This lesson gives you the number-handling habits that every later chapter assumes: which units thermodynamics uses, how to move between them without losing a factor of a thousand, why pressure has to be absolute and temperature has to be in kelvin before either goes into an equation, and how many digits an answer deserves. In a degree sequence this is the first week of the first course, and it is where most lost marks in the first exam come from, not from the physics.

Why units are the whole game in thermodynamics

Every thermodynamic equation is a statement that two physical quantities are equal, so both sides must carry the same units. That gives you a free error check on every line you write: if the units do not match, the algebra is wrong, no matter how confident you feel. It also lets you reconstruct half-remembered formulas. For example, if you remember that boundary work involves pressure and volume, the units settle the form: 1 kPa × 1 m³ = 1 (kN/m²) × m³ = 1 kN·m = 1 kJ. That identity, kPa·m³ = kJ, is used in almost every problem in this course, and you will use its cousin 1 bar·m³ = 100 kJ when data come in bar.

The course uses SI almost exclusively, with the English (USCS) system appearing in a few problems because some of the classic textbooks and most of the American industry still use it. The seven SI base units matter less than the four you will meet daily: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s) and kelvin (K). Everything else is built from them.

📘 DEFINITION

Dimension: the physical nature of a quantity (length, mass, time, temperature). Unit: the agreed size used to measure it (m, kg, s, K). A quantity can change units without changing dimension; 1 atm and 101.325 kPa are the same pressure.

Dimensional homogeneity: every additive term in a physically meaningful equation has the same dimensions. If your energy balance has a term in kJ and another in kJ/kg, one of them is missing a mass.

The derived units you use every day

QuantitySI unitBuilt fromEveryday size
Forcenewton, Nkg·m/s²an apple weighs about 1 N
Pressurepascal, Pa = N/m²kg/(m·s²)atmosphere ≈ 101 kPa; car tyre ≈ 220 kPa gauge
Energy, work, heatjoule, J = N·mkg·m²/s²lifting 1 kg by 10 cm ≈ 1 J; a kettle boil ≈ 300 kJ
Powerwatt, W = J/skg·m²/s³a person at rest ≈ 100 W; a kettle 1.5-3 kW; a car engine ≈ 100 kW; a large power station ≈ 1 GW
Specific volumem³/kg1/densityliquid water ≈ 0.001 m³/kg; room air ≈ 0.83 m³/kg
Specific energykJ/kgJ per kgboiling off 1 kg of water at 1 atm takes hfg = 2256 kJ/kg

Thermodynamics works in kJ and kPa rather than J and Pa because the numbers come out human-sized (a kettle delivers hundreds of kJ, a boiler runs at thousands of kPa) and because the kPa·m³ = kJ identity then needs no extra factor. The consequence is that you must watch the prefix on every single line. A specific volume table gives m³/kg; a density from a data sheet gives kg/m³; a heat capacity may be quoted in J/(g·K), which is numerically equal to kJ/(kg·K), or in J/(kg·K), which is a thousand times smaller.

Specific quantities. Any extensive property (one that scales with the amount of matter: volume V, internal energy U, enthalpy H, entropy S) divided by mass becomes an intensive, per-kilogram property written in lower case: v = V/m, u = U/m, h = H/m, s = S/m. Tables list the lower-case values; you multiply by the mass in the last line. Dividing by the number of moles instead gives molar quantities with a bar over the symbol in most textbooks (written here as v̄, ū, h̄), in m³/kmol and kJ/kmol.

Pressure: absolute, gauge and vacuum

Almost every gauge in the world measures the difference between the fluid and the surrounding atmosphere, because that is what a diaphragm or a Bourdon tube physically feels. Thermodynamic equations, however, need the true pressure relative to a perfect vacuum, because that is what the molecules exert. So every problem starts with a conversion:

📊 FIGURE — Absolute pressure and absolute temperature, drawn as ladders
Left: the gauge measures only the part above the local barometer, so 220 kPa gauge sits on 96 kPa. Right: ratios need kelvin, because the Celsius zero is arbitrary.
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Pabs = Pgauge + Patm and, for pressures below atmospheric, Pabs = Patm − Pvac

Pabs: absolute pressure, kPa, the number that goes into equations and tables. Pgauge: the reading on a gauge, kPa above atmospheric. Patm: the local atmospheric (barometric) pressure, kPa, which is 101.325 kPa at standard conditions but is given in the problem at altitude or on a weather day. Pvac: a vacuum gauge reading, kPa below atmospheric.

Conversions you can trust: 1 bar = 100 kPa exactly; 1 atm = 101.325 kPa exactly; 1 psi = 6.8948 kPa; 1 atm = 14.696 psi; 1 mm Hg (torr) = 0.13332 kPa; 1 MPa = 1000 kPa = 10 bar.

Two vocabulary points. First, in English units the letters are spelled out: psia is absolute, psig is gauge. Second, an absolute pressure can never be negative, and a gauge pressure can never be below −Patm; if either shows up in your working, you have subtracted in the wrong direction.

Temperature: why only Kelvin and Rankine may go into a ratio

Celsius and Fahrenheit are interval scales: their zero is a convention (the ice point, or Fahrenheit's brine), so \"twice as hot\" means nothing in them. Kelvin and Rankine are absolute scales whose zero is the absolute zero of thermodynamics, so ratios and products of temperatures mean something. The ideal gas law PV = mRT, the Carnot efficiency η = 1 − TL/TH, the entropy change Δs = c ln(T₂/T₁) and every radiation law all need absolute temperature. A temperature difference is the same size in kelvin and in degrees Celsius, so heat-capacity calculations of the form Q = m c ΔT are indifferent, which is exactly why the trap is so easy to fall into: the °C habit works nine times, then wrecks the tenth.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15, T(R) = T(°F) + 459.67, T(R) = 1.8 T(K), T(°F) = 1.8 T(°C) + 32

T(K): kelvin, no degree sign. T(R): degrees Rankine, the absolute Fahrenheit-sized scale. A change of 1 K equals a change of 1 °C equals a change of 1.8 R equals a change of 1.8 °F. Most textbooks round to 273 K only in quick estimates; use 273.15 in a worked answer.

Quick illustration: a heat engine between 500 °C and 30 °C. In kelvin the Carnot limit is 1 − 303.15/773.15 = 0.608, so 60.8 percent. Someone who divides the Celsius values gets 1 − 30/500 = 0.94, which is absurd for those temperatures and is the single most common wrong answer on a first exam.

Worked example: what is actually in a car tyre?

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A tyre gauge reads 220 kPa on a mountain day when the barometer reads 96 kPa. The air in the tyre is at 25 °C and the tyre holds 0.025 m³. Find the absolute pressure in kPa, bar and psi, the temperature in K, and the mass of air. Use R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K) for air.

  1. Absolute pressure. Pabs = Pgauge + Patm = 220 kPa + 96 kPa = 316 kPa. (Not 220 + 101.325: the problem gave the local barometer, so use it.)
  2. Other units. 316 kPa ÷ 100 kPa/bar = 3.16 bar; 316 kPa ÷ 6.8948 kPa/psi = 45.8 psia. As a gauge reading that is 220 ÷ 6.8948 = 31.9 psig, the familiar tyre number.
  3. Absolute temperature. T = 25 + 273.15 = 298.15 K (also 298.15 × 1.8 = 536.67 R).
  4. Mass from the ideal gas law. m = PV/(RT) = (316 kPa × 0.025 m³) / (0.287 kJ/(kg·K) × 298.15 K). Numerator: 316 × 0.025 = 7.90 kPa·m³ = 7.90 kJ. Denominator: 0.287 × 298.15 = 85.57 kJ/kg. So m = 7.90 / 85.57 = 0.0923 kg, about 92 g of air.
  5. Units check. kPa·m³ = kJ on top, kJ/(kg·K) × K = kJ/kg below, so kJ ÷ (kJ/kg) = kg. Correct.
  6. Sanity check. Density = 0.0923 kg / 0.025 m³ = 3.69 kg/m³, about three times room air (1.2 kg/m³) at three times atmospheric pressure. Plausible. With the gauge pressure by mistake you would get 0.064 kg; with 25 instead of 298.15 in the denominator you would get 1.10 kg, which is more than a bag of sugar of air in a tyre and should stop you cold.

Energy, power and the kilowatt-hour

Energy is the stock, power is the flow. A 1.5 kW kettle running for 3 minutes delivers 1.5 kW × 180 s = 270 kJ, which is also 1.5 kW × (3/60) h = 0.075 kWh. Since 1 kWh = 3600 kJ, the electricity bill unit is a large one. That 270 kJ would raise 1 kg of water by ΔT = Q/(m c) = 270 kJ / (1 kg × 4.18 kJ/(kg·K)) = 64.6 K, using c = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K) for liquid water. Both numbers are worth remembering as anchors for the sanity check at the end of any problem: a kettle-sized device moves hundreds of kJ in minutes; a power station moves the same in a millisecond.

English-unit equivalents, all of which follow from the exact SI definitions of the pound, inch and °F: 1 Btu = 1.0551 kJ, 1 hp = 0.7457 kW, 1 lbf = 4.4482 N, 1 lbm = 0.45359 kg, 1 ft = 0.3048 m. The English system also carries the constant gc = 32.174 lbm·ft/(lbf·s²) because the pound is used both as a mass and as a force; in SI, gc = 1 and disappears.

✅ VERIFIED

The 2019 SI fixes the Boltzmann constant at k = 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J/K and the Avogadro constant at NA = 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ exactly, so the universal gas constant is their product, Ru = 8.314462618 J/(mol·K) = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K), computed here rather than quoted. Dividing by the molar mass of air, 28.97 kg/kmol, gives Rair = 0.2870 kJ/(kg·K). NIST's CODATA page for R: physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/cuu/Value?r.

Significant figures and the discipline of the answer line

Property tables are good to four or five significant figures; measured pressures and temperatures in a problem are rarely better than three. Carry every digit through the working (do not round intermediate results; store them in the calculator or a variable) and round only the final answer, to three or four significant figures. Writing 0.09232310047 kg for the tyre pretends to a precision the gauge never had; writing 0.09 kg throws away real information. 0.0923 kg is right.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Gauge in, garbage out. Putting a gauge pressure into PV = mRT or into a steam table. The fix is mechanical: the first line under any pressure is \"Pabs = Pgauge + Patm = ...\".

Celsius in a ratio. T₂/T₁, P₂/P₁ = T₂/T₁ at constant volume, Carnot efficiencies and entropy logarithms all need kelvin. A ΔT may stay in °C; a T may not.

Prefix slip. Mixing kJ and J, or kPa and Pa, gives an answer off by 1000. If a tank of air weighs 90 kg or a kettle takes 270 000 kJ, look for the prefix.

Wrong R. Ru = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K) is per kmol; R = Ru/M is per kg and differs for every gas. Air 0.287, nitrogen 0.2968, helium 2.0769, CO₂ 0.1889 kJ/(kg·K).

★ ON THE EXAM

Expect the very first question to hide a unit trap: a pressure given as a gauge reading with an unusual barometer, a temperature in °C going into a ratio, or a density given where the table needs specific volume (v = 1/ρ). Write the conversion as its own line so the marker can give method marks even if you slip later.

Units are worth marks in their own right. Put a unit on every number in every line; an answer of \"0.0923\" with no unit is usually marked wrong even when the digits are right.

This lesson is the mathematical toolkit for the rest of the degree, kept to what thermodynamics actually uses: the three kinds of \"small change\" (d, Δ and ∂), the difference between exact and inexact differentials (which is the mathematical face of the difference between a property and a process), the two identities that let you rearrange partial derivatives, and the integral ∫P dV for the processes that appear in every cycle. Nothing here is beyond first-year calculus, but every idea returns in the chapters on the first law, entropy and property relations, so it is worth an hour now.

d, Δ and ∂: three symbols, three questions

Δ asks \"by how much did it change between two states\": ΔU = U₂ − U₁, a finite difference, in kJ. d asks \"how much does it change for an infinitesimal step along a path\": dU, which you integrate to recover ΔU. ∂ asks \"how fast does it change with one variable while another is held fixed\": (∂u/∂T)v, a partial derivative, with the subscript naming what is held constant. The subscript is not decoration. For a gas, the rate of change of internal energy with temperature is different at constant volume (that one is cv) from what it would be at constant pressure, because along a constant-pressure heating the volume also changes and drags u along with it.

📘 DEFINITION

A state function (a property) depends only on the current state of the system, not on how it got there: P, T, v, u, h, s. Its change between two states is the same along every path, so we write ΔU and it has an exact differential dU.

A path function depends on the route taken between the states: heat Q and work W. There is no \"amount of work in the system\", so ΔW is meaningless; the small amount transferred along a step of the path is written δW (or đW), an inexact differential, and its total is written W₁₂ or just W, never ΔW.

Exact and inexact differentials, and the test

Take any expression of the form dz = M(x, y) dx + N(x, y) dy. It is called exact if some function z(x, y) exists whose partial derivatives are M and N; then ∫dz around any closed loop is zero and ∫dz between two points is z₂ − z₁ regardless of path. Because mixed second derivatives of a smooth function are equal, there is a one-line test:

🧮 KEY EQUATION

dz = M dx + N dy is exact if and only if (∂M/∂y)x = (∂N/∂x)y

M and N: the coefficient functions, each a function of both x and y. If the equality fails, dz is inexact and its integral depends on the path. In thermodynamics x and y are any two independent properties (T and v, or T and P), z is any other property, and the test is what later gives you the Maxwell relations.

Apply it to a unit mass of ideal gas in a reversible process. The first law says δq = du + P dv, and for an ideal gas du = cv dT and P = RT/v, so δq = cv dT + (RT/v) dv. Here M = cv and N = RT/v, with x = T and y = v. Test: (∂M/∂v)T = 0 because cv is a constant, but (∂N/∂T)v = R/v ≠ 0. Not equal, so δq is inexact: heat is not a property, and \"the heat content of a gas\" is not a thing. Now divide by T: δq/T = (cv/T) dT + (R/v) dv. Test again: (∂/∂v)(cv/T) = 0 and (∂/∂T)(R/v) = 0. Equal, so δq/T is exact for a reversible process. That quantity is ds, the entropy, and this calculation is the mathematical reason entropy exists as a property. You will meet it formally in the entropy chapter; notice now that you already did the hard part.

The chain rule and the cyclic relation

Any property z of a simple compressible substance is a function of two others, z = z(x, y), so dz = (∂z/∂x)y dx + (∂z/∂y)x dy. Two consequences let you convert a derivative you cannot measure into ones you can:

🧮 KEY EQUATION

Reciprocity: (∂x/∂y)z = 1 / (∂y/∂x)z

Cyclic relation: (∂x/∂y)z (∂y/∂z)x (∂z/∂x)y = −1

x, y, z: any three properties linked by an equation of state. The minus sign is real and is the part people forget; the three derivatives, each holding a different variable fixed, multiply to −1, not +1.

Check it on the ideal gas Pv = RT, which you can differentiate directly. (∂P/∂T)v = R/v. (∂T/∂v)P = P/R. (∂v/∂P)T = −RT/P². Multiply: (R/v)(P/R)(−RT/P²) = −RT/(Pv) = −1, since Pv = RT. At 100 kPa and 300 K, where v = 0.287 × 300 / 100 = 0.861 m³/kg, the three factors are 0.3333 kPa/K, 348.4 K·kg/m³ and −0.00861 m³/(kg·kPa), whose product is −1.000. The physical use: (∂P/∂T)v is hard to measure for a liquid (you would need a rigid vessel that does not expand), but the relation turns it into −(∂v/∂T)P / (∂v/∂P)T, the ratio of the thermal expansion coefficient to the compressibility, both of which are in the handbooks.

Integrating P dV: the work of the standard processes

The boundary work of a quasi-equilibrium process is the area under the path on a P-V diagram, Wb = ∫₁² P dV, in kJ when P is in kPa and V in m³. Its value depends on the path, which is the geometric meaning of \"work is a path function\": two curves between the same end states enclose different areas. Three paths cover almost every textbook process:

ProcessPath P(V)Wb = ∫P dVNotes
Constant pressure (isobaric)P = P₀P₀ (V₂ − V₁)rectangle; heating in an open piston-cylinder
Constant volume (isochoric)V = V₀0a rigid tank; all heat goes to internal energy
Isothermal ideal gasPV = mRT = constP₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁) = mRT ln(V₂/V₁) = mRT ln(P₁/P₂)hyperbola; ln is the natural log
Polytropic, n ≠ 1PVn = C(P₂V₂ − P₁V₁)/(1 − n) = mR(T₂ − T₁)/(1 − n)n = k = 1.4 is the reversible adiabatic for air; n = 0 is isobaric; n → ∞ is isochoric

Where the polytropic formula comes from, because you will be asked to derive it: with P = C V−n, ∫C V−n dV = C [V1−n/(1 − n)] from V₁ to V₂ = (C V₂1−n − C V₁1−n)/(1 − n), and C V1−n = (C V−n) V = PV, giving (P₂V₂ − P₁V₁)/(1 − n). The n = 1 case is excluded because the power rule fails for ∫dV/V, which is the logarithm; that is the isothermal row.

Worked example: three ways to squeeze the same air into a fifth of its volume

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

0.5 kg of air (R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K)) at 100 kPa and 300 K is compressed in a piston-cylinder to one fifth of its initial volume, (a) isothermally, (b) polytropically with n = 1.3, (c) polytropically with n = 1.4. Find the boundary work for each and the final pressure.

📊 FIGURE — Three ways to compress 0.5 kg of air to a fifth of its volume
All three paths start at state 1 and end at the same volume. The higher the exponent n, the steeper the curve, the higher P2, and the larger the area under it: that area is the work.
  1. Initial volume. V₁ = mRT₁/P₁ = 0.5 kg × 0.287 kJ/(kg·K) × 300 K / 100 kPa = 43.05 kJ / 100 kPa = 0.4305 m³. Final volume V₂ = 0.4305/5 = 0.0861 m³. Note P₁V₁ = 43.05 kJ; it appears in every path.
  2. (a) Isothermal. W = P₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁) = 43.05 kJ × ln(0.2) = 43.05 × (−1.6094) = −69.3 kJ. P₂ = P₁V₁/V₂ = 43.05/0.0861 = 500 kPa. Negative work means 69.3 kJ of work was done on the air.
  3. (b) n = 1.3. P₂ = P₁ (V₁/V₂)n = 100 kPa × 51.3 = 100 × 8.103 = 810.3 kPa. W = (P₂V₂ − P₁V₁)/(1 − n) = (810.3 × 0.0861 − 43.05) kJ / (1 − 1.3) = (69.77 − 43.05)/(−0.3) = 26.72/(−0.3) = −89.1 kJ. Final temperature T₂ = P₂V₂/(mR) = 69.77/(0.5 × 0.287) = 486.2 K.
  4. (c) n = 1.4. P₂ = 100 × 51.4 = 951.8 kPa. W = (951.8 × 0.0861 − 43.05)/(1 − 1.4) = (81.95 − 43.05)/(−0.4) = 38.90/(−0.4) = −97.3 kJ. T₂ = 81.95/0.1435 = 571.1 K.
  5. Units check. kPa × m³ = kJ throughout; the (1 − n) is dimensionless. kJ ÷ (kg × kJ/(kg·K)) = K for the temperatures.
  6. Sanity check. The steeper the path on the P-V diagram, the more area under it: 69.3 < 89.1 < 97.3 kJ, exactly the order of n. The isothermal path is the cheapest way to compress a gas because the heat removed keeps the pressure low; the adiabatic (n = 1.4) is the most expensive because the temperature rises to 571 K. All three final pressures satisfy PVn = const, and the isothermal P₂ = 500 kPa is exactly five times P₁, as it must be.

Reading a slope off a P-v diagram

Differentiating the path gives the slope, and the slope tells you which process you are looking at. For an isotherm, Pv = C so (∂P/∂v)T = −P/v. For a polytrope, Pvn = C so dP/dv = −nP/v; the isentrope with n = k = 1.4 is 1.4 times steeper than the isotherm through the same point. At 100 kPa and v = 0.861 m³/kg the isotherm has slope −116 kPa per (m³/kg) and the isentrope −163 kPa per (m³/kg). Going the other way, if a sketch shows an adiabatic compression of air crossing an isotherm, the adiabatic must be the steeper curve, and if you have drawn it shallower, the diagram is wrong. Every cycle diagram in the gas-cycle chapters is built from these two curves and the horizontal (isobaric) and vertical (isochoric) lines.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

You already integrate numerically for a living. Sample the isothermal path above at 2001 points with numpy and apply the trapezoid rule (np.trapezoid(P, V), or np.trapz in older numpy): −69.286 kJ against the analytic −69.286 kJ. With only 21 points you get −69.42 kJ, and with 6 points −71.37 kJ, which is a nice demonstration of why the exam prefers the closed forms in the table.

The exact-differential test is also a data test: if a quantity is a state function, the loop integral around any closed cycle of measured states is zero to within noise. Regress the residual and you have a check on whether a measured \"property\" is really a property.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Writing ΔQ or ΔW. A path function has no \"before\" and \"after\" value, so the change makes no sense. Write Q, W, Q₁₂, Wnet, δQ, δW.

Using the isobaric formula on a non-isobaric path. P₁(V₂ − V₁) for the compression above gives −34.4 kJ, half the true isothermal work, because P rises during the process.

Log base. The ln in the isothermal formula is the natural log. Using log₁₀ divides the answer by 2.303.

Dropping the sign of (1 − n). For n > 1 and compression, the numerator P₂V₂ − P₁V₁ is positive and (1 − n) is negative, so W is negative: work done on the gas. Losing the sign turns a compressor into a turbine.

★ ON THE EXAM

Derive the polytropic work formula from ∫C V−n dV, and state why n = 1 needs the logarithm. Show that δq for an ideal gas is inexact and that δq/T is exact; both are standard short questions.

Given a P-V sketch with two paths between the same states, say which has more work and why (area under the curve). Given T₁, V₁/V₂ and n, compute W and T₂ and check that a compression gives negative W.

This lesson gives you a fixed procedure that turns any thermodynamics question, from a first-law piston problem this week to a combined-cycle plant in the capstone, into the same seven moves. Examiners grade the moves, not just the final number, and following them is also how you catch your own mistakes before anyone else does. Study it with the first two lessons open: the method is where the units discipline and the ∫P dV integrals get used.

Why a method beats cleverness

Thermodynamics problems look different on the surface (steam, air, refrigerant; tanks, turbines, engines) but underneath every one is the same three-part structure: a balance of mass and energy (and later entropy and exergy) across a boundary you chose, a set of property values found from tables or an equation of state, and a process description that supplies the missing relation between states. Students who solve by pattern-matching to a remembered example run out of patterns by the second exam. Students who run the same procedure every time slow down at first and then never get stuck, because the procedure tells them what to do when they cannot see the answer: find the next unknown.

📘 DEFINITION

System: the quantity of matter or the region of space you choose to analyse. Boundary: the real or imaginary surface separating the system from its surroundings. A closed system (control mass) has a fixed amount of matter and energy crosses the boundary as heat and work; an open system (control volume) also has mass crossing it, through inlets and exits.

Process: the change of a system from one equilibrium state to another; its path is the series of states passed through. A process description such as \"constant pressure\", \"isothermal\" or \"adiabatic\" is not a property of either end state; it is the extra equation that connects them.

The seven moves

📊 FIGURE — The seven moves, each applied to one constant-pressure heating
Read down the left column for the procedure; the right column shows what each move produced in the worked example. Moves 4 and 6 are where most marks are won or lost.
  1. Sketch the system and choose the boundary. Draw the hardware, then draw a dashed line around the thing you are analysing, and decide whether mass crosses it (open) or not (closed). Mark every energy crossing with an arrow: Q in, W out, mass flows with their h. A piston-cylinder problem changes entirely depending on whether the boundary is inside the gas (then the piston's weight is a pressure, not a work) or around the piston too.
  2. List knowns and unknowns with units, converting as you go: gauge to absolute, °C to K, bar to kPa, density to specific volume. Give each state a number and write what you know about it in a state table with columns P, T, v, u, h, s, x. Two independent intensive properties fix a state for a simple compressible substance, so any row with two entries can be completed from tables.
  3. Write the assumptions. Ideal gas or tables; constant specific heats or not; kinetic and potential energy negligible; quasi-equilibrium process; steady flow. Each assumption is a claim you can be asked to justify, and it tells the marker which equations you are entitled to use.
  4. Write the balance in words, then symbols, then numbers. \"Energy in minus energy out equals change in stored energy.\" Then Q − W = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE for a closed system, with the terms you are neglecting struck out explicitly. Only then substitute values. Writing the general form first is what protects you from forgetting a term.
  5. Find the properties. Fill the state table: tables for water and refrigerants, PV = mRT and Δu = cvΔT for ideal gases at moderate pressure. Add the process relation (isobaric: P₂ = P₁; isothermal ideal gas: P₂V₂ = P₁V₁; and so on) as the equation that links the rows.
  6. Solve, then check the sign. In this course, Q is positive into the system and W is positive when done by the system (some texts reverse the sign of W; use whichever your exam paper states, and state it yourself). A compression must come out with negative boundary work; a cooling with negative Q. If the sign surprises you, it is more often the bookkeeping than the physics.
  7. Check the magnitude and the units, and box the answer. Run the \"obviously wrong\" checklist below, round to three or four significant figures, write the unit, and state the one-line sanity check this course asks for on every answer.

The energy balance you will write hundreds of times

🧮 KEY EQUATION

Closed system, any process: Q − W = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE, and for a stationary system Q − Wb − Wother = m (u₂ − u₁)

Q: net heat added to the system, kJ (positive in). W: net work done by the system, kJ (positive out). ΔU = m(u₂ − u₁): change in internal energy, kJ, with u from tables or cvΔT for an ideal gas. ΔKE = ½m(V₂² − V₁²) and ΔPE = mg(z₂ − z₁), kJ when m is in kg, velocities in m/s and heights in m, divided by 1000.

For a constant-pressure closed process the boundary work P(V₂ − V₁) combines with ΔU to give Q = m (h₂ − h₁) = ΔH, because h = u + Pv. That is why enthalpy exists: it is the property that absorbs the flow-work and boundary-work terms. For an ideal gas with constant specific heats, Δh = cpΔT and Δu = cvΔT, with cp − cv = R.

Worked example: the method applied to a constant-pressure heating

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A piston-cylinder holds 0.2 kg of air at 150 kPa and 27 °C. The piston is free and carries a constant load, and heat is added until the air reaches 227 °C. Find the boundary work, the change in internal energy and the heat added. Air: R = 0.287, cv = 0.718, cp = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K), constant.

  1. System and boundary. Closed system: the air inside the cylinder. The boundary moves with the piston, so there is boundary work Wb out; heat Q in. No mass crosses.
  2. Knowns in absolute units. m = 0.2 kg. State 1: P₁ = 150 kPa (absolute, given), T₁ = 27 + 273.15 = 300.15 K. State 2: P₂ = P₁ = 150 kPa (free piston with constant load), T₂ = 227 + 273.15 = 500.15 K. ΔT = 200 K. Unknowns: Wb, ΔU, Q.
  3. Assumptions. Ideal gas (air at 150 kPa is far from its critical point); constant specific heats; quasi-equilibrium; ΔKE = ΔPE = 0.
  4. Balance. Energy in − energy out = change in stored energy: Q − Wb = ΔU, so Q = ΔU + Wb.
  5. Properties and process. V₁ = mRT₁/P₁ = 0.2 × 0.287 × 300.15 / 150 = 17.229/150 = 0.11486 m³. V₂ = mRT₂/P₂ = 0.2 × 0.287 × 500.15 / 150 = 28.709/150 = 0.19139 m³. Process: P constant, so Wb = P(V₂ − V₁).
  6. Boundary work. Wb = 150 kPa × (0.19139 − 0.11486) m³ = 150 × 0.07653 = 11.48 kJ (positive: the gas pushes the piston out). Cross-check: for an isobaric ideal gas Wb = mRΔT = 0.2 × 0.287 × 200 = 11.48 kJ. Same.
  7. Internal energy. ΔU = m cv ΔT = 0.2 kg × 0.718 kJ/(kg·K) × 200 K = 28.72 kJ.
  8. Heat. Q = ΔU + Wb = 28.72 + 11.48 = 40.20 kJ. Cross-check by the enthalpy route: Q = m cp ΔT = 0.2 × 1.005 × 200 = 40.20 kJ. Same, which confirms cp = cv + R.
  9. Signs, units, sanity. Q and W both positive: heat in, work out, as the story says. All terms in kJ. Of the 40.2 kJ supplied, 11.48/40.2 = 28.6 percent left as work and the rest stayed in the gas; that fraction equals R/cp = 0.287/1.005 = 0.286 for any constant-pressure heating of air, a nice invariant. Plausible: heating a gas at constant pressure always stores more than it pushes.

The checklist of ways a thermodynamics answer is obviously wrong

Run this before you box any answer. Each line is a physical impossibility or a size that experience rules out, and each has caught a real exam mistake.

  • An absolute temperature or absolute pressure that is negative, or a temperature below the surroundings in a device that only heats.
  • A heat-engine efficiency above the Carnot value 1 − TL/TH in kelvin, or above 100 percent; a refrigerator COP that is negative; a heat pump COP below 1.
  • A quality x outside 0 to 1, or a quality quoted for a state that is not in the wet region.
  • A specific volume for liquid water far from 0.001 m³/kg, or for room air far from 0.8 m³/kg; a density of a gas above that of a liquid.
  • Entropy generation that is negative, or heat flowing spontaneously from cold to hot (from the second-law chapters on).
  • A compression with positive boundary work, or a turbine with negative work, under the sign convention you stated.
  • Sizes: a kettle that draws 2 MW, a car engine of 3 kW, a power plant of 5 kW, a gas cylinder holding 90 kg of air, a house heated by 10 W. Compare with the anchors from lesson 1 (person 100 W, kettle 2 kW, car 100 kW, plant 1 GW).
  • Units missing from the answer, or a factor of 1000 between two terms that were added.
  • The answer is exactly the same as an intermediate value you already had, which usually means a term was dropped rather than computed.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Using cv for a constant-pressure heat, or cp for a constant-volume one. In the example, m cv ΔT = 28.72 kJ is ΔU, not Q; a rigid tank heated over the same ΔT would need only 28.72 kJ because it does no work. The rule: QP = ΔH = m cp ΔT, QV = ΔU = m cv ΔT.

Subtracting 273.15 from a ΔT. A temperature difference is identical in K and °C; \"ΔT = 200 − 273.15\" is a sign that the conversion was applied to the wrong thing.

Forgetting the work in a moving-boundary problem, which gives Q = ΔU = 28.72 kJ instead of 40.2 kJ; or getting the sign backwards, Q = ΔU − W = 17.24 kJ.

Skipping the state table. Most \"I do not know where to start\" moments dissolve when you write the two known properties of each state and ask which unknown row entry the process relation supplies.

★ ON THE EXAM

Markers award method marks for the sketch, the stated assumptions, the balance written in general form before substitution, and the units on each line. A correct final number with none of those typically earns half credit; a wrong number with all of them typically earns most of it.

Every long-answer question in this course, and in the engineering exams it mirrors, can be laid out as: sketch, state table, assumptions, balance, properties, solve, check. Practise writing those seven headings in the margin before you read the question a second time.

"}, "THERMO/concepts/s1": {"body": "

This lesson gives you the first move in every thermodynamics problem you will ever solve: drawing the box. By the end you will be able to choose a system, classify it as closed, open or isolated, say which of its properties are extensive and which are intensive, convert between total and specific properties, and explain why we are allowed to treat a gas as a smooth continuum at all. In the degree sequence this is the opening of Basic Concepts (Cengel & Boles chapter 1, Moran & Shapiro chapter 1); the first law, the second law and every control-volume analysis later in the course start with exactly this step.

\n\n

Drawing the box: what a system is

\n

Thermodynamics never analyses the whole universe. It picks a region of space or a fixed lump of matter, calls it the system, and calls everything outside it the surroundings. The real or imaginary surface separating the two is the boundary. Energy and mass are then counted only when they cross the boundary. Nothing about the physics changes when you move the boundary, but the bookkeeping changes completely, so the boundary is a modelling decision and the first line of every solution should state it.

\n

Three facts about the boundary are worth memorising now. It has zero thickness, so it contains no mass and no volume of its own. It can be fixed or moving: the inside face of a piston is a moving boundary, the wall of a rigid tank is a fixed one. And it can be real or imaginary: the tank wall is real, but the inlet plane of a nozzle where you decide to start counting is a surface you invented.

\n\n

The three kinds of system

\n
📘 DEFINITION

A closed system (also called a control mass) is a fixed quantity of matter. No mass crosses its boundary, but energy, as heat or work, may. A open system (a control volume) is a chosen region of space through which mass may flow; its boundary is the control surface. An isolated system is a closed system that exchanges neither mass nor energy with its surroundings.

📊 FIGURE — The three kinds of system and what may cross each boundary
The dashed line is the boundary you choose. Closed: only heat and work cross. Open: mass also flows in and out. Isolated: nothing crosses, so the total energy stays constant.

The gas trapped in a sealed piston-cylinder is closed. A water heater, a turbine, a nozzle, a garden hose are open. A perfectly insulated, rigid, sealed thermos is (approximately) isolated.

\n\n\n\n\n\n
System typeMass crosses boundary?Energy crosses boundary?Typical exampleWhich law form you will use
Closed (control mass)NoYes (heat and work)Gas in a cylinder, sealed rigid tank, a can of drink warming upQ − W = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE (chapter Energy)
Open (control volume)YesYes (heat, work and energy carried by the flow)Turbine, compressor, nozzle, heat exchanger, water heaterMass and energy balances with flow enthalpy (chapter Control Volumes)
IsolatedNoNoInsulated rigid sealed tank; the universe as a wholeTotal energy constant; entropy can only rise (chapter Entropy)
\n

A closed system can still change shape and volume. The classic case is gas in a cylinder under a piston: the mass is fixed, the boundary moves, and the work done on the moving boundary is what the next chapter calls boundary work. A rigid closed tank has a fixed boundary and therefore no boundary work at all, which is why so many exam problems use rigid tanks.

\n\n

The boundary is a choice: the same device, two boxes

\n

Take an electric kettle. If you draw the boundary around the water only, you have a closed system until it boils; once steam leaves the spout, mass is crossing and you have an open system. If you draw the boundary around the whole kettle including the heating element, electrical work enters through the cable and the same steam leaves. If you draw it around the kettle plus the room, the steam never leaves and you are back to a closed system that is merely getting more humid. Each choice is legitimate. The good choice is the one that puts the quantity you are asked about on the boundary and keeps as many unknowns as possible outside it.

\n

For open systems the control volume can be any shape, can have several inlets and exits, and can even move (the control volume around a rocket engine moves with the rocket). A moving boundary inside a control volume is still allowed: a reciprocating compressor is analysed as a control volume over one full cycle even though its piston moves.

\n

Rule of thumb for choosing

\n
    \n
  • If the question gives you a fixed mass ("2 kg of air is compressed"), start with a closed system around that mass.
    • \n
  • If the question gives you flow rates ("steam enters at 3 kg/s"), start with a control volume around the device, inlet to exit.
    • \n
  • If the question asks about a heat interaction, place the boundary where the temperature is known, because heat transfer is counted at the boundary temperature (this matters for entropy generation later).
    • \n
\n\n

Properties: extensive, intensive and specific

\n

A property is any measurable characteristic of a system whose value depends only on the state the system is in, not on how it got there: pressure P, temperature T, volume V, mass m, energy U, density ρ. Properties come in two families, and the test to tell them apart is the halving test: imagine a partition dividing the system into two equal halves and ask what happens to the property's value.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

An extensive property depends on the size (extent) of the system; it halves when the system is halved. Mass m, total volume V, total internal energy U, total enthalpy H, total entropy S are extensive. By convention they get capital letters.

An intensive property is independent of the size of the system; each half has the same value as the whole. Pressure P, temperature T, density ρ, and every specific property (an extensive property divided by mass: v = V/m, u = U/m, h = H/m, s = S/m) are intensive. Specific properties get lower-case letters.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

v = V / m   specific volume, m³/kg; V is total volume in m³ and m is mass in kg.

ρ = m / V = 1 / v   density, kg/m³; density and specific volume are reciprocals and you will use both, because gas tables list v while liquids are usually quoted by ρ.

U = m·u, H = m·h, S = m·s   any total (extensive) property is mass times the specific (intensive) one. Units: U in kJ, u in kJ/kg, m in kg.

v̄ = M·v   molar specific volume, m³/kmol, where M is the molar mass in kg/kmol (28.97 for air, 18.015 for water). Molar properties carry a bar and are also intensive.

\n

Two more intensive quantities appear constantly. Specific gravity (relative density) is SG = ρ / ρwater with ρwater = 1000 kg/m³ at 4 °C, so mercury with ρ = 13,600 kg/m³ has SG = 13.6 and it is dimensionless. Specific weight is γs = ρ·g in N/m³, the weight of a unit volume; it is what turns a column height into a pressure in the manometer work of section 3.

\n

Why does the distinction matter? Because the state of a system is fixed by intensive properties alone. Two kilograms of air at 300 K and 100 kPa are in the same state as two grams of air at 300 K and 100 kPa; they just have different amounts. Property tables therefore list only specific (intensive) values, and you multiply by the mass yourself at the end. Forgetting that multiplication, or doing it twice, is the most frequent arithmetic slip in first-law problems.

\n\n

The continuum assumption: why we can talk about "the pressure at a point"

\n

A gas is a swarm of molecules with empty space between them, yet thermodynamics treats density, pressure and temperature as smooth functions of position. That is the continuum assumption: the system is modelled as continuous, homogeneous matter with no holes, so a property can be defined at a point as the limit over a volume that is tiny compared with the system but still contains an enormous number of molecules. It is an idealisation, and it is a good one whenever the system is huge compared with the mean free path λ, the average distance a molecule travels between collisions.

\n

Kinetic theory gives the mean free path for a gas of hard spheres of diameter d as λ = k·T / (√2 · π · d² · P), with k the Boltzmann constant (1.380649 × 10−23 J/K), T in K, d in m and P in Pa. For air at 20 °C and 1 atm, taking the effective molecular diameter d ≈ 3.7 × 10−10 m, this gives λ ≈ 6.6 × 10−8 m, about 66 nm, which agrees with the widely quoted 67-68 nm. The same calculation gives the number of molecules per unit volume as n = P/(k·T) ≈ 2.5 × 1025 per m³, so one cubic millimetre of room air holds about 2.5 × 1016 molecules. Averaging over that many particles makes fluctuations utterly negligible, which is why the continuum works.

\n

The ratio of the mean free path to the size L of the system is the Knudsen number, Kn = λ / L. For a 1 mm gas passage at atmospheric pressure Kn ≈ 6.6 × 10−5; the continuum is safe. For a 1 μm channel Kn ≈ 0.066 and slip effects appear at the walls; in high vacuum (P ≈ 1 Pa) λ grows to roughly 6.7 mm and a laboratory vacuum chamber a few centimetres across is no longer a continuum but a rarefied gas, which needs the statistical treatment of the later chapter on statistical thermodynamics. Everything in the classical part of this course assumes Kn ≪ 1.

\n\n

Worked example: one tank, every kind of property

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A rigid tank of internal volume 2.0 m³ contains 5.0 kg of air at 300 K. Take air as an ideal gas with R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K and M = 28.97 kg/kmol. Find (a) the specific volume, (b) the density, (c) the pressure, (d) the amount of substance in kmol and the number of molecules, and (e) what each of these becomes if an imaginary partition splits the tank into two equal halves.

The point of the exercise is not the ideal-gas law (the Properties chapter treats it properly) but seeing which numbers change under the halving test and which do not.

\n
    \n
  1. Specific volume. v = V / m = 2.0 m³ / 5.0 kg = 0.40 m³/kg. Intensive: a specific property.
    2. \n
  2. Density. ρ = 1 / v = 1 / 0.40 m³/kg = 2.5 kg/m³. Check: m / V = 5.0 kg / 2.0 m³ = 2.5 kg/m³, the same.
    3. \n
  3. Pressure. From Pv = RT: P = RT / v = (0.287 kJ/kg·K × 300 K) / 0.40 m³/kg = 86.1 kJ/kg ÷ 0.40 m³/kg = 215.25 kPa. Units: kJ/m³ = kN·m/m³ = kN/m² = kPa. Intensive.
    4. \n
  4. Amount of substance. N = m / M = 5.0 kg / 28.97 kg/kmol = 0.1726 kmol. Number of molecules = N × NA = 0.1726 kmol × 6.02214 × 1026 molecules/kmol = 1.04 × 1026 molecules. Both extensive (the count doubles if you double the air).
    5. \n
  5. Halving test. Each half has m = 2.5 kg and V = 1.0 m³ (extensive, halved). Each half has v = 1.0 m³ / 2.5 kg = 0.40 m³/kg, ρ = 2.5 kg/m³, T = 300 K and P = 215.25 kPa (intensive, unchanged). The state of each half is identical to the state of the whole; only the amount differs.
    6. \n
\n

Answer: v = 0.40 m³/kg, ρ = 2.5 kg/m³, P = 215.25 kPa, N = 0.1726 kmol ≈ 1.04 × 1026 molecules. Sanity check: air at room temperature and about 2 atm should be roughly twice as dense as atmospheric air (about 1.2 kg/m³), and 2.5 kg/m³ is; the pressure of 215 kPa is about 2.1 atm, consistent.

\n\n
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Extensive versus intensive is exactly the aggregation question you meet in every dataset: a column that must be summed when you merge groups (sales, row counts, mass, volume, energy) versus a column that must be averaged or left alone (price per unit, temperature, density). When you build a property table in pandas, keep the specific (per-kg) quantities as columns and keep mass as a separate column; multiply out totals at the very end. It mirrors the way steam tables are laid out, and it stops the double-multiplication error before it starts.

A quick self-test in a notebook: generate a system, split it into k parts, and assert that sum(V_i) == V while all(v_i == v). If a quantity fails the second test but passes the first, it is extensive.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Calling a piston-cylinder an open system because the volume changes. Volume change is not mass transfer. If no matter crosses the boundary it is closed, however much the boundary moves.

Treating specific volume as extensive. v = V/m is per kilogram, so it does not halve when the system is halved; it is intensive. Same for u, h and s. Total V, U, H and S are the extensive ones.

Mixing molar and mass bases. R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K is per kilogram of air; Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K is per kilomole of anything. Using Ru with a mass in kg makes the pressure 29 times too large for air.

Forgetting that density and specific volume are reciprocals. If a table gives v = 0.40 m³/kg and you need ρ, it is 2.5 kg/m³, not 0.40.

\n

One further subtlety: "isolated" is stronger than "adiabatic". An adiabatic system has no heat transfer but may still receive work (a compressed insulated gas). An isolated system has neither heat nor work nor mass crossing. Exams like to describe a well-insulated rigid tank with a paddle wheel inside driven from outside: it is closed and adiabatic, but not isolated, because shaft work enters.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

Classification questions: you are shown a device (turbine, pressure cooker with the valve closed, pressure cooker venting, refrigerator, the whole Earth) and asked to name the system type and to say what crosses the boundary. Always answer with two facts: does mass cross, does energy cross.

Halving-test questions: a list of properties, tick the intensive ones. Expect pressure, temperature, density, specific volume, specific internal energy and molar mass in the intensive column and mass, volume, total energy and total enthalpy in the extensive column.

Short calculations that convert between total and specific properties, usually one step (U = m·u, ρ = 1/v) buried inside a larger first-law problem. The marks are lost by forgetting the mass, not by the physics.

A one-line justification of the continuum assumption: "the system dimension is very large compared with the mean free path (about 0.07 μm for air at atmospheric conditions), so Kn ≪ 1". Quote the order of magnitude and the criterion.

\n

Next section: once the box is drawn, we ask what it means for the contents to be in a definite state, how many properties it takes to pin that state down, and what distinguishes a property from something like heat or work that depends on the path.

"}, "THERMO/concepts/s2": {"body": "

This lesson turns the box from section 1 into something you can calculate with. By the end you will be able to say when a system is in equilibrium and therefore has a definite state, use the state postulate to decide how many numbers you need to fix that state, tell a point function (a property) from a path function (heat, work), read and draw process diagrams, and recognise the two special processes, quasi-equilibrium and steady flow, that make most of the degree tractable. It corresponds to the middle of the Basic Concepts chapter in Cengel & Boles and Moran & Shapiro, and it is the language the first law (next chapter) and the second law are written in.

\n\n

State and equilibrium in plain words

\n

Take a photograph of the system. If every property has a single, well-defined value throughout the system at that instant, the photograph is a state. Thermodynamics can only assign a state to a system that is not in the middle of some internal upheaval: no pressure waves sloshing about, no hot corner and cold corner, no chemical reaction half done. That condition is equilibrium, from a Latin root meaning "equal balance": nothing inside the system has any tendency to change on its own when it is isolated from the surroundings.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

A system is in thermodynamic equilibrium when it is simultaneously in thermal equilibrium (uniform temperature, no internal heat flow), mechanical equilibrium (no unbalanced force; pressure uniform apart from the small hydrostatic variation with height, which is normally neglected in gases), phase equilibrium (the mass of each phase is constant: no net evaporation or condensation) and chemical equilibrium (composition constant: no net reaction).

The state of a system in equilibrium is the complete set of its property values. Two states are the same if every property has the same value. A single property changing gives a new state.

\n

Only equilibrium states appear as points on a property diagram, and only they can be looked up in a property table. That is why a gas being violently stirred, or a liquid in the middle of flash boiling, is off-limits to the classical theory until it settles; we can still analyse the before and after states, which is what most first-law problems do.

\n\n

The state postulate: how many numbers fix a state?

\n

A system has dozens of properties (P, T, v, u, h, s, viscosity, refractive index, speed of sound ...). Happily they are not independent; once a few are set, the rest follow. How many? Experience, distilled into a postulate, gives the answer for the systems in this course.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

A simple compressible system is one in which the only relevant work mode is boundary (compression/expansion) work, with electrical, magnetic, gravitational, surface-tension and motion effects absent or negligible.

The state postulate: the state of a simple compressible system is completely specified by two independent intensive properties. More generally the number of independent intensive properties equals the number of relevant work modes plus one (the "plus one" is the thermal, heat-transfer mode).

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

nindependent intensive = (number of relevant work modes) + 1

For a simple compressible system: one work mode (boundary work) + 1 = 2. Any other intensive property is then a function of those two: u = u(T, v), h = h(T, P), s = s(T, P), and so on.

Two properties are independent if one can be varied while the other is held fixed. T and v are always independent. T and P are independent for a single-phase substance but not during a phase change: boiling water at 101.325 kPa is at 99.97 °C whatever you do, so P and T together do not fix how much has boiled.

\n

The last point is the one that matters in practice. In the Properties chapter you will meet saturated mixtures, where (P, T) is a useless pair and you must supply the quality x or the specific volume instead. In the ideal-gas region, by contrast, any two of P, T, v do the job because Pv = RT links the third. A quick preview: air at P = 200 kPa and T = 350 K has v = RT / P = (0.287 kJ/kg·K × 350 K) / 200 kPa = 0.5023 m³/kg; the state is fixed and u, h and s can all be read from the air table at 350 K.

\n\n

Processes, paths and quasi-equilibrium

\n
📘 DEFINITION

A process is any change of the system from one equilibrium state to another. The series of states the system passes through is the path of the process. A process is fully described by its initial state, its final state, its path and the interactions (heat and work) with the surroundings.

📊 FIGURE — One equilibrium state and the named processes through it
State 1 is one point, fixed by two properties. A quasi-equilibrium process is a continuous line from it; the named processes are the lines along which one property stays constant.

A quasi-equilibrium (quasi-static) process is one carried out so slowly that the system stays infinitesimally close to equilibrium at every instant; every intermediate state is an equilibrium state and the whole path can be drawn as a continuous line on a property diagram.

A cycle is a sequence of processes that returns the system to its initial state, so every property has the same value at the end as at the start.

\n

Quasi-equilibrium is an idealisation, but a useful one twice over: it is the easiest process to analyse (the pressure is uniform, so the work is ∫P dV), and it is the best a real device can do, delivering the most work in an expansion and consuming the least in a compression. Real machines are compared against it. Compressing a gas by shoving the piston in suddenly is not quasi-equilibrium: the gas piles up against the piston face, the pressure there exceeds the pressure elsewhere, and the process cannot be drawn as a line, only as a dashed guess between the two end points.

\n

Processes are named by the property held constant, and you must know the prefixes cold, because exam wording uses them without explanation:

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
NameWhat stays constantAppearance on the diagramTypical device
IsothermalTemperature THyperbola-like curve on P-v (ideal gas: Pv = const)Slow compression in a water-cooled cylinder
IsobaricPressure PHorizontal line on P-vPiston free to move under a fixed weight; boiling in an open pan
Isochoric (isometric)Specific volume vVertical line on P-vHeating a rigid tank
IsentropicEntropy sVertical line on T-s (chapter Entropy)Ideal turbine, compressor, nozzle
IsenthalpicEnthalpy hHorizontal line on h-P or the throttling line on T-sThrottling valve, expansion valve in a fridge
\n

A steady-flow process is a different kind of idealisation for open systems: the fluid flows through the control volume steadily, so that properties can vary from point to point inside the control volume but do not change with time at any given point. Turbines, compressors, boilers, condensers and nozzles are analysed this way once they have warmed up; the mass, volume and energy content of the control volume are constant, and the flows in and out are constant. The Control Volumes chapter lives on this idea.

\n\n

Point functions versus path functions

\n

This is the single most important distinction in the lesson and it decides how everything later is written. A property depends only on the state (the point on the diagram); it is a point function. Its change during a process depends only on the two end states, never on the route between them, and its differential is exact. Heat and work are not properties: how much heat and how much work a process involves depends on the route taken; they are path functions with inexact differentials.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

∫12 dV = V2 − V1 = ΔV   exact differential of a property: the change is the difference of the end values (V in m³; the same holds for P, T, u, h, s).

∫12 δW = W12 (never "ΔW")   inexact differential of a path function: the total work depends on the path and there is no such thing as "work at state 1". W in kJ; likewise δQ and Q12.

∮ dV = 0   around any cycle the net change in every property is zero, because the system returns to its starting state.

Wb = ∫12 P dV   quasi-equilibrium boundary work in kJ when P is in kPa and V in m³: the area under the process curve on a P-V diagram. Two paths with the same end states enclose different areas, which is exactly why work is a path function. (The Energy chapter derives this; here we only use the geometry.)

\n

The notation is not pedantry. Writing Δ in front of Q or W is marked wrong in every engineering thermodynamics course, because it claims that heat is a property the system possesses. A system does not contain heat or work; it contains energy, and heat and work are the two ways energy crosses the boundary during a process.

\n\n

Process diagrams

\n

Diagrams with properties on the axes are the working tool of the subject. Each equilibrium state is a point, each quasi-equilibrium process is a line, and a cycle is a closed loop. The three you will use constantly are:

\n
    \n
  • P-v (or P-V): the area under a process line is boundary work; the area enclosed by a cycle is the net work of the cycle. Clockwise loop = net work output (an engine); anticlockwise = net work input (a refrigerator or compressor cycle).
    • \n
  • T-s: the area under a reversible process line is heat transfer; enclosed area is net heat, which for a cycle equals net work. Introduced properly in the Entropy chapter.
    • \n
  • T-v and P-T: used in the Properties chapter to show phase boundaries, the dome of saturated states and the critical point.
    • \n
\n

On a P-v diagram the ideal-gas isotherm is the curve P = RT/v, a rectangular hyperbola; higher temperature isotherms sit further from the origin. Knowing this lets you sketch a process without any numbers, and a sketch is the first thing an examiner looks for.

\n\n

Worked example: same two states, three paths, three different works

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Air at state 1 (P1 = 100 kPa, V1 = 0.50 m³, T1 = 300 K) is compressed quasi-statically to state 2 at P2 = 400 kPa and the same temperature, T2 = 300 K. Treat air as an ideal gas (R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K). Find V2, then the boundary work for three different paths: (A) an isothermal compression; (B) an isobaric compression at 100 kPa to V2 followed by isochoric heating to 400 kPa; (C) isochoric heating to 400 kPa first, then isobaric compression at 400 kPa to V2. Comment on which quantities are the same for all three.

Sign convention throughout the course: work done by the system is positive, so a compression gives negative W.

\n
    \n
  1. Fix state 2. The state postulate says P2 and T2 (independent for an ideal gas) fix it. Since T2 = T1, Pv = RT gives P1V1 = P2V2, so V2 = P1V1 / P2 = (100 kPa × 0.50 m³) / 400 kPa = 0.125 m³.
    2. \n
  2. Mass (a check we will reuse). m = P1V1 / (R T1) = (100 kPa × 0.50 m³) / (0.287 kJ/kg·K × 300 K) = 50 kJ / 86.1 kJ/kg = 0.5807 kg. It is the same at every state; mass is a property of the closed system.
    3. \n
  3. Path A, isothermal. With P = P1V1/V, WA = ∫P dV = P1V1 ln(V2/V1) = 100 kPa × 0.50 m³ × ln(0.125/0.50) = 50 kJ × ln(0.25) = 50 kJ × (−1.3863) = −69.3 kJ.
    4. \n
  4. Path B, isobaric then isochoric. Along the isobar at 100 kPa: W = P(V2 − V1) = 100 kPa × (0.125 − 0.50) m³ = −37.5 kJ. Along the isochor dV = 0, so W = 0. Total WB = −37.5 kJ.
    5. \n
  5. Path C, isochoric then isobaric. Isochor: W = 0. Isobar at 400 kPa: W = 400 kPa × (0.125 − 0.50) m³ = −150.0 kJ. Total WC = −150.0 kJ. (During the isochoric heating the temperature rises to T = P2V1/(mR) = 400 kPa × 0.50 m³ / (0.5807 kg × 0.287 kJ/kg·K) = 1200 K before the isobaric step brings it back to 300 K.)
    6. \n
  6. Compare. The end states are identical for all three paths, so every property change is identical: ΔV = −0.375 m³, ΔT = 0, ΔP = +300 kPa, and, for an ideal gas whose internal energy depends only on temperature, ΔU = 0. The work is −37.5 kJ, −69.3 kJ or −150.0 kJ depending on the route: path B hugs the low-pressure axis and encloses the least area, path C runs along the high-pressure line and encloses the most, and the isotherm lies between them.
    7. \n
\n

Answer: V2 = 0.125 m³; WA = −69.3 kJ, WB = −37.5 kJ, WC = −150.0 kJ; all property changes are path-independent. Sanity check: the isothermal work must lie between the two rectangular paths because the hyperbola lies between the two horizontal lines on the P-V plot, and 37.5 < 69.3 < 150 confirms it.

\n

If the system were then taken from state 2 back to state 1 along path C in reverse (isobaric expansion at 400 kPa to 0.50 m³, then isochoric cooling to 100 kPa), the work would be +150.0 kJ and the cycle 1-A-2-C-1 would deliver net work of −69.3 + 150.0 = +80.7 kJ per cycle, the area enclosed by the loop, while every property returned to its original value: ∮dV = 0 but ∮δW ≠ 0.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Writing ΔQ or ΔW. Heat and work are path functions; write Q12 and W12 (or δQ, δW for infinitesimals). Δ is reserved for properties.

Using P and T to fix a state during boiling or condensing. Inside the saturation dome P and T are locked together and are not independent; you need a second property such as v, u, h, s or the quality x.

Drawing a non-quasi-equilibrium process as a solid line and integrating P dV along it. If the pressure is not uniform there is no single P to integrate; only the end states are defined. Draw a dashed line and use an energy balance instead.

Confusing steady with equilibrium. A turbine in steady flow has hot high-pressure steam at the inlet and cool low-pressure steam at the exit, so it is not in equilibrium; steady means no change in time at each point, not uniformity in space.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

State-postulate questions: "How many independent intensive properties fix the state of ..." (two for a simple compressible system) and "Which pair does not fix the state of water at 100 °C?" (P and T during a phase change).

Point/path identification: given a list (P, W, T, Q, h, v, s), sort into properties and non-properties, or spot the illegal notation ΔW in a candidate answer.

Area problems: two processes between the same states on a P-V diagram, compute the work along each (rectangles, triangles and logarithms only) and state which path gives more. The follow-up "is ΔU the same for both?" is a yes.

Vocabulary: the four kinds of equilibrium, the iso- prefixes, quasi-equilibrium, cycle, steady flow. These are worth marks and cost only memory.

\n

Next section: two of the properties that appear in every state, pressure and temperature, get their operational definitions, and the zeroth law explains why a thermometer works at all.

"}, "THERMO/concepts/s3": {"body": "

This lesson makes two of the properties from the state postulate measurable. By the end you will be able to convert between absolute, gauge and vacuum pressures, compute the pressure at depth in a liquid and read a manometer or barometer, state the zeroth law and explain why it is what makes temperature a property at all, and convert between the Celsius, Kelvin, Fahrenheit and Rankine scales without mixing up levels and differences. It closes the Basic Concepts chapter of the degree (Cengel & Boles chapter 1, Moran & Shapiro chapter 1) and every table lookup for the rest of the course silently assumes you have got absolute pressure and absolute temperature right.

\n\n

Pressure in plain words

\n

Pressure is the normal force a fluid exerts per unit area. In a gas it comes from molecules bouncing off the wall; in a liquid it also carries the weight of the fluid above. At a point inside a fluid at rest the pressure is the same in every direction: it is a scalar, not a vector, which is why a diver at 30 m feels the same squeeze on the top of the head and the soles of the feet. Pressure is only defined for fluids; the equivalent quantity in a solid is called normal stress.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Pressure P is the normal force per unit area exerted by a fluid: P = Fn / A. SI unit the pascal, 1 Pa = 1 N/m². Because a pascal is tiny, engineering work uses the kilopascal (1 kPa = 10³ Pa), the megapascal (1 MPa = 10⁶ Pa) and the bar (1 bar = 100 kPa). One standard atmosphere is 1 atm = 101.325 kPa = 1.01325 bar = 14.696 psi = 760 mmHg.

Absolute pressure Pabs is measured relative to a perfect vacuum; it is what appears in every equation of state and every property table, and it is never negative.

Gauge pressure Pgauge is what most pressure gauges read: the difference between the absolute pressure and the local atmospheric pressure. Vacuum pressure Pvac is the amount by which a pressure falls below atmospheric, reported as a positive number.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Pgauge = Pabs − Patm   (for pressures above atmospheric), all in kPa.

Pvac = Patm − Pabs   (for pressures below atmospheric), all in kPa.

Patm is the local atmospheric pressure, which the problem states or which you take as 101.325 kPa at sea level. Gauge and vacuum values are labelled psig, kPa (gauge) or "kPa vacuum"; anything used in Pv = RT or a steam table must be absolute.

\n

A tyre gauge reading 220 kPa on a day when the barometer reads 100 kPa means the air in the tyre is at 320 kPa absolute; a vacuum gauge on a condenser reading 90 kPa vacuum at the same barometer means the steam is at 10 kPa absolute. The second one is a classic trap: the reading is large but the absolute pressure is small.

\n\n

Pressure at depth: the hydrostatic relation

\n

In a fluid at rest, pressure does not vary horizontally but increases downward because each layer must support the weight of everything above it. A force balance on a thin slab of fluid of thickness Δz and density ρ gives ΔP = ρ g Δz. For a liquid ρ is essentially constant and the relation integrates to a straight line; for the atmosphere ρ falls with height and the variation is smaller and curved, but over the metre or so of a manometer the density of a gas is so low (about 1.2 kg/m³ for air, versus 1000 for water) that the pressure of a gas is taken as uniform throughout a container.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

P = Patm + ρ·g·h   absolute pressure at depth h (m) below the free surface of a liquid open to the atmosphere; ρ in kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s², result in Pa (divide by 1000 for kPa). The gauge pressure at depth is simply ρgh.

ΔP = P2 − P1 = ρ·g·Δz = γs·Δz   pressure difference across a height Δz of one fluid, with γs = ρg the specific weight in N/m³. Pressure rises going down and falls going up.

Patm = ρHg·g·h   the barometer: the height h of a mercury column supported by a vacuum-topped tube measures atmospheric pressure directly. With ρHg = 13,595 kg/m³ and g = 9.807 m/s², 760 mm gives 101.3 kPa.

\n

The manometer is the hydrostatic relation turned into an instrument: a U-tube containing a liquid of known density connects the point whose pressure you want to the atmosphere (or to a second point), and the difference in liquid levels gives the pressure difference. The rule for reading any manometer, however many fluids it contains, is mechanical: start at one end whose pressure you know, walk through the tube, add ρgh each time you go down through a fluid, subtract ρgh each time you go up, and stop at the other end. Two points at the same height in the same continuous fluid are at the same pressure, which lets you jump across the bottom of a U.

\n

A useful design fact: the manometer fluid's density sets the sensitivity. Water gives 9.81 kPa per metre of column and is convenient for small gas pressures; mercury gives 13.6 times that (about 133 kPa per metre) and keeps the tube short for pressures of a few atmospheres. That is the same reason barometers use mercury: a water barometer would be over 10 m tall.

\n\n

Worked example 1: manometer, vacuum gauge and barometer

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Three readings are taken in a laboratory where the barometer stands at 740 mmHg. (a) A mercury U-tube manometer attached to a gas tank shows the mercury 0.55 m higher on the open (atmospheric) side than on the tank side. Find the absolute pressure in the tank. (b) A vacuum gauge on a second vessel reads 30 kPa vacuum. Find its absolute pressure. (c) Check what the atmospheric pressure would be if the barometer read the standard 760 mm.

📊 FIGURE — Reading a mercury manometer, then placing all three readings
Left: mercury stands 0.55 m higher on the open side, so the tank is 73.38 kPa above atmospheric. Right: gauge readings add to the barometer, vacuum readings subtract from it.

Take ρHg = 13,595 kg/m³ and g = 9.807 m/s² for the barometer (the standard values), and ρHg = 13,600 kg/m³ with g = 9.81 m/s² for the manometer (the rounded values used in most textbook problems).

\n
    \n
  1. Local atmospheric pressure from the barometer. Patm = ρHg g h = 13,595 kg/m³ × 9.807 m/s² × 0.740 m = 98,661 N/m² = 98.66 kPa. (Units: kg/m³ × m/s² × m = kg/(m·s²) = N/m² = Pa.)
    2. \n
  2. Manometer. The mercury is higher on the open side, so the tank pressure is above atmospheric by one column of mercury. Walking from the open surface (at Patm) down 0.55 m to the level of the tank-side meniscus, then across the same fluid: Ptank = Patm + ρHg g h = 98.66 kPa + 13,600 kg/m³ × 9.81 m/s² × 0.55 m = 98.66 kPa + 73,379 Pa = 98.66 kPa + 73.38 kPa = 172.0 kPa absolute. The gauge pressure is 73.38 kPa.
    3. \n
  3. Vacuum gauge. Pabs = Patm − Pvac = 98.66 kPa − 30 kPa = 68.66 kPa absolute. Not 128.66 kPa: a vacuum reading is subtracted.
    4. \n
  4. Standard barometer check. 13,595 kg/m³ × 9.807 m/s² × 0.760 m = 101,328 Pa = 101.33 kPa, which reproduces the standard atmosphere of 101.325 kPa to four figures. The 740 mm reading is therefore a slightly low-pressure day or a laboratory a few hundred metres above sea level.
    5. \n
\n

Answer: Ptank = 172.0 kPa (abs), Pvessel = 68.7 kPa (abs), Patm = 98.66 kPa. Sanity check: 0.55 m of mercury is a bit under three-quarters of a standard atmosphere (0.76 m), so a gauge pressure of about 73 kPa is plausible, and the tank sits at about 1.7 atm.

\n

A second, multi-fluid case in the same style: a tank of air is connected to the atmosphere (100 kPa) through a manometer holding, in order from the tank, 0.20 m of water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³), 0.30 m of oil (SG 0.85, ρ = 850 kg/m³) and 0.40 m of mercury (ρ = 13,600 kg/m³), with the tube arranged so you go down through the water and oil and up through the mercury to reach the open end. Then Pair + 1000 × 9.81 × 0.20 + 850 × 9.81 × 0.30 − 13,600 × 9.81 × 0.40 = Patm, i.e. Pair + 1.962 kPa + 2.502 kPa − 53.366 kPa = 100 kPa, so Pair = 100 − 1.962 − 2.502 + 53.366 = 148.9 kPa. The same add-down, subtract-up walk works for any arrangement.

\n\n

The zeroth law and why temperature is a property

\n

Everyone knows temperature as "hotness", but hotness is a sensation, not a number you can put in a table. The way out is to notice what happens when two bodies are brought into contact: heat flows from one to the other until it stops, and we say they have reached thermal equilibrium. The zeroth law is the statement that this relation is transitive, and that single fact is what allows a third body, a thermometer, to compare two bodies that never touch each other.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Zeroth law of thermodynamics: if two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third body, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.

Consequence: all bodies in mutual thermal equilibrium share the value of some property, and that shared property is what we call temperature. Two bodies at the same temperature exchange no net heat when placed in contact, whatever their other properties (mass, material, pressure) may be.

\n

The law is called "zeroth" because it was recognised as a logically necessary foundation only after the first and second laws had been named and numbered; its content is older than its name. A thermometer works by being the third body: the mercury column, the resistance of a platinum wire or the voltage of a thermocouple reaches equilibrium with the object, and the zeroth law guarantees that any two objects giving the same reading would exchange no heat if they met.

\n\n

Temperature scales

\n

Any property that changes reproducibly with hotness can carry a scale (liquid expansion, electrical resistance, gas pressure), but different thermometric substances give slightly different scales except at the fixed points used to calibrate them. The way out is the ideal-gas temperature scale: in a constant-volume gas thermometer the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is proportional to temperature, and in the limit of vanishing gas pressure every gas gives the same result. That defines a temperature that does not depend on the substance, and it coincides with the absolute thermodynamic temperature scale that the second law provides later in the course.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15   and   T(R) = T(°F) + 459.67   absolute from relative scales. Kelvin and Rankine have their zero at absolute zero.

T(R) = 1.8 · T(K)   and   T(°F) = 1.8 · T(°C) + 32   the two systems differ by the size of the degree: one kelvin (or one Celsius degree) is 1.8 Rankine (or Fahrenheit) degrees.

ΔT(K) = ΔT(°C)   and   ΔT(R) = ΔT(°F) = 1.8 · ΔT(K)   temperature differences carry no offset: a rise of 20 °C is a rise of 20 K, which is a rise of 36 °F or 36 R.

T = 273.16 K × (P / Ptp)   constant-volume gas thermometer in the low-pressure limit: P is the gas pressure at the unknown temperature and Ptp its pressure at the triple point of water, which was assigned 273.16 K exactly on the scale in use from 1954 to 2019.

\n

Two housekeeping facts. First, since 2019 the SI defines the kelvin by fixing the Boltzmann constant at exactly 1.380649 × 10−23 J/K, so the triple point of water is now a measured 273.16 K (with a tiny uncertainty) rather than a defined one; nothing in this course is affected. Second, when writing units, the kelvin has no degree sign (300 K, not 300 °K), and the Rankine is written R or °R depending on the textbook.

\n

Which scale goes into which formula? Any equation with T multiplying something (Pv = RT, radiation σT4, Carnot efficiency 1 − TL/TH, entropy change with ln(T2/T1)) needs an absolute temperature. Any equation with only a difference of temperatures (Q = m c ΔT, conduction q = k A ΔT/L, sensible-heat calculations) is indifferent between Celsius and Kelvin, because the 273.15 cancels. Specific heats are quoted as kJ/kg·K and kJ/kg·°C interchangeably for exactly this reason.

\n\n

Worked example 2: the gas thermometer and the four scales

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A constant-volume gas thermometer holds a small amount of helium. Its pressure is 50.0 kPa when the bulb is at the triple point of water and 68.0 kPa when the bulb is immersed in a bath of unknown temperature. (a) Find the bath temperature in K, °C, R and °F. (b) A second bath is 20 °C warmer than the first; state its temperature on all four scales and the temperature difference on all four scales.

Treat the helium pressures as already extrapolated to the low-pressure limit, which is how such problems are posed.

\n
    \n
  1. Kelvin from the gas thermometer. T = 273.16 K × (P / Ptp) = 273.16 K × (68.0 kPa / 50.0 kPa) = 273.16 K × 1.36 = 371.5 K. The kPa cancel; the ratio is dimensionless.
    2. \n
  2. Celsius. T(°C) = 371.5 − 273.15 = 98.3 °C: just under the boiling point of water at 1 atm (99.97 °C), consistent with a hot-water bath.
    3. \n
  3. Rankine. T(R) = 1.8 × 371.5 K = 668.7 R.
    4. \n
  4. Fahrenheit. T(°F) = 668.7 − 459.67 = 209.0 °F; check by the other route, 1.8 × 98.3 + 32 = 209.0 °F, the same.
    5. \n
  5. The warmer bath. A rise of 20 °C is a rise of 20 K, of 1.8 × 20 = 36 R and of 36 °F. So the second bath is at 118.3 °C = 391.5 K = 704.7 R = 245.0 °F; and the difference between the baths is 20 °C = 20 K = 36 °F = 36 R. Notice that the difference in °F is not obtained by converting 20 °C to 68 °F: the 32 offset belongs to levels, not to differences.
    6. \n
\n

Answer: first bath 371.5 K = 98.3 °C = 668.7 R = 209.0 °F; second bath 20 K (36 R) warmer. Sanity check: the pressure rose by 36% above its triple-point value, and 371.5 K is 36% above 273.16 K, as the proportionality demands.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Putting a gauge pressure into Pv = RT or a steam table. Every equation of state and every table uses absolute pressure. Add the local atmospheric pressure first; if the problem gives none, use 101.325 kPa and say so.

Adding a vacuum reading instead of subtracting it. 30 kPa vacuum at 92 kPa atmospheric is 62 kPa absolute, not 122 kPa.

Using Celsius in a ratio or a product. Doubling the absolute temperature from 300 K to 600 K doubles the pressure of a fixed-volume gas; doubling 27 °C to 54 °C raises it by only 9%. Carnot efficiencies computed with °C come out absurd (negative or above 100%).

Adding 32 to a temperature difference. ΔT(°F) = 1.8 × ΔT(°C); the offset cancels.

Mixing the manometer sign. Going down through a fluid the pressure increases (add ρgh); going up it decreases (subtract). A mercury level that is higher on the open side means the measured pressure is above atmospheric.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

One-line conversions: gauge to absolute, vacuum to absolute, kPa to bar to psi, °C to K and °F to R. Fast marks, but each wrong one propagates through a whole cycle problem.

A manometer or barometer sketch with one to three fluids and a request for the pressure in a tank; sometimes the reverse, the column height needed to show a given pressure. Show the walk-through equation with the sign of each ρgh term.

A piston-cylinder in mechanical equilibrium: gas pressure = atmospheric pressure + piston weight/area (+ spring force/area if present). This is the hydrostatic idea applied to a solid piston, and it fixes the pressure for every constant-pressure process in the next chapters.

Conceptual: state the zeroth law and explain what it lets a thermometer do; explain why the ideal-gas scale is independent of the gas; say which formulas need absolute temperature and which do not.

\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

The remark that the zeroth law received its name in the 1930s, after the first and second laws were already established, is commonly repeated in textbooks; the precise attribution and date have not been checked here, so confirm before you rely on this in any written work.

\n

With systems, states, processes, pressure and temperature in hand, the next chapter introduces the quantities that actually cross the boundary, energy, work and heat, and writes the first law for a closed system.

"}, "THERMO/energy/s1": {"body": "

This lesson lets you take any object or lump of matter, name every form of energy it holds, put a number in kJ on each one, and say cleanly what heat is and is not. In the degree this is the opening of the first-law block: the next three lessons add work, the energy balance and specific heats, and every later chapter (cycles, entropy, exergy, heat transfer) quietly assumes you can do this bookkeeping without thinking.

\n\n

Energy in plain words: what the system has, and what crosses its boundary

\n

Thermodynamics splits energy into two very different ideas. The first is energy the system possesses because of its state: how fast it moves, how high it sits, how hot and how compressed it is. That is a property, and we call its total E. The second is energy that crosses the boundary while a process happens. Energy only crosses a closed-system boundary in two ways, as heat or as work, and neither of them is a property; they are things that happen during a process, not things a system contains.

📊 FIGURE — Stored energy E versus heat and work at the boundary, with numbers
Left: E = U + KE + PE lives inside the boundary; Q and W are only counted as they cross it. Right: the car’s KE and PE are small next to warming its mass of water by 1 K.
\n

The energy a system possesses is further split by scale:

\n
    \n
  • Macroscopic forms depend on the system as a whole relative to some outside reference frame: kinetic energy from its bulk velocity, potential energy from its height in a gravity field.
    • \n
  • Microscopic forms depend on molecular structure and activity and are independent of any outside frame. Their sum is the internal energy U: molecular translation, rotation and vibration (the sensible part, which is what temperature measures), the energy tied up in phase (the latent part), the energy of chemical bonds, and nuclear energy.
    • \n
\n
📘 DEFINITION

Internal energy U (kJ) is the sum of all microscopic forms of energy of a system. Per unit mass it is u = U/m (kJ/kg). In this course the chemical and nuclear parts are constant unless the chapter is about combustion, so a change in U means a change in sensible and latent energy only.

Total energy E (kJ) is internal + kinetic + potential energy: the sum of everything the system possesses. Per unit mass, e = E/m (kJ/kg).

\n\n

The equations, every symbol named

\n

E = U + KE + PE = U + m·V²/2 + m·g·z

\n

e = u + V²/2 + g·z

\n
    \n
  • E: total energy, kJ; e: total energy per unit mass, kJ/kg.
    • \n
  • U, u: internal energy, kJ and kJ/kg.
    • \n
  • m: mass, kg. V: velocity of the system relative to the reference frame, m/s. g: 9.81 m/s². z: elevation above the chosen datum, m.
    • \n
  • KE = m·V²/2 comes out in kg·m²/s² = N·m = J, so divide by 1000 to get kJ. Same for PE = m·g·z.
    • \n
\n

The \"1000\" is the trap: V²/2 with V in m/s gives J/kg, not kJ/kg. A car at 100 km/h has only 0.386 kJ/kg of kinetic energy (computed below), which is tiny beside the hundreds of kJ/kg that show up in internal energy changes. That is why most closed-system problems set ΔKE and ΔPE to zero: a system that sits in a tank has no bulk motion, and a change of a few metres in height is worth a few hundredths of a kJ/kg.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

E = U + m·V²/2 + m·g·z (kJ, with the mechanical terms divided by 1000 when m is in kg, V in m/s, z in m).
