For a stationary closed system ΔE = ΔU. That single line is what lets the first law collapse to Q − W = ΔU in Lesson 3.

\n\n

Heat: energy in transit, driven only by a temperature difference

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Heat Q (kJ) is energy transferred between a system and its surroundings because of a temperature difference across the boundary. It has meaning only while it crosses the boundary. Per unit mass, q = Q/m (kJ/kg); as a rate, Q̇ (kW). A process with no heat transfer is adiabatic: either the boundary is insulated or system and surroundings are at the same temperature.

\n

Three consequences of that definition come up on every exam:

\n
    \n
  • A body does not \"contain heat\". It contains internal energy. Heat is the name for energy while it moves across a boundary because of ΔT. The everyday phrase \"heat content\" is what we now call enthalpy or internal energy.
    • \n
  • Adiabatic is not isothermal. A gas compressed quickly in an insulated cylinder receives no heat, yet its temperature rises a lot, because work is being done on it. Isothermal means constant temperature; adiabatic means zero heat transfer. They are different constraints and only coincide in special cases.
    • \n
  • Heat has a direction, and the sign convention encodes it. The classical engineering convention used throughout this course: heat transferred to the system is positive, heat lost by the system is negative; work done by the system is positive, work done on the system is negative. Equivalently, write every term as a magnitude and label it Qin, Qout, Win, Wout, then keep the balance as Ein − Eout = ΔE. Both forms are correct; mixing them mid-problem is how signs go wrong.
    • \n
\n\n

The three modes of heat transfer, at a glance

\n

Thermodynamics tells you how much energy moves once the end states are known; heat transfer (its own chapter near the end of this course) tells you how fast. You need the three rate laws now only so that the words are familiar and so that you can tell which mode a problem is describing.

\n\n\n\n\n
ModeMechanismRate lawSymbols and units
ConductionEnergy passed molecule to molecule through a solid or a still fluidQ̇ = k·A·ΔT/L (Fourier's law for a plane wall)k thermal conductivity W/m·K; A area m²; ΔT temperature difference across the wall K; L wall thickness m
ConvectionConduction into a fluid plus the fluid carrying the energy away by bulk motionQ̇ = h·A·(Ts − T∞) (Newton's law of cooling)h convection coefficient W/m²·K; Ts surface temperature; T∞ fluid temperature far from the surface
RadiationElectromagnetic waves emitted by matter because of its temperature; needs no mediumQ̇ = ε·σ·A·(Ts⁴ − Tsurr⁴)ε emissivity, 0 to 1; σ = 5.670 × 10−8 W/m²·K⁴ (Stefan-Boltzmann constant); temperatures in kelvin, always
\n

Two habits to build now: radiation uses absolute temperature to the fourth power, so a Celsius value inside the bracket is meaningless; and a vacuum stops conduction and convection but not radiation, which is why a thermos flask is silvered as well as evacuated.

\n\n

Worked example 1: putting numbers on the forms of energy

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A 1500 kg car travels at 100 km/h at a point 120 m above the valley floor. Find its kinetic and potential energy in kJ and compare them with the energy needed to warm the same mass of water by just 1 K (cwater = 4.18 kJ/kg·K).

  1. Convert the speed: V = 100 km/h × (1000 m/km) / (3600 s/h) = 27.78 m/s. Units must be m/s before squaring, or the answer is wrong by a factor of 3.6² = 12.96.
  2. Kinetic energy: KE = m·V²/2 = 1500 kg × (27.78 m/s)² / 2 = 578 704 J = 578.7 kJ. Per unit mass: 578.7 kJ / 1500 kg = 0.386 kJ/kg.
  3. Potential energy: PE = m·g·z = 1500 kg × 9.81 m/s² × 120 m = 1 765 800 J = 1765.8 kJ. Per unit mass: 1.177 kJ/kg.
  4. Warming 1500 kg of water by 1 K: Q = m·c·ΔT = 1500 kg × 4.18 kJ/kg·K × 1 K = 6270 kJ.
  5. Sanity check: a whole car at motorway speed carries less kinetic energy than it takes to warm the same mass of water by one degree (6270 / 578.7 ≈ 10.8 times less). That is the everyday reason internal energy dominates in stationary systems and why ΔKE and ΔPE are usually dropped.
\n\n

Worked example 2: which mode carries the energy, and how much per hour

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A 0.5 m² steel plate has a surface temperature of 400 K in a room where the air and the walls are both at 300 K. The convection coefficient is 15 W/m²·K and the plate emissivity is 0.8. Find the rate of heat loss by convection, by radiation, and the total energy lost in 8 hours. Use σ = 5.670 × 10−8 W/m²·K⁴.

  1. Convection: Q̇conv = h·A·(Ts − T∞) = 15 W/m²·K × 0.5 m² × (400 − 300) K = 750 W.
  2. Radiation: first the fourth powers. 400⁴ = 2.56 × 1010 K⁴; 300⁴ = 0.81 × 1010 K⁴; difference = 1.75 × 1010 K⁴. Then Q̇rad = ε·σ·A·(Ts⁴ − Tsurr⁴) = 0.8 × 5.670 × 10−8 W/m²·K⁴ × 0.5 m² × 1.75 × 1010 K⁴ = 396.9 W.
  3. Total rate: Q̇ = 750 W + 396.9 W = 1146.9 W. Radiation is about a third of the total even at these modest temperatures: never drop it without checking.
  4. Energy over 8 h: Q = Q̇·Δt = 1146.9 W × 8 h × 3600 s/h = 33 030 720 J = 33 031 kJ ≈ 33.0 MJ. This is heat out of the plate, so in the sign convention Q = −33 031 kJ for the plate as the system.
  5. Sanity check: 1.1 kW is the output of a small space heater, plausible for a half-square-metre surface 100 K above room temperature.
\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Squaring km/h. Convert to m/s first; the error is a factor of 12.96.
  • Leaving KE and PE in joules and adding them to ΔU in kilojoules. Convert to kJ before adding anything.
  • Putting °C into the radiation law. T⁴ only works in kelvin; (127 °C)⁴ − (27 °C)⁴ gives 5.9 W in Worked example 2 instead of 396.9 W.
  • Writing (Ts − Tsurr)⁴. The law is the difference of the fourth powers, not the fourth power of the difference; the wrong form gives 2.3 W here.
  • Saying \"the gas gained heat\" when it was compressed adiabatically. If the boundary is insulated Q = 0 and the energy came in as work.
\n
★ ON THE EXAM

Expect a first question that asks you to classify energy terms: which are properties (U, KE, PE, E) and which are interactions (Q, W). Expect a numerical one that hides a unit conversion (km/h, cm, J vs kJ) in the kinetic or potential energy term and one that asks whether a process is adiabatic, isothermal, both or neither.

Write the sign convention at the top of your answer sheet in the first minute: Q in +, W out +. Then every later problem in the paper follows it.

"}, "THERMO/energy/s2": {"body": "

This lesson lets you compute the work for any mechanical, electrical or boundary-movement interaction a closed system can have, and, most importantly, evaluate the integral of P dV for the four process types that appear in almost every cycle. It sits between the definition of energy (Lesson 1) and the energy balance (Lesson 3): once you can put a number on W, Q − W = ΔU becomes a one-line calculation.

\n\n

Work in plain words

\n

Work is the other way energy crosses a boundary. Mechanically it is a force acting through a distance: push a piston, twist a shaft, stretch a spring, raise a weight. Electrically it is charge pushed through a potential difference. The test for whether an interaction is work rather than heat: could its sole effect on the surroundings have been the raising of a weight? If yes, it is work. A current flowing through a resistor inside the system is work crossing the boundary (the electrons could have driven a motor instead), even though the resistor gets hot.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Work W (kJ) is energy transferred across a system boundary by a force acting through a displacement, or by an equivalent mechanism such as electric current. Per unit mass w = W/m (kJ/kg); per unit time it is power Ẇ (kW). 1 kW = 1 kJ/s; 1 hp = 0.7457 kW.

Sign: work done by the system is positive; work done on the system is negative. A gas expanding against a piston does positive work; a gas being compressed has W < 0.

\n\n

Boundary work: the integral of P dV

\n

When a gas expands in a piston-cylinder it pushes the piston with force F = P·A through a distance ds, so δWb = P·A·ds = P·dV. Adding up every small step of a quasi-equilibrium process (one that passes only through equilibrium states, so a single P describes the whole gas at every instant):

\n

Wb = ∫12 P dV

\n
    \n
  • Wb: boundary work, kJ. P: absolute pressure of the gas, kPa. V: volume, m³. The product kPa·m³ = kJ exactly, which is why we keep pressure in kPa.
    • \n
  • On a P-V diagram the integral is the area under the process curve. Two processes between the same end states with different curves enclose different areas: work depends on the path, which is why W is written with a δ and is never called a property.
    • \n
\n

The integral can only be evaluated once you know how P varies with V along the path. The four cases you must know cold:

\n\n\n\n\n\n
ProcessP(V) relationBoundary work WbIdeal-gas form
Constant volume (isochoric)dV = 0Wb = 00, whatever the pressure does
Constant pressure (isobaric)P = P0Wb = P0·(V2 − V1)m·R·(T2 − T1)
Isothermal, ideal gasP·V = C = m·R·TWb = P1V1·ln(V2/V1)m·R·T·ln(V2/V1) = m·R·T·ln(P1/P2)
Polytropic, n ≠ 1P·Vn = CWb = (P2V2 − P1V1)/(1 − n)m·R·(T2 − T1)/(1 − n)
\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Wb = ∫ P dV in general; P0·ΔV at constant pressure; P1V1·ln(V2/V1) for an isothermal ideal gas; (P2V2 − P1V1)/(1 − n) for a polytropic process with n ≠ 1.

The polytropic exponent n is a number that describes the path: n = 0 is constant pressure, n = 1 is isothermal for an ideal gas, n = k (1.4 for air) is the reversible adiabatic case you meet in the entropy chapter, and n → ∞ is constant volume. The second state on a polytropic path follows from P2 = P1·(V1/V2)n.

\n\n

Shaft, electrical, spring and other work forms

\n
    \n
  • Shaft work. A torque T (N·m) turning through n revolutions moves the rim of the shaft a distance 2π·r·n against a force T/r, so Wsh = 2π·n·T (J, with n a pure number of turns). As a power: Ẇsh = 2π·ṅ·T with ṅ in revolutions per second (rpm/60). Paddle wheels, stirrers and fans deliver shaft work into a system.
    • \n
  • Electrical work. A potential difference 𝒱 (volts) pushing current I (amperes) for time Δt: We = 𝒱·I·Δt (J = V·A·s). Power Ẇe = 𝒱·I (W). A resistance heater inside a rigid tank is electrical work in, not heat in, if the boundary is drawn around the tank.
    • \n
  • Spring work. A linear spring of constant k (kN/m) stretched or compressed from x1 to x2: Wspring = ½·k·(x2² − x1²) (kJ with k in kN/m and x in m). When a piston pushes against a spring, part of the boundary work goes into the spring and part into the atmosphere.
    • \n
  • Raising a body and accelerating a body. W = m·g·(z2 − z1) and W = ½·m·(V2² − V1²): the work done equals the change in the body's potential or kinetic energy. Same J-to-kJ conversion as in Lesson 1.
    • \n
  • Non-mechanical forms (magnetic, electrical polarisation, surface tension) all take the shape \"generalised force × generalised displacement\" and rarely appear at this level.
    • \n
\n\n

Worked example 1: the same compression by three different paths

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Air, 0.2 m³ at 150 kPa and 300 K, is compressed in a piston-cylinder to 0.05 m³. Find the boundary work if the process is (a) polytropic with n = 1.3, (b) isothermal, (c) constant pressure at 150 kPa followed by constant-volume heating to the same final pressure as in (a). R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K for air.

📊 FIGURE — The same compression by four paths, and four different works
Every path starts at state 1 (0.2 m³, 150 kPa) and ends at 0.05 m³. The work is the area under each path, so the high-pressure path (d) costs six times as much as (c).
  1. Mass, for later: m = P1V1/(R·T1) = 150 kPa × 0.2 m³ / (0.287 kJ/kg·K × 300 K) = 0.3484 kg. (kPa·m³ = kJ, so the units cancel to kg.)
  2. (a) Final pressure on the polytropic path: P2 = P1·(V1/V2)n = 150 kPa × (0.2/0.05)1.3 = 150 kPa × 41.3 = 150 × 6.063 = 909.4 kPa.
  3. (a) Work: Wb = (P2V2 − P1V1)/(1 − n) = (909.4 kPa × 0.05 m³ − 150 kPa × 0.2 m³)/(1 − 1.3) = (45.47 − 30.00) kJ / (−0.3) = −51.6 kJ. Negative: work is done on the air. Cross-check by temperature: T2 = P2V2/(m·R) = 45.47 kJ / (0.3484 kg × 0.287 kJ/kg·K) = 454.7 K, and m·R·(T2 − T1)/(1 − n) = 0.3484 × 0.287 × (454.7 − 300)/(−0.3) = −51.6 kJ. Same number, good.
  4. (b) Isothermal: Wb = P1V1·ln(V2/V1) = 150 kPa × 0.2 m³ × ln(0.05/0.2) = 30 kJ × ln(0.25) = 30 kJ × (−1.386) = −41.6 kJ.
  5. (c) Constant pressure then constant volume: the constant-volume leg does no work, so Wb = P1·(V2 − V1) = 150 kPa × (0.05 − 0.2) m³ = −22.5 kJ. Had the order been reversed (constant volume up to 909.4 kPa first, then constant pressure), the work would be 909.4 × (−0.15) = −136.4 kJ.
  6. Sanity check: the four answers (−22.5, −41.6, −51.6, −136.4 kJ) are all negative (compression) and the polytropic value lies between the isothermal and the high-pressure isobaric one, exactly as the areas under the curves on a P-V sketch would show. Same end volumes, four different works: work is a path function.
\n\n

Worked example 2: electrical and shaft work

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

(a) A 12 V battery drives 3 A through a resistor inside a rigid insulated tank of gas for 30 minutes. (b) A stirrer in the same tank is driven by a motor that applies a torque of 150 N·m at 3000 rpm. Find the electrical work in kJ and the stirrer power in kW.

  1. (a) We = 𝒱·I·Δt = 12 V × 3 A × (30 × 60) s = 12 × 3 × 1800 = 64 800 J = 64.8 kJ. Sign: it is work done on the gas, so W = −64.8 kJ in the balance, or Win = 64.8 kJ.
  2. (b) Convert the speed: ṅ = 3000 rpm / 60 = 50 rev/s. Ẇsh = 2π·ṅ·T = 2π × 50 s−1 × 150 N·m = 47 124 W = 47.1 kW.
  3. Sanity check: 47 kW is about 63 hp, a realistic small industrial motor; the battery example is the energy in a few minutes of a car headlamp. Both are work interactions even though the gas ends up hotter: no temperature difference drove them across the boundary.
\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Using gauge pressure in P dV. Boundary work needs absolute pressure; a piston at \"200 kPa gauge\" is pushing at about 301 kPa absolute.
  • Sign of a compression. If V2 < V1 the boundary work is negative. Do not \"fix\" it to positive; the energy balance needs the sign.
  • Writing (n − 1) instead of (1 − n) in the polytropic formula. Both appear in textbooks with the numerator flipped accordingly; pick one pair and keep it.
  • Applying P1V1·ln(V2/V1) to steam. That formula assumes PV = constant, which is the ideal-gas isothermal case. Isothermal steam inside the dome is a constant-pressure process instead.
  • Forgetting that a rigid tank has Wb = 0 but can still receive shaft or electrical work. \"Rigid\" kills boundary work only.
  • Leaving rpm as rpm in 2π·ṅ·T: the answer comes out 60 times too large.
\n
★ ON THE EXAM

The classic exam item is a piston-cylinder with a P-V sketch: identify the process type from the words (\"constant pressure\", \"PV1.3 = constant\", \"the temperature is held constant\"), write the matching formula, and compute the area. The second favourite is a two-step path (isobaric then isochoric, or the reverse) where you must realise only one leg does work.

Always state the sign and the units of W and say which body did the work on which. A bare \"51.6 kJ\" earns half marks.

"}, "THERMO/energy/s3": {"body": "

This lesson lets you write the first law for any closed system, decide which terms survive, and solve for the one unknown, whether that is a final temperature, a heat transfer, a work, or a missing entry in a cycle table. It is the hinge of the whole degree: control volumes (next chapter), every power and refrigeration cycle, and even the second law all begin by writing this balance.

\n\n

The first law in plain words

\n

Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only moved and converted. For any system, whatever crosses the boundary inward, minus whatever crosses outward, is exactly the change in what the system holds. That sentence is the first law of thermodynamics; everything else in this lesson is notation and special cases.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

The energy balance for any system undergoing any process: Ein − Eout = ΔEsystem. Net energy transfer by heat, work and mass equals the change in internal + kinetic + potential energy. In rate form: Ėin − Ėout = dEsystem/dt (kW).

A closed system exchanges no mass, so only heat and work cross the boundary and the balance reduces to the form below.

\n\n

The closed-system form, every symbol named

\n

Q − W = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE

📊 FIGURE — The closed-system energy balance applied to a tank and a cycle
Left: work in and heat out enter Q − W = ΔU with their signs, giving +20 kJ. Right: ΔU sums to zero around the cycle, which fixes the missing entries shown in accent.
\n
    \n
  • Q: net heat transfer to the system, kJ (Q = Qin − Qout).
    • \n
  • W: net work done by the system, kJ (W = Wout − Win), including boundary, shaft and electrical work.
    • \n
  • ΔU = m·(u2 − u1): change in internal energy, kJ; u from tables or from cv·ΔT (Lesson 4).
    • \n
  • ΔKE = m·(V2² − V1²)/2, ΔPE = m·g·(z2 − z1): kJ after dividing by 1000. For a tank or a piston that does not move as a whole, both are zero.
    • \n
\n

Per unit mass, q − w = Δu + Δke + Δpe (kJ/kg). Most problems: stationary system, so Q − W = ΔU. Many students prefer to write Qin + Win − Qout − Wout = ΔU with every symbol a positive magnitude; the result is identical, and the sign errors are fewer.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Q − W = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE (closed system, any process). Stationary: Q − W = ΔU.

Constant volume, no shaft or electrical work: W = 0 so Q = ΔU = m·(u2 − u1).

Constant pressure, quasi-equilibrium, only boundary work: Wb = P·(V2 − V1), and Q − P·ΔV = ΔU rearranges to Q = ΔU + Δ(PV) = ΔH = m·(h2 − h1).

Cycle: the system returns to its initial state, ΔE = 0, so Qnet = Wnet, i.e. ΣQ = ΣW around the loop.

\n\n

Why enthalpy appears

\n

The constant-pressure case introduces the combination U + PV so often that it gets its own name and its own column in every property table.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Enthalpy H = U + P·V (kJ), or per unit mass h = u + P·v (kJ/kg with P in kPa and v in m³/kg). It is a property, because U, P and V are properties. Physically, for a closed system heated at constant pressure it is the total energy that must be supplied: the rise in internal energy plus the work pushed into the surroundings by the expanding boundary.

\n

Two warnings that pay off later. First, Q = ΔH is a result for a closed system at constant pressure with only boundary work; if a stirrer or heater is also running, Q − Wother = ΔH. Second, in the next chapter enthalpy appears again for flowing streams, for a different reason (the Pv term is the flow work needed to push mass across an open boundary). Same property, two different jobs.

\n\n

Worked example 1: rigid tank with a paddle wheel and heat loss

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A rigid, uninsulated tank holds 2 kg of air at 300 K. A paddle wheel does 30 kJ of work on the air while 10 kJ of heat leaks out to the room. Find the final temperature. Use cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K for air (constant, room-temperature value).

  1. System: the air in the tank (closed). Rigid, so Wb = 0; the only work is the paddle-wheel work on the air, W = −30 kJ. Heat leaves, so Q = −10 kJ. Stationary: ΔKE = ΔPE = 0.
  2. Energy balance: Q − W = ΔU gives (−10 kJ) − (−30 kJ) = ΔU, so ΔU = +20 kJ. In magnitude form: Win − Qout = ΔU, 30 − 10 = 20 kJ, the same thing.
  3. Air as an ideal gas with constant cv: ΔU = m·cv·(T2 − T1), so T2 − T1 = 20 kJ / (2 kg × 0.718 kJ/kg·K) = 13.93 K.
  4. T2 = 300 K + 13.93 K = 313.9 K (40.8 °C).
  5. Sanity check: two-thirds of the paddle energy stayed in the gas; the temperature rose modestly, which is right for a 20 kJ input into 2 kg of gas. Had the heat sign been flipped (treating the leak as heat in) the answer would be 327.9 K; had cp been used, 310.0 K. Both are classic exam distractors.
\n\n

Worked example 2: constant-pressure heating of a gas, and the enthalpy shortcut

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

0.5 kg of air in a frictionless piston-cylinder at 100 kPa is heated from 27 °C to 227 °C at constant pressure. Find the boundary work, the change in internal energy and the heat added. Constant specific heats: cp = 1.005, cv = 0.718, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K.

  1. Temperatures: 27 °C = 300.15 K, 227 °C = 500.15 K, so ΔT = 200 K. (A temperature difference is the same in K and °C; only absolute values need converting.)
  2. Boundary work at constant pressure for an ideal gas: Wb = P·(V2 − V1) = m·R·(T2 − T1) = 0.5 kg × 0.287 kJ/kg·K × 200 K = 28.7 kJ (positive: the air pushes the piston out).
  3. Internal energy: ΔU = m·cv·ΔT = 0.5 kg × 0.718 kJ/kg·K × 200 K = 71.8 kJ.
  4. Heat from the balance: Q = ΔU + Wb = 71.8 kJ + 28.7 kJ = 100.5 kJ.
  5. Enthalpy shortcut: Q = ΔH = m·cp·ΔT = 0.5 kg × 1.005 kJ/kg·K × 200 K = 100.5 kJ. Identical, and one line. Note that cp − cv = 0.287 = R is exactly why the two routes agree.
  6. Sanity check: 28.7 of the 100.5 kJ (29%) went into pushing the piston and 71% into the gas; for air the fraction R/cp = 0.287/1.005 = 0.286 is a fixed rule of thumb. Using the specific heats at the average temperature of 400 K (cp = 1.013, cv = 0.726 kJ/kg·K, Cengel and Boles Table A-2b) would give Q = 101.3 kJ, under 1% different.
\n\n

Worked example 3: filling in a cycle table

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A closed system executes a three-process cycle. Process 1-2: 120 kJ of heat in, 40 kJ of work out. Process 2-3: 50 kJ of heat out, no work. Process 3-1: 30 kJ of work in. Find ΔU for each process, the heat transfer in 3-1, and the net work of the cycle.

ProcessQ (kJ)W (kJ)ΔU = Q − W (kJ)
1-2+120+40+80
2-3−500−50
3-1−60−30−30
Cycle+10+100
  1. ΔU12 = 120 − 40 = +80 kJ; ΔU23 = −50 − 0 = −50 kJ.
  2. U is a property, so around a cycle ΣΔU = 0: ΔU31 = −(80 − 50) = −30 kJ.
  3. Q31 = ΔU31 + W31 = −30 + (−30) = −60 kJ: 60 kJ of heat rejected.
  4. Net work: Wnet = 40 + 0 − 30 = +10 kJ; net heat: 120 − 50 − 60 = +10 kJ. Qnet = Wnet, as a cycle demands. This machine takes 120 kJ, rejects 110 kJ and delivers 10 kJ of work: a heat engine with thermal efficiency 10/120 = 8.3%, poor but legal.
\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Getting the sign of W backwards. Paddle wheels, stirrers, resistance heaters and compressions are work in (W negative in Q − W = ΔU). Expansions are work out.
  • Using Q = m·cp·ΔT in a rigid tank. At constant volume the heat goes entirely into U, so it is cv. Using cp over-predicts Q for air by 40%.
  • Applying Q = ΔH when the pressure is constant but a stirrer is also running. The full statement is Q − Wother = ΔH.
  • Forgetting that a free expansion into a vacuum does no work. If the gas pushes against nothing, Wb = 0 even though V changes; the P dV formula needs a resisting pressure.
  • Assuming a cycle has ΔU = 0 for each process. Only the sum around the loop is zero; individual legs can have large ΔU.
\n
★ ON THE EXAM

The standard first-law item gives a tank or piston-cylinder, a list of interactions (heat leak, heater, paddle wheel, expansion) and asks for one unknown. Full marks come from four visible lines: the system sketch and boundary, the balance with the terms that vanish crossed out and the reason stated (\"rigid, so Wb = 0\"), the property relation for ΔU, and the arithmetic with units.

Cycle tables like Worked example 3 are a favourite because they test both Q − W = ΔU per process and ΣΔU = 0 around the loop in one question.

"}, "THERMO/energy/s4": {"body": "

This lesson lets you evaluate Δu and Δh for ideal gases, liquids and solids by the three accepted routes (property tables, average specific heats, constant specific heats), know when each is good enough, and use cp − cv = R and the ratio k without looking anything up. It completes the closed-system first-law block; from here the course moves to control volumes, and later to the property relations chapter, which derives these results for real substances.

\n\n

Specific heats in plain words

\n

A specific heat answers the question \"how much energy does it take to raise 1 kg of this stuff by 1 K?\" The answer depends on what the substance is allowed to do while it warms. Held at constant volume it can only store the energy internally. Held at constant pressure it also expands and pushes on the surroundings, so more energy is needed for the same temperature rise. That is why there are two specific heats, and why cp is always the larger.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Specific heat at constant volume cv = (∂u/∂T)v: the change in internal energy per unit temperature change with specific volume held fixed. Units kJ/kg·K (identical to kJ/kg·°C, because it is a per-degree quantity).

Specific heat at constant pressure cp = (∂h/∂T)p: the change in enthalpy per unit temperature change with pressure held fixed. Both are properties of the substance, defined by these derivatives, whatever process the substance later undergoes.

\n\n

Ideal gases: u and h depend on temperature only

\n

Joule's classic experiment showed that when an ideal gas expands into a vacuum with no heat transfer, its temperature does not change: internal energy of an ideal gas does not depend on volume or pressure, only on temperature. Since h = u + Pv = u + RT, enthalpy is also a function of temperature alone. The partial derivatives then become ordinary ones and the process constraint disappears:

\n

du = cv(T)·dT → Δu = ∫12 cv(T) dT

\n

dh = cp(T)·dT → Δh = ∫12 cp(T) dT

\n

These hold for any process of an ideal gas, not only constant-volume or constant-pressure ones. The subscripts on cv and cp record how they were defined, not where they may be used. Differentiating h = u + RT gives the relation everyone must know:

\n

cp = cv + R and k = cp/cv so cv = R/(k − 1), cp = k·R/(k − 1)

\n
    \n
  • R: the gas constant of the particular gas, kJ/kg·K, = Ru/M with Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K and M the molar mass in kg/kmol. Air: 0.287; helium: 2.0769; nitrogen: 0.2968; CO2: 0.1889 kJ/kg·K.
    • \n
  • k: specific heat ratio, dimensionless. Monatomic gases (He, Ar): cv = 3R/2, cp = 5R/2, k = 1.667, and these do not change with temperature. Diatomic gases near room temperature (air, N2, O2): k ≈ 1.4, falling slowly as T rises and vibration switches on.
    • \n
  • On a molar basis the same relations read c̄p = c̄v + Ru with c̄ = M·c in kJ/kmol·K.
    • \n
\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Δu = ∫ cv(T) dT ≈ cv,avg·(T2 − T1) and Δh = ∫ cp(T) dT ≈ cp,avg·(T2 − T1) for an ideal gas on any process.

cp − cv = R, k = cp/cv. Air at 300 K: cp = 1.005, cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, k = 1.4. Check: 1.005 − 0.718 = 0.287 = R.

\n\n

Three ways to get Δu and Δh, and when each is good enough

\n
    \n
  1. Ideal-gas tables (Cengel and Boles Table A-17 for air, A-18 to A-25 for other gases; Moran and Shapiro Table A-22). Someone has already integrated cp(T) from a reference temperature and listed u(T) and h(T). Read u1, u2 and subtract. Most accurate, any temperature range.
  2. Average specific heat: read cv or cp at the mean temperature (T1 + T2)/2 from a c(T) table (A-2b) and multiply by ΔT. Within a fraction of a percent for a few hundred kelvin of range.
  3. Constant room-temperature specific heat (A-2a values: 0.718 and 1.005 for air). Simplest; fine when the temperature range is a couple of hundred kelvin or the gas is monatomic; a few percent low for large ranges because cv of air rises with temperature.
    4. \n
\n\n

Worked example 1: the three routes compared for air, 300 K to 600 K

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Air is heated from 300 K to 600 K. Find Δu and Δh per kg by all three routes and state the error of the simplest one.

📊 FIGURE — How cv of air rises with temperature, and three routes to Δu
Δu is the area under cv(T). The constant 0.718 line misses the part of the curve above it (−2.4%); the average-temperature value 0.733 almost matches the area (−0.4%). Note the cv axis starts at 0.70.
  1. Tables (Cengel and Boles A-17 / Moran and Shapiro A-22, ideal-gas properties of air): u(300 K) = 214.07 kJ/kg, u(600 K) = 434.78 kJ/kg, h(300 K) = 300.19 kJ/kg, h(600 K) = 607.02 kJ/kg. So Δu = 434.78 − 214.07 = 220.71 kJ/kg and Δh = 607.02 − 300.19 = 306.83 kJ/kg. Check: Δh − Δu should equal R·ΔT = 0.287 × 300 = 86.1 kJ/kg; the tables give 306.83 − 220.71 = 86.12 kJ/kg. Consistent.
  2. Average specific heats at Tavg = 450 K (Table A-2b: cv = 0.733, cp = 1.020 kJ/kg·K): Δu = 0.733 × 300 = 219.9 kJ/kg, Δh = 1.020 × 300 = 306.0 kJ/kg. Error against the tables: −0.4%.
  3. Constant room-temperature values (cv = 0.718, cp = 1.005): Δu = 0.718 × 300 = 215.4 kJ/kg, Δh = 1.005 × 300 = 301.5 kJ/kg. Error: −2.4%, low because the true cv climbs from 0.718 to about 0.764 kJ/kg·K across this range.
  4. Sanity check: all three Δh values exceed the Δu values by about R·ΔT, and the errors grow in the expected order (tables, average, constant). For an exam question over a 300 K span any route is accepted if named; over 1000 K use the tables.
\n
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Table A-2c of Cengel and Boles gives c̄p(T) for common gases as a cubic, c̄p = a + b·T + c·T² + d·T³ in kJ/kmol·K. For air the listed coefficients are a = 28.11, b = 0.1967 × 10−2, c = 0.4802 × 10−5, d = −1.966 × 10−9, valid 273 to 1800 K. Integrating that polynomial in Python (numpy.polyint, or sympy) from 300 K to 600 K and dividing by M = 28.97 kg/kmol gives Δh = 308.6 kJ/kg, within 0.6% of the tabulated 306.83 kJ/kg; the polynomial also returns cp = 1.004 kJ/kg·K at 300 K, the familiar 1.005. That is the whole story of the ideal-gas tables: someone fitted cp(T) to data and integrated it.

Your regression instincts apply directly: if a lab hands you cp measurements at ten temperatures, a least-squares cubic and a numerical integral are the same job as the table, and you can put error bars on Δh. Treat the coefficient values above as a transcription to confirm against your own copy of the table before relying on them.

\n\n

Incompressible substances: liquids and solids

\n

For liquids and solids the specific volume barely changes with pressure or temperature, so the two specific heats collapse into one, written simply c. Internal energy is again a function of temperature only, but enthalpy picks up a pressure term because h = u + Pv and v is fixed:

\n

cp = cv = c, Δu = cavg·(T2 − T1), Δh = Δu + v·ΔP = cavg·ΔT + v·(P2 − P1)

\n
    \n
  • c: kJ/kg·K. Liquid water 4.18; iron about 0.45; copper 0.385; aluminium 0.90 (room-temperature values from Table A-3).
    • \n
  • v: specific volume, m³/kg, about 0.001 for water; with P in kPa, v·ΔP comes out in kJ/kg.
    • \n
  • Heating at constant pressure: Δh = c·ΔT (the v·ΔP term vanishes). Pumping at constant temperature: Δh = v·ΔP, and this is the pump work per kg you will use in the Rankine cycle chapter.
    • \n
\n\n

Worked example 2: gases from R and k, a solid, and a pumped liquid

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

(a) Helium has cp = 5.1926 kJ/kg·K and R = 2.0769 kJ/kg·K. Find cv and k. (b) A 5 kg iron block (c = 0.45 kJ/kg·K) is heated from 20 °C to 80 °C. Find the heat required. (c) Liquid water (v = 0.001 m³/kg) is pumped from 100 kPa to 5 MPa with negligible temperature change. Find Δh.

  1. (a) cv = cp − R = 5.1926 − 2.0769 = 3.1157 kJ/kg·K; k = cp/cv = 5.1926/3.1157 = 1.667. Check: helium is monatomic, so k should be 5/3 = 1.667 and R should be 8.314/4.003 = 2.077 kJ/kg·K. Both agree.
  2. (b) Solid, so Q = ΔU = m·c·ΔT = 5 kg × 0.45 kJ/kg·K × (80 − 20) K = 135 kJ. Using absolute temperatures inside the bracket changes nothing (353.15 − 293.15 = 60 K); using 353.15 K as if it were ΔT gives the absurd 794.6 kJ.
  3. (c) Δh = c·ΔT + v·ΔP = 0 + 0.001 m³/kg × (5000 − 100) kPa = 4.9 kJ/kg (m³·kPa/kg = kJ/kg). Compare: raising the same water by 1 K costs 4.18 kJ/kg, so a 49-fold pressure rise is worth about one degree of heating. This smallness is why pump work is so cheap in vapour power cycles.
  4. Sanity check: k = 1.667 is the theoretical monatomic value; 135 kJ warms a small engine block by 60 K, reasonable; 4.9 kJ/kg matches the pump-work numbers in every Rankine example (a few kJ/kg against hundreds for a turbine).
\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • \"cv is only for constant-volume processes.\" For an ideal gas Δu = cv·ΔT on every process, including constant pressure; Worked example 2 of Lesson 3 used exactly that.
  • Using cp for ΔU or cv for ΔH. The letters match: cv goes with u, cp goes with h.
  • Mixing molar and mass values: c̄p in kJ/kmol·K divided by M in kg/kmol gives cp in kJ/kg·K. Air: 29.1/28.97 = 1.005.
  • Forgetting that cp − cv = R uses the specific gas constant of that gas, not Ru = 8.314.
  • Writing Δh = c·ΔT for a liquid that is being pumped: the v·ΔP term is the whole answer when ΔT ≈ 0.
  • Saying steam is an ideal gas. Near the saturation dome it is not; use the steam tables (next chapter) and reserve cp·ΔT for gases far from condensation.
\n
★ ON THE EXAM

Expect: a \"find Δu by tables, by average cv, by constant cv and compare\" item exactly like Worked example 1; a \"given cp and R (or k and R) find the rest\" item; a rigid-tank or piston problem where the only decision is cv versus cp; and an incompressible-substance item where two bodies of different temperature reach equilibrium (set the heat lost by one equal to the heat gained by the other, e.g. 1 kg of iron at 200 °C dropped into 5 kg of water at 20 °C settles at 23.8 °C).

State which specific-heat route you used and its source. \"cv,avg = 0.733 kJ/kg·K at 450 K from Table A-2b\" is a marking-scheme phrase.

"}, "THERMO/props/s1": {"body": "

This lesson lets you name the five states a substance passes through as it boils, place any state on the T-v, P-v and P-T diagrams, and explain why temperature and pressure stop being independent inside the vapour dome. It is the first of three lessons on properties; the next two turn the pictures here into table look-ups and into the ideal-gas law. Everything in the cycle chapters (Rankine, refrigeration) is drawn on these diagrams, so the shapes are worth learning cold.

\n\n

Pure substances and phases in plain words

\n

A pure substance has one fixed chemical composition everywhere in the system. Water is pure whether it is ice, liquid or steam, and a mixture of liquid water and its vapour is still pure because both phases are H2O. Air counts as pure while it stays a gas, because its composition does not change; the moment part of it condenses the liquid is oxygen-rich and the gas is nitrogen-rich, so liquid-plus-vapour air is not a pure substance.

\n

A phase is a region of matter with a distinct molecular arrangement: in a solid the molecules sit in a lattice and vibrate, in a liquid they stay close but slide past each other, in a gas they are far apart and move almost freely. Thermodynamics only needs the phase idea to describe two things: when a substance changes phase, and how much energy it takes.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Saturation temperature Tsat: at a given pressure, the temperature at which a pure substance changes phase. Saturation pressure Psat: at a given temperature, the pressure at which it changes phase. They are the same curve read two ways: for water, Tsat at 101.325 kPa is 99.97 °C and Psat at 100 °C is 101.42 kPa (IAPWS-95 steam tables, as in Cengel & Boles Table A-4).

Latent heat of vaporisation hfg = hg − hf: the energy absorbed per kilogram when saturated liquid becomes saturated vapour at constant pressure. For water at 100 °C it is 2256.4 kJ/kg; it falls as pressure rises and is exactly zero at the critical point.

\n\n

Heating water at constant pressure: the five states

\n

Put 1 kg of liquid water at 20 °C in a piston-cylinder held at 100 kPa and add heat slowly. The table below is the whole story; the subscripts f and g are the steam-table labels for saturated liquid and saturated vapour. Values are computed from the IAPWS-95 formulation for water (the equation the modern steam tables are generated from; printed tables such as Cengel & Boles A-5 agree to within a unit or two in the last digit), saturated water by pressure at 100 kPa: Tsat = 99.61 °C, vf = 0.001043 m³/kg, vg = 1.6939 m³/kg.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
StateNameTv (m³/kg)What is happening
1Compressed (subcooled) liquid20 °C0.001002Liquid, not about to boil: T is below Tsat at this pressure. Adding heat raises T; v grows only slightly.
2Saturated liquid99.61 °C0.001043Still all liquid, but one more joule starts boiling. This is the left edge of the dome.
3Saturated liquid-vapour mixture99.61 °Cbetween 0.001043 and 1.6939Boiling. T stays constant while heat goes into the phase change; v rises as liquid turns to vapour.
4Saturated vapour99.61 °C1.6939The last drop has boiled. Right edge of the dome; one joule less and a drop condenses.
5Superheated vapour200 °C2.1724All vapour, T above Tsat. Adding heat raises T again.
\n

Two things in that table decide everything you do in the next lesson. First, between states 2 and 4 the temperature does not move: T and P are locked together by the saturation curve, so knowing both tells you nothing about how far the boiling has gone. Second, the specific volume jumps by a factor of roughly 1,600 across the dome at 100 kPa (1.6939 / 0.001043 = 1,624), which is why a boiler is a large, dangerous thing and why v is the property that tells you where inside the dome you are.

\n\n

The T-v diagram and the vapour dome

\n

Plot the process above with T on the vertical axis and v on the horizontal: a steep rise from 1 to 2 (liquid barely expands), a flat horizontal line from 2 to 4 (boiling at 99.61 °C), then a rising curve from 4 to 5. Repeat at higher pressures and the flat line moves up (Tsat rises: 120.21 °C at 200 kPa, 179.88 °C at 1 MPa, 263.94 °C at 5 MPa) and gets shorter, because vf grows and vg shrinks. The saturated-liquid points join into the saturated liquid line, the saturated-vapour points into the saturated vapour line, and together they form the vapour dome. Inside the dome is the two-phase mixture region, to its left the compressed-liquid region, to its right the superheated-vapour region.

📊 FIGURE — The vapour dome on a T-v diagram, with water heated at 100 kPa
Follow states 1 to 5 along the 100 kPa line: liquid, boiling at a flat 99.61 °C, then superheat. Higher-pressure lines boil hotter and shorter until they close at the critical point. Not to scale.
\n

The flat line shrinks to a single point at the critical point: for water Pcr = 22.06 MPa, Tcr = 373.95 °C, vcr = 0.003106 m³/kg. Above the critical pressure there is no boiling at all: the fluid goes from liquid-like to vapour-like continuously with no meniscus and no latent heat. By convention it is called compressed liquid below Tcr and superheated vapour above Tcr. Supercritical boilers in modern power stations operate here on purpose, and that is why the Rankine chapter later cares about the dome shape.

\n

The P-v diagram is the same dome with P on the vertical axis; the constant-temperature lines now slope downward to the right (a fluid compressed at fixed T loses volume) and are flat inside the dome. It is the diagram used for boundary work because the area under a process curve is ∫P dv, which you met in the energy chapter.

\n\n

The P-T diagram: three lines, a triple point and sublimation

\n

On a P-T plot the entire dome collapses into one line, because inside it P and T are not independent. Three phase-boundary lines meet at the triple point, where solid, liquid and vapour coexist: for water 0.01 °C and 0.6117 kPa. The vaporisation line runs from the triple point up to the critical point and stops there. The fusion (melting) line runs upward from the triple point; for water it leans very slightly to the left, meaning that raising the pressure lowers the melting point. That tilt and the fact that ice floats have the same cause: water expands when it freezes, so squeezing it favours the denser liquid. The sublimation line runs below the triple point: at pressures under 0.6117 kPa ice turns straight to vapour without melting. Freeze-drying and the disappearance of snow on a cold dry day are both sublimation.

\n

Because P-T diagrams show the phases as areas separated by lines, they are called phase diagrams. The three diagrams are one surface seen from three sides: the P-v-T surface. You never need to draw the surface, but you should be able to say which of the three plane views hides which information (P-T hides quality; T-v and P-v hide nothing about the state but cannot show the solid region clearly).

\n\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

For a closed system heated at constant pressure with negligible kinetic and potential energy, the boundary work and the internal-energy change combine into enthalpy, so the heat added is

Q = m (h2 − h1)

Q = heat added (kJ); m = mass (kg); h = specific enthalpy (kJ/kg) read from the table for each state. Across the dome alone this becomes the latent heat:

Qboil = m hfg = m (hg − hf)

hf, hg = saturated liquid and vapour enthalpy at the pressure of the process (kJ/kg); hfg = latent heat of vaporisation (kJ/kg).

\n\n

Worked example: heating 1 kg of water from 20 °C to 200 °C at 100 kPa

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A piston-cylinder holds 1 kg of water at 20 °C and 100 kPa. Heat is added at constant pressure until the water is at 200 °C. Find the volume at each of the five states, the heat needed for each leg, and the fraction of the total that goes into boiling. Source: IAPWS-95 formulation for water, evaluated with the CoolProp library (saturated water by temperature, saturated water by pressure and superheated vapour; the same layout as Cengel & Boles Tables A-4, A-5 and A-6).

\n
    \n
  1. State 1, compressed liquid at 20 °C. The compressed-liquid table has no entry this low, so use the standard approximation: treat it as saturated liquid at the same temperature. Saturated water at 20 °C: vf = 0.001002 m³/kg, hf = 83.91 kJ/kg (the liquid is at 100 kPa, far above Psat(20 °C) = 2.339 kPa, which is why it is compressed). V1 = 1 kg × 0.001002 m³/kg = 0.001002 m³ (about one litre).
    2. \n
  2. State 2, saturated liquid at 100 kPa. Table by pressure at 100 kPa: Tsat = 99.61 °C, vf = 0.001043 m³/kg, hf = 417.50 kJ/kg. V2 = 1 kg × 0.001043 m³/kg = 0.001043 m³.
    3. \n
  3. Heat for leg 1 to 2 (warming the liquid): Q12 = 1 kg × (417.50 − 83.91) kJ/kg = 333.6 kJ.
    4. \n
  4. State 4, saturated vapour at 100 kPa. Same table row: vg = 1.6939 m³/kg, hg = 2674.9 kJ/kg, so hfg = 2674.9 − 417.50 = 2257.4 kJ/kg. V4 = 1 kg × 1.6939 m³/kg = 1.6939 m³. State 3 is anywhere between V2 and V4 at 99.61 °C.
    5. \n
  5. Heat for leg 2 to 4 (boiling): Q24 = m hfg = 1 kg × 2257.4 kJ/kg = 2257.4 kJ, with the temperature stuck at 99.61 °C the whole time.
    6. \n
  6. State 5, superheated vapour at 100 kPa and 200 °C. Superheated table at 0.10 MPa, 200 °C: v = 2.1724 m³/kg, h = 2875.5 kJ/kg. V5 = 1 kg × 2.1724 m³/kg = 2.1724 m³.
    7. \n
  7. Heat for leg 4 to 5 (superheating): Q45 = 1 kg × (2875.5 − 2674.9) kJ/kg = 200.6 kJ.
    8. \n
  8. Total and fractions. Qtotal = 333.6 + 2257.4 + 200.6 = 2791.6 kJ, which equals m(h5 − h1) = 1 kg × (2875.5 − 83.91) kJ/kg = 2791.6 kJ, as it must. Boiling takes 2257.4 / 2791.6 = 80.9 % of the heat; warming the liquid takes 333.6 / 2791.6 = 11.9 % and superheating 200.6 / 2791.6 = 7.2 %.
    9. \n
  9. Sanity check. The volume grows by a factor of 2.1724 / 0.001002 = 2,168 from start to finish, the latent heat (2257.4 kJ) is 2257.4 / 333.6 = 6.8 times the heat needed to warm the liquid, and that liquid heating (333.6 kJ) agrees with the rough estimate c × ΔT = 4.18 kJ/kg-K × (99.61 − 20) K = 332.8 kJ: both are the familiar orders of magnitude for water, so the table reads are consistent.
    10. \n
\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Assuming temperature rises while a substance boils. It does not. From saturated liquid to saturated vapour at fixed pressure, all the heat goes into hfg and T stays at Tsat. If a question says \"water at 100 kPa and 99.61 °C\" you cannot tell whether it is liquid, vapour or a mixture; you need one more property, usually v, u, h or the quality x.

Treating \"100 °C\" as the boiling point of water. It is only the boiling point at 101.42 kPa. At 10 kPa (a power-station condenser) water boils at 45.81 °C; at 1 MPa it boils at 179.88 °C; at 5 MPa at 263.94 °C. Always read Tsat at the actual pressure.

\n
    \n
  • \"Saturated\" does not mean \"wet\": saturated vapour is 100 % vapour. It means \"on the edge of the dome\".
    • \n
  • Above Pcr = 22.06 MPa water never boils; any process at, say, 25 MPa crosses no dome and has no hfg.
    • \n
  • The P-T diagram cannot show quality: every mixture state at 100 kPa is the same point (100 kPa, 99.61 °C).
    • \n
  • Water is unusual in that its fusion line leans to the left (it expands on freezing); most substances contract on freezing and their line leans right. Do not generalise the ice behaviour to other substances.
    • \n
\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

Expect to be asked to sketch a constant-pressure process on a T-v diagram and label all five regions, to state what is constant during boiling, and to identify the phase from a pair of properties (\"water at 200 kPa and 150 °C is superheated, because 150 °C is above Tsat = 120.21 °C\"). Numerical questions give a pressure and ask for Tsat, vf, vg or hfg, or give a temperature and ask for Psat.

Say the words \"saturation line\", \"critical point\", \"triple point\" and \"sublimation\" correctly and know the three numbers for water: 22.06 MPa and 373.95 °C (critical), 0.01 °C and 0.6117 kPa (triple), 2256.4 kJ/kg (hfg at 100 °C).

\n
✅ VERIFIED

Every water property in this lesson was computed from the IAPWS-95 formulation with the CoolProp 8.0 library (coolprop.org) rather than copied from memory: Psat(100 °C) = 101.42 kPa, Tsat(101.325 kPa) = 99.97 °C, hfg(100 °C) = 2256.4 kJ/kg, the critical point 22.064 MPa and 373.95 °C, and the 100 kPa row used in the example. A printed table may differ from these in the last digit; use your own course's table in an exam.

"}, "THERMO/props/s2": {"body": "

This lesson lets you find v, u, h and s of water or R-134a at any state from the property tables: saturated by temperature, saturated by pressure, superheated, compressed liquid, and anywhere inside the dome using the quality x. It is the most-used skill in the whole degree: every Rankine, refrigeration and steady-flow problem in later chapters starts with three or four table look-ups, and most lost marks in those chapters are look-up errors made here.

\n\n

What each table holds and why there are so many

\n

No single equation fits water in every phase, so its properties are published as tables. In the Cengel & Boles numbering (other books use the same layout with different numbers): A-4 saturated water by temperature, A-5 saturated water by pressure, A-6 superheated vapour, A-7 compressed liquid, A-8 saturated ice-vapour; and for refrigerant-134a A-11 saturated by temperature, A-12 saturated by pressure, A-13 superheated. The two saturation tables contain the same information; one is convenient when you know T, the other when you know P. Each saturation row lists Tsat or Psat and then vf, vg, uf, ufg, ug, hf, hfg, hg, sf, sfg, sg. The superheated and compressed-liquid tables are two-dimensional: a block for each pressure, rows for each temperature, columns v, u, h, s.

\n

Tables list u, h and s relative to an arbitrary reference state, because only differences matter. Water tables set uf = 0 and sf = 0 for saturated liquid at the triple point (0.01 °C); the usual R-134a tables set hf = 0 and sf = 0 for saturated liquid at −40 °C (so uf there is slightly negative, −0.036 kJ/kg, because u = h − Pv). Never mix values from two books with different reference states in one calculation. The water values in this chapter are computed from the IAPWS-95 formulation with the CoolProp library; the R-134a values are computed with CoolProp's R-134a equation of state set to the −40 °C reference. Printed tables are generated from equations of the same kind but not always the same version, so the last digit can differ: a posted Cengel & Boles Table A-11 gives Psat(−40 °C) = 51.25 kPa, where CoolProp gives 51.21 kPa. In an exam, use the table you are given.

\n\n

Quality: the one extra property a mixture needs

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Quality x is the mass fraction of vapour in a saturated liquid-vapour mixture:

x = mvapour / (mliquid + mvapour)

x = 0 is saturated liquid, x = 1 is saturated vapour, and x has meaning only inside the dome. A mixture at 30 % quality by mass can be well over 99 % vapour by volume, because vg is so much larger than vf.

\n

Inside the dome T and P are tied together, so you need x (or any one of v, u, h, s) to fix the state. Because the two phases are simply mixed, every extensive property adds: V = Vf + Vg = mf vf + mg vg. Divide by the total mass and you get the mixing rule.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

For any property y (v, u, h or s) of a saturated mixture with quality x:

y = yf + x · yfg = (1 − x) yf + x yg

yf, yg = saturated liquid and vapour values at the mixture's T or P (same units as y); yfg = yg − yf. Solved for the quality:

x = (y − yf) / yfg

Linear interpolation between two table rows (T1, y1) and (T2, y2) uses exactly the same shape: y = y1 + (T − T1)/(T2 − T1) × (y2 − y1), the fraction f = (T − T1)/(T2 − T1) playing the role of x.

\n\n

The decision tree: which table, which row

\n

Every look-up starts by finding the phase. Given two independent properties, use whichever test below fits what you were told. The comparison is always against the saturation values at the known P or T.

\n
    \n
  1. Given T and P. Look up Tsat at that P (or Psat at that T). If T < Tsat (equivalently P > Psat): compressed liquid, use Table A-7 or the saturated-liquid approximation. If T > Tsat (P < Psat): superheated, use Table A-6 at that P and T. If T = Tsat exactly: you are somewhere in the dome and need a third property; the state is not fixed.
    2. \n
  2. Given T or P plus v, u, h or s. Read yf and yg from the saturation row. If y < yf: compressed liquid. If yf ≤ y ≤ yg: saturated mixture, x = (y − yf)/yfg. If y > yg: superheated; go to the superheated block at that P and find the row (interpolating) whose y matches.
    3. \n
  3. Given quality x. The word \"quality\" already tells you it is a mixture: read the saturation row and apply y = yf + x yfg for everything.
    4. \n
  4. Given \"saturated liquid\" or \"saturated vapour\". Read the f or g column directly; T or P alone fixes the state.
    5. \n
\n

For a compressed liquid, when the table has no row at your pressure (Table A-7 starts at 5 MPa), use the saturated-liquid approximation: v ≈ vf(T), u ≈ uf(T), s ≈ sf(T), and for enthalpy either h ≈ hf(T) or the better h ≈ hf(T) + vf(T) × (P − Psat(T)). The error is tiny because liquids barely compress: at 5 MPa and 80 °C the exact v is 0.0010267 m³/kg against vf(80 °C) = 0.001029 m³/kg, a 0.2 % difference, and exact u is 333.82 kJ/kg against uf = 334.96 kJ/kg (IAPWS-95 via CoolProp; the compressed-liquid table, Cengel & Boles A-7, lists this state).

\n\n

Worked example A: a rigid tank of water inside the dome

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A rigid tank of volume 0.5 m³ contains 4 kg of water at 150 °C. Find the pressure, the phase, the quality, the mass of vapour, the specific internal energy and the total internal energy, and the volume occupied by the liquid. Source: saturated water by temperature (the layout of Cengel & Boles Table A-4), values computed from IAPWS-95 with CoolProp, at 150 °C: Psat = 476.16 kPa, vf = 0.001091 m³/kg, vg = 0.39245 m³/kg, uf = 631.66 kJ/kg, ug = 2559.1 kJ/kg, hf = 632.18 kJ/kg, hg = 2745.9 kJ/kg.

📊 FIGURE — Quality as a lever: where 0.1250 m³/kg sits on the 150 °C tie line
The tie line runs from vf to vg at 150 °C (drawn to scale along the line). The state splits it 0.3166 : 0.6834, so 31.66 % of the 4 kg is vapour, yet the vapour fills almost the whole tank.
\n
    \n
  1. Specific volume from the givens: v = V/m = 0.5 m³ / 4 kg = 0.1250 m³/kg.
    2. \n
  2. Phase test: vf = 0.001091 < 0.1250 < vg = 0.39245 m³/kg, so the water is a saturated liquid-vapour mixture. Therefore P = Psat(150 °C) = 476.16 kPa; you do not get to choose it.
    3. \n
  3. Quality: x = (v − vf)/(vg − vf) = (0.1250 − 0.001091)/(0.39245 − 0.001091) = 0.123909/0.391359 = 0.3166.
    4. \n
  4. Masses: mg = x m = 0.3166 × 4 kg = 1.266 kg of vapour; mf = 4 − 1.266 = 2.734 kg of liquid.
    5. \n
  5. Specific internal energy: u = uf + x(ug − uf) = 631.66 + 0.3166 × (2559.1 − 631.66) kJ/kg = 631.66 + 0.3166 × 1927.44 = 1241.9 kJ/kg. (For reference h = 632.18 + 0.3166 × (2745.9 − 632.18) = 1301.4 kJ/kg.)
    6. \n
  6. Total internal energy: U = m u = 4 kg × 1241.9 kJ/kg = 4968 kJ.
    7. \n
  7. Liquid volume: Vf = mf vf = 2.734 kg × 0.001091 m³/kg = 0.00298 m³, about 3 litres; the vapour takes 1.266 kg × 0.39245 m³/kg = 0.4970 m³. Together 0.4999 m³ ≈ 0.5 m³, which checks.
    8. \n
  8. Sanity check: 68 % of the mass is liquid but it fills only 0.6 % of the tank; the tank looks almost empty with a puddle at the bottom, exactly what a 32 %-quality mixture should look like. u lies between uf and ug, as any mixture property must.
    9. \n
\n\n

Worked example B: R-134a that turns out to be superheated

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A 0.24 m³ tank holds 2 kg of refrigerant-134a at 200 kPa. Find the phase, the temperature and the enthalpy. Source: saturated R-134a by pressure and superheated R-134a (the layout of Cengel & Boles Tables A-12 and A-13), values computed with CoolProp using the −40 °C reference. Saturated at 200 kPa: Tsat = −10.08 °C, vf = 0.0007534 m³/kg, vg = 0.099877 m³/kg, hg = 244.47 kJ/kg. Superheated at 0.20 MPa: 30 °C, v = 0.118737 m³/kg, h = 278.89 kJ/kg; 40 °C, v = 0.123226 m³/kg, h = 287.72 kJ/kg.

\n
    \n
  1. Specific volume: v = 0.24 m³ / 2 kg = 0.120 m³/kg.
    2. \n
  2. Phase test: 0.120 > vg = 0.099877 m³/kg, so the refrigerant is superheated vapour. Quality is meaningless here; if you tried x = v/vg you would get 1.20, which is the signal that you are outside the dome.
    3. \n
  3. Find the row. In the 0.20 MPa superheated block, v = 0.120 falls between 30 °C (0.118737) and 40 °C (0.123226). Interpolation fraction f = (0.120 − 0.118737)/(0.123226 − 0.118737) = 0.001263/0.004489 = 0.2814.
    4. \n
  4. Temperature: T = 30 + 0.2814 × (40 − 30) = 32.8 °C.
    5. \n
  5. Enthalpy: h = 278.89 + 0.2814 × (287.72 − 278.89) kJ/kg = 278.89 + 0.2814 × 8.83 = 281.4 kJ/kg.
    6. \n
  6. Sanity check: the equation of state evaluated directly at v = 0.120 m³/kg gives T = 32.80 °C and h = 281.35 kJ/kg, so linear interpolation over a 10 °C step is good to about 0.03 kJ/kg. h is above hg = 244.47 kJ/kg, as superheated vapour must be, and the refrigerant is 43 °C above its saturation temperature, consistent with warm vapour at low pressure.
    7. \n
\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Writing v = x vg instead of v = vf + x vfg. For specific volume the error is small because vf is tiny (at 200 kPa, vf = 0.001061 and vg = 0.88568 m³/kg, and x = 0.4: 0.3549 versus 0.3543 m³/kg), which is why the habit survives, but for u, h and s the liquid part is large: at 150 °C and x = 0.25 the correct h = 632.18 + 0.25 × 2113.7 = 1160.6 kJ/kg, while 0.25 × hg = 0.25 × 2745.9 = 686.5 kJ/kg is 41 % too low. Always start from the f value.

Reading the wrong saturation row. Given a pressure, use the by-pressure table; given a temperature, the by-temperature table. Mixing them up (looking up \"200 kPa\" in the temperature table at 200 °C) gives numbers that are off by a factor of ten and still look plausible.

\n
    \n
  • A quality above 1 or below 0 is not an answer; it means the state is outside the dome and you must switch tables.
    • \n
  • Interpolate on the property you were given, then use the same fraction f for every other column. Do not interpolate T from v and then re-interpolate h from T with a fresh fraction; it is the same f.
    • \n
  • Units: v in m³/kg, u and h in kJ/kg, s in kJ/kg-K, P in kPa when multiplying P × v to get kJ/kg (kPa × m³/kg = kJ/kg).
    • \n
  • Compressed-liquid enthalpy at high pressure: at 20 MPa and 80 °C the exact h is 350.90 kJ/kg, hf(80 °C) = 335.01 kJ/kg is 15.9 kJ/kg low, and hf + vf(P − Psat) = 335.01 + 0.001029 × (20000 − 47.41) = 355.54 kJ/kg is 4.6 kJ/kg high. Use Table A-7 when it has your pressure. At 500 kPa the correction term is only 0.001029 × (500 − 47.41) = 0.47 kJ/kg and can be ignored.
    • \n
\n
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Table interpolation is exactly numpy.interp(x, xp, fp), and a superheated block is a tidy DataFrame indexed by (P, T). Loading the tables once as CSV and writing a five-line function state(P=..., T=...) that applies the decision tree above removes every transcription error, and the free CoolProp library (PropsSI('H','P',200e3,'T',305.95,'R134a')) gives the same numbers the tables were generated from. Use the code to check your hand look-ups, not to replace learning them: the exam is on paper.

Mind the reference state when you compare code with a book: CoolProp's default R-134a reference (h = 200 kJ/kg, s = 1 kJ/kg-K for saturated liquid at 0 °C) differs from the textbook's (h = s = 0 for saturated liquid at −40 °C); in Python, CoolProp.CoolProp.set_reference_state('R134a', 'ASHRAE') switches to the textbook convention; differences of properties agree, single values do not.

\n\n
✅ VERIFIED

The R-134a reference state (hf = 0 and sf = 0 for saturated liquid at −40 °C, Psat = 51.25 kPa) was checked against a posted copy of Cengel & Boles Table A-11: property tables and charts, Table A-11 (Université de Batna 2). The water and R-134a numbers in the two worked examples were computed with CoolProp 8.0 (coolprop.org), and every interpolation was checked against a direct evaluation of the equation of state.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

The standard question is a partly filled table of states (\"complete the table: P, T, v, phase description\") with four or five rows, each needing a different branch of the decision tree: one compressed liquid, one mixture given x, one mixture given v, one superheated needing interpolation. A second favourite is a rigid tank or piston-cylinder with a mass and a volume, exactly like Example A, sometimes followed by heating to a new state.

Write the phase test explicitly (\"vf < v < vg, therefore mixture\") before any number; markers award the method mark for it, and it is what stops you applying the quality formula to superheated vapour.

"}, "THERMO/props/s3": {"body": "

This lesson lets you use the ideal-gas equation of state correctly (right R, absolute T, absolute P), decide when a real gas, including water vapour, may be treated as ideal, correct it with the compressibility factor Z and the generalised chart when it may not, and use the van der Waals equation as the first step beyond ideal. Air, combustion gases and the working fluid of every gas cycle in later chapters are modelled this way, so this is the equation you will write more than any other.

\n\n

The equation of state in plain words

\n

An equation of state is any relation among P, v and T of a substance. The steam tables are one, in tabular form. For gases at low density the molecules are far apart, they interact only in brief collisions, and a single simple relation works for all of them: pressure times volume is proportional to absolute temperature and to the amount of gas. That is the ideal-gas model. \"Ideal\" describes the model, not the gas; nitrogen at 300 K and 1 atm obeys it to within 0.02 % (Z = 0.9998), while steam in a boiler can be 20 % off.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

An ideal gas is a gas whose P, v and T satisfy Pv = RT. Its internal energy and enthalpy then depend on temperature only (the energy chapter used this: du = cv dT, dh = cp dT).

The compressibility factor Z = Pv/(RT) measures the departure from ideal behaviour: Z = 1 for an ideal gas; Z < 1 means the gas is denser than ideal (attraction between molecules wins), Z > 1 means less dense (molecular volume wins).

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

P v = R T, equivalently P V = m R T, P V = N Ru T, P = ρ R T

P = absolute pressure (kPa); v = specific volume (m³/kg); V = volume (m³); m = mass (kg); T = absolute temperature (K); ρ = 1/v = density (kg/m³); N = number of kilomoles (kmol); Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol-K, the universal gas constant, the same for every gas; R = Ru/M, the specific gas constant (kJ/kg-K), with M the molar mass (kg/kmol), different for every gas. With P in kPa, V in m³ and R in kJ/kg-K the units close: kPa × m³ = kJ.

Between two states of a fixed mass: P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2.

Real gas: P v = Z R T, with Z read from the generalised compressibility chart at the reduced temperature TR = T/Tcr and reduced pressure PR = P/Pcr.

\n

Specific gas constants from R = 8.314/M, molar masses from Cengel & Boles Table A-1: air (M = 28.97) 0.2870, nitrogen (28.013) 0.2968, oxygen (31.999) 0.2598, carbon dioxide (44.01) 0.1889, water vapour (18.015) 0.4615, helium (4.003) 2.0769, hydrogen (2.016) 4.124 kJ/kg-K. Light gases have large R: a kilogram of helium contains seven times as many molecules as a kilogram of air and exerts seven times the pressure in the same tank at the same temperature.

\n\n

Is water vapour an ideal gas?

\n

Sometimes. The ideal-gas model works when the molecules are far apart relative to their size, which means low pressure compared with Pcr or high temperature compared with Tcr. Water has Tcr = 647.1 K and Pcr = 22.06 MPa, so at engineering pressures steam is often near saturation and not ideal. The table below is the ideal-gas v = RT/P (R = 0.4615 kJ/kg-K) against the steam-table v (IAPWS-95, computed with CoolProp):

📊 FIGURE — How far steam departs from Pv = RT at seven states
Each dot is Z for steam; the stem shows the gap to Z = 1 (ideal). Low pressure stays in the green band; near saturation or near the critical point the ideal-gas v is 6 to 26 % too high.
\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
Statev, steam table (m³/kg)v, ideal gas (m³/kg)Error of ideal gasZ
10 kPa, 50 °C14.867014.9134+0.31 %0.997
100 kPa, 150 °C1.93671.9528+0.84 %0.992
1 MPa, 200 °C0.206020.21836+6.0 %0.944
1 MPa, 300 °C0.257990.26451+2.5 %0.975
10 MPa, 400 °C0.026440.03107+17.5 %0.851
20 MPa, 500 °C0.014790.01784+20.6 %0.829
\n

The working rule from the table: below 10 kPa water vapour may be treated as an ideal gas regardless of temperature (even saturated vapour, the worst case, has Z = 0.9966 at 10 kPa and Z = 0.9993 at 1 kPa, errors of 0.3 % and under 0.1 %), which covers atmospheric humidity and air-conditioning, so the psychrometrics chapter will use Pv = RT for the vapour in air without apology. At higher pressures, use the tables unless the state is far above saturation; at 1 MPa the error falls from 6 % at 200 °C (only 20 °C above Tsat = 179.88 °C) to 2.5 % at 300 °C. Closer to the critical point the model gets worse fast: saturated vapour at 5 MPa (263.94 °C) has Z = 0.796, a 26 % error in v.

\n\n

The compressibility factor and the generalised chart

\n

The remarkable fact behind the chart is the principle of corresponding states: gases at the same reduced temperature TR and reduced pressure PR have very nearly the same Z, whatever the gas. Plotting Z against PR for lines of constant TR, measured for many gases, gives one chart (the Nelson-Obert generalised compressibility chart in most textbooks, Cengel & Boles Figure A-15) that works for all of them to within a few percent. Read it with three rules:

\n
    \n
  • At very low PR (roughly below 0.05) Z ≈ 1 whatever the temperature: every gas is ideal when dilute.
    • \n
  • At high TR (above about 2) Z ≈ 1 up to several times the critical pressure: hot gases stay ideal even when compressed. Nitrogen at 300 K has TR = 2.38, which is why air behaves ideally in every ordinary situation.
    • \n
  • Near the critical point (TR ≈ 1, PR ≈ 1) Z drops far below 1, to around 0.3 at the critical point itself, and the ideal-gas law can be wrong by a factor of three or more.
    • \n
\n

When P and v are known but not T (or v and T but not P), the chart cannot be entered from TR and PR directly; use the pseudo-reduced specific volume vR = v/(R Tcr/Pcr), which is drawn as a third family of lines on the chart. Note the definition uses R Tcr/Pcr, not the true critical volume, so that it can be computed from Table A-1 alone.

\n\n

Worked example: a nitrogen tank, then steam, then carbon dioxide

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Part 1. A 0.5 m³ tank holds nitrogen at 2 MPa and 300 K. Find the mass, and check whether the ideal-gas model is justified. Critical properties from Cengel & Boles Table A-1: Tcr = 126.2 K, Pcr = 3.39 MPa, M = 28.013 kg/kmol.

\n
    \n
  1. Gas constant: R = Ru/M = 8.314 kJ/kmol-K / 28.013 kg/kmol = 0.2968 kJ/kg-K.
    2. \n
  2. Absolute units: P = 2000 kPa (already absolute), T = 300 K (already absolute). Nothing to convert, but write it down; the classic error is using 27 °C.
    3. \n
  3. Mass: m = PV/(RT) = 2000 kPa × 0.5 m³ / (0.2968 kJ/kg-K × 300 K) = 1000 kJ / 89.04 kJ/kg = 11.23 kg.
    4. \n
  4. Is it ideal? TR = 300/126.2 = 2.377, PR = 2/3.39 = 0.590. The chart at TR ≈ 2.4 and PR ≈ 0.6 reads Z ≈ 1.00; the nitrogen equation of state (CoolProp) gives Z = 0.9972 and m = 11.23 kg / 0.9972 = 11.26 kg. The ideal-gas answer is within 0.3 %: justified.
    5. \n
\n

Part 2. Steam at 10 MPa and 400 °C: compare the ideal-gas specific volume with the table and with the chart. Tcr = 647.1 K, Pcr = 22.06 MPa, R = 0.4615 kJ/kg-K.

\n
    \n
  1. Ideal gas: v = RT/P = 0.4615 kJ/kg-K × 673.15 K / 10000 kPa = 0.03107 m³/kg.
    2. \n
  2. Steam table (superheated, 10 MPa, 400 °C): v = 0.02644 m³/kg. The ideal-gas value is high by (0.03107 − 0.02644)/0.02644 = 17.5 %.
    3. \n
  3. Chart: TR = 673.15/647.1 = 1.040, PR = 10/22.06 = 0.453. The true Z = Pv/(RT) = 0.02644/0.03107 = 0.851, and v = Z RT/P = 0.851 × 0.03107 = 0.02644 m³/kg recovers the table. On an exam you would read Z off the chart at TR = 1.04, PR = 0.45 instead; the chart is built from simple non-polar gases, so for a polar molecule such as water treat its reading as approximate and prefer the steam table whenever you have it.
    4. \n
\n

Part 3. Carbon dioxide in a 0.1 m³ cylinder at 5 MPa and 300 K (Tcr = 304.2 K, Pcr = 7.39 MPa, M = 44.01): how much mass is really inside?

\n
    \n
  1. R: 8.314/44.01 = 0.1889 kJ/kg-K.
    2. \n
  2. Ideal gas: m = 5000 kPa × 0.1 m³ / (0.1889 kJ/kg-K × 300 K) = 500 / 56.67 = 8.82 kg.
    3. \n
  3. Reduced state: TR = 300/304.2 = 0.986, PR = 5/7.39 = 0.677: just below the critical temperature and two-thirds of the critical pressure, the worst region for the ideal-gas model. The CO2 equation of state (CoolProp) gives Z = 0.687. (It is still a vapour: Psat of CO2 at 300 K is 6.71 MPa.)
    4. \n
  4. Real mass: m = PV/(Z R T) = 8.82 kg / 0.687 = 12.84 kg. The ideal-gas law under-counts the gas by 31 %: a CO2 cylinder holds far more than the ideal gas law says, and a tank sized by Pv = RT would be under-designed.
    5. \n
  5. Sanity check: all three Z values are below 1 and the nearer the state to the critical point, the lower Z (0.997, 0.851, 0.687), which is the pattern the chart shows. Nitrogen far above Tcr is ideal; CO2 at room temperature is not, because room temperature is CO2's critical temperature.
    6. \n
\n\n

Van der Waals and the other equations of state

\n

The van der Waals equation adds two corrections to Pv = RT: the molecules occupy volume b themselves, so only v − b is free, and they attract one another, which lowers the pressure at the wall by a/v²:

\n

(P + a/v²)(v − b) = R T

\n

P = pressure (kPa); v = specific volume (m³/kg) or molar volume (m³/kmol); a, b = constants for the gas, a in kPa·m⁶/kg² (or kPa·m⁶/kmol²) and b in m³/kg (or m³/kmol). They are fixed by requiring the critical isotherm to have an inflection at the critical point, which gives

\n

a = 27 R² Tcr² / (64 Pcr), b = R Tcr / (8 Pcr)

\n

On a molar basis with Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol-K: for nitrogen a = 27 × 8.314² × 126.2² / (64 × 3390) = 137.0 kPa·m⁶/kmol² and b = 8.314 × 126.2 / (8 × 3390) = 0.03869 m³/kmol; for carbon dioxide a = 365.2 kPa·m⁶/kmol² and b = 0.04278 m³/kmol. Applied to the nitrogen of Part 1 (the real molar volume from the nitrogen equation of state is v̄ = 0.044398 m³/kg × 28.013 kg/kmol = 1.2437 m³/kmol at 300 K): ideal gas gives P = 8.314 × 300 / 1.2437 = 2005.4 kPa, van der Waals gives P = 8.314 × 300 / (1.2437 − 0.03869) − 137.0 / 1.2437² = 2069.8 − 88.6 = 1981.2 kPa, against the true 2000 kPa. Both are within 1 % here, as they should be at TR = 2.4. For CO2 at 3 MPa and 350 K (real v̄ = 0.8819 m³/kmol) the ideal gas gives 8.314 × 350 / 0.8819 = 3299 kPa, 10 % high, while van der Waals gives 2998 kPa, essentially exact: the correction earns its keep near Tcr.

\n

Van der Waals is qualitatively right (it predicts a critical point and a dome) but only moderately accurate, and its predicted Zcr = 3/8 = 0.375 is higher than real gases show (water: 22 064 kPa × 0.003106 m³/kg / (0.4615 kJ/kg-K × 647.1 K) = 0.229). More accurate equations with more constants are the Beattie-Bridgeman (five constants), the Benedict-Webb-Rubin (eight constants) and the virial equation, a power series in 1/v whose coefficients can be linked to the forces between molecules. The steam tables and the CoolProp values in this chapter come from modern multi-parameter equations of the same family with dozens of terms; you are never asked to evaluate those by hand, but you should be able to say why they exist.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Celsius or gauge pressure in Pv = RT. The mass of the nitrogen above with T = 27 (°C) instead of 300 K comes out as 124.8 kg, eleven times too big. A tyre at 220 kPa gauge on a 100 kPa day is at 320 kPa absolute; using 220 kPa gives 69 % of the true mass. The only place Celsius survives is in a temperature difference, and P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2 is not a difference: heating a rigid tank from 27 °C to 327 °C doubles the pressure (600/300), it does not multiply it by 327/27 = 12.1.

Using Ru = 8.314 with mass in kg. Ru goes with kilomoles; with kilograms you need R = Ru/M. The density of air at 100 kPa and 27 °C is 100/(0.287 × 300.15) = 1.161 kg/m³; with 8.314 it would come out as 0.040 kg/m³, which should look absurd for air.

\n
    \n
  • Z is not a property of the gas alone; it depends on the state. \"Z for nitrogen\" means nothing without T and P.
    • \n
  • Water vapour in air at atmospheric humidity (partial pressure of a few kPa) is an ideal gas; steam in a boiler at several MPa is not. Same molecule, different state.
    • \n
  • Do not use the ideal-gas u = cv ΔT for steam near saturation; that is the tables' job.
    • \n
  • Reduced properties use absolute Tcr in kelvin and absolute Pcr; TR = 27/373.95 is meaningless.
    • \n
\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

Three question shapes: (1) a straight Pv = RT calculation (mass in a tank, pressure after heating, volume of a balloon) where the marks are for absolute units and the correct R; (2) \"can this be treated as an ideal gas?\", answered with TR and PR and a chart reading, often for steam so that you can compare with the tables; (3) evaluate the van der Waals or another equation of state at a given v and T and compare its pressure with the ideal gas and the table.

Write R = Ru/M with the molar mass shown, convert T and P to absolute values on their own line, and quote the percentage error when you compare models: markers look for those three lines.

"}, "THERMO/cv/s1": {"body": "

This lesson lets you take any pipe, duct, nozzle or turbine and write down how much mass passes through it each second and how much energy that mass carries with it. It is the hinge of the whole degree: the previous chapter closed the first law for a fixed lump of matter (a piston-cylinder), and from here on almost every device you will meet (turbines, compressors, boilers, condensers, air-conditioners, jet engines) is a region of space that fluid flows through. Get mass flow rate, the mass balance and flow work right and the steady-flow energy equation of the next lesson is one line of algebra.

\n\n

From a closed system to a control volume

\n

A closed system has a fixed identity: the same molecules stay inside the boundary while it moves, heats or expands. A control volume (CV) is the opposite idea. You draw a boundary (the control surface) around a region of space, often the metal casing of a device, and let matter stream in and out across it. The boundary may be rigid (a turbine casing) or moving (the inside of a balloon being inflated); it may have one inlet and one exit (a nozzle) or several (a mixing chamber). The price of this freedom is one extra piece of bookkeeping: mass now crosses the boundary, and every kilogram that crosses carries energy with it. So a control-volume analysis always has two balances, a mass balance and an energy balance, where the closed system had only one.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Control volume: a chosen region of space through which mass may flow. Its boundary is the control surface. Mass, heat and work can all cross the control surface.

Steady-flow process: a process in which no property inside the control volume changes with time. The fluid properties at a given point may differ from point to point, but at any one point they are constant in time; consequently the mass inside the CV, the energy inside it and the flow rates across the surface are all constant.

\n\n

Mass flow rate and volume flow rate

\n

Picture fluid moving through a pipe of cross-sectional area A at average speed V. In one second a slab of fluid of length V metres and area A square metres passes any chosen plane; its volume is A·V cubic metres and its mass is that volume times the density. That single sentence is the whole of the mass-flow-rate formula.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

V̇ = A · V (volume flow rate, m³/s)

ṁ = ρ · A · V = ρ · V̇ = V̇ / v (mass flow rate, kg/s)

Symbols: ṁ mass flow rate in kg/s; ρ density in kg/m³; v = 1/ρ specific volume in m³/kg; A flow area normal to the velocity in m²; V average velocity in m/s; V̇ volume flow rate in m³/s. The dot always means \"per unit time\".

\n

Two remarks. First, the velocity in a real pipe is not uniform (zero at the wall, fastest in the middle); V in the formula is the average velocity over the cross-section, defined precisely so that A·V equals the true volume flow rate. Second, for a liquid ρ is nearly constant so volume flow rate and mass flow rate are interchangeable; for a gas ρ changes strongly with pressure and temperature, so a compressor delivers the same mass per second at inlet and outlet but a much smaller volume per second at the high-pressure outlet. Mass is conserved; volume is not. If you need v for a gas, the ideal-gas relation v = R·T/P gives it (for air R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K); for steam or refrigerant, read it from the tables.

\n\n

The mass balance

\n

The conservation-of-mass principle for a control volume says: the rate at which mass accumulates inside equals the rate at which it enters minus the rate at which it leaves.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

dmCV/dt = Σ ṁin − Σ ṁout (general, kg/s)

Σ ṁin = Σ ṁout (steady flow: nothing accumulates)

ρ1 A1 V1 = ρ2 A2 V2 (steady flow, one inlet 1 and one exit 2)

A1 V1 = A2 V2 (steady and incompressible: ρ constant). mCV is the mass inside the control volume in kg; the sums run over every inlet and every exit.

\n

The last line is why water leaving a garden hose speeds up when you squeeze the end: the same volume per second must pass a smaller area. For the unsteady case (a tank filling up, lesson 4) the left-hand side is not zero and you integrate over the process: m2 − m1 = Σ min − Σ mout, with total masses in kg instead of rates.

\n\n

Flow work and the enthalpy shortcut

\n

Here is the idea that students most often accept without understanding, so slow down. For fluid to enter a control volume, something behind it has to push it in against the pressure at the inlet. Imagine a fluid element of volume v (per kilogram) just outside the inlet, in a pipe of area A, so its length is L = v/A. The fluid behind it presses on it with force F = P·A. To shove the element fully across the control surface the force acts through the distance L, doing work F·L = P·A·(v/A) = P·v. This is the flow work (or flow energy), and it is done on every kilogram that enters. At the exit the control volume must do the same amount of work, P·v evaluated at exit conditions, to push each kilogram out. It is not work you can harvest with a shaft; it is the toll charged for crossing the boundary.

📊 FIGURE — A control volume, with the flow work paid to push mass across it
Fluid behind the element pushes with force P·A through length v/A, doing P·v per kg to get it inside. Add that to u and you get h, which is why h, not u, rides with every stream.
\n
📘 DEFINITION

Flow work wflow = P·v (kJ/kg): the work required to push a unit mass of fluid into or out of a control volume against the local pressure. P is absolute pressure in kPa and v specific volume in m³/kg; the product kPa·m³/kg is exactly kJ/kg.

Enthalpy h = u + P·v exists precisely so that the internal energy the mass carries and the flow work needed to move it can be added in one symbol. Whenever mass crosses a control surface, h appears, not u.

\n

A flowing kilogram therefore carries three things across the boundary: its internal energy u, the flow work P·v that was done to move it, and its mechanical energies (kinetic and potential). Combining the first two into enthalpy gives the total energy of a flowing fluid, which the textbooks write as θ (theta):

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

θ = h + V²/2 + g·z (energy carried per kg of flowing fluid, kJ/kg)

Ėmass = ṁ · θ = ṁ · (h + V²/2 + g·z) (rate of energy transport by a stream, kW)

h specific enthalpy in kJ/kg; V velocity in m/s; g = 9.81 m/s²; z elevation in m. Because h is in kJ/kg but V²/2 and g·z come out in J/kg, divide those two terms by 1000 before adding.

\n

Compare with the closed-system energy per kilogram, e = u + V²/2 + g·z. The only change is u → h, and the reason is flow work. This single substitution is why the tables list h for every state: open systems are the common case in engineering.

\n\n

Worked example: a water pipe and a steam line

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Part A. Liquid water at 20 °C flows steadily through a 5.0 cm inside-diameter pipe at an average velocity of 3.0 m/s and leaves through a nozzle whose exit diameter is 2.0 cm. Find the volume flow rate, the mass flow rate and the exit velocity. Property source: saturated water, temperature table (Cengel & Boles Table A-4), vf at 20 °C = 0.001002 m³/kg, taken as the specific volume of the compressed liquid.

  1. Inlet area: A1 = π·D1²/4 = π·(0.050 m)²/4 = 1.963 × 10−3 m².
  2. Volume flow rate: V̇ = A1·V1 = 1.963 × 10−3 m² × 3.0 m/s = 5.890 × 10−3 m³/s = 5.89 L/s.
  3. Density: ρ = 1/vf = 1/0.001002 m³/kg = 998.0 kg/m³.
  4. Mass flow rate: ṁ = V̇/v = 5.890 × 10−3 m³/s ÷ 0.001002 m³/kg = 5.88 kg/s (about 21 tonnes per hour).
  5. Exit area: A2 = π·(0.020 m)²/4 = 3.142 × 10−4 m².
  6. Incompressible steady flow, so A1V1 = A2V2: V2 = V̇/A2 = 5.890 × 10−3 m³/s ÷ 3.142 × 10−4 m² = 18.8 m/s.
  7. Sanity check: the diameter fell by a factor 2.5, so the area fell by 2.5² = 6.25 and the velocity should rise by 6.25: 3.0 × 6.25 = 18.75 m/s. Agrees.
\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Part B. Superheated steam at 1 MPa and 300 °C flows through a 10 cm diameter line at 40 m/s. Find the mass flow rate, the flow work per kilogram, the total energy carried per kilogram and the rate of energy transport. Property source: superheated water table (Cengel & Boles Table A-6) at 1 MPa, 300 °C: v = 0.25799 m³/kg, u = 2793.7 kJ/kg, h = 3051.6 kJ/kg.

  1. Area: A = π·(0.10 m)²/4 = 7.854 × 10−3 m².
