  2. Mass flow rate: ṁ = A·V/v = 7.854 × 10−3 m² × 40 m/s ÷ 0.25799 m³/kg = 1.218 kg/s. (Notice that the same pipe carried 5.88 kg/s of water at only 3 m/s; steam at this state is about 260 times less dense than the water, since 0.25799/0.001002 = 257.)
  3. Flow work: P·v = 1000 kPa × 0.25799 m³/kg = 258.0 kJ/kg. Check against the table: h − u = 3051.6 − 2793.7 = 257.9 kJ/kg. Same number to rounding, which is exactly what h = u + Pv promises.
  4. Kinetic energy: V²/2 = (40 m/s)²/2 = 800 J/kg = 0.80 kJ/kg.
  5. Energy per kilogram (horizontal pipe, so g·z drops): θ = h + V²/2 = 3051.6 + 0.8 = 3052.4 kJ/kg.
  6. Rate of energy transport: Ė = ṁ·θ = 1.218 kg/s × 3052.4 kJ/kg = 3717 kW ≈ 3.72 MW.
  7. Sanity check: kinetic energy is 0.8/3052 = 0.03 % of the total. At 40 m/s it is negligible, which is why textbooks drop it for turbines and heat exchangers; it becomes important only above roughly 100 m/s, i.e. in nozzles and diffusers.
\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Mixing J and kJ. V²/2 with V in m/s gives J/kg; the tables give h in kJ/kg. Divide the kinetic and potential terms by 1000. Forgetting this makes a 40 m/s stream look 800 kJ/kg richer than it is, larger than the enthalpy of most liquids.
  • Gauge pressure in Pv. Flow work uses absolute pressure. A gauge reading of 400 kPa at sea level means 501 kPa absolute.
  • Diameter for radius. A = πD²/4, not πD². The factor of 4 is the single most common arithmetic slip on this topic.
  • Volume flow rate treated as conserved. Through a compressor or a heater the mass flow rate is the same at inlet and exit; the volume flow rate is not, because v changes. Always convert to ṁ before balancing.
  • Using u instead of h for a flowing stream. The stream carries h. Keep u for the mass sitting inside a tank.
\n
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Plant data comes as a time series of velocities, pressures and temperatures, never as mass flow rates. Turning a sensor log into ṁ is a two-line pandas job: compute v = R·T/P (gas) or look up vf (liquid), then mdot = A*V/v. Keep a column for every intermediate quantity with its unit in the column name (v_m3_per_kg, mdot_kg_per_s); the J-versus-kJ error is far easier to catch when the unit is in the name.

A steady-flow check is also a data-quality check: if Σ ṁin − Σ ṁout over a plant drifts away from zero, either a sensor is miscalibrated or there is a leak. Mass balances are the oldest anomaly detector in engineering.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM
  • Given diameter, velocity and a state, find ṁ (needs v from the tables or the ideal-gas law, and πD²/4).
  • Given ṁ at one section, find the velocity or the diameter at another section where the state is different (steady mass balance with two different v values).
  • Explain in words why enthalpy rather than internal energy appears in the energy balance of a control volume (the flow-work argument above, in two sentences).
  • Compute the energy transported by a stream and state which of h, V²/2 and gz matter (for typical pipe speeds and heights, only h).
  • Distinguish steady flow (properties inside constant in time) from uniform flow (properties constant across a section), and know that steady does not mean the properties are the same at inlet and exit.
"}, "THERMO/cv/s2": {"body": "

This lesson gives you the one equation that solves nearly every device question in the rest of the degree, the steady-flow energy equation, and then shows how each of the classic devices (nozzle, diffuser, turbine, compressor, throttling valve) is just that equation with two or three terms crossed out. Power cycles, refrigeration, jet propulsion and compressible flow are all built from these five building blocks, so the habit you form here, \"write the full equation, then justify each term you drop\", is worth more than any individual answer.

\n\n

The steady-flow energy equation

\n

Take the general energy balance for a control volume, rate of energy in minus rate out equals rate of change inside, and impose steady flow, so the inside does not change with time. Energy crosses the surface in three ways: as heat Q̇, as work Ẇ, and carried by mass at the rate ṁ·θ found in lesson 1. The result is the steady-flow energy equation (SFEE).

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Q̇ − Ẇ = Σ ṁout·(h + V²/2 + g·z)out − Σ ṁin·(h + V²/2 + g·z)in (kW, any number of streams)

q − w = (h2 − h1) + (V2² − V1²)/2 + g·(z2 − z1) (kJ/kg, one inlet 1, one exit 2, divide by ṁ)

Q̇ net rate of heat transfer into the CV in kW; Ẇ net rate of work done by the CV (shaft or electrical work; flow work is already inside h) in kW; q = Q̇/ṁ and w = Ẇ/ṁ in kJ/kg; subscripts 1 and 2 are inlet and exit. Kinetic and potential terms are in J/kg until divided by 1000.

\n

The sign convention is the same as for closed systems: heat in is positive, work out is positive. A turbine has positive w, a compressor negative w (or, as most people write it, a positive win on the left-hand side). Notice what is missing compared to the closed-system first law: there is no ΔU of the system, because in steady flow nothing inside changes; the energy change belongs to the fluid passing through, and it is written with h.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Steady-flow device: a device that operates for long periods under the same conditions, so that the mass and energy inside it and the properties at every point are constant in time. Turbines, compressors, pumps, nozzles, diffusers, heat exchangers and throttling valves are all modelled this way once they have warmed up.

Adiabatic device: one with negligible heat transfer (Q̇ ≈ 0), either because it is insulated or because the fluid passes through too quickly for much heat to cross the casing. Nozzles, diffusers, throttling valves and (usually) turbines and compressors are treated as adiabatic unless a heat loss is stated.

\n\n

The five devices and what each one drops

\n

Every device question is the SFEE with a set of justified simplifications. Learn the reasons, not just the crossings-out.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
DevicePurposewqΔKEΔPEReduced equation
NozzleRaise velocity, drop pressure0 (no shaft)≈0 (fast flow)the whole point0h1 + V1²/2 = h2 + V2²/2
DiffuserSlow the flow, raise pressure0≈0the whole point0same as nozzle
TurbineProduce shaft workwout > 0≈0 unless statedsmall unless V given0wout = h1 − h2
Compressor / pumpRaise pressure using workwin > 0≈0 unless cooledusually 00win = h2 − h1
Throttling valveDrop pressure with no work0≈0 (small device)≈0 (V roughly equal)0h2 = h1
\n

The nozzle and diffuser are the only devices where the kinetic-energy term is the answer rather than a nuisance; that is why nozzle velocities are hundreds of metres per second while turbine inlet speeds are tens. The throttling valve is the odd one out: it is a deliberately irreversible pressure drop (a partially closed valve, a porous plug, a capillary tube) whose only thermodynamic content is that enthalpy is conserved across it, an isenthalpic process. For an ideal gas h depends on temperature alone, so throttling an ideal gas leaves its temperature unchanged; for a real fluid, and above all for a refrigerant that enters as a liquid, a large temperature drop occurs, which is precisely how every household refrigerator makes cold.

\n\n

Worked example 1: an air diffuser

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Air at 80 kPa and 10 °C enters the diffuser of a jet engine steadily at 200 m/s through an inlet area of 0.40 m². The air leaves the diffuser at a velocity that is negligible compared with the inlet velocity. Find the mass flow rate and the exit temperature. Property source: air as an ideal gas with R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K and cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K (constant, near-room-temperature value).

  1. Inlet specific volume: v1 = R·T1/P1 = 0.287 kJ/kg·K × 283.15 K ÷ 80 kPa = 1.016 m³/kg. (Temperature in kelvin: 10 + 273.15.)
  2. Mass flow rate: ṁ = A1·V1/v1 = 0.40 m² × 200 m/s ÷ 1.016 m³/kg = 78.8 kg/s.
  3. Energy balance for a diffuser (q = 0, w = 0, ΔPE = 0): h2 − h1 = (V1² − V2²)/2. With V2 ≈ 0: h2 − h1 = (200 m/s)²/2 = 20 000 J/kg = 20.0 kJ/kg.
  4. Ideal gas with constant cp: ΔT = Δh/cp = 20.0 kJ/kg ÷ 1.005 kJ/kg·K = 19.9 K.
  5. Exit temperature: T2 = 283.15 K + 19.9 K = 303.05 K = 29.9 °C.
  6. Sanity check: a diffuser converts kinetic energy into enthalpy, so the air must get warmer, and 20 K for 200 m/s is the right order of magnitude (a jet at 250 m/s cruise sees a ram rise of about 30 K). Had the 1000 been forgotten, the answer would have been 19 900 K, which is absurd on sight.
\n\n

Worked example 2: a steam turbine with everything included

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Steam enters a turbine at 2 MPa and 400 °C with a velocity of 50 m/s at an elevation of 10 m, and leaves at 10 kPa with a quality of 0.90 at 180 m/s and an elevation of 6 m. The turbine loses 8.5 kJ of heat per kilogram of steam to the surroundings. Find the work output per kilogram and the power for a steam flow of 5 kg/s. Property sources: superheated water (Cengel & Boles Table A-6) at 2 MPa, 400 °C: h1 = 3248.4 kJ/kg; saturated water, pressure table (Table A-5) at 10 kPa: hf = 191.81 kJ/kg, hfg = 2392.1 kJ/kg.

📊 FIGURE — A steam turbine with its inlet and exit states and every energy term
Steam enters at state 1 and leaves at state 2. Of the 903.7 kJ/kg enthalpy drop, 880.3 leaves as shaft work; the rest goes to heat loss and to speeding the steam up.
  1. Exit enthalpy from the quality: h2 = hf + x·hfg = 191.81 + 0.90 × 2392.1 = 2344.7 kJ/kg.
  2. Enthalpy change: Δh = 2344.7 − 3248.4 = −903.7 kJ/kg.
  3. Kinetic-energy change: ΔKE = (180² − 50²)/2 = (32 400 − 2 500)/2 = 14 950 J/kg = 14.95 kJ/kg.
  4. Potential-energy change: ΔPE = 9.81 m/s² × (6 − 10) m = −39.2 J/kg = −0.039 kJ/kg.
  5. Heat transfer: the steam loses heat, so q = −8.5 kJ/kg.
  6. SFEE per kg, q − w = Δh + ΔKE + ΔPE, so w = q − Δh − ΔKE − ΔPE = −8.5 − (−903.7) − 14.95 − (−0.039) = 880.3 kJ/kg.
  7. Power: Ẇ = ṁ·w = 5 kg/s × 880.3 kJ/kg = 4401 kW ≈ 4.40 MW.
  8. Sanity check and lesson: of the 903.7 kJ/kg drop in enthalpy, 8.5 went out as heat (0.9 %), 14.95 went into speeding the steam up (1.7 %), 0.04 into elevation (0.004 %). Ignoring everything but Δh would give 903.7 kJ/kg, 2.7 % high. On an exam, if velocities and heights are not given, drop them and say so; if they are given, include them, because the examiner put them there.
\n\n

Worked example 3: throttling a refrigerant

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Refrigerant-134a enters the capillary tube of a refrigerator as saturated liquid at 0.8 MPa and is throttled to 0.12 MPa. Find the quality and the temperature drop. Property source: saturated R-134a, pressure table (Cengel & Boles Table A-12): at 0.8 MPa Tsat = 31.31 °C, hf = 95.47 kJ/kg; at 0.12 MPa Tsat = −22.32 °C, hf = 22.49 kJ/kg, hfg = 214.48 kJ/kg.

  1. Throttling: h2 = h1 = hf at 0.8 MPa = 95.47 kJ/kg.
  2. At 0.12 MPa, hf = 22.49 < 95.47 < hg = 22.49 + 214.48 = 236.97 kJ/kg, so the exit is a saturated mixture and its temperature is Tsat = −22.32 °C.
  3. Quality: x2 = (h2 − hf)/hfg = (95.47 − 22.49)/214.48 = 0.340; 34 % of the mass has flashed to vapour.
  4. Temperature drop: 31.31 − (−22.32) = 53.6 K.
  5. Sanity check: the enthalpy did not change, yet the temperature fell by 54 K. The energy to boil 34 % of the liquid came from cooling the remainder. This is the refrigeration effect, and it is available only because the fluid was a liquid near saturation; throttling an ideal gas would have produced no temperature change at all.
\n
✅ VERIFIED

The saturated-water values at 10 kPa used here (Tsat = 45.81 °C, hf = 191.81 kJ/kg, hfg = 2392.1 kJ/kg, hg = 2583.9 kJ/kg) are the Cengel & Boles Table A-5 entries, reproduced for example at coecs.ou.edu (Table A-5, saturated water by pressure).

The R-134a throttling result (saturated liquid at 0.8 MPa to 0.12 MPa gives x = 0.34 and a 53.6 K drop) matches the same textbook problem as posed at chegg.com (R-134a capillary-tube problem). Other editions and IAPWS/NIST-based tables differ in the third or fourth significant figure; name the table you used in every answer.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Sign of the compressor work. In q − w = Δh, a compressor has w negative. If you write win = h2 − h1 + qout you never see a minus sign and cannot get it backwards.
  • Turbine exit as saturated vapour. If the exit quality is 0.90, use hf + x·hfg, not hg. Using hg at 10 kPa in example 2 would have given 641 kJ/kg instead of 880.
  • Throttling is not isothermal. It is isenthalpic. Only for an ideal gas do the two coincide.
  • cv for cp. Flowing gases change enthalpy, Δh = cp·ΔT. cv belongs to closed rigid tanks. Using 0.718 instead of 1.005 in the diffuser example gives a 27.9 K rise instead of 19.9 K.
  • Celsius in the ideal-gas law. v = RT/P needs kelvin. Differences ΔT are the same in °C and K, which is the only place Celsius is safe.
\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM
  • Nozzle: inlet state and velocity, exit state, find exit velocity (V2 = √(2·(h1 − h2)·1000 + V1²)) and then the exit area from ṁ = A·V/v.
  • Turbine or compressor: inlet and exit states, find w and Ẇ; sometimes with a stated heat loss, sometimes with a required power and an unknown ṁ.
  • Throttling: given the inlet state and exit pressure, find exit temperature and quality (refrigerant) or state that T is unchanged (ideal gas) and explain why.
  • Justify each dropped term in one phrase: \"no shaft so w = 0\", \"insulated so q = 0\", \"velocities not given and typically small, ΔKE neglected\".
  • Write out a states table (state, P, T, h, x) before any arithmetic. Markers give method credit for the table even when the arithmetic slips.
"}, "THERMO/cv/s3": {"body": "

This lesson extends the steady-flow energy equation to devices with more than one stream (mixing chambers and heat exchangers) and to the humble but ubiquitous pipe, duct and pump. These are the devices that connect the glamorous ones: every power plant has a condenser and a feedwater pump, every air-conditioner has an evaporator, every building has ducts that lose heat. The new skill is choosing where to draw the control surface: the same heat exchanger gives you two different, equally correct, energy equations depending on whether the boundary encloses both fluids or only one.

\n\n

Several inlets and exits

\n

Nothing in the SFEE limits you to one stream. With several, the mass balance and the energy balance each become a sum over streams. In steady flow the inside does not change, so whatever enters must leave, in mass and in energy.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Σ ṁin = Σ ṁout (mass, kg/s)

Q̇ − Ẇ = Σ ṁout·hout − Σ ṁin·hin (energy, kW, kinetic and potential terms neglected)

Every stream carries ṁ·h in kW; Q̇ is heat into the CV; Ẇ is shaft or electrical work out of it. With n streams you have one mass equation and one energy equation, so at most two unknowns can be found. If more are unknown, the question has given you a ratio or an extra state.

\n\n

Mixing chambers

\n

A mixing chamber is any device where two or more streams merge into one: a T-junction where hot and cold water meet, the open feedwater heater of a power plant, the point where a spray of water meets a stream of steam. There is no work, heat loss is normally negligible, and the streams are all at (nearly) the same pressure because otherwise the higher-pressure stream would simply flow backwards up the lower-pressure pipe. So the balances become ṁ1 + ṁ2 = ṁ3 and ṁ1h1 + ṁ2h2 = ṁ3h3. The typical exam version gives all three temperatures and asks for the ratio of the two inlet flows.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Mixing chamber: a control volume in which two or more streams combine into one exit stream at a common pressure, with no work and (usually) no heat transfer.

Heat exchanger: a device in which two fluid streams exchange heat without mixing, separated by a wall. Condensers, evaporators, boilers, radiators and feedwater heaters (closed type) are heat exchangers. There is no shaft work and the pressure drop of each stream is usually neglected, so each stream's state is fixed by its temperature (or quality) and the known pressure.

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Hot water at 80 °C is mixed with cold water at 20 °C in a chamber at 250 kPa to produce a stream at 45 °C. Find the ratio of the hot-water to cold-water mass flow rates, and the hot-water flow required if the cold stream is 2.0 kg/s. Property source: saturated water, temperature table (Cengel & Boles Table A-4), taking the enthalpy of the compressed liquid at each temperature as hf at that temperature: hf(80 °C) = 335.02, hf(45 °C) = 188.44, hf(20 °C) = 83.915 kJ/kg. (All three are below the saturation temperature at 250 kPa, 127.4 °C, so each stream is a compressed liquid.)

  1. Mass balance: ṁhot + ṁcold = ṁ3.
  2. Energy balance (Q̇ = 0, Ẇ = 0, ΔKE = ΔPE = 0): ṁhot·hhot + ṁcold·hcold = (ṁhot + ṁcold)·h3.
  3. Gather the hot terms on the left: ṁhot·(hhot − h3) = ṁcold·(h3 − hcold). In words: the enthalpy the hot stream gives up equals the enthalpy the cold stream gains.
  4. Ratio: ṁhot/ṁcold = (h3 − hcold)/(hhot − h3) = (188.44 − 83.915)/(335.02 − 188.44) = 104.53/146.58 = 0.713.
  5. Hot flow: ṁhot = 0.713 × 2.0 kg/s = 1.43 kg/s.
  6. Sanity check: with a constant specific heat the same ratio is just the temperature differences, (45 − 20)/(80 − 45) = 25/35 = 0.714. The table value 0.713 agrees to three figures, which tells you cp of liquid water is very nearly constant over this range and the \"lever rule with temperatures\" is a fine mental check.
\n\n

Heat exchangers: where you draw the boundary

\n

A heat exchanger has two streams that never mix. You can analyse it in two ways, and exams test whether you know when to use which.

📊 FIGURE — One condenser, two control surfaces: steam side and whole unit
Boundary A (blue) wraps only the steam, so the heat through the tube wall crosses it: that gives Q̇. Boundary B wraps both fluids, Q̇ cancels inside it, and the balance gives the water flow.
\n
  • Boundary around the whole exchanger. Both streams enter and leave the CV. The heat transferred between them is internal to the CV and does not appear; if the outer casing is well insulated then Q̇ = 0 and the energy balance is simply ṁA·(hA,in − hA,out) = ṁB·(hB,out − hB,in): the enthalpy lost by the hot stream equals the enthalpy gained by the cold stream.
  • Boundary around one stream only. Now the heat crossing the separating wall is a boundary crossing: Q̇ = ṁ·(hout − hin) for that stream. This is the way to find the rate of heat transfer itself.
\n

The two are consistent: the Q̇ from the single-stream analysis is exactly the quantity that cancels in the whole-exchanger analysis. Draw the boundary with a pen on the diagram before writing any equation; most marks are lost by writing a Q̇ for a boundary that heat does not cross.

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Steam enters the condenser of a power plant at 10 kPa with a quality of 0.95 at a rate of 20 kg/s and leaves as saturated liquid at the same pressure. It is cooled by river water that enters at 20 °C and leaves at 30 °C. Find the rate of heat transfer from the steam and the mass flow rate of cooling water. Property sources: saturated water, pressure table (Cengel & Boles Table A-5) at 10 kPa: hf = 191.81, hfg = 2392.1 kJ/kg; saturated water, temperature table (Table A-4): hf(20 °C) = 83.915, hf(30 °C) = 125.74 kJ/kg for the compressed-liquid cooling water.

  1. Steam inlet enthalpy: h1 = 191.81 + 0.95 × 2392.1 = 2464.3 kJ/kg. Steam exit: h2 = hf = 191.81 kJ/kg.
  2. Boundary around the steam side only (heat leaves this CV, so Q̇out is positive as written): Q̇out = ṁs·(h1 − h2) = 20 kg/s × (2464.3 − 191.81) kJ/kg = 20 × 2272.5 = 45 450 kW = 45.4 MW.
  3. Boundary around the whole condenser (insulated, no work): ṁs·(h1 − h2) = ṁw·(h4 − h3).
  4. Cooling water: ṁw = 45 450 kW ÷ (125.74 − 83.915) kJ/kg = 45 450 ÷ 41.825 = 1087 kg/s, about 54 kg of river water per kg of steam.
  5. Sanity check: a 10 K rise in water carries about 42 kJ/kg, while condensing steam releases about 2270 kJ/kg, so a ratio near 2270/42 = 54 is right. This is why power stations sit beside rivers or the sea, and why the condenser is physically the largest heat exchanger in the plant.
\n\n

Pipe and duct flow with heat loss or heating

\n

Fluid moving through a pipe is a steady-flow device too. Usually there is no work, but there may be heat gain or loss through the wall, or an electric heater inside the duct (which counts as work in, Ẇe,in, since electrical energy crosses the boundary through wires). Velocities in pipes are low and the change in velocity is smaller still, so kinetic energy is neglected unless the pipe changes diameter or the fluid changes phase. The reduced equation is Q̇in + Ẇe,in = ṁ·(h2 − h1), and for a gas h2 − h1 = cp·(T2 − T1).

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Air at 100 kPa and 17 °C enters an electric heating duct at 150 m³/min. The heater draws 15 kW and the duct loses 200 W to the room. Find the exit temperature. Property source: air as an ideal gas, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K.

  1. Inlet specific volume: v1 = R·T1/P1 = 0.287 × 290.15 ÷ 100 = 0.8327 m³/kg.
  2. Mass flow rate: ṁ = V̇1/v1 = (150/60 m³/s) ÷ 0.8327 m³/kg = 2.50 ÷ 0.8327 = 3.002 kg/s.
  3. Net energy input: Ẇe,in − Q̇out = 15 kW − 0.2 kW = 14.8 kW.
  4. Energy balance: 14.8 kW = ṁ·cp·(T2 − T1), so T2 − T1 = 14.8 ÷ (3.002 × 1.005) = 4.91 K.
  5. Exit temperature: T2 = 17 + 4.91 = 21.9 °C.
  6. Sanity check: 15 kW is a large domestic heater but 3 kg/s is a lot of air (2.5 m³ every second), so a rise of only 5 K is reasonable. Ignoring the 200 W loss would change the answer by 0.07 K; ignoring the volume-to-mass conversion (using 2.5 as if it were kg/s) would give 5.9 K, which is the classic error.
\n\n

Pumps and the incompressible shortcut

\n

A pump is a compressor for liquids, and because liquids hardly change volume the work needed is tiny compared with a gas compressor between the same pressures. For a reversible steady-flow device the work is w = −∫v·dP (proved in the entropy chapter); with v constant this becomes a one-liner.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

wpump,in = v·(P2 − P1) (ideal pump, incompressible liquid, kJ/kg when v is in m³/kg and P in kPa)

Then h2 = h1 + wpump,in. Use v = vf at the inlet temperature or pressure. Example: water as saturated liquid at 10 kPa (vf = 0.001010 m³/kg, Table A-5) pumped to 5 MPa needs w = 0.001010 × (5000 − 10) = 5.04 kJ/kg; for 20 kg/s the pump power is 101 kW. Compare with a turbine producing 880 kJ/kg from the same flow: the pump uses under 1 % of the turbine output. This is the reason the Rankine cycle works and is the number you will keep re-using in the vapour-cycles chapter.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • A Q̇ that does not cross the boundary. If your CV encloses both streams of a heat exchanger, the heat between them is internal and must not appear. Draw the boundary first.
  • Compressed liquid enthalpy. For water below its boiling point at the given pressure, use h ≈ hf(T) from the temperature table, not hf at the pressure. At 250 kPa, hf(P) is 535 kJ/kg, which is the enthalpy of water at 127 °C, not at 45 °C.
  • Volume flow rate used as mass flow rate. 150 m³/min of air is 3.0 kg/s, not 150 kg/s or 2.5 kg/s.
  • Forgetting the pump work or using vg instead of vf in it. With vg at 10 kPa (14.67 m³/kg) the \"pump work\" comes out at 73 000 kJ/kg, which should trigger alarm bells.
  • Mixing a stream ratio with a mass. The energy balance of a mixing chamber gives a ratio of flows; you need one actual flow rate to get the others.
\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM
  • Mixing chamber: three temperatures (or a quality) given, find a flow ratio or a required flow rate; sometimes a steam stream mixed with a water stream, so one h comes from the superheated table and one from hf.
  • Heat exchanger: find the heat transfer rate (single-stream boundary) and the second fluid's flow rate or exit temperature (whole-exchanger boundary). Refrigerant condensers cooled by water and steam condensers are the favourites.
  • Duct with an electric heater and a stated heat loss: find the exit temperature or the required flow (the volume-to-mass conversion is the mark-earning step).
  • Pump: compute v·ΔP and add it to h1; state the incompressible assumption.
  • A one-sentence explanation of why the same exchanger can have Q̇ = 0 in one analysis and Q̇ = 45 MW in another.

This lesson deals with the processes where the control volume itself changes: a tank being filled from a supply line, a cylinder being discharged, a pressure cooker venting. The mass inside changes, so the steady-flow shortcut is gone and you are back to the full balance with a beginning state and an end state, exactly like a closed-system problem, except that mass crossing the boundary brings enthalpy with it. The signature result, that a tank charged from a line ends up hotter than the line, is the best test in the whole chapter of whether you truly understand flow work. It appears in every exam sequence and sits at the base of later material on compressed-gas storage and transient plant operation.

\n\n

Unsteady flow and the uniform-flow idealisation

\n

In an unsteady (transient) flow process the properties inside the control volume change with time. The general balances still hold: rate of accumulation equals rate in minus rate out. To make them solvable by hand, engineering thermodynamics uses the uniform-flow process idealisation with two assumptions: (1) at any instant the state of the mass inside the CV is uniform (the same everywhere inside), though it changes with time; and (2) the state of the fluid at each inlet or exit is constant for the whole process (uniform in time), though it may differ from the state inside. Under these assumptions the balances integrate cleanly from the initial state 1 to the final state 2.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Uniform-flow process: an unsteady control-volume process in which the fluid inside the CV is at a single uniform state at any instant, and the fluid crossing each inlet or exit has a fixed state throughout the process. Charging a tank from a large, steady supply line is the standard case.

The closed system is the special case with no inlets or exits; steady flow is the special case where the initial and final states inside are identical.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

m2 − m1 = Σ min − Σ mout (mass, kg, over the whole process)

Q − W + Σ min·θin − Σ mout·θout = m2·e2 − m1·e1 (energy, kJ)

Q − W + Σ min·hin − Σ mout·hout = m2·u2 − m1·u1 (kinetic and potential energies neglected)

m1, m2 mass inside the CV at the start and end in kg; u1, u2 its internal energy in kJ/kg; hin, hout the enthalpy of the streams crossing the boundary in kJ/kg; θ = h + V²/2 + g·z, e = u + V²/2 + g·z. Note the asymmetry: the mass inside is counted with u, the mass crossing is counted with h. This is the entire lesson in one line.

\n\n

Charging an evacuated tank: why it gets hotter than the line

\n

Take a rigid, insulated, initially evacuated tank connected by a valve to a supply line. Open the valve, let fluid flow in until the tank pressure equals the line pressure, close it. Rigid means W = 0; insulated means Q = 0; evacuated means m1 = 0; no exit. The energy balance collapses to min·hline = m2·u2, and since min = m2:

📊 FIGURE — Filling an evacuated tank: the line’s flow work heats the steam
Each kilogram arrives with u plus the flow work P·v done by the line. Inside the rigid tank that work has nowhere to go, so u₂ = h(line) and the steam ends at 456.1 °C, not 300 °C.
\n

u2 = hline

\n

The internal energy of the fluid in the tank equals the enthalpy of the fluid in the line. Because h = u + Pv > u, the fluid in the tank has more internal energy per kilogram than the fluid in the line, so it is hotter. Where did the extra energy come from? From flow work: the line pushed each kilogram into the tank, doing P·v of work on it, and with nowhere else to go that work became internal energy. For an ideal gas, u2 = cv·T2 and hline = cp·Tline, so

\n

T2 = (cp/cv)·Tline = k·Tline

\n

For air (k = 1.4) a line at 300 K fills an evacuated tank to 420 K, a 120 K rise with no heater anywhere. If the question says the tank is not insulated and ends at the line temperature instead, the difference is the heat that left: Qout = m2·(hline − u2).

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A rigid, insulated tank of volume 8 m³, initially evacuated, is connected to a supply line carrying steam at 1 MPa and 300 °C. The valve is opened and steam flows in until the tank pressure reaches 1 MPa, then the valve is closed. Find the final temperature of the steam in the tank and the mass that entered. Property source: superheated water table (Cengel & Boles Table A-6) at 1 MPa: 300 °C: h = 3051.6 kJ/kg; 400 °C: u = 2957.9 kJ/kg, v = 0.30661 m³/kg; 500 °C: u = 3125.0 kJ/kg, v = 0.35411 m³/kg.

  1. Assumptions: uniform-flow process, W = 0 (rigid), Q = 0 (insulated), m1 = 0, kinetic and potential energies of the line steam negligible.
  2. Mass balance: min = m2. Energy balance: min·hline = m2·u2, so u2 = hline = 3051.6 kJ/kg.
  3. Final state: P2 = 1 MPa and u2 = 3051.6 kJ/kg. In the 1 MPa column of the superheated table, u lies between the 400 °C row (2957.9) and the 500 °C row (3125.0), so the steam is superheated and hotter than 400 °C.
  4. Interpolation fraction: f = (3051.6 − 2957.9)/(3125.0 − 2957.9) = 93.7/167.1 = 0.561.
  5. Temperature: T2 = 400 + 0.561 × 100 = 456.1 °C. (Interpolating with the 450 °C row, where the table has one, changes this by a fraction of a degree.)
  6. Specific volume at the same fraction: v2 = 0.30661 + 0.561 × (0.35411 − 0.30661) = 0.3332 m³/kg.
  7. Mass: m2 = V/v2 = 8 m³ ÷ 0.3332 m³/kg = 24.0 kg.
  8. Sanity check: the tank ends 156 K hotter than the 300 °C line although nothing heated it; the energy is the flow work P·v = 1000 × 0.25799 = 258 kJ/kg done on each kilogram by the line. And 24 kg is less than the 31 kg you would get by wrongly assuming the tank steam was at the line state (8/0.25799), because hotter steam is less dense.
\n\n
✅ VERIFIED

The final temperature of about 456 °C for an evacuated insulated tank filled from a 1 MPa, 300 °C steam line agrees with the worked solution of the same problem in Purdue ME 200 course notes: engineering.purdue.edu (unsteady control-volume example).

\n\n

Charging a tank that already contains gas

\n

If the tank starts with mass m1 at state 1, the same balance keeps its first term: m2u2 − m1u1 = (m2 − m1)·hline. For an ideal gas there are two unknowns, m2 and T2, linked by the ideal-gas law at the final pressure, and the algebra is a short substitution.

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A rigid, insulated 2.0 m³ tank contains air at 100 kPa and 300 K. It is connected to a line carrying air at 600 kPa and 300 K and filled until the tank pressure is 600 kPa. Find the final temperature and the mass added. Property source: air as an ideal gas, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K.

  1. Initial mass: m1 = P1V/(R·T1) = 100 kPa × 2.0 m³ ÷ (0.287 kJ/kg·K × 300 K) = 2.323 kg.
  2. Energy balance (Q = 0, W = 0): m2·cv·T2 − m1·cv·T1 = (m2 − m1)·cp·Tline.
  3. Ideal-gas law at the end: m2·T2 = P2V/R = 600 × 2.0 ÷ 0.287 = 4181 kg·K. This lets the product m2T2 be replaced by a known number.
  4. Substitute: 0.718 × 4181 − 0.718 × 2.323 × 300 = (m2 − 2.323) × 1.005 × 300, i.e. 3002.0 − 500.4 = 301.5·m2 − 700.4.
  5. Solve: m2 = (3002.0 − 500.4 + 700.4)/301.5 = 10.62 kg, so the mass added is 10.62 − 2.32 = 8.30 kg.
  6. Final temperature: T2 = 4181/10.62 = 393.7 K (about 121 °C).
  7. Sanity check: the result sits between the initial 300 K and the evacuated-tank limit of k·Tline = 420 K, as it must, because the 2.32 kg already inside is compressed (and warmed) by the incoming gas while the incoming gas arrives with its flow work. Assuming the tank stayed at 300 K would give m2 = 600 × 2.0 ÷ (0.287 × 300) = 13.94 kg, i.e. 11.6 kg added, 40 % more than the true 8.30 kg.
\n\n

Discharging a tank

\n

Discharge is harder than charging, because the state of the fluid leaving the tank is the state inside the tank, and that changes during the process: the second uniform-flow assumption is violated. Two ways out are used. The exact way, for an insulated rigid tank of ideal gas discharged slowly, is to notice that the gas remaining in the tank has undergone a reversible adiabatic expansion (it did work pushing the leaving gas out and exchanged no heat), so it obeys the isentropic relation T2/T1 = (P2/P1)(k−1)/k, which the entropy chapter derives. The approximate way, used when the exit state changes little or when a mixture leaves at a fixed saturation state (a venting pressure cooker), is to take hout as the average of its initial and final values and apply the uniform-flow balance directly.

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A 1.0 m³ insulated rigid tank holds air at 500 kPa and 300 K. A valve is opened and air escapes slowly until the pressure is 200 kPa. Find the final temperature and the mass that escaped. Property source: air as an ideal gas, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, k = 1.4.

  1. Initial mass: m1 = P1V/(R·T1) = 500 × 1.0 ÷ (0.287 × 300) = 5.807 kg.
  2. The gas that stays expands isentropically: T2 = T1·(P2/P1)(k−1)/k = 300 K × (200/500)0.2857 = 300 × 0.7697 = 230.9 K (−42 °C).
  3. Final mass: m2 = P2V/(R·T2) = 200 × 1.0 ÷ (0.287 × 230.9) = 3.018 kg.
  4. Mass escaped: m1 − m2 = 5.807 − 3.018 = 2.79 kg.
  5. Sanity check: the tank gets cold, which is what you feel on a discharging CO₂ cartridge or a rapidly emptied scuba cylinder. Assuming the temperature stayed at 300 K would give m2 = 2.32 kg and 3.48 kg escaped, 25 % too much, because cold gas is denser and more of it stays behind. The uniform-flow approximation with an average exit enthalpy, he = cp·(T1 + T2)/2, gives T2 = 232 K, within 1.3 K of the exact result, which shows why that approximation is acceptable for modest pressure ratios.
\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • h for the tank, u for the line. It is the other way round. Mass inside: u. Mass crossing: h. Writing h2 = hline for a charged tank gives T2 = Tline and the tank mass about 29 % too high (31.0 kg instead of 24.0 kg in the steam example).
  • Applying the steady-flow equation. There is no ṁ in a filling problem; the balance is in total masses and total energies over the process.
  • Celsius in k·T. T2 = k·Tline needs kelvin: 1.4 × 300 K = 420 K, not 1.4 × 27 °C = 38 °C.
  • Forgetting the initial mass. If the tank is not evacuated, m1u1 stays in the balance and min = m2 − m1, not m2.
  • Discharge with a fixed exit state. Unless the fluid leaves at a fixed saturation state, the exit enthalpy changes during the process; use the isentropic relation for the remaining ideal gas or an average exit enthalpy, and say which.
\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM
  • Evacuated insulated tank filled from a steam or air line: find T2 (u2 = hline, then read the table or use k·T) and the mass (V/v2 or PV/RT2).
  • The same with heat loss so that the tank ends at a stated temperature: find Q.
  • Partly full tank charged from a line: two unknowns, ideal-gas law plus energy balance.
  • Pressure cooker or steam-tank venting at constant pressure: the leaving fluid is saturated vapour at the cooker pressure, so hout = hg is constant and the uniform-flow balance applies exactly.
  • The conceptual question: \"Explain why the temperature in a tank charged from a supply line exceeds the line temperature\" (flow work Pv becomes internal energy; u2 = hline; ideal gas T2 = k·Tline). Three sentences earn full marks.
"}, "THERMO/second/s1": {"body": "

This lesson lets you look at any device that takes in heat and delivers work, draw it as a box between two reservoirs, and compute its thermal efficiency from any two of the three energy flows. It also gives you the first formal statement of the second law, the Kelvin-Planck statement, which is the reason no engine anywhere converts all of its heat into work. In the degree this is the opening of the second-law block: everything in the entropy, exergy and cycle chapters rests on the vocabulary fixed here.

\n\n

A process can obey the first law and still never happen

\n

Leave a hot cup of coffee on a desk. It cools, and the room warms by exactly the energy the coffee lost. Now imagine the reverse: the room gives a little energy back to the coffee and the coffee heats up. Energy would still be conserved, so the first law is perfectly happy with it, yet it never happens. The same is true of a paddle wheel driven by a falling weight that warms a tank of water: the warm water never spontaneously turns the wheel and lifts the weight back up. The first law is a bookkeeping law; it says how much, never which way. The second law is the law of direction. It tells you which processes can actually run, and it gives every energy conversion an upper limit that no amount of engineering can beat.

\n

Three ideas appear in the next few sections and you should hold them together: a process runs in a definite direction; energy has quality as well as quantity (work is worth more than the same number of joules of heat, and hot heat is worth more than cold heat); and there is a best possible performance for every engine, refrigerator and heat pump, set only by the temperatures it works between.

\n\n

Thermal energy reservoirs

\n
📘 DEFINITION

A thermal energy reservoir is a body with such a large thermal energy capacity (mass × specific heat) that it can supply or absorb finite amounts of heat without any measurable change in its temperature. A reservoir that supplies heat is a source; one that absorbs heat is a sink.

\n

Oceans, lakes, rivers and the atmosphere are the standard examples, but the idea is relative to the process: a room is a reservoir for a television set, and a furnace with a steady fuel supply is a reservoir for the boiler of a power plant. Two-phase systems also behave as reservoirs while they boil or condense, because the heat goes into changing phase rather than temperature. The point of the abstraction is that once a reservoir has a single fixed temperature, TH or TL, every heat transfer to or from it happens at that temperature and the analysis becomes clean.

\n\n

Heat engines and thermal efficiency

\n

Work converts to heat directly and completely. Rub your hands, stir a fluid, pass a current through a resistor: all of the work ends up as internal energy. The reverse needs a special device. A heat engine is a device that (1) receives heat from a high-temperature source, (2) converts part of it to work, usually as a rotating shaft, (3) rejects the remaining heat to a low-temperature sink and (4) operates on a cycle. Steam power plants, gas turbines and car engines are the everyday examples; strictly a car engine does not run its working fluid on a closed cycle, but its energy balance is analysed the same way.

📊 FIGURE — Two heat engines drawn as boxes between a source and a sink
Heat QH comes down from the hot source, part leaves as net work, and the rest QL must go to the cold sink. Efficiency is net work over QH; any two flows give the third.
\n

Because the engine works on a cycle, its net change in internal energy over one cycle is zero and the first law reduces to net work equals net heat. With QH the heat supplied by the source and QL the heat rejected to the sink, both written as positive magnitudes:

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Wnet,out = QH − QL

ηth = Wnet,out / QH = 1 − QL / QH

Wnet,out is the net work output of the cycle (kJ, or kW for a rate); QH is the heat received from the high-temperature reservoir (kJ or kW); QL is the heat rejected to the low-temperature reservoir (kJ or kW); ηth is the thermal efficiency, dimensionless, always between 0 and 1.

\n

Thermal efficiency is a ratio of the output you wanted to the input you paid for. It is the yardstick for every engine that follows: spark-ignition engines around 25 to 30 percent, diesel engines around 35 to 40 percent, large gas-turbine plants a little higher and modern combined-cycle plants around 60 percent. Note that QL is not a design flaw that a better engineer could remove: rejecting heat to a sink is a requirement of a cyclic device, as the next section explains.

\n\n

Worked example: a steam power plant and a car engine

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem A. The furnace of a steam power plant transfers 280 MW to the steam in the boiler and the condenser rejects 165 MW to a river. Find the net power output and the thermal efficiency.

  1. Identify the flows: QH = 280 MW (source, the furnace), QL = 165 MW (sink, the river).
  2. Cycle energy balance: Wnet,out = QH − QL = 280 MW − 165 MW = 115 MW.
  3. Thermal efficiency: ηth = Wnet,out / QH = 115 MW / 280 MW = 0.4107 = 41.1%.
  4. Check by the other form: 1 − QL/QH = 1 − 165/280 = 1 − 0.5893 = 0.4107. Same answer, as it must be.

Sanity check: a large steam plant in the 35 to 45 percent range is exactly what the industry reports, so 41% is plausible. Note that the pump work inside the plant is already inside the \"net\" output; the 115 MW is what leaves the plant as electricity before generator losses.

Problem B. A car engine delivers 65 kW of net power at a thermal efficiency of 24%. What rate of heat must the fuel supply, and how much heat is thrown away through the radiator and exhaust?

  1. Rearrange the definition: QH = Wnet,out / ηth = 65 kW / 0.24 = 270.8 kW.
  2. Heat rejected: QL = QH − Wnet,out = 270.8 kW − 65 kW = 205.8 kW.
  3. Sanity check: more than three-quarters of the fuel energy leaves as heat, which is why a car has a large radiator and a hot exhaust. QL is larger than W, as it must be when ηth is below 0.5.
\n\n

The Kelvin-Planck statement

\n

Could a clever engine take heat from a single reservoir and turn all of it into work, so that QL = 0 and ηth = 100%? Think about the steam plant: the steam leaving the turbine is a low-pressure, mostly-vapour mixture. To close the cycle the pump has to push it back into the boiler, and a pump that handles vapour would consume most of the turbine's output. The only way to make the return cheap is to condense the steam first, and condensing means rejecting heat to the river. Every cyclic engine faces the same problem: to bring the working fluid back to its starting state, some heat has to be dumped at low temperature. This observation, confirmed by every experiment ever made, is elevated to a law:

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law: it is impossible for any device that operates on a cycle to receive heat from a single reservoir and produce a net amount of work.

\n

Two consequences are worth making explicit. First, a heat engine must exchange heat with at least two reservoirs at different temperatures; the low-temperature sink is not optional. Second, no heat engine, real or idealised, can have a thermal efficiency of 100%. What the maximum actually is, and why it depends only on the two temperatures, is the subject of the Carnot lessons later in this chapter. The statement is about cycles and net work: a single non-cyclic process (an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, say) can convert heat to work completely, because the system does not return to its initial state.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Mixing up the sign convention. In this chapter QH, QL and Wnet are magnitudes, all positive, and the direction is carried by the drawing. If you carry the signed convention from the first-law chapter (heat in positive, heat out negative) you will write W = QH + QL and get a wildly wrong efficiency. Draw the engine as a box with arrows before you write a single equation.

Dividing by the wrong quantity. Efficiency is work over heat supplied, never work over heat rejected. For the steam plant, 115/165 = 0.697 looks like an efficiency and is wrong. An efficiency you compute above about 65% for a real plant should make you suspicious.

Treating QL as a loss to be engineered away. QL is required by the Kelvin-Planck statement. Friction, leaks and poor insulation add to it, but even the perfect engine rejects heat.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM
  • Given any two of QH, QL and Wnet, find the third and the efficiency. Watch the units: kJ per cycle, kW, or kJ/h and MW are all common in one paper, and the ratio only works when both flows are in the same unit.
  • State the Kelvin-Planck statement precisely: the words \"single reservoir\", \"cycle\" and \"net work\" are what earn the marks. A vague \"you cannot turn all heat into work\" is marked down because a non-cyclic process can.
  • Explain why the condenser of a steam plant cannot be removed, using the pump-work argument above.
  • Distinguish a thermal energy reservoir from an ordinary body: the defining property is that its temperature does not change during the heat transfer in question.
"}, "THERMO/second/s2": {"body": "

This lesson lets you analyse the two machines that move heat the wrong way, from cold to hot: the refrigerator and the heat pump. You will compute their coefficients of performance from any two of the three energy flows, see why the two COPs always differ by exactly one, and meet the second formal statement of the second law, the Clausius statement. It closes with the two kinds of perpetual-motion machine, which are the standard exam way of testing whether you can tell a first-law violation from a second-law violation. In the degree this sits beside the heat-engine lesson and feeds directly into the refrigeration-cycle chapter.

\n\n

Heat only flows downhill on its own

\n

Heat transfer from a hot body to a cold one needs no help; it happens whenever the two are in contact. The reverse, taking heat out of a cold space and pushing it into a warmer one, never happens by itself. It can be made to happen, but only with a special device and only at a price: work has to be supplied. The device is a refrigerator when the purpose is to keep the cold space cold, and a heat pump when the purpose is to keep the warm space warm. The hardware can be identical; in fact many units run as both, cooling a house in summer and heating it in winter by reversing the flow.

\n

The most common form is the vapour-compression cycle: a refrigerant evaporates at low pressure in the cold space (absorbing QL), is compressed to high pressure by a compressor (receiving Wnet,in), condenses at high pressure in the warm surroundings (rejecting QH), and expands back to low pressure through a throttling valve. The details of that cycle are a later chapter; here we treat the machine as a box.

\n\n

Refrigerators and heat pumps: the same box, two goals

\n
📘 DEFINITION

A refrigerator is a cyclic device that transfers heat from a low-temperature medium to a high-temperature medium using a work input; its desired output is QL, the heat removed from the cold space. A heat pump is the same kind of device whose desired output is QH, the heat delivered to the warm space. The coefficient of performance (COP) is the ratio of the desired output to the required work input.

📊 FIGURE — A refrigerator and a heat pump: same cycle, different useful output
Both machines lift QL from cold to hot using work, and dump QH = QL + W. The accent arrow is the output each one is bought for; COP is that output divided by the work in.
\n

Because the device operates on a cycle, the first law for the cycle gives Wnet,in = QH − QL: the heat delivered to the warm side is the heat lifted from the cold side plus the work that did the lifting. This is why a heat pump can deliver more heat than the electricity it consumes. It is not creating energy; it is moving energy that was already in the outside air or the ground and adding the compressor work on top.

\n\n

Coefficient of performance

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

COPR = QL / Wnet,in = QL / (QH − QL) = 1 / (QH/QL − 1)

COPHP = QH / Wnet,in = QH / (QH − QL) = 1 / (1 − QL/QH)

COPHP = COPR + 1

QL is the heat removed from the cold space (kJ or kW), QH the heat rejected to the warm space (kJ or kW), Wnet,in the net work supplied, usually to the compressor (kJ or kW). Both COPs are dimensionless and can be, and usually are, greater than 1. The last line follows from subtracting the two definitions: (QH − QL)/W = 1, for the same machine with the same flows.

\n

Read the last equation carefully. It says that a heat pump's COP is never below 1 in theory: even if it moved no heat at all from outside, the compressor work would still end up as heat in the house, so W in gives at least W out as heat, and COPHP = 1 is the resistance-heater floor. In practice a heat pump in a very cold climate may fall to that level, which is why the COP is quoted with the temperatures it was measured at. Domestic refrigerators typically run at COPR around 2 to 3; air-source heat pumps at 2.5 to 4 in mild weather.

\n\n

Worked example: a refrigerator and a heat pump

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem A. The food compartment of a refrigerator is kept at 4 °C by removing heat from it at a rate of 360 kJ/min. The compressor draws 2 kW. Find the COP of the refrigerator and the rate at which heat is rejected to the kitchen.

  1. Put both flows in the same unit. QL = 360 kJ/min = 360/60 kJ/s = 6 kW. Wnet,in = 2 kW.
  2. COPR = QL / Wnet,in = 6 kW / 2 kW = 3.0. Every kilowatt of electricity removes 3 kW of heat from the food.
  3. Cycle energy balance: QH = QL + Wnet,in = 6 kW + 2 kW = 8 kW = 480 kJ/min to the kitchen.
  4. Sanity check: QH is larger than QL by exactly the work, and the kitchen receives more heat than the food loses, which is why a refrigerator with the door open warms a room. The 4 °C is not needed for this calculation; it would be needed to find the Carnot limit in lesson 4.

Problem B. A house loses heat at 80,000 kJ/h on a winter day and is kept at 21 °C by a heat pump with COPHP = 2.5. Find the electrical power the heat pump draws and the rate at which it extracts heat from the cold outside air.

  1. To hold the house steady, the heat pump must deliver exactly what the house loses: QH = 80,000 kJ/h.
  2. Wnet,in = QH / COPHP = 80,000 kJ/h / 2.5 = 32,000 kJ/h. Convert: 32,000 kJ/h ÷ 3600 s/h = 8.89 kW.
  3. Heat lifted from the outside air: QL = QH − Wnet,in = 80,000 − 32,000 = 48,000 kJ/h (13.3 kW).
  4. Sanity check: a resistance heater would need the full 80,000 kJ/h = 22.2 kW of electricity. The heat pump needs 8.89 kW, a 60% saving, consistent with a COP of 2.5 meaning 1/2.5 = 40% of the heat is paid for as electricity. The corresponding COPR of this machine is 48,000/32,000 = 1.5 = 2.5 − 1.
\n\n

The Clausius statement, and why two statements are one law

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Clausius statement of the second law: it is impossible to construct a device that operates on a cycle and produces no effect other than the transfer of heat from a lower-temperature body to a higher-temperature body.

\n

The phrase \"no effect other than\" is what makes the statement precise. A refrigerator does move heat from cold to hot, but it leaves another effect behind: work was consumed and the surroundings received QH greater than QL. What is forbidden is a refrigerator with COPR = ∞, one that needs no work at all.

\n

The Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements look different, one about engines and one about refrigerators, but each implies the other, so they are two phrasings of the same law. The standard proof runs like this. Suppose a Clausius-violating refrigerator existed: it moves QL from a cold reservoir at TL to a hot reservoir at TH with no work. Put an ordinary heat engine beside it, taking QH from the hot reservoir, producing W = QH − QL of work and rejecting exactly QL to the cold reservoir. Now look at the two devices together as one box. The cold reservoir receives QL from the engine and gives QL to the refrigerator: net zero, so it can be removed. What is left is a cyclic device that takes QH − QL from a single reservoir (the hot one) and produces an equal amount of work, which violates Kelvin-Planck. The mirror argument, using a Kelvin-Planck-violating engine to drive an ordinary refrigerator and produce a work-free heat transfer from cold to hot, shows that violating Kelvin-Planck violates Clausius. Two statements that each imply the other are equivalent.

\n\n

Perpetual-motion machines

\n

Any device that violates the first or the second law is called a perpetual-motion machine, and exam questions love them because they test whether you can name which law is broken.

\n
    \n
  • A perpetual-motion machine of the first kind (PMM1) violates the first law: it produces energy from nothing. The textbook example is a steam plant whose generator also powers the resistance heaters that boil its own water, with electricity left over to sell. Energy out exceeds energy in, so it is a PMM1.
    • \n
  • A perpetual-motion machine of the second kind (PMM2) conserves energy but violates the second law. The textbook example is a steam plant with the condenser removed, whose turbine exhaust is pumped straight back to the boiler: it exchanges heat with a single reservoir (the furnace) and produces net work, which the Kelvin-Planck statement forbids. A work-free refrigerator is also a PMM2.
    • \n
\n

The test is always the same two questions in order. Does energy balance? If not, PMM1. Does it exchange heat with a single reservoir and make net work, or move heat from cold to hot for free? If so, PMM2.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Using the wrong Q in the COP. A refrigerator is judged by the heat it removes (QL); a heat pump by the heat it delivers (QH). Using QH for a refrigerator overstates its COP by exactly 1; using QL for a heat pump understates it by 1. Ask \"what did the owner buy this machine to do?\" and use that flow.

Believing a COP above 1 breaks the first law. It does not. The heat delivered by a heat pump is QL + W: the extra came from the cold outdoor air, not from nowhere. Energy is conserved; the machine is a mover, not a generator.

Mixed units. Refrigeration loads arrive in kJ/min, kJ/h, kW and tons of refrigeration (1 ton = 211 kJ/min) while compressor power arrives in kW. Convert everything to kW before dividing, or the COP is off by a factor of 60 or 3600.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM
  • Given a refrigeration load and a compressor power, find COPR and the heat rejected; given a heating load and a COPHP, find the power drawn and the heat taken from outside. Always finish with the cycle balance QH = QL + W.
  • Prove that COPHP = COPR + 1 for the same machine in two lines from the definitions.
  • State the Clausius statement with the words \"cycle\" and \"no effect other than\"; then reproduce the two-device argument that shows violating one statement violates the other.
  • Classify a described device as a PMM1 or a PMM2 and say which law it breaks. Do the energy balance first; only if it balances do you look for a second-law violation.
"}, "THERMO/second/s3": {"body": "

This lesson lets you say precisely what \"reversible\" means, list the irreversibilities that make every real process fall short of it, and analyse the Carnot cycle, the reversible cycle that sets the ceiling for all heat engines and refrigerators. You will trace its four processes on P-v and T-s diagrams, compute a full set of states for a Carnot cycle running on air, and use the two Carnot principles to rank engines. In the degree this is where the second law stops being a prohibition and starts giving numbers.

\n\n

What \"reversible\" means

\n

Every process runs in a definite direction and, once it has happened, cannot be undone without leaving a trace. A pendulum in air slows and stops; nobody has seen a stopped pendulum start swinging by cooling the air around it. But we can imagine an idealised pendulum in a vacuum on a frictionless pivot that swings forever, and that idealisation is what the second law is built on.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

A reversible process is one that can be reversed without leaving any trace on the surroundings: at the end of the process and its reverse, both the system and the surroundings are back in their initial states. A process that is not reversible is irreversible. The factors that make a process irreversible are called irreversibilities.

\n

Reversible processes do not occur in nature; they are limits that real processes approach. They matter for two reasons. They are easy to analyse, because the system passes through a sequence of equilibrium states. And they deliver the most work (for a work-producing device) or consume the least work (for a work-consuming device) of any process between the same end states, so they are the yardstick against which real devices are measured. The less irreversible a device, the closer it comes to its reversible limit.

\n\n

The irreversibilities

\n

The exam list, with the reason each one is irreversible:

\n
    \n
  • Friction. Two surfaces in relative motion convert work into heat at the interface. Reversing the motion does not give the work back; it generates more heat. The same applies to fluid friction in pipes and turbines.
    • \n
  • Unrestrained expansion. A gas expanding into a vacuum, or a membrane bursting, does no work. To put the gas back you must compress it, which costs work, and the heat that compression generates must be dumped to the surroundings: they are not the same afterwards. The reversible alternative is a quasi-equilibrium expansion against a piston that is always just barely lighter than the gas pressure.
    • \n
  • Heat transfer across a finite temperature difference. Heat from a body at 100 °C to one at 20 °C cannot be sent back without a refrigerator, which needs work. Heat transfer is reversible only in the limit of an infinitesimal temperature difference, which would take infinite time or infinite area. This is the irreversibility that dominates boilers, condensers and every heat exchanger.
    • \n
  • Mixing. Two different gases mixing, or two streams at different temperatures merging, cannot be unmixed without a work input.
    • \n
  • Others. Electric resistance, inelastic deformation, chemical reactions, and any sudden change (a valve snapping open, a throttling process) where the system is not in equilibrium along the way.
    • \n
\n\n

Internally, externally and totally reversible

\n

A process is internally reversible if no irreversibilities occur inside the system boundary: the system passes through a series of equilibrium states, and the path can be retraced exactly. A quasi-equilibrium process is internally reversible. It is externally reversible if no irreversibilities occur outside the boundary; in practice this means heat crosses the boundary only between bodies at the same temperature. It is totally reversible (or simply reversible) when both hold. The distinction matters in the entropy chapter: the entropy relations are written for internally reversible processes, and the classic example is a heat transfer to a system at exactly 100 °C from a reservoir at 100 °C (totally reversible) versus from a reservoir at 300 °C (internally reversible, externally irreversible).

\n\n

The Carnot cycle

\n

Because reversible cycles deliver the most work, the best possible heat engine runs on one. The best known is the Carnot cycle, four reversible processes for a gas in a piston-cylinder:

📊 FIGURE — The Carnot cycle on air between 800 K and 300 K, on P-v and T-s
Heat enters on the 800 K isotherm (1-2) and leaves on the 300 K isotherm (3-4); the adiabats link them. On T-s the cycle is a rectangle and its area is the net work.
\n
    \n
  1. 1-2, reversible isothermal expansion at TH. The cylinder touches the hot reservoir; the gas expands slowly, doing work, while heat QH flows in to hold the temperature constant.
    2. \n
  2. 2-3, reversible adiabatic (isentropic) expansion. The cylinder is insulated; the gas keeps expanding and doing work, and its temperature falls from TH to TL.
    3. \n
  3. 3-4, reversible isothermal compression at TL. The cylinder touches the cold reservoir; the piston pushes in, and heat QL flows out to hold the temperature constant.
    4. \n
  4. 4-1, reversible adiabatic compression. Insulated again; compression raises the temperature from TL back to TH and closes the cycle.
    5. \n
\n

On a P-v diagram the four processes form a lens shape: two isotherms (hyperbola-like curves, P ∝ 1/v for an ideal gas) joined by two steeper adiabats (P ∝ 1/vk). The area enclosed is the net work per unit mass. On a T-s diagram the cycle is a rectangle: the isotherms are horizontal lines at TH and TL, and the isentropic legs are vertical lines. The area under the top edge is qH = TH Δs, the area under the bottom edge is qL = TL Δs, and the rectangle itself is the net work. That rectangle is the fastest way to remember the Carnot efficiency, which lesson 4 derives properly. Run the four processes in the opposite order (1-4-3-2-1) and you have the reversed Carnot cycle, the ideal refrigerator or heat pump, and the T-s rectangle is traced anticlockwise.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

For an ideal gas on the two isothermal legs (T constant, so Δu = 0 and q = w):

qH = R TH ln(v2/v1) and qL = R TL ln(v3/v4)

On the two isentropic legs (q = 0, ideal gas, constant specific heats):

T vk−1 = constant, so v3/v2 = v4/v1 = (TH/TL)1/(k−1)

qH, qL are heat per unit mass (kJ/kg); R is the gas constant (0.287 kJ/kg·K for air); TH, TL are the reservoir temperatures in kelvin; v is specific volume (m³/kg); k = cp/cv (1.4 for air). Because the two isentropic legs have the same temperature ratio, v3/v4 = v2/v1, and the ratio qL/qH collapses to TL/TH.

\n\n

Worked example: a Carnot cycle running on air

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem. Air (ideal gas, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, k = 1.4, constant specific heats) executes a Carnot cycle between reservoirs at TH = 800 K and TL = 300 K. At state 1 the pressure is 1000 kPa, and the isothermal expansion doubles the volume (v2/v1 = 2). Find all four states, the heat transfers, the net work and the efficiency.

  1. State 1. v1 = R T1/P1 = 0.287 kJ/kg·K × 800 K / 1000 kPa = 0.2296 m³/kg (kJ/kPa = m³).
  2. State 2 (isothermal, T2 = 800 K). v2 = 2 × 0.2296 = 0.4592 m³/kg. P2 = R T/v2 = 0.287 × 800 / 0.4592 = 500 kPa (the pressure halves when the volume doubles at constant T).
  3. Heat in on 1-2. qH = R TH ln(v2/v1) = 0.287 kJ/kg·K × 800 K × ln 2 = 0.287 × 800 × 0.6931 = 159.1 kJ/kg.
  4. State 3 (isentropic 2-3, T3 = 300 K). v3/v2 = (TH/TL)1/(k−1) = (800/300)2.5 = 11.61, so v3 = 11.61 × 0.4592 = 5.332 m³/kg. P3 = 0.287 × 300 / 5.332 = 16.15 kPa.
  5. State 4 (isothermal at 300 K, closing the cycle). The isentropic leg 4-1 has the same temperature ratio, so v4/v1 = 11.61 and v4 = 11.61 × 0.2296 = 2.666 m³/kg; equivalently v4 = v3/2. P4 = 0.287 × 300 / 2.666 = 32.29 kPa. Check: P1/P4 = 1000/32.29 = 30.97 and (TH/TL)k/(k−1) = (8/3)3.5 = 30.97. Consistent.
  6. Heat out on 3-4. qL = R TL ln(v3/v4) = 0.287 × 300 × ln 2 = 59.68 kJ/kg.
  7. Net work. wnet = qH − qL = 159.1 − 59.68 = 99.5 kJ/kg. (The adiabatic legs do work too, +cv(TH − TL) on 2-3 and the same amount negative on 4-1; they cancel.)
  8. Efficiency. ηth = wnet/qH = 99.5/159.1 = 0.625, and 1 − TL/TH = 1 − 300/800 = 0.625. Identical, which is the point of the Carnot cycle.
StateT (K)P (kPa)v (m³/kg)Process leaving it

Sanity check: the entropy change on each isothermal leg is q/T = 159.1/800 = 0.1989 kJ/kg·K and 59.68/300 = 0.1989 kJ/kg·K, equal and opposite, so the T-s rectangle closes. The huge volume range (v3 is 23 times v1) is why practical Carnot gas engines are not built.

\n\n

The Carnot principles

\n

Two statements follow from the second law and are proved by the same kind of two-device argument used in lesson 2:

\n
    \n
  1. The efficiency of an irreversible heat engine is always less than the efficiency of a reversible one operating between the same two reservoirs.
    2. \n
  2. The efficiencies of all reversible heat engines operating between the same two reservoirs are the same.
    3. \n
\n

Sketch of the proof of the first principle: suppose an irreversible engine were more efficient than a reversible engine between the same reservoirs, both taking the same QH. Run the reversible engine backwards as a refrigerator, driven by part of the irreversible engine's work. The reversible engine returns exactly QH to the hot reservoir, so the hot reservoir can be removed. What remains is a device that takes heat from the cold reservoir alone and produces net work, a Kelvin-Planck violation. So the assumption was wrong. The second principle follows by running the same argument with two reversible engines each way round.

\n

The second principle is what makes the Carnot efficiency universal: it cannot depend on the working fluid, the size of the engine or the mechanical design, only on the two reservoir temperatures. That is exactly what the worked example showed, and it is the door to the thermodynamic temperature scale in the next lesson.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Calling quasi-equilibrium \"reversible\". A slow, quasi-equilibrium process is internally reversible. If it receives heat across a finite temperature difference it is still externally irreversible. \"Reversible\" without qualification means totally reversible.

Using the wrong exponent on the isentropic legs. For an ideal gas, T vk−1 = constant and T P(1−k)/k = constant, so the volume ratio uses the exponent 1/(k − 1) = 2.5 for air and the pressure ratio uses k/(k − 1) = 3.5. Swapping them gives a volume ratio of 30.97 instead of 11.61.

Thinking the adiabatic legs contribute net work. They do work, but the expansion and compression legs cancel exactly for an ideal gas with constant specific heats, so the net work is qH − qL from the isothermal legs alone.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM
  • Define reversible, internally reversible and externally reversible, and give one example of each.
  • Name four irreversibilities and, for one of them, explain in a sentence why reversing the process would leave a trace on the surroundings.
  • Sketch the Carnot cycle on P-v and on T-s axes, label the four processes with what happens to Q, and mark which area is qH, qL and wnet. The T-s rectangle is the most-asked sketch in the course.
  • Compute states and heat transfers for a Carnot cycle on an ideal gas, exactly as in the worked example, and show that qL/qH = TL/TH.
  • State the two Carnot principles and reproduce the two-engine proof of the first.
"}, "THERMO/second/s4": {"body": "

This lesson lets you compute the best possible efficiency of any engine and the best possible COP of any refrigerator or heat pump from nothing more than two temperatures, and then judge a real machine, or a claimed one, against that ceiling. It also explains where the Kelvin scale comes from and why a joule of heat at 1000 K is worth more than a joule at 400 K. In the degree this closes the second-law block; the entropy chapter that follows takes the ratio Q/T defined here and turns it into a property.

\n\n

Where the Kelvin scale comes from

\n

The second Carnot principle says that the efficiency of a reversible engine depends only on the two reservoir temperatures, so the ratio QL/QH for a reversible engine must be some function of TH and TL alone. Stack two reversible engines in series (the first rejects to a middle reservoir, the second takes that heat) and compare with a single reversible engine spanning the outer reservoirs; the only way the function can be consistent for every choice of middle temperature is if it separates into a ratio, QH/QL = φ(TH)/φ(TL). Lord Kelvin chose the simplest possible φ, namely φ(T) = T, and that choice defines the thermodynamic (Kelvin) temperature scale:

\n
📘 DEFINITION

On the thermodynamic temperature scale, the ratio of two temperatures is defined as the ratio of the heats exchanged by a reversible heat engine operating between reservoirs at those temperatures:

(QH / QL)rev = TH / TL

The scale is fixed by assigning one number: the triple point of water is 273.16 K. It is independent of the properties of any substance, which is why it is called absolute. Kelvin temperatures on this scale agree with the ideal-gas temperature scale, and T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15.

\n

Nobody measures temperature with a Carnot engine; the point is conceptual. It says the kelvin is built into the second law itself, and that only kelvin temperatures may appear in the formulas below. Any \"efficiency\" computed with degrees Celsius is meaningless.

\n\n

The Carnot limits

\n

Substitute the definition into the efficiency and COP expressions from lessons 1 and 2, and the three ceilings appear:

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

ηth,rev = 1 − TL / TH (Carnot efficiency, the highest efficiency any heat engine can have between TH and TL)

COPR,rev = 1 / (TH/TL − 1) = TL / (TH − TL)

COPHP,rev = 1 / (1 − TL/TH) = TH / (TH − TL)

TH and TL are the absolute temperatures of the hot and cold reservoirs in kelvin; the results are dimensionless. For any real (irreversible) machine between the same reservoirs, ηth < ηth,rev, COPR < COPR,rev and COPHP < COPHP,rev. A claimed value above the ceiling is impossible, equal to it means reversible, below it is a real machine.

\n

Notice what the formulas say about design. Efficiency rises with TH and falls with TL, which is why power plants push boiler temperatures as high as metallurgy allows and reject heat to the coldest water available. The COPs, on the other hand, fall as the temperature gap widens: a refrigerator working to −30 °C in a 35 °C room, or a heat pump on a −20 °C night, has a low ceiling and an even lower real COP. Sizing the lift as small as possible is the single biggest lever in refrigeration and heat-pump design.

\n\n

Worked example: a Carnot engine and a Carnot heat pump

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem A. A Carnot heat engine receives 500 kJ of heat per cycle from a source at 652 °C and rejects heat to a sink at 30 °C. Find the thermal efficiency, the work output per cycle and the heat rejected per cycle.

  1. Convert to kelvin: TH = 652 + 273.15 = 925.15 K; TL = 30 + 273.15 = 303.15 K.
  2. ηth,rev = 1 − TL/TH = 1 − 303.15/925.15 = 1 − 0.3277 = 0.672 (67.2%).
  3. Wnet,out = ηth QH = 0.6723 × 500 kJ = 336.2 kJ per cycle.
  4. QL = QH − Wnet,out = 500 − 336.2 = 163.8 kJ per cycle. Check by the temperature ratio: QL = QH TL/TH = 500 × 303.15/925.15 = 163.8 kJ. Same.
  5. Sanity check: had you used Celsius, 1 − 30/652 = 0.954, an absurd 95% that no engine approaches. The 67% figure is a ceiling; a real steam plant with these reservoir temperatures achieves around 40%.

Problem B. A house is kept at 21 °C on a day when the outside air is −5 °C. (a) What is the highest COP any heat pump could have between these temperatures? (b) A real air-source heat pump on that day draws 2.5 kW and delivers 9 kW; what fraction of the ideal does it achieve?

  1. TH = 21 + 273.15 = 294.15 K; TL = −5 + 273.15 = 268.15 K; TH − TL = 26 K (a difference is the same in K and °C).
  2. COPHP,rev = TH/(TH − TL) = 294.15/26 = 11.3. The refrigerator ceiling for the same machine would be 268.15/26 = 10.3, one less, as always.
  3. Real COPHP = QH/W = 9 kW / 2.5 kW = 3.6.
  4. Ratio to ideal: 3.6/11.3 = 0.32. The real machine reaches about a third of the Carnot ceiling, which is typical; the exergy chapter names this ratio the second-law efficiency.
  5. Sanity check: 3.6 is below 11.3, so the machine is possible; a salesperson claiming COP 12 at these temperatures would be claiming a PMM2.
\n\n

Comparing real machines with their Carnot ceilings

\n

A useful habit: whenever a performance figure is quoted, compute the Carnot ceiling for the stated temperatures and put the two side by side. The table below does this for the machines in this chapter (the reservoir temperatures for the steam plant are assumed typical values, not data from a specific plant).

📊 FIGURE — How close four machines come to their Carnot ceilings
Each dashed bar is the Carnot limit for that machine’s two temperatures; the filled part is what the real machine achieves. A filled bar past the dashed end would be impossible.
\n\n\n\n\n\n
