\n
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

You already know how to build exactly this table in pandas: one row per machine, columns for the two temperatures, a computed column for the ceiling and a ratio column. Do it for the whole course as you go and you will have a dataset of real-versus-ideal performance across engines, refrigerators and heat pumps. Plot ratio against (TH − TL) and you will see the pattern the exam wants you to state in words: the wider the temperature lift, the smaller the fraction of the Carnot ceiling a real machine reaches. It is also the fastest error check available: any row where the real figure exceeds the ceiling is a data-entry mistake or a temperature in the wrong unit.

\n\n

The quality of energy

\n

The Carnot efficiency makes a claim about energy that the first law cannot: the same quantity of heat is worth different amounts of work depending on the temperature it is available at. Take 100 kJ of heat and a sink at 300 K. From a source at 1000 K, a reversible engine can turn 100 × (1 − 300/1000) = 70 kJ of it into work. From a source at 400 K, only 100 × (1 − 300/400) = 25 kJ. The rest is unavailable at that temperature no matter how well the engine is built. Energy therefore has quality as well as quantity, and the higher the temperature, the higher the quality. Work is the highest-quality form of all, because it can be converted to heat at any temperature with 100% efficiency but not the other way round.

\n

This idea explains a great deal of engineering practice. It is why heating a house with electric resistance is thermodynamically wasteful (high-quality work is degraded into low-temperature heat that a heat pump could have delivered for a third of the electricity), why solar thermal collectors that run hot are worth more per joule than ones that run warm, and why a power plant's exhaust heat, though large in kilojoules, is nearly worthless for making more work. The exergy chapter turns \"quality\" into a number.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Celsius in a ratio. Every temperature in a Carnot formula must be in kelvin. A difference TH − TL is the same in either unit, but the ratios TL/TH, TL/(TH − TL) and TH/(TH − TL) are not. The most common wrong answer in the whole chapter is 1 − 30/652 instead of 1 − 303.15/925.15.

Applying the Carnot formula to a real machine. η = 1 − TL/TH gives the ceiling. A real engine's efficiency is W/QH from measured flows, and it will be lower. Use the Carnot value only to check feasibility or to compute the reversible case.

Quoting a heat-pump COP against a refrigerator ceiling. The ceilings differ by exactly 1 (COPHP,rev = COPR,rev + 1), so compare like with like.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM
  • Compute ηth,rev, COPR,rev or COPHP,rev from two temperatures given in °C, then find W, QH or QL. The marks are for the kelvin conversion and for choosing the right one of the three formulas.
  • Judge a claim: \"an inventor claims an engine with η = 0.7 between 652 °C and 30 °C.\" Compute the ceiling (0.672), compare, and write the verdict as \"impossible: exceeds the Carnot efficiency, violates the second law\".
  • Explain what the thermodynamic temperature scale is and why the Kelvin scale is independent of the working substance; write (QH/QL)rev = TH/TL.
  • Explain \"quality of energy\" with a numerical comparison of the work obtainable from the same heat at two temperatures.
  • Rank three heat pumps (or refrigerators) by their Carnot COP given their operating temperatures, and say which direction a design change (smaller lift) moves the ceiling.
"}, "THERMO/entropy/s1": {"body": "

This lesson lets you take the second law, which so far has only said what a cycle cannot do, and turn it into a number you can compute for any process: entropy. By the end you can test whether a proposed engine is possible with one integral, define entropy as a property, and use the increase-of-entropy principle to compute how much irreversibility a process produced. In the degree this sits right after the Carnot chapter and before everything that uses an s column in a table: isentropic efficiencies, exergy, and every power and refrigeration cycle.

\n\n

The idea in plain words

\n

The Carnot chapter proved that no engine between two reservoirs can beat a reversible one, and that for a reversible engine QH/QL = TH/TL. Rewrite that as QH/TH − QL/TL = 0. In words: for a reversible cycle, the heat received divided by the temperature at which it is received sums to zero around the loop. Clausius showed that for any real (irreversible) cycle the same sum is negative. That is the Clausius inequality, and it is the only new physics in this whole chapter; everything else is bookkeeping built on it.

\n

The quantity δQ/T is special because its cyclic integral vanishes for every reversible cycle. Any quantity whose integral around a closed loop is zero depends only on the end states, which is exactly what a property is (volume and internal energy behave this way; work and heat do not). So δQrev/T defines a property. Clausius named it entropy, symbol S.

\n\n

Definitions

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Clausius inequality: for any thermodynamic cycle, ∮ δQ/T ≤ 0, where δQ is the heat transferred to the system at the boundary where the temperature is T (in kelvin). The equality holds for internally reversible cycles, the inequality for irreversible ones, and a cycle with ∮ δQ/T > 0 is impossible.

Entropy is the extensive property S (kJ/K) whose change between two states is ΔS = S₂ − S₁ = ∫₁² (δQ/T)int rev, evaluated along any internally reversible path joining the states. Specific entropy s = S/m has units kJ/kg·K.

Entropy generation Sgen (kJ/K) is the entropy created inside a system by irreversibilities (friction, unrestrained expansion, mixing, heat transfer across a finite temperature difference). It is never negative: Sgen > 0 for a real process, Sgen = 0 for a reversible one.

\n

Three things follow immediately. First, the definition only tells you entropy changes; absolute values come from the third law (statistical thermodynamics chapter) and tables just pick a reference state (for water, saturated liquid at the triple point has s = 0). Second, T must be absolute: a temperature in °C in a δQ/T makes the result meaningless and can even flip its sign. Third, the integral is along an internally reversible path even when the real process is irreversible, because entropy is a property and only the end states matter.

\n\n

The equations, symbol by symbol

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

ΔSsys = ∫₁² δQ/T + Sgen (closed system, kJ/K)

ΔSsys: change in the entropy of the system (kJ/K). ∫δQ/T: entropy transfer by heat, kJ/K, positive when heat comes in, with T the absolute temperature of the boundary where the heat crosses. Sgen: entropy generated inside the boundary, kJ/K, ≥ 0.

Sgen = ΔStotal = ΔSsys + ΔSsurr ≥ 0 (increase of entropy principle)

For an isolated system there is no entropy transfer at all, so ΔSisolated = Sgen ≥ 0: the entropy of an isolated system never decreases. A system plus everything it exchanges heat with is isolated, which is why the sum of the system change and the surroundings change is the generation.

ΔSreservoir = Q/T (a reservoir has constant T, so the integral is trivial; Q is signed, kJ; T in K)

\n

The one-line picture of every entropy problem: entropy change = entropy transfer + entropy generation. Heat carries entropy across the boundary (Q/T); work carries none; irreversibility creates it. That sentence is also the entropy balance of Lesson 4, so learn it here and you have already learned Lesson 4.

\n\n

Worked example 1: entropy generated by heat transfer across a temperature difference

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A source at 800 K transfers 1000 kJ of heat to a sink at 500 K through a metal bar. Find the entropy change of each reservoir and the entropy generated. (The bar is at steady state, so its own entropy does not change; the two reservoirs together form an isolated system.)

📊 FIGURE — Entropy bookkeeping when 1000 kJ flows from 800 K to 500 K
The same 1000 kJ is divided by 800 K on the way out but by 500 K on the way in, so the sink gains more entropy than the source loses. The 0.750 kJ/K difference is entropy generated.
  1. Source loses heat: Qsource = −1000 kJ, T = 800 K. ΔSsource = Q/T = (−1000 kJ)/(800 K) = −1.250 kJ/K.
  2. Sink gains heat: Qsink = +1000 kJ, T = 500 K. ΔSsink = (1000 kJ)/(500 K) = +2.000 kJ/K.
  3. Nothing else changes, so Sgen = ΔStotal = −1.250 kJ/K + 2.000 kJ/K = 0.750 kJ/K.
  4. Sanity check: Sgen is positive, so the process is possible and irreversible. Reverse it (1000 kJ from 500 K to 800 K by itself) and Sgen = −0.750 kJ/K, which is why heat never flows uphill on its own.
\n

Notice the pattern: the hot body loses less entropy than the cold body gains, because the same Q is divided by a smaller T on the cold side. The smaller the temperature difference, the smaller Sgen; in the limit Tsink → Tsource the transfer becomes reversible and generates nothing. That is the physical content of \"reversible heat transfer needs an infinitesimal ΔT\".

\n\n

Worked example 2: testing a claimed engine with the Clausius inequality

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

An inventor claims a heat engine receives 1000 kJ per cycle from a reservoir at 800 K and rejects 400 kJ per cycle to a reservoir at 300 K. Is it possible? What if it rejected only 300 kJ?

  1. Both heat transfers happen at constant reservoir temperatures, so ∮ δQ/T = QH/TH − QL/TL.
  2. Claim A: (1000 kJ)/(800 K) − (400 kJ)/(300 K) = 1.2500 kJ/K − 1.3333 kJ/K = −0.0833 kJ/K. Negative, so the cycle satisfies the inequality: possible, and irreversible.
  3. Cross-check with Carnot: ηclaimed = W/QH = (1000 − 400)/1000 = 0.600; ηCarnot = 1 − 300 K/800 K = 0.625. The claim is below the Carnot limit, consistent.
  4. Claim B: (1000 kJ)/(800 K) − (300 kJ)/(300 K) = 1.2500 − 1.0000 = +0.250 kJ/K. Positive, so the cycle is impossible. Its efficiency would be 0.700, above Carnot.
\n

Both tests (the inequality and the Carnot comparison) are the same physics. The inequality is more general: it works for any number of reservoirs and for heat transfer at varying temperature, where \"compare with Carnot\" is not defined.

\n\n

What entropy means physically

\n

Three views that will all be made precise later in the course:

\n
    \n
  • Entropy measures the quality of energy. 1000 kJ at 800 K can drive a Carnot engine to produce 1000 × (1 − 300/800) = 625 kJ of work against a 300 K environment; the same 1000 kJ at 500 K can produce only 400 kJ. The 0.750 kJ/K generated in Worked example 1 destroyed 300 K × 0.750 kJ/K = 225 kJ of work potential, which is precisely 625 − 400. The exergy chapter builds on this: work destroyed = T₀ · Sgen.
    • \n
  • Entropy measures dispersal. Energy that is spread over many molecules at low temperature is less available than the same energy concentrated at high temperature. Mixing, friction and free expansion all spread energy out without any heat crossing the boundary, and all generate entropy.
    • \n
  • Entropy counts microstates. Boltzmann's S = k ln W (k = 1.380649 × 10−23 J/K, W the number of microscopic arrangements consistent with the macroscopic state) is the subject of the statistical thermodynamics chapter. It is why entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero is zero.
    • \n
\n

Entropy is not conserved. Energy is conserved and can be traced; entropy is created by every real process and can only be moved out of a system by heat transfer (or mass flow for open systems). A refrigerator lowers the entropy of its contents by moving even more entropy into the kitchen; the total still rises.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Using °C in Q/T. ΔS of a reservoir at 25 °C receiving 500 kJ is 500/298.15 = 1.677 kJ/K, not 500/25 = 20 kJ/K. Every T in this chapter is kelvin.

Dividing by the wrong temperature. The T in the entropy transfer is the temperature of the boundary where heat crosses. If a system at 400 K receives heat from a reservoir at 600 K and you are computing the reservoir's entropy change, use 600 K; for the system, use its own boundary temperature (or, when the system temperature changes, integrate).

Concluding that ΔS < 0 is impossible. The entropy of a system can decrease (cool a gas, freeze water). What cannot decrease is the entropy of an isolated system, i.e. Sgen. Check the total before saying \"second law violation\".

Confusing entropy transfer with entropy generation. A reversible isothermal expansion has ΔS = Q/T > 0 with Sgen = 0; the entropy came in with the heat, it was not made.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

Typical questions from this section, in the order they appear in Cengel & Boles chapter 7 and Moran & Shapiro chapter 6:

  • \"A heat engine receives QH at TH and rejects QL at TL. Is it reversible, irreversible or impossible?\" Compute QH/TH − QL/TL: zero, negative, positive respectively.
  • \"Heat Q flows from a body at T₁ to a body at T₂. Find the total entropy change.\" Sgen = Q/T₂ − Q/T₁ (kelvin, T₂ < T₁).
  • \"During a process the entropy of the system decreases by 2 kJ/K. Is this possible?\" Yes if at least 2 kJ/K of entropy left with heat transfer, i.e. Qout/Tb ≥ 2 kJ/K.
  • \"Which of these is a property: Q, W, δQ/T, S?\" Only S (and the integral of δQrev/T that defines it).
  • Conceptual: entropy of an isolated system never decreases; Sgen is a measure of irreversibility, not a property; work transfers no entropy.
\n

Next lesson: how to get numbers for s from steam tables and from the ideal-gas relations, so that the ΔSsys term in these balances is never a mystery.

"}, "THERMO/entropy/s2": {"body": "

This lesson lets you put a number on Δs for any working fluid you will meet in the degree: water and refrigerants from tables, liquids and solids from one logarithm, and ideal gases from the two relations that every cycle chapter later uses. You also learn to read a T-s diagram, where reversible heat is an area, and to solve isentropic processes (the ideal turbine, compressor, pump and nozzle) with either constant specific heats or the relative-pressure columns of the air table. It sits between the definition of entropy (Lesson 1) and its use in device efficiencies (Lesson 3).

\n\n

Entropy is just another column in the table

\n

Because entropy is a property, a pure substance in a known state has a definite s, and the steam and refrigerant tables list it beside v, u and h. The rules are the same as for h in the properties chapter:

\n
    \n
  • Compressed liquid: s ≈ sf at the given temperature (pressure barely matters).
    • \n
  • Saturated mixture: s = sf + x·sfg, where x is the quality.
    • \n
  • Superheated vapour: read s directly from the superheat table at (P, T); interpolate if needed.
    • \n
\n

The reference state for water is saturated liquid at the triple point (0.01 °C), where sf = 0. Reference states differ between tables and between substances, which is harmless because only differences of s ever enter a calculation, but it means you must never mix two different tables inside one problem.

\n

Table: saturated water, selected rows by pressure (steam tables in the IAPWS-IF97 formulation, as printed in Cengel & Boles Table A-5; s in kJ/kg·K, h in kJ/kg).

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
P (kPa)Tsat (°C)hfhfghgsfsfgsg
1045.81191.812392.12583.90.64927.49968.1488
5081.32340.542304.72645.21.09126.50187.5930
10099.61417.502257.42674.91.30286.05617.3588
200120.21504.702201.52706.21.53025.59677.1269
1000179.88762.522014.62777.12.13814.44706.5850
\n
✅ VERIFIED

Every steam-table number in this chapter was recomputed from the IAPWS formulation with the open-source CoolProp library (coolprop.org) and agrees with the printed Cengel & Boles tables to the last digit or within 0.1 kJ/kg of rounding. A useful check you can do yourself: sfg must equal hfg/Tsat with Tsat in kelvin, e.g. at 50 kPa, 2304.7/(81.32 + 273.15) = 6.502 kJ/kg·K.

\n\n

The T-s and h-s diagrams

\n

On a T-s diagram the area under an internally reversible process curve is the heat transfer, because δQrev = T dS. This makes the diagram the natural home of cycles: a Carnot cycle is a rectangle (two isotherms, two vertical isentropes), and its efficiency is visibly the ratio of the enclosed rectangle to the area under the top edge. The saturation dome looks like the one on the T-v diagram, constant-pressure lines run up through the dome as horizontals and curve upward in the superheat region, and an adiabatic reversible process is a vertical line. The h-s (Mollier) diagram is the engineer's version for steady-flow devices, because Δh is the work of an adiabatic turbine or compressor and the vertical distance between the inlet point and the exit isobar at the same s is the isentropic work, read directly.

📊 FIGURE — The T-s diagram of water, with steam cooled at 1 MPa
Constant pressure is flat inside the dome and climbs in the superheat region. For a reversible path the area down to 0 K is the heat: shaded here for 1→2. A reversible adiabatic path is vertical.
\n\n

The Tds relations and the three families of substance

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Isentropic process: a process with constant entropy, s₂ = s₁. An internally reversible adiabatic process is isentropic. The converse is not guaranteed (an irreversible process that loses exactly the right amount of heat could also end with s₂ = s₁), but in the degree \"isentropic\" is used as the ideal model for adiabatic devices.

Relative pressure Pr and relative volume vr are dimensionless columns of the ideal-gas air table, defined so that for an isentropic process between two states, P₂/P₁ = Pr2/Pr1 and v₂/v₁ = vr2/vr1. They pack the variable-specific-heat integral into a lookup.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

T ds = du + P dv and T ds = dh − v dP (the Gibbs equations, per unit mass)

T: absolute temperature (K); ds: change in specific entropy (kJ/kg·K); du, dh: changes in specific internal energy and enthalpy (kJ/kg); P dv, v dP: pressure (kPa) times specific volume change (m³/kg), both in kJ/kg. They relate properties only, so they hold for every process, reversible or not; they were merely derived along a reversible path.

Incompressible substance (dv = 0, cp = cv = c): s₂ − s₁ = cavg ln(T₂/T₁). An isentropic process of a liquid or solid is therefore isothermal.

Ideal gas, constant specific heats: s₂ − s₁ = cv ln(T₂/T₁) + R ln(v₂/v₁) and s₂ − s₁ = cp ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(P₂/P₁), with R the gas constant (0.287 kJ/kg·K for air) and cp, cv evaluated at the average temperature.

Ideal gas, variable specific heats: s₂ − s₁ = s°₂ − s°₁ − R ln(P₂/P₁), where s°(T) = ∫₀T cp(T) dT/T is the tabulated standard-state entropy function (kJ/kg·K, Table A-17 for air).

Isentropic ideal gas, constant k = cp/cv: T₂/T₁ = (P₂/P₁)(k−1)/k = (v₁/v₂)k−1 and P vk = constant. With variable specific heats use P₂/P₁ = Pr2/Pr1 instead.

\n

Where the ideal-gas relations come from, in two lines: with dh = cp dT and v = RT/P, the second Gibbs equation gives ds = cp dT/T − R dP/P; integrate with cp constant to get the logarithms, or leave cp(T) inside the first integral and tabulate it as s°. Setting Δs = 0 in the constant-cp form and using cp − cv = R gives the (k−1)/k exponent.

\n\n

Worked example 1: steam cooled at constant pressure (tables)

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A piston-cylinder holds 2 kg of steam at 1 MPa, 300 °C. It is cooled at constant pressure to 200 °C by the surroundings at 25 °C. Find the entropy change of the steam, the heat transfer, and the entropy generated. Source: superheated water table (Cengel & Boles A-6, checked against IAPWS).

StatePTh (kJ/kg)s (kJ/kg·K)
1 superheated1 MPa300 °C3051.67.1246
2 superheated (Tsat at 1 MPa is 179.88 °C, so 200 °C is still vapour)1 MPa200 °C2828.36.6955

  1. Entropy change of the steam: ΔS = m(s₂ − s₁) = 2 kg × (6.6955 − 7.1246) kJ/kg·K = 2 × (−0.4291) = −0.858 kJ/K. Negative, as expected for cooling.
  2. Heat transfer at constant pressure equals the enthalpy change (boundary work is included in h): Q = m(h₂ − h₁) = 2 kg × (2828.3 − 3051.6) kJ/kg = −446.6 kJ (446.6 kJ leaves the steam).
  3. Surroundings receive 446.6 kJ at 298.15 K: ΔSsurr = 446.6/298.15 = +1.498 kJ/K.
  4. Sgen = ΔSsteam + ΔSsurr = −0.858 + 1.498 = 0.640 kJ/K.
  5. Sanity check: the steam's entropy fell, but the total rose; the generation is large because heat crossed a gap from 200-300 °C down to 25 °C.
\n\n

Worked example 2: air compressed and heated (ideal gas, both methods)

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Air goes from 100 kPa, 300 K to 600 kPa, 600 K. Find Δs (a) with constant specific heats at room temperature, (b) with cp at the average temperature, (c) with the variable-specific-heat table. Constants: R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K; cp(300 K) = 1.005 kJ/kg·K; cp(450 K) = 1.020 kJ/kg·K (Table A-2b); s°(300 K) = 1.70203, s°(600 K) = 2.40902 kJ/kg·K (Table A-17).

  1. Pressure term (same in every method): R ln(P₂/P₁) = 0.287 kJ/kg·K × ln(600/100) = 0.287 × 1.7918 = 0.5142 kJ/kg·K.
  2. (a) cp ln(T₂/T₁) = 1.005 × ln(600/300) = 1.005 × 0.6931 = 0.6966 kJ/kg·K; Δs = 0.6966 − 0.5142 = 0.1824 kJ/kg·K.
  3. (b) 1.020 × 0.6931 = 0.7070 kJ/kg·K; Δs = 0.7070 − 0.5142 = 0.1928 kJ/kg·K.
  4. (c) s°₂ − s°₁ = 2.40902 − 1.70203 = 0.7070 kJ/kg·K; Δs = 0.7070 − 0.5142 = 0.1928 kJ/kg·K.
  5. Sanity check: the table method is exact for an ideal gas; the average-cp method reproduces it to four decimals, while room-temperature cp is 5% low. Δs is positive: the heating (+0.707) outweighs the compression (−0.514).
\n\n

Worked example 3: isentropic expansion of air

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Air at 600 kPa, 500 K expands isentropically through a turbine to 100 kPa. Find the exit temperature with (a) k = 1.4 and (b) the relative-pressure column. Table A-17 values: Pr(500 K) = 8.411, Pr(300 K) = 1.3860, Pr(310 K) = 1.5546.

  1. (a) Exponent (k − 1)/k = 0.4/1.4 = 0.2857. T₂ = T₁ (P₂/P₁)0.2857 = 500 K × (100/600)0.2857 = 500 × 0.5995 = 299.7 K.
  2. (b) Pr2 = Pr1 × P₂/P₁ = 8.411 × (100/600) = 1.4018.
  3. Interpolate in the table between 300 K (1.3860) and 310 K (1.5546): T₂ = 300 + 10 × (1.4018 − 1.3860)/(1.5546 − 1.3860) = 300 + 10 × 0.0937 = 300.9 K.
  4. Sanity check: the two methods differ by about 1 K because cp varies little between 300 and 500 K; at 1000 K and above the gap grows to tens of kelvin and only method (b) is acceptable.
\n

One more family: incompressible substances. A 2 kg copper block (c = 0.385 kJ/kg·K, Table A-3) cooled from 400 K to 300 K has ΔS = 2 kg × 0.385 kJ/kg·K × ln(300/400) = 0.770 × (−0.2877) = −0.222 kJ/K. No pressure term appears, and a reversible adiabatic pumping of a liquid leaves its temperature (almost exactly) unchanged, which is why pump exit temperatures are never asked for.

\n
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

The whole s° column is one numerical integral: s°(T) = ∫ cp(T)/T dT from a reference temperature. With the polynomial cp(T) of Table A-2c and scipy.integrate.quad you can regenerate Table A-17 in five lines, and check any interpolation you are unsure of. The same script gives you Pr = exp(s°/R) up to a constant factor, which is exactly how the printed column was built. Treat the tables as a dataset with a known generating function, not as something to memorise.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Using cv with the pressure form or cp with the volume form. cp pairs with −R ln(P₂/P₁); cv pairs with +R ln(v₂/v₁). Mixing them changes the answer by R ln(T₂/T₁), which is usually the size of the answer itself.

Dropping the pressure term \"because it is a heating problem\". In Worked example 2 the pressure term is 0.514 kJ/kg·K against a total of 0.19; forgetting it turns the answer into 0.697.

Wrong exponent. T₂/T₁ = (P₂/P₁)(k−1)/k, not (P₂/P₁)k−1; and it is (v₁/v₂)k−1 with the volumes the other way up. For k = 1.4 the exponents are 0.2857 and 0.4.

Assuming an isentropic exit state is a vapour. Steam expanding isentropically from the superheat region usually ends inside the dome. Compare s₂ = s₁ with sg at the exit pressure: if s₂ < sg, compute the quality.

Mixing reference states: taking s₁ from one table (or software) and s₂ from another with a different zero. Use one source per problem.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM
  • \"Steam at P, T expands isentropically to P₂; find the exit quality and h₂.\" Set s₂ = s₁, read sf, sfg at P₂, x₂ = (s₂ − sf)/sfg, then h₂ = hf + x₂ hfg.
  • \"Air is compressed isentropically from (P₁, T₁) to P₂; find T₂.\" Constant k unless the temperatures are high or the question says \"account for variation of specific heats\", in which case use Pr.
  • \"Find Δs of the gas for the process A → B\" with a pressure change: the two-term formula with the correct sign on the pressure term.
  • \"Sketch the process on a T-s diagram and identify the area.\" Area under the curve = reversible heat; area inside a cycle = net work of the cycle (equal to net heat).
  • \"Which of the following processes is isentropic?\" Reversible and adiabatic; an isothermal process of an ideal gas is not (Δs = R ln(v₂/v₁)), and an adiabatic throttling is not (irreversible).
\n

Next lesson: the isentropic states you just learned to find become the benchmark for real turbines, compressors, pumps and nozzles.

"}, "THERMO/entropy/s3": {"body": "

This lesson turns the isentropic states of Lesson 2 into the yardstick for every real turbine, compressor, pump and nozzle. You will be able to compute the work a reversible steady-flow device needs, explain why pumping a liquid costs a few kJ/kg while compressing a gas costs hundreds, choose the intermediate pressure of a two-stage intercooled compressor, and use isentropic efficiencies to go from the ideal exit state to the real one. Every power and refrigeration cycle chapter later in the degree uses these four efficiencies on almost every problem.

\n\n

The idea in plain words

\n

A real adiabatic device is always worse than its reversible twin: friction, turbulence and shock waves turn some of the useful energy into internal energy of the fluid, so a turbine delivers less work and a compressor or pump demands more. The reversible adiabatic (isentropic) process is the natural best case, because it connects the same inlet state to the same exit pressure with no entropy generated. Two questions follow. First, how much work does the ideal device need? That comes from the Tds relation and turns into a single integral of v dP. Second, how close does the real device get? That is a ratio of actual to ideal work (or the reverse), called the isentropic efficiency, and it is a number the manufacturer or the examiner gives you.

\n\n

Reversible steady-flow work

\n

For a steady-flow device with one inlet and one exit, the energy balance per unit mass is δq − δw = dh + d(ke) + d(pe). If the process is internally reversible, δq = T ds, and the second Tds relation says T ds = dh − v dP. Substituting and cancelling dh leaves −δwrev = v dP + d(ke) + d(pe).

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

wrev,in = ∫₁² v dP + Δke + Δpe

wrev,in: reversible work input per unit mass (kJ/kg); v: specific volume (m³/kg); P: pressure (kPa), so v dP is in kPa·m³/kg = kJ/kg; Δke = (V₂² − V₁²)/2 and Δpe = gΔz, converted to kJ/kg by dividing J/kg by 1000. For a turbine the same expression is negative and its magnitude is the work output.

Pump (incompressible liquid, Δke = Δpe = 0): wpump,rev = v (P₂ − P₁)

Ideal gas, isentropic, constant k: wcomp,in = cp(T₂s − T₁) = (kRT₁)/(k − 1) · [(P₂/P₁)(k−1)/k − 1]

Ideal gas, polytropic Pvn = constant: wcomp,in = (nRT₁)/(n − 1) · [(P₂/P₁)(n−1)/n − 1]

Ideal gas, isothermal: wcomp,in = RT₁ ln(P₂/P₁). Here k = cp/cv (1.4 for air), n is the polytropic exponent, R is the gas constant (0.287 kJ/kg·K for air), and T₁ is the inlet temperature in kelvin.

\n

The whole story of compressors is in the factor v. Work is the area to the left of the process curve on a P-v diagram, so anything that keeps v small during compression saves work. A liquid has a tiny, nearly constant v. A gas has a large v that grows as the gas heats up during compression. Cooling the gas while it is being compressed pulls its v down, which is why the isothermal process (n = 1) needs the least work, the isentropic one (n = k) the most, and real cooled machines fall in between.

\n\n

Worked example 1: a liquid against a gas

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Compare the reversible work to raise (a) water and (b) air from 100 kPa to 1000 kPa, each entering at the inlet state below, with Δke and Δpe negligible. Then find (c) the isothermal work for the air and (d) the work of two isentropic stages with perfect intercooling. Sources: vf at 100 kPa = 0.001043 m³/kg (saturated water by pressure, Cengel & Boles Table A-5); air R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, k = 1.4; air enters at 300 K.

  1. (a) Pump, saturated liquid water in: w = v(P₂ − P₁) = 0.001043 m³/kg × (1000 − 100) kPa = 0.939 kJ/kg.
  2. (b) Isentropic exit temperature of the air: exponent (k − 1)/k = 0.4/1.4 = 0.2857; T₂s = 300 K × (1000/100)0.2857 = 300 K × 1.9307 = 579.2 K.
  3. Compressor work: w = cp(T₂s − T₁) = 1.005 kJ/kg·K × (579.2 − 300) K = 280.6 kJ/kg, about 299 times the pump work.
  4. (c) Isothermal: w = RT₁ ln(P₂/P₁) = 0.287 kJ/kg·K × 300 K × ln 10 = 0.287 × 300 × 2.3026 = 198.3 kJ/kg.
  5. (d) Two stages with intercooling back to 300 K: intermediate pressure Px = √(100 kPa × 1000 kPa) = 316.2 kPa; each stage has ratio 3.162, so Tx = 300 K × 3.1620.2857 = 416.8 K and each stage needs 1.005 × (416.8 − 300) = 117.4 kJ/kg; total 234.9 kJ/kg.
  6. Sanity check: 198.3 < 234.9 < 280.6 kJ/kg, so the two-stage machine sits between the isothermal ideal and single-stage isentropic compression, saving 16.3% of the single-stage work.
\n\n

Multistage compression with intercooling

\n

Real compressors cannot be cooled well enough through their casing to approach the isothermal line, so the practical trick is to compress part of the way, send the gas through a heat exchanger (the intercooler) that brings it back to near the inlet temperature, then compress again. Each extra stage moves the zigzag path closer to the isotherm. The saving is the area on the P-v diagram between the single-stage curve and the staged path.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Intercooling: cooling the gas at constant pressure between compression stages, ideally back to the first-stage inlet temperature.

Isentropic efficiency: a ratio that compares the actual device with an isentropic device that has the same inlet state and the same exit pressure. For devices that produce work it is actual/ideal; for devices that consume work it is ideal/actual, so it always lies between 0 and 1.

Isothermal efficiency: the benchmark for a compressor that is deliberately cooled, η = wisothermal/wactual; the isentropic benchmark is not a fair comparison for such a machine.

\n

For two stages with the same polytropic exponent and intercooling back to T₁, setting d(wtotal)/dPx = 0 gives the optimum intermediate pressure Px = √(P₁ P₂), which is the same as saying each stage should have the same pressure ratio, Px/P₁ = P₂/Px, and therefore the same work. For N stages each stage ratio is (P₂/P₁)1/N.

\n\n

Isentropic efficiencies of the four devices

\n\n\n\n\n\n
DeviceIsentropic efficiencyWhat you do with it
TurbineηT = wa/ws ≈ (h₁ − h₂a)/(h₁ − h₂s)h₂a = h₁ − ηT(h₁ − h₂s)
CompressorηC = ws/wa ≈ (h₂s − h₁)/(h₂a − h₁)h₂a = h₁ + (h₂s − h₁)/ηC
PumpηP = ws/wa = v(P₂ − P₁)/(h₂a − h₁)wa = v(P₂ − P₁)/ηP
NozzleηN = V₂a²/V₂s² ≈ (h₁ − h₂a)/(h₁ − h₂s)V₂a = √(2 ηN (h₁ − h₂s)) with Δh in J/kg
\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

ηT = (h₁ − h₂a)/(h₁ − h₂s) ηC = (h₂s − h₁)/(h₂a − h₁)

📊 FIGURE — Isentropic and actual paths of a turbine and a compressor on T-s
Both devices share inlet 1 and exit pressure. The ideal path (dashed) drops straight down or up at constant s; the real one (blue) ends to the right, at higher s and higher h, at state 2a.

h₁: inlet enthalpy (kJ/kg); h₂a: actual exit enthalpy (kJ/kg); h₂s: enthalpy at the exit pressure and the inlet entropy, s₂s = s₁ (kJ/kg). The approximations drop Δke and Δpe, which is standard for turbines and compressors. For an ideal gas with constant cp the enthalpy differences become cp times temperature differences, so ηC = (T₂s − T₁)/(T₂a − T₁). The nozzle ratio uses kinetic energies, so its efficiency applies to V², never to V.

\n

The procedure is always the same three moves: (1) fix the inlet state and read s₁; (2) find the ideal exit state at the actual exit pressure with s₂s = s₁; (3) apply the efficiency to the enthalpy difference to get h₂a, then use h₂a and P₂ to fix the real exit state. Because the actual exit has the same pressure but more enthalpy, it also has more entropy, which on a T-s or h-s diagram puts it to the right of the ideal exit on the same isobar.

\n
✅ VERIFIED

Steam values in Worked example 2 come from Cengel & Boles Tables A-5 (saturated water by pressure) and A-6 (superheated water); each was recomputed from the IAPWS formulation with the open-source CoolProp library (coolprop.org): at 3 MPa and 400 °C, h = 3231.7 kJ/kg and s = 6.9235 kJ/kg·K; at 50 kPa, hf = 340.54, hfg = 2304.7 kJ/kg, sf = 1.0912, sfg = 6.5018 kJ/kg·K.

\n\n

Worked example 2: a steam turbine with ηT = 0.85

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Steam enters an adiabatic turbine at 3 MPa, 400 °C and leaves at 50 kPa; ṁ = 20 kg/s and ηT = 0.85. Find the actual exit state, the power output and the entropy generated. Property source: the table named in the VERIFIED callout above.

StatePxh (kJ/kg)s (kJ/kg·K)
1 superheated, 400 °C3 MPan/a3231.76.9235
2s ideal exit50 kPa0.89702407.96.9235
2a actual exit50 kPa0.95062531.57.2721

  1. Ideal exit: s₂s = s₁ = 6.9235 kJ/kg·K is below sg = 7.5930 at 50 kPa, so the state is wet. x₂s = (s₂s − sf)/sfg = (6.9235 − 1.0912)/6.5018 = 0.8970.
  2. h₂s = hf + x₂shfg = 340.54 + 0.8970 × 2304.7 = 2407.9 kJ/kg.
  3. Isentropic work: ws = h₁ − h₂s = 3231.7 − 2407.9 = 823.8 kJ/kg.
  4. Actual work: wa = ηT ws = 0.85 × 823.8 kJ/kg = 700.2 kJ/kg, so h₂a = 3231.7 − 700.2 = 2531.5 kJ/kg.
  5. Actual exit quality: x₂a = (h₂a − hf)/hfg = (2531.5 − 340.54)/2304.7 = 0.9506.
  6. Power: Ẇ = ṁ wa = 20 kg/s × 700.2 kJ/kg = 14,004 kW ≈ 14.0 MW (the isentropic turbine would give 16.48 MW).
  7. Exit entropy: s₂a = sf + x₂asfg = 1.0912 + 0.9506 × 6.5018 = 7.2721 kJ/kg·K; Ṡgen = ṁ(s₂a − s₁) = 20 × (7.2721 − 6.9235) = 6.97 kW/K.
  8. Sanity check: the real exit is drier (0.9506 > 0.8970) and has higher entropy than the ideal one, exactly as friction heating predicts; Ṡgen is positive.
\n\n

Worked example 3: an air compressor, one stage or two

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Air (cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, k = 1.4, constant specific heats) is compressed from 100 kPa, 300 K to 800 kPa at ṁ = 0.5 kg/s, with ηC = 0.80. Find the power for (a) one stage and (b) two stages at the optimum intermediate pressure, intercooled to 300 K, each stage with ηC = 0.80.

  1. (a) T₂s = 300 K × (800/100)0.2857 = 300 × 1.8114 = 543.4 K.
  2. ws = cp(T₂s − T₁) = 1.005 × (543.4 − 300) = 244.7 kJ/kg.
  3. wa = ws/ηC = 244.7/0.80 = 305.8 kJ/kg; T₂a = 300 + 305.8/1.005 = 604.3 K.
  4. Ẇ = ṁ wa = 0.5 kg/s × 305.8 kJ/kg = 152.9 kW.
  5. (b) Px = √(100 × 800) = 282.8 kPa, stage ratio 2.828; Tx,s = 300 × 2.8280.2857 = 403.8 K.
  6. Isentropic work of both stages: 2 × 1.005 × (403.8 − 300) = 208.6 kJ/kg; actual: 208.6/0.80 = 260.7 kJ/kg.
  7. Ẇ = 0.5 × 260.7 = 130.4 kW, a saving of 14.7%.
  8. Sanity check: the single-stage actual entropy change is Δs = 1.005 ln(604.3/300) − 0.287 ln 8 = 0.107 kJ/kg·K, positive for an adiabatic device, as it must be.
\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Turning the efficiency upside down. Turbine: actual work = η × ideal. Compressor and pump: actual work = ideal ÷ η. If your compressor needs less work than the isentropic one, you multiplied when you should have divided.

Fixing the real exit state with s. The actual exit has s₂a > s₁. Use s₁ only to find the ideal state; the real state comes from h₂a and P₂.

Gauge pressures in the pressure ratio. (P₂/P₁)(k−1)/k needs absolute pressures; 700 kPa gauge over 0 kPa gauge is meaningless.

Applying ηN to velocity. Nozzle efficiency is a ratio of kinetic energies: V₂a = V₂s√ηN, not ηNV₂s. Also convert kJ/kg to J/kg before taking the square root.

Choosing the arithmetic mean as the intercooler pressure. The optimum is the geometric mean √(P₁P₂).

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM
  • Steam turbine with a stated ηT: find the actual exit quality or temperature and the power (Worked example 2).
  • Air compressor with ηC: find the actual exit temperature and the power; sometimes the reverse, find ηC from measured inlet and exit temperatures.
  • Pump work v ΔP ÷ ηP, usually as one line inside a Rankine-cycle problem.
  • Nozzle: find the exit velocity from ηN, or ηN from a measured velocity.
  • \"Show that the optimum intermediate pressure is √(P₁P₂)\" or \"find the work saved by two-stage intercooled compression\".
  • Conceptual: why a feed pump uses a tiny fraction of the turbine output while a gas-turbine compressor can take a large share of it.
\n

Next lesson: the entropy generated in Worked example 2 becomes the central quantity, measured by an entropy balance on any closed system or control volume.

"}, "THERMO/entropy/s4": {"body": "

This lesson gives you the last of the three balance equations of engineering thermodynamics. Mass and energy are conserved; entropy is not, and the entropy balance tells you exactly how much was created inside any closed system or control volume. With it you can decide whether a proposed device is possible, locate where a plant wastes its potential for work, and, in the exergy chapter that follows, convert Sgen into kilowatts of lost work. It closes the entropy chapter and is used in every later chapter that asks \"how irreversible is this?\"

\n\n

The idea in plain words

\n

Treat entropy like money in a bank account. It can be transferred in or out across the boundary, and it can be created inside, but it can never be destroyed. Transfers happen only two ways: with heat, and with mass that crosses the boundary. Work carries no entropy at all, which is the deepest reason why work is the more valuable form of energy. Whatever the account balance does that the transfers cannot explain must be generation, and generation is never negative. So a balance with a negative Sgen is not a surprising result, it is proof of an error or of an impossible claim.

\n\n

Definitions

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Entropy transfer by heat: heat Q crossing a part of the boundary that is at absolute temperature Tb carries entropy Q/Tb in the same direction as the heat.

Entropy transfer by mass: mass m crossing the boundary with specific entropy s carries entropy m·s (rate form ṁ·s).

Entropy generation Sgen: the entropy created by irreversibilities (friction, mixing, unrestrained expansion, heat transfer across a finite temperature difference, chemical reaction) within the chosen boundary. Sgen > 0 for an irreversible process, Sgen = 0 for a reversible one, Sgen < 0 never.

Boundary temperature Tb: the temperature of the surface where the heat crosses, not the average temperature of the system. Where it is chosen changes how much generation the balance counts, not whether the physics is right.

\n\n

The balance, symbol by symbol

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Sin − Sout + Sgen = ΔSsystem (general, kJ/K)

Closed system: S₂ − S₁ = Σ Qk/Tk + Sgen, where Qk is the heat into the system (kJ, negative if it leaves) through the part of the boundary at Tk (K).

Control volume, rate form: dSCV/dt = Σ Q̇k/Tk + Σ ṁisi − Σ ṁese + Ṡgen, with Q̇ in kW, ṁ in kg/s, s in kJ/kg·K and Ṡgen in kW/K; subscripts i and e are inlets and exits.

Steady flow (dSCV/dt = 0): Ṡgen = Σ ṁese − Σ ṁisi − Σ Q̇k/Tk

One stream: Ṡgen = ṁ(se − si) − Σ Q̇k/Tk; if the device is also adiabatic, se ≥ si, with equality only for the isentropic ideal of Lesson 3.

\n

Where to draw the boundary matters. If you draw it tight around a compressor casing, Tb is the casing temperature and Sgen counts only the irreversibility inside the machine. If you draw it a little further out, in the room air far enough away that the local temperature is the surroundings temperature T₀, the boundary also encloses the thin layer where heat drops from the casing temperature to T₀. This enlarged system gives a larger Sgen that includes the external irreversibility, and it is convenient because T₀ is usually the only temperature you know. Both are correct; they answer different questions.

\n

A preview: in the exergy chapter you will show that the work potential destroyed by a process is Xdestroyed = T₀ Sgen. That is why engineers care about the size of Sgen, not just its sign.

\n\n

Worked example 1: a closed system stirred by a paddle wheel

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

An insulated rigid tank holds 10 kg of liquid water at 20 °C. A paddle wheel does 200 kJ of work on it. Treat water as incompressible with c = 4.18 kJ/kg·K (liquid water near room temperature, Cengel & Boles Table A-3). Find the final temperature and the entropy generated.

  1. Energy balance (closed, rigid, adiabatic): Win = ΔU = m c (T₂ − T₁), so T₂ − T₁ = 200 kJ/(10 kg × 4.18 kJ/kg·K) = 4.785 K.
  2. T₁ = 20 + 273.15 = 293.15 K; T₂ = 293.15 + 4.785 = 297.935 K (24.8 °C).
  3. Entropy balance: no heat crosses, and work carries no entropy, so Sgen = ΔS = m c ln(T₂/T₁).
  4. Sgen = 10 kg × 4.18 kJ/kg·K × ln(297.935/293.15) = 41.8 kJ/K × 0.01619 = 0.677 kJ/K.
  5. Sanity check: positive, and it could not be undone: turning the paddle backwards does not cool the water. The same temperature rise produced by heat from a reservoir only slightly hotter than the water would generate almost nothing.
\n\n

Worked example 2: an adiabatic mixing chamber

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Hot water at 80 °C (ṁ₁ = 2 kg/s) and cold water at 20 °C (ṁ₂ = 3 kg/s) mix steadily at 200 kPa in an insulated chamber with no work. Treat the water as incompressible with c = 4.18 kJ/kg·K. Find the exit temperature and Ṡgen.

  1. Mass: ṁ₃ = 2 + 3 = 5 kg/s.
  2. Energy (Q̇ = Ẇ = 0, same c): ṁ₃T₃ = ṁ₁T₁ + ṁ₂T₂, so T₃ = (2 × 353.15 + 3 × 293.15)/5 = 317.15 K = 44.0 °C.
  3. Entropy (steady, adiabatic): Ṡgen = ṁ₁(s₃ − s₁) + ṁ₂(s₃ − s₂).
  4. Hot stream: 2 kg/s × 4.18 kJ/kg·K × ln(317.15/353.15) = −0.8989 kW/K.
  5. Cold stream: 3 kg/s × 4.18 kJ/kg·K × ln(317.15/293.15) = +0.9868 kW/K.
  6. Ṡgen = −0.8989 + 0.9868 = 0.0879 kW/K.
  7. Cross-check with the saturated-water table (Table A-4, compressed liquid taken as saturated liquid at the same T): sf(20 °C) = 0.2965, sf(80 °C) = 1.0756 kJ/kg·K; the mixed enthalpy (2 × 335.02 + 3 × 83.915)/5 = 184.36 kJ/kg gives T₃ = 44.02 °C and, again as saturated liquid at that temperature, s₃ = 0.6258 kJ/kg·K (IAPWS, via CoolProp); Ṡgen = 5 × 0.6258 − 2 × 1.0756 − 3 × 0.2965 = 0.0883 kW/K.
  8. Sanity check: the two methods agree within 0.5%, the small difference coming from c varying slightly with temperature. (Keep every state on the same basis: taking s₃ for compressed liquid at 200 kPa while the inlets use saturated-liquid values gives 0.0853 kW/K, a 3% error that comes purely from the mismatch.) The hot stream loses entropy, the cold one gains more, so the total rises even though energy is perfectly conserved.
\n\n

Worked example 3: a compressor that loses heat

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Air enters a compressor at 100 kPa, 300 K and leaves at 800 kPa, 560 K; ṁ = 0.5 kg/s and the power input is 150 kW. The surroundings are at 25 °C. With constant specific heats (cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K), find the heat loss and the entropy generated in the enlarged system whose boundary is at T₀.

📊 FIGURE — Entropy in, out and generated for a compressor that loses heat
Entropy enters with the inlet stream, leaves with the exit stream and with the heat; the work carries none. With the boundary at T₀ = 298.15 K the balance closes with 0.0801 kW/K generated.
  1. Energy balance (steady, Δke = Δpe = 0): Q̇ = ṁ cp(T₂ − T₁) − Ẇin = 0.5 kg/s × 1.005 kJ/kg·K × 260 K − 150 kW = 130.65 − 150 = −19.35 kW (19.35 kW leaves).
  2. Entropy change of the air: s₂ − s₁ = cp ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(P₂/P₁) = 1.005 × ln(560/300) − 0.287 × ln 8 = 0.6273 − 0.5968 = 0.0305 kJ/kg·K.
  3. ṁ(s₂ − s₁) = 0.5 kg/s × 0.0305 kJ/kg·K = 0.0152 kW/K.
  4. Heat term with Tb = T₀ = 298.15 K: −Q̇/T₀ = 19.35 kW/298.15 K = 0.0649 kW/K.
  5. Ṡgen = 0.0152 + 0.0649 = 0.0801 kW/K.
  6. Preview of the exergy chapter: T₀Ṡgen = 298.15 K × 0.0801 kW/K = 23.9 kW of work potential destroyed, about 16% of the 150 kW input.
  7. Sanity check: Ṡgen > 0. Most of it here is carried out with the lost heat, which leaves at the low temperature T₀.
\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

\"Steady means no entropy is generated.\" Steady means the entropy inside the control volume does not change; Ṡgen is carried out by the streams and the heat, and can be large.

Using the fluid temperature for Tb when the heat crosses at the wall or at the surroundings. Decide where the boundary is, then use the temperature there, in kelvin.

Wrong sign on the heat term. Heat leaving the system is negative in Σ Q/T, so −Σ Q̇/T in the steady-flow equation becomes a positive contribution to Ṡgen.

Giving work an entropy term. W/T does not exist; only heat and mass carry entropy.

Treating a throttle as isentropic because it is isenthalpic. he = hi in an adiabatic valve, but the pressure drop is unrestrained, so se > si.

Celsius inside a logarithm. ln(44/80) and ln(317.15/353.15) are very different numbers; only the second is right.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM
  • \"Find the rate of entropy generation\" for a turbine, compressor, valve, mixing chamber or heat exchanger: energy balance first for any unknown state, then one line of entropy balance.
  • Heat exchangers: take the whole exchanger, insulated, as the control volume; the two streams alone decide Ṡgen.
  • \"Is this claim possible?\" A device described by an inventor: compute Ṡgen; negative means impossible.
  • Closed-system problems with a reservoir: ΔS of the system plus Q/T of the reservoir, e.g. a hot block quenched in a lake.
  • \"Where would you draw the boundary to include the irreversibility of the heat transfer to the surroundings?\" At T₀, the enlarged system.
\n

With the three balances (mass, energy, entropy) in hand, the next chapter turns Sgen into exergy destroyed and asks how much work a system could ideally deliver.

"}, "THERMO/exergy/s1": {"body": "

This lesson lets you answer the question the first law cannot: not how much energy a system has, but how much work you could get out of it. That quantity is called exergy (older books say availability), and it sits at the hinge of the degree: it uses the entropy machinery of the previous chapter and it is the yardstick every cycle in the next three chapters is measured against. By the end you will be able to name the dead state, compute the exergy of kinetic and potential energy, separate useful work from the work spent pushing the atmosphere aside, and compute reversible work and irreversibility for a process.

The idea in plain words: energy has quality as well as quantity

A 1 kg brick at 40 °C in a 25 °C room and a phone battery may hold similar amounts of energy, yet nobody would try to run a phone on the brick. The first law counts joules; it says nothing about how usable those joules are. The second law does: work is the highest-grade form of energy (it can be converted to anything else without loss), while heat at a temperature close to the surroundings is nearly worthless because a heat engine running between 40 °C and 25 °C could convert only a few percent of it into work.

Exergy is the accounting tool that puts a single number on this. It asks: if this system were allowed to come, by the best possible (reversible) processes, into complete equilibrium with its environment, how much useful work would we collect on the way? That maximum is the exergy. Everything less than that maximum is lost, and the loss has a name (irreversibility) and, as the last section shows, a formula (T0·Sgen).

The dead state

📘 DEFINITION

The environment is the large body of surroundings (atmosphere, sea, ground) whose intensive properties are unaffected by anything the system does. Its temperature and pressure are written T0 and P0. Unless a problem says otherwise this course takes T0 = 25 °C = 298.15 K and P0 = 100 kPa (some texts use 101.325 kPa; always use the value the problem gives).

A system is at the dead state when it is in thermodynamic equilibrium with the environment: at T0 and P0, at rest relative to the environment, at the reference elevation, and with no chemical reaction or mixing possible with the environment. At the dead state the system has zero exergy: nothing more can be extracted from it. Properties at the dead state carry the subscript 0 (u0, h0, s0, v0).

Notice the words in equilibrium. A system at T0 and P0 but moving at 200 m/s is not dead; neither is a gas at T0 and P0 sitting on a 500 m tower. Nor, strictly, is pure oxygen at T0 and P0, because it could still mix with the atmosphere and that mixing could in principle drive a work-producing device. This course, like most first courses, ignores the chemical part and works with what is sometimes called the restricted dead state: thermal and mechanical equilibrium only. The combustion chapter reopens the chemical part.

Exergy defined

📘 DEFINITION

Exergy (symbol X for a total amount in kJ, x or φ or ψ per unit mass in kJ/kg) is the maximum useful work that could be obtained from a system in a given state as it comes to the dead state, exchanging heat only with the environment at T0. It is realised only by a fully reversible path.

Four facts follow. (1) Exergy is a property of the combination of system and environment, so changing T0 changes the exergy of a system that has not itself changed. (2) Exergy is never negative: a system not at the dead state can always drive a work-producing device, and at worst you get nothing. (3) Exergy is not conserved: real processes destroy it. (4) Exergy is the maximum for a work-producing device and the minimum input for a work-consuming one (the least work needed to bring the system from the dead state to the given state).

Exergy of kinetic and potential energy

Kinetic and potential energy are mechanical energy, which is already the highest grade. A reversible turbine could convert all of the kinetic energy of a stream into shaft work, and a reversible hydraulic machine could convert all of the potential energy of a lifted mass. So they count fully as exergy, whatever the temperature and pressure:

🧮 KEY EQUATION

xke = V²/2 and xpe = g·z

xke, xpe: exergy per unit mass (J/kg, divide by 1000 for kJ/kg); V: velocity relative to the environment (m/s); g = 9.81 m/s²; z: elevation above the environment reference level (m). For a mass m the totals are m·V²/2 and m·g·z (J). For a stream with mass flow rate ṁ (kg/s) the exergy rate is ṁ·V²/2 (W).

Two unit traps live here. V must be in m/s (divide km/h by 3.6), and V²/2 comes out in J/kg, not kJ/kg. At 12 m/s the specific kinetic energy is 72 J/kg = 0.072 kJ/kg, a tiny number per kilogram; wind power only works because the mass flow through a large rotor is enormous, as the worked example shows.

Surroundings work and useful work

When a piston pushes outward it has to shove the atmosphere out of the way, and that part of the work is not available to you. When the system is compressed the atmosphere helps push, so that part of the work is free. Exergy analysis therefore separates the two.

📊 FIGURE — Exergy, useful work and irreversibility from state to dead state
Top: exergy is the most useful work collected on a reversible trip to the dead state. Bottom left: expansion work spent pushing the atmosphere is not useful. Right: what a real process misses is I.
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Wsurr = P0·(V2 − V1) and Wu = W − Wsurr = W − P0·(V2 − V1)

Wsurr: work done on (or received from) the atmosphere (kJ); P0: environment pressure (kPa); V1, V2: initial and final system volume (m³); W: the actual work of the process by the sign convention of this course (work done by the system positive); Wu: useful work (kJ). kPa × m³ = kJ. For a rigid tank, a control volume or a cyclic device the volume does not change, Wsurr = 0 and Wu = W.

Reversible work and irreversibility

Fix the initial state, the final state and the environment. Of all the processes that connect the two states, the reversible one produces the most (or consumes the least) useful work. That amount is the reversible work Wrev. If the final state is the dead state, Wrev is the exergy; otherwise it is the maximum for that particular pair of states.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

I = Wrev,out − Wu,out (work-producing device) and I = Wu,in − Wrev,in (work-consuming device)

I: irreversibility, also called exergy destroyed, Xdestroyed (kJ); never negative; zero only for a totally reversible process. It is equal to T0·Sgen, which section 3 proves and uses. For a heat engine drawing QH from a reservoir at TH and rejecting to the environment, Wrev is the Carnot work: Wrev = (1 − T0/TH)·QH with temperatures in kelvin.

Irreversibility is the number a designer chases. Two engines with the same thermal efficiency can have very different irreversibilities if they run between different temperatures, which is why the second-law efficiency of the next section is a fairer score than ηth.

Worked examples

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A. Wind power potential. Wind at 12 m/s blows through a turbine rotor of diameter 40 m; air density 1.2 kg/m³. Find the specific exergy of the wind and the maximum power the rotor could produce.

  1. Kinetic exergy per kilogram: xke = V²/2 = (12 m/s)²/2 = 72 J/kg = 0.072 kJ/kg. (Mechanical energy is fully available, so no Carnot factor.)
  2. Swept area: A = π·(D/2)² = π·(20 m)² = 1256.6 m². (Use the radius, 20 m, not the diameter.)
  3. Mass flow through the rotor: ṁ = ρ·A·V = 1.2 kg/m³ × 1256.6 m² × 12 m/s = 18,096 kg/s.
  4. Exergy rate: Ẋ = ṁ·xke = 18,096 kg/s × 72 J/kg = 1,302,900 W = 1.30 MW.

Sanity check: 72 J/kg is tiny, but 18 tonnes of air per second makes it 1.3 MW; a real turbine of this size is rated around a third of that, because no rotor can stop the air completely and the flow is not reversible. Plausible.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

B. Heat engine irreversibility. An engine receives 500 kJ of heat from a furnace at 1200 K, produces 180 kJ of work and rejects the rest to the surroundings at 300 K. Find the reversible work, the irreversibility and the two efficiencies.

  1. Reversible (Carnot) work between 1200 K and the environment: Wrev = (1 − T0/TH)·QH = (1 − 300 K/1200 K) × 500 kJ = 0.75 × 500 kJ = 375 kJ.
  2. Irreversibility: I = Wrev − Wu = 375 kJ − 180 kJ = 195 kJ. (The engine is cyclic, so no surroundings work and Wu = W = 180 kJ.)
  3. Thermal efficiency: ηth = W/QH = 180 kJ/500 kJ = 0.36; Carnot efficiency ηrev = 1 − 300/1200 = 0.75.
  4. Ratio (the second-law efficiency of the next section): 180 kJ/375 kJ = 0.48: the engine delivers 48% of the work that was possible; 195 kJ of work potential was destroyed.

Sanity check: 320 kJ was rejected as heat; only 195 kJ of that was avoidable loss, the other 125 kJ had to be rejected even by a Carnot engine. Plausible.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

C. Useful work of a piston. A gas in a piston-cylinder expands from 0.1 m³ to 0.3 m³ doing 60 kJ of boundary work; the atmosphere is at 100 kPa.

  1. Surroundings work: Wsurr = P0·(V2 − V1) = 100 kPa × (0.3 − 0.1) m³ = 20 kJ.
  2. Useful work: Wu = W − Wsurr = 60 kJ − 20 kJ = 40 kJ.

Sanity check: a third of the boundary work went into pushing air out of the way, which is typical for a low-pressure expansion; the useful fraction rises as the gas pressure rises above P0.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Celsius inside a Carnot factor. (1 − 27/927) is not (1 − 300/1200). In example B the Celsius slip gives Wrev = 485 kJ instead of 375 kJ and an irreversibility that is 110 kJ too large. Every temperature that appears in a ratio or in an entropy term is absolute.

Forgetting that Wsurr can be negative. During a compression V2 < V1, so Wsurr is negative and the atmosphere supplies part of the compression work; the useful work you must provide is less than the boundary work. Apply the formula with signs and let it tell you.

Treating exergy as a property of the system alone. The same tank of hot water has more exergy in winter (low T0) than in summer. Always state the dead state you used.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

Three question shapes recur. (1) Compute the exergy of KE or PE: watch km/h and J versus kJ. (2) Given QH, TH, T0 and the actual work, find Wrev and I: Carnot factor first, subtract second. (3) Boundary work with an atmosphere: subtract P0·ΔV to get useful work; a rigid tank or a cyclic device has none.

Write the dead state on the first line of your answer (T0 = 298.15 K, P0 = 100 kPa) and keep every temperature in kelvin; markers look for exactly those two lines.

Section 1 gave the idea; this section gives the two formulas you will actually compute with, one for a fixed mass in a tank or cylinder (non-flow exergy, φ) and one for a stream passing through a turbine, nozzle or heat exchanger (flow exergy, ψ), plus the exergy carried by a quantity of heat. With those in hand you can score any device on a fair scale, the second-law efficiency, which compares what it did with the best that was thermodynamically possible. These are the property calculations the cycle chapters will repeat many times.

Why a fixed mass and a flowing stream need different formulas

Both formulas come from the same recipe: take the system from its state (P, T, V, z) to the dead state (P0, T0, at rest, at ground level) by reversible processes, exchange heat only with the environment at T0, and add up the useful work. The difference is the pressure term. A closed mass expanding to P0 must push the atmosphere aside, so the P0·(v − v0) surroundings work is subtracted. A flowing stream carries flow energy P·v that the upstream fluid supplied, and it delivers P0·v0 of it back to the environment at the exit; the net of the two is exactly why enthalpy h = u + P·v replaces internal energy.

Non-flow (closed-system) exergy

📘 DEFINITION

The non-flow exergy φ of a fixed mass is the maximum useful work per unit mass obtainable as it goes reversibly from its state to the dead state, with heat exchanged only with the environment.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

φ = (u − u0) + P0·(v − v0) − T0·(s − s0) + V²/2 + g·z

φ: non-flow exergy (kJ/kg); u, v, s: internal energy (kJ/kg), specific volume (m³/kg) and entropy (kJ/kg·K) at the state; u0, v0, s0: the same at the dead state (T0, P0); P0 in kPa so P0·v is kJ/kg; T0 in K; V²/2 and g·z in J/kg, divide by 1000. Total exergy X = m·φ (kJ). The change between two states, φ2 − φ1, drops the subscript-0 terms: Δφ = (u2 − u1) + P0·(v2 − v1) − T0·(s2 − s1) + ΔKE + ΔPE.

Read the terms as three stories. (u − u0) is the energy the system gives up on the way to the dead state. P0·(v − v0) is the work traded with the atmosphere (negative when the system must expand, positive when the atmosphere squeezes it). −T0·(s − s0) is the part that must leave as heat to the environment so that entropy is conserved on the reversible path; it is the tax the second law charges. For an ideal gas the pieces are u − u0 = cv·(T − T0), s − s0 = cp·ln(T/T0) − R·ln(P/P0) and v = R·T/P.

Flow exergy

🧮 KEY EQUATION

ψ = (h − h0) − T0·(s − s0) + V²/2 + g·z

ψ: flow exergy (kJ/kg), the maximum useful work per kilogram of a stream brought reversibly to the dead state; h, s: enthalpy (kJ/kg) and entropy (kJ/kg·K) of the stream; h0, s0: values of the same substance at T0, P0; other symbols as before. Exergy rate carried by a stream: Ẋ = ṁ·ψ (kW). The relation to non-flow exergy is ψ = φ + (P − P0)·v: a stream at pressure above P0 carries extra work potential in its flow work.

Change between inlet and exit of a steady-flow device: ψ2 − ψ1 = (h2 − h1) − T0·(s2 − s1) + ΔKE + ΔPE. The dead-state values cancel; you never need h0 for a change.

Exergy of heat

Heat is the low-grade carrier. A quantity Q crossing a boundary at absolute temperature T could at most drive a Carnot engine between T and T0, so its exergy is the Carnot work.

📊 FIGURE — How much of a quantity of heat is exergy, by temperature
The curve is the share of heat Q that a reversible engine to T0 could turn into work. It rises steeply above T0, is zero at T0, and turns negative for heat in a space colder than T0.
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Xheat = (1 − T0/T)·Q

Xheat: exergy carried by the heat (kJ); Q: the heat (kJ); T: absolute temperature of the boundary where the heat crosses (K); T0: environment temperature (K). If T varies during the transfer, integrate: Xheat = ∫(1 − T0/T)·δQ. At T = T0 the factor is zero: heat at environment temperature carries no exergy no matter how much of it there is. For T < T0 the factor is negative, which means heat leaving a cold space carries exergy into it; that is why a refrigerator delivers exergy to the cold box while removing heat from it.

Numbers to hold in your head with T0 = 298.15 K: 1000 kJ of heat at 800 K carries 627 kJ of exergy; the same 1000 kJ at 400 K carries only 255 kJ; at 298 K, zero. Same energy, very different value.

Worked examples

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A. Flow exergy of steam. Steam at 3 MPa and 400 °C flows at 30 m/s in a pipe at ground level. Environment: 25 °C, 100 kPa. Find ψ. Property source: Cengel & Boles steam tables (superheated water at 3 MPa, 400 °C; saturated liquid at 25 °C for the dead state), checked against IAPWS-95.

StatePTh (kJ/kg)s (kJ/kg·K)
1 (stream)3 MPa400 °C3231.76.9235
0 (dead state, compressed liquid ≈ saturated liquid at 25 °C)100 kPa25 °C104.830.3672
  1. Enthalpy difference: h − h0 = 3231.7 − 104.83 = 3126.87 kJ/kg.
  2. Entropy difference: s − s0 = 6.9235 − 0.3672 = 6.5563 kJ/kg·K.
  3. Entropy tax: T0·(s − s0) = 298.15 K × 6.5563 kJ/kg·K = 1954.76 kJ/kg.
  4. Kinetic term: V²/2 = (30 m/s)²/2 = 450 J/kg = 0.45 kJ/kg; g·z = 0.
  5. ψ = 3126.87 − 1954.76 + 0.45 = 1172.6 kJ/kg.

Sanity check: the exergy is well below the energy h − h0 (about 37% of it), as it must be for a substance whose work potential comes mostly through heat; the velocity term is negligible next to the thermal terms, which is typical below about 100 m/s.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

B. Non-flow exergy of compressed air. A 200 m³ rigid tank holds air at 1 MPa and 300 K; the environment is at 300 K and 100 kPa. Find the exergy of the air. Ideal gas with R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K.

  1. Because T = T0: u − u0 = cv·(T − T0) = 0, and no KE or PE.
  2. Specific volumes: v = R·T/P = 0.287 × 300/1000 = 0.0861 m³/kg; v0 = 0.287 × 300/100 = 0.861 m³/kg.
  3. Entropy: s − s0 = cp·ln(T/T0) − R·ln(P/P0) = 0 − 0.287 × ln(10) = −0.6608 kJ/kg·K.
  4. Entropy term: −T0·(s − s0) = −300 K × (−0.6608) = +198.25 kJ/kg.
  5. Atmosphere term: P0·(v − v0) = 100 kPa × (0.0861 − 0.861) m³/kg = −77.49 kJ/kg (the air must push the atmosphere aside as it expands ten-fold).
  6. φ = 0 + (−77.49) + 198.25 = 120.76 kJ/kg.
  7. Mass: m = P·V/(R·T) = 1000 kPa × 200 m³/(0.287 × 300) = 2322.9 kg. Total exergy X = m·φ = 2322.9 × 120.76 = 280,500 kJ ≈ 280 MJ.

Sanity check: the energy of the air (relative to the dead state) is zero because the temperature is T0, yet its exergy is 280 MJ; compressed air stores work potential in pressure, not in temperature. The isothermal expansion work R·T·ln(P/P0) = 198.25 kJ/kg minus the 77.49 kJ/kg paid to the atmosphere gives the same 120.76 kJ/kg, a good cross-check.

Second-law efficiency

📘 DEFINITION

The second-law efficiency ηII (also exergy efficiency or effectiveness) of a device is the ratio of the useful result it actually achieved to the best result a reversible device could have achieved under the same conditions. The most general form is ηII = exergy recovered / exergy supplied = 1 − exergy destroyed / exergy supplied. It lies between 0 and 1 and reaches 1 only for a totally reversible device.

🧮 KEY EQUATION
  • Heat engine: ηII = ηth/ηth,rev = Wu/Wrev, with ηth,rev = 1 − TL/TH.
  • Refrigerator or heat pump: ηII = COP/COPrev, with COPR,rev = TL/(TH − TL) and COPHP,rev = TH/(TH − TL).
  • Turbine, engine, any work producer: ηII = Wu/Wrev. Compressor, pump, any work consumer: ηII = Wrev/Wu.
  • Heat exchanger (two unmixed streams): ηII = ṁcold·(ψout − ψin)cold / ṁhot·(ψin − ψout)hot: exergy gained by the cold stream over exergy given up by the hot stream.
  • Mixing chamber: ηII = ṁ3·ψ3 / (ṁ1·ψ1 + ṁ2·ψ2): exergy leaving over exergy entering.

All temperatures in kelvin; all COPs and efficiencies dimensionless. ηII is not another name for isentropic efficiency: isentropic efficiency compares with an ideal device ending at a different exit state, second-law efficiency compares with a reversible device between the actual states and the actual environment.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

C. Two devices scored fairly. (i) A heat engine has ηth = 0.30 between 900 K and 300 K. (ii) A household refrigerator has COP = 3.0 keeping a freezer at −10 °C in a 25 °C kitchen.

  1. (i) ηth,rev = 1 − 300/900 = 0.6667. ηII = 0.30/0.6667 = 0.45. The engine wastes 55% of the work potential of its heat input.
  2. (ii) TL = −10 + 273.15 = 263.15 K; TH = T0 = 298.15 K. COPR,rev = 263.15/(298.15 − 263.15) = 263.15/35 = 7.519.
  3. (ii) ηII = 3.0/7.519 = 0.399: a COP of 3 sounds generous (300%!) but the refrigerator uses 2.5 times the minimum work.

Sanity check: both results are between 0 and 1, and a COP of 3 being a 40% second-law device is the usual finding for vapour-compression refrigerators; the refrigeration chapter will show where the other 60% goes.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Using ψ for a tank or φ for a pipe. The tank does not have flow work, so its formula has u and the P0·(v − v0) term; the pipe has h and no atmosphere term. In example B the wrong (flow) formula gives 198 kJ/kg instead of 121 kJ/kg, an error of 64%.

Dropping the T0·(s − s0) term. Then ψ collapses to h − h0 and you have computed energy, not exergy: 3127 kJ/kg instead of 1173 kJ/kg in example A.

Celsius in COPrev or in the Carnot factor. −10/(25 − (−10)) is negative; a negative COP is the tell-tale that a kelvin conversion was skipped.

Wrong dead-state substance. h0 and s0 are for the same fluid at T0, P0: for water that is compressed liquid at 25 °C, well approximated by the saturated-liquid values at 25 °C, not steam and not zero.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

Expect one full property calculation (ψ or φ from tables or ideal-gas relations, dead state stated, three or four numbered lines) and one short second-law-efficiency question (engine or refrigerator: compute the reversible figure, divide). The exergy-of-heat formula appears inside larger problems: whenever heat crosses a boundary at a known temperature, (1 − T0/T)·Q is the exergy that came with it.

Show the sign of P0·(v − v0) explicitly and say in words why it is negative for a gas above P0; markers reward that sentence.

This lesson gives you the third great balance of the subject. You already write an energy balance (energy in − energy out = change in stored energy) and an entropy balance (entropy in − entropy out + entropy generated = change in stored entropy). The exergy balance is their combination, and it has the property that makes it useful: the term that appears is a destruction, always positive, and it lands on the component that caused it. That lets you audit a whole power plant and say, in kJ, where the work potential of the fuel was lost. This is the analysis tool that the cycle chapters and the capstone design project will use.

The balance in words

📘 DEFINITION

The exergy balance for any system over any process: exergy in − exergy out − exergy destroyed = change in the exergy of the system. Exergy enters and leaves by heat, work and mass flow. Exergy destroyed is never negative (the decrease of exergy principle); it is zero only for a totally reversible process. The exergy destroyed is also called the irreversibility I.

BalanceTransfer termsGeneration or destruction termSign rule
Energyheat, work, massnone (conserved)always balances exactly
Entropyheat (Q/T), mass; not workSgen ≥ 0 addedSgen < 0 is impossible
Exergyheat (Carnot factor × Q), work, massXdestroyed = T0·Sgen ≥ 0 subtractedXdestroyed < 0 is impossible

Exergy transfer by heat, work and mass

🧮 KEY EQUATION
  • By heat crossing a boundary at absolute temperature Tk: Xheat = (1 − T0/Tk)·Qk (kJ). Sum over every boundary temperature.
  • By work: Xwork = W − Wsurr = W − P0·(V2 − V1) for boundary work of a closed system (kJ); Xwork = W for shaft or electrical work and for every control volume.
  • By mass: Xmass = m·ψ (kJ) or the rate ṁ·ψ (kW), with ψ the flow exergy of section 2.

Qk: heat crossing at Tk (kJ); W: work (kJ); m: mass crossing the boundary (kg); ψ: flow exergy (kJ/kg); T0, Tk in K. Note the asymmetry: entropy does not travel with work, but exergy does, all of it.

Exergy destruction equals T0 times the entropy generated

Take the energy balance for a closed system, multiply the entropy balance by T0, subtract, and rearrange. The heat terms combine into (1 − T0/Tk)·Qk, the stored-energy and stored-entropy terms combine into the exergy change of section 2, the entropy-generation term becomes T0·Sgen, and it appears with a minus sign. Nothing new was assumed: the exergy balance is the first law plus the second law with a common unit.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

Xdestroyed = I = T0·Sgen

Xdestroyed: exergy destroyed (kJ, or kW for a rate); T0: environment temperature (K), not the system temperature; Sgen: entropy generated inside the boundary you drew (kJ/K or kW/K). This is the fastest route in most problems: compute Sgen with the entropy balance you already know, multiply by T0.

Closed system, states 1 to 2: X2 − X1 = Σ(1 − T0/Tk)·Qk − [W − P0·(V2 − V1)] − T0·Sgen, with X = m·φ.

Steady-flow device, per unit mass, one inlet and one exit: (1 − T0/Tk)·qk − w + (ψ1 − ψ2) − xdestroyed = 0. Its reversible-work form: wrev = (ψ1 − ψ2) + (1 − T0/Tk)·qk, and for an adiabatic device simply wrev = ψ1 − ψ2.

If Sgen is the boundary-dependent quantity, so is Xdestroyed. Draw the boundary at the outer surface of a hot device, where heat leaves at T0, and the exergy destruction of the heat transfer is charged to the device; draw it at the hot inner wall and that destruction is charged to the surroundings instead. Say where your boundary is.

Worked examples

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A. Steam turbine with heat loss. Steam enters a turbine at 3 MPa, 400 °C and leaves at 50 kPa, 100 °C. The turbine loses 10 kJ/kg of heat to the surroundings at 25 °C; kinetic and potential energy changes are negligible. Find the work, the exergy destroyed, the reversible work and the second-law efficiency. Property source: Cengel & Boles superheated steam table (checked against IAPWS-95).

📊 FIGURE — Where a steam turbine’s work potential goes, per kilogram
Left: inlet and exit states, work out and a small heat leak. Right: of 779.4 kJ/kg that a reversible turbine could give, 539.3 is delivered and 240.1 is destroyed, T0 times s gen.
StatePTh (kJ/kg)s (kJ/kg·K)
1 inlet3 MPa400 °C3231.76.9235
2 exit50 kPa100 °C2682.47.6953
  1. Energy balance (steady flow, per kg): wout = h1 − h2 − qout = 3231.7 − 2682.4 − 10 = 539.3 kJ/kg.
  2. Entropy balance with the boundary at the outer surface (heat leaves at T0): sgen = s2 − s1 + qout/T0 = (7.6953 − 6.9235) + 10/298.15 = 0.7718 + 0.0335 = 0.8053 kJ/kg·K.
  3. Exergy destroyed: xdestroyed = T0·sgen = 298.15 K × 0.8053 kJ/kg·K = 240.1 kJ/kg.
  4. Reversible work: wrev = ψ1 − ψ2 = (h1 − h2) − T0·(s1 − s2) = 549.3 − 298.15 × (−0.7718) = 549.3 + 230.1 = 779.4 kJ/kg. (The heat leaves at T0, so it carries no exergy and adds nothing here.)
  5. Cross-check: wrev − wout = 779.4 − 539.3 = 240.1 kJ/kg, the same as step 3, as the balance demands.
  6. Second-law efficiency: ηII = wout/wrev = 539.3/779.4 = 0.692.

Sanity check: the 10 kJ/kg of heat loss costs only 10 kJ/kg of work, but the entropy rise inside the turbine (friction, throttling across blades) costs 230 kJ/kg of work potential; the loss that matters is the one that does not appear in the energy balance at all.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

B. Heat conduction through a wall. 1000 W flows steadily through a house wall whose inner surface is at 20 °C and outer surface at 5 °C; the outdoor environment is at 0 °C. Find the exergy destroyed in the wall.

  1. Kelvin first: Tin = 293.15 K, Tout = 278.15 K, T0 = 273.15 K.
  2. Entropy balance for the wall (steady, so no storage): Ṡgen = Q̇/Tout − Q̇/Tin = 1000/278.15 − 1000/293.15 = 3.5952 − 3.4112 = 0.1840 W/K.
  3. Ẋdestroyed = T0·Ṡgen = 273.15 K × 0.1840 W/K = 50.3 W.
  4. Cross-check by exergy transfer: in = (1 − 273.15/293.15) × 1000 = 68.2 W; out = (1 − 273.15/278.15) × 1000 = 18.0 W; destroyed = 68.2 − 18.0 = 50.2 W (rounding). Same answer.

Sanity check: the wall passes all 1000 W of energy but destroys three-quarters of the exergy that entered it. Heat transfer across a finite temperature difference is the most common irreversibility in engineering and this is what it looks like in numbers.

Where the losses really are in a power plant

Ask a first-law thinker where a steam plant loses most and the answer is the condenser: it throws away roughly 60% of the fuel energy as warm water. Ask the exergy balance and the answer is the boiler. The heat rejected in the condenser leaves at 30 to 40 °C, a few kelvin above T0, so it carries almost no exergy: energy, yes, work potential, no. The boiler, on the other hand, transfers heat from combustion gases at well over 1000 K to steam at 500 to 600 K. That temperature gap destroys exergy on a huge scale, and the combustion itself destroys more before the heat is even transferred.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

C. Boiler versus condenser. Per kilogram of steam a plant receives 2000 kJ of heat in the boiler from gases at an average 1500 K into steam at an average 550 K, and rejects 1300 kJ in the condenser from steam at 320 K to cooling water at the environment, 298.15 K. Compare the exergy destroyed.

  1. Boiler (heat transfer across the gas-to-steam gap): xdestroyed = T0·q·(1/Tsteam − 1/Tgas) = 298.15 × 2000 × (1/550 − 1/1500) = 298.15 × 2000 × 0.0011515 = 686.6 kJ/kg, which is 34% of the heat added.
  2. Condenser: xdestroyed = T0·q·(1/T0 − 1/Tsteam) = q·(1 − T0/Tsteam) = 1300 × (1 − 298.15/320) = 1300 × 0.0683 = 88.8 kJ/kg, 6.8% of the heat rejected.
  3. Ratio: the boiler destroys 686.6/88.8 ≈ 7.7 times more exergy than the condenser while the condenser handles the larger energy stream.

Sanity check: the exergy of the boiler heat on the gas side is 2000 × (1 − 298.15/1500) = 1602 kJ/kg and on the steam side 2000 × (1 − 298.15/550) = 916 kJ/kg; the difference, 686 kJ/kg, matches step 1. Raising the steam temperature (superheat, supercritical pressure, reheat) narrows the gap; that is the design lever the vapour-cycle chapter pulls.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

An exergy audit is a group-by. Put every component in a pandas DataFrame with columns for exergy in, exergy out and destroyed = T0·Sgen, add a column for the share of the fuel exergy destroyed, and sort descending. The top row is where the engineering effort should go, and the sum of the destroyed column plus the net work plus the exergy of the rejected heat must equal the fuel exergy, which is a one-line assertion that catches sign mistakes. The same table, drawn as a bar chart of shares, is the standard exergy-flow figure in plant reports.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Multiplying Sgen by the system temperature. Exergy destruction is T0·Sgen with the environment temperature, always. Using the turbine's own temperature in example A gives a meaningless number.

Forgetting the heat term in Sgen. For the turbine, s2 − s1 alone gives 230.1 kJ/kg destroyed instead of 240.1; the heat that leaves carries entropy out, so sgen is larger than the entropy rise of the fluid.

Reading a negative Xdestroyed as a result. It is a diagnosis: a temperature in Celsius, a sign slip in the heat direction, or a boundary drawn inconsistently between the energy and entropy balances.

Charging exergy to heat at the wrong temperature. (1 − T0/T) uses the temperature of the boundary where the heat crosses, which depends on where you drew the boundary; be explicit about it.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

The standard long problem is a steady-flow device (turbine, compressor, nozzle, heat exchanger, mixing chamber) with a heat loss: find the actual work from the energy balance, sgen from the entropy balance, multiply by T0, then quote wrev = w + xdestroyed and ηII. Always present the cross-check wrev = ψ1 − ψ2 + exergy of heat; two routes agreeing is worth marks.

Conceptual questions ask why the boiler, not the condenser, is the main exergy sink, and why heat transfer across a large ΔT is irreversible even though energy is conserved: answer with (1 − T0/T) at the two temperatures.
