This lesson gives you the modelling toolkit for every engine in the chapter: the air-standard assumptions that turn a messy, burning, flowing mixture into a clean closed cycle of air, the engine vocabulary (bore, stroke, top and bottom dead centre, displacement, compression ratio) that every exam problem uses without explaining, the mean effective pressure that lets you compare engines of different size, and the Carnot cycle as the ceiling against which all of them are judged. It sits right after the second law and entropy chapters in the degree: you already know that ηCarnot = 1 − TL/TH is the limit; now you learn why real gas engines do not even try to follow that cycle, and what they do instead.

\n\n

Why we model engines with ideal cycles

\n

A car engine does not run a thermodynamic cycle in the strict sense. Fresh air and fuel enter, burn, and leave as exhaust; the working fluid at the end is chemically different from the fluid at the start. A gas turbine is the same: air in, combustion products out. Analysing the real device needs chemistry, fluid mechanics and heat transfer all at once. The engineering trick is to replace the real engine with an ideal cycle: a closed, internally reversible cycle that keeps the essential shape of the real one (compression, heat addition, expansion, heat rejection) and drops everything else. The ideal cycle will overpredict the efficiency, but it gets the trends right: what happens when you raise the compression ratio, the pressure ratio or the peak temperature. That is what you use it for.

\n

Keep one principle from the second law in mind throughout. For any cycle, thermal efficiency rises when the average temperature at which heat is supplied rises, and when the average temperature at which heat is rejected falls. Every improvement in this chapter (higher compression ratio, regeneration, intercooling, reheating) can be explained by one of those two averages moving in the right direction.

\n\n

The air-standard assumptions

\n
📘 DEFINITION

The air-standard assumptions are:

  1. The working fluid is air, which circulates continuously in a closed loop and always behaves as an ideal gas.
  2. All processes in the cycle are internally reversible.
  3. The combustion process is replaced by heat addition from an external source.
  4. The exhaust process is replaced by heat rejection that returns the air to its initial state.

The cold-air-standard assumptions add one more: the specific heats of air are constant at their room-temperature (25 °C) values. In this chapter that means cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K and k = cp/cv = 1.4. Every example and quiz answer in this chapter is cold-air-standard unless it says otherwise.

\n

Why is this reasonable? In an engine the mixture is mostly nitrogen from the air (the fuel is a small fraction of the mass), so the working fluid really is close to air. The cost is accuracy: real specific heats rise with temperature, and at combustion temperatures of 1500 to 2500 K the cold-air-standard values are noticeably off, so cold-air-standard efficiencies come out higher than variable-specific-heat efficiencies. Textbooks then redo problems with the ideal-gas air table (variable specific heats); the method is identical, you just read u, h and the relative pressure and volume from a table instead of using cv·ΔT.

\n\n

Reciprocating engine vocabulary

\n

The reciprocating (piston-cylinder) engine is the engine of cars, trucks, small aircraft, ships and generators. The piston moves back and forth between two extreme positions. At top dead centre (TDC) the volume in the cylinder is smallest; at bottom dead centre (BDC) it is largest. The distance between them is the stroke, S, and the diameter of the piston is the bore, B. Air or air-fuel mixture enters through the intake valve, and combustion products leave through the exhaust valve.

📊 FIGURE — Piston-cylinder vocabulary and the meaning of mean effective pressure
Left: the piston travels the stroke between TDC and BDC, sweeping the displacement volume. Right: MEP is the constant pressure whose rectangle over V(d) has the same area as the cycle.
\n
📘 DEFINITION

Clearance volume Vmin (also VTDC): the cylinder volume with the piston at TDC. Displacement volume Vd: the volume the piston sweeps between TDC and BDC, Vd = Vmax − Vmin. The compression ratio r is the ratio of the largest to the smallest cylinder volume.

Two ignition families: spark-ignition (SI) engines ignite the mixture with a spark plug (petrol engines, modelled by the Otto cycle); compression-ignition (CI) engines compress air until it is hot enough to ignite injected fuel on its own (diesel engines, modelled by the Diesel cycle).

🧮 KEY EQUATION

Vd = (π/4)·B²·S

r = Vmax/Vmin = VBDC/VTDC = (Vd + Vc)/Vc

Wnet = MEP × (Vmax − Vmin) = MEP × Vd

Ẇnet = Wnet,cycle × ncyl × N / nR

Vd: displacement per cylinder (m³); B: bore (m); S: stroke (m); Vc = Vmin: clearance volume (m³); r: compression ratio (dimensionless, a volume ratio); MEP: mean effective pressure (kPa, so kPa × m³ = kJ); Wnet: net work per cylinder per cycle (kJ); Ẇnet: engine power (kW); ncyl: number of cylinders; N: crankshaft speed (rev/s); nR: crank revolutions per cycle, 2 for a four-stroke engine and 1 for a two-stroke. Per unit mass, MEP = wnet/(vmax − vmin) with w in kJ/kg and v in m³/kg.

\n

The mean effective pressure (MEP) is a fictitious constant pressure that, if it pushed on the piston for the whole power stroke, would produce the same net work as the real cycle. It is the fair way to compare engines of different size: work scales with displacement, so work divided by displacement is a measure of how hard each litre of the engine is working. Of two engines of equal displacement, the one with the larger MEP delivers more work per cycle and therefore more power at the same speed.

\n\n

The Carnot cycle as the benchmark, and why engines do not use it

\n

You met the Carnot cycle in the second law chapter: two reversible isothermal processes and two reversible adiabatic (isentropic) processes. It can be run with a gas in a piston-cylinder: isothermal expansion at TH while heat is added, isentropic expansion down to TL, isothermal compression at TL while heat is rejected, and isentropic compression back up to TH. Its efficiency depends only on the two reservoir temperatures.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

ηth,Carnot = 1 − TL/TH

ηth,Carnot: thermal efficiency of the Carnot cycle (dimensionless); TL, TH: absolute temperatures (K) at which heat is rejected and supplied. For isentropic processes of an ideal gas with constant specific heats you also need T2/T1 = (v1/v2)k−1 = (P2/P1)(k−1)/k, and for an isothermal process of an ideal gas q = R·T·ln(v2/v1) (kJ/kg).

\n

In practice nobody builds a Carnot gas engine. Isothermal heat transfer at a finite rate needs either a huge heat-exchange area or a very slow process; the isentropic legs need enormous pressure and volume ratios to span a useful temperature range; and, as the worked example shows, the net work per cycle is small compared with the volume swept, so the MEP is low and the engine would be huge for its power. The Carnot cycle is the yardstick, not the design.

\n\n

Worked example: engine geometry, MEP and power, then a Carnot gas cycle

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A. Geometry and power. A four-cylinder, four-stroke engine has a bore of 86 mm, a stroke of 86 mm and a compression ratio of 10.5. Each cylinder produces 0.55 kJ of net work per cycle at 3000 rpm. Find the displacement, clearance volume, MEP and power.

  1. Displacement per cylinder: Vd = (π/4)·B²·S = (π/4) × (0.086 m)² × 0.086 m = 4.996 × 10−4 m³ = 0.4996 L.
  2. Total displacement: 4 × 0.4996 L = 1.998 L, a \"2.0 litre\" engine.
  3. Clearance volume from r = (Vd + Vc)/Vc: Vc = Vd/(r − 1) = 0.4996 L/9.5 = 0.05258 L = 52.6 cm³.
  4. Largest volume: Vmax = Vd + Vc = 0.4996 + 0.0526 = 0.5521 L.
  5. MEP = Wnet/Vd = 0.55 kJ/(4.996 × 10−4 m³) = 1101 kPa ≈ 1.10 MPa.
  6. Speed: N = 3000 rev/min ÷ 60 = 50 rev/s. Four-stroke, so nR = 2 and each cylinder fires 25 times per second.
  7. Power: Ẇ = 0.55 kJ × 4 × 50 rev/s / 2 = 55.0 kW.

B. Carnot gas cycle. Air runs a Carnot cycle between TL = 300 K and TH = 1200 K and receives 200 kJ/kg of heat. At the largest volume (end of isentropic expansion, state 3) the pressure is 100 kPa. Find η, wnet, the peak pressure, the volume ratio and the MEP. States: 1→2 isothermal expansion at TH, 2→3 isentropic expansion, 3→4 isothermal compression at TL, 4→1 isentropic compression.

  1. η = 1 − 300 K/1200 K = 0.75; wnet = 0.75 × 200 kJ/kg = 150 kJ/kg; qout = 50 kJ/kg.
  2. Isothermal expansion volume ratio: ln(v2/v1) = qin/(R·TH) = 200/(0.287 × 1200) = 0.5807, so v2/v1 = 1.787 (the compression 3→4 has the same ratio, v3/v4 = 1.787).
  3. Pressure ratio across each isentropic leg: (TH/TL)k/(k−1) = 43.5 = 128.
  4. State 3: v3 = R·TL/P3 = 0.287 × 300/100 = 0.861 m³/kg. State 4: v4 = 0.861/1.787 = 0.4817 m³/kg.
  5. State 1 (isentropic from 4): v1 = v4·(TL/TH)1/(k−1) = 0.4817 × 0.252.5 = 0.4817 × 0.03125 = 0.01505 m³/kg.
  6. Peak pressure: P1 = R·TH/v1 = 0.287 × 1200/0.01505 = 22,880 kPa ≈ 22.9 MPa.
  7. Overall volume ratio v3/v1 = 0.861/0.01505 = 57.2.
  8. MEP = wnet/(v3 − v1) = 150 kJ/kg/(0.861 − 0.01505) m³/kg = 177 kPa.

Sanity check: the Carnot cycle needs a 57:1 volume ratio and a 23 MPa peak to deliver an MEP of only 177 kPa, about a sixth of the 1.1 MPa MEP of the ordinary engine in part A. That is the practical case against it in two numbers.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Compression ratio is a volume ratio, not a pressure ratio. r = Vmax/Vmin. In an isentropic compression the pressure ratio is rk (18.4 for r = 8), which is much larger. Gas turbines use the pressure ratio rp; piston engines use the volume ratio r. Do not swap them.

Clearance volume is Vd/(r − 1), not Vd/r. The compression ratio divides Vmax = Vd + Vc, not Vd, by Vc.

MEP divides by the displacement, Vmax − Vmin, never by Vmax alone.

A four-stroke engine fires once every two revolutions. Forgetting nR = 2 doubles the power.

Kelvin, always. η = 1 − TL/TH in degrees Celsius gives nonsense (27 °C and 1227 °C would give 97.8% instead of the correct 80%).

★ ON THE EXAM

Expect: (1) list the air-standard assumptions and say what cold-air-standard adds; (2) geometry from bore, stroke and compression ratio, including the clearance volume; (3) MEP from net work and displacement, and power from MEP, speed and the number of strokes; (4) a one-paragraph argument for why the Carnot cycle is the upper limit yet impractical for gas engines (isothermal heat transfer, huge pressure ratios, low MEP); (5) a statement that raising the average heat-addition temperature, or lowering the average rejection temperature, raises efficiency.

Always write down which assumptions you use and the property values (cp, cv, k, R); examiners give marks for the model as well as the number.

"}, "THERMO/gascycles/s2": {"body": "

This lesson lets you analyse the two ideal cycles behind almost every piston engine: the Otto cycle for spark-ignition (petrol) engines and the Diesel cycle for compression-ignition engines, plus the dual cycle that sits between them. By the end you can fill in a four-state table (P, T, v) for either cycle, compute heat in, heat out, net work, thermal efficiency and MEP, and explain from one formula why raising the compression ratio raises efficiency. In the degree this is the first full cycle analysis; the Brayton and Rankine chapters reuse exactly the same state-by-state method.

\n\n

What the piston actually does: four strokes and two

\n

In a four-stroke engine the piston makes four strokes (two crank revolutions) per thermodynamic cycle. Intake: the intake valve opens and the piston moves from TDC to BDC, drawing in fresh charge. Compression: both valves closed, the piston moves up and compresses the charge; near TDC a spark ignites it (SI) or fuel is injected into hot air and ignites (CI). Power (expansion): the high-pressure gas pushes the piston down; this is the only stroke that produces work. Exhaust: the exhaust valve opens and the piston pushes the burnt gas out. In a two-stroke engine all four functions happen in one crank revolution: the end of the power stroke and the start of the compression stroke are used to scavenge the cylinder through ports in the cylinder wall. Two-stroke engines are simpler and lighter for their power, but some fresh charge escapes with the exhaust and the burnt gas is expelled less completely, so they are generally less efficient.

\n

The ideal cycles below ignore the intake and exhaust strokes altogether. Under the air-standard assumptions the same air stays in the cylinder, and the exhaust-intake pair is replaced by a constant-volume heat rejection at BDC.

\n\n

The ideal Otto cycle

\n
📘 DEFINITION

The ideal Otto cycle is the air-standard model of a spark-ignition engine. It has four internally reversible processes: 1→2 isentropic compression; 2→3 constant-volume heat addition (combustion so fast that the piston does not move); 3→4 isentropic expansion (power stroke); 4→1 constant-volume heat rejection (the exhaust valve opening at BDC).

\n

Each process is a closed system with no kinetic or potential energy change, so the first law on each constant-volume leg is simply q = Δu. With constant specific heats, Δu = cv·ΔT. The isentropic legs have no heat, so their work is also a Δu, but you do not need it: net work is qin − qout for any cycle.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

qin = cv·(T3 − T2) qout = cv·(T4 − T1)

T2/T1 = T3/T4 = rk−1 P2/P1 = P3/P4 = rk

ηth,Otto = 1 − qout/qin = 1 − 1/rk−1

qin, qout: heat added and rejected per unit mass (kJ/kg); cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K; T1...T4: absolute temperatures (K); r = v1/v2 = v4/v3: compression ratio; k = 1.4. Derivation: η = 1 − (T4 − T1)/(T3 − T2); because T3/T4 = T2/T1, factor T1 and T2 out and the brackets cancel, leaving η = 1 − T1/T2 = 1 − r1−k.

\n

The result is remarkable: under cold-air-standard assumptions the Otto efficiency depends only on the compression ratio and k, not on how much heat you add or on the inlet temperature. Using k = 1.4 (computed): r = 4 gives 42.6%, r = 6 gives 51.2%, r = 8 gives 56.5%, r = 10 gives 60.2% and r = 12 gives 63.0%. The curve is steep at low r and flattens out, so each extra unit of compression ratio buys less. In terms of the two averages from Section 1: a higher compression ratio raises T2, so all the heat is added at a higher average temperature.

\n

Why not simply build a spark-ignition engine with r = 20? Because the air-fuel mixture is compressed together. Compress it too far and it becomes hot enough to ignite on its own before the spark, or ahead of the flame front; the result is autoignition, heard as engine knock, which is damaging. Knock, and the fuel's resistance to it, sets the upper limit of the compression ratio of spark-ignition engines. Note too that a monatomic gas (k = 1.67) would give a higher efficiency at the same r; the real mixture, with its larger molecules and higher specific heats at high temperature, has an effective k below 1.4, which is one reason real efficiencies are lower.

\n\n

The ideal Diesel cycle

\n
📘 DEFINITION

The ideal Diesel cycle is the air-standard model of a compression-ignition engine. It differs from the Otto cycle only in process 2→3: heat is added at constant pressure while the piston moves down, because fuel is injected over part of the power stroke and burns as it enters. The cutoff ratio rc = v3/v2 is the ratio of cylinder volume after and before combustion.

📊 FIGURE — Otto and Diesel cycles on P-v and T-s, states 1 to 4
Both cycles compress 1→2 and expand 3→4 at constant s, and reject heat 4→1 at constant v. They differ only in 2→3: constant volume for Otto, constant pressure (piston moving) for Diesel. Sketches, not to scale.
🧮 KEY EQUATION

qin = h3 − h2 = cp·(T3 − T2) qout = cv·(T4 − T1)

T3/T2 = v3/v2 = rc T4 = T3·(v3/v4)k−1 = T3·(rc/r)k−1

ηth,Diesel = 1 − (1/rk−1) · [ (rck − 1) / (k·(rc − 1)) ]

cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K; rc: cutoff ratio (dimensionless, > 1); other symbols as for the Otto cycle. The constant-pressure heat addition includes the boundary work P·Δv done while the piston moves, which is why qin is Δh, not Δu. The heat rejection 4→1 is still at constant volume, so qout uses cv.

\n

The square bracket is always greater than 1 for rc > 1 (it tends to 1 as rc → 1). So at the same compression ratio, ηOtto > ηDiesel; the Diesel cycle adds part of its heat during expansion, at a lower average temperature. The Diesel engine wins in practice because it compresses only air: nothing can knock during compression, so it can run at much higher compression ratios than a spark-ignition engine. A Diesel cycle at r = 18 beats an Otto cycle at r = 8. Efficiency also falls as rc rises (at r = 18, computed: rc = 1.5 gives 65.6%, 2 gives 63.2%, 3 gives 58.9%), so a diesel is most efficient at light load, when little fuel is injected.

\n\n

The dual cycle

\n

Real combustion is neither instantaneous nor perfectly at constant pressure. The dual cycle (also called the limited-pressure cycle) models it as heat added partly at constant volume (2→x, pressure ratio rp = P3/P2) and partly at constant pressure (x→3, cutoff ratio rc). Both Otto (rc = 1) and Diesel (rp = 1) are special cases.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

qin = cv·(Tx − T2) + cp·(T3 − Tx)

ηth,dual = 1 − (1/rk−1) · [ (rp·rck − 1) / ((rp − 1) + k·rp·(rc − 1)) ]

Tx: temperature at the end of the constant-volume part (K); rp = P3/P2: pressure ratio of the constant-volume part. Computed for r = 16: Otto 67.0%; dual with rp = 1.5, rc = 1.6 gives 64.5%; Diesel with rc = 1.6 gives 63.4%. At equal r and equal heat input the order is always Otto > dual > Diesel.

\n\n

Worked examples: an Otto cycle and a Diesel cycle

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A. Otto cycle. An ideal Otto cycle has r = 8. At the start of compression the air is at 95 kPa and 27 °C (300 K); 750 kJ/kg of heat is added. Cold-air-standard: cv = 0.718, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, k = 1.4. Find every state, η and MEP.

  1. State 1: v1 = R·T1/P1 = 0.287 × 300/95 = 0.9063 m³/kg.
  2. 1→2 isentropic: rk−1 = 80.4 = 2.2974 and rk = 81.4 = 18.379. T2 = 300 K × 2.2974 = 689.2 K; P2 = 95 kPa × 18.379 = 1746 kPa; v2 = 0.9063/8 = 0.1133 m³/kg.
  3. 2→3 constant volume: T3 = T2 + qin/cv = 689.2 + 750/0.718 = 689.2 + 1044.6 = 1733.8 K; P3 = P2·T3/T2 = 1746 × 1733.8/689.2 = 4392 kPa.
  4. 3→4 isentropic: T4 = 1733.8/2.2974 = 754.7 K; P4 = 4392/18.379 = 239.0 kPa.
  5. qout = cv·(T4 − T1) = 0.718 × (754.7 − 300) = 326.5 kJ/kg.
  6. wnet = 750 − 326.5 = 423.5 kJ/kg; η = 423.5/750 = 56.5%, identical to 1 − 1/80.4 = 0.5647.
  7. MEP = wnet/(v1 − v2) = 423.5/(0.9063 − 0.1133) = 423.5/0.7930 = 534 kPa.
StateP (kPa)T (K)v (m³/kg)

B. Diesel cycle. An ideal Diesel cycle has r = 18 and rc = 2. Air starts compression at 100 kPa and 300 K. Cold-air-standard.

  1. v1 = 0.287 × 300/100 = 0.861 m³/kg; v2 = 0.861/18 = 0.04783 m³/kg; v3 = 2 × 0.04783 = 0.09567 m³/kg.
  2. 1→2: 180.4 = 3.1777, 181.4 = 57.198. T2 = 300 × 3.1777 = 953.3 K; P2 = 100 × 57.198 = 5720 kPa.
  3. 2→3 constant pressure: T3 = rc·T2 = 2 × 953.3 = 1906.6 K; P3 = 5720 kPa. qin = cp·(T3 − T2) = 1.005 × 953.3 = 958.1 kJ/kg.
  4. 3→4 isentropic with v4/v3 = 0.861/0.09567 = 9.0: T4 = 1906.6/90.4 = 791.7 K; P4 = 100 × 791.7/300 = 263.9 kPa.
  5. qout = 0.718 × (791.7 − 300) = 353.0 kJ/kg.
  6. wnet = 958.1 − 353.0 = 605.0 kJ/kg; η = 605.0/958.1 = 63.2%. The formula gives 1 − (1/3.1777) × 1.1707 = 63.2% (the two differ in the fourth figure only because 1.005/0.718 = 1.3997, not exactly 1.4).
  7. MEP = 605.0/(0.861 − 0.04783) = 744 kPa.

Sanity check: the Otto cycle at the same r = 18 would reach 1 − 1/180.4 = 68.5%, higher than 63.2%, as the theory predicts; yet the Diesel at r = 18 beats the Otto at r = 8 (56.5%). Both efficiencies sit below the Carnot value between their extreme temperatures (1 − 300/1906.6 = 84.3% for the Diesel), as they must.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

cp versus cv. Otto heat addition is at constant volume: cv. Diesel heat addition is at constant pressure: cp. Both cycles reject heat at constant volume: cv. Using cv for the Diesel heat input (684.5 kJ/kg instead of 958.1 in example B) drops the efficiency to a wrong 48.4%.

Exponent k−1 for temperature, k for pressure. T2/T1 = rk−1; P2/P1 = rk. And r is a volume ratio; do not use (P2/P1)(k−1)/k with r in place of the pressure ratio.

Celsius in isentropic relations. 27 °C × 80.4 = 62 °C is meaningless; 300 K × 80.4 = 689 K is the answer.

Cutoff ratio in the expansion. The Diesel expansion ratio is v4/v3 = r/rc, not r.

★ ON THE EXAM

The classic question gives r (and rc for a Diesel), the state at the start of compression and either qin or Tmax, and asks for: the maximum temperature and pressure, the net work, the thermal efficiency and the MEP. Build the state table first; everything else is one line. Be ready to derive ηOtto = 1 − 1/rk−1 in four lines, to explain knock and why diesels run higher compression ratios, and to rank Otto, dual and Diesel at the same r.

A frequent twist: \"the same Diesel engine with variable specific heats\". Same states, but u, h and the isentropic relations come from the air table (relative pressure Pr and relative volume vr); the answer comes out a few percentage points lower.

"}, "THERMO/gascycles/s3": {"body": "

This lesson lets you analyse the gas turbine, the engine of jet aircraft and of most new fossil-fuelled power stations, using the ideal Brayton cycle. You will compute its efficiency from the pressure ratio, measure how much of the turbine's output the compressor eats (the back-work ratio), add real compressor and turbine losses, and then quantify the three classic improvements: regeneration, intercooling and reheating. The method is the steady-flow energy equation you already know, applied to four devices in series; the same device-by-device bookkeeping carries straight over to the Rankine and combined cycles of the next chapter.

\n\n

From an open gas turbine to the closed Brayton cycle

\n

A real gas turbine is an open system. Air is drawn in and compressed, fuel is burned in the compressed air in a combustion chamber at nearly constant pressure, the hot gas expands through a turbine that drives the compressor and delivers net shaft work, and the exhaust leaves to the atmosphere. Applying the air-standard assumptions closes the loop: combustion becomes heat addition at constant pressure, and the exhaust-plus-fresh-intake becomes heat rejection at constant pressure to the atmosphere.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

The ideal Brayton cycle has four internally reversible steady-flow processes: 1→2 isentropic compression in a compressor; 2→3 constant-pressure heat addition; 3→4 isentropic expansion in a turbine; 4→1 constant-pressure heat rejection. The pressure ratio is rp = P2/P1. The back-work ratio is the fraction of the turbine work used to drive the compressor, bwr = wcomp,in/wturb,out.

\n

Every device is steady flow with negligible kinetic and potential energy changes, so for each one the first law is q − w = Δh = cp·ΔT. That is why every energy term below uses cp, including the compressor and turbine work.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

wcomp,in = cp·(T2 − T1) wturb,out = cp·(T3 − T4) qin = cp·(T3 − T2) qout = cp·(T4 − T1)

T2/T1 = T3/T4 = rp(k−1)/k

ηth,Brayton = 1 − 1/rp(k−1)/k

w, q: work and heat per unit mass flow (kJ/kg); multiply by the mass flow ṁ (kg/s) to get kW. cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K; T: absolute temperatures (K); rp: pressure ratio (dimensionless); (k−1)/k = 0.2857 for k = 1.4. The efficiency derivation mirrors the Otto one: because T3/T4 = T2/T1, qout/qin reduces to T1/T2.

\n

Efficiency rises with pressure ratio (computed: rp = 8 gives 44.8%, 12 gives 50.8%, 20 gives 57.5%). But efficiency is not the only target. The turbine inlet temperature T3 is capped by what the blades can survive, and at fixed T1 and T3 the net work first rises with rp and then falls: at rp = 1 nothing happens, and at the very high rp where T2 reaches T3 there is no room left to add heat. In between, the net work per kilogram peaks at

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

rp,max work = (T3/T1)k/[2(k−1)] wnet,max = cp·(√T3 − √T1)²

At this pressure ratio T2 = T4 = √(T1·T3). A small net work per kilogram means a larger mass flow, and a bigger machine, for the same power; designers therefore trade efficiency against size.

\n

The back-work ratio is the gas turbine's weak point. Compressing a gas takes far more work than pumping a liquid, so a large fraction of the turbine's output (41% in the ideal example below, 55% once component losses are included) goes straight back into the compressor. In a steam power plant the pump takes only a tiny fraction of the turbine work, because the liquid it pumps has a specific volume roughly a thousandth that of air (0.001 m³/kg for liquid water against 0.861 m³/kg for air at 100 kPa and 300 K). This is why small losses in the compressor and turbine hurt a gas turbine so badly.

\n\n

Deviations of real gas turbines from the ideal cycle

\n

Real compressors and turbines are not isentropic. Their performance is described by isentropic efficiencies, which you met in the entropy chapter. There are also pressure drops in the combustor and exhaust ducts, and some heat loss, but the component efficiencies dominate.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

ηC = (h2s − h1)/(h2a − h1) ≈ (T2s − T1)/(T2a − T1) ηT = (h3 − h4a)/(h3 − h4s) ≈ (T3 − T4a)/(T3 − T4s)

Subscript s: the ideal (isentropic) exit state at the actual exit pressure; subscript a: the actual exit state. A real compressor needs more work than the ideal (divide by ηC); a real turbine delivers less (multiply by ηT).

\n\n

Regeneration

\n

In many gas turbines the exhaust leaves the turbine hotter than the air leaves the compressor (T4 > T2). A regenerator (recuperator) is a counter-flow heat exchanger that uses that hot exhaust to preheat the compressed air before it enters the combustor. The fuel then only has to raise the air from the regenerator exit temperature T5 to T3, so qin falls while the compressor and turbine work, and hence the net work, stay the same. In terms of the two averages: heat is now added at a higher average temperature and rejected at a lower one.

📊 FIGURE — A regenerative gas turbine: layout and T-s diagram, states 1 to 6
Hot exhaust 4→6 preheats the compressed air 2→5, so the combustor only lifts it from 725.1 K to 1400 K. Same turbine and compressor work, less fuel. Ideal regenerator; r(p) = 10 example.
\n
📘 DEFINITION

The effectiveness ε of a regenerator is the actual heat transferred to the compressed air divided by the maximum possible, which would bring the air up to the turbine exhaust temperature: ε = (h5 − h2)/(h4 − h2) ≈ (T5 − T2)/(T4 − T2). For the ideal Brayton cycle with an ideal regenerator (ε = 1): ηth,regen = 1 − (T1/T3)·rp(k−1)/k.

T5: temperature of the compressed air leaving the regenerator (K). Regeneration only helps when T4 > T2, which is true at low pressure ratios and high turbine inlet temperatures; the ideal-regeneration formula shows efficiency now falls with rp.

\n\n

Intercooling and reheating

\n

Compressor work per kilogram is ∫v·dP; the colder the gas, the smaller v and the less work. Splitting compression into stages with an intercooler between them, which cools the gas back towards T1, reduces compressor work. By the same argument, turbine work ∫v·dP rises if the gas is hot, so expanding in stages with a reheater (a second combustor) between them, bringing the gas back to T3, raises turbine work. For two stages with perfect intercooling and reheating, the work is best split evenly: each stage has pressure ratio √rp. With many stages, compression and expansion approach isothermal processes.

\n

The catch: without a regenerator, intercooling lowers the temperature at which heat addition starts, and reheating adds heat at the high turbine exit pressure where the gas is still hot, so the net work rises but the thermal efficiency usually falls. Combine them with a regenerator and the exhaust, now hotter, and the compressor exit, now cooler, give the regenerator more to work with; efficiency then rises well above the simple cycle, approaching the Ericsson cycle of Section 4.

\n\n

Worked examples

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A. Ideal Brayton cycle. rp = 10, compressor inlet 300 K and 100 kPa, turbine inlet 1400 K. Cold-air-standard, cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, k = 1.4.

  1. rp0.2857 = 100.2857 = 1.9307.
  2. T2 = 300 × 1.9307 = 579.2 K; T4 = 1400/1.9307 = 725.1 K.
  3. wcomp,in = 1.005 × (579.2 − 300) = 280.6 kJ/kg; wturb,out = 1.005 × (1400 − 725.1) = 678.2 kJ/kg.
  4. wnet = 678.2 − 280.6 = 397.6 kJ/kg; bwr = 280.6/678.2 = 41.4%.
  5. qin = 1.005 × (1400 − 579.2) = 824.9 kJ/kg; η = 397.6/824.9 = 48.2% (formula: 1 − 1/1.9307 = 0.482).

B. Same cycle with ηC = 0.85 and ηT = 0.88.

  1. T2a = T1 + (T2s − T1)/ηC = 300 + 279.2/0.85 = 628.5 K; wcomp,in = 1.005 × 328.5 = 330.1 kJ/kg.
  2. T4a = T3 − ηT·(T3 − T4s) = 1400 − 0.88 × 674.9 = 806.1 K; wturb,out = 1.005 × 593.9 = 596.9 kJ/kg.
  3. wnet = 596.9 − 330.1 = 266.7 kJ/kg (a third less than ideal); bwr = 55.3%.
  4. qin = 1.005 × (1400 − 628.5) = 775.4 kJ/kg; η = 266.7/775.4 = 34.4%.

C. Add a regenerator with ε = 0.80 to cycle B.

  1. T4a − T2a = 806.1 − 628.5 = 177.6 K, positive, so regeneration is worthwhile.
  2. T5 = T2a + ε·(T4a − T2a) = 628.5 + 0.80 × 177.6 = 770.6 K.
  3. qin = 1.005 × (1400 − 770.6) = 632.6 kJ/kg; wnet unchanged at 266.7 kJ/kg.
  4. η = 266.7/632.6 = 42.2%, up from 34.4%. The exhaust leaves the regenerator at 806.1 − (770.6 − 628.5) = 664.0 K.

D. Intercooling and reheating. Ideal cycle, overall rp = 16, T1 = 300 K, T3 = 1400 K, two compression stages with perfect intercooling and two expansion stages with perfect reheat.

  1. Stage pressure ratio √16 = 4; 40.2857 = 1.4860. Each compressor stage exits at 300 × 1.4860 = 445.8 K; each turbine stage exits at 1400/1.4860 = 942.1 K.
  2. wcomp,in = 2 × 1.005 × 145.8 = 293.1 kJ/kg; wturb,out = 2 × 1.005 × 457.9 = 920.3 kJ/kg; wnet = 627.3 kJ/kg, bwr = 31.8%.
  3. No regenerator: qin = 1.005 × (1400 − 445.8) + 1.005 × (1400 − 942.1) = 1419.1 kJ/kg; η = 627.3/1419.1 = 44.2%.
  4. Ideal regenerator (air heated to 942.1 K): qin = 2 × 1.005 × (1400 − 942.1) = 920.3 kJ/kg; η = 627.3/920.3 = 68.2%.
  5. For comparison, the simple ideal cycle at rp = 16: wnet = 405.6 kJ/kg and η = 54.7%.

Sanity check: intercooling and reheating raised net work by 55% (627.3 against 405.6 kJ/kg) but cut efficiency from 54.7% to 44.2%; the regenerator turned that into 68.2%, still below the Carnot limit 1 − 300/1400 = 78.6%.

\n
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

The optimum pressure ratio is a one-variable optimisation, so treat it like one. In Python, rp = np.linspace(2, 40, 400); x = rp**(0.4/1.4); w = 1.005*((1400 - 1400/x) - (300*x - 300)); eta = 1 - 1/x, then plot w and η against rp on twin axes and read off rp[w.argmax()]. You get about 14.8 and 405.9 kJ/kg, matching the closed form (1400/300)1.75 = 14.8 and 1.005 × (√1400 − √300)² = 405.9 kJ/kg. Add component efficiencies to the same arrays and watch the optimum move to lower rp; that sensitivity study takes one line in pandas and would take an afternoon by hand.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Otto exponent in a Brayton problem. The Brayton cycle is specified by a pressure ratio, so the exponent is (k−1)/k = 0.2857, not k−1 = 0.4. For rp = 12, 1 − 1/120.4 = 63.0% is wrong; 1 − 1/120.2857 = 50.8% is right.

cv in a steady-flow device. Compressor and turbine work are Δh = cp·ΔT, not cv·ΔT.

Isentropic efficiency upside down. Divide the ideal compressor temperature rise by ηC (the real rise is bigger); multiply the ideal turbine drop by ηT. Multiplying for the compressor gives 537 K instead of 628.5 K in example B.

Regenerating when T4 < T2. At high pressure ratios the \"hot\" exhaust is colder than the compressed air, and a regenerator would heat the exhaust and cool the air, reducing efficiency.

★ ON THE EXAM

Standard questions: (1) ideal Brayton with rp and T3 given: find T2, T4, works, bwr, η and the mass flow for a given net power (ṁ = Ẇnet/wnet); (2) the same with ηC and ηT; (3) add a regenerator of given effectiveness and find the new η and exhaust temperature; (4) two-stage compression and expansion with intercooling, reheat and regeneration; (5) explain in words why intercooling and reheating alone lower the efficiency and why a regenerator reverses that.

Draw the T-s diagram before any arithmetic: it shows at once whether T4 > T2 and where every heat and work term sits.

This lesson takes the Brayton cycle into the air and then back to the ideal. First you will analyse a turbojet: the same compressor, combustor and turbine as a power-station gas turbine, but with a diffuser in front and a nozzle behind, and with the useful output being a fast jet rather than shaft work. You will compute thrust, propulsive power and the efficiencies that measure a jet engine. Then you will meet the Stirling and Ericsson cycles, the two cycles that, with a perfect regenerator, reach the Carnot efficiency while using practical processes. This closes the gas-cycle part of the degree; the vapour and combined cycles come next.

\n\n

The ideal turbojet cycle

\n

An aircraft gas turbine does not try to turn all the turbine output into shaft work. Its turbine produces just enough power to drive the compressor (and small accessories such as a generator and pumps). The gas leaving the turbine is still at high pressure and temperature, and it expands through a nozzle to the ambient pressure, leaving at high velocity. The change in momentum of the air is the thrust. At the front, a diffuser slows the incoming air, which raises its pressure before the compressor even starts: this is ram compression, and it is free.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

The ideal turbojet cycle (analysed in the aircraft's frame, so the air arrives at the flight speed V1): 1→2 isentropic deceleration in the diffuser to negligible velocity; 2→3 isentropic compression; 3→4 constant-pressure heat addition; 4→5 isentropic expansion in the turbine, just far enough that wturb = wcomp; 5→6 isentropic expansion in the nozzle to ambient pressure, producing the exit velocity V6.

Thrust is the net force the engine exerts on the aircraft. Propulsive power ẆP is the thrust times the aircraft speed: the rate at which the engine does useful work pushing the aircraft.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

Diffuser: T2 = T1 + V1²/(2·cp) Nozzle: V6 = √[2·cp·(T5 − T6)]

F = ṁ·(Vexit − Vinlet) ẆP = F·Vaircraft = ṁ·(Vexit − Vinlet)·Vaircraft

ηP = ẆP/Q̇in ηFroude = 2/(1 + Vexit/Vaircraft)

V: velocity (m/s); cp in J/kg·K here (1005) so that V²/(2cp) comes out in K; T: absolute temperature (K); F: thrust (N); ṁ: air mass flow (kg/s), fuel mass neglected; ẆP: propulsive power (W); Q̇in = ṁ·qin: rate of heat (fuel energy) input (W). The thrust formula assumes the exit pressure equals ambient pressure. Two efficiency definitions are in use: Cengel & Boles call ẆP/Q̇in the propulsive efficiency; many aircraft-propulsion texts call that ratio the overall efficiency and reserve \"propulsive efficiency\" for the Froude ratio ẆP/(rate of kinetic energy increase) = 2/(1 + Vexit/V). Overall = thermal × Froude. State which you are using.

\n

The Froude expression explains the design of modern aircraft engines. Thrust needs Vexit > V, but every m/s of extra jet speed carries kinetic energy that is simply left behind in the atmosphere. To get the same thrust with less wasted kinetic energy, accelerate more air by a smaller amount.

\n\n

Turbofans, turboprops, ramjets and afterburners

\n
  • Turbofan (bypass engine). A large fan at the front, driven by the turbine, pushes a big mass of air around the core engine (the bypass stream) as well as through it. The bypass ratio is the mass flow of bypass air divided by the mass flow of air through the combustor. More air at a lower jet velocity gives higher Froude efficiency and a quieter engine, which is why airliners use high-bypass turbofans.
  • Turboprop. Take the bypass idea to the limit: the turbine drives a propeller through a gearbox, and most of the thrust comes from the propeller moving a very large mass of air slowly. Very efficient at lower flight speeds; propeller efficiency falls as blade tips approach the speed of sound.
  • Ramjet. No compressor and no turbine: at high flight speed the diffuser alone provides enough ram compression. It produces no thrust at rest, so it must be launched or accelerated by another engine first. A scramjet keeps the flow supersonic through the combustor.
  • Afterburner. Extra fuel is burned in the gas between the turbine and nozzle. This raises the nozzle inlet temperature and hence Vexit and thrust, at a large cost in fuel; used for take-off and combat in military aircraft.
\n\n

Worked example: an ideal turbojet

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem. A turbojet flies at 250 m/s where the air is at 40 kPa and 240 K. The compressor pressure ratio is 12 and the turbine inlet temperature is 1400 K; air mass flow 50 kg/s. Treat every component as ideal, cold-air-standard (cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, k = 1.4). Find the jet velocity, thrust, propulsive power and efficiencies.

📊 FIGURE — An ideal turbojet: components, states 1 to 6 and the T-s path
Air is slowed and compressed (1→3), heated (3→4), expanded just enough in the turbine to drive the compressor (4→5), then accelerated in the nozzle to 1013 m/s (5→6). Numbers are the worked example.
  1. Diffuser: V1²/(2cp) = 250²/(2 × 1005) = 31.1 K, so T2 = 240 + 31.1 = 271.1 K. P2 = 40 × (271.1/240)3.5 = 61.27 kPa (ram pressure ratio 1.53).
  2. Compressor: P3 = 12 × 61.27 = 735.2 kPa; 120.2857 = 2.0339, so T3 = 271.1 × 2.0339 = 551.4 K. wcomp,in = 1.005 × (551.4 − 271.1) = 281.7 kJ/kg.
  3. Combustor: T4 = 1400 K, P4 = 735.2 kPa; qin = 1.005 × (1400 − 551.4) = 852.9 kJ/kg; Q̇in = 50 × 852.9 = 42,640 kW.
  4. Turbine drives compressor: T5 = T4 − wcomp/cp = 1400 − 281.7/1.005 = 1119.7 K; P5 = 735.2 × (1119.7/1400)3.5 = 336.4 kPa.
  5. Nozzle to 40 kPa: T6 = 1119.7 × (40/336.4)0.2857 = 609.4 K; V6 = √[2 × 1005 × (1119.7 − 609.4)] = 1013 m/s.
  6. Thrust: F = 50 kg/s × (1012.8 − 250) m/s = 38,140 N ≈ 38.1 kN.
  7. Propulsive power: ẆP = 38,140 N × 250 m/s = 9535 kW (190.7 kJ per kg of air).
  8. ηP (Cengel, = overall) = 9535/42,640 = 22.4%. Froude efficiency = 2/(1 + 1012.8/250) = 39.6%. Thermal efficiency (kinetic energy gain/heat) = [(1012.8² − 250²)/2]/1000/852.9 = 481.6/852.9 = 56.5%; check 0.565 × 0.396 = 0.224.
StateP (kPa)T (K)V (m/s)
1 inlet40240.0250
2 diffuser exit61.27271.1≈0
3 compressor exit735.2551.4≈0
4 turbine inlet735.21400.0≈0
5 turbine exit336.41119.7≈0
6 nozzle exit40609.41013

Sanity check: the thermal efficiency equals 1 − T1/T3 = 1 − 240/551.4 = 56.5%, the Brayton efficiency for the overall pressure ratio P3/P1 = 18.4, exactly as an ideal Brayton cycle should; the jet is four times the flight speed, which is why the Froude efficiency is only about 40%.

\n\n

Stirling and Ericsson cycles: Carnot efficiency with regeneration

\n

The Otto, Diesel and Brayton cycles all fall short of Carnot because they add and reject heat over a range of temperatures. The Carnot cycle avoids that with isothermal heat transfer, but its isentropic legs cause the huge pressure ratios and low MEP you saw in Section 1. The Stirling and Ericsson cycles keep the two isothermal heat transfers and replace the isentropic legs with processes in which heat is passed internally from the gas to a regenerator and later returned. If the regenerator is perfect, the only external heat transfers are at TH and TL, and the efficiency equals Carnot's.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Stirling cycle: 1→2 isothermal expansion at TH (heat from the external source); 2→3 constant-volume regeneration (gas gives heat to the regenerator and cools to TL); 3→4 isothermal compression at TL (heat to the sink); 4→1 constant-volume regeneration (gas takes the heat back and warms to TH).

Ericsson cycle: the same, but the two regeneration processes are at constant pressure. A steady-flow Ericsson machine is the limit of a gas turbine with infinitely many stages of intercooling and reheating plus an ideal regenerator.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

ηth,Stirling = ηth,Ericsson = ηth,Carnot = 1 − TL/TH (perfect regeneration)

Stirling, ideal gas: qin = R·TH·ln(vmax/vmin) qout = R·TL·ln(vmax/vmin) qregen = cv·(TH − TL)

R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K for air; T in K; the volume ratio is the same on both isotherms because the regeneration legs are at constant volume. For the Ericsson cycle replace ln(v ratio) by ln(P ratio) and cv by cp.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Stirling cycle. Air runs an ideal Stirling cycle between 1000 K and 300 K with a volume ratio of 10.

  1. qin = 0.287 × 1000 × ln 10 = 0.287 × 1000 × 2.3026 = 660.8 kJ/kg.
  2. qout = 0.287 × 300 × 2.3026 = 198.3 kJ/kg.
  3. wnet = 660.8 − 198.3 = 462.6 kJ/kg; η = 462.6/660.8 = 70.0% = 1 − 300/1000.
  4. Heat stored and returned by the regenerator: cv·(TH − TL) = 0.718 × 700 = 502.6 kJ/kg, three quarters of qin.
  5. Without the regenerator that 502.6 kJ/kg would have to come from the source: η = 462.6/(660.8 + 502.6) = 39.8%.

Sanity check: equal to Carnot with a perfect regenerator, as the theory requires; the regenerator carries almost as much heat as the source, so its quality decides the whole engine. Stirling engines burn fuel outside the cylinder (external combustion), so they can use any heat source, and they run quietly, but the heat exchangers and regenerator make them large and costly.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Thrust from the exit velocity alone. F = ṁ·(Vexit − Vinlet). Using ṁ·Vexit in the example gives 50.6 kN instead of 38.1 kN; the engine has to accelerate air that was already arriving at 250 m/s.

Units in V²/2. V² in m²/s² divided by 2 gives J/kg; divide by 1000 for kJ/kg, or use cp = 1005 J/kg·K. Forgetting this turns a 31 K ram temperature rise into 31,000 K.

Turbine output is not net work in a turbojet. The ideal turbine produces exactly the compressor work; the \"output\" is the kinetic energy of the jet.

Stirling without regeneration is not Carnot. The Carnot result needs the regenerator to return every joule it stores; with no regenerator the example drops from 70.0% to 39.8%.

★ ON THE EXAM

Expect a full ideal turbojet: diffuser, compressor, combustor, turbine balancing the compressor, nozzle to ambient pressure; then thrust, propulsive power and propulsive efficiency. Always build the state table (P, T, V) first. Word questions ask why turbofans beat turbojets for airliners (more mass, lower jet speed, higher Froude efficiency), why a ramjet cannot take off on its own, what an afterburner does, and why Stirling and Ericsson cycles reach Carnot efficiency (isothermal heat transfer at TH and TL, all other heat exchanged internally).

Say which efficiency definition you use for jets; examiners accept either if you define it.

This lesson lets you draw the ideal Rankine cycle on a T-s diagram, write the energy balance for each of its four components, pull every state from the steam tables and compute the thermal efficiency, pump work and back work ratio of a real steam plant. It is the vapour-cycle counterpart of the gas cycles you just finished, and it is the base on which the reheat, regeneration and combined cycles in the next three lessons are built. Every steam power station on Earth is a modified Rankine cycle, so this is the single most-examined cycle in the degree.

\n\n

Why not just run Carnot on steam?

\n

Carnot gives the highest efficiency between two temperatures, and inside the vapour dome a Carnot cycle is almost easy to build: boiling at constant pressure is also at constant temperature, so the isothermal heat addition costs nothing extra. The problems appear when you try to make the other three legs work.

\n
    \n
  • The heat-addition temperature is capped. Isothermal heat addition inside the dome cannot exceed the critical temperature of water, 373.95 °C (critical point 22.06 MPa, 373.95 °C). Any Carnot cycle that stays under the dome is limited to roughly TL/TH of (30 + 273.15)/(374 + 273.15) at the very best, which caps the ideal at about 53% even before any losses.
    • \n
  • The turbine runs wet. Isentropic expansion from saturated vapour lands deep in the two-phase region. Droplets erode turbine blades, and in practice quality below about 0.90 at the exit is not tolerated.
    • \n
  • Compressing a wet mixture is impractical. The Carnot cycle needs an isentropic compressor that takes a liquid-vapour mixture and delivers saturated liquid. Nobody can build a machine that handles two phases at once with any efficiency, and controlling the condensation to end exactly at the saturated-liquid line is impossible.
    • \n
\n

The fix is the Rankine cycle: condense all the way to saturated liquid (so the pump handles only liquid), pump it as a liquid (which is cheap because liquid is nearly incompressible), and heat it at constant pressure through the liquid, mixture and superheated regions. Heat addition is no longer isothermal, which costs efficiency, but every component becomes buildable.

\n\n

The four processes of the ideal Rankine cycle

\n
📘 DEFINITION

The ideal Rankine cycle is the closed cycle of a working fluid (almost always water) through four internally reversible steady-flow devices: 1-2 isentropic compression in a pump, 2-3 constant-pressure heat addition in a boiler, 3-4 isentropic expansion in a turbine, 4-1 constant-pressure heat rejection in a condenser. State 1 is saturated liquid at the condenser pressure; state 3 is saturated or superheated vapour at the boiler pressure.

📊 FIGURE — The ideal Rankine cycle: four devices and its T-s loop, states 1-4
Left: pump, boiler, turbine, condenser with states 1-4 and the energy per kg from the worked example. Right: the same states on T-s; the shaded loop is the net work.
\n

On the T-s diagram: 1-2 is a nearly vertical line so short you can barely see it (the pump raises pressure but the liquid temperature rises only a fraction of a degree); 2-3 follows the boiler isobar up the liquid line, across the dome as a horizontal boiling segment, and then curves up into the superheat region; 3-4 is a vertical drop into the dome; 4-1 is the horizontal condensation line back to saturated liquid. The area enclosed is the net work per unit mass, and the area under 2-3 is the heat added. Because the T-s and the h-s (Mollier) diagrams both show this, examiners often ask you to sketch it, label the states and mark which areas are qin, qout and wnet.

\n\n

Energy balance of each component

\n

All four devices are steady-flow devices, so the control-volume first law from the open-systems chapter applies. Neglecting kinetic and potential energy, per unit mass of steam:

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

wpump,in = h2 − h1 ≈ v1 (P2 − P1)

qin = h3 − h2

wturb,out = h3 − h4

qout = h4 − h1

ηth = wnet / qin = 1 − qout / qin, with wnet = wturb,out − wpump,in = qin − qout

h is specific enthalpy in kJ/kg, v1 is the specific volume of saturated liquid at the condenser pressure in m³/kg, P is pressure in kPa (so v·ΔP comes out directly in kJ/kg because 1 kPa·m³ = 1 kJ), and w and q are per kilogram of steam in kJ/kg. ηth is dimensionless.

\n

The pump formula comes from the reversible steady-flow work relation wrev = ∫v dP with v treated as constant, which is accurate to well under 1% for liquid water below its critical pressure. That relation is why you use vf at the pump inlet pressure and why the answer is tiny: vf is about 0.001 m³/kg, a thousand times smaller than the vapour that expands in the turbine.

\n\n

Worked example: a 3 MPa, 350 °C plant condensing at 75 kPa

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Steam enters the turbine of an ideal Rankine cycle at 3 MPa and 350 °C and is condensed at 75 kPa. Find the pump work, turbine work, heat added, heat rejected, thermal efficiency and back work ratio. Property source: Cengel & Boles steam tables, saturated water by pressure (A-5) and superheated water (A-6).

State table (all values from the tables or computed below):

StatePTConditionh (kJ/kg)s (kJ/kg·K)
175 kPa91.76 °Csat. liquid, v1 = 0.001037 m³/kg384.441.2132
23 MPa≈ 92 °Ccompressed liquid387.471.2132
33 MPa350 °Csuperheated3116.16.7450
475 kPa91.76 °Cmixture, x4 = 0.88612403.16.7450
  1. State 1 is saturated liquid at 75 kPa: h1 = hf = 384.44 kJ/kg, v1 = vf = 0.001037 m³/kg.
  2. Pump work: wpump = v1(P2 − P1) = 0.001037 m³/kg × (3000 − 75) kPa = 3.03 kJ/kg. Then h2 = 384.44 + 3.03 = 387.47 kJ/kg.
  3. State 3 is superheated steam at 3 MPa, 350 °C: h3 = 3116.1 kJ/kg, s3 = 6.7450 kJ/kg·K.
  4. State 4: isentropic, so s4 = s3 = 6.7450 kJ/kg·K at 75 kPa. Since sf = 1.2132 < 6.7450 < sg = 7.4558, it is a mixture: x4 = (6.7450 − 1.2132)/6.2426 = 0.8861. So h4 = 384.44 + 0.8861 × 2278.0 = 2403.1 kJ/kg.
  5. Heat added: qin = h3 − h2 = 3116.1 − 387.47 = 2728.6 kJ/kg.
  6. Heat rejected: qout = h4 − h1 = 2403.1 − 384.44 = 2018.6 kJ/kg.
  7. Turbine work: wturb = h3 − h4 = 3116.1 − 2403.1 = 713.0 kJ/kg; net work wnet = 713.0 − 3.03 = 710.0 kJ/kg (check: qin − qout = 2728.6 − 2018.6 = 710.0 kJ/kg).
  8. Efficiency: ηth = 710.0/2728.6 = 0.260, i.e. 26.0%. Back work ratio = 3.03/713.0 = 0.0043 (0.43%).

Sanity check: the Carnot limit between 350 °C and 91.76 °C is 1 − 364.91/623.15 = 41.4%, and even between the boiling temperature 233.85 °C and 91.76 °C it is 28.0%. A Rankine result of 26.0% sits below both, as it must. The turbine exit quality of 0.886 is on the low side (below 0.90), which is exactly the moisture problem the next lesson fixes with superheat and reheat.

\n\n

Why the pump work is so small, and when it matters

\n

The back work ratio of a steam plant, wpump/wturb, is typically under 1%. Compare that with the Brayton cycle from the gas-cycles chapter, where the compressor consumes 40-80% of the turbine output. The difference is entirely the phase change: the pump handles liquid with v ≈ 0.001 m³/kg, while the turbine expands vapour with v of order 1 m³/kg, and the steady-flow work is ∫v dP. Because the pump term is so small, many quick calculations drop it and take h2 ≈ h1; in the example above that would give η = (3116.1 − 2403.1)/(3116.1 − 384.44) = 26.1% instead of 26.0%. The error is small but an examiner will still expect you to include the pump when the question asks for \"the\" efficiency, and in supercritical plants at 25-30 MPa the pump work reaches 30 kJ/kg and is no longer negligible.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Using the wrong specific volume in the pump. The pump formula needs vf at the condenser (inlet) pressure, about 0.00101-0.00104 m³/kg. Grabbing vg instead (14.67 m³/kg at 10 kPa) for a 10 kPa to 8 MPa pump gives 14.67 × 7990 ≈ 117,000 kJ/kg, which should trigger an immediate sanity alarm.

Mixing MPa and kPa. v(P2 − P1) only comes out in kJ/kg when P is in kPa. With P in MPa you get an answer 1000 times too small (0.003 kJ/kg instead of 3.03 kJ/kg).

Reading s4 from the wrong pressure. State 4 shares the turbine inlet entropy but the condenser pressure. Always check sf < s4 < sg at the condenser pressure before computing a quality; if s4 > sg the exit is superheated and quality is meaningless.

Treating qout as h4 − h2. The condenser returns the fluid to state 1, not state 2. qout = h4 − h1.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

The standard question gives boiler pressure and temperature plus condenser pressure and asks for the four energy quantities, ηth, the exit quality and sometimes the mass flow rate for a stated power (mass flow = power / wnet). Set up the four-state table first, fill it from the tables, then compute; that ordering is where the marks are.

Conceptual variants: \"Explain three reasons the Carnot vapour cycle is impractical\" (temperature capped at Tcrit, wet turbine expansion, two-phase compression) and \"Sketch the T-s diagram and shade the area representing net work\".

Watch for a turbine inlet given as saturated vapour rather than superheated: then h3 = hg and s3 = sg at the boiler pressure, read from the saturation table, not the superheat table.

"}, "THERMO/vapcycles/s2": {"body": "

This lesson lets you predict, with numbers, how each design lever of a steam plant moves the thermal efficiency and the turbine exit quality: lowering the condenser pressure, superheating the steam, raising the boiler pressure, and reheating between turbine stages. The idea underneath every lever is the same one you met with Carnot: raise the average temperature at which heat is added, or lower the average temperature at which it is rejected. Reheat is examined as a full cycle calculation, so this lesson ends with the standard reheat worked example.

\n\n

One principle, four levers

\n

Write the Rankine efficiency as η = 1 − qout/qin, and remember that for internally reversible heat transfer, q = ∫T ds. Then qin = TH,avg × (s3 − s2) and qout = TL,avg × (s4 − s1), where the averages are entropy-weighted. Since s3 − s2 = s4 − s1 (the two isentropic legs), the efficiency is simply:

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

ηth = 1 − TL,avg / TH,avg

TH,avg is the entropy-averaged absolute temperature (K) of heat addition along 2-3 and TL,avg the entropy-averaged temperature (K) of heat rejection along 4-1; for a condenser inside the dome TL,avg is just the condenser saturation temperature. Anything that raises TH,avg or lowers TL,avg raises efficiency.

\n
    \n
  • Lower the condenser pressure. Dropping Pcond from 75 kPa to 10 kPa lowers Tsat from 91.76 °C to 45.81 °C, lowering TL,avg directly. The cost: the exit quality falls (more moisture), the specific volume of the exhaust rises so the last turbine stages and condenser get bigger, and air leaks into a condenser that is far below atmospheric pressure. The floor is set by the cooling water: with 20 °C cooling water and a 10 °C temperature difference the steam cannot condense below about 30 °C, which corresponds to about 4.2 kPa.
    • \n
  • Superheat the steam. Raising T3 at fixed pressure adds heat at high temperature, so TH,avg rises, and it shifts state 4 to the right, raising the exit quality. Both effects are good. The ceiling is metallurgical: turbine inlet temperatures are limited to about 620 °C in current plants.
    • \n
  • Raise the boiler pressure. At fixed T3 this raises the boiling temperature and TH,avg, but the T-s diagram shifts left and state 4 moves deeper into the dome: quality drops. Modern plants use 30 MPa supercritical boilers (above the 22.06 MPa critical pressure there is no boiling at all, the liquid simply becomes vapour).
    • \n
  • Reheat. Expand partly, send the steam back through the boiler to reheat it (usually to the same T3), and expand again. This lets you use high boiler pressure without wet exhaust.
    • \n
\n\n

The effect of each lever with numbers

\n

Take the plant from Lesson 1 (3 MPa, 350 °C) and work each change with the same condenser temperature basis. Property source throughout: Cengel & Boles Tables A-5 and A-6. Saturated water at 10 kPa: vf = 0.001010 m³/kg, hf = 191.81, hfg = 2392.1 kJ/kg, sf = 0.6492, sfg = 7.4996 kJ/kg·K. Superheated steam: 3 MPa/350 °C h = 3116.1, s = 6.7450; 3 MPa/600 °C h = 3682.8, s = 7.5103; 15 MPa/600 °C h = 3583.1, s = 6.6796 (kJ/kg and kJ/kg·K).

\n\n\n\n\n\n

Base (Lesson 1)3 MPa, 350 °C75 kPa3.030.8862728.62018.626.0%

\n

Read the table the way an examiner does. Lowering the condenser pressure from 75 to 10 kPa gained 7.4 percentage points but pushed the exit quality from 0.886 down to 0.813. Superheating to 600 °C gained 3.9 points and rescued the quality to 0.915. Raising the pressure to 15 MPa gained another 5.7 points but dropped the quality back to 0.804, which is unacceptable for the blades. That is the motivation for reheat: it is the lever that lets you keep case (c)'s pressure with case (b)'s quality.

\n
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

This table is a small designed experiment: three factors (Pcond, T3, Pboil), two responses (η and x4). Put the four rows in a pandas DataFrame and plot η against each lever; you will see the diminishing returns of pressure (43.0% at 15 MPa needs five times the pressure of 37.3% at 3 MPa) and the trade-off between η and x4 that a two-axis chart makes obvious. If you want more points, loop the same five-line calculation over a grid of pressures and temperatures in Python (the iapws package gives steam properties) and fit η against each factor; you will have built your own design chart.

\n\n

The ideal reheat Rankine cycle

\n
📘 DEFINITION

The ideal reheat Rankine cycle splits the expansion into two stages. Steam expands isentropically in a high-pressure turbine from state 3 to state 4 (the reheat pressure), returns to the boiler where it is reheated at constant pressure to state 5 (usually the original inlet temperature), and then expands isentropically in a low-pressure turbine to the condenser pressure at state 6. Heat is added in two pieces and work is extracted in two pieces.

📊 FIGURE — Reheat Rankine cycle: 15 MPa, 600 °C, reheated at 4 MPa, states 1-6
Steam expands 3→4 in the HP turbine, is reheated 4→5 back to 600 °C, then expands 5→6. Reheat moves the exhaust right: x = 0.896 instead of the 0.804 of the dashed single expansion.
\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

qin = qprimary + qreheat = (h3 − h2) + (h5 − h4)

wturb,out = wHP + wLP = (h3 − h4) + (h5 − h6)

qout = h6 − h1

All enthalpies in kJ/kg; state 4 is found from s4 = s3 at the reheat pressure (usually superheated, so it needs interpolation in the superheat table), and state 6 from s6 = s5 at the condenser pressure. The optimum reheat pressure is roughly one-quarter of the boiler pressure; Cengel & Boles quote an improvement of about 4 to 5 percent for a single reheat in a modern plant (the idealised example below gains 2.0 points). The theoretical gain from a second reheat is only about half that of the first, and more than two reheat stages are not practical.

\n\n

Worked example: 15 MPa, 600 °C with reheat at 4 MPa

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Steam enters the high-pressure turbine of an ideal reheat Rankine cycle at 15 MPa and 600 °C, is reheated at 4 MPa to 600 °C, and is condensed at 10 kPa. Find the turbine exit quality, the total heat added and the thermal efficiency. Property source: Cengel & Boles Tables A-5 and A-6. The relevant table values are: 15 MPa/600 °C h = 3583.1 kJ/kg, s = 6.6796 kJ/kg·K; at 4 MPa with s = 6.6796 the superheat table interpolates to T = 375.5 °C, h = 3155.0 kJ/kg; 4 MPa/600 °C h = 3674.9 kJ/kg, s = 7.3706 kJ/kg·K.

  1. State 1: saturated liquid at 10 kPa, h1 = 191.81 kJ/kg, v1 = 0.001010 m³/kg.
  2. Pump: wpump = 0.001010 m³/kg × (15000 − 10) kPa = 15.14 kJ/kg, so h2 = 191.81 + 15.14 = 206.95 kJ/kg.
  3. State 3: h3 = 3583.1 kJ/kg, s3 = 6.6796 kJ/kg·K.
  4. State 4: P4 = 4 MPa, s4 = s3 = 6.6796 kJ/kg·K. At 4 MPa sg = 6.0696 < 6.6796, so state 4 is superheated: h4 = 3155.0 kJ/kg (T4 = 375.5 °C).
  5. State 5: 4 MPa, 600 °C: h5 = 3674.9 kJ/kg, s5 = 7.3706 kJ/kg·K.
  6. State 6: 10 kPa, s6 = 7.3706: x6 = (7.3706 − 0.6492)/7.4996 = 0.8962, h6 = 191.81 + 0.8962 × 2392.1 = 2335.7 kJ/kg. Exit moisture = 1 − 0.896 = 10.4%, compared with 19.6% without reheat (case (c) above).
  7. Heat added: qprimary = 3583.1 − 206.95 = 3376.2 kJ/kg; qreheat = 3674.9 − 3155.0 = 519.9 kJ/kg; qin = 3896.1 kJ/kg.
  8. Heat rejected: qout = 2335.7 − 191.81 = 2143.9 kJ/kg.
  9. Turbine work: wHP = 3583.1 − 3155.0 = 428.1 kJ/kg; wLP = 3674.9 − 2335.7 = 1339.2 kJ/kg; wnet = 428.1 + 1339.2 − 15.14 = 1752.2 kJ/kg (check: 3896.1 − 2143.9 = 1752.2 kJ/kg).
  10. Efficiency: ηth = 1 − 2143.9/3896.1 = 0.450, i.e. 45.0%.

Sanity check: the same plant without reheat (case (c)) gave 43.0% with 19.6% exit moisture. Reheat gained 2.0 percentage points and halved the moisture, and 45.0% is well below the Carnot limit between 600 °C and 45.81 °C of 1 − 318.96/873.15 = 63.5%. Plausible.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Forgetting the reheat heat input. qin has two pieces. Using only h3 − h2 = 3376.2 kJ/kg in the example gives η = 1752.2/3376.2 = 51.9% instead of 45.0%, a wrong answer that still sits below Carnot and so looks plausible, which is the dangerous kind.

Assuming state 4 is a mixture. After partial expansion at 4 MPa the steam is still superheated (s4 = 6.6796 > sg = 6.0696). Compare s4 with sg at the reheat pressure before you reach for the lever rule.

Believing reheat is mainly about efficiency. Its main job is to keep the turbine exhaust dry enough to use a high boiler pressure; the efficiency gain is a side effect of the higher average heat-addition temperature. Reheating without raising pressure gains very little.

Using Celsius in TL/TH. The averaged-temperature form of the efficiency and every Carnot comparison need Kelvin; 1 − 45.81/600 = 92.4% is meaningless.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

Three question types recur. (1) \"State and explain three methods of increasing the efficiency of the Rankine cycle and the practical limit of each\": lower Pcond (limited by cooling-water temperature and exit moisture), superheat (limited by metallurgy, about 620 °C), higher Pboil (limited by exit moisture, fixed by reheat). (2) A full reheat calculation exactly like the worked example, often asking for the reheat pressure that produces a stated exit quality: fix x6, find s6, set s5 = s6 at T5 and search the superheat table for the pressure. (3) A T-s sketch of a reheat cycle: two vertical expansions with a constant-pressure reheat \"hump\" between them.

Know the numbers: a single reheat improves efficiency by about 4 to 5 percent in a modern plant (Cengel & Boles), the optimum reheat pressure is about one-quarter of the boiler pressure, and the practical moisture limit at the turbine exit is about 10%.

This lesson lets you analyse the regenerative Rankine cycle, in which steam bled from the turbine preheats the feedwater before it enters the boiler. You will write the mass and energy balances for an open (direct-contact) feedwater heater and a closed (shell-and-tube) feedwater heater, solve for the fraction of steam extracted, and compute the efficiency of a regenerative cycle with the steam tables. Regeneration is used in essentially every large steam plant (large plants use several heaters, up to about eight) and it is a favourite exam calculation because it forces you to track mass fractions as well as enthalpies.

\n\n

Why regeneration raises the efficiency

\n

Look at the boiler isobar 2-3 on the T-s diagram. The feedwater enters the boiler at state 2, only about 46 °C in a 10 kPa-condenser plant, and is heated by burning fuel all the way to the boiling temperature. That low-temperature stretch of heat addition drags TH,avg down. The idea of regeneration is to do that low-temperature heating with steam that has already done some work in the turbine, instead of with fuel. Steam is extracted (bled) from the turbine at an intermediate pressure and used to heat the feedwater in a feedwater heater (FWH). The fuel then only has to heat the water from the heater exit temperature upward, so the average temperature of external heat addition rises and ηth = 1 − TL,avg/TH,avg rises with it. A side benefit: the extracted steam never reaches the condenser, so the condenser and the low-pressure turbine stages shrink, and the heaters also deaerate the feedwater, removing dissolved oxygen that would corrode the boiler.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Regeneration is the transfer of heat from steam that has partly expanded in the turbine to the feedwater on its way to the boiler. The device that does it is a feedwater heater. In an open (direct-contact) feedwater heater the extracted steam and the feedwater mix and leave as a single stream, ideally saturated liquid at the heater pressure. In a closed feedwater heater the two streams do not mix: the extracted steam condenses on tubes carrying the feedwater, and the condensate (the \"drain\") is either pumped forward into the feedwater line or throttled backward to a lower-pressure heater or the condenser.

The extraction fraction y is the mass of steam bled per unit mass of steam leaving the boiler: y = ṁextracted/ṁboiler.

\n\n

The open feedwater heater: mass and energy balances

\n

Number the states as in the standard cycle: 1 condenser exit (saturated liquid), 2 after pump I, 3 heater exit (saturated liquid at the extraction pressure), 4 after pump II (boiler pressure), 5 turbine inlet, 6 extraction point, 7 turbine exhaust. Per kilogram of steam leaving the boiler: y kg is extracted at state 6 and (1 − y) kg continues to state 7, through the condenser and pump I, and arrives at the heater at state 2. The heater is an adiabatic mixing chamber, so the steady-flow energy balance is:

📊 FIGURE — One open feedwater heater: where the bled fraction y goes, states 1-7
A fraction y of the steam is bled at state 6 and mixed with the pumped condensate (2) in the heater; only 1 − y reaches the condenser. The panel solves the heater balance for y.
\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

y h6 + (1 − y) h2 = 1 × h3, so y = (h3 − h2) / (h6 − h2)

qin = h5 − h4

qout = (1 − y)(h7 − h1)

wturb,out = (h5 − h6) + (1 − y)(h6 − h7)

wpump,in = (1 − y) wpump I + wpump II, with wpump I = v1(P2 − P1) and wpump II = v3(P4 − P3)

All h in kJ/kg, v in m³/kg, P in kPa, y dimensionless, everything per kilogram of steam leaving the boiler. There are two pumps because the open heater works at the extraction pressure: the condensate must be raised to that pressure to enter it, and the mixed stream must then be raised to boiler pressure. Notice that both the condenser heat and the low-pressure turbine work are scaled by (1 − y), and pump I is scaled by (1 − y) too.

\n\n

Worked example: one open feedwater heater at 1.2 MPa

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Steam enters the turbine at 15 MPa and 600 °C and is condensed at 10 kPa. Some steam is extracted at 1.2 MPa and sent to an open feedwater heater, which delivers saturated liquid. Find the fraction extracted and the thermal efficiency. Property source: Cengel & Boles Tables A-5 and A-6. At 1.2 MPa: hf = 798.33 kJ/kg, vf = 0.001138 m³/kg, Tsat = 187.96 °C. State 6 (1.2 MPa, s = 6.6796 kJ/kg·K) is superheated and interpolates to h6 = 2860.2 kJ/kg at T6 = 218.4 °C.

21.2 MPacompressed liquid (after pump I)193.01
31.2 MPasat. liquid, v3 = 0.001138 m³/kg798.33
415 MPacompressed liquid (after pump II)814.03

61.2 MPasuperheated, s6 = s52860.2
710 kPamixture, x7 = 0.80412115.3
  1. Pump I: wpI = 0.001010 m³/kg × (1200 − 10) kPa = 1.20 kJ/kg; h2 = 191.81 + 1.20 = 193.01 kJ/kg.
  2. Pump II: wpII = 0.001138 m³/kg × (15000 − 1200) kPa = 15.70 kJ/kg; h4 = 798.33 + 15.70 = 814.03 kJ/kg.
  3. State 7: x7 = (6.6796 − 0.6492)/7.4996 = 0.8041; h7 = 191.81 + 0.8041 × 2392.1 = 2115.3 kJ/kg.
  4. Extraction fraction: energy balance on the heater, y h6 + (1 − y) h2 = h3: y = (798.33 − 193.01)/(2860.2 − 193.01) = 605.32/2667.2 = 0.2269, about 22.7% of the steam.
  5. Heat added: qin = h5 − h4 = 3583.1 − 814.03 = 2769.1 kJ/kg.
  6. Heat rejected: qout = (1 − 0.2269)(2115.3 − 191.81) = 0.7731 × 1923.5 = 1486.9 kJ/kg.
  7. Efficiency: ηth = 1 − 1486.9/2769.1 = 0.463, i.e. 46.3%.
  8. Check via work: wturb = (3583.1 − 2860.2) + 0.7731 × (2860.2 − 2115.3) = 722.9 + 575.9 = 1298.8 kJ/kg; wpump = 0.7731 × 1.20 + 15.70 = 16.63 kJ/kg; wnet = 1282.1 kJ/kg; η = 1282.1/2769.1 = 0.463. The two routes agree.

Sanity check: the same plant with no regeneration (Lesson 2, case (c)) gave 43.0%, so one open heater gained 3.3 percentage points, and the net work per kilogram fell from 1452.7 to 1282.1 kJ/kg because 22.7% of the steam does not expand through the low-pressure stages. Higher efficiency, less work per kilogram: that trade-off is the signature of regeneration and is exactly what the exam expects you to notice.

\n\n

Closed feedwater heaters

\n

A closed FWH is a heat exchanger. The feedwater passes through tubes at boiler pressure (so only one main pump is needed for any number of closed heaters), and the extracted steam condenses on the outside of the tubes. The condensed extraction steam leaves as saturated liquid at the extraction pressure, and there are two ways to dispose of it: (i) pump it forward with a small drain pump into the feedwater line downstream of the heater, or (ii) throttle it backward through a trap to the next lower-pressure heater or the condenser. Throttling is cheaper (no pump) and is the usual choice; it is an isenthalpic process, so the trap exit has the same enthalpy as the drain but a lower pressure and a small vapour fraction.

\n

In the ideal closed heater the feedwater leaves at the saturation temperature of the extraction steam (in practice a \"terminal temperature difference\" of a few degrees remains). Because the streams do not mix, the energy balance has the feedwater on one side and the steam on the other. For a closed heater where y kg of steam at hext condenses to saturated liquid hdrain and heats 1 kg of feedwater from hfw,in to hfw,out:

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

y (hext − hdrain) = 1 × (hfw,out − hfw,in), so y = (hfw,out − hfw,in) / (hext − hdrain)

hext is the enthalpy of the extracted steam (kJ/kg), hdrain = hf at the extraction pressure, and the feedwater enthalpies are at the boiler pressure (approximated with hf at the corresponding temperature plus the v·ΔP correction if you want to be precise). If the drain is throttled back to a lower heater, that heater's balance gains an extra inlet stream y hdrain, so with several heaters you solve the balances from the highest pressure down.

\n

Open versus closed in one sentence each: open heaters are simple, cheap and good heat exchangers (the streams mix, so the feedwater reaches saturation) but every one needs its own pump; closed heaters need no extra pump and can all sit on one high-pressure feedwater line, but they are more expensive and less effective (a terminal temperature difference remains). Real plants use several closed heaters plus one open heater which doubles as the deaerator.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Forgetting to weight by (1 − y). The condenser heat and the low-pressure turbine work are per kilogram of steam that actually goes there, which is (1 − y) kg. Using h7 − h1 = 1923.5 kJ/kg for qout instead of 1486.9 kJ/kg in the example gives η = 30.5%, badly wrong.

Wrong denominator in y. The denominator is h6 − h2 (steam enthalpy minus incoming feedwater enthalpy), not h6 − h3. The latter gives y = 0.294 in the example instead of 0.227.

Using h2 instead of h4 in qin. The boiler receives the feedwater after the heater and the second pump: qin = h5 − h4 = 2769.1 kJ/kg, not h5 − h2 = 3390.1 kJ/kg.

Expecting more net work. Regeneration raises efficiency but lowers wnet per kilogram of boiler steam, so a regenerative plant needs a larger steam flow (and a larger boiler) for the same power. If your regenerative wnet came out higher than the simple cycle, you have made an error.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

The classic question is the open-heater calculation above: find y, qin, qout (or wnet) and ηth. Draw the schematic and the T-s diagram first and label every state on both; the T-s diagram of a regenerative cycle shows the expansion line 5-6-7 with a branch at 6 and the feedwater path 1-2-3-4 climbing the liquid line in two pumped steps.

Two-heater questions (one closed with drain throttled to one open, for instance) ask for two extraction fractions: write the closed-heater balance first (it has one unknown), then the open-heater balance, which contains both. Show each balance as an equation with the unknowns before substituting numbers.

Conceptual questions: \"Explain how regeneration increases efficiency\" (raises TH,avg by removing the low-temperature part of external heat addition), \"Compare open and closed feedwater heaters\" (mixing versus heat exchange, pumps, cost, effectiveness, deaeration) and \"Why does the net work per kilogram fall?\" (extracted steam does not expand through the low-pressure stages).
