This lesson lets you move from the ideal cycle to a real plant: apply isentropic efficiencies to the turbine and pump, account for pressure and heat losses, and then extend the Rankine cycle in the two directions that matter most in industry, cogeneration (using the steam for both power and process heat) and the combined gas-vapour cycle, which is how the most efficient thermal power stations in the world reach about 60% efficiency. It closes the vapour-cycle chapter and connects backward to the Brayton cycle and forward to the refrigeration chapter, where the same isentropic-efficiency tools reappear for compressors.

\n\n

Where the real cycle loses

\n

A real steam plant departs from the ideal cycle in three ways. Fluid friction causes pressure drops in the boiler, the condenser and every pipe, so the pump must deliver a higher pressure than the turbine sees. Heat loss from the steam to the surroundings in the pipes and turbine means more heat must be added in the boiler for the same output. And the turbine and pump are irreversible: entropy rises through both, so the turbine delivers less work than the isentropic drop and the pump consumes more. The first two are handled by specifying the actual pressures and temperatures at each state; the third is handled with isentropic efficiencies exactly as defined in the entropy chapter.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

The isentropic efficiency of a turbine is the actual work output divided by the work that an isentropic expansion between the same inlet state and the same exit pressure would give: ηT = wa/ws. The isentropic efficiency of a pump is the isentropic work divided by the actual work for the same inlet state and exit pressure: ηP = ws/wa. Both are defined so that they lie between 0 and 1; textbook problems typically use values around 0.85-0.90 for steam turbines and 0.75-0.85 for feed pumps.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

ηT = (h3 − h4a) / (h3 − h4s), so h4a = h3 − ηT(h3 − h4s)

ηP = (h2s − h1) / (h2a − h1), so h2a = h1 + v1(P2 − P1) / ηP

Subscript s means the isentropic end state (same entropy as the inlet, at the exit pressure) and subscript a the actual end state. h in kJ/kg, v1 in m³/kg, P in kPa. The turbine multiplies the ideal work by ηT (less out); the pump divides the ideal work by ηP (more in). On the T-s diagram both actual processes lean to the right of the vertical isentropic lines, and the actual turbine exhaust is drier than the isentropic one, which is the one kind thing irreversibility does for a steam turbine.

\n\n

Worked example: an actual cycle with ηT = 0.85 and ηP = 0.80

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A steam plant runs between 8 MPa, 500 °C at the turbine inlet and a 10 kPa condenser. The turbine has an isentropic efficiency of 85% and the pump 80%. Find the net work, the thermal efficiency and the actual turbine exit quality, and compare with the ideal cycle. Property source: Cengel & Boles Tables A-5 and A-6: 8 MPa/500 °C h3 = 3399.5 kJ/kg, s3 = 6.7266 kJ/kg·K; at 10 kPa hf = 191.81, hfg = 2392.1 kJ/kg, sf = 0.6492, sfg = 7.4996 kJ/kg·K, vf = 0.001010 m³/kg.

📊 FIGURE — Ideal vs actual steam turbine: 3→4s vertical, 3→4a leaning right
The dashed line is the isentropic expansion; the real turbine generates entropy, so 4a lies right of 4s: less work, a drier exhaust. The table sets the two cycles side by side.
  1. Isentropic turbine exit: x4s = (6.7266 − 0.6492)/7.4996 = 0.8104; h4s = 191.81 + 0.8104 × 2392.1 = 2130.3 kJ/kg.
  2. Isentropic turbine work: wT,s = 3399.5 − 2130.3 = 1269.2 kJ/kg.
  3. Actual turbine work: wT,a = 0.85 × 1269.2 = 1078.8 kJ/kg; h4a = 3399.5 − 1078.8 = 2320.7 kJ/kg.
  4. Actual exit quality: x4a = (2320.7 − 191.81)/2392.1 = 0.890, drier than the isentropic 0.810.
  5. Isentropic pump work: wP,s = 0.001010 m³/kg × (8000 − 10) kPa = 8.07 kJ/kg.
  6. Actual pump work: wP,a = 8.07/0.80 = 10.09 kJ/kg; h2a = 191.81 + 10.09 = 201.90 kJ/kg.
  7. Heat added: qin = h3 − h2a = 3399.5 − 201.90 = 3197.6 kJ/kg.
  8. Net work and efficiency: wnet = 1078.8 − 10.09 = 1068.7 kJ/kg; ηth = 1068.7/3197.6 = 0.334, i.e. 33.4%.
  9. Ideal comparison: wnet,ideal = 1269.2 − 8.07 = 1261.1 kJ/kg; qin,ideal = 3399.5 − 199.88 = 3199.6 kJ/kg; ηideal = 0.394, i.e. 39.4%.
  10. Plant size: for 100 MW net, the steam flow is 100,000 kW ÷ 1068.7 kJ/kg = 93.6 kg/s.

Sanity check: the turbine inefficiency alone removed 15% of the turbine work, and the efficiency fell from 39.4% to 33.4%, a drop of about the same relative size (15%), which is what you expect when the pump term is negligible. The actual exhaust at x = 0.890 is drier than the isentropic exhaust, as it must be for an irreversible adiabatic expansion (entropy rises, state moves right).

\n\n

Cogeneration: power plus process heat

\n

Many industries (chemical, paper, food, district heating) need large quantities of heat at 150-200 °C. Supplying that heat by burning fuel in a dedicated boiler wastes the fuel's work potential (its exergy), because heat at 200 °C is far less valuable than heat at 1500 °C from a flame. A cogeneration plant instead raises high-pressure steam, expands it through a turbine to make electricity, and extracts or exhausts steam at the pressure the process needs. The heat that would have gone to the condenser is used, so the fraction of fuel energy put to use can reach 70-80% rather than the 30-45% of a power-only plant.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

The utilisation factor εu of a cogeneration plant is the fraction of the heat input that is used for any purpose: εu = (Ẇnet + Q̇process)/Q̇in = 1 − Q̇out/Q̇in, where Q̇out is the heat rejected in the condenser only. It replaces thermal efficiency as the performance measure because a cogeneration plant has two useful products.

\n

In the ideal cogeneration plant no heat is rejected in the condenser at all (all the turbine exhaust goes to the process), so εu = 100%. Real plants must follow a process-heat demand that varies, so a practical layout has an extraction point for process steam, a bypass (throttling) valve to send boiler steam straight to the process heater when heat demand is high, and a condenser for when it is low. Per unit time, with a steam flow ṁ split into a process fraction and a condenser fraction, the energy balances are the usual component balances with each stream's own mass flow rate. As an illustration: a plant with Q̇in = 120 MW that produces Ẇnet = 30 MW and delivers Q̇process = 50 MW has εu = (30 + 50)/120 = 0.667, even though its thermal efficiency as a power plant is only 30/120 = 0.25.

\n\n

The combined gas-vapour cycle

\n

A gas turbine (Brayton cycle) takes in heat at 1400-1600 °C but exhausts at 500-600 °C, wasting a lot of high-temperature energy. A steam plant takes in heat below about 620 °C but rejects it at 30-45 °C. Stacking them removes both weaknesses: the gas turbine exhaust becomes the heat source for the steam cycle in a heat recovery steam generator (HRSG), no extra fuel is burned for the steam side (except optional supplementary firing), and the combined plant adds heat at gas-turbine temperatures while rejecting it at condenser temperatures. Combined-cycle plants are the most efficient fossil-fuel power stations in operation, with thermal efficiencies of about 60% for the best modern units.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

If all the gas-turbine exhaust heat goes to the steam cycle and the HRSG has no stack loss: ηcc = ηgas + ηsteam − ηgas ηsteam

In general, with a heat-recovery fraction f of the gas exhaust captured by the HRSG: Ẇtotal = ηgas Q̇in + ηsteam × f × (1 − ηgas) Q̇in and ηcc = Ẇtotal/Q̇in

ηgas and ηsteam are the individual cycle efficiencies (dimensionless), Q̇in is the fuel heat rate into the gas turbine combustor in MW, and f is the fraction of the gas exhaust energy (1 − ηgas)Q̇in transferred to the steam in the HRSG. The steam-side energy balance that examiners set is the HRSG balance: ṁgas cp(Texhaust,in − Tstack) = ṁsteam(hsteam,out − hfeedwater,in), which fixes the ratio of steam flow to gas flow.

\n

Numbers: with ηgas = 0.38 and ηsteam = 0.30 and perfect heat recovery, ηcc = 0.38 + 0.30 − 0.38 × 0.30 = 0.566, i.e. 56.6%. With a more realistic 70% recovery in the HRSG and a 32% steam cycle: gas work = 38 MW per 100 MW of fuel, exhaust = 62 MW, heat to steam = 0.70 × 62 = 43.4 MW, steam work = 0.32 × 43.4 = 13.9 MW, total 51.9 MW, ηcc = 51.9%. Either way the combined plant beats both of its parts by a wide margin. In the 70% recovery case the gas turbine supplies 38 of the 51.9 MW (about 73%) and the steam turbine the rest; the gas turbine is the larger contributor in combined-cycle plants.

\n\n

Binary vapour cycles

\n

Water is a poor fluid at the top of the cycle (its critical temperature of 373.95 °C is too low, so high-temperature heat addition needs very high pressure) and a good fluid at the bottom (low condenser pressures of 5-10 kPa are manageable). A binary vapour cycle uses two working fluids in two Rankine cycles coupled by a heat exchanger: a topping fluid with a high critical temperature and low vapour pressure, historically mercury, that condenses by boiling water in the bottoming cycle. Mercury-water plants have been built in the past, but mercury is toxic and expensive, and today the topping role is filled far more practically by the gas turbine of a combined cycle. Organic fluids are used in the opposite role as bottoming cycles (organic Rankine cycles) for low-temperature heat sources such as geothermal brine and engine exhaust.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Applying ηP the wrong way round. The pump's actual work is larger than isentropic: divide by ηP (8.07/0.80 = 10.09 kJ/kg), never multiply (8.07 × 0.80 = 6.46 kJ/kg is wrong). The turbine's actual work is smaller: multiply by ηT.

Computing qin with the isentropic h2s. Once you have an actual pump exit enthalpy, the boiler heat input is h3 − h2a. In the example this changes qin from 3199.6 to 3197.6 kJ/kg, small here but marked.

Reporting thermal efficiency for a cogeneration plant. The performance measure is the utilisation factor; quoting ηth = 25% for a plant that uses 67% of its fuel energy misses the point of cogeneration.

Adding the two cycle efficiencies. ηgas + ηsteam = 68% is not a combined-cycle efficiency; the steam cycle only sees the (1 − ηgas) fraction of the fuel energy, so the cross term ηgas ηsteam must be subtracted.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

The actual-cycle question is the ideal Rankine question with two extra lines: find h4s and h2s as before, then h4a = h3 − ηT(h3 − h4s) and h2a = h1 + wP,s/ηP. Sometimes the actual turbine exit temperature or quality is given instead of ηT; then compute ηT from it. Pressure drops are given as \"the boiler outlet is at 8 MPa but the turbine inlet is at 7.5 MPa\": use the turbine inlet conditions for state 3 and the boiler pressure for the pump.

Cogeneration questions give the process-steam pressure and heat demand and ask for the turbine extraction flow, the net power and the utilisation factor. Draw the schematic with mass flows on every line, then balance the process heater (Q̇process = ṁprocess(hin − hout)) before anything else.

Combined-cycle questions almost always come down to the HRSG energy balance for the steam-to-gas mass-flow ratio, then ηcc = (Ẇgas + Ẇsteam)/Q̇in. Use cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K for air-like exhaust unless variable-specific-heat tables are supplied, and remember the gas side rejects only the stack loss, not the whole exhaust, once the HRSG is present.

This lesson lets you take a refrigerator or heat pump described in a problem, draw its cycle on a P-h diagram, read four enthalpies from the R-134a tables and compute the cooling load, the compressor power and the coefficient of performance. In the degree sequence it sits right after the vapour power cycles: a vapour-compression refrigerator is essentially a Rankine cycle run backwards, with the turbine replaced by a throttling valve. Everything here rests on the steady-flow energy equation from the control-volume chapter and on the second-law limits from the Carnot chapter.

Refrigerators and heat pumps: one machine, two purposes

Heat flows on its own from hot to cold. Moving it the other way, from a cold space to a warmer one, needs a device and needs work. A refrigerator is such a device whose purpose is the heat it removes from the cold space (the inside of the fridge, the cold room, the cabin). A heat pump is the same device whose purpose is the heat it delivers to the warm space (the house in winter). The hardware is identical; only the quantity we care about changes, so the performance measure changes with it.

📘 DEFINITION

The coefficient of performance (COP) is the desired heat transfer divided by the work that had to be paid for. For a refrigerator the desired effect is the heat absorbed from the cold space, QL; for a heat pump it is the heat delivered to the warm space, QH.

A COP can be, and usually is, greater than 1. It is not an efficiency and nothing is being violated: the work is not converted into cooling, it is used to move heat that already exists.

COPR = QL / Wnet,in

COPHP = QH / Wnet,in

COPHP = COPR + 1

QL is the heat removed from the low-temperature space (kJ or kW), QH the heat rejected to the high-temperature surroundings (kJ or kW), Wnet,in the net work input (kJ or kW). The third line follows from the first law for a cycle, QH = QL + Wnet,in; it holds for any cycle, ideal or real, as long as the same machine and the same two heat flows are meant.

Cooling capacity is often quoted in tons of refrigeration. One ton is the rate of heat removal needed to freeze one short ton (2,000 lb) of liquid water at 0 °C into ice at 0 °C in 24 hours. In SI it is 211 kJ/min, which is 3.517 kW; in US units it is 12,000 Btu/h (Cengel & Boles, Chapter 11). A domestic refrigerator is a small fraction of a ton; a supermarket plant is tens of tons.

The reversed Carnot cycle: the ceiling nobody builds

Every process of the Carnot cycle is reversible, so running it backwards gives a refrigerator: isentropic compression 1-2, isothermal heat rejection 2-3 at TH, isentropic expansion 3-4, isothermal heat absorption 4-1 at TL. Because the heat transfers are isothermal, Q = T Δs and the COP depends on the two temperatures alone.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

COPR,Carnot = TL / (TH − TL)

COPHP,Carnot = TH / (TH − TL)

TL is the temperature of the cold space and TH that of the warm surroundings, both in kelvin (K). These are the highest COPs any refrigerator or heat pump can have between those two temperatures; a real machine between the same temperatures is always lower.

Two things about this formula shape the whole subject. First, the COP falls as the temperature difference grows: cooling a freezer at −20 °C in a 35 °C kitchen is far more expensive per kilojoule than cooling a room at 20 °C. Second, it is not built in practice. Inside the vapour dome the isothermal processes are easy (boiling and condensing at constant pressure are isothermal), but process 1-2 would compress a wet liquid-vapour mixture, which damages compressors, and process 3-4 would expand a mostly-liquid mixture through a turbine that would recover very little work for its cost. The fixes to those two processes define the practical cycle.

The ideal vapour-compression refrigeration cycle

Two changes turn the reversed Carnot cycle into something a manufacturer will build: compress the refrigerant only after it has become saturated (or slightly superheated) vapour, and replace the turbine with a cheap throttling valve or capillary tube. The four processes, with the state numbering used in Cengel & Boles and on most exam papers, are:

ProcessDeviceWhat happensIdeal model
1 to 2CompressorSaturated vapour at the evaporator pressure is compressed to the condenser pressure; it leaves superheated and hotIsentropic: s2 = s1
2 to 3CondenserHot vapour is desuperheated, condensed and leaves as saturated liquid, rejecting QH to the surroundingsConstant pressure, no work
3 to 4Throttling valveLiquid flashes to a low-pressure, low-temperature liquid-vapour mixtureIsenthalpic: h4 = h3
4 to 1EvaporatorThe mixture boils at the low pressure, absorbing QL from the cold space, and leaves as saturated vapourConstant pressure, no work

The throttling step is where the ideal vapour-compression cycle gives up its claim to reversibility. Throttling is irreversible, so this "ideal" cycle is internally irreversible and its COP is below the reversed Carnot value between the same two saturation temperatures, even before any real-world losses are added. It is still called ideal because every device is modelled as perfectly as its type allows.

The P-h diagram

Refrigeration engineers use the pressure-enthalpy (P-h) diagram rather than the T-s diagram because three of the four processes are straight lines on it. The condenser (2-3) and evaporator (4-1) are horizontal lines at the two pressures; the throttling process (3-4) is a vertical line, since h is constant; only the compression 1-2 curves, following a line of constant entropy up and to the right in the superheated region. The horizontal length of line 4-1 is the refrigeration effect qL per kilogram; the horizontal length of 2-3 is qH; their difference, the horizontal run of 1-2, is the compressor work. You can therefore see the COP as a ratio of two lengths before you compute anything.

📊 FIGURE — Ideal vapour-compression cycle: four states on the loop and on P-h
Left: the loop the refrigerant runs through. Right: the same states 1-4 on P-h. The horizontal lengths are q_L (4-1), w_in (1-2) and q_H (2-3), so COP_R is a ratio of two lengths.

The energy balances

Each device is a steady-flow control volume with negligible kinetic and potential energy changes, so the steady-flow energy equation reduces to q − w = hout − hin. Applied to each device in turn:

qL = h1 − h4

win = h2 − h1

qH = h2 − h3

h4 = h3

COPR = (h1 − h4) / (h2 − h1)

All h are specific enthalpies in kJ/kg, q and w are per kilogram of refrigerant in kJ/kg, and multiplying by the mass flow rate ṁ (kg/s) gives rates in kW. Everything therefore comes down to finding four enthalpies: h1 = hg at the evaporator pressure, h3 = hf at the condenser pressure, h4 = h3, and h2 from the superheated table at the condenser pressure and s2 = s1, which almost always needs an interpolation.

Worked example: an R-134a refrigerator between 0.14 MPa and 0.8 MPa

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A refrigerator uses R-134a on the ideal vapour-compression cycle between 0.14 MPa (evaporator) and 0.8 MPa (condenser). The mass flow rate is 0.05 kg/s. Find the refrigeration rate, the compressor power, the heat rejected, the COP, and compare with the reversed Carnot COP. Property source: Cengel & Boles, Tables A-12 (saturated R-134a by pressure) and A-13 (superheated R-134a), 7th edition values; other editions and NIST tables differ in the second decimal, which does not change any answer below to three figures.

  1. State 1, saturated vapour at 0.14 MPa (Table A-12): Tsat = −18.77 °C, h1 = hg = 239.16 kJ/kg, s1 = sg = 0.94456 kJ/kg·K.
  2. State 3, saturated liquid at 0.8 MPa (Table A-12): Tsat = 31.31 °C, h3 = hf = 95.47 kJ/kg.
  3. State 4, throttling: h4 = h3 = 95.47 kJ/kg at 0.14 MPa (a wet mixture at −18.77 °C).
  4. State 2, 0.8 MPa and s2 = 0.94456 kJ/kg·K. In Table A-13 at 0.8 MPa the saturation row (31.31 °C) has h = 267.29 kJ/kg, s = 0.91835 kJ/kg·K and the 40 °C row has h = 276.45 kJ/kg, s = 0.94779 kJ/kg·K. The target entropy lies between them, so interpolate: fraction = (0.94456 − 0.91835)/(0.94779 − 0.91835) = 0.02621/0.02944 = 0.8903. Then h2 = 267.29 + 0.8903 × (276.45 − 267.29) = 267.29 + 8.16 = 275.45 kJ/kg, and T2 ≈ 31.31 + 0.8903 × 8.69 ≈ 39.0 °C. (The textbook, interpolating on a finer grid, quotes 275.39 kJ/kg; the 0.02 % difference is invisible in the answers.)
  5. Refrigeration effect: qL = h1 − h4 = 239.16 − 95.47 = 143.69 kJ/kg, so QL = 0.05 kg/s × 143.69 kJ/kg = 7.18 kW (7.18/3.517 = 2.04 tons).
  6. Compressor: win = h2 − h1 = 275.45 − 239.16 = 36.29 kJ/kg, so Win = 0.05 × 36.29 = 1.81 kW.
  7. Condenser: qH = h2 − h3 = 275.45 − 95.47 = 179.98 kJ/kg, so QH = 0.05 × 179.98 = 9.00 kW. Check: QL + Win = 7.18 + 1.81 = 8.99 kW, equal to QH within rounding.
  8. COPR = qL/win = 143.69/36.29 = 3.96. As a heat pump the same machine would have COPHP = 179.98/36.29 = 4.96 = 3.96 + 1.
  9. Reversed Carnot between the two saturation temperatures: TL = 273.15 − 18.77 = 254.38 K, TH = 273.15 + 31.31 = 304.46 K, COPR,Carnot = 254.38/(304.46 − 254.38) = 254.38/50.08 = 5.08.
  10. Quality after the valve, for the picture: x4 = (h4 − hf)/(hg − hf) at 0.14 MPa with hf = 27.08 kJ/kg: (95.47 − 27.08)/(239.16 − 27.08) = 68.39/212.08 = 0.32, so about a third of the mass flashes to vapour in the valve and does no cooling.

Sanity check: the COP of 3.96 is below the Carnot ceiling of 5.08 (78 % of it), the compressor outlet is superheated (39 °C is above the 31.31 °C saturation temperature at 0.8 MPa), and QH exceeds QL by exactly the work. All plausible.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Celsius in the Carnot COP. COP = TL/(TH − TL) needs kelvin in the numerator; the difference in the denominator is the same in °C and K, which is exactly why the error survives a quick glance. With TL = −10 °C and TH = 30 °C the correct COP is 263.15/40 = 6.58, not −0.25.

Reading h4 as hf at the evaporator pressure. State 4 is a mixture, not saturated liquid; its enthalpy is fixed by the throttling, h4 = h3 = hf at the condenser pressure.

Stopping at the saturation row for state 2. The compressor outlet is superheated; if you use hg at the condenser pressure you underestimate the work and overstate the COP.

Mixing up which COP was asked. The same machine has COPHP = COPR + 1; a refrigerator answer given as a heat-pump COP is off by exactly 1, and graders look for it.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

The interpolation in step 4 is the same operation you do when you resample a time series: numpy.interp(0.94456, [0.91835, 0.94779], [267.29, 276.45]) returns 275.45 in one line. If you load the superheated R-134a table into a pandas DataFrame indexed by pressure and temperature, every cycle in this chapter becomes a five-line script, and you can sweep the condenser pressure to plot COP against it, which is exactly the design question the next lesson asks.

It also protects you from the classic error: interpolating on the wrong column. Name the columns and the code will not let you read h off the s column.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

The standard question gives two pressures (or two saturation temperatures) and a mass flow rate or a cooling load, and asks for QL, Win, QH and COP. Full marks need: a labelled sketch of the cycle on a T-s or P-h diagram, a table of the four states with P, T, h and s, the interpolation for h2 shown explicitly, and the answers in kW with a COP to three significant figures.

Variants: the cooling load is given in tons (convert with 1 ton = 3.517 kW to get ṁ = QL/qL); the quality at the evaporator inlet is asked (x4 from h4); the reversed Carnot COP between the same saturation temperatures is asked for comparison.

The one-mark conceptual questions: why the turbine is replaced by a throttling valve (cost and the small work recovered from expanding a liquid), why compression starts from saturated vapour (liquid droplets damage compressors), and why the ideal cycle is still internally irreversible (the throttling).

This lesson lets you analyse a real refrigeration cycle whose states no longer sit neatly on the saturation lines, judge a refrigerant the way a design engineer does, and size a heat pump for a building. It is the bridge between the idealised cycle of the last lesson and the machines that are actually installed, and it draws on the isentropic-efficiency idea from the entropy chapter. The next lesson stacks these cycles for larger temperature spans.

Where the real cycle leaves the ideal one

An actual vapour-compression cycle differs from the ideal one mainly through fluid friction, which causes pressure drops, and heat transfer to or from the surroundings, which happens in every pipe. Walk around the loop and list the departures:

  • Superheat at the compressor inlet. The evaporator cannot be controlled precisely enough to deliver exactly saturated vapour, so the refrigerant is deliberately superheated by a few degrees before the compressor. This guarantees a dry compressor inlet (no liquid droplets) but raises the specific volume, so the compressor moves less mass per stroke and the work per kilogram rises.
  • Pressure drop in the suction line and the evaporator lowers the compressor inlet pressure, which again raises the specific volume and the work.
  • Non-isentropic compression. Friction and heat transfer make the real compressor outlet state 2a differ from the isentropic 2s. If the compressor is well cooled the entropy can even decrease; if it is not, entropy increases and the outlet is hotter than 2s.
  • Subcooling in the condenser. The liquid is cooled below its saturation temperature before the valve. This is a good departure: it lowers h3, hence h4, hence increases the refrigeration effect h1 − h4 at no cost in compressor work.
  • Pressure drop in the condenser and heat gain in the lines between the condenser and the valve, and between the evaporator and the compressor, each of which costs a little capacity.
📘 DEFINITION

The isentropic efficiency of a compressor is the work the compressor would need if it were isentropic between the same inlet state and the same outlet pressure, divided by the work it actually needs. Because it compares two work inputs, the ideal one is the smaller and sits in the numerator.

Superheat is the temperature of the vapour above its saturation temperature at the same pressure; subcooling is the temperature of the liquid below its saturation temperature at the same pressure. Both are quoted in kelvin (or °C difference).

🧮 KEY EQUATION

ηC = ws / wa = (h2s − h1) / (h2a − h1)

h1 is the actual compressor inlet enthalpy (kJ/kg), h2s the outlet enthalpy at the condenser pressure with s = s1 (kJ/kg), h2a the actual outlet enthalpy (kJ/kg). Given ηC and h2s, the actual outlet is h2a = h1 + (h2s − h1)/ηC: you divide by the efficiency, never multiply.

The energy balances of the last lesson do not change: qL = h1 − h4, win = h2a − h1, qH = h2a − h3. What changes is that the states are now found from the superheated and compressed-liquid data rather than from the saturation lines, and that compressed liquid is approximated, as with water, by the saturated liquid at the same temperature: h3 ≈ hf@T3.

Worked example: an actual R-134a cycle with superheat, subcooling and pressure drops

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

R-134a enters the compressor at 0.14 MPa and −10 °C (superheated) at 0.05 kg/s and leaves at 0.8 MPa and 50 °C. It is cooled in the condenser to 26 °C at 0.72 MPa and throttled to 0.15 MPa. Neglecting heat transfer in the lines, find the refrigeration rate, the compressor power, the compressor isentropic efficiency and the COP. Property source: Cengel & Boles Tables A-11 (saturated R-134a by temperature), A-12 and A-13, 7th edition values.

📊 FIGURE — The actual R-134a cycle on P-h: superheat, subcooling, 2s vs 2a
Solid line: the real cycle of the worked example; dashed: the isentropic compression 1-2s. State 1 sits right of the vapour line (superheat), state 3 left of the liquid line (subcooling).
  1. State 1 (0.14 MPa, −10 °C; saturation temperature at this pressure is −18.77 °C, so the vapour has 8.8 K of superheat). Table A-13: h1 = 246.36 kJ/kg, s1 = 0.97236 kJ/kg·K.
  2. State 2a (0.8 MPa, 50 °C), Table A-13: h2a = 286.69 kJ/kg.
  3. State 2s (0.8 MPa, s = 0.97236 kJ/kg·K). Table A-13 at 0.8 MPa: 40 °C row h = 276.45, s = 0.94779; 50 °C row h = 286.69, s = 0.97992. Fraction = (0.97236 − 0.94779)/(0.97992 − 0.94779) = 0.02457/0.03213 = 0.7647; h2s = 276.45 + 0.7647 × (286.69 − 276.45) = 276.45 + 7.83 = 284.28 kJ/kg.
  4. State 3 (0.72 MPa, 26 °C). Saturation pressure at 26 °C is 685.84 kPa, below 720 kPa, so this is compressed (subcooled) liquid; Table A-11: h3 ≈ hf@26 °C = 87.83 kJ/kg. Since Tsat at 0.72 MPa is a little above 26 °C, the subcooling is about 1 to 2 K.
  5. State 4: h4 = h3 = 87.83 kJ/kg at 0.15 MPa.
  6. Refrigeration: qL = 246.36 − 87.83 = 158.53 kJ/kg; QL = 0.05 × 158.53 = 7.93 kW.
  7. Compressor: wa = 286.69 − 246.36 = 40.33 kJ/kg; Win = 0.05 × 40.33 = 2.02 kW.
  8. Isentropic efficiency: ws = 284.28 − 246.36 = 37.92 kJ/kg; ηC = 37.92/40.33 = 0.940 (94.0 %).
  9. COPR = 158.53/40.33 = 3.93. Condenser load QH = 0.05 × (286.69 − 87.83) = 0.05 × 198.86 = 9.94 kW = 7.93 + 2.02 within rounding.

Sanity check: the COP (3.93) is close to the ideal cycle between the same pressures (3.96): the subcooling to 26 °C raised the refrigeration effect from 143.69 to 158.53 kJ/kg, which almost paid for the extra work of compressing superheated vapour with a 94 % efficient compressor. Both effects are the right size and the right sign.

Choosing a refrigerant

A refrigerant is chosen by the temperatures the job needs, then filtered by safety, environment, cost and compatibility with the compressor oil. The temperature requirement works like this: to absorb heat the evaporator must be colder than the space it cools, and to reject heat the condenser must be hotter than the surroundings. Practical heat exchangers need a difference of roughly 5 to 10 K at each end. A cold room held at −10 °C therefore needs an evaporator at about −20 °C, and a condenser cooled by 30 °C air runs at about 40 °C. Those two temperatures fix the two saturation pressures through the refrigerant’s own vapour-pressure curve, and that is where the choice of fluid matters:

  • Evaporator pressure above atmospheric. If the evaporator is below 1 atm, air leaks in, carrying moisture that freezes in the valve. R-134a boils at −26.1 °C at 1 atm, so it is a natural fit for domestic and automotive work down to about −25 °C; ammonia boils at −33.3 °C at 1 atm and reaches lower.
  • Condenser pressure not too high. High pressures mean heavy, expensive components. The condensing temperature must also sit well below the critical temperature, otherwise there is no latent heat to reject; R-134a’s critical point (101.1 °C, 4.06 MPa) is comfortably above 40 °C, whereas CO2 (critical temperature 31.0 °C) must run a transcritical cycle whenever the surroundings are warm.
  • Large enthalpy of vaporisation means less mass flow for a given load; a small vapour specific volume means a smaller compressor.
  • Environment. The chlorine in CFCs (R-12) and HCFCs (R-22) destroys stratospheric ozone; the Montreal Protocol of 1987 phased CFCs out and HCFCs are following. The HFCs that replaced them (R-134a, R-410A) have zero ozone depletion potential but large global warming potentials, and the 2016 Kigali Amendment phases them down in turn, pushing the industry towards HFOs (R-1234yf), CO2, ammonia and hydrocarbons.
  • Safety. ASHRAE Standard 34 classifies refrigerants by toxicity (A = lower, B = higher) and flammability (1 = none, 2L = mildly flammable, 2 and 3 = flammable). Ammonia is B2L: efficient and cheap but toxic, so it is confined to industrial plants with trained staff. Propane is A3: excellent thermodynamically but flammable, so charges are kept small.

Later IPCC reports revise them by a few per cent; quote the basis when you cite one.

Heat pump systems

A heat pump is the refrigerator of the last lesson with the condenser inside the building. The attraction is the COP: every kilowatt of electricity delivers COPHP kilowatts of heat, whereas a resistance heater delivers exactly one. The Carnot limit for a house at 21 °C with −5 °C outside is 294.15/(294.15 − 268.15) = 294.15/26 = 11.3, and real machines typically achieve a COP in the range of about 2 to 4, which still cuts the electricity bill for heating by more than half.

Air-source heat pumps take heat from outdoor air. They are cheap to install, but their capacity and COP fall as the outdoor temperature falls, which is exactly when the house needs the most heat; the Carnot formula shows why, since TH − TL grows. Below roughly 0 °C the outdoor coil also frosts over and must be defrosted periodically, usually by running the machine in reverse for a few minutes, which costs capacity. Most units include a reversing valve that swaps the roles of the two coils, so the same unit cools the house in summer.

Ground-source (geothermal) heat pumps take heat from the soil or groundwater a few metres down, where the temperature stays close to the yearly average of the location all year round. The source is warmer than the winter air and cooler than the summer air, so the COP is higher in both seasons and there is no defrost penalty. The cost is the buried loop: trenches or boreholes make the installation several times more expensive than an air-source unit. Water-source units use a lake, river or well for the same reason.

Sizing is a first-law calculation: the heat loss of the building (kW) at the design outdoor temperature is QH; the electricity demand is W = QH/COPHP; the heat drawn from the source is QL = QH − W. The outdoor coil must therefore be big enough to absorb QL from cold air or soil, which is why the outdoor unit is larger than intuition suggests.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Multiplying by the isentropic efficiency. For a compressor the actual work is the isentropic work divided by ηC: with ws = 36.23 kJ/kg and ηC = 0.80 the actual work is 36.23/0.80 = 45.3 kJ/kg, not 36.23 × 0.80 = 29.0 kJ/kg. Turbines multiply; compressors and pumps divide.

Reading a subcooled liquid at its pressure. Compressed liquid enthalpy follows the temperature, not the pressure: h3 ≈ hf at T3. Using hf at 0.72 MPa in the example above would have given roughly 90 kJ/kg instead of 87.83 kJ/kg and thrown the refrigeration effect off by about 2 kJ/kg.

Computing ηC from the temperatures. The isentropic efficiency of a real-gas compressor is a ratio of enthalpy differences; (T2s − T1)/(T2a − T1) is only valid for an ideal gas with constant cp, and R-134a vapour near saturation is not one.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

The actual-cycle question gives the compressor inlet as superheated vapour (P and T), the compressor outlet (P and T) or an isentropic efficiency, and the condenser exit as subcooled liquid (P and T). You must locate every state in the correct table: A-13 for the two vapour states, A-11 by temperature for the subcooled liquid. Then the same four energy balances as before, plus ηC. Quote the tables you used.

A second favourite: "explain the effect on COP of (a) 5 K of superheat at the compressor inlet, (b) 5 K of subcooling at the condenser exit, (c) a pressure drop in the suction line". Answers: (a) slightly lowers COP through higher specific volume and work per kg, though it protects the compressor; (b) raises COP by increasing qL at no work cost; (c) lowers COP, more work per kg.

Refrigerant-selection questions are short-answer: name two thermodynamic criteria (evaporator pressure above atmospheric, condensing temperature below critical, large hfg) and two non-thermodynamic ones (ODP, GWP, toxicity, flammability), and say why ammonia is used in warehouses but not homes.

"}, "THERMO/refrig/s3": {"body": "

This lesson lets you handle the refrigeration problems that a single vapour-compression cycle cannot: very low temperatures, where a cascade or a multistage system is used; heat-driven cooling, where an absorption cycle replaces the compressor with a pump and a heat source; and gas-cycle cooling, used on aircraft and in gas liquefaction. It completes the cycles part of the degree; the property-relations and mixtures chapters that follow supply the tools these systems are designed with.

Why one stage runs out

Suppose a process needs −60 °C while the condenser rejects heat to 30 °C air. A single R-134a cycle would need an evaporator pressure far below atmospheric and a pressure ratio across the compressor of well over ten. Three things go wrong at once: the compressor discharge becomes very hot (the isentropic compression line on the P-h diagram climbs steeply through the superheated region), the compressor’s volumetric efficiency collapses so it moves little mass per stroke, and the throttling loss grows because a large fraction of the liquid flashes uselessly in the valve. The remedy in every case is the same idea used for gas compressors in the control-volume chapter: split the pressure ratio into stages and remove heat in between.

Cascade refrigeration systems

A cascade system is two (or more) complete vapour-compression cycles stacked in series and coupled by a heat exchanger. The evaporator of the upper cycle is the condenser of the lower cycle. The two cycles can use different refrigerants: one suited to the low pressures of the cold end (its evaporator pressure kept above atmospheric) and one suited to the moderate pressures of the warm end. The two mass flow rates are not equal; they are related by the energy balance on the coupling heat exchanger, which is treated as adiabatic on its outside.

📊 FIGURE — Two-stage cascade: cycle A above cycle B, coupled at 0.32 MPa
The heat exchanger is A’s evaporator and B’s condenser at once. On P-h the two cycles share the 0.32 MPa line; B throttles from there, not from 0.8 MPa, so less of it flashes.
🧮 KEY EQUATION

ṁA (h5 − h8) = ṁB (h2 − h3)

COPR,cascade = QL / (Wcomp,A + Wcomp,B) = ṁB(h1 − h4) / [ṁA(h6 − h5) + ṁB(h2 − h1)]

Subscript A is the upper (warm) cycle with states 5-6-7-8, B the lower (cold) cycle with states 1-2-3-4; ṁ in kg/s, h in kJ/kg. The left side of the first line is the heat absorbed by the upper cycle’s evaporator, the right side the heat rejected by the lower cycle’s condenser; they are equal because the exchanger is adiabatic.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A two-stage cascade system operates between 0.8 MPa and 0.14 MPa with R-134a in both loops. Each stage is an ideal vapour-compression cycle. Heat is transferred between the loops in an adiabatic counterflow exchanger where both streams are at 0.32 MPa; the lower loop’s refrigerant leaves it as saturated liquid and the upper loop’s as saturated vapour. The upper loop’s mass flow rate is 0.05 kg/s. Find the lower loop’s mass flow rate, the refrigeration rate, the total compressor power and the COP. Property source: Cengel & Boles Tables A-12 and A-13, 7th edition; the two superheated enthalpies at 0.32 MPa and 0.8 MPa are interpolations in Table A-13.

  1. Upper loop (A), 0.32 to 0.8 MPa. State 5, saturated vapour at 0.32 MPa: h5 = 251.88 kJ/kg, s5 = 0.93006 kJ/kg·K (Tsat = 2.46 °C). State 6 at 0.8 MPa and s = 0.93006: between the saturation row (h = 267.29, s = 0.91835) and the 40 °C row (h = 276.45, s = 0.94779): fraction = (0.93006 − 0.91835)/0.02944 = 0.3978, h6 = 267.29 + 0.3978 × 9.16 = 270.93 kJ/kg. State 7, saturated liquid at 0.8 MPa: h7 = 95.47 kJ/kg; h8 = h7 = 95.47 kJ/kg.
  2. Lower loop (B), 0.14 to 0.32 MPa. State 1, saturated vapour at 0.14 MPa: h1 = 239.16 kJ/kg, s1 = 0.94456 kJ/kg·K. State 2 at 0.32 MPa and s = 0.94456, interpolated in Table A-13: h2 = 255.93 kJ/kg. State 3, saturated liquid at 0.32 MPa: h3 = 55.16 kJ/kg; h4 = 55.16 kJ/kg.
  3. Heat-exchanger balance: ṁB = ṁA(h5 − h8)/(h2 − h3) = 0.05 × (251.88 − 95.47)/(255.93 − 55.16) = 0.05 × 156.41/200.77 = 0.0390 kg/s. The cold loop carries less mass because each kilogram of it rejects more heat (200.77 kJ) than each kilogram of the warm loop absorbs (156.41 kJ).
  4. Refrigeration rate: QL = ṁB(h1 − h4) = 0.03895 × (239.16 − 55.16) = 0.03895 × 184.00 = 7.17 kW.
  5. Compressor power: WA = 0.05 × (270.93 − 251.88) = 0.05 × 19.05 = 0.953 kW; WB = 0.03895 × (255.93 − 239.16) = 0.03895 × 16.77 = 0.653 kW; total Win = 1.61 kW.
  6. COP: 7.17/1.61 = 4.46.

Sanity check: a single-stage cycle between the same 0.14 and 0.8 MPa (last lesson) gave 7.18 kW of cooling for 1.81 kW and a COP of 3.96. The cascade delivers almost the same cooling for 11 % less power, a 12.7 % gain in COP, because the cold loop throttles from 0.32 MPa instead of 0.8 MPa (h4 = 55.16 instead of 95.47 kJ/kg) so far less of it flashes in the valve. The gain is modest here because the pressure span is small; for a real low-temperature cascade it is decisive.

Multistage compression with a flash chamber

📘 DEFINITION

A flash chamber is a vessel at an intermediate pressure into which the condensed liquid is throttled. The vapour that flashes off is separated and fed to the high-pressure compressor inlet, where it mixes with and cools the vapour leaving the low-pressure compressor; only the remaining saturated liquid is throttled again to the evaporator.

When both stages use the same refrigerant this replaces the cascade heat exchanger with a mixing chamber, which is cheaper and has no temperature difference to lose.

Take the same limits, 0.14 and 0.8 MPa, with the flash chamber at 0.32 MPa (per kilogram leaving the condenser). Throttling the saturated liquid from 0.8 MPa gives h6 = 95.47 kJ/kg at 0.32 MPa, and the quality there is x6 = (95.47 − 55.16)/(251.88 − 55.16) = 40.31/196.72 = 0.2049: about 20 % of the flow flashes and is sent straight to the second compressor, and only 0.795 kg reaches the evaporator. The mixing chamber receives (1 − x6) kg of vapour from the low-pressure compressor at h2 = 255.93 kJ/kg and x6 kg of saturated vapour at h3 = 251.88 kJ/kg, so the second compressor inlet has h9 = 0.7951 × 255.93 + 0.2049 × 251.88 = 255.10 kJ/kg, cooler than the low-stage discharge. The refrigeration effect per kilogram of condenser flow is qL = (1 − x6)(h1 − h8) = 0.7951 × (239.16 − 55.16) = 146.3 kJ/kg, and the work is the sum of both stages, win = (1 − x6)(h2 − h1) + (h4 − h9) with h4 read at 0.8 MPa and s9. Finishing the interpolation gives a COP of about 4.47 (Cengel & Boles, Example 11-4; the last digit depends on the table edition), essentially the same as the cascade, which is the general result: for the same intermediate pressure the two arrangements perform alike, and the choice is made on cost and on whether different refrigerants are needed.

Absorption refrigeration: cooling driven by heat

Compressing a vapour is expensive; pumping a liquid is almost free. An absorption system exploits this by dissolving the refrigerant vapour leaving the evaporator into a liquid, pumping the solution to the condenser pressure, and then boiling the refrigerant out again with heat. The classic pair is ammonia (refrigerant) in water (absorbent); the other common pair, for air-conditioning above 0 °C, is water (refrigerant) in lithium bromide solution. The condenser, valve and evaporator are the same as before. The compressor is replaced by an absorber, a pump, a generator and a regenerator:

  1. In the absorber, ammonia vapour from the evaporator dissolves in weak aqueous ammonia; dissolving releases heat, so the absorber is cooled (by cooling water) because ammonia dissolves better in cold water.
  2. The strong solution is pumped to the high pressure; the pump work is tiny because the fluid is a liquid.
  3. In the generator, heat Qgen from a burner, steam, waste heat or a solar collector boils ammonia out of the solution. A rectifier strips the water vapour that came with it so that only ammonia goes to the condenser (water in the evaporator would freeze).
  4. The now-weak hot solution flows back to the absorber through a regenerator that preheats the strong solution going the other way, and through a throttling valve that drops its pressure.

The performance measure is the cooling per unit of heat supplied, since the pump work is negligible:

COPabs = QL / Qgen

The reversible limit comes from treating the generator heat as driving a Carnot engine between the source temperature Ts and the ambient T0, whose work drives a Carnot refrigerator between T0 and the cold space TL:

COPabs,max = (1 − T0/Ts) × TL/(T0 − TL)

Ts is the temperature of the heat source, T0 that of the environment that receives the rejected heat, TL that of the refrigerated space, all in K. For a source at 120 °C (393.15 K), an environment at 25 °C (298.15 K) and a cold space at −10 °C (263.15 K): (1 − 298.15/393.15) = 0.2416 and 263.15/(298.15 − 263.15) = 263.15/35 = 7.519, so COPabs,max = 0.2416 × 7.519 = 1.82. Actual absorption systems achieve COPs well below 1; they are chosen not for efficiency but because they run on cheap or free heat, are quiet, and have almost no moving parts.

Gas refrigeration: the reversed Brayton cycle

Run the Brayton gas-turbine cycle backwards and the gas never changes phase: it is compressed (1-2), cooled at constant pressure by rejecting heat to the surroundings (2-3), expanded in a turbine (3-4), which drops its temperature far below the surroundings, and then warmed at constant pressure by absorbing heat from the cold space (4-1). The turbine’s work helps drive the compressor, so the net work is the difference. On the cold-air-standard assumptions (ideal gas, constant specific heats, isentropic turbomachinery):

qL = cp(T1 − T4)

wnet,in = cp(T2 − T1) − cp(T3 − T4)

T2/T1 = T3/T4 = rp(k−1)/k

COPR,gas = 1 / (rp(k−1)/k − 1)

rp is the compressor pressure ratio, k the specific heat ratio (1.4 for air), cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K for air, temperatures in K. The COP depends on the pressure ratio alone and falls as it rises, exactly like the Carnot COP falls with temperature span.

A short example, computed with cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K and k = 1.4: air enters the compressor at 0 °C (273.15 K) and the turbine at 35 °C (308.15 K), rp = 4, mass flow 0.1 kg/s. Then rp0.2857 = 40.2857 = 1.486; T2 = 273.15 × 1.486 = 405.9 K (132.7 °C); T4 = 308.15/1.486 = 207.4 K (−65.8 °C). Refrigeration qL = 1.005 × (273.15 − 207.4) = 66.1 kJ/kg; compressor w = 1.005 × (405.9 − 273.15) = 133.4 kJ/kg; turbine w = 1.005 × (308.15 − 207.4) = 101.3 kJ/kg; net w = 32.1 kJ/kg. So QL = 0.1 × 66.1 = 6.61 kW (1.88 tons) for Wnet = 3.21 kW, COP = 66.1/32.1 = 2.06, and the formula check 1/(1.486 − 1) = 2.06 agrees. Sanity check: the reversed Carnot COP between 273.15 K and 308.15 K is 273.15/35 = 7.80, so the gas cycle reaches only about a quarter of it. That is typical: the heat transfers are not isothermal, so the gas cycle is intrinsically poor.

Gas cycles are nevertheless used where their other properties dominate. Aircraft cabin cooling uses an open reversed Brayton cycle with bleed air from the engine compressor: the "refrigerant" is the cabin air itself, the equipment is light and simple, and the very low turbine exit temperature is an asset. Gas liquefaction and cryogenics use a regenerative version, in which the gas leaving the low-temperature side pre-cools the high-pressure gas before the turbine, so the turbine exit reaches temperatures no vapour cycle can.

Thermoelectric refrigeration in words

When two dissimilar conductors are joined in a loop and the two junctions are held at different temperatures, a small voltage and current appear (the Seebeck effect, the basis of the thermocouple). Run the current the other way from an external source and one junction cools while the other warms (the Peltier effect). A thermoelectric cooler is a stack of semiconductor pairs arranged so that all the cold junctions face the cooled object and all the hot junctions face a heat sink. There is no refrigerant, no compressor and no moving part, it can be made tiny, and reversing the current swaps heating and cooling. The price is a COP far below a vapour-compression machine, so it is confined to small loads: portable coolers, electronic component cooling, laboratory sample stages.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Equal mass flows in a cascade. The two loops have different mass flow rates fixed by the exchanger balance ṁA(h5 − h8) = ṁB(h2 − h3); use the lower-loop flow for QL and each loop’s own flow for its compressor.

Using the whole flow in the evaporator of a flash system. Only (1 − x6) of the condenser flow reaches the evaporator; the flashed vapour x6 bypasses it. Forgetting this overstates qL by about a quarter in the example above.

Quoting the absorption COP against Carnot’s refrigerator COP. An absorption COP of 0.7 is not "terrible compared with 5": the denominators are different quantities (heat versus work). Compare it with COPabs,max = (1 − T0/Ts)·TL/(T0 − TL).

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

Cascade: two pressure limits, an intermediate pressure, one mass flow rate; find the other mass flow rate from the exchanger balance, then QL, total W and COP. Eight enthalpies, two interpolations. Draw both loops on one T-s diagram with the overlap at the intermediate pressure.

Flash chamber: find x6 from the throttled enthalpy at the intermediate pressure, the mixed enthalpy h9 by a mass-weighted average, then qL and win per kilogram of condenser flow.

Absorption: state why the pump work is negligible, name the four components that replace the compressor, and compute COPabs,max from three temperatures in kelvin.

Gas cycle: cold-air-standard temperatures from the pressure ratio, then qL, wnet and COP; explain in two lines why it is used on aircraft despite its low COP. Thermoelectric: define Seebeck and Peltier and give one application.

"}, "THERMO/relations/s1": {"body": "

This lesson gives you the mathematical toolkit that the rest of the chapter, and the chemical-equilibrium chapter later, are built on. By the end you will be able to write the total differential of any property, test whether a differential is exact, use the reciprocity and cyclic relations to rearrange partial derivatives, define the Helmholtz and Gibbs functions, and derive the four Maxwell relations from the four Gibbs equations rather than memorise them. In a degree sequence this is the first lesson of the \"property relations\" block (Cengel & Boles chapter 12, Moran & Shapiro chapter 11), and it is the point where thermodynamics stops reading tables and starts explaining where the tables come from.

\n\n

Why we need property relations at all

\n

In the lab you can measure pressure, volume and temperature with instruments, and you can measure specific heats with a calorimeter. You cannot measure internal energy, enthalpy or entropy directly: there is no \"entropy meter\". Every u, h and s value in the steam tables was calculated from measured P-v-T data and specific heats. The bridge between what can be measured and what cannot is a small set of exact mathematical relations among partial derivatives, and this lesson builds that bridge.

\n

Everything rests on one fact from earlier chapters: the state postulate. A simple compressible substance has exactly two independent intensive properties, so every property can be written as a function of two others, for example u = u(T, v) or s = s(T, P). A function of two variables has a total differential, and that is where the calculus starts.

\n\n

Total differentials, exactness, reciprocity and the cyclic relation

\n

Take any property z that depends on two independent properties x and y, z = z(x, y). A small change in z is the sum of the change caused by x moving with y frozen and the change caused by y moving with x frozen:

\n

dz = (∂z/∂x)y dx + (∂z/∂y)x dy = M dx + N dy

\n

Here (∂z/∂x)y is the partial derivative of z with respect to x holding y constant; the subscript names the variable that is held fixed and is not optional in thermodynamics, because (∂u/∂T)v and (∂u/∂T)P are different numbers. M and N are just short names for the two coefficients.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

A differential dz = M dx + N dy is exact when z is a genuine function of the state (x, y), so that the integral of dz between two states does not depend on the path. Every property (P, v, T, u, h, s, a, g) has an exact differential; heat δq and work δw do not, which is why they are written with δ instead of d.

The test for exactness is that the mixed second derivatives agree: (∂M/∂y)x = (∂N/∂x)y, because both equal ∂²z/∂x∂y and the order of differentiation of a smooth function does not matter.

\n

Two further identities follow from writing the same relation both ways round. Write x = x(y, z) and z = z(x, y), substitute one differential into the other, and compare coefficients of dy and dz. The algebra (four lines, worth doing once by hand) gives:

\n

(∂x/∂y)z = 1 / (∂y/∂x)z (the reciprocity relation)

\n

(∂x/∂y)z (∂y/∂z)x (∂z/∂x)y = −1 (the cyclic relation)

\n

The reciprocity relation says you may flip a partial derivative upside down as long as the same variable stays constant. The cyclic relation is the surprising one: three partials that look as if they should multiply to +1 by \"cancelling\" actually multiply to −1, because a different variable is held constant in each factor. Check it once on the ideal gas so that you trust it:

\n
    \n
  1. Ideal gas: P = RT/v, so (∂P/∂T)v = R/v.
    2. \n
  2. Solve for T: T = Pv/R, so (∂T/∂v)P = P/R.
    3. \n
  3. Solve for v: v = RT/P, so (∂v/∂P)T = −RT/P².
    4. \n
  4. Multiply: (R/v)(P/R)(−RT/P²) = −RT/(Pv) = −RT/(RT) = −1. The cyclic relation holds, with the minus sign coming from the P² in the denominator of step 3.
    5. \n
\n\n

The four thermodynamic potentials: u, h, a and g

\n

You already use two energy-like properties, internal energy u and enthalpy h = u + Pv. Two more are defined for the same reason enthalpy was: they make certain processes simple.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Helmholtz function (specific): a = u − Ts, units kJ/kg. For a closed system at constant temperature, the decrease in a is the maximum work the system can deliver; it is the natural energy function of a constant-T, constant-v process.

Gibbs function (specific): g = h − Ts = u + Pv − Ts, units kJ/kg. For a process at constant temperature and pressure, the decrease in g is the maximum work other than boundary work; g is constant across a phase change at fixed T and P (gf = gg) and it drives chemical equilibrium in a later chapter.

\n

Both are properties because they are built only from properties. Neither has an absolute zero that matters: like u and h, only differences in a and g enter any calculation.

\n\n

The four Gibbs equations

\n

Start from the first Tds relation from the entropy chapter, which combines the first law with the definition of entropy for a simple compressible substance:

\n

du = T ds − P dv (Gibbs equation 1)

\n

Now differentiate the other three potentials and substitute this line into each, one step at a time:

\n
    \n
  1. h = u + Pv, so dh = du + P dv + v dP. Substitute du: dh = T ds − P dv + P dv + v dP, hence dh = T ds + v dP (Gibbs equation 2).
    2. \n
  2. a = u − Ts, so da = du − T ds − s dT. Substitute du: da = T ds − P dv − T ds − s dT, hence da = −s dT − P dv (Gibbs equation 3).
    3. \n
  3. g = h − Ts, so dg = dh − T ds − s dT. Substitute dh: dg = T ds + v dP − T ds − s dT, hence dg = −s dT + v dP (Gibbs equation 4).
    4. \n
\n

Read the pattern: each equation tells you the two \"natural variables\" of its potential. u is naturally a function of (s, v), h of (s, P), a of (T, v) and g of (T, P). The last two pairs are the measurable ones, which is why a and g are so useful: a(T, v) and g(T, P) are expressed entirely in quantities you can put a gauge on.

\n\n

The four Maxwell relations, derived not memorised

\n

Each Gibbs equation has the form dz = M dx + N dy with z a property, so each differential is exact and the exactness test applies. Do it for the fourth Gibbs equation in full:

📊 FIGURE — From potentials to Gibbs equations to the four Maxwell relations
Each row: define the potential, differentiate it and substitute du (or dh) to get its Gibbs equation, then apply the exactness test. The a and g rows swap an entropy derivative for measurable P-v-T data.
\n
    \n
  1. dg = −s dT + v dP, so here x = T, y = P, M = −s, N = v.
    2. \n
  2. Exactness demands (∂M/∂P)T = (∂N/∂T)P.
    3. \n
  3. Substitute: (∂(−s)/∂P)T = (∂v/∂T)P.
    4. \n
  4. Move the sign: (∂s/∂P)T = −(∂v/∂T)P. This is the fourth Maxwell relation.
    5. \n
\n

The same four lines applied to the other three Gibbs equations give the full set.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

(∂T/∂v)s = −(∂P/∂s)v (from du = T ds − P dv)

(∂T/∂P)s = (∂v/∂s)P (from dh = T ds + v dP)

(∂s/∂v)T = (∂P/∂T)v (from da = −s dT − P dv)

(∂s/∂P)T = −(∂v/∂T)P (from dg = −s dT + v dP)

Symbols: T temperature in K, P pressure in kPa, v specific volume in m³/kg, s specific entropy in kJ/kg·K. Every term in one relation has the same units; for example both sides of the last relation are m³/kg·K. The two relations from a and g are the useful ones, because they replace a derivative of entropy (unmeasurable) by a derivative of P-v-T data (measurable).

\n

Notice how the sign works: a minus sign appears exactly when the pair of variables being swapped is (T, v) against (P, s) in the \"crossed\" order. If you ever doubt a sign, re-derive from the Gibbs equation in four lines rather than trusting memory; that is the point of learning the derivation.

\n\n

Worked example: testing the fourth Maxwell relation on superheated steam

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem. Verify (∂s/∂P)T = −(∂v/∂T)P for steam at 250 °C and 300 kPa, using finite differences over neighbouring table entries. Property source: IAPWS-95 water (the same formulation behind the Cengel & Boles superheated-steam table A-6), evaluated with CoolProp; the values agree with the printed table to the last digit shown.

Step 1: the left side. Hold T = 250 °C and step P either side of 300 kPa. s(250 °C, 200 kPa) = 7.7100 kJ/kg·K and s(250 °C, 400 kPa) = 7.3804 kJ/kg·K.
(∂s/∂P)T ≈ (7.3804 − 7.7100) kJ/kg·K / (400 − 200) kPa = −0.3296/200 = −0.001648 (kJ/kg·K)/kPa. Since 1 kJ/kPa = 1 m³, this is −0.001648 m³/kg·K.

Step 2: the right side. Hold P = 300 kPa and step T either side of 250 °C. v(300 kPa, 200 °C) = 0.71642 m³/kg and v(300 kPa, 300 °C) = 0.87534 m³/kg.
−(∂v/∂T)P ≈ −(0.87534 − 0.71642) m³/kg / (300 − 200) K = −0.15892/100 = −0.001589 m³/kg·K. (A difference of 100 °C is a difference of 100 K, so Celsius is fine here.)

Step 3: compare. −0.001648 against −0.001589 m³/kg·K: same sign, same magnitude to within 3.6%. The gap is the error of a 200 kPa / 100 K central difference, not a failure of the relation: the exact derivatives from the equation of state are (∂s/∂P)T = −0.001587 m³/kg·K and −(∂v/∂T)P = −0.001587 m³/kg·K, identical to four significant figures.

Sanity check. If steam at 300 kPa behaved as an ideal gas, −(∂v/∂T)P = −R/P = −0.4615/300 = −0.001538 m³/kg·K. The real value is 3% larger in magnitude, which is the expected small departure from ideal behaviour for low-pressure superheated steam.

\n
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

A steam table is a grid, and a Maxwell relation is a statement about the partial derivatives of that grid. If you load a table into pandas, numpy.gradient along the pressure axis of the entropy column and along the temperature axis of the volume column gives you both sides of the fourth relation for every cell at once; plotting their ratio is a quick consistency check on any property data set, including one you have curve-fitted yourself.

The 3.6% gap in the example is the classic central-difference truncation error, proportional to the step size squared; halving the step (if the table has the rows) cuts the gap by about four.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Dropping the subscript. (∂v/∂T)P and (∂v/∂T)s differ hugely (one is positive for steam, the other negative). A partial derivative in thermodynamics has no meaning until you say what is held constant, and every Maxwell relation pairs a specific constant on each side.

Reading the cyclic relation as +1. It is −1. The three partials do not cancel like fractions because the constant variable changes from factor to factor.

Using absolute temperature in Celsius. In dg = −s dT + v dP the dT is a difference and Celsius survives; in a = u − Ts the T multiplies s and must be in kelvin. The rule: any T that is multiplied or divided is in K.

Mixing up which Gibbs equation produced which Maxwell relation. If asked to \"derive\" a Maxwell relation, write the Gibbs equation, name M and N, apply the exactness test. Writing the result from memory earns little credit and is where sign errors come from.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

Derive one Maxwell relation from a named Gibbs equation (four lines: Gibbs equation, identify M and N, exactness test, rearrange). This is the most common short question in this chapter.

Verify a Maxwell relation numerically from a table extract using central differences, as in the worked example, then comment on the size of the discrepancy. Show units on the finite-difference quotient and convert kJ/kPa to m³.

Use the cyclic and reciprocity relations to rewrite an awkward derivative, typically turning (∂P/∂T)v into −(∂v/∂T)P / (∂v/∂P)T, which is the ratio of volume expansivity to isothermal compressibility used in the next lesson.

State the natural variables of u, h, a and g, or explain in one sentence why the Helmholtz and Gibbs functions are worth defining.

"}, "THERMO/relations/s2": {"body": "

This lesson turns the Maxwell relations into working tools. You will derive the Clapeyron equation and use it to get an enthalpy of vaporisation from nothing but saturation P-v-T data, use its Clausius-Clapeyron approximation to extrapolate a vapour-pressure table, write the general relations for du, dh and ds that hold for any simple compressible substance, prove that the internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone, and derive cp − cv for a real substance (with the Mayer relation cp − cv = R as its ideal-gas special case). In the degree sequence this is the core of the property-relations chapter and the source of several of the \"show that\" questions on the final.

\n\n

The Clapeyron equation in plain words

\n

Along the saturation dome, pressure and temperature are locked together: at 100 °C water boils at 101.42 kPa, at 105 °C at 120.90 kPa. The slope of that vapour-pressure curve, dP/dT along the saturation line, can be measured with a thermometer and a pressure gauge. The Clapeyron equation says that this slope alone, together with the volume change on boiling, fixes the enthalpy of vaporisation. It is the reason the hfg column of the steam tables exists without anyone having boiled a measured kilogram in a calorimeter at every temperature.

\n

The derivation uses the third Maxwell relation, (∂s/∂v)T = (∂P/∂T)v, applied inside the two-phase region:

\n
    \n
  1. Inside the dome, at fixed T the pressure is Psat(T), which does not depend on v. So (∂P/∂T)v is simply the slope of the saturation curve, written (dP/dT)sat, and is the same number at every v between vf and vg.
    2. \n
  2. Substitute and integrate the Maxwell relation across the dome at constant T: ∫ ds = (dP/dT)sat ∫ dv from the saturated-liquid state to the saturated-vapour state, giving sg − sf = (dP/dT)sat (vg − vf), i.e. (dP/dT)sat = sfg/vfg.
    3. \n
  3. The phase change is at constant T and P, so from dh = T ds + v dP with dP = 0: hfg = T sfg, hence sfg = hfg/T.
    4. \n
  4. Substitute: (dP/dT)sat = hfg / (T vfg).
    5. \n
\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Clapeyron equation (any phase change, any substance): (dP/dT)sat = hfg / (T vfg)

(dP/dT)sat slope of the saturation curve in kPa/K; hfg enthalpy of vaporisation in kJ/kg; T saturation temperature in K (it multiplies, so kelvin is compulsory); vfg = vg − vf in m³/kg. Check the units: kJ/kg divided by (K · m³/kg) = kJ/(m³·K) = kPa/K.

Clausius-Clapeyron equation (low pressure, vapour treated as ideal gas, hfg taken constant): ln(P2/P1) = (hfg/R) (1/T1 − 1/T2), with R the gas constant of the vapour in kJ/kg·K (0.4615 for water) and both temperatures in K.

\n

The same equation with hif and vif describes melting, and with hig and vig sublimation. It is why the melting line of water leans backwards on a P-T diagram: ice is less dense than liquid water, so vif is negative while hif is positive, and the slope dP/dT of the fusion line comes out negative.

\n\n

From Clapeyron to Clausius-Clapeyron

\n

Far from the critical point, the vapour is so much less dense than the liquid that vfg ≈ vg, and at low pressure the vapour is close to an ideal gas, vg ≈ RT/P. Substituting both into Clapeyron:

\n
    \n
  1. dP/dT = hfg P / (R T²), so dP/P = (hfg/R) dT/T².
    2. \n
  2. Take hfg as constant over the interval and integrate from state 1 to state 2: ln(P2/P1) = (hfg/R)(1/T1 − 1/T2).
    3. \n
\n

This is the equation behind every \"vapour pressure versus 1/T is a straight line\" plot: ln P is linear in 1/T with slope −hfg/R. The straight-line form is also what makes it a regression problem, which the data-edge note in the previous lesson hinted at.

\n\n

Worked examples: hfg of water from the slope of the vapour-pressure curve

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem A. Estimate hfg of water at 100 °C from saturation P-v-T data alone and compare with the tabulated value. Property source: IAPWS-95 water via CoolProp, which reproduces the Cengel & Boles saturated-water tables A-4/A-5.

📊 FIGURE — hfg of water from the slope of the vapour-pressure curve at 100 °C
The dashed chord through the 95 °C and 105 °C points estimates the slope dP/dT at 100 °C. Clapeyron turns that slope and v fg into h fg, within 0.28% of the table.

Step 1: slope by central difference. Psat(95 °C) = 84.608 kPa, Psat(105 °C) = 120.903 kPa.
(dP/dT)sat ≈ (120.903 − 84.608) kPa / (105 − 95) K = 36.295/10 = 3.6295 kPa/K.

Step 2: volume change. At 100 °C, vf = 0.001043 m³/kg and vg = 1.67177 m³/kg, so vfg = 1.67177 − 0.001043 = 1.67073 m³/kg.

Step 3: Clapeyron. T = 100 + 273.15 = 373.15 K.
hfg = T vfg (dP/dT)sat = 373.15 K × 1.67073 m³/kg × 3.6295 kPa/K = 2262.7 kJ/kg (m³·kPa = kJ).

Step 4: compare. The table gives hfg(100 °C) = 2675.57 − 419.17 = 2256.4 kJ/kg; the estimate 2262.7 kJ/kg is 0.28% high. Using the exact slope from the equation of state, 3.6193 kPa/K, the Clapeyron equation returns 2256.4 kJ/kg exactly, so the whole 0.28% is the finite-difference error in step 1.

Sanity check. sfg = hfg/T = 2256.4/373.15 = 6.0469 kJ/kg·K, which is exactly the sfg column of the table at 100 °C: the hfg = T sfg step of the derivation is confirmed.

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem B. Using only the boiling point at 1 atm (100 °C, 101.42 kPa) and hfg = 2256.4 kJ/kg, estimate the vapour pressure of water at 50 °C with Clausius-Clapeyron. R = 0.4615 kJ/kg·K for water vapour (Ru/M = 8.314/18.015).

Step 1: temperatures in kelvin. T1 = 373.15 K, T2 = 323.15 K.

Step 2: the bracket. 1/T1 − 1/T2 = 1/373.15 − 1/323.15 = 0.0026799 − 0.0030945 = −4.1465 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹.

Step 3: the prefactor. hfg/R = 2256.4 kJ/kg / 0.4615 kJ/kg·K = 4889.3 K.

Step 4: solve. ln(P2/P1) = 4889.3 K × (−4.1465 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹) = −2.0273, so P2 = 101.42 kPa × e−2.0273 = 101.42 × 0.13169 = 13.36 kPa.

Step 5: compare. The table value at 50 °C is 12.352 kPa, so the estimate 13.36 kPa is 8.1% high. The error comes from holding hfg at its 100 °C value: at 50 °C it is 2381.9 kJ/kg. Repeating with the mean of the two, 2319.2 kJ/kg, gives 12.62 kPa (2.2% high). Over a 50 K interval Clausius-Clapeyron is a good estimate, not a table replacement.

Sanity check. The pressure must fall as the temperature falls, and 13 kPa is the right order for warm water under vacuum (a 50 °C condenser runs at about 12 kPa absolute). Two classic slips give absurd numbers: with °C in the bracket the exponent becomes −48.9 and P2 comes out at 10⁻¹⁹ kPa; with Ru = 8.314 instead of R = 0.4615 the exponent is −0.113 and P2 = 90.6 kPa, barely below 1 atm.

\n\n

General relations for du, dh and ds

\n

Now the promised bridge: expressions for the unmeasurable u, h and s in terms of T, P, v and the specific heats, valid for any substance. Take u = u(T, v). Its total differential is

\n

du = (∂u/∂T)v dT + (∂u/∂v)T dv = cv dT + (∂u/∂v)T dv

\n

where cv = (∂u/∂T)v by definition (kJ/kg·K). The second coefficient is the one that needs work:

\n
    \n
  1. Write s = s(T, v) too: ds = (∂s/∂T)v dT + (∂s/∂v)T dv.
    2. \n
  2. Put this into the first Gibbs equation du = T ds − P dv: du = T(∂s/∂T)v dT + [T(∂s/∂v)T − P] dv.
    3. \n
  3. Both expressions for du must agree coefficient by coefficient, because dT and dv are independent. Coefficient of dT: cv = T(∂s/∂T)v. Coefficient of dv: (∂u/∂v)T = T(∂s/∂v)T − P.
    4. \n
  4. Replace the entropy derivative by the third Maxwell relation, (∂s/∂v)T = (∂P/∂T)v: (∂u/∂v)T = T(∂P/∂T)v − P.
    5. \n
\n

Exactly the same four steps with h = h(T, P), the second Gibbs equation and the fourth Maxwell relation give the enthalpy result. Collecting everything:

\n

du = cv dT + [T(∂P/∂T)v − P] dv

\n

dh = cp dT + [v − T(∂v/∂T)P] dP

\n

ds = (cv/T) dT + (∂P/∂T)v dv (from steps 1 and 3 above)

\n

ds = (cp/T) dT − (∂v/∂T)P dP (the same route through h)

\n

Every bracket contains only P, v, T and their derivatives, which an equation of state supplies. Two immediate pay-offs:

\n
    \n
  • Ideal gas. P = RT/v gives (∂P/∂T)v = R/v, so T(∂P/∂T)v − P = RT/v − P = P − P = 0. Hence (∂u/∂v)T = 0: the internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature only. The same substitution in the dh bracket gives v − T(R/P) = v − v = 0, so h = h(T) as well. Earlier chapters asserted this; now it is proved.
    • \n
  • Van der Waals gas, P = RT/(v − b) − a/v². Here (∂P/∂T)v = R/(v − b), so T(∂P/∂T)v − P = RT/(v − b) − RT/(v − b) + a/v² = a/v². Thus du = cv dT + (a/v²) dv: at constant temperature the internal energy of a van der Waals gas rises on expansion, because work is done against the intermolecular attraction that the constant a represents. This is the microscopic reason real gases cool when they expand freely.
    • \n
\n

Two more relations come from applying the exactness test to the ds equations: (∂cv/∂v)T = T(∂²P/∂T²)v and (∂cp/∂P)T = −T(∂²v/∂T²)P. For an ideal gas both second derivatives are zero, so cv and cp of an ideal gas cannot depend on v or P; they are functions of T only, which is what the ideal-gas specific-heat tables assume.

\n\n

cp − cv for any substance, and the Mayer relation

\n

Set the two ds equations equal to each other and solve for dT:

\n
    \n
  1. (cv/T) dT + (∂P/∂T)v dv = (cp/T) dT − (∂v/∂T)P dP.
    2. \n
  2. Collect dT: (cp − cv) dT = T(∂P/∂T)v dv + T(∂v/∂T)P dP.
    3. \n
  3. Compare with the total differential of T = T(v, P), dT = (∂T/∂v)P dv + (∂T/∂P)v dP. The dP coefficients must match: (cp − cv)(∂T/∂P)v = T(∂v/∂T)P.
    4. \n
  4. Use the cyclic relation on (P, v, T) to rewrite (∂P/∂T)v = −(∂v/∂T)P (∂P/∂v)T, then substitute (with reciprocity for (∂T/∂P)v): cp − cv = −T (∂v/∂T)P² (∂P/∂v)T.
    5. \n
\n
📘 DEFINITION

Volume expansivity (isobaric expansion coefficient): β = (1/v)(∂v/∂T)P, units 1/K. How much a substance swells per kelvin at fixed pressure.

Isothermal compressibility: α = −(1/v)(∂v/∂P)T, units 1/kPa (or 1/Pa). How much it shrinks per unit pressure at fixed temperature; the minus sign makes α positive because volume always falls when pressure rises. Some books write κT for the same quantity.

In terms of these two measurable coefficients: cp − cv = v T β² / α. Since v, T, β² and α are all positive (α is positive for every stable substance), cp ≥ cv always, with equality only where β = 0, for example liquid water at its density maximum near 4 °C.

\n

For an ideal gas, β = 1/T and α = 1/P, so cp − cv = v T (1/T²)(P) = Pv/T = R: the Mayer relation, which you have used since the first-law chapter (air: 1.005 − 0.718 = 0.287 kJ/kg·K). For solids and liquids the difference is usually small but not always negligible, as the next example shows.

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem C. Find cp − cv for liquid water at 20 °C and 100 kPa from β and α, and compare with the direct values. Source: IAPWS-95 via CoolProp; handbook values of β and α for water at 20 °C agree with these to three figures.

Step 1: data. v = 0.001002 m³/kg, β = 2.068 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹, α = 4.589 × 10⁻¹⁰ Pa⁻¹, T = 293.15 K.

Step 2: compute. cp − cv = v T β²/α = 0.001002 m³/kg × 293.15 K × (2.068 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹)² / (4.589 × 10⁻¹⁰ Pa⁻¹).
Numerator: 0.001002 × 293.15 × 4.277 × 10⁻⁸ = 1.256 × 10⁻⁸ m³/kg·K. Divide by α: 1.256 × 10⁻⁸ / 4.589 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 27.4 Pa·m³/kg·K = 27.4 J/kg·K = 0.0274 kJ/kg·K.

Step 3: compare. Directly, cp = 4184.1 J/kg·K and cv = 4156.7 J/kg·K, difference 27.4 J/kg·K: identical. So for cold water cp and cv differ by 0.65%, which is why the tables give a single \"c\" for liquids.

Sanity check and a warning. The difference scales with β². At 80 °C water expands three times faster (β = 6.41 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹), and the same formula gives 324 J/kg·K, an 8% gap between cp = 4197 and cv = 3873 J/kg·K. \"Liquids have cp = cv\" is a cold-water approximation, not a law.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Celsius inside Clapeyron or Clausius-Clapeyron. T multiplies vfg in one and sits under 1/T in the other; both need kelvin. The example shows the Celsius version predicting a vapour pressure of 10⁻¹⁹ kPa.

Using Ru with mass-based hfg. If hfg is in kJ/kg, R must be the specific gas constant of the vapour in kJ/kg·K (0.4615 for water). Mixing them changes the exponent by a factor of 18.

Forgetting vf. vfg = vg − vf. At low pressure it hardly matters (0.06% at 100 °C), but near the critical point vf and vg are comparable and Clausius-Clapeyron, which drops vf and assumes an ideal vapour, fails completely.

Treating (∂u/∂v)T = 0 as general. It is an ideal-gas result. For a van der Waals gas it equals a/v², and for liquids it is large; the \"u depends on T only\" shortcut belongs to ideal gases alone.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

Derive the Clapeyron equation from the third Maxwell relation (the four numbered steps above), then state the two approximations that turn it into Clausius-Clapeyron.

Numerical Clapeyron: given three neighbouring rows of a saturation table (or of a refrigerant table), estimate hfg and compare with the tabulated value. Always take the central difference across the target temperature, not a one-sided one.

\"Show that\" questions: show that (∂u/∂v)T = 0 for an ideal gas, or equals a/v² for a van der Waals gas; show that cp − cv = R for an ideal gas from the general expression; show that cp of an ideal gas is independent of pressure.

Estimate cp − cv for a liquid or solid from tabulated β and α, and comment on whether the difference is negligible.

"}, "THERMO/relations/s3": {"body": "

This lesson answers two practical questions that the ideal-gas model cannot: why does a real gas change temperature when it is throttled, and how do you get h and s for a real gas at high pressure when no table exists for it? The first is the Joule-Thomson coefficient, which is the working principle of every gas liquefier and of the expansion valve in a refrigerator; the second is the method of departure functions with the generalised charts, which lets you handle any gas from its critical temperature and pressure alone. In the degree sequence this closes the property-relations chapter and feeds directly into the real-gas parts of the gas-mixtures and compressible-flow chapters.

\n\n

Throttling revisited: the Joule-Thomson coefficient in plain words

\n

Throttling is a steady flow through a restriction with no work, negligible heat transfer and negligible change in kinetic energy, so the energy balance from the control-volume chapter reduces to h2 = h1. For an ideal gas h depends on T only, so the outlet temperature equals the inlet temperature. For a real gas h depends on pressure as well, so the temperature must move to keep h fixed while P drops. Whether it moves down (nitrogen, air, CO2 at room temperature) or up (hydrogen and helium at room temperature) is decided by one property of the gas.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Joule-Thomson coefficient: μJT = (∂T/∂P)h, units K/kPa (often quoted in K/bar or K/MPa). It is the slope of a constant-enthalpy line on a T-P diagram.

Because the pressure always falls across a throttle (dP < 0): μJT > 0 means the gas cools on throttling, μJT < 0 means it warms, and μJT = 0 means the temperature is unchanged, which is the ideal-gas case. The locus of states where μJT = 0 is the inversion line; its intercept on the zero-pressure axis is the maximum inversion temperature, above which no amount of throttling can cool the gas.

\n\n

Deriving μJT from the general enthalpy relation

\n

Take the general dh from the previous lesson and set dh = 0 along the throttling line:

\n
    \n
  1. dh = cp dT + [v − T(∂v/∂T)P] dP = 0.
    2. \n
  2. Solve for dT/dP at constant h: (∂T/∂P)h = −[v − T(∂v/∂T)P] / cp.
    3. \n
  3. Tidy the sign: μJT = (1/cp) [T(∂v/∂T)P − v].
    4. \n
\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

μJT = (∂T/∂P)h = (1/cp) [ T (∂v/∂T)P − v ]

cp in kJ/kg·K, T in K, v in m³/kg, (∂v/∂T)P in m³/kg·K. The bracket has units m³/kg; divided by kJ/kg·K it gives m³·K/kJ = K/kPa. The bracket is the same one that appears in dh: μJT is zero exactly when the enthalpy is independent of pressure.

Ideal gas: v = RT/P so T(∂v/∂T)P = T(R/P) = v, the bracket vanishes and μJT = 0 at every state. Van der Waals gas at low pressure (expand P(v − b) = RT − a/v + ab/v² to first order in 1/v): μJT ≈ (1/cp) (2a/RT − b), which changes sign at the low-pressure inversion temperature Tinv = 2a/(Rb) = (27/4) Tcr.

\n

The van der Waals result makes the physics visible. The term 2a/RT is the attraction between molecules: pulling them apart during expansion costs energy, which is taken from the kinetic energy, so the gas cools. The term b is the finite molecular size: at short range molecules repel, and expansion releases that stored repulsive energy as heat, so the gas warms. Attraction wins at low temperature, repulsion wins at high temperature, and the crossover is the inversion temperature. Since a and b scale with Tcr and Pcr, a gas with a very low critical temperature (helium 5.2 K, hydrogen 33.1 K) has a very low inversion temperature and warms on throttling from room temperature, which is why those two must be pre-cooled (with liquid nitrogen, for instance) before a Joule-Thomson stage can liquefy them.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
Gas (Tcr)μJT at 300 K, 1 barMax. inversion T (van der Waals, 27Tcr/4)Max. inversion T (reference equation of state)
Nitrogen (126.2 K)+0.212 K/bar (cools)852 K607 K
Air+0.225 K/bar (cools)——
Carbon dioxide (304.1 K)+1.076 K/bar (cools strongly)——
Hydrogen (33.1 K)−0.030 K/bar (warms)224 K200 K
Helium (5.2 K)−0.063 K/bar (warms)35 K45 K
\n

All values computed with CoolProp from the reference (Helmholtz-energy) equations of state for each fluid; the van der Waals column uses a and b from the same critical constants. Notice that van der Waals gets the sign and the ordering right and the magnitudes only roughly: it overshoots nitrogen's inversion temperature by 40%. That is typical of the cubic equations: good for insight, adequate for estimates, not a substitute for a fitted equation of state.

\n\n

Worked example: μJT of nitrogen and a real throttling calculation

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem A. Estimate the Joule-Thomson coefficient of nitrogen at 300 K and low pressure from the van der Waals constants, and compare with the equation-of-state value. Data: Tcr = 126.19 K, Pcr = 3.3958 MPa, M = 28.013 kg/kmol, Ru = 8.3145 J/mol·K, c̄p(300 K) = 29.17 J/mol·K (= 1.041 kJ/kg·K).

📊 FIGURE — Joule-Thomson inversion curve and the nitrogen throttling path
Sketch of the T-P plane for nitrogen. Inside the inversion line throttling cools the gas. The red arrow follows one constant-enthalpy line from 300 K, 20 MPa to 271.5 K, 1 MPa.

Step 1: van der Waals constants from the critical point. a = 27 Ru² Tcr² / (64 Pcr) = 27 × 8.3145² × 126.19² / (64 × 3.3958 × 10⁶) = 0.13676 Pa·m⁶/mol²; b = Ru Tcr / (8 Pcr) = 8.3145 × 126.19 / (8 × 3.3958 × 10⁶) = 3.862 × 10⁻⁵ m³/mol.

Step 2: the bracket. 2a/(RuT) = 2 × 0.13676 / (8.3145 × 300) = 1.0966 × 10⁻⁴ m³/mol, so 2a/RuT − b = 1.0966 × 10⁻⁴ − 0.3862 × 10⁻⁴ = 7.104 × 10⁻⁵ m³/mol. Positive: attraction dominates at 300 K, nitrogen cools.
