Step 3: divide by c̄p. μJT ≈ 7.104 × 10⁻⁵ m³/mol / 29.17 J/mol·K = 2.435 × 10⁻⁶ K/Pa = 0.244 K/bar (m³/J = 1/Pa).

Step 4: compare. The reference equation of state gives μJT = 0.212 K/bar at 300 K and 1 bar, so van der Waals is 15% high but has the right sign and size. Low-pressure inversion temperature from step 1: Tinv = 2a/(Rub) = 2 × 0.13676 / (8.3145 × 3.862 × 10⁻⁵) = 852 K, against 607 K from the reference equation.

Sanity check. 0.2 K/bar means throttling nitrogen across a 10 bar drop cools it by roughly 2 K: small, which is why practical liquefiers use pressure ratios of 100 or more and recover the cold with a counter-flow heat exchanger.

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem B. Nitrogen at 300 K and 20 MPa is throttled to 1 MPa. Find the exit temperature (a) assuming an ideal gas, (b) assuming μJT stays at its low-pressure value of 0.244 K/bar, (c) exactly, from h2 = h1 with the reference equation of state (CoolProp, Span-Wagner nitrogen).

(a) Ideal gas: h = h(T) only, so T2 = T1 = 300 K. No cooling at all.

(b) Constant μJT: ΔP = 1 − 20 = −19 MPa = −190 bar. ΔT ≈ μJT ΔP = 0.244 K/bar × (−190 bar) = −46.4 K, so T2 ≈ 253.6 K.

(c) Exact: h(300 K, 20 MPa) fixed, solve for T at 1 MPa: T2 = 271.5 K, a drop of 28.5 K. The mean coefficient over the process is 28.5 K / 190 bar = 0.150 K/bar, well below the 1 bar value, because μJT falls as the pressure rises towards the inversion line.

Sanity check. The exact answer lies between the ideal-gas answer (no cooling) and the constant-coefficient answer (too much cooling), as it must: the ideal gas ignores the effect entirely and the constant coefficient overstates it. Real nitrogen at 20 MPa is at PR = 5.9, deep in non-ideal territory, so neither shortcut is acceptable in a design calculation.

\n\n

Departure functions: enthalpy and entropy of a real gas from the generalised charts

\n

Suppose you need h and s for nitrogen at 220 K and 10 MPa, or for a gas nobody has tabulated. The strategy is to split each property into an ideal-gas part, which you already know how to compute from cp(T), plus a correction called the departure that depends only on how non-ideal the gas is at that state:

\n

h(T, P) = h*(T) + [h(T, P) − h*(T, P)], where the asterisk marks the ideal gas at the same T and P.

\n

Derive the correction from the general dh at constant temperature: dh = [v − T(∂v/∂T)P] dP. Integrate from P = 0 (where every gas is ideal, so h = h*) up to P at fixed T, and subtract the same integral for the ideal gas (for which the bracket is zero):

\n

h − h* = ∫0P [v − T(∂v/∂T)P] dP (at constant T)

\n

Substituting v = ZRT/P and switching to reduced variables TR = T/Tcr, PR = P/Pcr turns the integrand into a function of Z and its derivative with respect to TR, which by the principle of corresponding states is roughly the same function for all gases. The result is tabulated once, as the generalised enthalpy-departure chart, in the dimensionless form

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Enthalpy departure factor: Zh = (h̄* − h̄)T,P / (Ru Tcr), so h̄ − h̄* = −Ru Tcr Zh (kJ/kmol; divide by M for kJ/kg)

Entropy departure factor: Zs = (s̄* − s̄)T,P / Ru, so s̄ − s̄* = −Ru Zs (kJ/kmol·K)

Change between two states: h̄2 − h̄1 = (h̄2 − h̄1)ideal − Ru Tcr (Zh2 − Zh1) and s̄2 − s̄1 = (s̄2 − s̄1)ideal − Ru (Zs2 − Zs1), with the ideal parts from the ideal-gas tables or c̄p(T2 − T1) and c̄p ln(T2/T1) − Ru ln(P2/P1).

Zh and Zs are read from the generalised charts (Lee-Kesler) at (TR, PR), both dimensionless and both positive for almost all states: a real gas has less enthalpy and less entropy than the ideal gas at the same T and P, because attraction lowers the energy and pulls the molecules into a smaller volume. Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K, Tcr in K.

\n

The charts are only as good as corresponding states, roughly within a few per cent for simple, nearly spherical molecules and worse for polar ones like water and ammonia. Where a fitted equation of state exists, use it; the charts are for gases without one and for exam questions. The next example computes the departures analytically with the van der Waals equation so that every number is traceable, then compares with the reference equation of state.

\n\n

Worked example: enthalpy and entropy departure of nitrogen at 220 K, 10 MPa

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem C. Nitrogen at 220 K and 10 MPa. Find Z, the enthalpy departure and the entropy departure with the van der Waals equation, express them as Zh and Zs, and compare with the reference equation of state. Then find the enthalpy change when the gas is heated at 10 MPa from 220 K to 300 K. Constants from Problem A: a = 0.13676 Pa·m⁶/mol², b = 3.862 × 10⁻⁵ m³/mol, Tcr = 126.19 K, M = 28.013 kg/kmol.

Step 1: reduced state. TR = 220/126.19 = 1.743, PR = 10/3.3958 = 2.945. Well above Tcr but at three times Pcr: gas, but not ideal.

Step 2: molar volume from the cubic. Rearranging P = RuT/(v̄ − b) − a/v̄² gives P v̄³ − (Pb + RuT) v̄² + a v̄ − ab = 0. With P = 10⁷ Pa, T = 220 K the three roots are one real, 1.5541 × 10⁻⁴ m³/mol, and a complex pair (discarded). So v̄ = 1.5541 × 10⁻⁴ m³/mol, against the ideal value RuT/P = 8.3145 × 220 / 10⁷ = 1.8292 × 10⁻⁴ m³/mol.

Step 3: compressibility factor. Z = P v̄/(RuT) = 10⁷ × 1.5541 × 10⁻⁴ / (8.3145 × 220) = 0.850. The reference equation gives 0.904; van der Waals overstates the compression.

Step 4: internal-energy and enthalpy departure. From du = cv dT + (a/v̄²) dv̄ at constant T, integrating from v̄ = ∞ (ideal gas) to v̄: ū − ū* = −a/v̄ = −0.13676 / 1.5541 × 10⁻⁴ = −880.0 J/mol. Then h̄ − h̄* = (ū − ū*) + (P v̄ − RuT) = −880.0 + (1554.1 − 1829.2) = −880.0 − 275.1 = −1155.1 J/mol, i.e. −1155.1/28.013 = −41.2 kJ/kg. As a chart factor: Zh = 1155.1 / (8.3145 × 126.19) = 1155.1/1049.2 = 1.101. Reference equation of state: h̄ − h̄* = −1102.5 J/mol, Zh = 1.051, so van der Waals is 5% high.

Step 5: entropy departure. From ds = (cv/T)dT + (∂P/∂T)v dv̄ with (∂P/∂T)v = Ru/(v̄ − b), integrating at constant T from the ideal-gas state at the same P (where v̄* = RuT/P): s̄ − s̄* = Ru ln[ P(v̄ − b) / (RuT) ] = 8.3145 × ln[10⁷ × (1.5541 − 0.3862) × 10⁻⁴ / 1829.2] = 8.3145 × ln(0.6385) = 8.3145 × (−0.4487) = −3.731 J/mol·K, i.e. −0.133 kJ/kg·K, and Zs = 0.449. Reference equation: −3.977 J/mol·K, Zs = 0.478.

Step 6: enthalpy change 220 K to 300 K at 10 MPa. Ideal part with c̄p = 29.12 J/mol·K (mean over the interval from the ideal-gas nitrogen table): (h̄2 − h̄1)ideal = 29.12 × (300 − 220) = 2329 J/mol. Repeating steps 2 to 4 at 300 K, 10 MPa gives v̄ = 2.403 × 10⁻⁴ m³/mol, Z = 0.963 and Zh2 = 0.630. Then h̄2 − h̄1 = 2329 − 1049.2 × (0.630 − 1.101) = 2329 + 494 = 2823 J/mol = 100.8 kJ/kg. The reference equation gives 103.0 kJ/kg; the ideal-gas value alone, 83.1 kJ/kg, is 19% low.

Sanity check. The departure is larger (more negative) at the colder state, so heating at high pressure requires more enthalpy than the ideal gas needs: the correction adds to the ideal-gas value, and the sign of the −RuTcr(Zh2 − Zh1) term confirms it. Both departures are negative, both chart factors positive, as the theory says.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Reading the inversion condition backwards. Below the inversion temperature (and inside the inversion curve) μJT > 0 and the gas cools; above it the gas warms. Room-temperature hydrogen and helium warm because 300 K is above their inversion temperatures, not because their coefficient is \"large\".

Treating μJT as a constant over a big pressure drop. It varies strongly with P and T; Problem B shows a 60% overestimate of the cooling. For a large ΔP use h2 = h1 with real property data.

Reduced properties in Celsius or with Pcr in the wrong unit. TR needs kelvin; PR needs P and Pcr in the same unit (10 MPa / 3.3958 MPa, not 10 000 kPa / 3.3958).

Sign of the departure. The charts give Zh = (h̄* − h̄)/RuTcr, a positive number, so h̄ = h̄* − RuTcrZh: subtract. Adding it is the most common single error in this topic.

Molar versus mass. RuTcrZh is in kJ/kmol. Divide by M before combining with a mass-based cpΔT, or keep everything molar until the last line.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

Derive μJT = (1/cp)[T(∂v/∂T)P − v] from the general dh, and show it is zero for an ideal gas. Sketch constant-h lines on a T-P diagram with the inversion line through their maxima.

Estimate μJT from a table extract: two states at the same h and neighbouring pressures give μJT ≈ ΔT/ΔP; state whether the gas cools or warms.

Chart problem: a real gas (nitrogen, methane, CO2, propane) between two states at high pressure. Compute TR and PR at each state, read Zh and Zs, compute the ideal-gas changes from the tables, then apply the two-state formulas. Show the units conversion from kJ/kmol to kJ/kg.

Conceptual: explain why helium must be pre-cooled before Joule-Thomson liquefaction, or why the generalised charts are less reliable for water vapour than for nitrogen.

"}, "THERMO/mixtures/s1": {"body": "

This lesson lets you treat a mixture of ideal gases (air, natural gas, combustion products, the contents of a scuba cylinder) as if it were one gas with its own molar mass, gas constant and specific heats, so that every equation from the ideal-gas and first-law chapters works on it unchanged. You will convert between mass and mole fractions, split the total pressure into partial pressures with Dalton's law, compute u, h and s of the mixture, and find the entropy generated when separate gases mix. In the degree it opens the mixtures chapter (Cengel & Boles chapter 13, Moran & Shapiro chapter 12) and is the foundation for psychrometrics in the next lesson and for combustion and chemical equilibrium later.

\n

A mixture is described by how much of each gas it holds

\n

A gas mixture has no single chemical formula, so before you can use PV = mRT you have to say what is in it. There are two natural ways to count: by mass (kilograms of each component) or by amount of substance (kilomoles of each component). Mass is what a scale measures and what energy balances use; moles are what pressure responds to, because in an ideal gas every molecule contributes equally to the pressure regardless of how heavy it is. Most mixture problems start by converting from one count to the other.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Mass fraction and mole fraction. For a mixture of k components with masses mi (kg) and mole numbers Ni (kmol):

  • Total mass mm = Σ mi; total moles Nm = Σ Ni; the two are linked for each component by mi = NiMi, Mi the molar mass (kg/kmol).
  • Mass fraction mfi = mi/mm (dimensionless); mole fraction yi = Ni/Nm (dimensionless). Each set sums to 1.
  • Apparent (average) molar mass Mm = mm/Nm = Σ yiMi (kg/kmol); apparent gas constant Rm = Ru/Mm (kJ/kg·K).

Mass and mole fractions are equal only when all components have the same molar mass. A light gas has a larger mole fraction than mass fraction; a heavy gas the reverse.

\n

The two fractions convert through the molar masses: mfi = yiMi/Mm. A useful check on any mixture calculation: Mm must lie between the smallest and largest Mi, and it is pulled towards the component with the largest mole fraction, not the largest mass fraction.

\n\n

Dalton and Amagat: two ways to split the mixture

\n

Imagine the mixture in a tank at temperature Tm and pressure Pm with volume Vm. There are two thought experiments for asking how much each component contributes.

📊 FIGURE — Dalton splits the pressure, Amagat the volume, of one gas mixture
The tank from the worked example, split two ways (values computed from the stated masses). Each gas’s share of the pressure (Dalton) or of the volume (Amagat) equals its mole fraction.
\n
  • Dalton's law of additive pressures. Take component i alone and let it fill the whole tank (Vm) at the mixture temperature Tm. The pressure it exerts is its component pressure Pi. Dalton's law states that these add up to the mixture pressure: Pm = Σ Pi(Tm, Vm).
  • Amagat's law of additive volumes. Take component i alone at the mixture temperature and the mixture pressure (Tm, Pm). The volume it occupies is its component volume Vi. Amagat's law states Vm = Σ Vi(Tm, Pm).
\n

For ideal gases both laws hold exactly, because ideal-gas molecules do not interact and occupy no volume of their own, so each gas behaves as if the others were absent. Dividing PV = NRuT for one component by the same equation for the mixture gives the result used constantly in this chapter and in combustion:

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Ideal-gas mixtures: pressure fraction = volume fraction = mole fraction.

Pi/Pm = Vi/Vm = Ni/Nm = yi

PmVm = NmRuTm = mmRmTm

Pi is the partial pressure of component i (kPa), Vi its component volume (m³), Ni its moles (kmol), Pm, Vm, Tm the mixture pressure (kPa), volume (m³) and absolute temperature (K), Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K and Rm = Ru/Mm. Gas analyses quoted \"by volume\" are therefore mole fractions.

\n

For real gases at high pressure the two laws are approximations that give different answers, because molecular interactions in the mixture differ from those in each pure gas. One option is to use a compressibility factor for each component in either law: Zm = Σ yiZi, with Zi evaluated at (Tm, Vm) for Dalton or at (Tm, Pm) for Amagat. The simpler route is Kay's rule: treat the whole mixture as a single pure substance whose pseudo-critical temperature and pressure are the mole-fraction averages of the components' critical properties, T'cr,m = Σ yiTcr,i and P'cr,m = Σ yiPcr,i. You then form a reduced temperature Tm/T'cr,m and reduced pressure Pm/P'cr,m and read one Zm off the generalized compressibility chart, exactly as for a pure gas. In words: a mixture of real gases is approximated by a fictitious pure gas with averaged critical properties.

\n\n

Energy and entropy of an ideal-gas mixture

\n

Because ideal-gas components ignore one another, the extensive properties of the mixture are simply the sums of the component properties, each evaluated at the mixture temperature. For U and H this is all you need, since ideal-gas u and h depend on temperature only. Entropy also depends on pressure, and here the partial pressure matters: each component in the mixture behaves as if it alone occupied the full volume at its own partial pressure Pi, not at the total pressure.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Properties of an ideal-gas mixture (mass basis; divide extensive totals by mm):

Um = Σ miui(Tm), Hm = Σ mihi(Tm), Sm = Σ misi(Tm, Pi)

cp,m = Σ mficp,i, cv,m = Σ mficv,i (kJ/kg·K)

Δsi = cp,i ln(T2/T1) − Ri ln(Pi,2/Pi,1)

On a mole basis the same sums use yi and molar properties (c̄p,m = Σ yic̄p,i in kJ/kmol·K). Mass-specific cp values are averaged with mass fractions, molar ones with mole fractions; mixing the two is the classic error.

\n

Entropy of mixing

\n

Put several ideal gases, each at the same T and P, in separate compartments and remove the partitions. The temperature does not change (no energy is exchanged and h depends on T only), the total pressure does not change, but each gas expands from pressure P to its partial pressure yiP in the combined volume. Its entropy rises by −Ri ln yi per kg, which is positive because yi < 1. Summing on a mole basis:

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Entropy generated by mixing ideal gases initially at the mixture T and P:

ΔSmix = Sgen = −Ru Σ Ni ln yi (kJ/K)

Ni in kmol, yi the final mole fraction, Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K. The result depends only on the mole fractions, not on which gases they are, as long as they are different gases. Mixing two samples of the same gas generates no entropy, because nothing distinguishable has spread out.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem. A rigid tank holds 6 kg of N2, 3 kg of O2 and 1 kg of CO2 at 300 K and 150 kPa. Find (a) the mass and mole fractions, (b) the apparent molar mass and gas constant, (c) the tank volume and the partial pressures, (d) the heat needed to warm the mixture to 400 K at constant volume and, for comparison, at constant pressure, and (e) the entropy generated when the three gases, originally in separate compartments at 300 K and 150 kPa, were allowed to mix. Molar masses from Cengel & Boles Table A-1: N2 28.013, O2 31.999, CO2 44.01 kg/kmol. Specific heats at 300 K from Table A-2: cp = 1.039, 0.918, 0.846 kJ/kg·K and cv = 0.743, 0.658, 0.657 kJ/kg·K respectively.

  1. Total mass: mm = 6 + 3 + 1 = 10 kg. Mass fractions: mfN2 = 6/10 = 0.600, mfO2 = 0.300, mfCO2 = 0.100.
  2. Moles, N = m/M: NN2 = 6 kg / 28.013 kg/kmol = 0.21419 kmol; NO2 = 3/31.999 = 0.09375 kmol; NCO2 = 1/44.01 = 0.02272 kmol. Total Nm = 0.33066 kmol.
  3. Mole fractions: yN2 = 0.21419/0.33066 = 0.6478; yO2 = 0.2835; yCO2 = 0.0687 (sum 1.0000). The heavy CO2 has a smaller mole fraction than mass fraction, as expected.
  4. Apparent molar mass: Mm = mm/Nm = 10 kg / 0.33066 kmol = 30.24 kg/kmol (check: Σ yiMi gives the same 30.24). Gas constant Rm = 8.314/30.24 = 0.2749 kJ/kg·K.
  5. Volume: V = mmRmT/P = 10 kg × 0.2749 kJ/kg·K × 300 K / 150 kPa = 5.50 m³.
  6. Partial pressures Pi = yiPm: PN2 = 0.6478 × 150 kPa = 97.16 kPa; PO2 = 42.53 kPa; PCO2 = 10.31 kPa (sum 150.00 kPa).
  7. Mixture specific heats (mass-fraction weighted): cv,m = 0.6(0.743) + 0.3(0.658) + 0.1(0.657) = 0.7089 kJ/kg·K; cp,m = 0.6(1.039) + 0.3(0.918) + 0.1(0.846) = 0.9834 kJ/kg·K. Their difference, 0.2745 kJ/kg·K, matches Rm to within table rounding.
  8. Heat at constant volume (rigid tank, no work): Q = mmcv,mΔT = 10 kg × 0.7089 kJ/kg·K × 100 K = 709 kJ. At constant pressure it would be 10 × 0.9834 × 100 = 983 kJ; the extra 274 kJ is the boundary work of expansion. Both use constant specific heats at 300 K, adequate over 100 K.
  9. Entropy of mixing: Sgen = −8.314 kJ/kmol·K × [0.21419 ln 0.6478 + 0.09375 ln 0.2835 + 0.02272 ln 0.0687] = 2.26 kJ/K, or 0.226 kJ/kg·K of mixture. With a dead state at T0 = 300 K, the exergy destroyed is T0Sgen = 300 K × 2.26 kJ/K = 678 kJ.

Sanity check: Mm = 30.24 lies between 28.01 and 44.01 and close to N2, the dominant component; the partial pressures sum to the total; Sgen is positive, as the second law requires of spontaneous mixing.

\n

The 678 kJ of destroyed exergy is the minimum work a separation plant would need to pull these gases apart again at 300 K. This is why separating air into oxygen and nitrogen, or capturing CO2 from flue gas, always costs work: the entropy of mixing must be undone.

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Averaging with the wrong fraction. The apparent molar mass is Σ yiMi (mole fractions), while the mass-specific cp,m is Σ mficp,i (mass fractions). Weighting kJ/kg·K values by mole fractions, or molar masses by mass fractions, gives a plausible-looking but wrong number. In the example, weighting the mass-specific cp values by mole fractions would give 0.9914 kJ/kg·K instead of 0.9834 kJ/kg·K, an error small enough to go unnoticed; always check that the unit of the averaged property matches the basis of the fraction.

Using the total pressure in the entropy of a component. In Δsi = cp,i ln(T2/T1) − Ri ln(Pi,2/Pi,1), the pressures are the component's partial pressures. If the composition does not change, Pi,2/Pi,1 = Pm,2/Pm,1 and the distinction vanishes; the moment gases mix or separate, only partial pressures give the right answer.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n

Exam problems on ideal-gas mixtures follow a fixed script: convert a mass analysis to a mole analysis (or back), find Mm and Rm, apply PV = mRmT, then either a first-law balance using mixture cv or cp, or an entropy balance component by component. Tabulate the components in rows (mi, Mi, Ni, yi, mfi, Pi) before you compute anything else; it prevents almost every slip.

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

Typical questions: \"a gas mixture is 40% CO2 and 60% N2 by volume; find the mass fractions\"; \"two gases at different temperatures and pressures mix adiabatically in a rigid tank; find the final T, P and the entropy generated\"; \"find the minimum work to separate air into its components\". For adiabatic mixing of gases at different initial temperatures, first find the final T from an energy balance (Σ micv,i(Tf − Ti) = 0 for a rigid tank), then compute each Δsi from its own initial T and partial-pressure change.

Know that \"by volume\" means mole fraction, that partial pressure equals mole fraction times total pressure, and that the entropy of mixing depends only on the yi.

"}, "THERMO/mixtures/s2": {"body": "

This lesson lets you describe the air in a room, a duct or a weather report quantitatively: how much water vapour it carries, how close it is to condensing, how much energy it holds, and how a thermometer with a wet wick tells you all of that. These quantities, and the psychrometric chart that plots them, are the working language of air conditioning, drying, meteorology and cooling towers. In the degree this is the application of the previous lesson to the single most important gas mixture, atmospheric air (Cengel & Boles chapter 14, Moran & Shapiro chapter 12), and it is the foundation for every air-conditioning process in the next lesson.

\n

Air is a two-component mixture: dry air plus water vapour

\n

Atmospheric air is nitrogen, oxygen, argon and a little CO2, whose composition barely changes, plus a variable amount of water vapour. Psychrometrics lumps the first group together as dry air (treated as one ideal gas, M = 28.97 kg/kmol, Ra = 0.287 kJ/kg·K) and tracks the vapour separately. Between about −10 °C and 50 °C both can be treated as ideal gases with small error: the vapour's partial pressure is only a few kPa, far below the pressures at which steam departs from ideal behaviour. Dalton's law from the previous lesson then gives P = Pa + Pv, with Pa the partial pressure of dry air and Pv that of vapour.

\n

The key simplification: because an ideal gas's enthalpy depends only on temperature, the enthalpy of the vapour at low pressure is essentially the enthalpy of saturated vapour at the same temperature, hv(T, low P) ≈ hg(T). That lets you read vapour enthalpies straight from the saturated-water temperature table.

\n

The water content is what changes in air-conditioning processes, while the mass of dry air flowing through a duct stays constant. So every psychrometric property is quoted per kilogram of dry air, never per kilogram of moist air. Hold on to that; it is the source of most errors.

\n\n

Specific humidity, relative humidity and dew point

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Specific (absolute) humidity ω: the mass of water vapour per unit mass of dry air, ω = mv/ma (kg vapour/kg dry air).

Relative humidity φ: the amount of vapour the air holds relative to the maximum it could hold at the same temperature, φ = mv/mg = Pv/Pg, where Pg = Psat at the air temperature. φ runs from 0 (dry air) to 1 (saturated air).

Dew-point temperature Tdp: the temperature at which condensation begins when the air is cooled at constant pressure, Tdp = Tsat at Pv.

Dry-bulb temperature T: the ordinary air temperature, as read by a dry thermometer.

\n

Specific and relative humidity answer different questions. ω is an inventory: grams of water per kilogram of air, unchanged by heating or cooling as long as no water is added or removed. φ is a comfort and condensation measure: how near the air is to saturation. Heat a room without adding water and ω stays the same while φ falls, because Pg rises steeply with temperature. That is why heated winter air feels dry.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Moist-air relations (P total pressure in kPa, T in °C for the enthalpy fit):

ω = 0.622 Pv / (P − Pv)

φ = ωP / [(0.622 + ω) Pg] and Pv = φPg

h = ha + ωhg ≈ 1.005 T + ω(2500.9 + 1.82 T) (kJ/kg dry air)

Pv is the vapour partial pressure (kPa), Pg the saturation pressure of water at the dry-bulb temperature (kPa), 0.622 = Mv/Ma = 18.015/28.97, h the enthalpy of the moist air per kg of dry air, cp,a = 1.005 kJ/kg·K for dry air, hg the saturated-vapour enthalpy at T from the steam table. The fit 2500.9 + 1.82T reproduces tabulated hg to within about 0.2 kJ/kg between 5 and 40 °C (it gives 2546.4 kJ/kg at 25 °C against the table's 2546.5). Enthalpy is referenced to dry air at 0 °C and liquid water at 0.01 °C.

\n

The 0.622 comes from dividing the ideal-gas equations for vapour and dry air in the same volume: ω = mv/ma = (PvV/RvT)/(PaV/RaT) = (Ra/Rv)(Pv/Pa) = 0.622 Pv/Pa.

\n
✅ VERIFIED

Saturation pressures and enthalpies of water used in this chapter are from Cengel & Boles Table A-4 (saturated water, temperature table): Psat = 0.8725, 1.2281, 1.7057, 2.3392, 3.1698, 4.2469, 5.6291, 7.3851 kPa at 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40 °C; hg = 2519.2, 2528.3, 2537.4, 2546.5, 2555.6, 2564.6, 2573.5 kJ/kg at 10 to 40 °C; hf = 62.982, 83.915, 104.83, 125.74, 167.53 kJ/kg at 15, 20, 25, 30, 40 °C.

They were cross-checked against an IAPWS-IF97 implementation (agreement within 0.01%) and against a published copy of the table: Table A-4, saturated water, temperature table.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem A: the air in a room. A 4 m × 5 m × 3 m room holds air at 25 °C, relative humidity 60% and 101.325 kPa. Find the vapour and dry-air partial pressures, the specific humidity, the enthalpy per kg of dry air, the masses of dry air and vapour, and the dew point. Steam data from Table A-4; Ra = 0.287 kJ/kg·K; cp,a = 1.005 kJ/kg·K.

  1. Saturation pressure at 25 °C (Table A-4): Pg = 3.1698 kPa. Vapour pressure Pv = φPg = 0.60 × 3.1698 kPa = 1.9019 kPa.
  2. Dry-air partial pressure: Pa = P − Pv = 101.325 − 1.9019 = 99.423 kPa.
  3. Specific humidity: ω = 0.622 × 1.9019 kPa / 99.423 kPa = 0.01190 kg H2O/kg dry air (11.9 g/kg).
  4. Enthalpy: h = cp,aT + ωhg = 1.005 kJ/kg·K × 25 °C + 0.01190 × 2546.5 kJ/kg = 25.13 + 30.30 = 55.42 kJ/kg dry air. More than half the enthalpy sits in the 12 g of vapour.
  5. Dry-air mass: V = 60 m³, T = 298.15 K. ma = PaV/(RaT) = 99.423 kPa × 60 m³ / (0.287 kJ/kg·K × 298.15 K) = 69.71 kg.
  6. Vapour mass: mv = ωma = 0.01190 × 69.71 kg = 0.829 kg (the ideal-gas law for vapour alone, with Rv = 0.4615 kJ/kg·K, gives the same 0.829 kg).
  7. Dew point: Tdp = Tsat at 1.9019 kPa, which lies between 15 °C (1.7057 kPa) and 20 °C (2.3392 kPa). Linear interpolation: 15 + 5 × (1.9019 − 1.7057)/(2.3392 − 1.7057) = 16.5 °C. (The exact IAPWS value is 16.7 °C; linear interpolation of the curved Psat(T) slightly under-reads.)

Sanity check: 12 g/kg and a dew point in the mid-teens are typical of a comfortable, slightly humid room; any wall or window colder than about 16.5 °C will fog.

\n\n

Measuring humidity: adiabatic saturation and the wet-bulb temperature

\n

Relative humidity is hard to measure directly, but temperatures are easy. The trick is to let the air evaporate water and see how much it cools. Imagine a long insulated channel with a pool of water in it. Unsaturated air enters at T1, ω1; water evaporates into it, the latent heat comes from the air itself, so the air cools and gains moisture until it leaves saturated at the adiabatic saturation temperature T2. Make-up water enters at T2. Mass and energy balances on this steady-flow device give ω1 from two temperatures.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Specific humidity from the adiabatic saturation temperature:

ω1 = [cp,a(T2 − T1) + ω2hfg2] / (hg1 − hf2), ω2 = 0.622 Pg2/(P − Pg2)

T1 is the entering dry-bulb temperature, T2 the adiabatic saturation temperature (air leaves saturated, φ2 = 100%), hfg2 and hf2 are at T2, hg1 at T1, all in kJ/kg. For air-water vapour mixtures at atmospheric pressure the wet-bulb temperature Twb read by a thermometer with a wetted wick in moving air is approximately equal to T2, so the same equation is used with T2 = Twb.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem B: a sling psychrometer. A sling psychrometer reads a dry-bulb temperature of 25 °C and a wet-bulb temperature of 15 °C at 101.325 kPa. Find ω, φ, h and the dew point.

  1. Saturated state at the wet bulb, 15 °C (Table A-4): Pg2 = 1.7057 kPa, hf2 = 62.982 kJ/kg, hfg2 = hg − hf = 2528.3 − 62.982 = 2465.3 kJ/kg. At 25 °C: hg1 = 2546.5 kJ/kg, Pg1 = 3.1698 kPa.
  2. ω2 = 0.622 × 1.7057 / (101.325 − 1.7057) = 0.010650 kg/kg dry air.
  3. Numerator: 1.005 kJ/kg·K × (15 − 25) K + 0.010650 × 2465.3 kJ/kg = −10.05 + 26.26 = 16.21 kJ/kg. Denominator: 2546.5 − 62.982 = 2483.5 kJ/kg.
  4. ω1 = 16.21/2483.5 = 0.00653 kg H2O/kg dry air.
  5. Pv1 = ω1P/(0.622 + ω1) = 0.00653 × 101.325/(0.62853) = 1.052 kPa, so φ1 = 1.052/3.1698 = 0.332 (33%).
  6. h1 = 1.005 × 25 + 0.00653 × 2546.5 = 41.7 kJ/kg dry air.
  7. Dew point: 1.052 kPa lies between 5 °C (0.8725 kPa) and 10 °C (1.2281 kPa); linear interpolation gives about 7.5 °C.

Sanity check: Tdp (7.5 °C) < Twb (15 °C) < Tdb (25 °C), the ordering every unsaturated air sample must obey. The saturated exit enthalpy, 1.005 × 15 + 0.010650 × 2528.3 = 42.0 kJ/kg, exceeds h1 by exactly (ω2 − ω1)hf2 = 0.26 kJ/kg, the enthalpy of the make-up water.

\n\n

The psychrometric chart

\n

Every calculation above can be read off one chart, drawn for a single total pressure (usually 1 atm). Learn its geometry once and you can sketch any air-conditioning process on it.

📊 FIGURE — Psychrometric chart: a 25 °C, 60% room and its 16.5 °C dew point
Dry-bulb temperature across, ω up the right side. Cooling the room air at constant ω (move left) meets the saturation curve at the dew point; the green dashed line is its constant enthalpy.
\n
  • Horizontal axis: dry-bulb temperature. Vertical axis (right side): specific humidity ω. A horizontal line is constant ω, which is also constant Pv and constant dew point.
  • Saturation curve (φ = 100%): the curved upper-left boundary. The other relative-humidity curves have the same shape and lie below it.
  • Constant wet-bulb lines slope down to the right and are almost parallel to constant-enthalpy lines, because h changes only by the small (ω2 − ω1)hf along an adiabatic saturation path. Enthalpy is read on a scale along the saturation curve.
  • Specific-volume lines (m³/kg dry air) are steeper, almost vertical.
  • On the saturation curve, dry-bulb, wet-bulb and dew-point temperatures are equal. For any state: dew point is found by moving horizontally left to the saturation curve; wet bulb by following the wet-bulb line up-left to it.
\n

Check Problem A on a chart: at 25 °C and 60% you should read ω ≈ 11.9 g/kg, h ≈ 55 kJ/kg, Tdp ≈ 16.7 °C and v ≈ 0.86 m³/kg dry air (RaT/Pa = 0.287 × 298.15/99.423 = 0.861 m³/kg).

\n
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

A psychrometric chart is a lookup table drawn by hand. You can replace it with five lines of Python: a function Pg(T) (fitted to Table A-4 or taken from a library such as iapws or CoolProp), then vectorised formulas for ω, φ, h and a root-finder for dew point and wet bulb. With pandas you can then take a year of hourly weather-station readings (dry bulb and relative humidity) and compute enthalpy for every hour, which is exactly how building engineers size cooling coils from design-day data. The chart is still worth knowing for exams and for seeing processes at a glance.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Per kg of mixture instead of per kg of dry air. ω and h are per kg of dry air. When you multiply by a mass flow rate, it must be the dry-air mass flow ṁa = PaV̇/(RaT), computed with the dry-air partial pressure Pa, not the total pressure.

Using P instead of P − Pv. ω = 0.622Pv/(P − Pv). Using P in the denominator underestimates ω by about 2% at room conditions and more in hot humid air.

Treating φ as a fraction of ω. φ is a ratio of pressures, not of specific humidities: φ ≠ ω/ωsat exactly (they differ by a factor (P − Pg)/(P − Pv)). And Pg must be taken at the dry-bulb temperature, not at the dew point or wet bulb.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

Expect: (1) given T and φ (or T and Twb, or T and Tdp), find the other properties, including the masses of air and vapour in a room; (2) will a surface at a given temperature sweat? Compare it with the dew point; (3) derive ω = 0.622Pv/(P − Pv) and the adiabatic-saturation relation from balances; (4) read a state off the psychrometric chart and check it by calculation.

Always list the three temperatures in order Tdp ≤ Twb ≤ Tdb as a check, and state which steam table (temperature table) your Pg values came from.

"}, "THERMO/mixtures/s3": {"body": "

This lesson lets you size the hardware of air conditioning: how much heat a cooling coil must remove, how much water drains from it, how much water an evaporative cooler or humidifier needs, what comes out when two air streams are mixed, and how much air and make-up water a power-plant cooling tower uses. Every problem is the same three balances (dry air, water, energy) applied to a steady-flow control volume with the psychrometric properties of the previous lesson. In the degree this closes the mixtures chapter (Cengel & Boles chapter 14, Moran & Shapiro chapter 12) and is where HVAC and power-plant heat rejection meet thermodynamics.

\n

Three balances for every process

\n

An air-conditioning device is a steady-flow control volume through which moist air passes, with possibly a stream of liquid water or steam added or drained, a heat transfer and occasionally fan work. Because psychrometric properties are per kg of dry air, the bookkeeping is done with the dry-air mass flow rate ṁa, which enters and leaves unchanged.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Steady-flow balances for moist air (all flows in kg/s, h in kJ/kg dry air for air streams and kJ/kg for liquid water):

Dry air: Σ ṁa,in = Σ ṁa,out

Water: Σ ṁa,inωin + Σ ṁw,in = Σ ṁa,outωout + Σ ṁw,out

Energy: Q̇in + Ẇin + Σ ṁhin = Q̇out + Ẇout + Σ ṁhout

ṁw is a liquid-water (or steam) stream, ω the specific humidity, and for each air stream ṁh means ṁah. The dry-air mass flow comes from the volume flow: ṁa = V̇/v with v = RaT/Pa (m³/kg dry air). Kinetic and potential energy changes are negligible in HVAC equipment.

📘 DEFINITION

The standard air-conditioning processes. Simple heating or cooling: temperature changes at constant ω (no water added or removed). Humidification: water or steam added, ω rises. Cooling with dehumidification: air cooled below its dew point so that vapour condenses and drains. Evaporative cooling: water evaporates into dry air adiabatically, at nearly constant wet-bulb temperature and enthalpy. Adiabatic mixing: two air streams combine without heat transfer. Wet cooling tower: warm water is cooled by partly evaporating into an air stream.

\n\n

Simple heating and cooling; heating with humidification

\n

A heating coil or a dry cooling coil (one warmer than the dew point) changes only the temperature. With ω1 = ω2 the balances reduce to q = h2 − h1 per kg of dry air. On the chart the process is a horizontal line; φ falls on heating and rises on cooling. Take outdoor air at 10 °C and 70% heated to 25 °C at 101.325 kPa: Pv = 0.70 × 1.2281 = 0.8597 kPa, ω = 0.622 × 0.8597/(101.325 − 0.8597) = 0.00532 kg/kg, h1 = 1.005 × 10 + 0.00532 × 2519.2 = 23.46 kJ/kg and h2 = 1.005 × 25 + 0.00532 × 2546.5 = 38.68 kJ/kg, so q = 15.22 kJ/kg dry air. The relative humidity drops from 70% to φ2 = 0.8597/3.1698 = 27%, uncomfortably dry. That is why winter systems follow the heater with a humidifier. Injecting steam raises ω with a small temperature rise; spraying liquid water raises ω while the air cools slightly, since the latent heat comes from the air. The water balance gives the water added, ṁw = ṁa(ω3 − ω2), and the energy balance across the humidifier is ṁah2 + ṁwhw = ṁah3.

\n\n

Cooling with dehumidification

\n

In summer the air must lose both heat and water. The cooling coil is colder than the dew point, so the air cools at constant ω until it reaches saturation, then continues down the saturation curve while vapour condenses and drains. The condensate leaves at about the exit air temperature.

📊 FIGURE — Cooling coil (A) and evaporative cooler (B) on the psychrometric chart
A: the coil cools at constant ω to the dew point, then follows the saturation curve down while water drains. B: an evaporative cooler trades temperature for moisture at nearly constant enthalpy.
\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem A. Air at 30 °C, φ = 70% and 101.325 kPa enters a cooling coil at 25 m³/min and leaves saturated at 15 °C. Condensate leaves at 15 °C. Find the dry-air mass flow, the rate of condensate removal and the cooling load. Table A-4: Pg = 4.2469 kPa and hg = 2555.6 kJ/kg at 30 °C; Pg = 1.7057 kPa, hg = 2528.3 kJ/kg and hf = 62.982 kJ/kg at 15 °C.

  1. Inlet: Pv1 = 0.70 × 4.2469 = 2.9728 kPa; Pa1 = 101.325 − 2.9728 = 98.352 kPa; ω1 = 0.622 × 2.9728/98.352 = 0.01880 kg/kg dry air.
  2. h1 = 1.005 × 30 + 0.01880 × 2555.6 = 78.20 kJ/kg dry air.
  3. Specific volume v1 = RaT1/Pa1 = 0.287 kJ/kg·K × 303.15 K / 98.352 kPa = 0.8846 m³/kg dry air, so ṁa = 25 m³/min / 0.8846 m³/kg = 28.26 kg/min.
  4. Exit (saturated, φ2 = 1): ω2 = 0.622 × 1.7057/(101.325 − 1.7057) = 0.01065 kg/kg; h2 = 1.005 × 15 + 0.01065 × 2528.3 = 42.00 kJ/kg dry air.
  5. Water balance: ṁw = ṁa(ω1 − ω2) = 28.26 × (0.01880 − 0.01065) = 0.230 kg/min of condensate (13.8 kg/h).
  6. Energy balance: Q̇out = ṁa(h1 − h2) − ṁwhw = 28.26 × 78.20 − 28.26 × 42.00 − 0.230 × 62.982 = 2209.9 − 1187.0 − 14.5 = 1008.4 kJ/min = 16.8 kW.

Sanity check: the inlet dew point (Tsat at 2.97 kPa, about 23.8 °C by interpolation) is above the 15 °C exit, so condensation must happen; the condensate term is under 2% of the load, which is why it is often neglected.

\n

About 56% of that load, 28.26 × (0.01880 − 0.01065) × roughly 2450 kJ/kg ≈ 564 kJ/min, is latent (condensing vapour) rather than sensible cooling; in humid climates the dehumidification dominates. The 15 °C saturated air is often too cold and clammy to supply directly, so it is reheated at constant ω before entering the room.

\n\n

Evaporative cooling

\n

In hot, dry climates you can cool air without a refrigerator by letting it evaporate water from a wet pad. No heat or work crosses the boundary, so the air's enthalpy is essentially constant (strictly, it rises by the tiny enthalpy of the liquid water added). The process follows a constant wet-bulb line, and the lowest temperature reachable is the wet-bulb temperature of the entering air.

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem B. Desert air at 40 °C, φ = 15% and 101.325 kPa passes through an evaporative cooler and leaves at 25 °C. Find the exit relative humidity and the water evaporated per kg of dry air. Table A-4: Pg = 7.3851 kPa, hg = 2573.5 kJ/kg at 40 °C; Pg = 3.1698 kPa, hg = 2546.5 kJ/kg at 25 °C.

  1. Inlet: Pv1 = 0.15 × 7.3851 = 1.1078 kPa; ω1 = 0.622 × 1.1078/(101.325 − 1.1078) = 0.006875 kg/kg dry air.
  2. h1 = 1.005 × 40 + 0.006875 × 2573.5 = 40.20 + 17.69 = 57.89 kJ/kg dry air.
  3. Adiabatic, h2 ≈ h1: 1.005 × 25 + ω2 × 2546.5 = 57.89, so ω2 = (57.89 − 25.13)/2546.5 = 0.01287 kg/kg dry air.
  4. Pv2 = ω2P/(0.622 + ω2) = 0.01287 × 101.325/0.63487 = 2.054 kPa; φ2 = 2.054/3.1698 = 0.648 (65%).
  5. Water evaporated: ω2 − ω1 = 0.01287 − 0.00688 = 0.00599 kg/kg dry air (6.0 g per kg of air).

Sanity check: the neglected liquid-water enthalpy, 0.00599 × 104.83 = 0.63 kJ/kg, would raise φ2 by about one percentage point; the 15 °C of cooling was bought with 6 g of water per kg of air and no compressor.

\n\n

Adiabatic mixing of two airstreams

\n

Buildings mix fresh outdoor air with recirculated room air before conditioning it. With no heat or work, the three balances give ṁa3 = ṁa1 + ṁa2, ω3 and h3 as dry-air-mass-weighted averages, and a geometric rule for the chart.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Adiabatic mixing of streams 1 and 2 into state 3:

ṁa1/ṁa2 = (ω2 − ω3)/(ω3 − ω1) = (h2 − h3)/(h3 − h1)

State 3 lies on the straight line joining 1 and 2 on the psychrometric chart, dividing it in the inverse ratio of the dry-air mass flows: it sits closer to the stream with the larger flow. Temperatures are not strictly mass-weighted, but nearly so.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem C. Stream 1, outdoor air at 10 °C, φ = 80%, 30 m³/min, mixes adiabatically at 101.325 kPa with stream 2, room air at 30 °C, φ = 60%, 50 m³/min. Find ω3, h3, T3 and φ3. Table A-4 values at 10 °C: Pg = 1.2281 kPa, hg = 2519.2 kJ/kg; at 30 °C as in Problem A.

  1. Stream 1: Pv1 = 0.80 × 1.2281 = 0.9825 kPa; Pa1 = 100.343 kPa; ω1 = 0.006090; h1 = 1.005 × 10 + 0.006090 × 2519.2 = 25.39 kJ/kg; v1 = 0.287 × 283.15/100.343 = 0.8099 m³/kg; ṁa1 = 30/0.8099 = 37.04 kg/min.
  2. Stream 2: Pv2 = 0.60 × 4.2469 = 2.5481 kPa; Pa2 = 98.777 kPa; ω2 = 0.016046; h2 = 1.005 × 30 + 0.016046 × 2555.6 = 71.16 kJ/kg; v2 = 0.287 × 303.15/98.777 = 0.8808 m³/kg; ṁa2 = 50/0.8808 = 56.77 kg/min.
  3. ṁa3 = 37.04 + 56.77 = 93.81 kg/min. ω3 = (37.04 × 0.006090 + 56.77 × 0.016046)/93.81 = 0.01211 kg/kg dry air. h3 = (37.04 × 25.39 + 56.77 × 71.16)/93.81 = 53.09 kJ/kg dry air.
  4. Temperature from h3 = 1.005T3 + ω3(2500.9 + 1.82T3): T3 = (53.09 − 0.01211 × 2500.9)/(1.005 + 1.82 × 0.01211) = 22.2 °C.
  5. Pv3 = 0.01211 × 101.325/0.63411 = 1.936 kPa. Linear interpolation in Table A-4 between 20 and 25 °C gives Pg ≈ 2.703 kPa at 22.2 °C, so φ3 = 1.936/2.703 = 0.72 (72%).

Sanity check: T3 = 22.2 °C lies between 10 and 30 °C, nearer the larger stream; the lever rule holds, since ṁa1/ṁa2 = 0.653 = (ω2 − ω3)/(ω3 − ω1). The exact Pg at 22.2 °C is 2.676 kPa, giving 72.3%.

\n\n

Wet cooling towers

\n

A power plant or large chiller must reject heat from its condenser cooling water. A wet cooling tower sprays the warm water down over packing while air is drawn up through it; a small fraction of the water evaporates, and the latent heat that takes cools the rest. The water can in principle be cooled to the wet-bulb temperature of the entering air, well below its dry-bulb temperature. The evaporated water must be replaced by make-up water, ṁmakeup = ṁa(ω2 − ω1).

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem D. Cooling water enters a tower at 40 °C and 100 kg/s and leaves at 25 °C. Air enters at 20 °C, φ = 60%, 101.325 kPa and leaves saturated at 30 °C. Fan power is neglected. Find the dry-air mass flow, the volume flow of entering air and the make-up water rate. Table A-4: hf = 167.53 kJ/kg at 40 °C, 104.83 kJ/kg at 25 °C; at 20 °C Pg = 2.3392 kPa, hg = 2537.4 kJ/kg.

  1. Air in (1): Pv1 = 0.60 × 2.3392 = 1.4035 kPa; ω1 = 0.622 × 1.4035/99.921 = 0.008737; h1 = 1.005 × 20 + 0.008737 × 2537.4 = 42.27 kJ/kg dry air.
  2. Air out (2): ω2 = 0.622 × 4.2469/97.078 = 0.027211; h2 = 1.005 × 30 + 0.027211 × 2555.6 = 99.69 kJ/kg dry air.
  3. Water in (3) and out (4): ṁ3 = 100 kg/s, h3 = 167.53 kJ/kg; ṁ4 = ṁ3 − ṁa(ω2 − ω1), h4 = 104.83 kJ/kg.
  4. Energy balance ṁah1 + ṁ3h3 = ṁah2 + ṁ4h4, rearranged: ṁa = ṁ3(h3 − h4) / [(h2 − h1) − (ω2 − ω1)h4] = 100 × 62.70 / (57.42 − 1.94) = 6270 kW / 55.48 kJ/kg = 113.0 kg/s of dry air.
  5. Volume flow in: v1 = 0.287 × 293.15/99.921 = 0.8420 m³/kg; V̇1 = 113.0 × 0.8420 = 95.1 m³/s.
  6. Make-up water: ṁa(ω2 − ω1) = 113.0 × (0.027211 − 0.008737) = 2.09 kg/s.

Sanity check: evaporating about 2% of the water flow removes 6.27 MW, consistent with 2.09 kg/s × roughly 2,400 kJ/kg of latent heat plus a little sensible heating of the air.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Forgetting the water stream in the energy balance. In cooling towers and humidifiers the liquid or steam stream carries enthalpy (ṁwhw). In a tower the water leaving is less than the water entering by the evaporated amount; setting ṁ4 = ṁ3 gives the wrong ṁa.

Using volume flow rates as if they were mass flows. Mixing and balances weight by dry-air mass flow, ṁa = V̇/v, and v differs between streams (0.81 against 0.88 m³/kg in Problem C).

Assuming dehumidification without checking the dew point. A coil only removes water if the air reaches its dew point; above it the process is simple cooling at constant ω.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

Each process appears as a standard problem: heating plus humidification (find heat input and water or steam added), cooling plus dehumidification (cooling load and condensate, often with reheat), evaporative cooling (exit φ or T), adiabatic mixing (state 3 from two streams), and a cooling tower (air flow and make-up water). Write the three balances first, draw the process on a sketch of the chart, then fill in properties.

Conceptual favourites: why an evaporative cooler fails in humid weather (small wet-bulb depression), why a cooling tower cannot cool water below the air wet-bulb temperature, and why summer air conditioning needs reheat.

"}, "THERMO/combust/s1": {"body": "

This lesson lets you write the balanced equation for burning any hydrocarbon in air, convert it into an air-fuel ratio, express how much air was supplied as percent theoretical air, excess air or equivalence ratio, and predict the temperature at which the water in the exhaust starts to condense. In the degree sequence this is the first lesson of the chemical-reactions block: everything in the next two lessons (enthalpy of formation, heating values, flame temperature, exergy destruction) is built on a correctly balanced reaction, so the bookkeeping here is not optional preparation, it is the part that most exam marks are lost on.

What burns, and what it burns in

Combustion is a chemical reaction in which a fuel is oxidised rapidly and releases energy. In an engineering course the fuels are almost always hydrocarbons, written CnHm: methane CH4 (the main component of natural gas), propane C3H8 (bottled gas), octane C8H18 (used as a stand-in for petrol/gasoline) and dodecane C12H26 (a stand-in for diesel). Alcohols such as methanol CH3OH and ethanol C2H5OH also appear, and so do hydrogen H2 and carbon monoxide CO. When a hydrocarbon burns completely, all of its carbon becomes CO2 and all of its hydrogen becomes H2O. Nothing else is produced by the fuel itself.

The oxidiser is almost always air, and the whole chapter uses one standard simplification for it: dry air is 21% O2 and 79% N2 by volume (mole), with the argon and traces lumped into the nitrogen. So every kmol of O2 drags 79/21 = 3.76 kmol of N2 with it, and one kmol of O2 plus its nitrogen is 4.76 kmol of air. The molar mass of air is Mair = 28.97 kg/kmol. The nitrogen is treated as inert: it passes through the reaction unchanged, but it still has to be heated, which is why it matters enormously for the flame temperature in lesson 3.

📘 DEFINITION

Theoretical (stoichiometric) air is the minimum amount of air that supplies exactly enough oxygen for complete combustion: every C atom ends up in CO2, every H atom in H2O, and no free O2 is left in the products. Combustion with theoretical air is called theoretical or stoichiometric combustion. Complete combustion means no unburned fuel, no CO, no H2 and no free carbon in the products; it needs at least theoretical air, but supplying enough air does not guarantee it (mixing and time also matter).

Balancing the reaction: the recipe

Balancing is atom bookkeeping. Write the fuel on the left with an unknown amount ath of (O2 + 3.76 N2), write CO2, H2O and N2 on the right, and balance C, then H, then O, then N. For a pure hydrocarbon the oxygen requirement can be written down directly:

📊 FIGURE — Balancing octane in air: C, then H, then O, then N
Balance the atoms in the order shown; the oxygen step fixes a th = 12.5. The bars show the products with theoretical air and with 50% excess air (AF values computed from the balanced equations).

CnHm + ath (O2 + 3.76 N2) → n CO2 + (m/2) H2O + 3.76 ath N2, with ath = n + m/4

Here n and m are the numbers of C and H atoms in one molecule of fuel (dimensionless), ath is the kmol of O2 needed per kmol of fuel, and 3.76 ath is the kmol of N2 that come along. The n counts one O2 per CO2; the m/4 counts one O atom (half an O2) per H2O and there are m/2 of them. If the fuel already contains oxygen (an alcohol CnHmOp), subtract p/2 from ath, because that oxygen is already in the fuel. Check with octane: n = 8, m = 18, so ath = 8 + 18/4 = 12.5 kmol O2 per kmol C8H18, and the stoichiometric equation is C8H18 + 12.5 (O2 + 3.76 N2) → 8 CO2 + 9 H2O + 47 N2. Count the oxygen atoms: 25 on the left, 16 + 9 = 25 on the right.

Air-fuel ratio, percent theoretical air, excess air and equivalence ratio

Engineers do not talk in kmol; they talk in kg of air per kg of fuel. The conversion from the balanced equation is a one-line multiplication:

🧮 KEY EQUATION

AF = mair / mfuel = (Nair Mair) / (Nfuel Mfuel)

AF is the air-fuel ratio on a mass basis (kg air / kg fuel); Nair = 4.76 a kmol of air per kmol fuel (a is the actual kmol of O2 supplied); Mair = 28.97 kg/kmol; Nfuel = 1 kmol; Mfuel is the fuel molar mass in kg/kmol (C8H18: 114.23, CH4: 16.04, C3H8: 44.10, from atomic masses C = 12.011, H = 1.008 kg/kmol). The fuel-air ratio FA is simply 1/AF.

percent theoretical air = 100 × a / ath percent excess air = 100 × (a − ath) / ath φ = AFst / AFactual = FAactual / FAst

a is the kmol of O2 (equivalently of air) actually supplied per kmol fuel, ath the theoretical amount; 150% theoretical air is the same thing as 50% excess air. φ (phi) is the equivalence ratio, dimensionless: φ = 1 is stoichiometric, φ < 1 is a lean mixture (excess air), φ > 1 is a rich mixture (deficiency of air, so CO and unburned fuel must appear). Note that φ is defined with the actual ratio in the denominator, so it moves opposite to percent theoretical air: 150% theoretical air is φ = 1/1.5 = 0.667.

Most real burners run lean. Boilers and gas turbines use anything from 10% to several hundred percent excess air so that every fuel molecule finds oxygen; a petrol engine with a three-way catalyst runs at φ ≈ 1 because the catalyst needs a stoichiometric exhaust. Rich mixtures are used deliberately only where the maximum power per kg of air matters more than efficiency.

Incomplete combustion and the dry (Orsat) analysis

With less than theoretical air, or with poor mixing, the products contain CO, H2, unburned hydrocarbons or soot. A textbook rule for balancing such cases: hydrogen is assumed to burn to H2O first, and whatever oxygen is left over is shared between CO and CO2. In practice the product composition is measured, historically with an Orsat apparatus: a sample of exhaust is bubbled through absorbers that remove CO2, then O2, then CO, and the volume that disappears at each stage gives that gas as a fraction of the sample. Because the sample is collected over water, its own water vapour is already condensed out, so the result is a dry analysis: mole fractions of the products with the H2O removed, and the rest of the gas (N2) taken by difference. Modern electrochemical and infrared analysers report the same dry-basis numbers. The exam skill is to run the balance backwards: given the dry analysis, find how much air was really used.

Dew point of the products

Combustion of any hydrogen-containing fuel makes water vapour, and that vapour condenses when the exhaust cools to its dew point. Condensation is a problem (acidic condensate corrodes flues; water in engine exhaust pipes) or an opportunity (condensing boilers recover the latent heat). The dew point follows from the water vapour's partial pressure, exactly as in the psychrometrics chapter:

Pv = yH2O Pprod = (NH2O / Nprod,total) Pprod, Tdp = Tsat at Pv

Pv is the partial pressure of the water vapour (kPa), yH2O its mole fraction in the wet products (all product species counted, including N2), Pprod the total product pressure (kPa, usually 101.325 kPa), and Tsat comes from the saturated-water-by-pressure table. Once the exhaust is below Tdp, part of the water is liquid and the vapour left in the gas is at the saturation pressure for that temperature.

Worked example 1: octane with 50% excess air

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Liquid octane C8H18 is burned completely with 150% theoretical air (50% excess air). Find (a) the balanced equation, (b) the air-fuel ratio, (c) the equivalence ratio and (d) the dew point of the products at 101.325 kPa.

  1. Theoretical oxygen. n = 8, m = 18: ath = 8 + 18/4 = 12.5 kmol O2/kmol fuel.
  2. Actual oxygen. a = 1.5 × 12.5 = 18.75 kmol O2/kmol fuel, bringing 3.76 × 18.75 = 70.5 kmol N2. The unused oxygen is 18.75 − 12.5 = 6.25 kmol O2 and it appears unchanged in the products.
  3. Balanced equation (per kmol fuel). C8H18 + 18.75 (O2 + 3.76 N2) → 8 CO2 + 9 H2O + 6.25 O2 + 70.5 N2. Oxygen check: 37.5 atoms in, 16 + 9 + 12.5 = 37.5 out.
  4. Air-fuel ratio. Air supplied = 4.76 × 18.75 = 89.25 kmol; mass = 89.25 kmol × 28.97 kg/kmol = 2585.6 kg air. Fuel mass = 1 kmol × 114.23 kg/kmol = 114.23 kg. AF = 2585.6 / 114.23 = 22.63 kg air / kg fuel. (Stoichiometric: 12.5 × 4.76 × 28.97 / 114.23 = 15.09 kg/kg.)
  5. Equivalence ratio. φ = AFst / AF = 15.09 / 22.63 = 1 / 1.5 = 0.667 (lean).
  6. Total product moles. Nprod = 8 + 9 + 6.25 + 70.5 = 93.75 kmol per kmol fuel.
  7. Water partial pressure. yH2O = 9 / 93.75 = 0.0960; Pv = 0.0960 × 101.325 kPa = 9.727 kPa.
  8. Dew point. Saturated water by temperature (Cengel & Boles Table A-4): Psat = 9.5953 kPa at 45 °C and 12.352 kPa at 50 °C. Interpolating: Tdp = 45 + 5 × (9.727 − 9.5953)/(12.352 − 9.5953) = 45 + 5 × 0.0478 = 45.2 °C.

Sanity check: gasoline engines run near AF ≈ 15 at stoichiometric, so 22.6 for 50% excess air is the right size; a dew point in the 40s (°C) is why cold exhaust pipes drip water on a winter morning.

Worked example 2: from a dry exhaust analysis back to the air-fuel ratio

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Methane is burned with an unknown amount of air. A dry analysis of the products gives 9.17% CO2, 4.59% O2 and 86.24% N2 by volume, with no CO. Find the percent theoretical air and the air-fuel ratio.

  1. Take 100 kmol of dry products as the basis and let x kmol of CH4 and a kmol of O2 (with 3.76 a N2) have produced them, plus b kmol of H2O that the analyser removed: x CH4 + a (O2 + 3.76 N2) → 9.17 CO2 + 4.59 O2 + 86.24 N2 + b H2O.
  2. Carbon balance: x = 9.17 kmol CH4.
  3. Nitrogen balance: 3.76 a = 86.24, so a = 22.94 kmol O2.
  4. Hydrogen balance: 4x = 2b, so b = 2 × 9.17 = 18.34 kmol H2O.
  5. Oxygen check (atoms): in, 2 × 22.94 = 45.88; out, 2 × 9.17 + 2 × 4.59 + 18.34 = 45.86. The balance closes to rounding, which confirms the analysis is self-consistent and there is no CO.
  6. Per kmol of fuel: divide by x: a / x = 22.94 / 9.17 = 2.50 kmol O2 per kmol CH4. Theoretical is ath = 1 + 4/4 = 2. Percent theoretical air = 100 × 2.50 / 2 = 125% (25% excess air, φ = 0.80).
  7. Air-fuel ratio: AF = 2.50 × 4.76 × 28.97 / 16.04 = 21.5 kg air / kg fuel (stoichiometric methane is 2 × 4.76 × 28.97 / 16.04 = 17.2 kg/kg).

Sanity check: 4.59% free O2 in dry flue gas corresponds to roughly a quarter more air than needed, which is the typical excess for a gas boiler; the nitrogen balance is the key step because N2 is the one species that only comes from the air.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Mixing molar and mass ratios. A balanced equation gives kmol of air per kmol of fuel (59.5 for octane). Reported AF ratios are kg per kg (15.1 for octane). Never quote a molar ratio as an AF ratio, and always multiply by 28.97/Mfuel, not by 32/Mfuel (oxygen only) and not by 3.76 × 28.97 (nitrogen only).

Wet versus dry mole fractions. The dew point uses the mole fraction of H2O in the wet products (denominator includes the water). An Orsat analysis is dry: its percentages have the water removed, so the denominator excludes it. Using the dry total in the dew-point calculation overstates Pv and the dew point by several degrees.

Percent theoretical air versus percent excess air. 150% theoretical is 50% excess; 200% theoretical is 100% excess. If a question says 20% excess air, the multiplier is 1.20, not 0.20.

Forgetting that unused O2 appears in the products. With excess air the products carry (a − ath) kmol of O2; leaving it out breaks the oxygen balance and the total-moles count used for the dew point.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Balancing is a linear system: unknown coefficients times an atom matrix equals zero. A four-species combustion is a tiny numpy solve, and a whole fuel table can be processed at once with a dataframe whose columns are C, H, O atom counts: ath = C + H/4 − O/2, AFst = 4.76 ath × 28.97 / M. Build that table once (methane 17.2, propane 15.6, octane 15.1 kg/kg) and you will instantly recognise an answer that is off by a factor of 3.76 or 4.76.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

Three question types account for nearly all of the marks on this section: (1) balance a fuel with a given percent theoretical or excess air and report AF, the product composition and the dew point; (2) run the balance backwards from a dry product analysis to find percent theoretical air and AF, including the case where CO is present; (3) a short conceptual item on the meaning of φ, lean/rich, complete versus theoretical combustion, or why the analysis is on a dry basis.

Working habits that score: write the equation per 1 kmol of fuel, balance C, H, O, N in that order, do an oxygen-atom check before going on, and state the basis (wet or dry, molar or mass) beside every ratio you report.

This lesson lets you put an enthalpy on every reactant and product of a combustion reaction, so that the first law can be applied across a flame the same way it was applied across a turbine or a boiler. You will use the enthalpy of formation, add the sensible enthalpy from the ideal-gas tables, compute the enthalpy of combustion and the two heating values of a fuel, and find the heat released by a steady-flow burner and by a rigid combustion bomb. In the degree this is where the first law (chapters 3 and 5) meets chemistry; the flame-temperature and exergy calculations of the next lesson are the same energy balance solved for a different unknown.

Why the ordinary property tables are not enough

Every property table you have used so far picks an arbitrary zero: steam tables set u = 0 for saturated liquid at the triple point, the ideal-gas tables set h = 0 at 0 K. That is harmless when the substance stays the same substance, because only differences matter. In a reaction the substances change: CH4 and O2 go in, CO2 and H2O come out, and if each has its own private zero the difference Hproducts − Hreactants is meaningless. Chemists solved this by agreeing on one common reference for all substances, the standard reference state, 25 °C (298.15 K) and 1 atm, and by giving each compound an enthalpy at that state that measures the energy locked in its chemical bonds relative to the elements it is made from.

📘 DEFINITION

The enthalpy of formation h̄f° of a compound is the enthalpy change when one kmol of the compound is formed from its elements, each element in its most stable form, with reactants and product all at the standard reference state of 25 °C and 1 atm. By convention the enthalpy of formation of every stable element in its natural form (O2, N2, H2, C as graphite) is zero. A negative h̄f° means heat is released when the compound is formed (an exothermic formation, as for CO2 and H2O); a positive one means energy must be supplied (endothermic, as for acetylene C2H2, +226,730 kJ/kmol).

The bar over a symbol (h̄, s̄) means a molar quantity, per kmol, which is the natural unit for reactions because balanced equations are written in kmol.

The values used in this chapter are the standard ones tabulated in Cengel & Boles, Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach, Table A-26 (enthalpy of formation, Gibbs function of formation and absolute entropy at 25 °C, 1 atm), which are drawn from the JANAF thermochemical tables. All are in kJ/kmol:

SubstanceFormulah̄f° (kJ/kmol)
Carbon (graphite), oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogenC(s), O2(g), N2(g), H2(g)0
Carbon dioxideCO2(g)−393,520
Carbon monoxideCO(g)−110,530
Water vapourH2O(g)−241,820
Liquid waterH2O(l)−285,830
MethaneCH4(g)−74,850
PropaneC3H8(g)−103,850
Octane (liquid)C8H18(l)−249,950
Octane (vapour)C8H18(g)−208,450

Two things to notice. Liquid and vapour water differ by 285,830 − 241,820 = 44,010 kJ/kmol, which is the enthalpy of vaporisation of water at 25 °C (2442 kJ/kg × 18.015 kg/kmol). And liquid and vapour octane differ by 41,500 kJ/kmol, its enthalpy of vaporisation. The phase of the fuel and of the product water must always be stated, because the number changes.

Enthalpy at any temperature: formation plus sensible

🧮 KEY EQUATION

h̄(T, P) = h̄f° + (h̄T − h̄298)

h̄(T, P) is the enthalpy of one kmol of the substance at the state of interest (kJ/kmol); h̄f° is its enthalpy of formation at 25 °C, 1 atm (kJ/kmol); h̄T − h̄298 is the sensible enthalpy change from 298 K to T, read from the ideal-gas tables on a molar basis (Cengel & Boles Tables A-18 to A-23 for N2, O2, CO2, CO, H2 and H2O) or, for a fuel with no table, from c̄p(T − 298). For an ideal gas the pressure does not enter. The 298 K entries of those tables (N2 8669, O2 8682, CO2 9364, H2O 9904 kJ/kmol) are not zero because the tables count from 0 K, which is exactly why the subtraction is needed.

H = Σ Ni [h̄f° + h̄T − h̄298]i

The enthalpy of a stream or a mixture of reactants or products is the sum over species i of the kmol Ni of each (per kmol of fuel) times its molar enthalpy. Reactants and products are summed separately.

Example of the bookkeeping: CO2 at 1000 K has h̄ = −393,520 + (42,769 − 9364) = −360,115 kJ/kmol, still strongly negative because the chemical term dwarfs the sensible term. For the mixtures of ideal gases in combustion each component is at its own partial pressure, but since ideal-gas enthalpy does not depend on pressure the mixture enthalpy is just the sum of the component enthalpies.

Enthalpy of combustion and heating values

📘 DEFINITION

The enthalpy of combustion hC of a fuel is Hproducts − Hreactants for complete combustion at a given temperature and pressure, usually 25 °C and 1 atm; it is negative. The heating value HV is the same quantity with the sign flipped, the heat released per unit of fuel. The higher heating value HHV counts the water in the products as liquid (its latent heat has been recovered); the lower heating value LHV counts it as vapour. HHV − LHV = (kmol of H2O per kmol fuel) × 44,010 kJ/kmol, converted to the fuel basis being used.

📊 FIGURE — Heat released by burning methane: LHV and HHV as enthalpy drops
Left: the steady-flow energy balance. Right: reactants and products at 25 °C on one enthalpy scale; the drop is the heat released, larger when the product water leaves as liquid (HHV).

hC = Σ Np h̄f,p° − Σ Nr h̄f,r° (at 25 °C, 1 atm) HHV = −hC with H2O(l), LHV = −hC with H2O(g)

Np and Nr are the stoichiometric kmol of each product and reactant per kmol of fuel; the h̄f° are the table values above. At 25 °C the sensible terms all vanish, so the enthalpy of combustion is purely a combination of formation enthalpies. Nitrogen, excess oxygen and any other inert drop out because their h̄f° is zero and they appear identically on both sides.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Find the enthalpy of combustion of methane at 25 °C and 1 atm, and its higher and lower heating values per kg.

  1. Reaction (air not needed for this calculation): CH4 + 2 O2 → CO2 + 2 H2O.
  2. Products as liquid water: hC = [1 × (−393,520) + 2 × (−285,830)] − [1 × (−74,850) + 2 × 0] = −393,520 − 571,660 + 74,850 = −890,330 kJ/kmol CH4.
  3. HHV per kg: MCH4 = 12.011 + 4 × 1.008 = 16.043 kg/kmol; HHV = 890,330 / 16.043 = 55,500 kJ/kg.
  4. Products as vapour: hC = [−393,520 + 2 × (−241,820)] + 74,850 = −802,310 kJ/kmol; LHV = 802,310 / 16.043 = 50,010 kJ/kg.
  5. Check the difference: HHV − LHV = 88,020 kJ/kmol = 2 kmol H2O × 44,010 kJ/kmol, as it must be; per kg of fuel that is 5,490 kJ/kg, about 10% of the heating value, which is what a condensing boiler can recover and a conventional one sends up the flue.

Sanity check: natural-gas heating values are quoted around 50 to 55 MJ/kg, the highest of any hydrocarbon because methane has the most hydrogen per carbon; a value near 45 MJ/kg would suggest an octane-type fuel, and one near 30 MJ/kg an alcohol.

The first law for a steady-flow reacting system

A burner, furnace, gas-turbine combustor or boiler is a steady-flow device with a chemical change inside. Nothing about the first law changes; only the enthalpies now carry the formation term. With kinetic and potential energy neglected and everything per kmol of fuel:

🧮 KEY EQUATION

Qnet,in − Wnet,out = Σ Np [h̄f° + h̄T − h̄298]p − Σ Nr [h̄f° + h̄T − h̄298]r = HP − HR

Qnet,in is the heat transferred into the combustion chamber per kmol of fuel (kJ/kmol fuel; a negative value is heat lost or delivered to a boiler); Wnet,out the work delivered (zero for a plain burner); HP the enthalpy of the product stream and HR that of the reactant streams, each evaluated at its own temperature. If the products are hotter than 25 °C their sensible terms are positive and less heat comes out; if the air is preheated HR rises and more heat comes out.

Q − W = Σ Np [h̄f° + h̄T − h̄298 − P v̄]p − Σ Nr [h̄f° + h̄T − h̄298 − P v̄]r

For a closed system (a rigid bomb or a piston-cylinder) the first law is in internal energy, and ū = h̄ − P v̄. For an ideal gas P v̄ = Ru T with Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K; for a liquid or solid the P v̄ term is negligible. The correction only matters when the number of kmol of gas changes across the reaction.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Propane gas at 25 °C is burned steadily and completely with 100% theoretical air, also at 25 °C, in a furnace. The products leave at 1000 K. Find the heat delivered by the furnace per kmol and per kg of propane. (Ideal-gas molar enthalpies at 298 K / 1000 K from Cengel & Boles Tables A-18, A-20, A-23: N2 8669 / 30,129; CO2 9364 / 42,769; H2O 9904 / 35,882 kJ/kmol.)

  1. Balance: ath = 3 + 8/4 = 5. C3H8 + 5 (O2 + 3.76 N2) → 3 CO2 + 4 H2O + 18.8 N2. No O2 is left over.
  2. Reactants at 25 °C: every sensible term is zero and O2 and N2 have h̄f° = 0, so HR = 1 × (−103,850) = −103,850 kJ/kmol fuel.
  3. Products at 1000 K, term by term: CO2: 3 × [−393,520 + 42,769 − 9364] = 3 × (−360,115) = −1,080,345 kJ. H2O (vapour at 1000 K): 4 × [−241,820 + 35,882 − 9904] = 4 × (−215,842) = −863,368 kJ. N2: 18.8 × [0 + 30,129 − 8669] = 18.8 × 21,460 = 403,448 kJ.
  4. Sum: HP = −1,080,345 − 863,368 + 403,448 = −1,540,265 kJ/kmol fuel.
  5. First law with W = 0: Qin = HP − HR = −1,540,265 − (−103,850) = −1,436,415 kJ/kmol fuel. The negative sign means heat leaves the furnace: Qout = 1,436,000 kJ per kmol of propane.
  6. Per kg: MC3H8 = 3 × 12.011 + 8 × 1.008 = 44.10 kg/kmol; Qout = 1,436,415 / 44.10 = 32,570 kJ/kg fuel.

Sanity check: the LHV of propane from the same table is 2,043,990 kJ/kmol (46,350 kJ/kg), so the furnace delivers 1,436,415 / 2,043,990 = 70% of the fuel energy and sends the other 30% out of the stack as sensible heat in 1000 K products, which is the right order for an uninsulated, un-recuperated furnace. Preheating the air to 500 K (N2 14,581, O2 14,770 kJ/kmol) raises HR to −103,850 + 5 × (14,770 − 8682) + 18.8 × (14,581 − 8669) = +37,736 kJ/kmol and the heat output to 1,578,000 kJ/kmol, a 10% gain, which is why recuperators exist.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A rigid, well-cooled vessel contains 1 kmol of H2 and 0.5 kmol of O2 at 25 °C. The mixture is ignited and the products are brought back to 25 °C, at which point the water is liquid. Find the heat removed.

  1. Reaction: H2 + 0.5 O2 → H2O(l). Closed system, W = 0 (rigid), so Q = UP − UR with ū = h̄ − P v̄.
  2. Enthalpy part: HP − HR = 1 × (−285,830) − (0 + 0) = −285,830 kJ.
  3. P v̄ part: reactants are 1.5 kmol of ideal gas: Σ Nr P v̄ = 1.5 × Ru T = 1.5 × 8.314 × 298.15 = 3718 kJ. The product is liquid, so Σ Np P v̄ ≈ 0.
  4. Combine: Q = (HP − Σ Np P v̄) − (HR − Σ Nr P v̄) = (−285,830 − 0) − (0 − 3718) = −282,112 kJ per kmol H2, i.e. 282,100 kJ of heat is removed (139,900 kJ per kg of H2).

Sanity check: the constant-volume heat is 1.3% less than the constant-pressure value 285,830 kJ because at constant pressure the atmosphere does 3718 kJ of work on the shrinking gas, and that work shows up as extra heat out; a bomb calorimeter measures the ΔU number and the tables convert it to the ΔH heating value.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Forgetting to subtract h̄298. The ideal-gas tables start from 0 K, so h̄T alone is not the sensible enthalpy above 25 °C; CO2 at 1000 K is −393,520 + 42,769 − 9364, not −393,520 + 42,769. The error is 9364 kJ per kmol of CO2 and it accumulates over every species.

Wrong phase of water. Products hot enough to be gaseous (any furnace exhaust) carry H2O(g), −241,820. Only when the products are cooled below the dew point may some water be liquid, and then only the condensed fraction gets −285,830. Using the liquid value for hot products overstates the heat release by 44,010 kJ per kmol of water.

Sign of the enthalpy of combustion. hC is negative (products have less enthalpy than reactants); the heating value is its magnitude. A first-law answer with Qin negative simply means the heat flows out; report it as Qout positive with a clear direction.

Per kmol versus per kg. Table A-26 is per kmol; heating values in fuel data sheets are per kg. Divide by the fuel molar mass, and by the fuel's, not the product's.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Formation enthalpies are a lookup table and a reaction is a vector of stoichiometric coefficients (negative for reactants, positive for products). The enthalpy of combustion is the dot product of the two, and the sensible correction is a second dot product against the interpolated table column at T. A pandas frame indexed by species with columns h_f, h_298 and an interpolator for h(T) turns every example in this chapter into three lines, and lets you plot Qout against product temperature to see the linear fall-off that a furnace designer trades against.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

Expect one full first-law problem: fuel and air states given (often preheated air, sometimes a liquid fuel, sometimes excess air), product temperature given, find the heat transfer per kmol or per kg of fuel, or per kg of air. Expect one short calculation of an enthalpy of combustion or HHV/LHV from formation enthalpies, and a conceptual item on the reference state, on why elements have zero h̄f°, or on which heating value a condensing boiler or an engine test uses.

Method that scores: balance first, tabulate species with columns N, h̄f°, h̄298, h̄T, then N × (sum), for reactants and products separately; state the phase of water; keep every number per kmol of fuel until the last line; quote the table used.
