This lesson lets you find the highest temperature a flame can reach, explain what excess air and dissociation do to it, and then turn the second law on a combustion process: assign an absolute entropy to every species with the third law, compute the entropy generated and the exergy destroyed, and see in numbers why burning fuel, the step at the heart of every power plant, is also its biggest single loss. In the degree this closes the first-law story of the previous lesson and connects the reactions block to the exergy chapter; the equilibrium chapter that follows explains the dissociation only mentioned here.

The adiabatic flame temperature in plain words

In the furnace example of lesson 2 the products left at 1000 K because the furnace took heat away. Insulate the chamber perfectly and take no work out, and all of the energy released by the reaction has nowhere to go except into the products themselves: their temperature rises until their enthalpy, formation plus sensible, equals the enthalpy of the reactants that came in. That temperature is the adiabatic flame temperature. It is the theoretical ceiling for the combustion chamber, so it drives the choice of materials and cooling for combustors and furnace walls.

📘 DEFINITION

The adiabatic flame temperature Tad is the temperature of the products when a fuel is burned in a steady-flow chamber with no heat transfer, no work, and negligible changes in kinetic and potential energy. For a given fuel it is highest with theoretical air and complete combustion; excess air, incomplete combustion, dissociation of the products and heat losses all lower it, while preheating the air or the fuel raises it.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

HP = HR → Σ Np [h̄f° + h̄Tad − h̄298]p = Σ Nr [h̄f° + h̄T − h̄298]r

The symbols are those of the first law in lesson 2 with Q = 0 and W = 0: Np, Nr are the kmol of each product and reactant per kmol of fuel, h̄f° the enthalpies of formation, h̄T − h̄298 the sensible enthalpies from the ideal-gas tables in kJ/kmol. The unknown Tad is buried inside every h̄T on the left, so the equation cannot be solved in closed form: you move all the known numbers to the right, then hunt for the temperature at which the left-hand sum of table values matches, bracket it between two table rows and interpolate.

A fast first guess: treat all the products as if they were N2 (the majority species), so Σ Np h̄N2(T) ≈ right-hand side gives an estimate of h̄N2(T) and a starting row in the nitrogen table. The true Tad is a little lower, because CO2 and H2O hold more enthalpy per kmol than N2.

Worked example: liquid octane, theoretical air and 400% theoretical air

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Liquid octane enters an insulated steady-flow combustor at 25 °C and is burned completely with air at 25 °C. Find the adiabatic flame temperature for (a) 100% theoretical air and (b) 400% theoretical air. Formation enthalpies (Cengel & Boles Table A-26, kJ/kmol): C8H18(l) −249,950; CO2 −393,520; H2O(g) −241,820. Ideal-gas molar enthalpies (Tables A-18 to A-23, kJ/kmol): at 298 K, N2 8669, O2 8682, CO2 9364, H2O 9904; at 2350 K, CO2 122,091, H2O 100,846, N2 77,496; at 2400 K, CO2 125,152, H2O 103,508, N2 79,320; at 900 K, CO2 37,405, H2O 31,828, O2 27,928, N2 26,890; at 1000 K, CO2 42,769, H2O 35,882, O2 31,389, N2 30,129.

📊 FIGURE — Adiabatic flame temperature of octane by trial and interpolation
Each panel: the product enthalpy at two trial temperatures brackets the target set by the reactants; interpolation gives T ad. Four times the air spreads the same heat and drops T ad from 2394.5 K to 962 K.
  1. (a) Balance with theoretical air: ath = 8 + 18/4 = 12.5 kmol O2/kmol fuel, and 12.5 × 3.76 = 47 kmol N2/kmol fuel. C8H18(l) + 12.5 (O2 + 3.76 N2) → 8 CO2 + 9 H2O + 47 N2 (all in kmol per kmol fuel).
  2. Reactant enthalpy: everything enters at 25 °C, so HR = 1 × (−249,950) = −249,950 kJ/kmol fuel.
  3. Product enthalpy as a function of Tad: HP = 8 [−393,520 + h̄CO2 − 9364] + 9 [−241,820 + h̄H2O − 9904] + 47 [h̄N2 − 8669].
  4. Move the known numbers to the right: 8 h̄CO2 + 9 h̄H2O + 47 h̄N2 = −249,950 + 8 × 393,520 + 9 × 241,820 + 8 × 9364 + 9 × 9904 + 47 × 8669 = −249,950 + 3,148,160 + 2,176,380 + 74,912 + 89,136 + 407,443 = 5,646,081 kJ/kmol fuel.
  5. First guess (all products as N2): 8 + 9 + 47 = 64 kmol of products, so h̄N2 ≈ 5,646,081 kJ / 64 kmol = 88,220 kJ/kmol, which the nitrogen table puts above 2400 K (79,320). The true value is lower, so try 2400 K first.
  6. Trial at 2400 K: 8 × 125,152 + 9 × 103,508 + 47 × 79,320 = 1,001,216 + 931,572 + 3,728,040 = 5,660,828 kJ/kmol fuel, slightly above the target, so Tad < 2400 K.
  7. Trial at 2350 K: 8 × 122,091 + 9 × 100,846 + 47 × 77,496 = 976,728 + 907,614 + 3,642,312 = 5,526,654 kJ/kmol fuel, below the target. The answer is bracketed.
  8. Interpolate: Tad = 2350 K + 50 K × (5,646,081 − 5,526,654)/(5,660,828 − 5,526,654) = 2350 K + 50 K × 119,427/134,174 = 2350 K + 44.5 K = 2394.5 K ≈ 2395 K (about 2121 °C).
  9. (b) Balance with 400% theoretical air: a = 4 × 12.5 = 50 kmol O2/kmol fuel and 50 × 3.76 = 188 kmol N2/kmol fuel: C8H18(l) + 50 (O2 + 3.76 N2) → 8 CO2 + 9 H2O + 37.5 O2 + 188 N2. HR is the same −249,950 kJ/kmol fuel.
  10. New right-hand side: the extra 37.5 O2 and 141 N2 add their 298 K table values: 5,646,081 + 37.5 × 8682 + 141 × 8669 = 5,646,081 + 325,575 + 1,222,329 = 7,193,985 kJ/kmol fuel, to be matched by 8 h̄CO2 + 9 h̄H2O + 37.5 h̄O2 + 188 h̄N2.
  11. Trial at 1000 K: 8 × 42,769 + 9 × 35,882 + 37.5 × 31,389 + 188 × 30,129 = 342,152 + 322,938 + 1,177,088 + 5,664,252 = 7,506,430 kJ/kmol fuel (too high). At 900 K: 8 × 37,405 + 9 × 31,828 + 37.5 × 27,928 + 188 × 26,890 = 299,240 + 286,452 + 1,047,300 + 5,055,320 = 6,688,312 kJ/kmol fuel (too low).
  12. Interpolate: Tad = 900 K + 100 K × (7,193,985 − 6,688,312)/(7,506,430 − 6,688,312) = 900 K + 100 K × 505,673/818,118 = 900 K + 61.8 K = 962 K (about 689 °C).

Sanity check: Cengel & Boles (Chapter 15, the liquid-octane adiabatic-flame example) report the same 962 K for 400% theoretical air and 2395 K for theoretical air; quadrupling the air spreads the same heat over roughly four times the mass of gas and drops the temperature to just under 1000 K, which is the range gas-turbine combustors deliberately operate in so that the turbine blades survive.

What pulls the real flame temperature down: excess air, dissociation, losses

The 2395 K above is an upper bound and a real flame does not reach it, for three reasons. First, excess air: the surplus O2 and N2 absorb sensible heat without contributing any, so Tad falls steadily as the percent theoretical air rises; the example spans 2395 K to 962 K. Second, incomplete combustion: with less than theoretical air some carbon stops at CO, releasing 282,990 kJ/kmol less than going all the way to CO2 (393,520 − 110,530), so the flame is cooler on the rich side as well; the peak sits at or very slightly rich of stoichiometric. Third, dissociation: at the temperatures of a near-stoichiometric flame the products themselves begin to fall apart, CO2 into CO and O2, H2O into H2, OH, H and O, and N2 and O2 into NO. Dissociation is endothermic, it re-absorbs part of the heat of reaction, and it is the reason the equilibrium flame temperature of a stoichiometric hydrocarbon-air flame comes out around a hundred kelvin below the no-dissociation value (the verified methane figures below). The equilibrium chapter computes the dissociated composition; here you need only the direction and rough size of the effect. Real combustors also lose heat through their walls and by radiation.

✅ VERIFIED

For a stoichiometric methane-air mixture entering at 298.15 K and 1 atm, a published calculation with NASA CEA and Cantera gives an adiabatic flame temperature of 2326 K for complete combustion to CO2, H2O and N2, the method of this lesson, and 2224 K at chemical equilibrium with dissociation included: dissociation costs about 102 K. Source: O. A. Marzouk, adiabatic flame temperatures computed with NASA CEARUN, arxiv.org/pdf/2503.11826.

The third law and absolute entropy

For the second law the same reference-state problem returns, and it is solved more elegantly. Entropy, unlike enthalpy, has a natural zero:

📘 DEFINITION

The third law of thermodynamics: the entropy of a pure crystalline substance at absolute zero temperature is zero. Because every substance then starts from the same zero, entropies measured from it are absolute entropies, and they can be compared and subtracted across a chemical reaction without any convention about elements. Table A-26 lists the absolute entropy s̄° at 25 °C and 1 atm (kJ/kmol·K): C(s) 5.74, O2 205.04, N2 191.61, CO2 213.80, H2O(g) 188.83, H2O(l) 69.92. The ideal-gas tables give s̄°(T) at other temperatures, still at 1 atm.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

s̄i(T, Pi) = s̄i°(T) − Ru ln (yi Pm / P0)

s̄i is the entropy of species i in the mixture (kJ/kmol·K); s̄i°(T) its absolute entropy at temperature T and the reference pressure P0 = 1 atm, from the tables; Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K; yi its mole fraction in the mixture; Pm the mixture pressure. The product yi Pm is the partial pressure of i; the logarithm is the ideal-gas pressure correction. Because yi < 1 the correction is positive: a gas spread through a mixture has more entropy than alone at the mixture pressure. For a solid or liquid the pressure term is dropped.

Sgen = SP − SR + Qout/Tsurr Xdestroyed = T0 Sgen Wrev = Σ Nr (h̄ − T0 s̄)r − Σ Np (h̄ − T0 s̄)p

SP and SR are Σ N s̄ over products and reactants (kJ/kmol fuel·K); Qout the heat rejected to surroundings at Tsurr (for an adiabatic combustor this term is zero); T0 the dead-state temperature, 298.15 K here; Xdestroyed the exergy destroyed (kJ/kmol fuel); Wrev the reversible work, the most work the reaction could have produced. When reactants and products are all at T0, h̄ − T0 s̄ is the Gibbs function ḡ and Wrev = −ΔG = Σ Nr ḡf,r° − Σ Np ḡf,p° using the tabulated Gibbs functions of formation. In any process with no actual work, Xdestroyed = Wrev: the whole work potential is thrown away.

Worked example: entropy generation and exergy destruction in burning carbon

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Carbon (graphite) at 25 °C burns steadily and completely with theoretical air at 25 °C and 1 atm; the products are cooled back to 25 °C and 1 atm, the heat going to surroundings at 25 °C. Per kmol of carbon find the heat rejected, the entropy generated, the exergy destroyed and the reversible work.

  1. Balance: C + (O2 + 3.76 N2) → CO2 + 3.76 N2. Reactant gas is 4.76 kmol of air per kmol C; products are 4.76 kmol of gas per kmol C.
  2. First law (everything at 25 °C, no sensible terms): Qin = HP − HR = 1 × (−393,520) − 0 = −393,520 kJ, so Qout = 393,520 kJ/kmol C.
  3. Mole fractions and pressure corrections: yO2 = 1/4.76 = 0.2101, yN2 = 3.76/4.76 = 0.7899, and in the products yCO2 = 0.2101, yN2 = 0.7899 (same moles). With Pm = P0: −Ru ln 0.2101 = −8.314 kJ/kmol·K × (−1.560) = +12.97 kJ/kmol·K; −Ru ln 0.7899 = −8.314 kJ/kmol·K × (−0.2358) = +1.96 kJ/kmol·K.
  4. Reactant entropies (kJ/kmol·K): C(s): 5.74. O2: 205.04 + 12.97 = 218.01. N2: 191.61 + 1.96 = 193.57, times 3.76 kmol = 727.83 kJ/K. SR = 5.74 + 218.01 + 727.83 = 951.58 kJ/kmol C·K.
  5. Product entropies (kJ/kmol·K): CO2: 213.80 + 12.97 = 226.77. N2: 727.83 kJ/K as before. SP = 954.60 kJ/kmol C·K. The reaction itself changes the entropy of the matter by only SP − SR = +3.02 kJ/kmol·K.
  6. Entropy generation: Sgen = SP − SR + Qout/Tsurr = 3.02 kJ/kmol·K + 393,520 kJ/kmol / 298.15 K = 3.02 + 1319.87 = 1322.9 kJ/kmol C·K. Almost all of it is the heat dumped into the surroundings at 25 °C.
  7. Exergy destroyed: Xdestroyed = T0 Sgen = 298.15 K × 1322.9 kJ/kmol·K = 394,420 kJ/kmol C, or 394,420 / 12.011 = 32,840 kJ per kg of carbon.
  8. Reversible work: no actual work was produced, so Wrev = Xdestroyed = 394,420 kJ/kmol C. Cross-check with the Gibbs function: the mixing terms cancel exactly here (CO2 leaves at the same mole fraction 0.2101 at which O2 entered, and the N2 is unchanged), so Wrev = −(ΔH − T0 ΔS°) = 393,520 kJ/kmol + 298.15 K × 3.02 kJ/kmol·K = 394,420 kJ/kmol. The tabulated ḡf°(CO2) = −394,360 kJ/kmol (Table A-26) gives 394,360 kJ/kmol, within 60 kJ (0.015%), which is rounding in the tabulated data.

Sanity check: the reversible work (394,420 kJ) slightly exceeds the heating value (393,520 kJ) because the reaction has a small positive entropy change and could in principle draw a little heat from the surroundings while producing work, as a fuel cell does; a real furnace produces none of it, so the entire work potential of the coal is destroyed the moment it is burned to make hot gas and the hot gas is cooled.

Why combustion is so irreversible

The carbon example is the extreme case: burning and cooling to ambient destroys 100% of the fuel exergy. An adiabatic combustor keeps part of it in the hot products, but still loses a large fraction, by mechanisms you know from the exergy chapter: (1) the chemical reaction itself runs across an enormous, uncontrolled difference in chemical potential, like discharging a battery through a short circuit instead of a motor; (2) the energy released heats the products through a temperature difference of thousands of kelvin, which is heat transfer across a finite ΔT on a grand scale; (3) fuel, air and products mix, and mixing generates entropy. This is the deepest reason even the best combined-cycle plants reach only about 60% and why fuel cells, which take the reaction along a controlled electrochemical path, can in principle exceed them: they avoid the combustion step altogether.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Iterating on the wrong side. If the trial temperature gives a product enthalpy sum larger than the right-hand side, Tad is lower, not higher. Write "too high" or "too low" beside every trial so the bracket is explicit before you interpolate.

Forgetting the excess air and nitrogen on the right-hand side. Excess O2 and all of the N2 contribute nothing to HR at 25 °C, but their 298 K table values do belong on the known side when you move h̄298 across, and their h̄T belongs on the trial side. Dropping them makes the flame impossibly hot.

Entropy at 1 atm instead of at the partial pressure. Using s̄° straight from the table for every gas in a mixture omits the −Ru ln yi term; in the carbon example that is 12.97 kJ/kmol·K for the oxygen alone. The correction is also needed when the mixture pressure differs from 1 atm.

Treating the reaction entropy change as the entropy generation. SP − SR was only 3 kJ/kmol·K; the generation was 1323 kJ/kmol·K because of the heat rejected. For an adiabatic flame the Q term is zero and Sgen is exactly SP(Tad) − SR, evaluated with the high-temperature s̄° values.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

The adiabatic flame temperature problem is the single most predictable long question in this chapter: a fuel (often liquid, sometimes with air preheated), a stated percent theoretical air, find Tad by bracketing between two table rows and interpolating. Marks go to the balance, the assembled right-hand side, both trials with a stated conclusion, and the interpolation. A follow-up often asks what happens to Tad with more excess air, with preheated air, or with dissociation.

The second-law question is shorter: entropy of a gas in a mixture at its partial pressure, Sgen and Xdestroyed for combustion at 25 °C, or the reversible work from Gibbs functions of formation; and a one-liner on the third law and why absolute entropies need no formation convention.

This lesson lets you answer the question the combustion chapter had to dodge: when products such as CO2 and H2O sit at 2,500 K, how much of them have fallen apart again into CO, H2, O2 and radicals? You will derive the criterion for chemical equilibrium (minimum Gibbs function at fixed T and P), turn it into the equilibrium constant KP for ideal-gas mixtures, read KP from a table, and solve for an equilibrium composition by hand. In the degree this sits right after combustion (Cengel & Boles chapter 16, Moran & Shapiro chapter 14) and feeds directly into the flame-temperature corrections of the next lesson.

\n\n

Equilibrium in plain words

\n

Take a rigid, insulated vessel, put in 2 kmol of CO and 1 kmol of O2, and light it. Chapter 14 (combustion) would say \"complete reaction gives 2 kmol CO2\". Real hot products disagree: at 2,600 K a measurable fraction of the CO2 is dissociated back into CO and O2. The mixture stops changing not when the reactants run out but when the forward and backward reactions run at the same rate. That resting point is chemical equilibrium, and thermodynamics tells you exactly where it is without any kinetics: the composition settles where the Gibbs function of the mixture, at the given T and P, is as low as it can be.

\n

Why the Gibbs function? The increase-of-entropy principle says any spontaneous change in an isolated system raises S. A reacting mixture held at constant T and P is not isolated, so the second law is rewritten in terms of a system-only property. From the first and second laws for a closed system at constant T and P, dGT,P ≤ 0: any spontaneous change at constant temperature and pressure must lower G, and the process stops when G cannot fall further.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Criterion for chemical equilibrium. A chemically reacting system at a fixed temperature T and pressure P is in equilibrium when its total Gibbs function G = H − TS is at a minimum: (dG)T,P = 0. Any composition change from that point would raise G, so none happens spontaneously.

For the general ideal-gas reaction νAA + νBB ⇌ νCC + νDD this becomes νCḡC + νDḡD − νAḡA − νBḡB = 0, where each ḡi (kJ/kmol) is the molar Gibbs function of component i at its own partial pressure in the mixture and νi is its stoichiometric coefficient.

\n\n

From the criterion to the equilibrium constant

\n

The criterion above is exact but not yet useful, because ḡi depends on the (unknown) composition. For an ideal gas the dependence is simple. At temperature T, the Gibbs function of component i at partial pressure Pi is

\n

ḡi(T, Pi) = ḡi*(T) + RuT ln Pi

\n

where ḡi*(T) (kJ/kmol) is the Gibbs function of pure i at 1 atm and temperature T, Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K, and Pi is in atmospheres (the \"1 atm\" reference is what makes the logarithm dimensionless). Substitute this into the criterion, collect the starred terms into one number and the logarithms into another:

\n

ΔG*(T) = νCḡC*(T) + νDḡD*(T) − νAḡA*(T) − νBḡB*(T)

\n

ΔG*(T) is the standard-state Gibbs function change of the reaction (kJ/kmol of reaction as written), a function of temperature only. The criterion then reads ΔG*(T) = −RuT ln[(PCνC PDνD)/(PAνA PBνB)], and the bracket is given a name.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Equilibrium constant of an ideal-gas reaction (Pi and P in atm, Ni in kmol):

KP = (PCνC · PDνD) / (PAνA · PBνB)

KP = exp[ −ΔG*(T) / (RuT) ]

KP = [(NCνC · NDνD) / (NAνA · NBνB)] · (P / Ntotal)Δν, Δν = νC + νD − νA − νB

Symbols: Pi = partial pressure of i (atm) = yiP; Ni = kmol of i present at equilibrium; Ntotal = kmol of everything in the mixture, including inert gases that take no part in the reaction; P = total mixture pressure (atm); T in kelvin; Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K; ΔG* in kJ/kmol. KP is dimensionless only because every pressure is measured in atmospheres.

\n

The third form is the one you actually solve with, because you count kmol, not partial pressures. It comes from Pi = yiP = (Ni/Ntotal)P. Three consequences of the definition are worth memorising:

\n
    \n
  • KP depends on T only (through ΔG*(T)), not on pressure or on how much inert gas is present.
    • \n
  • Write the reaction backwards and KP becomes 1/KP; double every coefficient and KP becomes KP2. The table is only useful if you match its stoichiometry.
    • \n
  • Large KP (say ln KP above +7, KP above 1,000) means the reaction goes essentially to completion; very small KP (ln KP below −7) means it essentially does not occur. In between, you must solve.
    • \n
\n\n

Reading the KP table

\n

Textbooks tabulate ln KP for a handful of dissociation reactions against temperature; in Cengel & Boles this is Table A-28, \"Natural logarithms of the equilibrium constant KP\", and Moran & Shapiro give log10K in Table A-27 (mind the base). The entries below are the ones used in this chapter's examples and quizzes. The 298 K entries can be recomputed from the Gibbs functions of formation in Table A-26: for CO2 ⇌ CO + ½O2, ΔG* = (−137,150) − (−394,360) = +257,210 kJ/kmol, so ln KP = −257,210 / (8.314 × 298.15) = −103.76, which reproduces the table.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
T (K)H2 ⇌ 2HH2O ⇌ H2 + ½O2CO2 ⇌ CO + ½O2½N2 + ½O2 ⇌ NO

\n

Reading the columns: every dissociation constant rises steeply with temperature (the next lesson explains why), and at 298 K they are absurdly small, ln KP = −92 for water means KP ≈ 10−40, so room-temperature water simply does not split. NO formation from air has a comparatively large constant even at 2,000 K, which is why engines make nitric oxide.

\n\n

Worked example: CO burning in excess oxygen at 2,600 K

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem. 2 kmol of CO and 3 kmol of O2 are heated to 2,600 K at 304 kPa. Assuming the equilibrium mixture contains only CO2, CO and O2, find its composition. (Cengel & Boles Example 16-3; numbers recomputed here.)

📊 FIGURE — Gibbs function of the CO + O2 mixture: equilibrium sits at its minimum
G of the whole mixture against how much CO2 has formed. G falls almost all the way, then turns up just before complete reaction; the lowest point, x = 1.906 kmol, is the equilibrium composition.
  1. Stoichiometric (complete) reaction: 2CO + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 2O2. Complete reaction would give 2 kmol CO2 and leave 2 kmol O2.
  2. Actual reaction with unknown x: 2CO + 3O2 → x CO2 + (2 − x) CO + (3 − x/2) O2. The carbon balance gives the CO term; the oxygen balance gives the O2 term (each kmol of CO2 formed consumes half a kmol of O2). Total moles Ntotal = x + (2 − x) + (3 − x/2) = 5 − x/2 kmol.
  3. Pick the table reaction. Table A-28 lists CO2 ⇌ CO + ½O2; at 2,600 K, ln KP = −2.801, so KP,diss = e−2.801 = 0.06075. The reaction we want, CO + ½O2 ⇌ CO2, is its reverse: KP = 1/0.06075 = 16.46 (dimensionless).
  4. Pressure in atm: P = 304 kPa / 101.325 kPa·atm−1 = 3.000 atm. Δν for CO + ½O2 → CO2 is 1 − 1 − ½ = −½.
  5. Write KP in terms of x: 16.46 = [x / ((2 − x)(3 − x/2)½)] · (3.000 / (5 − x/2))−½.
  6. Solve. This is nonlinear in x, so iterate or use a root finder (a bisection between x = 0 and x = 2 converges in a few steps). Try x = 1.9: left side [1.9/(0.1 × 2.05½)] × (3/4.05)−½ = 13.27 × 1.162 = 15.4, slightly below 16.46, so x must be a little larger. Root: x = 1.906 kmol.
  7. Composition: CO2 = 1.906 kmol, CO = 2 − 1.906 = 0.094 kmol, O2 = 3 − 0.953 = 2.047 kmol; Ntotal = 4.047 kmol. Mole fractions: yCO2 = 0.471, yCO = 0.023, yO2 = 0.506.
  8. Answer: 1.906 kmol CO2, 0.094 kmol CO, 2.047 kmol O2; about 4.7% of the CO stays unburned at equilibrium.

Sanity check: KP = 16 is large-ish, so the reaction should go nearly but not entirely to completion, and it does (95.3% of the CO converted). At 298 K the same KP would be e+103.8 and the residual CO would be zero to every decimal place.

\n\n

What temperature, pressure and inert gases do

\n

KP is fixed by T, but the composition also responds to pressure and dilution through the factor (P/Ntotal)Δν. The three rules, with numbers for 1 kmol of CO2 dissociating at 3,000 K (ln KP = −1.111, KP = 0.329, Δν = +½; α = fraction dissociated, so the mixture is (1 − α) CO2, α CO, α/2 O2, Ntotal = 1 + α/2):

\n
    \n
  • Temperature: raising T raises KP of every dissociation (endothermic) reaction, so more dissociation. At 2,000 K the same CO2 would have KP = e−6.635 = 0.0013 and barely dissociate at all.
    • \n
  • Pressure: for Δν > 0 (moles increase) higher pressure pushes the reaction back toward fewer moles. Computed: α = 0.675 at 0.1 atm, 0.437 at 1 atm, 0.241 at 10 atm. For Δν = 0 (e.g. ½N2 + ½O2 ⇌ NO) pressure has no effect at all.
    • \n
  • Inert gas: adding an inert gas at fixed total pressure raises Ntotal, which acts exactly like lowering the pressure. Adding 5 kmol of N2 to the 1 kmol of CO2 at 1 atm and 3,000 K raises α from 0.437 to 0.601. The N2 appears in Ntotal but nowhere else in the KP expression.
    • \n
\n

All three are Le Chatelier's principle in equation form: the system shifts in the direction that partly undoes the disturbance.

\n\n

Simultaneous reactions

\n

Real combustion products contain CO2, CO, H2O, H2, O2, OH, H, O, NO, N2 and more. The procedure scales: the number of independent KP equations you need equals (number of species) − (number of elements), and the elements supply the remaining balances. For products of CO2, CO, O2 and O (four species, two elements) you need two equilibrium relations, e.g. CO2 ⇌ CO + ½O2 and O2 ⇌ 2O, plus a carbon and an oxygen balance: four equations in four unknowns. Each KP is written with the same Ntotal that counts every species. By hand you solve two coupled nonlinear equations; in practice engineers use a Gibbs-minimisation code (NASA CEA, Cantera), which does exactly the same minimisation over all species at once.

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Using kPa in KP. The tabulated KP assumes partial pressures in atmospheres because the reference state is 1 atm. Feed P = 304 kPa into (P/Ntotal)Δν and every answer is wrong by a factor 101.325Δν. Convert first.

Forgetting Ntotal. Ntotal is the kmol of everything present at equilibrium: products, leftover reactants and inert nitrogen. Leaving out the 3.76 N2 per O2 in an air-fed problem changes the composition noticeably.

Using the table's KP for a reaction written the other way round or with different coefficients. Reversed reaction: 1/KP. Doubled coefficients: KP2. Halved: √KP. Check the stoichiometry line of the table before you lift a number.

\n
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

An equilibrium problem is a root-finding problem, and you already own the tool. Write the KP expression as f(x) = 0 and call scipy.optimize.brentq (or a five-line bisection) with a bracket such as (10−6, 1.9999). The worked example above converges to x = 1.9060 in microseconds, and you can then loop over pressure or temperature and plot α against P to see Le Chatelier instead of memorising it. For simultaneous reactions use scipy.optimize.fsolve on the vector of KP and element-balance equations.

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

The standard question gives reactants, a temperature and a pressure, names the species allowed in the products, and asks for the equilibrium composition. Full marks need: (1) the complete-reaction line, (2) the actual-reaction line with one unknown per independent reaction and element balances written out, (3) the table reaction identified and KP adjusted for direction and coefficient, (4) P converted to atm and Δν stated, (5) the solved composition with a plausibility comment.

Quick-fire variants: \"what happens to the amount of NO if pressure is doubled?\" (nothing, Δν = 0); \"how does adding argon at constant pressure affect dissociation?\" (increases it if Δν > 0); \"KP for the reverse reaction?\" (reciprocal); \"why does the answer not depend on kinetics?\" (equilibrium is a state, fixed by G minimisation).

"}, "THERMO/equil/s2": {"body": "

This lesson gives you the temperature dependence of KP and puts it to work. You will derive the van't Hoff equation, use two table entries to back out an enthalpy of reaction, solve a degree-of-dissociation problem for the temperature that produces a given split, and see why dissociation caps the adiabatic flame temperature that Chapter 14 over-predicted. In the degree sequence this is the second half of the chemical-equilibrium chapter (Cengel & Boles 16-4 and 16-5) and it is the part examiners like best, because one short equation links a table column to a physical quantity.

\n\n

Why KP climbs with temperature

\n

Every dissociation column in the KP table rises with T: for H2O ⇌ H2 + ½O2, ln KP goes from −92 at 298 K to −8.1 at 2,000 K and −3.1 at 3,000 K. The reason is buried in the definition. ln KP = −ΔG*(T)/(RuT) and ΔG* = ΔH* − TΔS*, so

📊 FIGURE — ln KP against 1/T is a straight line whose slope is −hR/Ru
Table A-28 values plotted against 1/T (T falls to the right). Each reaction lies on a line; the triangle is worked example 1 and the large dot worked example 2 (3,535 K).
\n

ln KP = −ΔH*/(RuT) + ΔS*/Ru

\n

Splitting a molecule costs energy (ΔH* = h̄R, the enthalpy of reaction, is positive for dissociation, about +251,700 kJ/kmol for water), so the first term is a large negative number that shrinks toward zero as T grows. The entropy term is positive (more particles, more disorder) and roughly constant. At low T the enthalpy term wins and KP is tiny; at high T the entropy term takes over and KP heads toward one and beyond. Differentiating the expression with respect to T, and allowing h̄R to be the enthalpy of reaction at the actual temperature, gives the exact form.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Enthalpy of reaction h̄R(T) (kJ/kmol of reaction as written): the enthalpy of the products minus that of the reactants when both are at temperature T and the reaction proceeds once as written. It is positive for endothermic (dissociation) reactions and negative for exothermic (combustion) reactions; reversing the reaction flips its sign.

Degree of dissociation α (dimensionless, 0 to 1): the fraction of the original kmol of a compound that has split at equilibrium. Starting from 1 kmol of AB dissociating as AB ⇌ A + B, the mixture holds (1 − α) AB, α A and α B, Ntotal = 1 + α.

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

The van't Hoff equation (differential and integrated forms):

d(ln KP)/dT = h̄R(T) / (RuT2)

ln(KP2/KP1) ≈ (h̄R/Ru) · (1/T1 − 1/T2)

Symbols: KP1, KP2 = equilibrium constants at absolute temperatures T1, T2 (K); h̄R = enthalpy of reaction (kJ/kmol), treated as constant over the interval in the integrated form; Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K. Because h̄R actually drifts slowly with T, the integrated form is an approximation that is excellent over a few hundred kelvin. Same shape as the Clapeyron-Clausius equation for vapour pressure, and for the same reason: both are Gibbs-function equalities differentiated along the equilibrium line.

\n

Two uses follow at once. Given h̄R and one KP, predict KP at another temperature (which is how the missing rows of a table are estimated). Given two KP values, back out h̄R, which turns a column of equilibrium data into a calorimetric quantity. The sign is a useful check: if KP increases with T, h̄R must be positive (endothermic), which is Le Chatelier again.

\n\n

Worked example 1: enthalpy of reaction from two table entries

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem. Estimate the enthalpy of reaction h̄R for the combustion H2 + ½O2 → H2O at 2,000 K using KP data, and compare with the value from enthalpy tables (Cengel & Boles Example 16-6, recomputed).

  1. Bracket 2,000 K with two table rows. Table A-28 lists the dissociation H2O ⇌ H2 + ½O2: ln KP = −9.826 at T1 = 1,800 K and −6.768 at T2 = 2,200 K. Our reaction is the reverse, so ln KP1 = +9.826 and ln KP2 = +6.768 (dimensionless).
  2. Rearrange van't Hoff: h̄R = Ru · ln(KP2/KP1) / (1/T1 − 1/T2).
  3. Numerator: 8.314 kJ/kmol·K × (6.768 − 9.826) = 8.314 × (−3.058) = −25.42 kJ/kmol·K.
  4. Denominator: 1/1800 K − 1/2200 K = 5.5556 × 10−4 − 4.5455 × 10−4 = 1.0101 × 10−4 K−1.
  5. Divide: h̄R = −25.42 / 1.0101 × 10−4 = −251,700 kJ/kmol (of H2 burned, at about 2,000 K).
  6. Compare. Evaluating h̄R = Σ Np(h̄f° + h̄ − h̄°)p − Σ Nr(h̄f° + h̄ − h̄°)r directly from the ideal-gas enthalpy tables at 2,000 K gives −251,663 kJ/kmol (Cengel & Boles), a difference of 0.01%.

Sanity check: the 298 K value (the enthalpy of formation of steam) is −241,820 kJ/kmol; the reaction releases slightly more per kmol at 2,000 K because the products' cp rises less than the reactants' between 298 K and 2,000 K. Sign negative because combustion is exothermic and KP for combustion falls with temperature. Plausible.

\n\n

Degree of dissociation

\n

Dissociation problems start from a known amount of one compound and ask how much has split at given T and P, or the reverse: at what T does a given fraction split. Set up the mixture with α, count Ntotal, and write KP. For a diatomic gas X2 ⇌ 2X starting from 1 kmol:

\n

KP = (2α)2/(1 − α) · (P/(1 + α))1

\n

with NX = 2α, NX2 = 1 − α, Ntotal = 1 + α, Δν = 2 − 1 = 1, P in atm. For the forward problem (T and P known) solve the quadratic in α; for the reverse problem (α and P known) evaluate KP, take its logarithm and interpolate the table for T.

\n

Worked example 2: the temperature for 10% dissociation of hydrogen

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem. At what temperature does 10 percent of diatomic hydrogen dissociate into monatomic hydrogen at a pressure of 10 atm? (Cengel & Boles Example 16-4, recomputed.)

  1. Mixture at equilibrium from 1 kmol H2 with α = 0.10: NH2 = 0.90 kmol, NH = 2 × 0.10 = 0.20 kmol, Ntotal = 1.10 kmol.
  2. Δν for H2 ⇌ 2H is 2 − 1 = 1; P = 10 atm (already in atm).
  3. KP = (0.20)2/0.90 × (10/1.10)1 = 0.04444 × 9.0909 = 0.4040 (dimensionless).
  4. Logarithm: ln KP = ln 0.4040 = −0.9062.
  5. Interpolate Table A-28, column H2 ⇌ 2H: ln KP = −1.516 at 3,400 K and −0.609 at 3,600 K. T = 3400 K + 200 K × (−0.9062 − (−1.516)) / (−0.609 − (−1.516)) = 3400 + 200 × 0.6098/0.907 = 3400 + 134.5 = 3,535 K.

Sanity check: hydrogen's bond is strong (h̄R ≈ +436,000 kJ/kmol at 298 K, from 2 × 218,000 for atomic H), so serious dissociation needs well over 3,000 K; and at 1 atm instead of 10 atm the same 10% would occur at a lower T, since Δν > 0 makes low pressure favour dissociation. Both directions agree.

\n\n

Dissociation and the adiabatic flame temperature

\n

Chapter 14 computed adiabatic flame temperatures by assuming complete combustion and letting all the heating value warm the products. Above about 1,800 K that overstates the temperature, for two reasons that both come from this lesson. First, dissociation is endothermic: every kmol of H2O that splits absorbs roughly 250,000 kJ that would otherwise have raised the product temperature. Second, the dissociated fragments (CO, H2, OH, H, O) still hold chemical energy that is only released if they recombine, which they do as the gases cool in the turbine or the exhaust. The result: real peak flame temperatures of hydrocarbons in air are around 2,200 to 2,400 K, not the 2,500 K+ that complete-combustion arithmetic gives, and the correction grows quickly with temperature. Some computed degrees of dissociation for pure steam at 1 atm show how sharp the onset is:

\n\n\n\n\n\n
T (K)ln KP (H2O ⇌ H2 + ½O2)KPα at 1 atmα at 10 atm
2000−8.1452.90 × 10−40.0055 (0.55%)lower still
2500 (interpolated between 2400 and 2600)−5.135.9 × 10−30.040 (4.0%)−
3000−3.0864.57 × 10−20.148 (14.8%)0.072 (7.2%)
\n

The α values solve KP = [α(α/2)½/(1 − α)] · (P/(1 + α/2))½, from 1 kmol H2O giving (1 − α) H2O, α H2, α/2 O2. The iterative flame-temperature procedure is: guess Tad, find the equilibrium composition at that T, do the energy balance with that composition, get a new Tad, repeat. High pressure (gas turbines, rocket chambers) suppresses dissociation and pushes the flame temperature back up, which is one more reason cycle pressure matters.

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Celsius in van't Hoff. 1/T1 − 1/T2 must use kelvin. Using 1,527 °C and 1,927 °C in Worked Example 1 gives h̄R ≈ −187,000 kJ/kmol, 26% off, with no warning.

Wrong sign for the reverse reaction. The table gives ln KP for the dissociation; for combustion you must negate it (KP → 1/KP). Forgetting this flips the sign of h̄R and you \"prove\" that burning hydrogen absorbs heat.

Confusing α with mole fraction. α = 0.10 for H2 means 0.20 kmol of H atoms in 1.10 kmol total, so yH = 0.182, not 0.10. Set up the Ni column before you write KP.

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

Three standard forms: (a) \"using KP at T1 and T2, estimate h̄R\" (Worked Example 1, four lines); (b) \"find the temperature at which x% dissociates at P\" (Worked Example 2, evaluate KP, then interpolate ln KP in the table); (c) \"explain why the actual adiabatic flame temperature is below the complete-combustion value and how pressure affects it\" (dissociation is endothermic; Δν > 0 so pressure suppresses it).

Show the interpolation explicitly with both bracketing rows quoted; the marker checks the rows, not just the result. State that h̄R was assumed constant over the interval.

This lesson moves from reacting gases to the equilibrium between phases: why water at 100 °C and 1 atm can be liquid, vapour or both, how many variables you may fix before a multi-phase, multi-component system is pinned down, and how the composition of a vapour above a two-component liquid, or of a gas dissolved in a liquid, is found. You will apply the Gibbs-function criterion to phases, use the Gibbs phase rule, and work two examples with Raoult's law and Henry's law. In the degree this closes the equilibrium chapter (Cengel & Boles 16-6 and 16-7) and is the thermodynamic underpinning of distillation, absorption refrigeration (ammonia-water) and dissolved-gas problems in environmental engineering.

\n\n

One component, two phases: gf = gg

\n

Put saturated liquid water and saturated vapour together in a cylinder at fixed T and P. The two phases are two \"species\" that can convert into one another, so the same criterion as for a chemical reaction applies: at equilibrium the total Gibbs function G = mfgf + mggg is a minimum. Let a small mass dmf evaporate (dmg = −dmf) at constant T and P. Then dG = gf dmf + gg dmg = (gf − gg) dmf, and requiring dG = 0 for any dmf gives

\n

gf = gg

\n

The specific Gibbs functions (kJ/kg) of the two phases are equal at equilibrium. If gf > gg, evaporation lowers G and liquid keeps evaporating until it is gone (superheated region); if gf < gg, vapour condenses. Check with steam-table numbers at 100 °C: g = h − Ts, so gg − gf = hfg − T sfg = 2,256 kJ/kg − 373.15 K × 6.046 kJ/kg·K = 2,256 − 2,256 = 0 (sfg = hfg/Tsat by definition of the reversible phase change). Differentiating gf = gg along the saturation line is exactly how the Clapeyron equation dP/dT = hfg/(T vfg) of the property-relations chapter was obtained; the same idea, in words, is that phase equilibrium is a curve in the T-P plane, not a region.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Phase equilibrium. Two or more phases of a substance coexist without net transfer of mass between them when the specific (or molar) Gibbs function of each component is the same in every phase: gi(1) = gi(2) = … for every component i. For a single component this holds only on the saturation curve; at the triple point all three phases have equal g.

Independent variable (degree of freedom). An intensive property (T, P, or a phase composition) that may be set freely without leaving the equilibrium state. Once the allowed number are fixed, every other intensive property is determined.

\n\n

The Gibbs phase rule

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Gibbs phase rule for a non-reacting system:

📊 FIGURE — The phase rule on water’s P-T diagram: 2, 1 or 0 free variables
Inside a region you may set T and P freely (IV = 2); on a two-phase line only one (fix T and P is fixed); at the triple point none. The box does the same count with IV = C − PH + 2.

IV = C − PH + 2

IV = number of independent intensive variables (degrees of freedom); C = number of components (chemically distinct species); PH = number of phases in equilibrium; the 2 stands for temperature and pressure. Counting is by intensive properties only, so the amounts of each phase do not appear: a 20% and an 80% quality mixture at 100 °C have the same IV.

\n

Where the 2 comes from: each phase has (C − 1) independent mole fractions plus T and P, giving PH(C − 1) + 2 variables; equilibrium imposes (PH − 1) Gibbs-function equalities per component, C(PH − 1) constraints; the difference is C − PH + 2. Apply it to water:

\n
    \n
  • Single phase (C = 1, PH = 1): IV = 2. Superheated steam needs both T and P, which is why Table A-6 is two-dimensional.
    • \n
  • Two phases (PH = 2): IV = 1. Fix T and Psat follows, which is why Tables A-4 and A-5 are one-dimensional. Quality x is a ratio of phase amounts, not an intensive variable of either phase, so it is not counted.
    • \n
  • Three phases (PH = 3): IV = 0. The triple point is a point: 0.01 °C and 0.6117 kPa, no freedom at all.
    • \n
  • Two components, two phases (ammonia-water, PH = 2, C = 2): IV = 2. Fix T and the liquid composition, and both the pressure and the vapour composition are determined. That is the next worked example.
    • \n
\n\n

Two components, two phases: Raoult's law

\n

For a mixture of two volatile liquids in equilibrium with their vapour, the criterion giliquid = givapour for each component becomes, for an ideal solution with an ideal-gas vapour, Raoult's law:

\n

Pi = yi,gas P = xi,liquid Psat,i(T)

\n

Pi = partial pressure of component i in the vapour (kPa); yi,gas = mole fraction of i in the vapour; P = total pressure (kPa); xi,liquid = mole fraction of i in the liquid; Psat,i(T) = saturation pressure of pure i at the mixture temperature (kPa). In words: each component's vapour pressure above the solution is its pure vapour pressure scaled down by its share of the liquid molecules. The total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures, and the vapour is always richer than the liquid in the more volatile component, which is the whole basis of distillation. Real solutions deviate (ammonia-water deviates strongly), so Raoult's law is a first estimate, and engineering practice uses measured equilibrium diagrams (the T-x-y diagram) for design.

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem. A liquid-vapour mixture of ammonia and water is in equilibrium at 30 °C. The liquid is 60% NH3 and 40% H2O by mole. Estimate the vapour composition and the total pressure, treating the solution as ideal (Raoult's law). (After Cengel & Boles Example 16-7; numbers recomputed.)

  1. Pure-component saturation pressures at 30 °C: water Psat = 4.2469 kPa (steam tables, saturated water by temperature); ammonia Psat ≈ 1,167 kPa (saturated ammonia, NIST WebBook).
  2. Partial pressures from Raoult's law: PNH3 = xNH3 Psat,NH3 = 0.60 × 1,167 kPa = 700.2 kPa; PH2O = 0.40 × 4.2469 kPa = 1.699 kPa.
  3. Total pressure: P = 700.2 + 1.699 = 701.9 kPa (about 7 bar).
  4. Vapour mole fractions: yNH3 = 700.2/701.9 = 0.9976; yH2O = 1.699/701.9 = 0.0024.
  5. Answer: vapour is 99.76% NH3 and 0.24% H2O at about 702 kPa, while the liquid is only 60% NH3.

Sanity check: ammonia's vapour pressure is 275 times water's at this temperature, so the vapour must be almost pure ammonia; and the total pressure, 702 kPa, lies between the two pure-component saturation pressures as it must for an ideal solution. The same fact is why an absorption refrigerator can drive nearly pure NH3 vapour off a weak ammonia-water solution with a little heat.

\n\n

Gases dissolving in liquids: Henry's law

\n

The second common two-phase, two-component case is a gas sparingly soluble in a liquid, e.g. air in a lake, CO2 in a soft drink, O2 in blood plasma. The dissolved gas is so dilute that its behaviour in the liquid is not that of a pure substance at all, so Raoult's law is replaced by an empirical proportionality with a measured constant:

\n

yi,gas side · P = H · yi,liquid side (so yi,liquid = Pi,gas / H)

\n

yi,gas side P = Pi,gas = partial pressure of the gas above the liquid (bar); yi,liquid side = mole fraction of the dissolved gas in the liquid; H = Henry's constant (bar), a property of the gas-liquid pair that depends on temperature. Read it as: the dissolved mole fraction is proportional to the gas's partial pressure and inversely proportional to H, so a big H means a poorly soluble gas. H rises with temperature for most gases in water, which is why warm water holds less oxygen and why a warm soda goes flat faster. Henry's constants in bar for water (Cengel & Boles Table 16-2, low to moderate pressures):

\n\n\n\n\n\n
Gas290 K300 K310 K320 K
Air62,00074,00084,00092,000
O238,00045,00052,00057,000
CO21,2801,7102,1702,720
\n
✅ VERIFIED

Cross-check of the CO2 row: the NIST Chemistry WebBook (CO2, Henry's law data) gives kH ≈ 0.035 mol/(kg·bar) at 298 K. Converting: 0.035 mol of CO2 per 55.5 mol of water per bar is a mole fraction of 6.3 × 10−4 per bar, i.e. H ≈ 1,590 bar at 298 K, consistent with 1,280 bar at 290 K and 1,710 bar at 300 K in the table. Cross-check of the O2 row: the calculation below gives 8.4 mg of dissolved O2 per kg of air-saturated water at 300 K, in line with the well-known 8 to 9 mg/L saturation of dissolved oxygen near 25 °C.

\n

Two short applications (computed with the table above):

\n
    \n
  1. Air dissolved at the surface of a lake at 17 °C (290 K) under 92 kPa. The gas phase is saturated air, so first remove the water vapour: Psat(17 °C) = 1.938 kPa, hence Pdry air = 92 − 1.938 = 90.06 kPa = 0.9006 bar. Then yair,liquid = 0.9006 bar / 62,000 bar = 1.45 × 10−5, about 15 air molecules per million water molecules. (Cengel & Boles Example 16-8; recomputed.)
    2. \n
  2. Dissolved oxygen in the same water at 300 K under ordinary air at 1.013 bar. PO2 = 0.21 × 1.013 = 0.2127 bar; yO2,liquid = 0.2127/45,000 = 4.73 × 10−6. Per kg of water (1000/18.015 = 55.5 mol) that is 4.73 × 10−6 × 55.5 mol = 2.62 × 10−4 mol of O2, × 32.0 g/mol = 8.4 mg O2 per kg water, the oxygen fish breathe.
    3. \n
  3. CO2 in a soft drink at 300 K, CO2 partial pressure 3.0 bar absolute. y = 3.0/1,710 = 1.754 × 10−3; per kg water nCO2 = y/(1 − y) × 55.5 mol = 0.0976 mol, × 44.01 g/mol = 4.3 g CO2 per kg water. Chill the same can to 290 K (H = 1,280 bar) and it holds 5.7 g at the same pressure, which is why drinks are carbonated cold.
    4. \n
\n

Two more things engineers need to know in words. Solubility of solids in liquids is tabulated directly (kg of salt per 100 kg of water at each temperature) because neither law above applies. And for a gas that is very soluble (ammonia in water), neither Henry's nor Raoult's law is accurate over the full range and measured equilibrium charts are used.

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Forgetting the water vapour above a liquid. The gas over an open water surface is saturated with vapour. Use the partial pressure of the dry gas (total minus Psat), not the total pressure, in Henry's law. At 17 °C the error is only 2%, at 60 °C it is 20%.

Mixing up which side x and y are on. Raoult's law scales the liquid mole fraction by the pure saturation pressure to get the vapour partial pressure. Henry's constant multiplies the liquid mole fraction to give the gas partial pressure. In both, the liquid side is the small number.

Counting quality as a degree of freedom. The phase rule counts intensive properties of the phases. The quality of a wet mixture is an extensive ratio and is not one of the IV, so water at 100 °C and 101.42 kPa has IV = 1, whether the cylinder is 1% or 99% vapour.

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

Typical questions: (1) \"Show that gf = gg at equilibrium\" (the dG = (gf − gg)dmf argument, four lines); (2) \"How many independent properties fix the state of …\" (phase rule; state C and PH explicitly and say what the variables are, e.g. T and P for superheated steam); (3) a Raoult's-law vapour composition from a liquid composition; (4) a Henry's-law dissolved mole fraction, usually with the water-vapour correction hidden in the wording (\"the lake surface\", \"saturated air\").

For a two-component two-phase question always report both the composition and the pressure, and say which law you used and why (dilute gas → Henry; volatile ideal solution → Raoult).

"}, "THERMO/compflow/s1": {"body": "

This lesson lets you take any gas stream whose speed matters, a jet engine inlet, a wind-tunnel test section, a leaking high-pressure line, and describe it with two extra numbers, the stagnation state and the Mach number, that make the first and second laws easy to apply. It sits at the end of the applied half of the degree: it uses the steady-flow energy equation from the control-volume chapter, the isentropic relations from the entropy chapter, and it feeds the gas-turbine and jet-propulsion material you have already met. Everything here is for an ideal gas with constant specific heats; air with k = 1.4, R = 0.287 kJ/kg-K and cp = 1.005 kJ/kg-K unless the problem says otherwise.

1. Why fast flow needs new bookkeeping

In every open-system problem so far the kinetic energy term V²/2 was either zero or a rounding error. Water at 5 m/s carries V²/2 = 12.5 J/kg, which is nothing next to the 2,000 kJ/kg of a boiler. Air leaving a jet nozzle at 800 m/s carries 320 kJ/kg, which is about a third of its enthalpy. Once the kinetic energy is that large, the temperature and pressure you would measure with a probe that stops the flow are very different from the temperature and pressure of the moving gas, and the two must be kept apart with clear names.

The trick that makes the whole chapter tidy is to bundle the kinetic energy into the enthalpy. The steady-flow energy equation for a nozzle or diffuser with no heat transfer and no shaft work says h + V²/2 stays constant along the flow. So we give that sum a name, the stagnation enthalpy, and then describe every point in the flow by the state the gas would reach if it were brought to rest without loss. That imaginary state is the stagnation state, and it is the reference against which everything in compressible flow is measured.

📘 DEFINITION

The stagnation state (also called the total state) of a moving fluid is the state it would reach if it were decelerated to zero velocity adiabatically and reversibly, that is, isentropically, with no shaft work. Its properties carry a subscript 0: h0, T0, P0, ρ0.

The static state (T, P, ρ, h with no subscript) is the actual state of the moving gas, what a thermometer moving with the flow would read. Static and stagnation states coincide only when V = 0.

2. Stagnation enthalpy, temperature and pressure

Write the steady-flow energy equation for a unit mass with q = 0 and w = 0 and no change in elevation. What is conserved is the sum of enthalpy and kinetic energy:

h0 = h + V²/2

h0 is the stagnation enthalpy in J/kg, h the static enthalpy in J/kg, V the velocity in m/s. The units only work in J/kg: if you keep h in kJ/kg you must divide V²/2 by 1,000. For an ideal gas with constant cp, h = cpT, so dividing through by cp gives the stagnation temperature:

T0 = T + V²/(2 cp)

T0 is the stagnation temperature in K, T the static temperature in K, cp in J/kg-K (1,005 for air). The added term V²/(2cp) is sometimes called the dynamic temperature; it is the temperature rise a probe experiences when the flow stops on it. Nothing in this equation required the deceleration to be reversible, only adiabatic, so T0 and h0 are well defined even in flows with friction or shocks.

Pressure is different. To go from T0 to P0 you need a process path, and the definition specifies an isentropic one, so the isentropic relation for an ideal gas applies:

P0/P = (T0/T)k/(k−1) and ρ0/ρ = (T0/T)1/(k−1)

P0 and P are the stagnation and static pressures (any unit, as long as both are absolute), ρ0 and ρ the densities in kg/m³, and k = cp/cv the specific heat ratio, dimensionless (1.4 for air, so the exponents are 3.5 and 2.5). Because P0 is defined through an isentropic path, it is the quantity that falls when the flow has friction or passes through a shock, while T0 stays constant. That asymmetry is the single most examined idea in the chapter.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

h0 = h + V²/2 (J/kg; valid for any adiabatic flow with no shaft work)

T0 = T + V²/(2cp) (ideal gas, constant cp in J/kg-K)

P0 = P (T0/T)k/(k−1) (isentropic path from static to stagnation)

For a turbine or compressor with fluid moving fast at inlet and outlet, replace h by h0 everywhere in the energy equation: w = h01 − h02 for a turbine, with the kinetic energy already inside. Stagnation properties are what a real engine test measures.

3. The speed of sound and the Mach number

A small pressure disturbance travels through a gas as a sound wave. Applying mass and momentum conservation to a control volume moving with the wave, with the process taken as isentropic because the wave is weak and fast, gives the speed of sound c² = (∂P/∂ρ)s. For an ideal gas Pvk = constant along an isentrope, so the derivative is kP/ρ = kRT:

c = √(k R T)

c is the speed of sound in m/s, k dimensionless, R the gas constant in J/kg-K (287 for air, not 0.287), T the static temperature in kelvin. Three things are worth staring at. The speed of sound depends on temperature only, not on pressure; on a given day sound travels no faster at sea level than on a mountain at the same temperature. It depends on the gas through kR = kRu/M, so light gases are fast: at 300 K, air gives 347.2 m/s, helium (k = 1.667, R = 2,077 J/kg-K) gives 1,019 m/s and carbon dioxide (k = 1.289, R = 188.9 J/kg-K) gives 270 m/s. And it is the local speed: as a gas accelerates through a nozzle and cools, the speed of sound in it falls at the same time as the velocity rises.

The Mach number is the ratio of the local velocity to the local speed of sound:

M = V / c = V / √(k R T)

M is dimensionless, V in m/s, c in m/s at the same point and the same static temperature. The stagnation relations can then be written in terms of M alone, which is what the isentropic tables tabulate. Substituting V = Mc and cp = kR/(k − 1) into the T0 equation:

T0/T = 1 + ((k−1)/2) M²

P0/P = [1 + ((k−1)/2) M²]k/(k−1) ρ0/ρ = [1 + ((k−1)/2) M²]1/(k−1)

For air these are T0/T = 1 + 0.2M², P0/P = (1 + 0.2M²)3.5 and ρ0/ρ = (1 + 0.2M²)2.5. The flow regimes are named by M:

RegimeMach numberWhat changes
Incompressible (a useful limit)M < about 0.3Density changes under a few per cent; Bernoulli works. At M = 0.3 the exact (P0 − P)/P of 0.0644 is only 2.2% above the Bernoulli value ½kM² = 0.0630.
SubsonicM < 1Pressure signals travel upstream; the flow adjusts ahead of an obstacle
SonicM = 1Occurs at a throat; the critical (starred) state
Transonicroughly 0.8 to 1.2Mixed sub- and supersonic pockets, shocks form on wings
SupersonicM > 1No upstream warning; disturbances confined to a Mach cone of half-angle μ = arcsin(1/M), which is 30° at M = 2
HypersonicM > about 5Stagnation temperatures so high that k is no longer constant; at M = 5 and T = 220 K, T0 = 220 × (1 + 0.2 × 25) = 1,320 K

4. Worked example: an aircraft in cruise

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

An aircraft flies at 250 m/s through air at 250 K and 50 kPa (absolute). Find the speed of sound, the flight Mach number, and the stagnation temperature and pressure the air reaches at the nose of the fuselage, where it is brought to rest. Take k = 1.4, R = 287 J/kg-K, cp = 1,005 J/kg-K.

📊 FIGURE — Static and stagnation states of air meeting an aircraft at M = 0.789
Air arriving at 250 m/s is brought to rest on the probe: T rises to T0 = 281.1 K and P to P0 = 75.4 kPa. The bar places M = 0.789 among the named flow regimes.
  1. Speed of sound at the static temperature (kelvin, because the ideal-gas law is in kelvin): c = √(kRT) = √(1.4 × 287 J/kg-K × 250 K) = √(100,450 m²/s²) = 316.9 m/s.
  2. Mach number: M = V/c = 250 m/s ÷ 316.9 m/s = 0.789. Subsonic, in the high-subsonic band typical of airliners, and well above 0.3, so compressibility cannot be ignored.
  3. Stagnation temperature from the energy equation: T0 = T + V²/(2cp) = 250 K + (250 m/s)² ÷ (2 × 1,005 J/kg-K) = 250 K + 62,500 m²/s² ÷ 2,010 J/kg-K = 250 K + 31.1 K = 281.1 K. (Check with the Mach form: 250 × (1 + 0.2 × 0.789²) = 250 × 1.1244 = 281.1 K. Same answer, as it must be.)
  4. Stagnation pressure along an isentropic path: P0 = P (T0/T)k/(k−1) = 50 kPa × (281.09/250)3.5 = 50 kPa × (1.1244)3.5 = 50 kPa × 1.507 = 75.4 kPa.
  5. Density, for interest: ρ = P/(RT) = 50,000 Pa ÷ (287 J/kg-K × 250 K) = 0.697 kg/m³, and ρ0 = ρ (T0/T)2.5 = 0.697 × 1.12442.5 = 0.934 kg/m³, which agrees with P0/(RT0) = 75,360 ÷ (287 × 281.09) = 0.934 kg/m³.

Sanity check: the kinetic energy is 31.25 kJ/kg, about an eighth of cpT = 251 kJ/kg, so a 12% rise in absolute temperature and a 51% rise in pressure are the right size. A pitot tube on the nose would read 75.4 kPa, not 50 kPa, and an air-data computer works backwards from that pair to get M.

5. The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Mixing kJ and J. V²/2 with V in m/s is in J/kg. Add it to cp = 1,005 J/kg-K, or divide it by 1,000 and use 1.005 kJ/kg-K. Adding 62,500 to a cp of 1.005 gives a stagnation temperature of about 31,000 K, which should stop you immediately.

Celsius in the speed of sound. c = √(kRT) needs kelvin. Air at 27 °C gives √(1.4 × 287 × 27) = 104 m/s if you forget, against the correct 347 m/s at 300 K.

Using cv or forgetting the ½. T0 − T = V²/(2cp). With cv = 718 the rise for 200 m/s comes out 27.9 K instead of 19.9 K; without the ½ it comes out 39.8 K.

Treating P0 as conserved like T0. Across friction or a shock, T0 (and h0) stay the same because the flow is still adiabatic, but P0 drops because entropy rose. Stagnation pressure is the bookkeeping quantity for losses.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Every isentropic table in this chapter is a one-line function of M. In pandas, M = np.linspace(0, 3, 301) then T_T0 = 1/(1 + 0.2*M**2), P_P0 = T_T0**3.5 and so on gives you the whole table at any resolution, with no interpolation. The inverse problem (given P/P0, find M) is np.interp on a monotonic column, or a one-line algebraic inversion M = √(5[(P0/P)2/7 − 1]) for air.

Fit check: plot log(P0/P) against log(T0/T) from any dataset of static and pitot readings and the slope should be k/(k − 1) = 3.5. A slope that drifts from 3.5 at high speed is your first sign that the probe is behind a shock or that k is falling with temperature.

6. What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

The chapter opener is always a three-liner: given V, T and P, find c, M, T0, P0 (or the reverse: given pitot and static pressures, find M then V). Write c = √(kRT) with T in kelvin and R in J/kg-K, quote the Mach number to three figures, then use T0 = T + V²/2cp and P0 = P(T0/T)3.5.

Expect a conceptual part: \"which of T0, P0, s stay constant across an adiabatic irreversible process?\" (T0 yes, P0 no, s rises) and \"does the speed of sound in a gas rise with pressure?\" (no, with temperature only).

Compressor and turbine questions in this chapter give inlet and outlet stagnation temperatures and expect w = cp(T02 − T01) with no separate kinetic-energy term. Write \"stagnation\" next to the symbols so the marker sees you know why.

"}, "THERMO/compflow/s2": {"body": "

This lesson lets you size a nozzle: given a supply pressure and temperature, you will be able to say how big the throat must be for a required mass flow, whether the flow will reach the speed of sound, how much exit area is needed to reach a given supersonic Mach number, and what happens when the back pressure is not the one the nozzle was designed for. It is the working heart of the compressible-flow chapter, and it is where the isentropic relations from the entropy chapter finally earn their keep. The flow is one-dimensional, steady, isentropic and of an ideal gas with constant k (1.4 for air).

1. Why a throat is needed to go supersonic

Intuition from garden hoses says that squeezing a duct speeds the fluid up, and for subsonic flow that is right. But combine the three governing laws for a differential slice of isentropic duct flow, mass conservation d(ρAV) = 0, the energy equation dh + V dV = 0, and the isentropic relation dh = dP/ρ, and use c² = dP/dρ to eliminate the density change. The result is the area-velocity relation:

dA/A = (M² − 1) · dV/V

A is the duct area in m², V the velocity in m/s, M the local Mach number. Read it for the three cases. Subsonic (M < 1): the bracket is negative, so a decreasing area raises the velocity, as expected. Supersonic (M > 1): the bracket is positive, so the velocity rises only if the area increases; the density is now falling faster than the velocity is rising, and the duct must widen to pass the same mass. Sonic (M = 1): dA must be zero, so the speed of sound can be reached only where the area is a minimum, at a throat. A converging duct can therefore never deliver more than M = 1 at its exit, and to accelerate a gas from rest to supersonic speed you need a converging section, a throat, and a diverging section: the converging-diverging (de Laval) nozzle. Run backwards, the same shape decelerates supersonic flow in a supersonic diffuser.

📘 DEFINITION

The critical state (starred: T*, P*, ρ*, A*) is the state of the flow where M = 1. For a given stagnation state it is fixed: T*/T0 = 2/(k + 1), P*/P0 = [2/(k + 1)]k/(k−1), ρ*/ρ0 = [2/(k + 1)]1/(k−1). For air, T*/T0 = 0.8333, P*/P0 = 0.5283 and ρ*/ρ0 = 0.6339.

A* is the area the flow would need at M = 1; it is used as the reference area for every point in an isentropic flow even when the duct never actually reaches sonic speed. A flow is choked when M = 1 is reached at the throat: the mass flow rate is then the largest the throat can pass for that stagnation state, and lowering the back pressure further cannot raise it.

2. Properties along the nozzle in terms of M

Because the flow is isentropic, the stagnation state is the same everywhere in the nozzle, and each local state is fixed by its Mach number alone through the relations from the previous lesson (T/T0 = 1/(1 + 0.2M²) and so on for air). The mass flow rate through any cross-section is ṁ = ρAV = (P/RT) · A · M√(kRT). Replacing P and T by P0 and T0 gives:

ṁ = A · M · P0 · √(k/(R T0)) · [1 + ((k−1)/2) M²]−(k+1)/(2(k−1))

ṁ in kg/s, A in m², P0 in Pa, R in J/kg-K, T0 in K. Since the flow rate is the same at every section, setting M = 1 at the throat and dividing gives the area ratio, the column of the isentropic table that lets you go from a nozzle shape to a Mach number:

A/A* = (1/M) · [ (2/(k+1)) · (1 + ((k−1)/2) M²) ](k+1)/(2(k−1))

This ratio is 1 at M = 1 and larger on both sides, so every A/A* above 1 corresponds to two Mach numbers, one subsonic and one supersonic; which one the flow takes depends on the back pressure. Setting M = 1 also gives the choked mass flow rate, the most useful single formula in the lesson:

ṁmax = A* · P0 · √(k/(R T0)) · [2/(k+1)](k+1)/(2(k−1))

For air the trailing group collapses to a number: √1.4 × (2/2.4)3 = 0.6847, so ṁmax = 0.6847 · A* · P0/√(R T0) with A* in m², P0 in Pa, R = 287 J/kg-K and T0 in K. Two things control a choked flow: raise P0 and the flow rises in proportion; raise T0 and it falls as 1/√T0 because the gas is less dense. The back pressure does not appear at all.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

A/A* = (1/M)[(2/(k+1))(1 + ((k−1)/2)M²)](k+1)/(2(k−1)) (isentropic; for air the outer exponent is 3)

ṁmax = 0.6847 A* P0 / √(R T0) (air, choked; A* m², P0 Pa, R = 287 J/kg-K, T0 K, ṁ kg/s)

P*/P0 = 0.5283, T*/T0 = 0.8333, ρ*/ρ0 = 0.6339 (air at the throat when choked; V* = c* = √(kRT*))

A short isentropic table for air, computed from the relations above (the isentropic-flow table in Cengel & Boles, Table A-32 in recent editions, tabulates the same functions at finer steps):

3. Worked example: a converging-diverging nozzle for Mach 2

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Air from a reservoir at P0 = 1.0 MPa and T0 = 800 K expands isentropically through a converging-diverging nozzle with a throat area of 20 cm². The nozzle is designed to deliver M = 2 at the exit. Find (a) the throat conditions and velocity, (b) the mass flow rate, (c) the exit area, and (d) the exit temperature, pressure and velocity. Take k = 1.4, R = 287 J/kg-K, cp = 1,005 J/kg-K.

📊 FIGURE — Converging-diverging nozzle for Mach 2: Mach regions and pressure
Top: the nozzle, subsonic (blue) up to the sonic throat, supersonic (yellow) after it. Bottom: P/P0 along it; the solid line is the design flow, the dashed one what a high back pressure gives.
  1. Is the throat sonic? The exit is supersonic, so the throat must be at M = 1 and the flow is choked. Throat properties are the critical ones: T* = 0.8333 × 800 K = 666.7 K; P* = 0.5283 × 1,000 kPa = 528.3 kPa.
  2. Throat density and velocity: ρ* = P*/(RT*) = 528,280 Pa ÷ (287 J/kg-K × 666.67 K) = 2.761 kg/m³. V* = c* = √(1.4 × 287 × 666.67) = √267,867 = 517.6 m/s.
  3. Mass flow rate, from the throat: ṁ = ρ*A*V* = 2.761 kg/m³ × 0.0020 m² × 517.6 m/s = 2.858 kg/s. Check with the choked formula: 0.6847 × 0.0020 m² × 1,000,000 Pa ÷ √(287 × 800) = 1,369.4 ÷ 479.2 = 2.858 kg/s. Same.
  4. Exit area from the area ratio at M = 2: A/A* = (1/2) × [(2/2.4)(1 + 0.2 × 4)]3 = 0.5 × (0.8333 × 1.8)3 = 0.5 × 1.53 = 1.6875, so Ae = 1.6875 × 20 cm² = 33.75 cm².
  5. Exit temperature and pressure from the M = 2 row: Te = 800 K ÷ (1 + 0.2 × 4) = 800/1.8 = 444.4 K; Pe = 1,000 kPa × 1.8−3.5 = 1,000 × 0.1278 = 127.8 kPa.
  6. Exit velocity: ce = √(1.4 × 287 × 444.44) = 422.6 m/s, so Ve = 2 × 422.6 = 845.2 m/s. Energy check: cp(T0 − Te) = 1,005 × (800 − 444.4) = 357.3 kJ/kg, and Ve²/2 = 845.2² ÷ 2 = 357.2 kJ/kg (the 0.05% gap is cp = 1,005 against the exact kR/(k − 1) = 1,004.5).
  7. Mass check at the exit: ρe = 127,800 ÷ (287 × 444.44) = 1.002 kg/m³; ρeAeVe = 1.002 × 0.003375 × 845.2 = 2.858 kg/s. Continuity holds.

Sanity check: the exit pressure of 128 kPa is close to atmospheric, so this nozzle would run at its design point exhausting to sea-level air; the exit velocity is 1.63 times the throat velocity while the area grew by 1.69 times, which fits the supersonic rule that density falls faster than velocity rises.

4. Operating regimes: what the back pressure does

A nozzle exhausts into a region at the back pressure Pb. Lowering Pb from P0 walks the nozzle through a sequence of regimes. For a converging nozzle there are only two: while Pb ≥ P*, the exit pressure equals Pb, the exit Mach number is below 1, and the mass flow rises as Pb falls; once Pb drops to P* = 0.5283 P0 (for air) the exit goes sonic and the flow chokes. Any further drop in Pb cannot be felt inside the nozzle, because pressure signals travel at the speed of sound and the exit flow is already moving that fast. The exit pressure stays at P*, the mass flow stays at ṁmax, and the extra expansion from P* down to Pb happens outside the nozzle in a fan of expansion waves.

For a converging-diverging nozzle with a fixed area ratio there are five distinct pictures as Pb falls:

  1. Subsonic throughout (Pb just below P0): the diverging section acts as a diffuser, the throat is the fastest point but Mthroat < 1, and the mass flow depends on Pb.
  2. Choked, subsonic diverging section: Pb has fallen to the value that makes the throat exactly sonic; the flow then decelerates isentropically in the diverging section. The mass flow is now ṁmax and stays there for every lower Pb.
  3. Normal shock inside the diverging section: the flow goes supersonic after the throat, then a normal shock (next lesson) jumps it back to subsonic and the rest of the nozzle diffuses it up to Pb. Lower Pb pushes the shock towards the exit.
  4. Overexpanded: the shock has reached the exit plane and then moved outside as oblique shocks; the flow inside is fully isentropic and supersonic, but the exit pressure is below Pb, so the jet is compressed back up outside the nozzle.
  5. Design condition and underexpanded: at exactly the design Pb the exit pressure equals Pb and the jet leaves cleanly. Below that the nozzle is underexpanded: the exit pressure exceeds Pb and the jet keeps expanding outside through expansion waves. Rocket nozzles pass through overexpanded, design and underexpanded as they climb through falling ambient pressure.

5. The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Using the back pressure in the choked-flow formula. ṁmax depends on P0, T0 and A* only. If Pb < P* the answer is the same whether Pb is 100 kPa or 1 kPa. Always compare Pb with 0.5283 P0 first to decide whether the nozzle is choked.

Applying the critical temperature ratio to pressure. T*/T0 = 0.8333 but P*/P0 = 0.5283 and ρ*/ρ0 = 0.6339. For P0 = 500 kPa the throat pressure is 264 kPa, not 417 kPa.

Unit slips in ṁmax. The formula wants Pa and m². With A* = 5 cm² = 0.0005 m², P0 = 800 kPa and T0 = 400 K, ṁ = 0.6847 × 0.0005 × 800,000 ÷ √(287 × 400) = 0.808 kg/s. Leaving P in kPa gives 0.0008 kg/s; leaving A in cm² gives 8,084 kg/s. Both are absurd, and you should notice.

Picking the wrong branch of A/A*. Every area ratio above 1 has a subsonic and a supersonic solution. In the diverging section of a choked nozzle you must decide from the back pressure which one applies; the tables will happily give you either.

6. What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

The classic question gives P0, T0, a throat area and either an exit area or an exit Mach number, and asks for the mass flow and the exit state. Steps: (1) check choking, (2) throat state from the starred ratios, (3) ṁ from ρ*A*V* or the 0.6847 formula, (4) exit state from the isentropic table at the exit M or by inverting A/A*. Say explicitly \"flow is choked because Pb < P*\"; that sentence is often worth a mark on its own.

The conceptual favourite: \"The back pressure on a choked converging nozzle is halved. What happens to the mass flow?\" Nothing. And its twin: \"The supply pressure is doubled at the same T0?\" The mass flow doubles.

Expect one sketch question: draw the pressure distribution along a converging-diverging nozzle for the regimes above, or state where a shock sits for a given Pb. Label the throat, P*, and the design exit pressure.

"}, "THERMO/compflow/s3": {"body": "

This lesson lets you handle the three ways a real high-speed flow departs from the clean isentropic picture: a normal shock, a heat-transfer or friction effect along a duct, and the strange behaviour of steam that expands so fast it has no time to condense. You will be able to compute the state on the far side of a normal shock and the entropy it generates, explain in words what an oblique shock does, say which way Rayleigh and Fanno flows drive the Mach number, and estimate the exit velocity of a steam nozzle from the tables. It closes the compressible-flow chapter and connects forward to the statistical-thermodynamics and heat-transfer chapters that end the degree.

1. What a shock is, in plain words

A supersonic gas has no way to receive a warning that an obstacle or a higher pressure lies ahead, because the warning would travel at the speed of sound and the gas is outrunning it. When the flow finally has to adjust, it does so all at once, across a layer only a few molecular mean free paths thick. That layer is a shock wave. Across it the velocity drops abruptly, and the pressure, temperature and density jump up. The process is adiabatic (too fast and thin for heat transfer) but violently irreversible, so the entropy rises. A normal shock stands perpendicular to the flow and turns supersonic flow into subsonic flow; an oblique shock is inclined to the flow and can leave it supersonic. This lesson computes the normal one and describes the oblique one.

📘 DEFINITION

A normal shock is a very thin adiabatic region, perpendicular to the flow, across which a supersonic stream (M1 > 1) becomes subsonic (M2 < 1) with a discontinuous rise in P, T and ρ and a fall in V, while the stagnation temperature is unchanged and the stagnation pressure drops. It is governed by conservation of mass, momentum and energy across the layer, with the ideal-gas relations closing the system.

The curve of states satisfying mass and energy for a given upstream state is the Fanno line; the curve satisfying mass and momentum is the Rayleigh line. A normal shock is the jump between the two points where the lines intersect, and the second law picks the direction of the jump: the state with the higher entropy, which is always the subsonic one.

2. The normal-shock relations

Take a thin control volume around the shock with the same area on both faces. Mass: ρ1V1 = ρ2V2. Energy with no heat or work: h01 = h02, so T01 = T02. Momentum: P1 − P2 = ρ2V2² − ρ1V1², which with the ideal-gas law becomes P1(1 + kM1²) = P2(1 + kM2²). Combining the three gives the downstream Mach number in terms of the upstream one and nothing else:

M2² = (M1² + 2/(k−1)) / (2k M1²/(k−1) − 1)

M1 and M2 are the Mach numbers before and after the shock (dimensionless), k the specific heat ratio. For air the numerator is M1² + 5 and the denominator 7M1² − 1. The property ratios then follow:

P2/P1 = (1 + kM1²)/(1 + kM2²) = 1 + (2k/(k+1))(M1² − 1)

ρ2/ρ1 = V1/V2 = (k+1)M1² / (2 + (k−1)M1²)

T2/T1 = (1 + ((k−1)/2)M1²) / (1 + ((k−1)/2)M2²)

P in any absolute unit, T in kelvin, ρ in kg/m³, V in m/s. The temperature ratio is simply the ratio of the two static-to-stagnation factors because T0 is the same on both sides. The density ratio has a ceiling: as M1 → ∞ it tends to (k + 1)/(k − 1) = 6 for air, while the pressure ratio grows without limit. The stagnation pressure ratio, P02/P01, is what the shock tables list as the loss; it is found by converting each side to its stagnation pressure with the isentropic relation at its own Mach number. And the entropy generated per kilogram is the ideal-gas entropy change across the two static states:

s2 − s1 = cp ln(T2/T1) − R ln(P2/P1) = −R ln(P02/P01)

s in kJ/kg-K with cp = 1.005 and R = 0.287 kJ/kg-K for air. The second form follows because T02 = T01. If you plug M1 < 1 into these formulas you get an \"expansion shock\" with M2 > 1, falling pressure and a negative entropy change (for M1 = 0.8 in air the formulas give M2 = 1.27 and s2 − s1 = −4.8 J/kg-K). The second law forbids it, which is why shocks only ever go from supersonic to subsonic.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

M2² = (M1² + 5)/(7M1² − 1) (air, normal shock)

P2/P1 = 1 + (7/6)(M1² − 1), ρ2/ρ1 = 6M1²/(M1² + 5), T2/T1 = (P2/P1)/(ρ2/ρ1) (air)

T02 = T01, P02 < P01, s2 − s1 = −R ln(P02/P01) > 0

A short normal-shock table for air, computed from these relations (the normal-shock table in Cengel & Boles, Table A-33 in recent editions, has the finer version):

1.50.7012.4581.3201.8620.93021.0

Notice how fast the loss grows: a Mach 1.2 shock costs under 1% of stagnation pressure, a Mach 2 shock 28%, a Mach 3 shock 67%. That is why supersonic engine inlets use several weak oblique shocks rather than one strong normal shock.

3. Worked example: a normal shock at Mach 2

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Air at M1 = 2.0, P1 = 40 kPa and T1 = 250 K passes through a normal shock. Find the downstream Mach number, pressure, temperature and velocity, the stagnation pressures before and after, and the entropy generated. Take k = 1.4, R = 287 J/kg-K, cp = 1,005 J/kg-K.

📊 FIGURE — A normal shock at Mach 2: the state on each side and what jumps
Top: the worked example on each side of the shock (arrow length is speed). Bottom: each property after the shock as a multiple of its upstream value; T0 is unchanged, P0 falls 28 %.
  1. Downstream Mach number: M2² = (M1² + 5)/(7M1² − 1) = (4 + 5)/(28 − 1) = 9/27 = 0.3333, so M2 = 0.577. Subsonic, as it must be.
  2. Pressure ratio: P2/P1 = 1 + (7/6)(4 − 1) = 1 + 3.5 = 4.5, so P2 = 4.5 × 40 kPa = 180 kPa.
  3. Density ratio: ρ2/ρ1 = 6 × 4/(4 + 5) = 24/9 = 2.667. Temperature ratio: T2/T1 = 4.5/2.667 = 1.6875, so T2 = 1.6875 × 250 K = 421.9 K.
  4. Velocities: c1 = √(1.4 × 287 × 250) = 316.9 m/s, V1 = 2.0 × 316.9 = 633.9 m/s. c2 = √(1.4 × 287 × 421.87) = 411.7 m/s, V2 = 0.5774 × 411.7 = 237.7 m/s. Check: V1/V2 = 633.9/237.7 = 2.667 = ρ2/ρ1. Mass is conserved.
  5. Stagnation temperature (same both sides): T01 = 250 × (1 + 0.2 × 4) = 450 K; T02 = 421.87 × (1 + 0.2 × 0.3333) = 421.87 × 1.0667 = 450 K. Energy is conserved.
  6. Stagnation pressures: P01 = 40 kPa × 1.83.5 = 40 × 7.824 = 313.0 kPa; P02 = 180 kPa × 1.06673.5 = 180 × 1.2534 = 225.6 kPa. Ratio P02/P01 = 0.7209, matching the table row for M1 = 2.
  7. Entropy generated: s2 − s1 = cp ln(T2/T1) − R ln(P2/P1) = 1.005 × ln 1.6875 − 0.287 × ln 4.5 = 1.005 × 0.5232 − 0.287 × 1.5041 = 0.5259 − 0.4317 = 0.0942 kJ/kg-K. Check: −R ln(P02/P01) = −0.287 × ln 0.7209 = 0.0939 kJ/kg-K (the last digit differs through rounding P02).

Sanity check: the entropy change is positive, the static pressure jumped 4.5 times while the stagnation pressure lost 28%, and T0 came out identical from both sides. A pitot tube in this Mach 2 stream would read about 226 kPa, not 313 kPa, because a bow shock forms in front of it; supersonic pitot readings must always be corrected with the shock relations.

4. Oblique shocks and expansion waves, in words

When supersonic flow meets a wedge or a ramp it does not need to stop; it turns. It does so through an oblique shock inclined at a wave angle β to the incoming flow. Only the velocity component normal to the shock is affected, and that component behaves exactly like a normal shock with an effective upstream Mach number M1 sin β; the tangential component passes through unchanged. Because only part of the velocity is processed, the losses are smaller than for a normal shock at the same M1, and the downstream flow can still be supersonic. For a given M1 and turning angle θ there are two solutions: a weak shock (smaller β, downstream usually supersonic), which nature almost always picks for an attached shock, and a strong shock (larger β, downstream subsonic). Above a maximum turning angle for that Mach number no attached solution exists and the shock detaches into a curved bow shock standing ahead of the body, which is why blunt bodies at supersonic speed carry a bow shock and sharp wedges do not. The weakest possible oblique shock is a Mach wave, at the Mach angle μ = arcsin(1/M1), 30° at M1 = 2 and 19.5° at M1 = 3.

Turn the flow the other way, around a convex corner, and it cannot shock: it expands through a continuous fan of Mach waves, a Prandtl-Meyer expansion. Across the fan the Mach number rises, pressure and temperature fall, and because each wave is infinitesimally weak the process is isentropic. Overexpanded nozzle jets adjust to the ambient pressure through oblique shocks; underexpanded jets through expansion fans; and the diamond pattern in a supersonic exhaust is the two alternating as the waves reflect off the jet boundary.

5. Rayleigh flow and Fanno flow, in words

Two idealised duct flows describe what heat transfer and friction do to a compressible stream in a constant-area duct. Rayleigh flow is frictionless with heat transfer; it is the model of a combustor or a duct with heat exchange. Fanno flow is adiabatic with wall friction; it is the model of a long insulated pipe. The single most useful fact is that both drive the Mach number towards 1. Heating a subsonic flow speeds it up and heating a supersonic flow slows it down; friction does the same in both regimes. Either process can only push the flow as far as M = 1, at which point the duct is choked: adding more heat (thermal choking) or more length (friction choking) cannot be absorbed at that mass flow, and the upstream conditions must change, typically by the inlet Mach number dropping so that less mass enters.
