The Rayleigh oddity in the subsonic column is worth remembering: between M = 0.845 and M = 1 adding heat to air makes its static temperature fall, because the gas accelerates so fast that the kinetic-energy gain exceeds the heat added. In both flows the stagnation pressure drops even when heat is being added: heating a moving gas is a loss of work potential, which is one of the reasons combustors are designed for low inlet Mach numbers.

6. Steam nozzles and supersaturation

Steam is not an ideal gas, and its nozzles are handled from the tables rather than with k. The energy equation is the same, h0 = h + V²/2, and for an isentropic nozzle the exit enthalpy is read at the exit pressure and the inlet entropy. In kJ/kg the velocity becomes

V = √(2(h0 − h)) = 44.72 √(h0 − h) (V in m/s when h0 − h is in kJ/kg)

The factor 44.72 is √2,000 and is nothing more than the unit conversion from kJ/kg to J/kg under the root. If the tables give an isentropic enthalpy drop of 280 kJ/kg, the exit velocity is 44.72 × √280 = 748 m/s; using 280 without the conversion gives 23.7 m/s, which is a bicycle, not a turbine nozzle. For a rough design, superheated steam is sometimes treated as an ideal gas with k ≈ 1.3, which makes the critical pressure ratio P*/P0 = (2/2.3)1.3/0.3 = 0.546 rather than the 0.528 of air.

The physics that is special to steam is supersaturation. When superheated steam expands through a nozzle it reaches the saturation line in a fraction of a millisecond, far faster than condensation nuclei can form and droplets can grow. The steam therefore continues to expand as a dry vapour below its saturation temperature: a metastable, supersaturated (undercooled) state that the equilibrium tables do not describe. Condensation finally occurs suddenly a little further down the nozzle, at the Wilson line, releasing the latent heat in a \"condensation shock\" that raises the pressure and temperature slightly. Two consequences follow: the actual enthalpy drop up to the Wilson line is smaller than the isentropic-table drop because the steam is behaving as a gas rather than condensing, so the exit velocity is a little lower; and the mass flow rate is a little higher than the equilibrium calculation predicts because the supersaturated vapour is denser than the equilibrium mixture at the same pressure. The design fix is to size the nozzle with the gas-like behaviour (the k ≈ 1.3 approximation is one way) up to the Wilson line and use the tables only after it.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

Textbooks often quote k ≈ 1.135 for wet steam (which would give P*/P0 = 0.577) and place the Wilson line roughly at 3 to 4 per cent moisture on the Mollier chart; the exact figures vary between sources and depend on the expansion rate, so confirm before you rely on this in a design or an exam answer.

7. The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Using the isentropic relation across a shock. P2/P1 is not (T2/T1)3.5 across a shock, because the shock is not isentropic. Use the shock relations or table for the jump; use the isentropic relations only on each side separately to get P01 and P02.

Taking M2 = 1/M1. Tempting and wrong: at M1 = 1.5 the true M2 is 0.701, not 0.667, and at M1 = 2 it is 0.577, not 0.5. Also do not forget the square root after computing M2².

Believing a shock destroys stagnation temperature or energy. T0 and h0 are unchanged; what is destroyed is stagnation pressure, and the measure of it is the entropy generated, −R ln(P02/P01).

Steam velocities with kJ. V = √(2Δh) needs Δh in J/kg; with Δh in kJ/kg use 44.72 √Δh. A \"nozzle\" that gives 20 m/s is telling you the units are wrong.

8. What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

The standard shock question is the worked example above: M1, P1, T1 given; find M2, P2, T2, V2, the stagnation pressure loss and the entropy generated, and comment that Δs > 0. A variant places the shock at a stated location in a converging-diverging nozzle: use A/A* to get M1 at that section, the shock table for M2, then note that the flow after the shock is isentropic with a new A* (since P0 has dropped, A* has risen in the ratio P01/P02).

Short-answer favourites: why a shock cannot run from subsonic to supersonic (entropy would fall); why T0 is unchanged but P0 falls; which way heating and friction move the Mach number (towards 1); what supersaturation is and whether it raises or lowers the nozzle mass flow (raises it slightly).

For steam nozzles show the tables explicitly: inlet h and s, exit h at the same s and the exit pressure, then V = 44.72 √(Δh). Quote the property source (superheated or saturated table) beside every number.

This lesson lets you explain where entropy comes from. Everything before this chapter treated entropy as a bookkeeping quantity defined by dS = δQrev/T; here you see it is a count of the number of ways molecules can be arranged, so that the second law becomes a statement about probability. In a degree sequence this is the first lecture of statistical thermodynamics, and it is the piece that turns the Clausius definition from a rule you accept into a result you can derive.

The idea in plain words

Take four coins and toss them. You can describe the outcome in two ways. The detailed description lists each coin: heads, tails, tails, heads. The coarse description only counts: two heads. There are 16 detailed outcomes but only five coarse ones (0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 heads), and the coarse outcomes are not equally likely: \"two heads\" can happen six ways, \"four heads\" only one way. Nothing pushes the coins toward two heads; two heads simply has more ways of happening.

A gas is the same story with 1025 coins. The detailed description (where every molecule is and how fast it moves) is the microstate. The coarse description you can actually measure (pressure, temperature, volume, how much gas is in the left half) is the macrostate. Entropy measures how many microstates belong to a macrostate. Systems drift toward high entropy for the same reason four coins usually show two heads: those macrostates own almost all of the microstates.

Definitions

📘 DEFINITION

Microstate: one complete specification of every particle in the system (position and momentum in classical mechanics, quantum state in quantum mechanics). All accessible microstates of an isolated system at fixed energy are taken to be equally probable; this is the fundamental postulate of statistical mechanics.

Macrostate: the state described by the few measurable properties you used in earlier chapters (U, V, N, or P, T, composition). One macrostate contains an enormous number of microstates.

Multiplicity W (also written Ω): the number of microstates that produce a given macrostate. W is a pure count with no units.

Counting microstates

The basic counting tool is the number of ways to put N distinguishable particles into groups of n1, n2, ... nm:

📊 FIGURE — Four molecules in a two-part box: all 16 microstates by macrostate
Each small box is one microstate (dot left or right of the dashed line). Columns are macrostates, counted by W = 4!/(n!(4−n)!); the even split owns the most microstates, so it has the highest S = k ln W.

W = N! / (n1! · n2! · ... · nm!)

N is the total number of particles, ni is how many sit in group i (a box, an energy level, a velocity bin), and the factorial n! = n·(n−1)·...·1. With only two groups (left half of a box and right half) this is the binomial coefficient C(N, n1).

Four molecules free to be in either half of a box give these macrostates (computed from 4!/(n!(4−n)!)):

Molecules in left halfW (ways)Probability W/16
010.0625
140.25
260.375
340.25
410.0625

The total is 24 = 16 microstates. Now raise N to 100. The evenly split macrostate has W = C(100, 50) = 1.009 × 1029 microstates, the 60/40 split has C(100, 60) = 1.375 × 1028 (7.3 times fewer), and the \"all in one half\" macrostate still has exactly W = 1. Its probability is 1/2100 = 7.9 × 10−31. With 100 molecules you would already never see the gas spontaneously crowd into one half; with 1025 molecules the word \"never\" is an understatement.

The Boltzmann entropy S = k ln W

🧮 KEY EQUATION

S = k ln W

S is the entropy of the macrostate in J/K; k is the Boltzmann constant, 1.380649 × 10−23 J/K (it equals Ru/NA = 8.314 J/mol·K ÷ 6.02214 × 1023 mol−1); W is the multiplicity (dimensionless); ln is the natural logarithm.

For a change between two macrostates of the same system: ΔS = k ln (W2/W1), so you only ever need the ratio of multiplicities, which is usually much easier to count than W itself.

Why the logarithm? Two independent systems A and B have WAB = WA × WB (every microstate of A can pair with every microstate of B), but entropy in the classical chapters was additive: SAB = SA + SB. The only function that turns products into sums is the logarithm. The constant k is then fixed by demanding that this S agree numerically with the Clausius entropy in J/K, which is exactly what the worked example below checks.

Because W involves factorials of huge numbers, you will almost always use Stirling's approximation, ln N! ≈ N ln N − N. Its accuracy improves with N: for N = 100 the exact value of ln 100! is 363.74 and the approximation gives 360.52 (0.9 % low); for N = 1000 it is 5912.13 versus 5907.76 (0.07 % low); for N ≈ 1025 the error is negligible.

Worked example: the free expansion, counted twice

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem. One kmol of an ideal gas at constant temperature is allowed to expand freely into an evacuated chamber so that its volume doubles. Find ΔS (a) by counting microstates and (b) from the classical ideal-gas entropy change, and compare.

  1. Count the molecules. N = n NA = (1 kmol)(1000 mol/kmol)(6.02214 × 1023 mol−1) = 6.022 × 1026 molecules.
  2. Count the position choices. Doubling the volume doubles the number of places each molecule can be, so each molecule has 2× as many position microstates. The molecules choose independently, so the multiplicity ratio is W2/W1 = 2N (the momentum part is unchanged because T, and therefore the speed distribution, is unchanged).
  3. Apply S = k ln W. ΔS = k ln(2N) = N k ln 2 = (6.022 × 1026)(1.380649 × 10−23 J/K)(0.6931) = 5.763 × 103 J/K = 5.763 kJ/K.
  4. Classical route. For an ideal gas at constant T, ΔS = n Ru ln(V2/V1) = (1 kmol)(8.314 kJ/kmol·K)(ln 2) = (8.314)(0.6931) kJ/K = 5.763 kJ/K.
  5. Compare. The two agree to four figures because N k = n NA k = n Ru; the identity Ru = NA k is the bridge between the molecular and the macroscopic descriptions.

Sanity check: ΔS is positive for an irreversible free expansion, as the increase-of-entropy principle requires, and 5.76 kJ/K per kmol is Ru ln 2, the number that appears in every mixing and free-expansion problem.

Scaled to a familiar mass: 1 kg of air (M = 28.97 kg/kmol) contains 2.079 × 1025 molecules, so doubling its volume gives ΔS = N k ln 2 = 198.9 J/K = 0.1989 kJ/kg·K, which is R ln 2 with R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K. The log of the multiplicity ratio, ln(W2/W1) = N ln 2 = 1.44 × 1025, is a number with 25 digits: multiplicities themselves are never written out, only their logarithms.

Why entropy increases

The second law now reads: an isolated system, left alone, moves from macrostates with fewer microstates to macrostates with more, simply because a random walk through microstates spends almost all of its time in the biggest macrostate. For small N the fluctuations are visible (four coins show four heads one time in sixteen). For thermodynamic N the most probable macrostate is so overwhelmingly dominant that the relative fluctuation, which scales as 1/√N, is about 3 × 10−13 for 1025 molecules. That is why pressure and temperature look like exact, steady numbers on a gauge.

This also tells you what entropy is not. It is not \"disorder\" in a visual sense, and it is not a force. Heat flows from hot to cold because the combined multiplicity of the two bodies is larger when the energy is shared in that way; the arrangement with more ways wins.

The connection to the classical definition

Three checks tie S = k ln W to the entropy of the earlier chapters:

  • Same numbers. The worked example shows N k ln(V2/V1) equals the tabulated n Ru ln(V2/V1). The same holds for temperature changes once the momentum microstates are counted (next lesson).
  • Temperature. Define 1/T = (∂S/∂U)V,N. Two bodies in contact exchange energy until this derivative is equal for both, which is precisely the equilibrium condition, and it makes T the quantity that a thermometer reads. In the statistical picture temperature measures how fast the number of microstates grows when you add energy.
  • The third law. A perfect crystal at absolute zero has one microstate (W = 1), so S = k ln 1 = 0. The absolute entropies in Table A-26 of Cengel & Boles are counted from that state.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Using log10. The formula needs the natural log. For W = 20 the entropy is k ln 20 = 4.14 × 10−23 J/K; k log10 20 = 1.80 × 10−23 J/K is wrong by the factor ln 10 = 2.303.
  • Mixing k and Ru. k goes with a number of molecules N; Ru goes with kmol; R = Ru/M goes with kg. All three give the same ΔS if the counting quantity matches.
  • Treating W as a probability. W is a count (≥ 1). The probability of a macrostate is W divided by the total number of microstates.
  • Forgetting that W multiplies, S adds. Two independent samples: W doubles as a product, so S = k ln(WAWB) = SA + SB, never k ln(WA + WB).
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

The two-box count is a binomial distribution: the number of molecules in the left half is Binomial(N, 0.5). Its standard deviation is √N/2, so the relative spread is 1/√N, which is the whole argument for why macroscopic properties look steady. In Python, scipy.stats.binom.pmf(50, 100, 0.5) returns 0.0796 and math.comb(100, 50) returns 1.009 × 1029; try N = 20, 100, 1000 and watch the histogram sharpen.

Stirling's approximation is the same trick you use when a log-likelihood has factorials in it: ln N! is replaced by N ln N − N so the expression can be differentiated.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM
  • Count W for a small system (4 to 8 particles, two boxes or two energy levels) and compute S = k ln W in J/K.
  • Find ΔS for a free expansion or a mixing process from ΔS = N k ln(W2/W1) and show it equals n Ru ln(V2/V1).
  • Explain in two or three sentences why entropy increases, using the words microstate, macrostate and most probable.
  • State why the third law follows from W = 1.

This lesson lets you predict how molecules share energy at a given temperature and, from that single rule, derive the internal energy, entropy and specific heat of a gas. It is the engine room of statistical thermodynamics: the Boltzmann distribution explains why cv of argon is 3/2 R, why air is close to 5/2 R at room temperature, and why the cp tables you have been reading from since the Properties chapter rise with temperature.

The idea in plain words

Molecules can hold energy in discrete levels (a ladder). Thermal energy is handed around in random collisions, and the natural size of one hand-out is kT: at 300 K that is 4.14 × 10−21 J, or 0.02585 eV per molecule. A level that costs much more than kT to reach is rarely occupied; a level that costs much less than kT is nearly as populated as the ground level. The Boltzmann distribution makes this exact: the population falls off exponentially with the energy divided by kT.

The Boltzmann factor and the partition function

📘 DEFINITION

Boltzmann distribution: for a system in equilibrium at temperature T, the probability that a particle is in a state of energy εi is proportional to exp(−εi/kT). The factor exp(−εi/kT) is the Boltzmann factor.

Partition function Z: the sum of Boltzmann factors over every state, Z = Σi gi exp(−εi/kT). It is the normalising constant of the distribution and, as the next section shows, it encodes every thermodynamic property of the system.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

ni/nj = (gi/gj) exp[−(εi − εj)/kT]

pi = gi exp(−εi/kT) / Z, with Z = Σi gi exp(−εi/kT)

ni is the number of particles in level i; pi is the fraction in level i (dimensionless); εi is the energy of level i in J (or eV, then use k = 8.617 × 10−5 eV/K); gi is the degeneracy, the number of distinct states sharing energy εi; k = 1.380649 × 10−23 J/K; T is the absolute temperature in K. Z is dimensionless.

The distribution is the most probable one: it is what you get when you maximise W = N!/Π ni! from the previous lesson subject to fixed N and fixed total energy U = Σ ni εi, using Stirling's approximation and Lagrange multipliers. The multiplier attached to the energy constraint turns out to be 1/kT, which is how temperature enters the molecular picture.

From Z to U, S and cv

Once Z(T, V) is known, every property follows by differentiation. For N independent particles:

U = N k T2 (∂ ln Z/∂T)V

S = U/T + N k ln Z (distinguishable particles; for an ideal gas of identical molecules subtract k ln N! to avoid over-counting, which is the Sackur-Tetrode correction)

cv = (∂U/∂T)V, and the Helmholtz function F = U − TS = −N k T ln Z

U is internal energy in J, S is entropy in J/K, cv is the heat capacity at constant volume in J/K (divide by mass for kJ/kg·K or by kmol for kJ/kmol·K). The first formula is worth understanding: U = Σ ni εi = N Σ εi exp(−εi/kT)/Z, and differentiating ln Z with respect to T brings down exactly εi/kT2, which is the same sum.

Worked example: a two-level system

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem. Each of N = 1 mol of molecules can be in a ground state (ε0 = 0) or one excited state ε1 = 0.020 eV (both non-degenerate). At T = 300 K find the population ratio, Z, the fraction excited, the internal energy, the molar entropy and the molar cv. Constants: k = 8.617 × 10−5 eV/K = 1.380649 × 10−23 J/K, 1 eV = 1.602 × 10−19 J, Ru = 8.314 J/mol·K.

📊 FIGURE — Boltzmann populations: a ladder of levels and the two-level example
Bar length is the share of molecules on each level. Left: each step of kT cuts the population by the same factor e. Right: the worked example, where 0.020 eV is just below kT at 300 K.
  1. Thermal energy. kT = (8.617 × 10−5 eV/K)(300 K) = 0.02585 eV. The dimensionless ratio is x = ε1/kT = 0.020 eV / 0.02585 eV = 0.7736.
  2. Population ratio. n1/n0 = exp(−0.7736) = 0.4613. The excited level holds 46 % as many molecules as the ground level.
  3. Partition function. Z = exp(0) + exp(−0.7736) = 1 + 0.4613 = 1.4613.
  4. Fractions. p0 = 1/Z = 0.6843; p1 = 0.4613/1.4613 = 0.3157. Check: 0.6843 + 0.3157 = 1.0000.
  5. Internal energy. Per molecule U/N = p1 ε1 = (0.3157)(0.020 eV) = 0.006314 eV = 1.012 × 10−21 J. For one mole: U = (1.012 × 10−21 J)(6.022 × 1023 mol−1) = 609 J/mol.
  6. Entropy. S = U/T + N k ln Z, so per mole S/Ru = x p1 + ln Z = (0.7736)(0.3157) + ln 1.4613 = 0.2442 + 0.3793 = 0.6236 and S = (0.6236)(8.314 J/mol·K) = 5.18 J/mol·K.
  7. Heat capacity. Differentiating U gives cv = Ru x2 ex/(1 + ex)2 = (8.314 J/mol·K)(0.7736)2(2.1676)/(3.1676)2 = 1.075 J/mol·K, which is 0.129 Ru.

Sanity check: the entropy cannot exceed the value for equal populations, Ru ln 2 = 5.76 J/mol·K, and 5.18 is below it; at 3000 K the same formulas give n1/n0 = 0.926, close to the equal-population limit, and cv falls to 0.0015 Ru because the levels are saturated. A two-level system is the one case where cv falls at high T; molecules with a ladder of many levels never saturate.

Equipartition of energy

When the level spacing is much smaller than kT the ladder looks continuous and the Boltzmann sum becomes an integral. For any energy term that is quadratic in a coordinate or a momentum (½mvx2, ½Iω2, ½κx2), that integral gives the same answer:

<ε> = ½ k T per quadratic term (\"degree of freedom\"), so U = (f/2) N k T = (f/2) n Ru T

cv = (f/2) R and cp = cv + R = (f/2 + 1) R, k = cp/cv = (f + 2)/f

f is the number of active quadratic terms; R is the gas constant of the particular gas in kJ/kg·K (Ru/M), or Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K if you work per kmol; here k in the ratio cp/cv is the usual specific-heat ratio, not the Boltzmann constant. The count of f:

  • Monatomic (He, Ar, Ne): three translational terms, f = 3. cv = 3/2 Ru = 12.47 kJ/kmol·K, cp = 20.79 kJ/kmol·K, ratio 5/3 = 1.667.
  • Diatomic at room temperature (N2, O2, H2, CO): three translational plus two rotational terms (rotation about the bond axis has negligible moment of inertia), f = 5. cv = 5/2 Ru = 20.79 kJ/kmol·K, cp = 7/2 Ru = 29.10 kJ/kmol·K, ratio 7/5 = 1.4.
  • Diatomic with vibration fully active: the bond adds a kinetic and a potential term, f = 7. cv = 7/2 Ru, ratio 9/7 = 1.286.

Compare with the ideal-gas specific heats at 300 K in Table A-2(a) of Cengel & Boles (values computed here from (f/2)Ru/M with Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K):

GasM (kg/kmol)fcv equipartition (kJ/kg·K)cp equipartition (kJ/kg·K)cp table, 300 K (kJ/kg·K)
Ar39.94830.31220.52030.5203
He4.00333.1155.1925.193
N228.01350.74201.03881.039
O231.99950.64960.90940.918
Air28.9750.71751.00451.005

The monatomic gases match to four figures. Nitrogen and air match to 0.1 %. Oxygen sits 1 % above 5/2 R because its vibrational temperature is lower, so a little vibration is already awake at 300 K. Nothing in classical thermodynamics explains these numbers; equipartition predicts them from the shape of the molecule alone.

Why cv rises with temperature

Equipartition assumes every quadratic term is fully excited, which requires kT to be large compared with the level spacing. Rotation of N2 has a characteristic temperature θrot = 2.9 K, so it is fully classical at any temperature you will meet. Vibration is different: the vibrational level spacing of N2 corresponds to θvib = hcω/k = 3393 K (from the fundamental wavenumber ω = 2358.6 cm−1). At 300 K only exp(−3393/300) = 1.2 × 10−5 of the molecules are vibrationally excited, so the vibration is frozen and f = 5. As T rises the vibrational term switches on gradually, and cv climbs from 5/2 R toward 7/2 R. The exact contribution for a harmonic vibrator follows from the partition function Zvib = 1/(1 − e−θ/T):

cv,vib/R = (θvib/T)2 eθvib/T / (eθvib/T − 1)2

For N2 (R = 8.314/28.013 = 0.2968 kJ/kg·K), computed with θvib = 3393 K and compared with the cp polynomial of Table A-2(c), cp = 28.90 − 0.1571 × 10−2 T + 0.8081 × 10−5 T2 − 2.873 × 10−9 T3 kJ/kmol·K:

T (K)θvib/Tcv,vib/Rcv model (kJ/kg·K)cp model (kJ/kg·K)cp polynomial (kJ/kg·K)
30011.310.0020.7421.0391.038
6005.6550.1130.7751.0721.080
10003.3930.4140.8651.1621.162
15002.2620.6640.9391.2361.251

A single harmonic oscillator with one measured constant reproduces the table to within 1.2 % over 1200 K. The remaining difference is anharmonicity of the real bond and vibration-rotation coupling. The same reasoning explains the ratio k = cp/cv dropping from 1.400 at 300 K to (3.5 + 0.414)/(2.5 + 0.414) = 1.343 at 1000 K, which is why the Gas Power Cycles chapter warned against using k = 1.4 for a hot turbine.

✅ VERIFIED

The N2 fundamental vibrational wavenumber 2358.6 cm−1 and rotational constant B = 1.998 cm−1 used above are the constants listed for the ground electronic state of nitrogen in the NIST Chemistry WebBook, https://webbook.nist.gov/cgi/cbook.cgi?ID=C7727379&Mask=1000; θ = hcω/k with h = 6.62607 × 10−34 J·s and c = 2.99792 × 1010 cm/s gives 3393 K and 2.875 K.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Dropping the minus sign. exp(+0.7736) = 2.17 would put more molecules in the higher level than the lower one, which never happens at positive temperature.
  • Celsius in kT. 0.020 eV at \"27\" gives exp(−0.020/0.002326) = 1.8 × 10−4 instead of 0.461. T is always kelvin.
  • Ratio versus fraction. n1/n0 = 0.461 is the ratio; the fraction of all molecules in level 1 is p1 = 0.316. Read the question.
  • Counting rotation for a monatomic gas or a third rotation for a linear molecule. Argon has f = 3, N2 has f = 5, not 6.
  • Confusing cv and cp. Equipartition gives cv = (f/2)R; cp is R higher. For argon cv = 0.312 and cp = 0.520 kJ/kg·K.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM
  • Compute a population ratio or Z for a two- or three-level system at a stated T, then U and S from it. Keep x = ε/kT as a named intermediate.
  • State the equipartition value of cv, cp and k for a monatomic and a diatomic gas and convert between per-kmol and per-kg using M.
  • Explain, with θvib and kT, why cp of a diatomic gas rises with temperature while a monatomic gas stays at 5/2 Ru forever.
  • Derive U = N k T2 d(ln Z)/dT from U = Σ ni εi in three lines.

This lesson lets you derive P v = R T from molecules bouncing off a wall, read the temperature of a gas as the average kinetic energy of its molecules, and estimate molecular speeds, mean free paths and collision rates. It is the second half of the statistical-thermodynamics introduction in a degree sequence, and it is where the ideal-gas model finally gets its justification and its limits.

The idea in plain words

Gas pressure is not a smooth push. It is the drum-roll of roughly 1028 molecules per square metre per second hitting the wall and bouncing back. Each impact transfers a tiny momentum; the average rate of momentum transfer per unit area is the pressure. Faster molecules hit harder and more often, so pressure grows with the square of the speed, and since the average kinetic energy is what temperature measures, pressure grows with T. Everything else in this lesson is that sentence written out with algebra.

Pressure from molecular collisions

Consider N molecules of mass m in a box of volume V. A molecule with x-velocity vx bounces elastically off the right wall and its momentum changes by 2 m vx. It returns to that wall every 2L/vx seconds, so the average force it exerts is (2 m vx)/(2L/vx) = m vx2/L. Summing over molecules and dividing by the wall area A (with V = A L):

P = (N m <vx2>)/V = (1/3)(N m <v2>)/V

The factor 1/3 appears because no direction is special, so <vx2> = <vy2> = <vz2> = <v2>/3. Here P is in Pa, N is the number of molecules, m the mass of one molecule in kg, V in m3, and <v2> is the mean of the squared speed in m2/s2.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

P V = (1/3) N m vrms2 = (2/3) N (½ m vrms2)

Comparing with the ideal-gas law P V = N k T gives ½ m vrms2 = (3/2) k T and therefore

vrms = √(3 k T / m) = √(3 Ru T / M)

vrms = √<v2> is the root-mean-square speed in m/s; k = 1.380649 × 10−23 J/K; T in K; m in kg per molecule; Ru = 8314 J/kmol·K (note the units) and M in kg/kmol. Temperature is, by this equation, a measure of the average translational kinetic energy per molecule: (3/2)kT per molecule, (3/2)RuT per kmol.

The Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution

Applying the Boltzmann factor of the previous lesson to translational kinetic energy ½mv2, and counting how many velocity states lie in a shell of radius v (proportional to v2), gives the fraction of molecules with speed between v and v + dv:

📊 FIGURE — Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution of nitrogen at 300 K and 600 K
Height is the share of molecules at each speed. At 300 K the three marked speeds are those of the worked example; doubling T flattens the hump and fattens the fast tail.

f(v) = 4π (m / 2πkT)3/2 v2 exp(−m v2 / 2kT)

f(v) has units of s/m, and ∫f(v)dv from 0 to ∞ equals 1. The v2 factor kills the curve at zero speed, the exponential kills it at high speed, and in between there is a hump. Three speeds summarise it:

📘 DEFINITION

Most probable speed vmp = √(2RT/M): the peak of f(v).

Mean speed vmean = √(8RT/πM): the arithmetic average, used for collision rates and effusion.

Root-mean-square speed vrms = √(3RT/M): the speed that carries the average kinetic energy, used for pressure and temperature. Always vmp < vmean < vrms in the ratio 1 : 1.128 : 1.225. Here R means Ru/M in J/kg·K, i.e. Ru = 8314 J/kmol·K with M in kg/kmol.

The distribution is wide. Integrating f(v) numerically for N2 shows that 1.05 % of molecules at 300 K move faster than 1000 m/s (about twice vrms), and at 600 K that fraction is 13.2 %. This high-speed tail is what drives evaporation and chemical reactions: only the fast molecules have enough energy to escape or react, and their number grows exponentially with T.

Mean free path and collision rate

A molecule of diameter d sweeps out a collision cylinder of cross-section πd2. With n = N/V molecules per m3 and the √2 correction for the relative motion of the targets, the average distance between collisions is

λ = 1 / (√2 π d2 n) = k T / (√2 π d2 P), and the collision frequency is z = vmean / λ

λ is the mean free path in m, d the effective molecular diameter in m, n the number density in m−3 (n = P/kT for an ideal gas), P in Pa, and z the number of collisions one molecule suffers per second.

Worked example: nitrogen at room conditions

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Problem. Nitrogen (M = 28.013 kg/kmol, effective diameter d = 3.64 × 10−10 m from viscosity data) is at 300 K and 101.325 kPa. Find vrms, vmean, vmp, the number density, the pressure predicted by kinetic theory, the mean free path and the collision frequency. Constants: Ru = 8314 J/kmol·K, k = 1.380649 × 10−23 J/K, NA = 6.02214 × 1026 kmol−1.

  1. Speeds. 3RuT/M = 3(8314 J/kmol·K)(300 K)/(28.013 kg/kmol) = 2.671 × 105 m2/s2, so vrms = √(2.671 × 105) = 516.8 m/s. Then vmean = vrms√(8/3π) = 516.8 × 0.9213 = 476.2 m/s and vmp = vrms√(2/3) = 516.8 × 0.8165 = 422.0 m/s.
  2. Number density. n = P/kT = (101 325 Pa)/[(1.380649 × 10−23 J/K)(300 K)] = 101 325 / 4.142 × 10−21 = 2.446 × 1025 m−3.
  3. Mass of one molecule. m = M/NA = 28.013 kg/kmol ÷ 6.02214 × 1026 kmol−1 = 4.652 × 10−26 kg.
  4. Pressure from collisions. P = (1/3) n m vrms2 = (1/3)(2.446 × 1025 m−3)(4.652 × 10−26 kg)(2.671 × 105 m2/s2) = 1.013 × 105 Pa = 101.3 kPa, the pressure we started from. Kinetic energy per molecule: ½ m vrms2 = ½(4.652 × 10−26)(2.671 × 105) = 6.213 × 10−21 J, and (3/2)kT = 1.5 × 4.142 × 10−21 = 6.213 × 10−21 J. Same number.
  5. Mean free path. √2 π d2 = 1.4142 × 3.1416 × (3.64 × 10−10 m)2 = 5.887 × 10−19 m2. λ = kT/(√2 π d2 P) = (4.142 × 10−21 J)/[(5.887 × 10−19 m2)(101 325 Pa)] = 4.142 × 10−21/5.965 × 10−14 = 6.94 × 10−8 m = 69.4 nm.
  6. Collision frequency. z = vmean/λ = (476.2 m/s)/(6.944 × 10−8 m) = 6.86 × 109 collisions per second, i.e. one collision every 0.146 ns.

Sanity check: vrms of about 500 m/s is 1.5 times the speed of sound in air (343 m/s at 20 °C), as it must be since sound is carried by these molecules; λ = 69 nm is about 190 molecular diameters, so the gas is dilute and the ideal-gas assumptions hold.

The ideal-gas law derived, and where it fails

Combine P V = (1/3) N m vrms2 with the equipartition result ½ m vrms2 = (3/2) k T and you get P V = N k T. Writing N = n NA gives P V = n Ru T, and dividing by mass gives P v = R T with R = Ru/M. The gas constant of the Properties chapter is Boltzmann's constant counted per kilogram instead of per molecule. The derivation used four assumptions, and each one names a way the law can fail:

  1. Molecules occupy negligible volume. Fails at high density: the free volume is less than V, so the real pressure is higher than ideal. Van der Waals corrects this with (v − b).
  2. No forces between molecules except during collisions. Fails near condensation: attractions pull molecules back from the wall, so the real pressure is lower. Van der Waals corrects this with −a/v2.
  3. Collisions are elastic and molecules are in random motion. Fails for rarefied gases where λ becomes comparable to the container (Knudsen number λ/L approaching 1): molecules then hit the walls more than each other, and the notion of local pressure and temperature weakens. At 1 Pa the mean free path of N2 at 300 K is already 7 mm.
  4. Classical statistics. Fails at very low T or very high density where quantum effects matter (electrons in metals, helium below a few kelvin).

How big are the corrections for nitrogen at 300 K? Using the van der Waals constants a = 137.0 kPa·m6/kmol2 and b = 0.0387 m3/kmol (equivalently 1.370 bar·L2/mol2 and 0.0387 L/mol), P = RuT/(v − b) − a/v2, the compressibility factor Z = Pv/RuT works out to 0.9993 at 1 atm, 0.9937 at 10 atm and 0.963 at 100 atm. The ideal-gas law is good to 0.1 % at atmospheric pressure and 4 % low at 100 atm, which is the same message the generalized compressibility chart gave in the Properties chapter, now with a molecular reason attached.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Ru in the wrong units. With M in kg/kmol you need Ru = 8314 J/kmol·K. Using 8.314 with M = 28.013 gives vrms = 16.3 m/s, wrong by √1000 = 31.6.
  • Celsius. √(3 × 8314 × 27/28.013) = 155 m/s is not the speed of nitrogen at 27 °C; use 300 K and get 517 m/s.
  • Which speed? Pressure and temperature use vrms; collision rate and effusion use vmean; a question about the peak of the distribution wants vmp. They differ by up to 22 %.
  • Pressure in kPa inside λ. kT/(√2πd2P) needs P in Pa; using 101.325 gives 69 µm instead of 69 nm.
  • Forgetting √2 in the mean free path (gives 98 nm instead of 69 nm), or using d instead of d2.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM
  • Derive P = (1/3) n m <v2> from momentum transfer at a wall, stating where the 2, the 1/3 and the 2L/vx come from.
  • Compute vrms, vmean and vmp for a named gas at a given T and rank them.
  • Compute a mean free path and collision rate and comment on whether the continuum (ideal-gas) description holds.
  • Explain which ideal-gas assumption fails at high pressure and which near the saturation line, and what sign of error each produces.
  • Show that (3/2)kT per molecule leads to cv = (3/2)R for a monatomic gas.

This lesson lets you take any wall, pipe, tank or insulated wire, draw it as a chain of thermal resistances, and compute the heat flow and every interface temperature. It is the first of three heat-transfer lessons that sit alongside the thermodynamics sequence: thermodynamics told you how much heat a process needs; heat transfer tells you how fast it can move and through what. Conduction is the mode you meet first because it has the cleanest law and the resistance picture you learn here is reused for convection and radiation.

Conduction in plain words

Put one end of a metal spoon in hot tea and the handle warms up. No material moved along the spoon; the fast-vibrating atoms and free electrons at the hot end handed energy to their slower neighbours, and so on down the handle. That is conduction: energy transfer through a medium by molecular interaction, always from higher temperature to lower, with no bulk motion. Three things obviously set the rate. A bigger temperature difference drives more heat. A thicker or longer path slows it. And the material matters enormously: a copper spoon burns your fingers, a wooden one never does. Fourier's law puts those three observations into one equation.

Fourier's law and thermal conductivity

📘 DEFINITION

Fourier's law of heat conduction: the rate of heat conduction through a layer is proportional to the area normal to the flow and to the temperature gradient across it, and opposite in sign to the gradient (heat flows downhill in temperature). The proportionality constant is the material's thermal conductivity k, in W/m·K: the heat rate through a 1 m thick slab of 1 m² area with 1 K across it.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

Q̇cond = −k A (dT/dx)

Q̇ heat transfer rate (W); k thermal conductivity (W/m·K); A area normal to the flow (m²); dT/dx temperature gradient (K/m). The minus sign makes Q̇ positive in the direction of decreasing T. For a plane layer of thickness L in steady state with surface temperatures T1 > T2 the gradient is uniform and the law integrates to Q̇ = k A (T1 − T2) / L. Heat flux is q̇ = Q̇/A in W/m².

Thermal conductivity spans about five orders of magnitude, which is why material choice dominates every conduction problem. Values at roughly room temperature from the property tables in Cengel & Ghajar, Heat and Mass Transfer (Tables A-3, A-9 and A-15) and the Engineering ToolBox:

Materialk (W/m·K)Class
Copper (pure)401Metal, excellent conductor
Aluminium (pure)237Metal
Stainless steel (AISI 304)≈ 15Alloy; alloying always lowers k
Common brick0.72Building material
Water (liquid, 25 °C)0.607Liquid
Gypsum plaster / plasterboard0.17Building material
Glass-fibre batt insulation≈ 0.04Insulation (trapped still air)
Air (still, 25 °C)0.0255Gas; the reason insulation works

Notice that good insulators are mostly trapped air: glass fibre, foam and feathers all work by holding air still so it cannot convect. Metals conduct through free electrons as well as lattice vibrations, which is why electrical and thermal conductivity go together (the Wiedemann-Franz relation). k also varies with temperature; degree-level problems usually let you take it constant at the mean temperature of the layer.

The thermal resistance analogy

Rewrite the plane-wall result as Q̇ = (T1 − T2) / R with R = L/(kA) and it looks exactly like Ohm's law: temperature difference is the voltage, heat rate is the current, and R (in K/W) is the resistance. That is not a coincidence, it is the same linear diffusion mathematics. The payoff is that layers in series simply add their resistances, parallel paths add their conductances (1/R), and a surface exchanging heat with a fluid by convection is just one more resistor in the chain. Every steady one-dimensional conduction problem becomes: draw the circuit, add the resistances, divide.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

Plane wall: Rwall = L / (k A)   (K/W)

Cylindrical shell of length L, inner radius r1, outer r2: Rcyl = ln(r2/r1) / (2π k L)

Spherical shell: Rsph = (r2 − r1) / (4π k r1 r2)

Convection film on a surface of area A with coefficient h (W/m²·K): Rconv = 1 / (h A)

Series chain: Q̇ = (T∞,1 − T∞,2) / ΣR; the temperature at any node follows from Tnode = T∞,1 − Q̇ · ΣR(up to that node). The overall heat transfer coefficient is defined by Q̇ = U A ΔT so U A = 1/ΣR.

The cylinder formula has a logarithm because the area 2πrL grows with radius: the same heat rate crosses a bigger area further out, so the gradient flattens. For a thin shell (r2/r1 close to 1) it collapses to the plane-wall form with the mean area. Two more resistances appear in practice. Thermal contact resistance: two solid faces pressed together touch only at high spots, and the gaps hold air, so the interface behaves like a thin extra resistor Rc = 1/(hc A); hc is measured, typically thousands to tens of thousands of W/m²·K, and thermal grease or a soft foil raises it. Fouling on heat-exchanger surfaces is the same idea with a deposit layer.

Worked example: a composite house wall

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A wall 15 m² in area is, from inside to outside, 2 cm of gypsum plaster (k = 0.17 W/m·K), 20 cm of common brick (k = 0.72 W/m·K) and 5 cm of glass-fibre insulation (k = 0.04 W/m·K). Room air is 22 °C with hi = 10 W/m²·K; outside air is -5 °C with ho = 25 W/m²·K. Find the heat loss, the U-value, the temperature of every interface, and how much the insulation is doing.

📊 FIGURE — The composite house wall: temperature profile and resistance chain
Top: the wall with the temperature at each interface; the steepest drop is across the insulation. Bottom: the same wall as five resistors in series. Add them, then Q = ΔT/ΣR.
  1. Draw the circuit: five resistors in series, room air → inside film → plaster → brick → insulation → outside film → outside air. All share the same A = 15 m² (plane wall).
  2. Inside film: Ri = 1/(hiA) = 1/(10 W/m²·K × 15 m²) = 0.00667 K/W.
  3. Plaster: Rp = L/(kA) = 0.02 m /(0.17 W/m·K × 15 m²) = 0.00784 K/W.
  4. Brick: Rb = 0.20 m /(0.72 W/m·K × 15 m²) = 0.01852 K/W.
  5. Insulation: Rins = 0.05 m /(0.04 W/m·K × 15 m²) = 0.08333 K/W.
  6. Outside film: Ro = 1/(25 W/m²·K × 15 m²) = 0.00267 K/W.
  7. Total: ΣR = 0.11903 K/W. The insulation alone is 70% of it.
  8. Heat loss: Q̇ = (Ti − To)/ΣR = (22 − (-5)) K / 0.11903 K/W = 227 W (flux 15.1 W/m²).
  9. U-value: U = 1/(ΣR · A) = 1/(0.11903 K/W × 15 m²) = 0.560 W/m²·K.
  10. Interface temperatures, walking the circuit from the room: inside surface T1 = 22 − 227 W × 0.00667 K/W = 20.5 °C; plaster/brick T2 = 20.5 − 227 × 0.00784 = 18.7 °C; brick/insulation T3 = 18.7 − 227 × 0.01852 = 14.5 °C; outer surface T4 = 14.5 − 227 × 0.08333 = -4.4 °C. One more step, -4.4 − 227 × 0.00267, returns -5 °C, the outside air, which closes the check.
  11. Without the insulation: ΣR = 0.03569 K/W, Q̇ = 756 W, i.e. 3.3 times the loss, and the inside surface would sit at 17.0 °C, cold enough to feel and to risk condensation.

Sanity check: the biggest temperature drop (18.9 K) is across the biggest resistor (the insulation) and the drops sum to the 27 K total; both must hold in any series circuit.

Cylinders, pipes and the critical radius of insulation

Pipes are the same circuit with the logarithmic resistance and with different areas at the inside and outside films. A steam line: stainless steel pipe (k = 15 W/m·K) inner radius 2.5 cm, outer radius 3.0 cm, wrapped in 3 cm of glass wool (k = 0.038 W/m·K), 20 m long; steam at 150 °C with hi = 80 W/m²·K inside, air at 20 °C with ho = 10 W/m²·K outside. Computed step by step: Ri = 1/(hi·2πr1L) = 0.00398 K/W; Rsteel = ln(3.0/2.5)/(2π·15·20) = 0.000097 K/W, negligible; Rwool = ln(6.0/3.0)/(2π·0.038·20) = 0.14516 K/W; Ro = 1/(ho·2πr3L) = 0.01326 K/W. ΣR = 0.16249 K/W, so Q̇ = 800 W (40 W per metre) and the outer surface sits at 30.6 °C, safe to touch. Bare, the same pipe would lose 4248 W. The metal wall is irrelevant; the insulation and the outside film are the whole story, which is the normal pattern.

Adding insulation to a cylinder does two opposing things: it adds conduction resistance, but it also enlarges the outer area and so lowers the convection resistance 1/(h·2πroL). Differentiating the total with respect to ro gives a minimum at the critical radius rcr,cyl = k/h (and rcr,sph = 2k/h for a sphere). Below rcr, adding insulation increases heat loss. For a 1.5 mm radius wire with plastic insulation k = 0.15 W/m·K in air with h = 12 W/m²·K, rcr = 0.15/12 = 12.5 mm, and the resistance per metre of the insulation-plus-film computes to 8.84 K/W bare, 5.16 at 3 mm, 3.68 at 6 mm, 3.31 at the critical 12.5 mm, and back up to 3.62 at 30 mm. So insulating an electrical wire helps it shed heat (good for the wire) up to 12.5 mm; for a large pipe, whose radius is already far past k/h, insulation always helps, and the \"trap\" only bites on thin wires and small tubes.

Fins, in words

When the convection resistance 1/(hA) dominates, the cheap fix is more A: extended surfaces or fins, the ridges on a CPU heat sink or a motorcycle engine. Heat conducts along the fin while leaking out of its sides by convection, so the fin cools along its length and its tip is nearly at the fluid temperature: the far end does little. Two numbers describe a fin. Fin efficiency ηfin is the actual heat rate divided by the rate if the whole fin were at the base temperature; it falls as the fin gets longer or thinner, or the material less conductive, through the parameter m = √(h p / (k Ac)) (p is the perimeter, Ac the cross-section). Fin effectiveness εfin is the heat rate with the fin divided by the rate from the bare base area; a fin is only worth having if εfin is well above 1, which is why fins are made of aluminium or copper, are thin and many, and are used on the gas side (low h) of a heat exchanger rather than the liquid side.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Using the plane-wall formula L/(kA) for a pipe with A taken at the inside radius. For thick shells that can be wrong by a factor of two; use ln(r2/r1)/(2πkL). Also: forgetting the two convection films (that alone changes the wall answer above from 227 W to 246 W), mixing cm and m in L (a thousandfold error in L/k), and writing the temperature at a node as T∞ minus Q̇ times the wrong partial sum. And note that ΔT in kelvin equals ΔT in degrees Celsius, so conduction problems never need the 273.15 conversion; radiation problems always do.

★ ON THE EXAM

The standard question is a composite wall or insulated pipe with convection on both sides: draw the circuit, tabulate every R with units, get Q̇, then one interior temperature, then \"what thickness of insulation halves the loss?\" (solve ΣR = 2 × old ΣR for L). Critical radius appears as a short conceptual or one-line numerical: rcr = k/h, cylinder; 2k/h, sphere. Fins are tested in words: what ηfin and εfin mean and why fins go on the gas side.

✅ VERIFIED

Property values used here: air at 1 atm (k = 0.02551 W/m·K at 25 °C, and the 40 °C values used in the next lesson) from Cengel Table A-15, reproduced at cecs.wright.edu (Cengel appendix tables); brick, plaster and fibreglass conductivities cross-checked against the Engineering ToolBox thermal-conductivity table. Convection coefficients in the examples (h = 10, 25, 80, 12 W/m²·K) are assumed inputs, not measured values.
