This lesson lets you estimate the convection coefficient h for a real flow, from picking the right empirical correlation to checking its validity range, and then combine h with wall conduction into the overall coefficient U that sizes a heat exchanger. In the degree it is the middle third of the heat-transfer introduction and the one that leans hardest on fluid mechanics: everything about h comes from what the fluid is doing in the thin layer next to the wall.

Convection in plain words

Blow on hot soup and it cools faster. The air touching the soup warms by conduction, but your breath keeps replacing that warm air with cool air, so the temperature difference at the surface stays large. Convection is conduction at a surface plus bulk fluid motion carrying the energy away. If a fan or pump drives the motion it is forced convection; if the fluid moves only because heated fluid is lighter and rises (a radiator, a candle plume) it is natural (free) convection. Phase change (boiling, condensation) gives the highest rates of all because latent heat is carried at nearly constant temperature. In every case the rate is proportional to the surface area and to the temperature difference between the surface and the fluid far from it, and everything else is bundled into one coefficient.

Newton's law of cooling and the coefficient h

📘 DEFINITION

Convection heat transfer coefficient h (W/m²·K): the heat rate per unit surface area per unit temperature difference between the surface and the undisturbed fluid. It is not a property of the fluid alone; it depends on the fluid, the velocity, the geometry, the surface roughness and whether the flow is laminar or turbulent.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

Q̇conv = h As (Ts − T∞)

As surface area in contact with the fluid (m²); Ts surface temperature; T∞ free-stream (or bulk) fluid temperature. The convection resistance is Rconv = 1/(h As). Right at the wall the fluid is stationary (no-slip), so the heat actually enters the fluid by conduction: q̇ = −kfluid (∂T/∂y)y=0 = h (Ts − T∞). That equality is where h comes from.

Typical ranges (Cengel & Ghajar, Table 1-5): free convection of gases 2-25 W/m²·K; free convection of liquids 10-1,000; forced convection of gases 25-250; forced convection of liquids 50-20,000; boiling and condensation 2,500-100,000. These orders of magnitude are worth memorising: they tell you at a glance that the air side of any air-to-water exchanger is the bottleneck, and they let you sanity-check a computed h.

Boundary layers and the dimensionless numbers

Fluid approaching a plate at speed V is slowed to zero at the wall; the slowed region, the velocity boundary layer, grows in thickness δ along the plate. Similarly the fluid heated by the wall forms a thermal boundary layer δt. Near the leading edge both are thin, the gradients are steep and h is high; downstream they thicken and h falls, until at some distance the laminar layer trips into turbulence, eddies stir the layer and h jumps back up. Turbulent flow is the friend of heat transfer and the enemy of pumping power. Rather than solving the boundary-layer equations for every case, engineers compress the physics into dimensionless groups:

NumberDefinitionMeaning
Reynolds ReV Lc/ν = ρ V Lc/μinertia / viscous forces; laminar vs turbulent. Flat plate: transition near 5 × 10⁵; pipe: turbulent above about 10,000 (laminar below 2,300)
Prandtl Prν/α = μ cp/kmomentum diffusivity / thermal diffusivity; δ vs δt. Gases ≈ 0.7, water 2-7, oils 100+, liquid metals ≪ 1
Nusselt Nuh Lc/kfluidconvection / pure conduction across the same layer; Nu = 1 is a stagnant film. The output of every correlation
Grashof Grg β (Ts − T∞) Lc³/ν²buoyancy / viscous forces; plays the role of Re in natural convection. β = 1/Tfilm (K) for an ideal gas
Rayleigh RaGr · Prthe single parameter of natural-convection correlations; laminar below about 10⁹

Lc is the characteristic length: plate length for a flat plate, diameter for a pipe or cylinder, height for a vertical wall. The whole subject of convection is then a library of fits of the form Nu = C Rem Prn (forced) or Nu = C Ran (natural), each valid only for one geometry, one flow regime and a stated range.

Using an empirical correlation correctly

The recipe, which the exam expects you to follow in this order:

  1. Fix the film temperature Tf = (Ts + T∞)/2 (external flow) or the bulk mean temperature (internal flow) and look up k, ν (or μ and ρ), Pr there.
  2. Compute Re (or Ra) with the correct characteristic length and decide the regime.
  3. Choose the correlation for that geometry and regime and check its stated validity range for Re and Pr.
  4. Compute Nu, then h = Nu k/Lc, then Q̇ = h A ΔT. Keep 10-25 % uncertainty in mind; correlations are fits to data, not laws.

The standard set you should recognise:

  • Flat plate, laminar (ReL < 5 × 10⁵), average over the plate: Nu = 0.664 ReL1/2 Pr1/3 (Pr > 0.6). Local value at x: 0.332 Rex1/2 Pr1/3.
  • Flat plate, turbulent from the leading edge: Nu = 0.037 ReL4/5 Pr1/3; mixed laminar-then-turbulent: Nu = (0.037 ReL4/5 − 871) Pr1/3.
  • Fully developed turbulent pipe flow (Dittus-Boelter): Nu = 0.023 Re0.8 Prn, n = 0.4 when the fluid is heated, 0.3 when cooled; Re > 10,000, 0.7 ≤ Pr ≤ 160.
  • Fully developed laminar pipe flow: Nu = 3.66 for constant wall temperature, 4.36 for constant heat flux, independent of Re.
  • Natural convection, vertical plate: Nu = 0.59 RaL1/4 for 10⁴ < Ra < 10⁹ and Nu = 0.1 RaL1/3 for 10⁹ < Ra < 10¹³.

Worked example: air over a flat plate

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Air at 20 °C and 1 atm flows at 8 m/s along a flat plate 0.5 m long and 1 m wide held at 60 °C. Find the average convection coefficient and the heat rate from the top surface.

📊 FIGURE — Laminar boundary layer on the heated plate, and how h falls along it
Top: the velocity layer (solid) and thermal layer (dashed) thicken with distance; arrows show the velocity profile. Bottom: local h falls as x^−1/2; its average over the plate is 15.4 W/m²·K.
  1. Film temperature Tf = (60 + 20)/2 = 40 °C. Air at 40 °C, 1 atm (Cengel Table A-15): k = 0.02662 W/m·K, ν = 1.702 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s, Pr = 0.7255.
  2. ReL = V L/ν = (8 m/s × 0.5 m)/(1.702 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s) = 235,018. This is below 5 × 10⁵, so the boundary layer is laminar over the whole plate.
  3. Laminar average correlation, Pr = 0.7255 > 0.6, valid: Nu = 0.664 ReL1/2 Pr1/3 = 0.664 × (235,018)0.5 × (0.7255)1/3 = 0.664 × 484.8 × 0.8986 = 289.2.
  4. h = Nu k/L = 289.2 × 0.02662 W/m·K / 0.5 m = 15.4 W/m²·K. Check against the table of ranges: forced convection of a gas, 25-250 W/m²·K; a slow laminar flow landing just below the range is plausible.
  5. Q̇ = h A (Ts − T∞) = 15.4 W/m²·K × (0.5 × 1) m² × (60 − 20) K = 308 W.
  6. Boundary-layer thickness at the trailing edge, δ ≈ 5 L/√ReL = 5 × 0.5 m / 484.8 = 5.2 mm: a few millimetres of air are doing all the work.

Sanity check: had the flow been turbulent (0.037 Re0.8 Pr1/3) the answer would be Nu = 659, h = 35.1 W/m²·K, Q̇ = 701 W, more than double: choosing the regime is the single most consequential step.

The overall heat transfer coefficient U

A heat exchanger wall separates two fluids: hot fluid → inside film → wall → outside film → cold fluid. The series resistance per unit area is 1/U = 1/hi + twall/kwall + 1/ho for a thin wall of thickness t (for a tube, use the log resistance and pick which area U refers to). Fouling deposits add Rf,i and Rf,o in m²·K/W to the sum. Example: water at 40 °C (Cengel Table A-9: ρ = 992.1 kg/m³, μ = 0.653 × 10⁻³ kg/m·s, k = 0.631 W/m·K, Pr = 4.32) flows at 1 m/s through a 20 mm stainless tube (wall 1 mm, k = 15 W/m·K) that is being heated on the outside by a condensing vapour with ho = 1500 W/m²·K. Re = ρVD/μ = 992.1 × 1 × 0.02 / 0.653 × 10⁻³ = 30,386, turbulent and above 10,000, Pr within 0.7-160, so Dittus-Boelter with n = 0.4 (heating) applies: Nu = 0.023 × 30,3860.8 × 4.320.4 = 159, hi = Nu k/D = 5024 W/m²·K. Then 1/U = 1/5024 + 0.001/15 + 1/1500 = 1.99e-04 + 6.67e-05 + 6.67e-04 = 9.32e-04 m²·K/W, so U = 1073 W/m²·K. The water film is the largest resistance, the wall is negligible; if this were air on one side, that side alone would set U.

Heat exchangers: LMTD and effectiveness-NTU in words

Along an exchanger the hot fluid cools and the cold fluid warms, so the driving ΔT changes from one end to the other. Integrating Q̇ = U dA ΔT along the length shows that the correct average is the log mean temperature difference:

🧮 KEY EQUATION

Q̇ = U As ΔTlm,   ΔTlm = (ΔT1 − ΔT2) / ln(ΔT1/ΔT2)

ΔT1 and ΔT2 are the hot-minus-cold differences at the two ends of the exchanger. Parallel flow: both fluids enter at the same end, so ΔT1 = Th,in − Tc,in. Counterflow: they enter at opposite ends, so ΔT1 = Th,in − Tc,out and ΔT2 = Th,out − Tc,in. Cross-flow and shell-and-tube use ΔTlm,counterflow times a correction factor F ≤ 1 read from charts. Energy balances on each stream give Q̇ = ṁh cp,h(Th,in − Th,out) = ṁc cp,c(Tc,out − Tc,in).

Numbers: hot water cools from 120 to 50 °C while heating 0.5 kg/s of cold water from 20 to 40 °C (cp = 4.18 kJ/kg·K) in a counterflow exchanger with U = 500 W/m²·K. Q̇ = 0.5 × 4.18 × (40 − 20) = 41.8 kW. End differences: ΔT1 = 120 − 40 = 80 K, ΔT2 = 50 − 20 = 30 K; ΔTlm = (80 − 30)/ln(80/30) = 51.0 K. Area A = Q̇/(U ΔTlm) = 41800 W/(500 × 51.0) = 1.64 m². The arithmetic mean (55 K) would have given 1.52 m², a small error here but a large one when the end differences differ a lot; in parallel flow the same temperatures give ΔTlm = 39.1 K and A = 2.14 m²: counterflow always needs less area for the same duty, and it is the only arrangement in which the cold outlet can exceed the hot outlet.

LMTD is convenient when all four temperatures are known and you want the area (design). When you know the exchanger and want the outlet temperatures (rating), the LMTD route needs iteration, and the effectiveness-NTU method is used instead. Define the heat-capacity rates C = ṁ cp for each stream; the smaller, Cmin, limits the exchange, because that stream would reach the other stream's inlet temperature first in an infinitely long exchanger. So Q̇max = Cmin(Th,in − Tc,in), the effectiveness is ε = Q̇/Q̇max, and the size of the exchanger relative to that stream is the number of transfer units NTU = U A/Cmin. For each flow arrangement ε is a known function of NTU and the ratio c = Cmin/Cmax, so with U, A and the inlet temperatures you read ε and get Q̇ and both outlets directly. In the example above Ch = 41.8/(120 − 50) = 0.597 kW/K, Cc = 2.09 kW/K, so Cmin = 0.597 kW/K, Q̇max = 0.597 × (120 − 20) = 59.7 kW, ε = 41.8/59.7 = 0.70 and NTU = 500 × 1.64/597 = 1.37. Effectiveness rises with NTU but with diminishing returns; beyond NTU ≈ 3 extra area buys little.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Evaluating the fluid properties at T∞ or Ts instead of the film temperature; using the local Nu (0.332…) when the question asks for the average over the plate (a factor of two); applying Dittus-Boelter to laminar flow or to a Pr outside 0.7-160; using the radius where the correlation wants the diameter (Re off by two, Nu off by 20.8); and forgetting that natural convection needs the temperature difference in Gr and β = 1/Tf with Tf in kelvin. In LMTD problems the classic error is taking ΔT1 and ΔT2 as the temperature changes of the two streams instead of the end-to-end hot-cold differences.

★ ON THE EXAM

Expect one \"find h\" problem following the six-step recipe above (film temperature, properties, Re, regime, correlation with its range stated, Nu → h → Q̇), and one heat-exchanger problem: energy balance for the unknown temperature or flow, ΔTlm for the stated arrangement, then A from Q̇ = U A ΔTlm. Conceptual marks go to: why turbulence raises h, why the air side controls U, why counterflow beats parallel flow, and when you would reach for ε-NTU instead of LMTD.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Every correlation here is a power-law fit, Nu = C Rem Prn, which becomes linear in logs: ln Nu = ln C + m ln Re + n ln Pr. If you ever have measured data, an ordinary least-squares regression on the log-transformed columns recovers C, m and n directly, and the residual plot tells you where the fit (and the regime assumption) breaks. Dittus-Boelter's 0.8 exponent is exactly such a slope on a log-log plot. Treat the textbook correlation as a model with a stated domain, the way you would any regression, and never extrapolate it.

"}, "THERMO/heat/s3": {"body": "

This lesson lets you compute radiation exchange between surfaces: how much a hot surface emits, how much of it a second surface receives, and the net rate between them, including the two everyday puzzles the syllabus names, a clear night sky that frosts a car roof at +3 °C air temperature and a parked car that cooks its interior. It completes the three modes; in the degree, radiation is the mode that behaves least like the other two, because it needs no medium and depends on absolute temperature to the fourth power.

Radiation in plain words

Stand near a bonfire: your face feels the heat instantly, even in cold air, and turning away stops it. Nothing conducted through the air quickly enough to explain that; the energy travelled as electromagnetic waves, at the speed of light, straight from the flames to your skin. Every body above absolute zero emits thermal radiation, mostly in the infrared at ordinary temperatures, shifting into the visible when things glow red then white. Radiation is a surface phenomenon for opaque solids (it comes from the top few microns), it needs no medium (it is how the Sun heats the Earth across vacuum), and unlike conduction and convection it depends on T⁴, so it is negligible between objects near room temperature only in comparison with strong forced convection, and it dominates at furnace temperatures and in still air.

The blackbody: Stefan-Boltzmann, Planck and Wien

📘 DEFINITION

A blackbody is the ideal surface: it absorbs all incident radiation at every wavelength and direction, and at a given temperature no surface can emit more. A small hole in the wall of a large cavity behaves as one. The emissive power E is the radiation emitted per unit area (W/m²); the blackbody value is Eb.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

Eb = σ T4   (Stefan-Boltzmann law),   σ = 5.670 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²·K⁴,   T in kelvin, always.

λmax T = 2897.8 μm·K   (Wien's displacement law): the wavelength at which the blackbody spectrum peaks.

Planck's distribution gives the spectrum Ebλ(λ, T) behind both: integrating it over all wavelengths gives σT⁴, differentiating it gives Wien. Numbers: the Sun's photosphere at 5772 K emits Eb = σ × 5772⁴ = 6.29e+07 W/m² and peaks at 0.50 μm (green-yellow, the middle of the visible band); a 300 K room surface peaks at 9.7 μm, deep in the infrared; an 800 K electric-stove element peaks at 3.6 μm and is only just visibly red because its spectrum's short tail reaches 0.7 μm.

Real surfaces: emissivity, absorptivity and Kirchhoff's law

A real surface emits a fraction ε of the blackbody value: E = ε σ T4, with the emissivity 0 ≤ ε ≤ 1. Radiation arriving at a surface (the irradiation G, W/m²) is split three ways: absorbed (fraction α, absorptivity), reflected (ρ, reflectivity) and transmitted (τ, transmissivity), with α + ρ + τ = 1; for an opaque surface τ = 0 so α + ρ = 1. In general ε and α depend on wavelength and direction. A gray surface has properties independent of wavelength and a diffuse surface independent of direction; the gray-diffuse model is what degree problems use.

📘 DEFINITION

Kirchhoff's law: for a surface in thermal equilibrium with its surroundings, the emissivity equals the absorptivity at each wavelength, ελ = αλ, and so for a gray surface ε = α. Good emitters are good absorbers. The law applies at the same wavelength: a white-painted roof has α ≈ 0.2-0.3 for short-wave solar radiation but ε ≈ 0.9 at long infrared wavelengths, which is exactly why white roofs stay cool, and it is not a violation.

Total emissivities of common surfaces at ordinary temperatures (Cengel & Ghajar Table A-18; polished aluminium also checked against the Engineering ToolBox emissivity table):

SurfaceεNote
Aluminium, highly polished≈ 0.03-0.05Polished metals are poor emitters and good reflectors: radiation shields, foil-backed insulation
Aluminium, anodised≈ 0.8An oxide layer raises ε enormously; oxidation and dirt do the same to any metal
Black paint0.98Close to a blackbody; the inside of a solar collector
White paint (acrylic)≈ 0.9Nearly as high as black in the infrared; colour tells you about the visible band only
Human skin0.95Infrared-camera makers quote 0.97-0.98; either way, nearly black in the infrared
Water0.96Also nearly black in the infrared
Red brick≈ 0.93Most building materials sit between 0.85 and 0.95
Snow≈ 0.8-0.9Reflects sunlight (low αsolar) but emits well in the infrared

Net exchange between surfaces

A surface both emits and absorbs; what matters is the net. Three cases carry most of the marks.

📊 FIGURE — Radiation between two parallel plates, with and without a shield
The furnace-wall example: emissivities below 1 add surface resistances and cut the black-body flux to 12,726 W/m²; one ε = 0.1 foil shield between the plates brings it down to 2,828 W/m².
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Small gray object (area As, emissivity ε, temperature Ts) inside a large enclosure at Tsurr: Q̇net = ε σ As (Ts4 − Tsurr4). The enclosure's emissivity does not appear because a large enclosure behaves as a blackbody to whatever is inside it (a person in a room, a pipe in a hall, a satellite in space).

Two large parallel gray plates facing each other: q̇12 = σ (T14 − T24) / (1/ε1 + 1/ε2 − 1) (W/m²). Each thin radiation shield of emissivity ε3 on both faces adds another term (1/ε3 + 1/ε3 − 1) to the denominator; N identical shields between identical plates cut the flux by a factor N + 1.

Radiation coefficient, for putting radiation in a resistance circuit alongside convection: hrad = ε σ (Ts + Tsurr)(Ts2 + Tsurr2), so that Q̇rad = hrad As (Ts − Tsurr) and the combined coefficient is hconv + hrad.

Example of the plate formula: a furnace wall at 800 °C (ε = 0.2) faces a parallel plate at 300 °C (ε = 0.7). Blackbody exchange would be σ(1073.15⁴ − 573.15⁴) = 69,083 W/m²; with the real emissivities the denominator is 1/0.2 + 1/0.7 − 1 = 5.429 and q̇ = 12,726 W/m². Inserting one aluminium shield with ε = 0.1 on both faces makes the denominator (1/0.2 + 1/0.1 − 1) + (1/0.1 + 1/0.7 − 1) = 24.429 and the flux falls to 2,828 W/m², a reduction to 22 % with one thin sheet of foil: this is why multilayer foil insulation works in cryostats and spacecraft.

View factors, in words

When neither surface encloses the other, only part of what surface 1 emits lands on surface 2. The view factor F12 is the fraction of the radiation leaving surface 1 that strikes surface 2 directly; it is pure geometry, between 0 and 1, and is tabulated or charted for standard pairs (parallel discs, perpendicular rectangles, coaxial cylinders). Three rules let you find most of them without charts: reciprocity, A1F12 = A2F21; the summation rule, the view factors from a surface to all surfaces of an enclosure (including itself, if it is concave) add to 1; and superposition, the view factor to a combined surface is the sum of the view factors to its parts. For two black surfaces the net exchange is Q̇12 = A1F12σ(T1⁴ − T2⁴); for gray surfaces each surface contributes a surface resistance (1 − ε)/(εA) and each pair a space resistance 1/(A1F12), and the enclosure becomes a resistance network solved exactly like the conduction circuits of the first lesson. The \"small object in a large enclosure\" formula is the special case F12 = 1 with the enclosure's surface resistance vanishing because its area is huge.

Worked example: a person in a cold room, and the temperature of the Earth

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

(a) A person with exposed skin and clothing area 1.6 m², ε = 0.95, surface temperature 30 °C stands in a room whose walls are at 15 °C. Find the net radiation loss, and repeat for walls at 25 °C.

  1. Convert to kelvin: Ts = 30 + 273.15 = 303.15 K; Tsurr = 15 + 273.15 = 288.15 K. The room is a large enclosure, so its wall emissivity is irrelevant.
  2. Q̇ = ε σ A (Ts⁴ − Tsurr⁴) = 0.95 × 5.670 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²·K⁴ × 1.6 m² × (303.15⁴ − 288.15⁴) K⁴ = 134 W.
  3. With walls at 25 °C (298.15 K): Q̇ = 0.95 × 5.670 × 10⁻⁸ × 1.6 × (303.15⁴ − 298.15⁴) = 47 W. A 10 K change in wall temperature nearly triples the loss, which is why a room with cold walls feels cold at the same air temperature.
  4. Gross figures behind the net: the person emits εσATs⁴ = 728 W and absorbs 594 W from the 15 °C walls; only the 134 W difference is felt.
  5. Radiation coefficient for the cold-wall case: hrad = 0.95 × 5.670 × 10⁻⁸ × (303.15 + 288.15)(303.15² + 288.15²) = 5.57 W/m²·K, comparable to natural convection in still air (2-25), so radiation carries roughly half of a resting person's heat loss indoors.

(b) Treat the Earth as a sphere that absorbs solar radiation over its cross-section πR² and emits as a blackbody over its whole surface 4πR², with albedo (reflected fraction) 0.30. The solar constant is 1361 W/m² (NASA SORCE/TSIS). Find the effective radiating temperature.

  1. Absorbed: (1 − 0.30) × 1361 W/m² × πR². Emitted: σTe⁴ × 4πR². Equate and cancel πR²: σTe⁴ = (1 − 0.30) × 1361/4 = 238.17 W/m².
  2. Te = (238.17 / 5.670 × 10⁻⁸)1/4 = 254.6 K = -18.6 °C.

Sanity check: Earth's measured mean surface temperature is about 15 °C, roughly 33 K warmer than this. The difference is the natural greenhouse effect described below: the atmosphere is largely transparent to the incoming 0.5 μm sunlight but absorbs and re-emits the outgoing 10 μm infrared. Forgetting the albedo would give 278 K; forgetting the factor 4 (emitting area versus intercepted area) would give 360 K, obviously wrong.

Why the sky is cold and why a parked car heats up

The cold sky. A horizontal roof exchanges radiation with the sky, not with the air. On a clear dry night the atmosphere is nearly transparent in the 8-13 μm \"window\", so the roof looks straight out to space, and the sky behaves like a blackbody at an effective sky temperature far below the air, commonly 230-285 K depending on humidity and cloud (clouds and moist air close the window and raise it). A roof at 10 °C (ε = 0.9) facing a 250 K sky loses 0.9 × 5.670 × 10⁻⁸ × (283.15⁴ − 250⁴) = 129 W/m², more than still air can supply by convection, so the roof falls below the air temperature and below 0 °C: frost on a car at +3 °C, dew on grass, and the ancient technique of making ice in shallow trays on clear desert nights. The same window is used by modern radiative-cooling paints.

The greenhouse effect, in a car. Ordinary glass transmits most radiation below about 3 μm, which is where the Sun's 5772 K spectrum lives (peak 0.50 μm), but is nearly opaque to the long-wave infrared emitted by objects at 300-350 K (peak around 10 μm). Sunlight passes in, the dashboard absorbs it (dark surfaces have α ≈ 0.9), warms up and re-emits at 10 μm, which the glass absorbs and partly re-emits back inside. The glass also stops convection from carrying warm air away. The interior therefore climbs until the losses through the glass by conduction and convection, plus the leakage of infrared, balance the solar input, which can be tens of kelvin above ambient. The planetary version replaces glass with water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane, which are the reason the surface sits near 15 °C rather than the -19 °C computed above.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Using Celsius in T⁴. The person-in-a-room calculation with 30⁴ − 15⁴ gives 0.07 W instead of 134 W; the fourth power of an absolute temperature is not a difference you can shift. Related: writing (Ts − Tsurr)⁴ instead of Ts⁴ − Tsurr⁴; multiplying by the enclosure's emissivity; using a blackbody (ε = 1) for skin (141 W, 5 % high); and assuming that a white surface has low emissivity because it has low visible absorptivity, which confuses two wavelength bands.

★ ON THE EXAM

Expect: (1) emissive power or peak wavelength of a surface at a given temperature (Stefan-Boltzmann, Wien, kelvin); (2) net exchange for a small object in a large enclosure, often combined with convection through hrad; (3) parallel plates with and without a shield; (4) a short explanation of Kirchhoff's law, why polished metals make good shields, why the sky is cold, or how a greenhouse works. State kelvin conversions explicitly; markers look for them.

✅ VERIFIED

Solar constant 1361 W/m² and the Sun's 5772 K effective temperature: NASA GSFC Solar Irradiance Science. Polished-aluminium emissivity ≈ 0.04 and skin ≈ 0.98 (camera makers) from FLIR, How does emissivity affect thermal imaging; the 0.95 used in the example is Cengel Table A-18.

"}, "THERMO/capstone/s1": {"body": "

This lesson lets you do what a graduating thermodynamics student is expected to do without a textbook problem statement: take a real energy system, decide where the boundaries go, gather its states, run the first law for the energy flows, run the second law for the entropy generation, turn that into exergy destruction component by component, and then propose one change and put a number on it. It is the capstone of the degree because it uses the property tables (Properties), the steady-flow energy equation (Control Volumes), entropy balances (Entropy), exergy (Exergy) and a whole cycle (Vapour Power Cycles or Refrigeration) in one piece of work. Every number below was computed step by step; the water properties come from the IAPWS-IF97 formulation (the same basis as the steam tables in Cengel & Boles) and the R-134a properties from the CoolProp library.

\n\n

1. What the project is, in plain words

\n

A design project is a cycle problem turned inside out. A homework problem hands you the states and asks for the efficiency. A project hands you a plant and asks where the losses are and what you would change. The work has six steps, and the same six steps apply whether the system is a coal-fired steam plant, a gas turbine or the refrigerator in a supermarket:

\n
    \n
  1. Pick the system and draw the boundaries. One boundary around the whole plant (for the overall efficiency) and one around each component (for the losses).
    2. \n
  2. Gather the states. Two independent properties at every numbered point; fill a state table with P, T, h, s and x.
    3. \n
  3. Run the first law on each component and on the whole cycle: work, heat, thermal efficiency, back-work ratio.
    4. \n
  4. Run the second law: entropy generation in each component, then exergy destruction Xd = T0·Sgen, and the second-law efficiency of the plant.
    5. \n
  5. Propose one improvement and quantify it by re-running steps 2 to 4 with the change.
    6. \n
  6. Present the result as a ranked table and a sensitivity table, the way a data analyst would present any model.
    7. \n
\n
📘 DEFINITION

Exergy destruction of a component is the work potential lost inside that component because of its irreversibilities: Xd = T0·Sgen, where T0 is the dead-state (environment) temperature in kelvin and Sgen is the entropy generated inside the component boundary. It is always positive for a real device, zero only for a reversible one, and the sum over all components equals the exergy supplied minus the useful work delivered.

The dead state is the environment the plant sits in: here T0 = 25 °C = 298.15 K and P0 = 100 kPa. Every exergy number is measured against it, so state it before any calculation.

\n\n

2. Step 1: the system and its boundaries

\n

The worked system is a simple steam plant of the kind every textbook uses, with real (not isentropic) machines:

\n
    \n
  • Boiler delivers steam at 8 MPa, 500 °C (state 3); the heat comes from combustion gases modelled as a reservoir at TH = 1500 K.
    • \n
  • Turbine: isentropic efficiency ηt = 0.85, exhaust to the condenser at 10 kPa (state 4).
    • \n
  • Condenser: saturated liquid out at 10 kPa (state 1); heat rejected to the environment at T0 = 298.15 K.
    • \n
  • Pump: isentropic efficiency ηp = 0.80, delivers 8 MPa (state 2).
    • \n
  • Mass flow rate ṁ = 50 kg/s. Kinetic and potential energy changes neglected; no pressure drops in the boiler or condenser.
    • \n
\n

The boundary choice matters: the boiler boundary is drawn around the heat-transfer surface and the flue gas, so that the temperature at which heat crosses it is 1500 K. That is what makes the boiler's exergy destruction appear inside the boiler rather than vanishing into a fictitious \"external\" loss. Draw the condenser the same way, with heat leaving at T0.

\n\n

3. Step 2: the state table

\n

Two properties fix each state. State 1 is saturated liquid by pressure; state 3 is superheated by P and T; states 2 and 4 come from the pump and turbine efficiencies. Property source: IAPWS-IF97 water, computed in Python (the values agree with the Cengel & Boles steam tables to the last printed digit of those tables).

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
StateP (kPa)T (°C)h (kJ/kg)s (kJ/kg·K)xHow it was fixed
11045.81191.810.64920 (sat. liquid)P and x = 0; v1 = 0.001010 m³/kg
2s8000—199.870.6492compressed liquids2s = s1; h2s = h1 + v1ΔP
2800046.56201.900.6556compressed liquidh2 = h1 + wp,s/ηp
380005003399.376.7264superheatedP and T
4s1045.812130.176.72640.8103s4s = s3, inside the dome
41045.812320.557.32330.8899h4 = h3 − ηt(h3 − h4s)
\n

Pump work first, because state 2 depends on it: wp,s = v1(P2 − P1) = 0.001010 m³/kg × (8000 − 10) kPa = 8.07 kJ/kg (1 kPa·m³ = 1 kJ); wp = 8.07/0.80 = 10.09 kJ/kg; h2 = 191.81 + 10.09 = 201.90 kJ/kg. Turbine: wt,s = 3399.37 − 2130.17 = 1269.21 kJ/kg; wt = 0.85 × 1269.21 = 1078.83 kJ/kg; h4 = 3399.37 − 1078.83 = 2320.55 kJ/kg, and at 10 kPa that enthalpy sits at quality x4 = (2320.55 − 191.81)/(2583.89 − 191.81) = 0.890, so s4 is read as a mixture, 7.3233 kJ/kg·K.

\n\n

4. Step 3: the first law on every component

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Steady-flow energy balance per unit mass, one inlet and one exit, ΔKE = ΔPE = 0:

q − w = hexit − hinlet

q: heat into the component (kJ/kg); w: work out of it (kJ/kg); h: specific enthalpy (kJ/kg). Cycle results: ηth = wnet/qin = (wt − wp)/(h3 − h2) and the back-work ratio bwr = wp/wt.

Exergy destroyed per unit mass in a steady-flow component with heat qk crossing its boundary at temperature Tk: xd = T0·sgen = T0·[(sexit − sinlet) − qk/Tk], with qk positive into the component, T in kelvin, result in kJ/kg.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
ComponentBalanceValue (kJ/kg)× ṁ = 50 kg/s
Boilerqin = h3 − h2 = 3399.37 − 201.903197.47159.87 MW
Turbinewt = h3 − h4 = 3399.37 − 2320.551078.8353.94 MW
Condenserqout = h4 − h1 = 2320.55 − 191.812128.73106.44 MW
Pumpwp = h2 − h1 = 201.90 − 191.8110.090.50 MW
Cyclewnet = 1078.83 − 10.09 (check: qin − qout = 3197.47 − 2128.73 = 1068.74)1068.7453.44 MW
\n

ηth = 1068.74/3197.47 = 0.3342 = 33.4%; bwr = 10.09/1078.83 = 0.0094, under 1%, which is why steam plants can afford irreversible pumps. Sanity check: the same plant with isentropic machines gives η = 39.4%, and Carnot between 1500 K and 298.15 K would give 80.1%; a real subcritical plant at 33% is plausible.

\n\n

5. Step 4: the second law, component by component

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Dead state T0 = 298.15 K. Heat enters the boiler from the 1500 K gas and leaves the condenser to the 298.15 K environment; the turbine and pump are adiabatic (qk = 0).

📊 FIGURE — Where the steam plant loses work: exergy destroyed in each component
The plant from the project with the boiler boundary drawn around the 1500 K gas. The bars rank each component’s exergy destruction: the boiler loses more work potential than the plant delivers.
  1. Pump: xd = 298.15 K × (0.6556 − 0.6492) kJ/kg·K = 1.90 kJ/kg (0.09 MW).
  2. Boiler: sgen = (6.7264 − 0.6556) − 3197.47/1500 = 6.0708 − 2.1316 = 3.9392 kJ/kg·K; xd = 298.15 × 3.9392 = 1174.46 kJ/kg (58.72 MW).
  3. Turbine: xd = 298.15 × (7.3233 − 6.7264) = 298.15 × 0.5969 = 177.96 kJ/kg (8.90 MW).
  4. Condenser: sgen = (0.6492 − 7.3233) + 2128.73/298.15 = −6.6741 + 7.1398 = 0.4657 kJ/kg·K; xd = 298.15 × 0.4657 = 138.87 kJ/kg (6.94 MW).
  5. Total destroyed: 1.90 + 1174.46 + 177.96 + 138.87 = 1493.18 kJ/kg = 74.66 MW.
  6. Exergy supplied with the heat: xin = qin(1 − T0/TH) = 3197.47 × (1 − 298.15/1500) = 3197.47 × 0.8012 = 2561.92 kJ/kg (128.10 MW).
  7. Closure check: xin − wnet = 2561.92 − 1068.74 = 1493.18 kJ/kg, equal to the sum of the four destructions to the last digit. The exergy balance closes, so no component was forgotten and no sign is wrong.
  8. Second-law efficiency: ηII = wnet/xin = 1068.74/2561.92 = 0.417 = 41.7%. Sanity: ηII = ηth/ηCarnot = 0.3342/0.8012 = 0.417, the same number by the other route.
\n

Ranked by share of the 74.66 MW destroyed: boiler 78.7%, turbine 11.9%, condenser 9.3%, pump 0.1%. That ranking is the single most important output of the project. It says the turbine, which looks \"inefficient\" at ηt = 0.85, wastes one eighth of what the boiler wastes, and the boiler wastes it not through friction but by transferring heat from 1500 K gas to steam that is mostly boiling at 295 °C (Tsat at 8 MPa), a temperature gap of about 930 K.

\n\n

6. Step 5: propose one improvement and quantify it

\n

The ranking points at the boiler, and the lever a plant engineer actually has is the average temperature at which heat is added. Raising the turbine-inlet temperature from 500 °C to 560 °C (within the range of ordinary alloy steels) and re-running the whole calculation gives:

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
QuantityBase, 500 °CImproved, 560 °CChange
h3, s33399.37 kJ/kg, 6.7264 kJ/kg·K3546.00 kJ/kg, 6.9091 kJ/kg·K—
Turbine work wt1078.83 kJ/kg1153.93 kJ/kg+75.10 kJ/kg
qin3197.47 kJ/kg3344.10 kJ/kg+146.63 kJ/kg
ηth33.42%34.21%+0.78 points
Net power at 50 kg/s53.44 MW57.19 MW+3.76 MW
Turbine exit quality x40.8900.920less blade erosion
Boiler xd per kJ of heat added1174.46/3197.47 = 0.3671199.78/3344.10 = 0.359−0.8 points
ηII41.72%42.69%+0.97 points
\n

Notice the trap: the boiler's absolute destruction rises (58.72 to 59.99 MW) because more heat now flows through it; the honest comparison is destruction per unit of heat supplied, or the second-law efficiency of the whole plant, both of which improve. A second candidate, lowering the condenser pressure from 10 kPa to 7.5 kPa, gives ηth = 34.08% and 54.87 MW but drops x4 to 0.883, so the superheat change wins on both counts.

\n\n

7. Step 6: present it as a data analyst would

\n
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

You already know how to present a model. Do the same three things here. (1) A ranked bar chart or table of Xd by component with a cumulative-share column (a Pareto view): boiler 78.7%, then 90.6% with the turbine, 99.9% with the condenser. (2) A sensitivity table: the same script run for a sweep of the design variable, below. (3) A closure line, \"supplied − delivered − destroyed = 0.00\", printed under every table, which is the thermodynamic equivalent of checking that your group-by totals match the grand total.

Write the cycle as a Python function of its design variables and call it in a loop; every table in this lesson came out of one such function, and the sweep below took one line.

\n\n\n\n\n\n
Turbine inlet T (°C)ηthNet power (MW)x4ηII
45032.80%50.360.86340.93%
500 (base)33.42%53.440.89041.72%
55034.07%56.560.91542.53%
60034.74%59.760.93943.36%
\n

Roughly +0.65 efficiency points and +3.1 MW per 50 °C of superheat, almost linear over this range: that slope, with its units, is the sentence a decision-maker wants.

\n\n

8. The refrigeration variant of the project

\n

If you would rather analyse a supermarket or heat-pump system, the six steps are identical; only the cycle and the definition of \"useful output\" change. A compact run for an R-134a vapour-compression cycle (evaporator 140 kPa, condenser 800 kPa, compressor ηc = 0.80, saturated vapour into the compressor, saturated liquid out of the condenser, ṁ = 0.05 kg/s, cold space at −10 °C = 263.15 K, T0 = 298.15 K; CoolProp R-134a, whose enthalpy reference differs from the textbook tables, so only differences are comparable):

\n
    \n
  • Tsat at 140 kPa = −18.8 °C; Tsat at 800 kPa = 31.3 °C. h1 = 387.32, h2s = 423.53, h2 = 387.32 + (423.53 − 387.32)/0.80 = 432.59, h3 = h4 = 243.65 kJ/kg.
    • \n
  • qL = 387.32 − 243.65 = 143.67 kJ/kg; wc = 45.27 kJ/kg; COPR = 143.67/45.27 = 3.17; cooling 7.18 kW = 2.04 tons; COP of a reversed Carnot cycle between 263.15 K and 298.15 K = 263.15/35 = 7.52.
    • \n
  • Exergy destruction (kJ/kg): compressor 8.53 (32.6%), expansion valve 7.66 (29.3%), evaporator 5.61 (21.4%), condenser 4.36 (16.7%); total 26.16. Exergy of the cooling delivered = qL(T0/TL − 1) = 143.67 × (298.15/263.15 − 1) = 19.11 kJ/kg; closure 45.27 − 19.11 − 26.16 = 0.00; ηII = 19.11/45.27 = 42.2%.
    • \n
  • The ranking says the compressor and the throttling valve are the targets, which is why real systems add subcooling, an expander or a two-stage flash chamber, all covered in the Refrigeration chapter.
    • \n
\n\n

9. The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Computing the boiler exergy destruction with qin/Tsteam instead of qin/TH. The entropy transfer term uses the temperature at which heat crosses your boundary. If the boundary hugs the steam, the boiler shows almost no destruction and the loss silently moves to a \"furnace\" you never analyse. Draw the boundary at the gas side and use TH.

Using h4 − h4s as the turbine exergy destruction. 190.38 kJ/kg is the lost work relative to an isentropic turbine exhausting at the same pressure, not T0·sgen = 177.96 kJ/kg; they differ because the exhaust exergy is not the same in the two cases.

Judging an improvement by absolute Xd of one component. Compare per unit of heat input, or the plant ηII, or you will reject the 560 °C change because the boiler number grew.

\n

Also: state 4 for a real turbine is fixed by (P4, h4), never by s3; the pump work uses v1 of the liquid, about 0.001 m³/kg, not v of the vapour; and every T in an exergy formula is in kelvin.

\n\n

10. What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

University finals and the FE both compress this project into one question: \"For the cycle shown, find (a) the net work and thermal efficiency, (b) the exergy destroyed in the turbine, (c) the second-law efficiency of the cycle.\" Expect to write the state table in the first five minutes; every later part is arithmetic on it.

A common variant gives the exergy destruction numbers and asks which component to improve first and why; the answer is the largest share per unit of exergy supplied, and the reason is always a named irreversibility (finite-ΔT heat transfer, throttling, friction).

The closure check (supplied − delivered − destroyed = 0) is also asked directly, usually as \"show that the exergy balance is satisfied\". It is free marks if you kept every sign consistent.

\n

Property sources used above: water, IAPWS-IF97 via the Python package iapws; R-134a, CoolProp. If you repeat the project with printed steam tables, expect agreement within one unit in the last printed digit and small differences in the third significant figure of sgen.

"}, "THERMO/capstone/s2": {"body": "

This lesson turns the eighteen chapters of thermodynamics before it into something you can execute under a clock. By the end you will recognise which of eight recurring problem archetypes a question belongs to within ten seconds, know the first equation to write for each, budget your time across an exam paper, and run a 30-second check that catches the four errors (table, sign, unit, temperature scale) responsible for most lost marks. It applies to the NCEES Fundamentals of Engineering (FE) exam, where thermodynamics is a small block of short multiple-choice items, and to a university final, where it is three or four long problems with full working.

\n\n

1. The two exam formats and what each rewards

\n
✅ VERIFIED

The FE exam has 110 questions in 5 hours 20 minutes of testing time inside a 6-hour appointment (the rest is the non-disclosure agreement, a tutorial and a 25-minute scheduled break). That is about 2.9 minutes per question, with no individually timed sections, and the only reference allowed is the on-screen NCEES FE Reference Handbook, which contains the property tables and charts. Source: NCEES, ncees.org/exams/fe-exam.

A university final in engineering thermodynamics is typically two to three hours with three to five multi-part problems, steam and refrigerant tables supplied; the exact format is set by the course, so check the syllabus, not this page.

\n

The FE rewards speed and recognition: pick the archetype, find the one equation in the handbook, plug, choose. The university final rewards method: a correct energy balance with a wrong table lookup still earns most of the marks, while a right number with no balance earns few. The archetype method below serves both, because the first line you write is the same in each.

\n\n

2. The eight archetypes

\n
📘 DEFINITION

A problem archetype is a family of exam questions that share the same system type, the same governing balance and the same property source, so that the first two lines of the solution are identical whatever the numbers. Almost every undergraduate thermodynamics question belongs to one of eight.

📊 FIGURE — The eight exam archetypes and the first line to write for each
Match the question to a card, write its blue first line, and watch for the grey trap. The bar underneath splits the exam time into the three passes.
\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
#ArchetypeFirst line to writeProperty sourceClassic trap
1Closed system, one process (piston, rigid tank)Q − W = m(u2 − u1); W = ∫P dVTables (u, not h) or ideal gas cvUsing cp for Δu; forgetting W = 0 for a rigid tank
2Steady-flow device (turbine, nozzle, valve, pump)q − w = Δh + ΔV²/2000 + gΔz/1000Tables (h) or cpΔTKinetic energy in J/kg added to kJ/kg
3Unsteady flow (tank charging, discharging)m2u2 − m1u1 = mihi − mehe + Q − WIdeal gas or tablesUsing u for the line and h for the tank (it is the reverse)
4Engine, refrigerator, heat pump vs Carnotη = W/QH; ηmax = 1 − TL/THNone: only temperatures in kelvinCelsius in the ratio; COPHP = COPR + 1 forgotten
5Entropy generation / isentropic efficiencySgen = ΔSsys − ΣQk/Tk ≥ 0; ηt = wa/wss from tables or s° tables / PrFixing the real exit state by s instead of by (P, h)
6Whole cycle (Rankine, Otto, Diesel, Brayton, vapour compression)The state table 1-2-3-4, then η or COPSteam or R-134a tables; air tables or cold-air kQuality outside 0-1 accepted; pump work omitted
7Mixtures and psychrometricsω = 0.622 Pv/(P − Pv); dry-air mass balancePsat of water; psychrometric chartUsing Pv where Psat belongs; balances per kg of moist air instead of dry air
8Combustion and reacting systemsBalance C, H, O, N; then Σnp(h̄f° + Δh̄)p = Σnr(h̄f° + Δh̄)rEnthalpy of formation table; ideal-gas tables in kJ/kmolAir-fuel ratio by mole quoted as by mass; forgetting 3.76 N2
\n

Two archetypes hide inside others. Property lookup (which table, interpolation, quality) is a sub-skill of 1, 2, 5 and 6; exergy questions are archetype 5 with one extra multiplication by T0.

\n\n

3. Time budgeting: the three passes

\n
    \n
  • Pass 1 (first 40% of the time): answer every question you can classify and solve in one equation. On the FE that is most of the thermodynamics items; on a final it is parts (a) and (b) of every problem. Never spend more than twice the average per-item time on anything in this pass.
    • \n
  • Pass 2 (next 40%): the archetype-6 cycle problems and anything needing a state table. Build the table completely before computing any efficiency; a complete table earns method marks even if the last arithmetic goes wrong.
    • \n
  • Pass 3 (last 20%): the 30-second check on every answer (section 7), then the questions you skipped. On a multiple-choice paper, a skipped question answered by elimination beats a blank.
    • \n
\n

Concretely on the FE: 2.9 minutes per item means a cycle problem at 6 minutes must be paid for by four one-minute recognition items. On a three-hour final with four equal problems, 45 minutes each with 5 minutes reserved for checking is the plan; write it on the cover page and stick to it.

\n\n

4. Property-table traps

\n
    \n
  1. Which region? Compare the given T with Tsat at the given P (or P with Psat at T). T < Tsat: compressed liquid. T = Tsat: mixture, you need x. T > Tsat: superheated. If the givens are (P, h) or (P, s), compare with hf, hg (or sf, sg) at that pressure.
    2. \n
  2. Compressed liquid: use the saturated-liquid values at the given temperature, y ≈ yf@T, not at the given pressure; for h add vf(P − Psat) only when the pressure is high.
    3. \n
  3. Quality: x = (y − yf)/yfg. A result outside 0 to 1 means the state is not a mixture; go back to step 1.
    4. \n
  4. Interpolation: linear between the two bracketing rows; on the FE, the nearest row is usually accepted only if the options are far apart. Write the fraction (T − T1)/(T2 − T1) once and reuse it for h, s and v.
    5. \n
  5. Ideal gas or table? Water vapour below about 10 kPa, or superheated far from the dome, can be treated as ideal; steam at boiler conditions cannot. Air, N2, O2, CO2 at ordinary pressures are ideal; check Z if PR > about 0.1 and TR is near 1.
    6. \n
\n\n

5. Sign-convention traps

\n

The course uses Q positive into the system, W positive done by the system, so the closed-system first law is Q − W = ΔU. Every trap here is a sign flipped by habit:

\n
    \n
  • A compressor or pump does work on the fluid: in the \"q − w = Δh\" form, w is negative, or write win = hexit − hinlet as a positive number and say so.
    • \n
  • Heat lost from a pipe or turbine is negative Q. A \"well-insulated\" device means Q = 0, not W = 0.
    • \n
  • In Sgen = ΔS − ΣQk/Tk, Qk keeps its sign: heat rejected makes −Qk/Tk positive. A negative Sgen is never an answer; it is a sign error or an impossible device.
    • \n
  • Boundary work of a compression is negative (∫P dV with dV < 0), and the ideal-gas isothermal formula W = mRT ln(V2/V1) delivers that sign by itself if you leave the logarithm alone.
    • \n
\n\n

6. Unit traps

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
TrapRuleSymptom of getting it wrong
kPa·m³ versus kJ1 kPa·m³ = 1 kJ; 1 bar·m³ = 100 kJ; 1 MPa·m³ = 1000 kJPump work 1000× too small or too large
Gauge versus absolutePabs = Pgauge + Patm before any Pv = RT or table lookupMass in a tyre 30% low
Celsius versus kelvinΔT is the same in both; any T that stands alone (Pv = RT, TL/TH, T0·Sgen) is in kelvinCarnot efficiency above 100% or a negative absolute temperature
Kinetic energyV²/2 is in J/kg when V is in m/s; divide by 1000 for kJ/kgA nozzle exit temperature of tens of thousands of kelvin
kmol versus kgRu = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K; R = Ru/M in kJ/kg·K; enthalpy of formation is per kmolAir mass 30× too small (Ru used as R)
Tons and horsepower1 ton of refrigeration = 211 kJ/min = 3.517 kW; 1 hp = 0.7457 kWCOP 60× off
\n\n

7. Worked example: an FE-style item under the clock

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Isentropic relation and real work of an adiabatic ideal-gas turbine with constant specific heats:

T2s = T1(P2/P1)(k−1)/k  and  wa = ηt·cp(T1 − T2s) = cp(T1 − T2)

T in kelvin; P2/P1 dimensionless; k = cp/cv; cp in kJ/kg·K; w in kJ/kg. For air use k = 1.4 and cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K (values at 300 K; at 800 K the variable-specific-heat tables give slightly different numbers, which the FE handbook problems accept as a stated assumption).

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Question: Air enters an adiabatic turbine at 800 K and 1 MPa and leaves at 100 kPa. The isentropic efficiency is 85%. With k = 1.4 and cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, the exit temperature is most nearly: (A) 273 K (B) 414 K (C) 472 K (D) 566 K.

  1. Classify (5 s): archetype 2 plus 5, steady flow, ideal gas, adiabatic.
  2. Isentropic exit: (k − 1)/k = 0.4/1.4 = 0.2857; (100/1000)0.2857 = 0.5179; T2s = 800 K × 0.5179 = 414.36 K.
  3. Isentropic work: ws = 1.005 kJ/kg·K × (800 − 414.36) K = 387.57 kJ/kg.
  4. Actual work: wa = 0.85 × 387.57 = 329.43 kJ/kg.
  5. Actual exit temperature: T2 = 800 K − 329.43/1.005 = 800 − 327.80 = 472.20 K, answer (C).
  6. Sanity (10 s): the real exit must be hotter than the isentropic one (472 > 414) and colder than the inlet; both hold. Total time about 90 seconds.
\n

The three wrong options are not random. (A) 273 K comes from putting 800 − 273.15 = 526.85 °C into the isentropic relation; (B) is the isentropic temperature, the answer for a question that was not asked; (D) 566 K comes from using cv = 0.718 for the work and cp to convert it back (w = 0.85 × 0.718 × 385.64 = 235.36 kJ/kg, T2 = 800 − 235.36/1.005 = 565.8 K). Examiners build distractors from exactly the traps in sections 4 to 6, so recognising the trap tells you which option to avoid.

\n

A second one-liner, archetype 1: 2 kg of air in a rigid tank is heated from 300 K to 400 K. Rigid means W = 0, so Q = m cv ΔT = 2 kg × 0.718 kJ/kg·K × 100 K = 143.6 kJ. The cp version, 201.0 kJ, is the answer for a constant-pressure piston, and the difference, 57.4 kJ = mRΔT, is exactly the boundary work the piston would do.

\n\n

8. The 30-second check

\n

Run these in order on every answer before moving on; each takes a few seconds and each catches a family of errors:

\n
    \n
  1. Direction: did the fluid get hotter or colder, faster or slower, in the direction physics says? (A real turbine exit is hotter than the isentropic one; a throttled refrigerant is colder; a charged tank is hotter than the line.)
    2. \n
  2. Bound: is η below Carnot, COP below the reversed-Carnot value, Sgen ≥ 0, 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, T > 0 K?
    3. \n
  3. Magnitude: pump work a few kJ/kg, turbine work hundreds to about a thousand kJ/kg for steam, hfg of water around 2000 kJ/kg, cp of air about 1 kJ/kg·K; anything ten times off means a unit slipped.
    4. \n
  4. Units: write the unit on the final line and check it came out of the algebra, not from habit.
    5. \n
  5. The question asked: exit temperature, not isentropic exit temperature; net work, not turbine work; per kg or total; rate or amount.
    6. \n
\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Answering the intermediate quantity. Distractor (B) above is the single most common way to lose an FE thermodynamics mark: the isentropic value, the heat-pump COP instead of the refrigerator COP, the turbine work instead of the net work. Re-read the last sentence of the question before choosing.

Treating \"insulated\" and \"rigid\" as the same word. Insulated sets Q = 0; rigid sets Wb = 0. A rigid insulated tank being stirred by a paddle has Q = 0, Wb = 0 and Wshaft ≠ 0, so ΔU = −Wshaft > 0.

\n\n

9. What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

On the FE, thermodynamics items are almost all archetypes 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 with ideal gases or a single table lookup; expect the handbook's steam table and P-h chart to be provided and the answer choices to be about 10% apart, so two significant figures are enough.

On a university final, expect one problem from each of: a closed system with tables, a steady-flow device or two, a complete cycle, and a second-law question (Sgen, exergy destruction or second-law efficiency). Later courses add a psychrometric or combustion problem.

The marking scheme rewards, in order: the sketch and boundary, the balance written in symbols, the property values with their table named, the arithmetic, the units, and the one-line sanity check. Write all six even when short of time; the last two are the cheapest marks on the paper.

"}, "THERMO/capstone/s3": {"body": "

This lesson is the whole degree on one page: for each of the eighteen chapters, a small table with the equation you will actually use, what it assumes, its units and the misuse that loses the most marks. Around the tables sit a map of how the chapters connect, one worked problem that runs through four chapters, and what to study next. Use it the week before an exam, or whenever a formula looks familiar but you cannot say when it is allowed.

\n\n

1. How to read a review sheet

\n

A thermodynamics equation is a balance (always true) specialised by a model (true only under assumptions). Q − W = ΔU holds for any closed system; Q = mcvΔT is that balance plus three assumptions: ideal gas or incompressible substance, constant cv, and no work. Most wrong answers in the course are the specialised form used after one assumption has quietly failed.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

An equation's assumption set is the list of conditions under which it follows from the general balances: the substance model (ideal gas, incompressible, table data), the process (steady, adiabatic, reversible, constant pressure) and what was neglected (ΔKE, ΔPE, heat loss).

A misuse is applying the equation when one item on that list is false. The arithmetic is right and the answer is wrong, so a quick re-check of the numbers will not catch it.

\n\n

2. The four balances and the map of the course

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Every chapter specialises four balances on a control volume (CV):

📊 FIGURE — How the eighteen chapters connect around the four balances
Read top to bottom: the language and property chapters feed the chain of balances, the applications run those balances on loops and on several species, and Heat Transfer adds how fast.

dmCV/dt = Σṁin − Σṁout
dECV/dt = Q̇ − Ẇ + Σṁinθin − Σṁoutθout, with θ = h + V²/2 + gz
dSCV/dt = ΣQ̇k/Tk + Σṁinsin − Σṁoutsout + Ṡgen, with Ṡgen ≥ 0
Ẋdestroyed = T₀Ṡgen

ṁ: mass flow (kg/s); E: energy in the CV (kJ); Q̇: heat rate into the CV (kW); Ẇ: work rate out (kW); h: enthalpy (kJ/kg); V: velocity (m/s; V²/2 comes out in J/kg, divide by 1000); g = 9.81 m/s²; z: height (m); Tk: temperature where Q̇k crosses the boundary (K); s: entropy (kJ/kg·K); Ṡgen: entropy generation (kW/K); T₀: dead-state temperature (K); Ẋ: exergy rate (kW).

\n
    \n
  1. Language: Foundations and Basic Concepts give units, systems, state and temperature.
    2. \n
  2. Properties: Pure Substances supplies every h, u, s; Property Relations extends it to real gases; Statistical Thermodynamics explains where cv and s come from.
    3. \n
  3. The balances: Energy (closed) → Control Volumes (open) → Second Law → Entropy → Exergy.
    4. \n
  4. Applications: Gas Cycles, Vapour Cycles and Refrigeration run the balances around a loop; Mixtures, Combustion and Equilibrium extend the property model to several species; Compressible Flow keeps the kinetic energy.
    5. \n
  5. Rates: Heat Transfer answers the question thermodynamics never does: how fast.
    6. \n
\n\n

3. The review sheets, one per chapter

\n

T is in kelvin and P is absolute unless marked. \"Tables\" means steam or refrigerant tables.

\n

Foundations

\n\n

4. One problem through four chapters

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Air is compressed steadily and adiabatically from 100 kPa, 300 K to 800 kPa by a compressor with ηc = 0.85, ṁ = 2 kg/s, T₀ = 300 K. Find the power, the exit temperature, the exergy destroyed and ηII. Properties: air R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, k = 1.4 (cold-air values at 300 K).

  1. Isentropic exit (Entropy): (k − 1)/k = 0.4/1.4 = 0.2857; (800/100)0.2857 = 1.8114; T₂s = 300 K × 1.8114 = 543.43 K.
  2. Isentropic work (Control Volumes): ws = 1.005 kJ/kg·K × (543.43 − 300) K = 244.65 kJ/kg.
  3. Actual work: wa = ws/ηc = 244.65 kJ/kg / 0.85 = 287.83 kJ/kg; power = 2 kg/s × 287.83 kJ/kg = 575.65 kW.
  4. Actual exit (energy balance): T₂ = 300 K + 287.83 kJ/kg / 1.005 kJ/kg·K = 300 + 286.39 = 586.39 K.
  5. Entropy change (Properties + Entropy): Δs = 1.005 ln(586.39/300) − 0.287 ln(800/100) = 0.67356 − 0.59680 = 0.07676 kJ/kg·K; adiabatic, so sgen = Δs.
  6. Exergy destroyed (Exergy): xd = 300 K × 0.07676 kJ/kg·K = 23.03 kJ/kg; rate = 2 kg/s × 23.03 kJ/kg = 46.06 kW.
  7. Second-law efficiency: minimum work to reach the same exit state, wrev = ψ₂ − ψ₁ = wa − xd = 287.83 − 23.03 = 264.80 kJ/kg; ηII = 264.80/287.83 = 0.920 = 92.0%.
\n

Sanity check: T₂ = 586 K is above T₂s = 543 K and sgen > 0, as a real compressor requires. ηII (92.0%) beats ηc (85%) because ηc compares with an isentropic machine, while ηII credits the extra exergy of the hotter exit air. (Δs at the isentropic state computes to 0.0003 kJ/kg·K, not zero, because the rounded 1.005, 0.287 and 1.4 are not perfectly consistent.)

\n\n

5. The misuses that cost the most marks

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Three misuses appear in almost every chapter's table, so learn them once:

  1. The wrong scale or basis. Celsius in a ratio or a logarithm, gauge pressure in Pv = RT, kJ mixed with J (V²/2, c = √(kRT)), kmol mixed with kg (Ru for R), moist air for dry air.
  2. A reversible formula for a real device. Isentropic relations, Carnot ratios and isentropic stagnation relations describe ideal limits; a real turbine exit, a real engine's QL/QH and the flow behind a shock all need an efficiency or a different relation.
  3. The model outside its range. Ideal gas near the dome, cold-air k at 1500 K, Clausius-Clapeyron near the critical point, a convection correlation outside its Reynolds-number range.
\n\n

6. What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM

Finals rarely ask you to recite an equation; they ask you to choose one. Expect questions of the form \"state the assumptions you made\" (a mark each), \"why can this equation not be used here\" (the misuse column) and multi-part problems that cross chapters, like the compressor above: properties, energy balance, entropy, exergy.

Beside every specialised equation, write its assumptions in a few words (\"ideal gas, const cp, adiabatic\"). It costs ten seconds and earns method marks even when the arithmetic goes wrong.

\n\n

7. What to study next

Tables list the specific value; you supply the mass.", "distractors": {"2": "214.07 kJ is the specific value with the wrong unit; the mass was never multiplied in.", "0": "71.4 kJ is u divided by m instead of multiplied by it.", "3": "428.1 kJ uses 2 kg instead of the 3 kg given."}, "topic": "Systems, boundaries and the control volume"}, {"id": "concepts-s1-q3", "text": "A pressure cooker is on the stove with the regulator valve lifting so that steam vents steadily from the top. If the boundary is drawn around the contents of the cooker, what kind of system is it while venting?", "options": ["Open, because mass leaves through the valve", "Closed and adiabatic, because no heat can escape a metal pot", "Isolated, because the cooker is sealed and hot", "Closed, because the lid is clamped shut"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Mass (steam) crosses the boundary through the valve, so by definition the contents form an open system (control volume) while venting; heat also crosses from the stove.", "distractors": {"3": "A clamped lid does not stop mass leaving through the regulator; mass transfer is what decides the classification.", "2": "Heat enters from the stove and steam leaves, so both mass and energy cross the boundary; the opposite of isolated.", "1": "The metal wall conducts heat readily, and in any case steam is leaving, which rules out closed."}, "topic": "Systems, boundaries and the control volume"}, {"id": "concepts-s1-q4", "text": "Imagine a partition dividing a tank of gas into two equal halves. Which list contains only properties whose values are the same in each half as in the whole?", "options": ["Mass, temperature, pressure", "Temperature, total enthalpy, density", "Volume, internal energy, specific volume", "Pressure, specific enthalpy, density"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Pressure, specific enthalpy and density are all intensive: they do not depend on how much matter is present, so each half has the same value as the whole. Any total quantity such as mass, volume or total enthalpy would halve.", "distractors": {"0": "Mass halves when the system is halved; it is extensive.", "2": "Volume and total internal energy are extensive and halve; only specific volume in that list is intensive.", "1": "Total enthalpy H is extensive and halves; the other two are intensive."}, "topic": "Systems, boundaries and the control volume"}, {"id": "concepts-s1-q5", "text": "A rigid, well-insulated, sealed tank contains air. A paddle wheel inside the tank is spun by an electric motor located outside the tank. How should the air be classified?", "options": ["Open, because energy from the motor flows in", "Isolated, because it is sealed and insulated", "Closed and adiabatic, but not isolated, because shaft work enters", "Closed and isolated, because the tank is rigid"], "correct": 2, "explain": "No mass crosses (closed) and no heat crosses (adiabatic), but work does cross via the rotating shaft, so energy is exchanged and the system is not isolated.", "distractors": {"1": "Isolated requires no energy transfer of any kind; the paddle wheel delivers work across the boundary.", "0": "Energy crossing the boundary does not make a system open; only mass transfer does.", "3": "Rigidity rules out boundary work but not shaft work, so the system is still exchanging energy."}, "topic": "Systems, boundaries and the control volume"}, {"id": "concepts-s1-q6", "text": "Under which condition does the continuum assumption used throughout classical thermodynamics stop being valid?", "options": ["When the temperature falls below 0 °C", "When the mean free path is no longer negligible compared with the system size", "When the system contains less than one kilomole of gas", "When the gas pressure rises above 1 atm"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The continuum treats matter as smooth, which needs a very large number of molecules in any volume of interest; that holds when the Knudsen number λ/L is very small. When λ becomes comparable to L (rarefied gas or micro-scale device) the assumption fails.", "distractors": {"3": "Higher pressure shortens the mean free path and makes the continuum assumption better, not worse.", "0": "Temperature alone does not decide it; a cold dense gas is still a continuum.", "2": "One kilomole is about 6 × 10²⁶ molecules; far smaller amounts, even a cubic millimetre of air, are still overwhelmingly continuous."}, "topic": "Systems, boundaries and the control volume"}, {"id": "concepts-s1-q7", "text": "The mean free path of air at 1 atm and 20 °C is about 66 nm. Estimate the Knudsen number for air flowing through a micro-channel 2 μm wide.", "options": ["0.66", "30", "3.3 × 10⁻⁵", "0.033"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Kn = λ / L = (66 × 10⁻⁹ m) / (2 × 10⁻⁶ m) = 0.033. That is not negligible, so slip effects begin to appear and the plain continuum model needs correction.", "distractors": {"1": "30 is L/λ, the inverse ratio; the Knudsen number puts the mean free path on top.", "0": "0.66 would need a 0.1 μm channel, ten times narrower than given.", "2": "3.3 × 10⁻⁵ is the value for a 2 mm channel, a thousand times wider than the one given."}, "topic": "Systems, boundaries and the control volume"}, {"id": "concepts-s1-q8", "text": "An oil has a density of 850 kg/m³. Taking water at 1000 kg/m³ as the reference, what is the specific gravity of the oil?", "options": ["0.85", "850", "1.18", "0.85 kg/m³"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Specific gravity is the ratio of the substance's density to that of water: SG = 850 / 1000 = 0.85. Being a ratio of two densities it carries no units.", "distractors": {"1": "850 is the density itself in kg/m³, not the ratio to water.", "3": "Specific gravity is dimensionless; attaching kg/m³ is a units error.", "2": "1.18 is 1000/850, the ratio inverted; oil is lighter than water so SG must be below 1."}, "topic": "Systems, boundaries and the control volume"}], "THERMO/concepts/s2": [{"id": "concepts-s2-q1", "text": "A gas in a piston-cylinder is compressed at a constant pressure of 150 kPa from a volume of 0.35 m³ to 0.20 m³ in a quasi-equilibrium process. What is the boundary work, using the convention that work done by the gas is positive?", "options": ["22.5 kJ done by the gas (W = +22.5 kJ)", "22.5 kJ done on the gas (W = −22.5 kJ)", "52.5 kJ done on the gas (W = −52.5 kJ)", "0.15 kJ done on the gas (W = −0.15 kJ)"], "correct": 1, "explain": "For a constant-pressure quasi-equilibrium process W = P(V2 − V1) = 150 kPa × (0.20 − 0.35) m³ = −22.5 kJ; negative because the volume shrinks, so work is done on the gas.", "distractors": {"0": "The magnitude is right but the sign is wrong: a compression is work done on the gas, so W is negative in the by-the-system convention.", "2": "52.5 kJ is P × V1, the full area under the line down to zero volume, not the area over the change in volume.", "3": "0.15 is just the volume change in m³ with the wrong unit; it must be multiplied by the pressure of 150 kPa."}, "topic": "State, process, cycle and the state postulate"}, {"id": "concepts-s2-q2", "text": "An ideal gas is compressed isothermally and quasi-statically at 200 kPa initial pressure from 0.30 m³ to 0.10 m³. How much boundary work is involved, and in which direction?", "options": ["−40.0 kJ (work done on the gas)", "−65.9 kJ (work done on the gas)", "+65.9 kJ (work done by the gas)", "−120 kJ (work done on the gas)"], "correct": 1, "explain": "For an isothermal ideal-gas process W = P1V1 ln(V2/V1) = 200 kPa × 0.30 m³ × ln(0.10/0.30) = 60 kJ × (−1.0986) = −65.9 kJ; negative means work was done on the gas.", "distractors": {"0": "−40.0 kJ is what you get from P1(V2 − V1), treating the process as constant pressure; the pressure triples during an isothermal compression.", "2": "Right magnitude, wrong sign: volume decreases so the surroundings do work on the gas and W is negative.", "3": "−120 kJ is P2(V2 − V1) using the final pressure of 600 kPa throughout; that path is isobaric at high pressure, not isothermal."}, "topic": "State, process, cycle and the state postulate"}, {"id": "concepts-s2-q3", "text": "Which of the following pairs of intensive properties fails to fix the state of water, and why?", "options": ["Pressure and temperature while the water is boiling, because they are not independent", "Temperature and specific internal energy, because u depends on T", "Temperature and specific volume, because v is not measurable", "Pressure and specific volume, because they are both mechanical quantities"], "correct": 0, "explain": "During a phase change P and T are locked together by the saturation curve, so specifying both gives no information about how much has vaporised; a second independent property such as v, u, h, s or quality is needed.", "distractors": {"2": "T and v are always independent and always fix the state; specific volume is perfectly measurable.", "3": "P and v are independent and fix the state, including inside the saturation dome.", "1": "T and u fix the state of water; u changes strongly across the dome even at constant T, so they are independent there."}, "topic": "State, process, cycle and the state postulate"}, {"id": "concepts-s2-q4", "text": "A student writes the energy balance for a process as ΔQ − ΔW = ΔU. What is wrong with this notation?", "options": ["ΔU should be written U because internal energy is a path function", "Q and W are path functions, so their amounts are written Q12 and W12, not as changes Δ of a property", "Nothing; it is the standard form of the first law", "The signs are reversed: it should read ΔW − ΔQ = ΔU"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Δ denotes the change of a point function (a property) between two states. Heat and work depend on the path and a system does not possess a quantity of heat or work, so their process totals are written Q12 and W12 with inexact differentials δQ and δW.", "distractors": {"2": "The first law is written Q − W = ΔU; the Δ in front of Q and W wrongly implies that heat and work are properties.", "0": "Internal energy is a property, so ΔU is exactly right; it is Q and W that must lose their Δ.", "3": "The sign convention Q − W is correct for work done by the system; the issue is the Δ on the path functions."}, "topic": "State, process, cycle and the state postulate"}, {"id": "concepts-s2-q5", "text": "A gas is compressed by slamming the piston inwards very rapidly. Which statement about analysing this process is correct?", "options": ["It is a quasi-equilibrium process because the gas returns to equilibrium afterwards", "The work can be found from ∫P dV using the pressure read at the piston face", "Only the end states are equilibrium states; the path cannot be drawn and ∫P dV cannot be evaluated", "It can be drawn as a solid line on a P-v diagram because the end states are known"], "correct": 2, "explain": "During a sudden compression the gas near the piston is at a higher pressure than the gas far from it, so there is no single system pressure at intermediate instants; the intermediate states are non-equilibrium, shown only as a dashed line, and the work must come from an energy balance instead.", "distractors": {"3": "A solid line implies every intermediate state is an equilibrium state, which is false for a rapid compression.", "1": "The piston-face pressure is not the pressure of the whole non-uniform gas, so that integral is not the system's boundary work in the usual sense.", "0": "Returning to equilibrium at the end does not make the intermediate path quasi-static; quasi-equilibrium requires slow, near-balanced steps throughout."}, "topic": "State, process, cycle and the state postulate"}, {"id": "concepts-s2-q6", "text": "A steam turbine has been running at constant load for an hour. Inlet steam is at 8 MPa and 500 °C, exit steam at 10 kPa. Which description of the turbine is correct?", "options": ["It is an unsteady process because inlet and exit states differ", "It is in thermodynamic equilibrium because nothing changes with time", "It is an isolated system because its casing is insulated", "It is a steady-flow process: properties vary with position but not with time at any point"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Steady flow means every property at every fixed location is constant in time, while properties may and do vary from inlet to exit. The turbine as a whole is not in equilibrium, since the inlet and exit fluid states differ, but its analysis is time-independent.", "distractors": {"1": "Equilibrium requires uniform temperature and pressure throughout; a turbine with 8 MPa at one end and 10 kPa at the other is far from uniform.", "0": "Different inlet and exit states are normal in steady flow; unsteady means the properties at a point change with time, which they do not here.", "2": "Insulation stops heat transfer, but mass and shaft work cross the boundary, so it is an open system, not isolated."}, "topic": "State, process, cycle and the state postulate"}, {"id": "concepts-s2-q7", "text": "According to the state postulate, how many independent intensive properties are needed to fix the state of nitrogen gas in a rigid tank where only compression work is relevant, and which pair below is always a valid choice?", "options": ["Two; pressure and temperature under all conditions", "One; temperature alone", "Two; temperature and specific volume", "Three; pressure, temperature and specific volume"], "correct": 2, "explain": "A simple compressible system has one work mode, so one plus one equals two independent intensive properties. Temperature and specific volume are independent everywhere, including inside a saturation region, so they are always a valid pair.", "distractors": {"1": "One property cannot fix the state; the same temperature can correspond to many pressures and specific volumes.", "3": "Three intensive properties are more than needed; once two are set the third is determined by the equation of state.", "0": "P and T are a valid pair only in single-phase regions; during a phase change they are not independent."}, "topic": "State, process, cycle and the state postulate"}], "THERMO/concepts/s3": [{"id": "concepts-s3-q1", "text": "A pressure gauge on an air compressor receiver reads 250 kPa on a day when the local barometric pressure is 101 kPa. What absolute pressure must be used for the air in an ideal-gas calculation?", "options": ["352.3 kPa", "351 kPa", "250 kPa", "149 kPa"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Gauges read relative to the local atmosphere, so P_abs = P_gauge + P_atm = 250 + 101 = 351 kPa. Only absolute pressures may be used in Pv = RT or property tables.", "distractors": {"3": "149 kPa subtracts the atmospheric pressure, which is the treatment for a vacuum reading, not a positive gauge reading.", "2": "250 kPa is the gauge reading itself; using it directly ignores the atmosphere pressing on the outside of the gauge.", "0": "352.3 kPa uses the standard 101.325 kPa instead of the stated local barometric pressure of 101 kPa."}, "topic": "Pressure, temperature and the zeroth law"}, {"id": "concepts-s3-q2", "text": "A mercury manometer (ρ = 13,600 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²) connected to a gas pipe shows a 300 mm difference in levels, with the mercury higher on the side open to the atmosphere. Atmospheric pressure is 101 kPa. What is the absolute pressure of the gas?", "options": ["40.0 kPa", "40,126 kPa", "61.0 kPa", "141.0 kPa"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The gas is above atmospheric by one mercury column: ρgh = 13,600 × 9.81 × 0.300 = 40,025 Pa = 40.0 kPa, so P_gas = 101 + 40.0 = 141.0 kPa absolute.", "distractors": {"2": "61.0 kPa subtracts the column; but mercury standing higher on the open side means the gas pressure exceeds atmospheric.", "0": "40.0 kPa is the gauge pressure (the column alone); the question asks for absolute pressure.", "1": "40,126 kPa comes from using h = 300 m instead of 0.300 m (ρgh = 40,025 kPa, plus 101 kPa); always convert millimetres to metres."}, "topic": "Pressure, temperature and the zeroth law"}, {"id": "concepts-s3-q3", "text": "Steam in a condenser is at 15 kPa absolute while the atmosphere is at 100 kPa. What does a vacuum gauge on the condenser read, and what error is made by adding rather than subtracting it?", "options": ["85 kPa gauge; adding gives the correct 185 kPa", "85 kPa vacuum; adding gives a wrong 185 kPa", "115 kPa vacuum; adding gives a wrong 215 kPa", "15 kPa vacuum; adding gives a wrong 115 kPa"], "correct": 1, "explain": "P_vac = P_atm − P_abs = 100 − 15 = 85 kPa vacuum. A vacuum reading is subtracted from atmospheric to recover the absolute value; adding it would wrongly give 185 kPa.", "distractors": {"3": "15 kPa is the absolute pressure, not the amount below atmospheric that the gauge reports.", "2": "115 kPa would be the sum of the two pressures, which has no meaning here.", "0": "The reading is a vacuum, not a positive gauge pressure, and 185 kPa is the erroneous result, not the correct one."}, "topic": "Pressure, temperature and the zeroth law"}, {"id": "concepts-s3-q4", "text": "The temperature of a gas in a rigid tank is raised from 25 °C to 175 °C. By what factor does its absolute pressure change, assuming ideal-gas behaviour?", "options": ["0.66", "1.50", "7.0", "0.503"], "correct": 1, "explain": "At constant volume P is proportional to absolute temperature: T1 = 298.15 K, T2 = 448.15 K, so P2/P1 = 448.15/298.15 = 1.50. Ratios must use kelvin.", "distractors": {"2": "7.0 is 175/25, the ratio of Celsius temperatures, which is meaningless because the Celsius zero is not absolute zero.", "3": "0.503 is ΔT/T1 = 150/298.15, the fractional increase (P2 − P1)/P1; the factor asked for is P2/P1 = 1 + 0.503 = 1.50.", "0": "0.66 is the inverse ratio; heating a fixed volume raises the pressure, so the factor must exceed one."}, "topic": "Pressure, temperature and the zeroth law"}, {"id": "concepts-s3-q5", "text": "During a test, the temperature of a heat-exchanger tube wall rises by 40 °C. Express this temperature rise in kelvin and in degrees Fahrenheit.", "options": ["40 K and 104 °F", "313.15 K and 72 °F", "313.15 K and 104 °F", "40 K and 72 °F"], "correct": 3, "explain": "A temperature difference has no offset: a 40 °C rise is exactly 40 K, and the Fahrenheit degree is 1/1.8 of a Celsius degree, so the rise is 1.8 × 40 = 72 °F.", "distractors": {"2": "313.15 K and 104 °F are conversions of a temperature level of 40 °C, not of a rise of 40 °C.", "0": "40 K is correct, but 104 °F adds the 32 offset that applies only to temperature levels.", "1": "313.15 K adds 273.15 to a difference; the kelvin and Celsius degrees are the same size, so the rise is 40 K."}, "topic": "Pressure, temperature and the zeroth law"}, {"id": "concepts-s3-q6", "text": "A vertical piston-cylinder contains gas. The frictionless piston has a mass of 40 kg and a cross-sectional area of 0.010 m², and the atmospheric pressure outside is 95 kPa (g = 9.81 m/s²). What is the absolute pressure of the gas while the piston floats in equilibrium?", "options": ["55.8 kPa", "39.2 kPa", "95.4 kPa", "134.2 kPa"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Mechanical equilibrium of the piston: P_gas A = P_atm A + m g, so P_gas = 95 kPa + (40 × 9.81 N)/(0.010 m²) = 95 kPa + 39,240 Pa = 134.2 kPa.", "distractors": {"1": "39.2 kPa is the piston-weight contribution alone, the gauge pressure; the atmosphere also presses on the piston top.", "0": "55.8 kPa subtracts the piston weight, which would be right only if the piston pulled up on the gas.", "2": "95.4 kPa forgets to divide the weight by the area properly (uses 392 Pa instead of 39,240 Pa)."}, "topic": "Pressure, temperature and the zeroth law"}, {"id": "concepts-s3-q7", "text": "Why does the zeroth law of thermodynamics matter for the practical act of reading a thermometer?", "options": ["It states that heat flows from hot to cold, so the thermometer always warms up", "It requires that all substances expand by the same amount per degree", "It guarantees that if the thermometer is in equilibrium with two bodies separately, the two bodies are at the same temperature as each other", "It defines the kelvin in terms of the triple point of water"], "correct": 2, "explain": "The zeroth law makes thermal equilibrium transitive: a third body (the thermometer) that reads the same when in equilibrium with A and with B proves A and B would be in equilibrium with each other, which is what allows temperature to be a shared, measurable property.", "distractors": {"0": "The direction of heat flow is a second-law statement, not the zeroth law.", "3": "The numerical definition of the kelvin is a matter of the SI scale, not of the zeroth law.", "1": "Different substances expand differently; the zeroth law is about equilibrium, not expansion coefficients."}, "topic": "Pressure, temperature and the zeroth law"}, {"id": "concepts-s3-q8", "text": "A diver descends to 30 m in sea water of density 1025 kg/m³ where the surface pressure is 101.3 kPa (g = 9.81 m/s²). Which value is the absolute pressure on the diver, and which the gauge pressure?", "options": ["Absolute 131.3 kPa, gauge 30.0 kPa", "Absolute 403.0 kPa, gauge 301.7 kPa", "Absolute 301.7 kPa, gauge 200.4 kPa", "Absolute 301.7 kPa, gauge 301.7 kPa"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Gauge pressure at depth is ρgh = 1025 × 9.81 × 30 = 301,658 Pa = 301.7 kPa; absolute pressure adds the surface pressure, 301.7 + 101.3 = 403.0 kPa, about four atmospheres.", "distractors": {"2": "This subtracts the atmosphere from ρgh rather than adding it; the sea surface already sits at 101.3 kPa.", "3": "Absolute and gauge pressures differ by the atmospheric pressure, so they cannot be equal.", "0": "131.3 kPa treats the depth as if it were 1 kPa per metre; the specific weight of sea water is about 10 kPa per metre."}, "topic": "Pressure, temperature and the zeroth law"}], "THERMO/energy/s1": [{"id": "energy-s1-q1", "text": "A 1200 kg delivery van is moving at 72 km/h on a flat road.
