The speed must be in m/s before squaring and the joules divided by 1000.", "distractors": {"2": "This squares 72 km/h without converting to m/s; the factor of 3.6² makes it 13 times too large.", "0": "The one-half in m·V²/2 was dropped, doubling the true value.", "3": "The magnitude is right but the unit is wrong by a factor of 1000: the kg·m²/s² result is in joules, and 240 000 J = 240 kJ."}, "topic": "Forms of energy and energy transfer by heat"}, {"id": "energy-s1-q2", "text": "A 0.5 m² surface at 400 K with emissivity 0.8 faces surroundings at 300 K. Using σ = 5.670 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²·K⁴, what is the net radiation heat transfer rate?", "options": ["2.3 W", "397 W", "496 W", "5.9 W"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Q̇ = ε·σ·A·(Ts⁴ − Tsurr⁴) = 0.8 × 5.670e-8 × 0.5 × (400⁴ − 300⁴) = 0.8 × 5.670e-8 × 0.5 × 1.75e10 = 396.9 W. The fourth powers are taken separately and in kelvin.", "distractors": {"0": "This uses (Ts − Tsurr)⁴ = 100⁴ instead of the difference of the fourth powers.", "2": "The emissivity of 0.8 was left out; a real surface radiates less than a blackbody.", "3": "The temperatures were put in as 127 °C and 27 °C; the radiation law only works with absolute temperatures."}, "topic": "Forms of energy and energy transfer by heat"}, {"id": "energy-s1-q3", "text": "A gas in a well-insulated cylinder is compressed rapidly and its temperature rises from 300 K to 450 K. Which statement about heat transfer during this process is correct?", "options": ["The process is isothermal because the cylinder is insulated", "Heat flowed out of the gas because it became hotter than the surroundings", "The process is adiabatic: no heat was transferred, the energy entered as work", "The gas received heat, which is why its temperature rose"], "correct": 2, "explain": "An insulated boundary blocks heat transfer, so Q = 0 by definition of adiabatic. The temperature rise came from the compression work done on the gas, stored as internal energy.", "distractors": {"3": "Heat is energy crossing a boundary because of a temperature difference; an insulated boundary blocks it. The energy entered as work.", "0": "Isothermal means constant temperature, which contradicts the stated rise; insulation gives adiabatic, not isothermal.", "1": "Insulation prevents heat flow in either direction regardless of which side is hotter."}, "topic": "Forms of energy and energy transfer by heat"}, {"id": "energy-s1-q4", "text": "Which of these is a property of a system rather than an interaction that occurs during a process?", "options": ["Boundary work W", "Internal energy U", "Heat transfer Q", "Shaft work delivered by a stirrer"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Internal energy is a state function: it depends only on the current condition of the system. Heat and all forms of work are energy in transit across the boundary and exist only while a process happens.", "distractors": {"2": "Heat is energy crossing the boundary because of a temperature difference; a system does not contain heat.", "0": "Boundary work is the integral of P dV along a path and depends on the path, so it is not a property.", "3": "Shaft work is a work interaction during a process, not something the system possesses."}, "topic": "Forms of energy and energy transfer by heat"}, {"id": "energy-s1-q5", "text": "A sealed thermos flask has a double wall with a vacuum between the walls and silvered surfaces. Which heat transfer modes does the vacuum stop, and which does the silvering address?", "options": ["The vacuum stops all three modes; the silvering is decorative", "The vacuum stops conduction and convection; the silvering reduces radiation", "The vacuum stops radiation; the silvering stops conduction", "The vacuum stops convection only; the silvering stops conduction and radiation"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Conduction and convection need matter in the gap, so a vacuum blocks them. Radiation crosses a vacuum, so the low-emissivity silvered surfaces are added to reduce it.", "distractors": {"2": "Radiation is the one mode that passes through a vacuum; the silvering exists precisely because of that.", "0": "Radiation needs no medium and continues across the gap; the low-emissivity coating is what limits it.", "3": "Conduction also needs matter between the walls, so the vacuum stops it as well as convection; silvering does not affect conduction across a vacuum."}, "topic": "Forms of energy and energy transfer by heat"}, {"id": "energy-s1-q6", "text": "Using the convention Q positive into the system and W positive out of it, a system loses 40 kJ of heat while a paddle wheel does 15 kJ of work on it. What are Q and W?", "options": ["Q = −40 kJ, W = +15 kJ", "Q = −40 kJ, W = −15 kJ", "Q = +40 kJ, W = −15 kJ", "Q = +40 kJ, W = +15 kJ"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Heat leaving the system is negative in this convention, so Q = −40 kJ. Work done on the system (by the paddle wheel) is negative, so W = −15 kJ.", "distractors": {"3": "Both signs are flipped: the heat leaves and the work is done on the system.", "0": "The heat sign is right but paddle-wheel work done on the system is negative, not positive.", "2": "Heat lost by the system must be negative; the work sign here is right but the heat sign is wrong."}, "topic": "Forms of energy and energy transfer by heat"}, {"id": "energy-s1-q7", "text": "A 50 kg block of water is lifted 30 m. With Q = 0 it follows T₂/T₁ = (P₂/P₁)^((k−1)/k), a reversible adiabatic expansion.", "distractors": {"1": "The leaving air carries enthalpy; the cooling is best seen through the remaining gas doing work.", "2": "T ∝ P holds only for fixed mass at constant volume; here mass is leaving.", "3": "Throttling affects the escaping stream, and for an ideal gas it causes no temperature change."}, "topic": "Unsteady flow"}, {"id": "cv-s4-q7", "text": "Which pair of assumptions defines the uniform-flow process used for tank charging problems?", "options": ["Steady flow at the inlet and zero heat transfer", "Negligible kinetic energy and an ideal gas", "A uniform state inside the control volume at each instant, and a fixed state at each inlet and exit during the process", "Constant mass inside and constant temperature at the inlet"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Uniform flow means the contents have one state at each moment (though it changes), and each crossing stream has a state fixed in time. What is its thermal efficiency?", "options": ["67%", "40%", "167%", "60%"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Net work per cycle is 50 − 30 = 20 kJ, and η = W/Q_H = 20/50 = 0.40, the same as 1 − 30/50.", "distractors": {"3": "60% is Q_L/Q_H, the fraction rejected, not the fraction converted to work.", "0": "67% is W/Q_L, work divided by the rejected heat instead of the supplied heat.", "2": "An efficiency over 100% would create energy from nothing and breaks the first law."}, "topic": "Why a first law is not enough"}, {"id": "second-s1-q2", "text": "A diesel generator set produces 700 kW of shaft power with a thermal efficiency of 35%. What is wrong with the claim?", "options": ["It violates the first law because 1200 kJ in and only 450 kJ out do not balance", "It violates the second law: with no heat rejection, the device would need an efficiency of 100%", "It violates the first law because energy is created inside the device", "Nothing; efficiency below 100% is allowed"], "correct": 0, "explain": "A cycle has ΔU = 0, so energy in must equal energy out. 1200 kJ enters, but only 450 kJ leaves as work and nothing leaves as heat: 750 kJ has vanished, which the first law forbids. What is the rate of entropy generation in the valve?", "options": ["0.733 kW/K", "−1.467 kW/K", "1.467 kW/K", "0 kW/K"], "correct": 2, "explain": "For an adiabatic single-stream device Ṡ_gen = ṁ(s_e − s_i) = 2 kg/s × (7.8581 − 7.1246) kJ/kg·K = 1.467 kW/K.", "distractors": {"3": "Zero assumes the throttle is isentropic because it is isenthalpic; the unrestrained pressure drop is irreversible, so s rises.", "0": "0.733 kW/K is the per-kilogram entropy rise; it has not been multiplied by the 2 kg/s flow rate.", "1": "−1.467 kW/K uses inlet minus exit; a negative generation is impossible, which is the clue that the subtraction is the wrong way round."}, "topic": "The entropy balance for closed systems and control volumes"}, {"id": "entropy-s4-q2", "text": "An electric resistance heater draws 2 kW steadily. The fraction of boiler steam extracted is:", "options": ["0.279", "0.773", "0.227", "0.294"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Energy balance on the adiabatic mixing chamber: y h6 + (1 − y) h2 = h3, so y = (h3 − h2)/(h6 − h2) = (798.33 − 193.01)/(2860.2 − 193.01) = 0.227.", "distractors": {"3": "This uses h6 − h3 in the denominator; the correct denominator is the difference between the extracted steam and the incoming feedwater, h6 − h2.", "1": "This is 1 − y, the fraction that continues to the condenser, not the extracted fraction.", "0": "This is h3/h6, a ratio of enthalpies with no physical basis; the balance must be written on enthalpy differences."}, "topic": "Regeneration with open and closed feedwater heaters"}, {"id": "vapcycles-s3-q2", "text": "A closed feedwater heater raises the feedwater enthalpy from 200 kJ/kg to 740 kJ/kg using extracted steam at 2900 kJ/kg that condenses to saturated liquid at 762.51 kJ/kg (drain leaves as saturated liquid). The actual work output is:", "options": ["1078.8 kJ/kg", "1269.2 kJ/kg", "1493.2 kJ/kg", "190.4 kJ/kg"], "correct": 0, "explain": "w_actual = η_T × (h3 − h4s) = 0.85 × (3399.5 − 2130.3) = 0.85 × 1269.2 = 1078.8 kJ/kg. What is the highest possible COP of a refrigerator working between these two temperatures?", "options": ["0.132", "6.58", "−0.25", "7.58"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The reversed Carnot COP is T_L/(T_H − T_L) with kelvin in the numerator: 263.15 K/(303.15 − 263.15) K = 263.15/40 = 6.58.", "distractors": {"3": "7.58 is T_H/(T_H − T_L), the Carnot heat-pump COP, which is the refrigerator value plus one.", "2": "−0.25 comes from putting −10 °C in the numerator; the numerator must be in kelvin.", "0": "0.132 is (T_H − T_L)/T_H, the Carnot engine efficiency, not a refrigerator COP."}, "topic": "The reversed Carnot cycle and the ideal vapour-compression cycle"}, {"id": "refrig-s1-q2", "text": "A chiller removes heat from a process at a steady 35 kW. a valve or capillary tube does the pressure drop for almost nothing.", "distractors": {"2": "Turbines operate between any two pressures; the vapour power cycle does exactly that.", "0": "For the same outlet pressure the isentropic expansion reaches the same saturation temperature; What fraction of the mass has become vapour when it enters the evaporator?", "options": ["0.40", "0.68", "0.32", "0.00"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Throttling fixes h4 = h3 = 95.47 kJ/kg, so x4 = (95.47 − 27.08)/(239.16 − 27.08) = 68.39/212.08 = 0.32.", "distractors": {"0": "0.40 would follow from dividing by h_g alone (95.47/239.16) instead of by h_fg.", "3": "Zero quality would mean saturated liquid at the low pressure, but the enthalpy is fixed at 95.47 kJ/kg, well above h_f = 27.08 kJ/kg.", "1": "0.68 is the liquid fraction, 1 − x4, not the vapour fraction."}, "topic": "The reversed Carnot cycle and the ideal vapour-compression cycle"}], "THERMO/refrig/s2": [{"id": "refrig-s2-q1", "text": "The isentropic compressor work in a refrigeration cycle is 36.23 kJ/kg and the compressor's isentropic efficiency is 80 %. How much work does the compressor actually consume per kilogram of refrigerant?", "options": ["9.06 kJ/kg", "29.0 kJ/kg", "36.2 kJ/kg", "45.3 kJ/kg"], "correct": 3, "explain": "For a compressor η_C = w_s/w_a, so w_a = w_s/η_C = 36.23/0.80 = 45.3 kJ/kg; the real machine needs more work than the ideal one.", "distractors": {"1": "29.0 kJ/kg is 36.23 × 0.80, which would make the real compressor need less work than the isentropic one.", "2": "36.2 kJ/kg is the isentropic work itself; the efficiency has not been applied.", "0": "9.06 kJ/kg is the extra work 45.3 − 36.23 lost to irreversibility, not the total."}, "topic": "Actual cycles, refrigerant selection and heat pump systems"}, {"id": "refrig-s2-q2", "text": "A heat pump with a COP of 3.5 is driven by a 2.5 kW compressor. How much heat does it deliver to the house, and how much does it draw from the outside air?", "options": ["11.25 kW delivered, 8.75 kW drawn from outside", "6.25 kW delivered, 3.75 kW drawn from outside", "8.75 kW delivered, 6.25 kW drawn from outside", "8.75 kW delivered, 8.75 kW drawn from outside"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Q_H = COP_HP × W = 3.5 × 2.5 = 8.75 kW, and the first law gives Q_L = Q_H − W = 8.75 − 2.5 = 6.25 kW from the outdoor coil.", "distractors": {"3": "The outdoor coil cannot supply all of Q_H; the compressor work accounts for 2.5 kW of the delivered heat.", "0": "11.25 kW treats 3.5 as the refrigerator COP and adds one; the question states the heat-pump COP.", "1": "6.25 kW is the heat drawn from outside, not the heat delivered; the two are swapped."}, "topic": "Actual cycles, refrigerant selection and heat pump systems"}, {"id": "refrig-s2-q3", "text": "In a real vapour-compression cycle the liquid leaving the condenser is cooled several degrees below its saturation temperature before the expansion valve. What is the effect on the cycle?", "options": ["The compressor work per kilogram falls, so the COP rises", "The refrigeration effect falls because the liquid carries less energy into the evaporator", "Nothing changes because the throttling is isenthalpic either way", "The refrigeration effect per kilogram increases with no change in compressor work, so the COP rises"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Subcooling lowers h3 and therefore h4, so h1 − h4 grows; the compressor sees the same inlet and outlet states, so w_in is unchanged and the COP increases.", "distractors": {"0": "The compressor's states are unaffected by what happens after the condenser; its work per kilogram is the same.", "1": "A lower h4 means more enthalpy can be absorbed in the evaporator, so the refrigeration effect rises, not falls.", "2": "Throttling is isenthalpic, but the enthalpy being held constant is now lower, which changes the evaporator inlet state."}, "topic": "Actual cycles, refrigerant selection and heat pump systems"}, {"id": "refrig-s2-q4", "text": "R-134a leaves a condenser at 0.72 MPa and 26 °C. To find its enthalpy from the standard tables you should use:", "options": ["h_f from the saturation-by-pressure table at 0.72 MPa", "h_g from the saturation-by-pressure table at 0.72 MPa", "the superheated table at 0.72 MPa and 26 °C", "h_f from the saturation-by-temperature table at 26 °C"], "correct": 3, "explain": "At 26 °C the saturation pressure is 685.84 kPa, below 720 kPa, so the state is compressed liquid, and compressed-liquid enthalpy is approximated by the saturated liquid at the same temperature: h ≈ h_f@26 °C = 87.83 kJ/kg.", "distractors": {"0": "h_f at 0.72 MPa is the liquid at that pressure's saturation temperature, which is higher than 26 °C, so it overstates h3 by a few kJ/kg.", "1": "h_g is the saturated vapour, not the liquid leaving the condenser.", "2": "There is no superheated entry for this state: the liquid is below its saturation temperature, not the vapour above it."}, "topic": "Actual cycles, refrigerant selection and heat pump systems"}, {"id": "refrig-s2-q5", "text": "A refrigerant is being chosen for a freezer whose evaporator must run at −20 °C. Which thermodynamic property makes a fluid unsuitable for this duty on its own?", "options": ["Its saturation pressure at −20 °C is well below atmospheric pressure", "It has zero ozone depletion potential", "Its critical temperature is above 100 °C", "Its enthalpy of vaporisation at −20 °C is large"], "correct": 0, "explain": "An evaporator below atmospheric pressure lets air and moisture leak in, which causes ice in the valve and non-condensable gas in the condenser; the fluid's vapour-pressure curve must give a pressure above 1 atm at the evaporator temperature.", "distractors": {"2": "A high critical temperature is desirable: it keeps the condensing temperature well below the critical point.", "3": "A large h_fg is desirable because it reduces the mass flow needed for a given cooling load.", "1": "Zero ODP is an environmental advantage, not a thermodynamic drawback."}, "topic": "Actual cycles, refrigerant selection and heat pump systems"}, {"id": "refrig-s2-q6", "text": "Why does a ground-source heat pump generally achieve a higher seasonal COP than an air-source unit heating the same house?", "options": ["Ground-source units do not need a condenser", "The ground loop replaces the compressor with a pump", "The soil a few metres down stays near the yearly average temperature, so the source is warmer in winter and the temperature lift is smaller", "Ground-source units use a refrigerant with a higher enthalpy of vaporisation"], "correct": 2, "explain": "The COP of any heat pump falls as T_H − T_L grows; the ground is warmer than the winter air (and there is no frost to defrost), so the lift is smaller and the COP higher, at the cost of an expensive buried loop.", "distractors": {"3": "Both types use the same range of refrigerants; the difference is the temperature of the source.", "1": "The ground loop is only a heat exchanger; a compressor still drives the vapour-compression cycle.", "0": "Every vapour-compression heat pump needs a condenser; in heating mode it is the indoor coil."}, "topic": "Actual cycles, refrigerant selection and heat pump systems"}, {"id": "refrig-s2-q7", "text": "A house at 21 °C loses heat to outdoor air at −5 °C. What is the maximum COP any heat pump could have while heating it, and what does a more realistic COP of 3 mean for the electricity used per kilowatt of heat?", "options": ["0.81; about 3 kW of electricity per kW of heat", "10.3; about 0.33 kW of electricity per kW of heat", "11.3; about 3 kW of electricity per kW of heat", "11.3; about 0.33 kW of electricity per kW of heat"], "correct": 3, "explain": "COP_HP,Carnot = T_H/(T_H − T_L) = 294.15/(294.15 − 268.15) = 294.15/26 = 11.3; with a real COP of 3 the electricity is W = Q_H/3 = 0.33 kW per kW of heat.", "distractors": {"1": "10.3 is the refrigerator Carnot COP T_L/(T_H − T_L); a heat pump's is one higher.", "0": "0.81 comes from using 21 °C in the numerator instead of 294.15 K.", "2": "A COP of 3 means the electricity is one third of the heat delivered, not three times it."}, "topic": "Actual cycles, refrigerant selection and heat pump systems"}], "THERMO/refrig/s3": [{"id": "refrig-s3-q1", "text": "An absorption chiller is driven by waste steam at 150 °C, rejects heat to surroundings at 30 °C and cools a space at −5 °C. What is the highest COP (cooling per unit of generator heat) that the second law allows?", "options": ["2.17", "7.66", "5.49", "0.284"], "correct": 0, "explain": "COP_abs,max = (1 − T0/Ts) × T_L/(T0 − T_L) = (1 − 303.15/423.15) × 268.15/(303.15 − 268.15) = 0.2836 × 7.661 = 2.17.", "distractors": {"1": "7.66 is only the Carnot refrigerator factor T_L/(T0 − T_L); it ignores that the driving heat must first be converted with Carnot efficiency.", "3": "0.284 is only the Carnot engine efficiency 1 − T0/Ts of the heat source; it must be multiplied by the refrigerator COP.", "2": "5.49 is (T0/Ts) × T_L/(T0 − T_L) = 0.7164 × 7.661: the engine factor must be the Carnot efficiency 1 − T0/Ts, not the ratio T0/Ts."}, "topic": "Cascade, multistage, absorption and gas refrigeration cycles"}, {"id": "refrig-s3-q2", "text": "A gas refrigeration cycle uses air (k = 1.4) with a compressor pressure ratio of 3 on the cold-air-standard model. What is its COP?", "options": ["0.50", "0.27", "2.71", "7.80"], "correct": 2, "explain": "COP = 1/(r_p^((k−1)/k) − 1) = 1/(3^0.2857 − 1) = 1/(1.3687 − 1) = 2.71.", "distractors": {"0": "0.50 is 1/(r_p − 1), forgetting the exponent (k − 1)/k on the pressure ratio.", "1": "0.27 is 1 − 1/r_p^((k−1)/k), the Brayton power-cycle efficiency, not the refrigerator COP.", "3": "7.80 is a reversed Carnot COP between 0 °C and 35 °C; the gas cycle's COP depends only on the pressure ratio and is far lower."}, "topic": "Cascade, multistage, absorption and gas refrigeration cycles"}, {"id": "refrig-s3-q3", "text": "In a two-stage cascade system the lower loop's condenser is the upper loop's evaporator. Which relation fixes the ratio of the two mass flow rates?", "options": ["The ratio of the two compressor pressure ratios", "The two mass flow rates are always equal because the loops share the intermediate pressure", "The ratio of the saturation temperatures at the two pressure limits", "An energy balance on the adiabatic heat exchanger: ṁ_A(h5 − h8) = ṁ_B(h2 − h3)"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The exchanger transfers all the heat rejected by the lower loop's condenser to the upper loop's evaporator, so the two ṁ Δh products are equal; the flows differ because the enthalpy changes differ.", "distractors": {"1": "The loops are separate closed circuits; sharing a pressure level says nothing about their mass flows.", "0": "Pressure ratios set the compressor work per kilogram, not how much mass each loop circulates.", "2": "Saturation temperatures fix the states, but only the energy balance links the two flows."}, "topic": "Cascade, multistage, absorption and gas refrigeration cycles"}, {"id": "refrig-s3-q4", "text": "Saturated liquid R-134a at 0.8 MPa (h = 95.47 kJ/kg) is throttled into a flash chamber at 0.32 MPa, where h_f = 55.16 kJ/kg and h_g = 251.88 kJ/kg. What fraction of the flow is separated as vapour and sent to the high-pressure compressor?", "options": ["0.379", "0.795", "0.160", "0.205"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The throttling is isenthalpic, so x = (95.47 − 55.16)/(251.88 − 55.16) = 40.31/196.72 = 0.205; about a fifth of the flow bypasses the evaporator.", "distractors": {"0": "0.379 is 95.47/251.88, dividing by h_g instead of by h_fg after subtracting h_f.", "1": "0.795 is the liquid fraction that continues to the evaporator, 1 − x.", "2": "0.160 is 40.31/251.88, the numerator divided by h_g rather than by h_fg."}, "topic": "Cascade, multistage, absorption and gas refrigeration cycles"}, {"id": "refrig-s3-q5", "text": "What is the main reason an absorption refrigeration system needs far less work input than a vapour-compression system of the same capacity?", "options": ["Ammonia has a much larger enthalpy of vaporisation than R-134a", "The generator recovers the throttling loss", "The refrigerant is raised to the condenser pressure as a liquid solution by a pump, and the vapour is released by heating rather than by mechanical compression", "The absorber condenses the refrigerant at the low pressure so no condenser is needed"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Pumping a liquid takes very little work (small specific volume), so the mechanical input is tiny; the energy to separate the refrigerant is supplied as heat in the generator, which is why the COP is defined per unit of heat.", "distractors": {"3": "The absorber dissolves vapour into a liquid; the refrigerant is still condensed in a separate condenser at the high pressure.", "0": "Ammonia's h_fg is large, but that affects the mass flow, not whether the pressure rise is done by pump or compressor.", "1": "The throttling loss is the same as in any vapour cycle; the generator supplies heat, it does not recover it."}, "topic": "Cascade, multistage, absorption and gas refrigeration cycles"}, {"id": "refrig-s3-q6", "text": "Aircraft cabin cooling systems use an open reversed Brayton cycle with engine bleed air even though its COP is much lower than a vapour-compression unit's. Why?", "options": ["Air has a larger enthalpy of vaporisation than any refrigerant", "The equipment is light and simple, the working fluid is the cabin air itself, and the very cold turbine exit is useful", "The gas cycle has a higher COP at the low pressures found at altitude", "Vapour-compression cycles cannot operate at altitude"], "correct": 1, "explain": "On an aircraft weight and simplicity outweigh efficiency; compressed air is already available from the engine, no refrigerant or condenser is needed, and the turbine exit air can be delivered directly to the cabin.", "distractors": {"3": "Vapour-compression cycles work at any altitude; they are simply heavier and more complex for this application.", "2": "The gas cycle's COP depends only on its pressure ratio and is always well below a vapour cycle's between the same temperatures.", "0": "Air does not change phase in the cycle; enthalpy of vaporisation is irrelevant to it."}, "topic": "Cascade, multistage, absorption and gas refrigeration cycles"}, {"id": "refrig-s3-q7", "text": "Which of the following correctly describes a thermoelectric (Peltier) cooler?", "options": ["Heat is pumped by the Seebeck voltage generated at the hot junction with a COP close to the Carnot value", "A vapour is compressed electrostatically between the junctions", "A temperature difference across the junctions drives a current that runs a small compressor", "A current through junctions of dissimilar semiconductors makes one set of junctions absorb heat and the other reject it, with no moving parts and a low COP"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The Peltier effect is the reverse of the Seebeck effect: forcing current through the junctions moves heat from the cold junctions to the hot ones; the device is silent and compact but its COP is far below a vapour-compression machine's.", "distractors": {"2": "A temperature difference producing a current is the Seebeck effect (a thermocouple); a cooler uses the reverse and has no compressor.", "1": "There is no vapour and no compression of any kind in a thermoelectric device.", "0": "Thermoelectric coolers have COPs far below Carnot; the Seebeck voltage is what a thermocouple produces, not what pumps the heat."}, "topic": "Cascade, multistage, absorption and gas refrigeration cycles"}], "THERMO/relations/s1": [{"id": "relations-s1-q1", "text": "A superheated-steam table at 500 kPa lists v = 0.47443 m³/kg at 250 °C and v = 0.57015 m³/kg at 350 °C. Using a Maxwell relation and a central difference, what is the best estimate of (∂s/∂P)T for steam at 300 °C and 500 kPa?", "options": ["−0.000923 m³/kg·K", "+0.000957 m³/kg·K", "−0.000957 m³/kg·K", "−0.001914 m³/kg·K"], "correct": 2, "explain": "From dg = −s dT + v dP, (∂s/∂P)T = −(∂v/∂T)P ≈ −(0.57015 − 0.47443)/(350 − 250) = −0.09572/100 = −0.000957 m³/kg·K. The direct entropy difference from the same table (s at 400 and 600 kPa) gives −0.000969, confirming the estimate.", "distractors": {"1": "Drops the minus sign of the fourth Maxwell relation; entropy falls as pressure rises at fixed T.", "3": "Divides the 100 K volume difference by 50 K, the half-interval, which doubles the slope.", "0": "This is the ideal-gas shortcut −R/P = −0.4615/500, not the table estimate the question asks for."}, "topic": "Partial derivatives, the Gibbs functions and the Maxwell relations"}, {"id": "relations-s1-q2", "text": "Air (ideal gas, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K) is compressed isothermally at 300 K until its specific volume is halved. What is the change in its specific Helmholtz function, Δa?", "options": ["−59.7 kJ/kg", "+59.7 kJ/kg", "+5.37 kJ/kg", "+209.0 kJ/kg"], "correct": 1, "explain": "At constant T, Δa = Δu − TΔs. For an ideal gas Δu = 0 at constant T and Δs = R ln(v2/v1) = 0.287 ln 0.5 = −0.1989 kJ/kg·K, so Δa = −300 × (−0.1989) = +59.7 kJ/kg, the minimum work needed to compress it.", "distractors": {"0": "Sign error: entropy falls on isothermal compression, so −TΔs and hence Δa are positive.", "2": "Uses T = 27 °C instead of 300 K; T multiplies s here, so it must be in kelvin.", "3": "Uses cp = 1.005 in place of R; the isothermal entropy change of an ideal gas involves R, not a specific heat."}, "topic": "Partial derivatives, the Gibbs functions and the Maxwell relations"}, {"id": "relations-s1-q3", "text": "Saturated water at 150 °C has hf = 632.18 kJ/kg, sf = 1.8418 kJ/kg·K, hg = 2745.9 kJ/kg and sg = 6.8371 kJ/kg·K. What is the specific Gibbs function of the saturated vapour, gg?", "options": ["+2113.7 kJ/kg", "+1720.3 kJ/kg", "−147.2 kJ/kg", "0 kJ/kg"], "correct": 2, "explain": "gg = hg − T sg = 2745.9 − 423.15 × 6.8371 = −147.2 kJ/kg. The liquid gives gf = 632.18 − 423.15 × 1.8418 = −147.2 kJ/kg as well: g is equal in the two phases at the same T and P, which is the condition for phase equilibrium.", "distractors": {"1": "Uses T = 150 in Celsius: 2745.9 − 150 × 6.8371 = 1720.3. T multiplies s, so it must be 423.15 K.", "0": "This is hfg = hg − hf, the enthalpy of vaporisation, not a Gibbs function.", "3": "Confuses gg − gf = 0 with gg = 0; the two phases have equal g, not zero g."}, "topic": "Partial derivatives, the Gibbs functions and the Maxwell relations"}, {"id": "relations-s1-q4", "text": "Apply the exactness test to the Gibbs equation for enthalpy, dh = T ds + v dP. Which Maxwell relation results?", "options": ["(∂s/∂v)T = (∂P/∂T)v", "(∂T/∂P)s = (∂v/∂s)P", "(∂s/∂P)T = −(∂v/∂T)P", "(∂T/∂v)s = −(∂P/∂s)v"], "correct": 1, "explain": "With x = s, y = P, M = T and N = v, exactness requires (∂M/∂P)s = (∂N/∂s)P, i.e. (∂T/∂P)s = (∂v/∂s)P. No minus sign appears because both coefficients in dh are positive.", "distractors": {"0": "This comes from the Helmholtz equation da = −s dT − P dv, whose natural variables are T and v.", "3": "This comes from du = T ds − P dv; the minus sign is inherited from the −P dv term.", "2": "This comes from the Gibbs function dg = −s dT + v dP, not from dh."}, "topic": "Partial derivatives, the Gibbs functions and the Maxwell relations"}, {"id": "relations-s1-q5", "text": "A classmate multiplies (∂P/∂T)v, (∂T/∂v)P and (∂v/∂P)T for an ideal gas, cancels the symbols like ordinary fractions, and announces the product must be +1. What is the product really, and why?", "options": ["+1, because every variable appears once on top and once underneath", "−1, because a different variable is held constant in each factor, so they cannot be cancelled like fractions", "0, because the ideal gas has no intermolecular forces", "−1 only for an ideal gas; for real substances it is +1"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The cyclic relation gives −1 for any three variables linked by one equation of state. For the ideal gas: (R/v)(P/R)(−RT/P²) = −RT/(Pv) = −1. The held-constant subscripts differ, so fraction-style cancelling is invalid.", "distractors": {"0": "Fraction-style cancelling ignores that each partial derivative holds a different variable fixed.", "2": "The product is a mathematical identity among partial derivatives and has nothing to do with molecular forces.", "3": "The cyclic relation is pure calculus and holds for any substance with a smooth equation of state."}, "topic": "Partial derivatives, the Gibbs functions and the Maxwell relations"}, {"id": "relations-s1-q6", "text": "Why are the Helmholtz and Gibbs functions more convenient than u and h for building property relations from laboratory data?", "options": ["They are always numerically smaller than u and h", "They are not properties, so they can depend on the path", "They have an absolute zero, while u and h do not", "Their natural variables, (T, v) for a and (T, P) for g, are directly measurable, unlike entropy"], "correct": 3, "explain": "da = −s dT − P dv and dg = −s dT + v dP, so a and g are naturally functions of T with v or P. Their Maxwell relations replace entropy derivatives with derivatives of measurable P-v-T data, whereas u(s, v) and h(s, P) keep entropy as an independent variable.", "distractors": {"0": "Their size is irrelevant, and since only differences matter they can be negative or positive.", "1": "a and g are built only from properties (u, h, T, s), so they are properties with exact differentials.", "2": "Like u and h, only differences in a and g matter; neither has a meaningful absolute zero."}, "topic": "Partial derivatives, the Gibbs functions and the Maxwell relations"}, {"id": "relations-s1-q7", "text": "A proposed property z has the differential dz = 2xy dx + (x² + 3) dy. What does the exactness test tell you?", "options": ["Exact, because (∂M/∂y)x = 2x and (∂N/∂x)y = 2x, so z could be a property", "Not exact, because M and N have different units", "Not exact, because (∂M/∂y)x = 2x while (∂N/∂x)y = 2x + 3", "Exact only along paths of constant y"], "correct": 0, "explain": "M = 2xy and N = x² + 3. Then ∂M/∂y = 2x and ∂N/∂x = 2x: equal, so dz is exact and z = x²y + 3y is a state function whose change is path independent.", "distractors": {"2": "The constant 3 vanishes when N is differentiated with respect to x, so ∂N/∂x is 2x, not 2x + 3.", "3": "Exactness is a property of the differential itself, not of any particular path.", "1": "M dx and N dy must share units with dz; M and N themselves need not share units, and that is not the test."}, "topic": "Partial derivatives, the Gibbs functions and the Maxwell relations"}], "THERMO/relations/s2": [{"id": "relations-s2-q1", "text": "R-134a saturation data: Psat = 387.61 kPa at 8 °C and 443.01 kPa at 12 °C; at 10 °C, vf = 0.000793 m³/kg and vg = 0.049442 m³/kg. Estimate hfg at 10 °C with the Clapeyron equation.", "options": ["0.00238 kJ/kg", "3.11 kJ/kg", "6.74 kJ/kg", "190.8 kJ/kg"], "correct": 3, "explain": "(dP/dT)sat ≈ (443.01 − 387.61)/4 = 13.851 kPa/K; vfg = 0.049442 − 0.000793 = 0.048649 m³/kg; hfg = T vfg (dP/dT) = 283.15 × 0.048649 × 13.851 = 190.8 kJ/kg, within 0.03% of the tabulated 190.74 kJ/kg (reference equation of state for R-134a, evaluated with CoolProp).", "distractors": {"2": "Uses T = 10 °C instead of 283.15 K; T multiplies vfg in the Clapeyron equation, so kelvin is compulsory.", "1": "Uses vf in place of vfg; the volume change on boiling is vg − vf, dominated by vg.", "0": "Divides by T instead of multiplying: hfg = T vfg (dP/dT)sat, so T belongs on top."}, "topic": "The Clapeyron equation and general relations for du, dh, ds, cv and cp"}, {"id": "relations-s2-q2", "text": "Water boils at 2.3393 kPa at 20 °C, where hfg = 2453.5 kJ/kg. The steam table gives 4.247 kPa: Clausius-Clapeyron is excellent over a 10 K step.", "distractors": {"3": "Uses Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K with a mass-based hfg in kJ/kg; the exponent shrinks by a factor of 18.", "0": "Swaps the order in the bracket (1/T2 − 1/T1), which makes the pressure fall as the temperature rises.", "1": "Puts Celsius temperatures in 1/T1 − 1/T2; reciprocal temperatures must be in kelvin."}, "topic": "The Clapeyron equation and general relations for du, dh, ds, cv and cp"}, {"id": "relations-s2-q3", "text": "Liquid water at 60 °C and 100 kPa has v = 0.0010171 m³/kg, volume expansivity β = 5.233 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹ and isothermal compressibility α = 4.450 × 10⁻¹⁰ Pa⁻¹. What is cp − cv?", "options": ["37.6 J/kg·K", "208.5 J/kg·K", "398 kJ/kg·K", "0 J/kg·K, since cp = cv for any liquid"], "correct": 1, "explain": "cp − cv = v T β²/α = 0.0010171 × 333.15 × (5.233 × 10⁻⁴)² / 4.450 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 208.5 J/kg·K. enthalpy has no such natural zero and needs the formation convention instead.", "distractors": {"1": "Entropy generation is positive for any real reaction; the carbon example gave over 1300 kJ/kmol·K.", "3": "Zero enthalpy for the elements is the enthalpy-of-formation convention, not a law of thermodynamics.", "2": "That is a consequence of the first law energy balance, not the third law."}, "topic": "Adiabatic flame temperature and second-law analysis of reactions"}, {"id": "combust-s3-q7", "text": "A fuel is burned adiabatically in a combustor and the hot products then heat steam in a boiler. From a second-law point of view, why is the combustion step usually the largest single source of exergy destruction in the plant?", "options": ["Because the products are at 1 atm and exergy is zero at atmospheric pressure", "An uncontrolled reaction across a huge chemical-potential difference, heating of products across thousands of kelvin, and mixing", "Because the enthalpy of formation of the products is negative, which counts as lost energy", "Because the combustor loses more heat through its walls than any other component"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Adiabatic combustion generates entropy even with no heat loss: the chemical reaction, the internal heating across a large ΔT and the mixing are all irreversible, which is why fuel cells that avoid the flame can in principle do better.", "distractors": {"3": "The combustor in the question is adiabatic; the destruction happens inside the process, not through heat loss.", "2": "A negative enthalpy of formation is a bookkeeping value, not an energy loss; energy is conserved in the combustor.", "0": "Exergy at 1 atm is not zero when the temperature and composition differ from the dead state; the hot products carry a great deal of exergy."}, "topic": "Adiabatic flame temperature and second-law analysis of reactions"}, {"id": "combust-s3-q8", "text": "Methane and oxygen react at 25 °C and 1 atm to CO2 and liquid water, each species at the standard state. With Gibbs functions of formation (kJ/kmol) CH4 −50,790, CO2 −394,360, H2O(l) −237,180 and H2O(g) −228,590, what is the maximum work per kmol of methane, as an ideal fuel cell would deliver?", "options": ["868,720 kJ", "817,930 kJ", "890,330 kJ", "800,750 kJ"], "correct": 1, "explain": "W_rev = Σ N_r ḡf°_r − Σ N_p ḡf°_p = (−50,790 + 0) − (−394,360 + 2 × (−237,180)) = 817,930 kJ per kmol CH4, about 92% of the 890,330 kJ/kmol higher heating value.", "distractors": {"3": "This uses the vapour-phase Gibbs function of water, but the question states the water leaves as liquid.", "0": "This drops the methane term; the fuel’s own Gibbs function of formation is part of the reactant sum.", "2": "This is the enthalpy of combustion (the HHV), the heat released, not the Gibbs-function change that limits the work."}, "topic": "Adiabatic flame temperature and second-law analysis of reactions"}], "THERMO/equil/s1": [{"id": "equil-s1-q1", "text": "A reacting ideal-gas mixture is held at fixed temperature and pressure. Which statement correctly describes the condition at chemical equilibrium?", "options": ["The enthalpy of the mixture is at a minimum", "The total Gibbs function of the mixture is at a minimum", "The total entropy of the mixture is at a maximum", "The forward reaction has stopped and only the reverse proceeds"], "correct": 1, "explain": "At constant T and P the second law reduces to dG ≤ 0 for any spontaneous change, so the equilibrium composition is the one that minimises G.", "distractors": {"2": "Maximum entropy is the criterion for an isolated system, not for one held at constant T and P by exchanging heat with its surroundings.", "0": "Enthalpy alone ignores the entropy contribution; G = H − TS is the relevant function.", "3": "Equilibrium is dynamic: forward and reverse reactions proceed at equal rates, neither stops."}, "topic": "The criterion for chemical equilibrium and the equilibrium constant KP"}, {"id": "equil-s1-q2", "text": "Table A-28 gives ln KP = −2.801 for CO2 ⇌ CO + ½O2 at 2,600 K. What is KP for the reaction 2CO + O2 ⇌ 2CO2 at the same temperature?", "options": ["−5.60", "0.0607", "271", "16.5"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Reversing gives KP = e^(+2.801) = 16.46; doubling every coefficient squares it: 16.46² = 271.", "distractors": {"3": "16.5 is KP for CO + ½O2 ⇌ CO2, the reversed reaction with the original coefficients; doubling the coefficients squares it.", "1": "0.0607 is e^(−2.801), the constant for the dissociation as tabulated, without reversing or doubling.", "0": "−5.60 is 2 × ln KP for the tabulated reaction; KP itself is always positive and this is a logarithm, not a constant."}, "topic": "The criterion for chemical equilibrium and the equilibrium constant KP"}, {"id": "equil-s1-q3", "text": "At 3,000 K and 1 atm, 43.7% of a sample of pure CO2 is dissociated into CO and O2. What happens to the fraction dissociated, and why?", "options": ["It rises because compression heats the gas and raises KP", "It falls to exactly 4.37% because dissociation scales as 1/P", "It stays at 43.7% because KP depends only on temperature", "It falls (to about 24%) because Δν = +½ and higher pressure favours fewer moles"], "correct": 3, "explain": "KP is unchanged but the factor (P/N_total)^Δν with Δν = +½ grows with P, so the mole-number ratio must shrink: α drops from 0.437 to 0.241.", "distractors": {"2": "KP is indeed fixed by T, but the composition also contains the (P/N_total)^Δν factor, which changes with pressure.", "0": "The temperature is held at 3,000 K; there is no heating in the statement and KP does not change.", "1": "The dependence is through a square-root factor inside a nonlinear equation, not a simple 1/P scaling; the computed value is 24%, not 4.4%."}, "topic": "The criterion for chemical equilibrium and the equilibrium constant KP"}, {"id": "equil-s1-q4", "text": "One kmol of CO2 dissociates at 3,000 K and a fixed total pressure of 1 atm. Five kmol of nitrogen, which does not react, are added while the total pressure is kept at 1 atm. What does the nitrogen do to the amount of CO2 dissociated?", "options": ["Increases it, because N_total rises and (P/N_total)^Δν falls, like lowering the pressure", "Decreases it, because the nitrogen dilutes the CO and O2", "Nothing, because nitrogen does not appear in the KP expression", "Increases it only if the nitrogen is added at a different temperature"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Inert gas enters only through N_total; with Δν = +½ the factor (P/N_total)^½ shrinks, so the reaction shifts toward more moles: α rises from 0.437 to 0.601.", "distractors": {"2": "Nitrogen is absent from the mole-number ratio but present in N_total, which multiplies the whole expression.", "1": "Dilution lowers every partial pressure, and with Δν > 0 that favours the side with more moles, i.e. more dissociation, not less.", "3": "The temperature is held fixed; the effect exists at any temperature and comes purely from N_total."}, "topic": "The criterion for chemical equilibrium and the equilibrium constant KP"}, {"id": "equil-s1-q5", "text": "The Gibbs functions of formation at 298 K are −394,360 kJ/kmol for CO2 and −137,150 kJ/kmol for CO, and zero for O2. Using Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K, what is ln KP for CO2 ⇌ CO + ½O2 at 298.15 K?", "options": ["−103.8 (KP is tiny)", "+103.8 (KP is huge)", "−0.348", "−10.4"], "correct": 0, "explain": "ΔG* = (−137,150 + 0) − (−394,360) = +257,210 kJ/kmol; ln KP = −ΔG*/(RuT) = −257,210/(8.314 × 298.15) = −103.8, matching Table A-28.", "distractors": {"1": "+103.8 has the wrong sign: ln KP = −ΔG*/(RuT), and ΔG* is positive for this dissociation.", "2": "−0.348 divides by the temperature twice (−103.76/298.15); in ln KP = −ΔG*/(RuT) the temperature appears in the denominator only once.", "3": "−10.4 results from dividing by 10 × RuT, e.g. using Ru = 83.14; Ru is 8.314 kJ/kmol·K."}, "topic": "The criterion for chemical equilibrium and the equilibrium constant KP"}, {"id": "equil-s1-q6", "text": "Products of combustion at high temperature are assumed to consist of CO2, CO, O2 and O atoms only. How many independent equilibrium-constant relations are needed to fix the composition, in addition to the element balances?", "options": ["Two", "One", "Four", "Three"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Number of KP equations = species − elements = 4 − 2 = 2, for example CO2 ⇌ CO + ½O2 and O2 ⇌ 2O, plus a carbon and an oxygen balance.", "distractors": {"1": "One KP relation plus two element balances gives only three equations for four unknown mole numbers.", "2": "Four would be more equations than unknowns after adding the element balances; the count is species minus elements.", "3": "Three KP relations would over-determine the system; only two of the possible reactions among these species are independent."}, "topic": "The criterion for chemical equilibrium and the equilibrium constant KP"}, {"id": "equil-s1-q7", "text": "In a gas turbine combustor the pressure is 20 atm. A student argues that the high pressure will reduce the equilibrium amount of NO formed by ½N2 + ½O2 ⇌ NO compared with 1 atm at the same temperature. What is the flaw?", "options": ["NO formation is exothermic, so the argument should be about temperature, not pressure", "Nitrogen is inert and cannot take part in an equilibrium calculation", "Δν = 0 for this reaction, so pressure has no effect on the equilibrium NO fraction", "KP increases with pressure, so NO actually rises"], "correct": 2, "explain": "For ½N2 + ½O2 ⇌ NO the mole count is unchanged (Δν = 1 − ½ − ½ = 0), so (P/N_total)^Δν = 1 and the NO mole fraction depends on temperature only.", "distractors": {"3": "KP never depends on pressure; it is a function of temperature alone.", "0": "NO formation from N2 and O2 is endothermic, and in any case the question is about the pressure dependence, which vanishes because Δν = 0.", "1": "N2 is a reactant here, not an inert; it is inert only in reactions in which it is not written."}, "topic": "The criterion for chemical equilibrium and the equilibrium constant KP"}], "THERMO/equil/s2": [{"id": "equil-s2-q1", "text": "For CO2 ⇌ CO + ½O2, Table A-28 gives ln KP = −6.635 at 2,000 K and −3.860 at 2,400 K. Using the integrated van't Hoff equation with Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K, estimate the enthalpy of this dissociation reaction near 2,200 K.", "options": ["+212,000 kJ/kmol", "+23.1 kJ/kmol", "+277,000 kJ/kmol (endothermic)", "−277,000 kJ/kmol (exothermic)"], "correct": 2, "explain": "hR = Ru·ln(K2/K1)/(1/T1 − 1/T2) = 8.314 × (−3.860 + 6.635)/(1/2000 − 1/2400) = 23.07/(8.333 × 10⁻⁵) = +276,900 kJ/kmol; positive because splitting CO2 absorbs heat.", "distractors": {"3": "The sign is wrong: KP rises with temperature, which by van't Hoff requires a positive (endothermic) hR. −277,000 would be the combustion of CO.", "0": "+212,000 kJ/kmol is what you get by using 1,727 °C and 2,127 °C instead of kelvin in 1/T1 − 1/T2.", "1": "+23.1 kJ/kmol is only Ru × Δ(ln KP); it still has to be divided by (1/T1 − 1/T2) ≈ 8.3 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹."}, "topic": "The van't Hoff equation and dissociation"}, {"id": "equil-s2-q2", "text": "Diatomic hydrogen at 1 atm is 5% dissociated into H atoms. Table A-28 gives ln KP = −3.685 at 3,000 K and −2.534 at 3,200 K for H2 ⇌ 2H. What is the temperature?", "options": ["About 3,150 K", "About 2,600 K", "About 3,535 K", "About 2,840 K"], "correct": 3, "explain": "With α = 0.05: N_H = 0.10, N_H2 = 0.95, N_total = 1.05, KP = 0.10²/0.95 × (1/1.05) = 0.01003, ln KP = −4.60. What does the van't Hoff equation let you conclude about the reaction, before doing any arithmetic?", "options": ["Its enthalpy of reaction is positive: the reaction absorbs heat", "Its equilibrium constant is independent of pressure only above some temperature", "It produces fewer moles of gas than it consumes", "Its entropy change is negative"], "correct": 0, "explain": "d(ln KP)/dT = hR/(RuT²): a positive slope requires hR > 0, i.e. an endothermic reaction such as a dissociation.", "distractors": {"3": "The temperature slope of ln KP is set by hR, not by ΔS; a dissociation in fact has a positive entropy change.", "2": "Mole-number change governs the pressure effect on composition, not the temperature dependence of KP.", "1": "KP is independent of pressure at every temperature; this is not what the trend shows."}, "topic": "The van't Hoff equation and dissociation"}, {"id": "equil-s2-q4", "text": "Hydrogen is burned adiabatically in oxygen. Which statement best explains why the real equilibrium flame temperature is much lower?", "options": ["Some hydrogen fails to ignite at high temperature, so less fuel burns", "Radiation from the flame becomes dominant and removes heat faster than combustion supplies it", "The specific heat of steam drops sharply above 2,000 K, so less energy is stored", "Dissociation of H2O into H2, O2, OH, H and O absorbs a large part of the released energy"], "correct": 3, "explain": "At high temperature KP for the dissociation reactions is no longer negligible; the endothermic splitting of products soaks up energy, and the iterative equilibrium calculation gives a far lower T_ad.", "distractors": {"2": "The specific heat of steam rises with temperature, which is already included in the complete-combustion calculation and is not the missing effect.", "0": "Ignition is not the issue; the reaction proceeds, but at equilibrium the products are partly dissociated.", "1": "Adiabatic flame temperature is by definition computed without heat loss; the lowering comes from the equilibrium composition, not radiation."}, "topic": "The van't Hoff equation and dissociation"}, {"id": "equil-s2-q5", "text": "A rocket combustion chamber runs at 70 atm rather than 1 atm. What went wrong?", "options": ["The student should have used degrees Celsius in the reciprocal temperatures", "The value should have been divided by two because ½O2 appears in the reaction", "The two temperatures are too far apart for van't Hoff to be valid, so the result is meaningless", "Nothing in the arithmetic, but the table reaction is the dissociation; combustion is the reverse, so hR = −251,700 kJ/kmol"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The table lists the endothermic dissociation; combustion is its reverse, with KP → 1/KP, ln KP → −ln KP and hR → −hR. The magnitude is right, the sign must be flipped.", "distractors": {"2": "A 400 K interval gives an answer within 0.01% of the tabulated enthalpy of reaction, so the approximation is excellent here.", "0": "Van't Hoff needs absolute temperatures; Celsius would introduce a 26% error, not fix the sign.", "1": "The enthalpy is per kmol of reaction as written, and the ½ is already inside the tabulated KP; no extra division is needed."}, "topic": "The van't Hoff equation and dissociation"}, {"id": "equil-s2-q7", "text": "One kmol of a diatomic gas X2 is heated until a fraction α has dissociated into atoms at total pressure P (atm). Which expression gives KP for X2 ⇌ 2X in terms of α and P?", "options": ["KP = α²/(1 − α) × P, no total-moles factor", "KP = (2α)²/(1 − α) × P/(1 + α), atoms squared, pressure over total moles", "KP = 2α/(1 − α) × (P/(1 + α))^½, atoms not squared, square-root factor", "KP = (2α)²/(1 − α) × (1 + α)/P, total moles over pressure"], "correct": 1, "explain": "N_X = 2α, N_X2 = 1 − α, N_total = 1 + α and Δν = 2 − 1 = 1, so KP = N_X²/N_X2 × (P/N_total)^1.", "distractors": {"0": "This uses α instead of 2α for the atoms formed and forgets N_total; each dissociated X2 gives two atoms.", "3": "The pressure factor is (P/N_total)^Δν with Δν = +1, not its reciprocal.", "2": "The atom count must be squared (ν_X = 2) and Δν is 1, not ½."}, "topic": "The van't Hoff equation and dissociation"}], "THERMO/equil/s3": [{"id": "equil-s3-q1", "text": "A liquid at 30 °C is 60 mol% ammonia and 40 mol% water. Taking the pure saturation pressures as 1,167 kPa for NH3 and 4.25 kPa for H2O and assuming an ideal solution, what is the mole fraction of ammonia in the equilibrium vapour?", "options": ["0.600", "0.998", "0.400", "0.0024"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Raoult's law: P_NH3 = 0.6 × 1,167 = 700.2 kPa, P_H2O = 0.4 × 4.25 = 1.70 kPa, P = 701.9 kPa, y_NH3 = 700.2/701.9 = 0.9976 ≈ 0.998.", "distractors": {"0": "0.600 is the liquid composition; the vapour is far richer in the volatile component.", "3": "0.0024 is the mole fraction of water in the vapour, i.e. 1 − y_NH3, not the ammonia fraction.", "2": "0.400 is the liquid mole fraction of water, not of ammonia in the vapour."}, "topic": "Phase equilibrium"}, {"id": "equil-s3-q2", "text": "Water at 300 K sits under air at 101.3 kPa total pressure; Henry's constant for O2 in water at 300 K is 45,000 bar and air is 21% O2 by mole. Estimate the mole fraction of dissolved oxygen in the water.", "options": ["4.7 × 10⁻⁴ (0.00047)", "2.3 × 10⁻⁵ (0.000023)", "2.1 × 10⁻¹ (0.21)", "4.7 × 10⁻⁶ (0.0000047)"], "correct": 3, "explain": "P_O2 = 0.21 × 1.013 bar = 0.2127 bar; y_O2,liquid = P_O2/H = 0.2127/45,000 = 4.7 × 10⁻⁶.", "distractors": {"1": "2.3 × 10⁻⁵ uses the total air pressure 1.013 bar instead of the oxygen partial pressure.", "0": "4.7 × 10⁻⁴ arises from putting the partial pressure in kPa (21.3) rather than bar into P/H.", "2": "0.21 is the oxygen mole fraction in the air, not in the water."}, "topic": "Phase equilibrium"}, {"id": "equil-s3-q3", "text": "How many independent intensive properties are needed to fix the state of a mixture of ice, liquid water and steam in equilibrium, and what is the practical consequence?", "options": ["One: choosing T fixes P, as along the vapour-pressure curve", "Three: T, P and the quality", "Two: T and P can both be chosen freely", "None: the triple point occurs at one fixed T and P (0.01 °C, 0.6117 kPa)"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Gibbs phase rule with C = 1 and PH = 3 gives IV = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0; three-phase equilibrium of a pure substance exists at a single point.", "distractors": {"0": "One degree of freedom is the two-phase (saturation) case, PH = 2.", "2": "Two degrees of freedom describe a single-phase region such as superheated steam.", "1": "Quality is a ratio of phase amounts, not an intensive property counted by the phase rule, and three-phase equilibrium has no freedom at all."}, "topic": "Phase equilibrium"}, {"id": "equil-s3-q4", "text": "Saturated liquid water and saturated vapour coexist in a cylinder at 100 °C and 101.42 kPa. Which quantity is equal in the two phases and is the reason no net evaporation or condensation occurs?", "options": ["The specific Gibbs function g = h − Ts", "The specific enthalpy h", "The specific internal energy u", "The specific entropy s"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Minimising G at fixed T and P for a mass transfer between phases gives (g_f − g_g)dm_f = 0, hence g_f = g_g; the steam-table check is h_fg − T s_fg = 2,256 − 373.15 × 6.046 ≈ 0.", "distractors": {"1": "Enthalpies differ by h_fg = 2,256 kJ/kg at 100 °C.", "3": "Entropies differ by s_fg ≈ 6.05 kJ/kg·K; the equality is of g, which combines h and Ts.", "2": "Internal energies differ by u_fg ≈ 2,087 kJ/kg at 100 °C."}, "topic": "Phase equilibrium"}, {"id": "equil-s3-q5", "text": "A student computes the amount of air dissolved in lake water at 40 °C from Henry's law using the full atmospheric pressure of 101 kPa as the air pressure. Roughly how large is the error, and in which direction?", "options": ["About 8% too low, because dissolved water must be subtracted from the liquid", "Negligible, because Henry's constant already accounts for vapour", "About 8% too high, because 7.4 kPa of the 101 kPa above the water is water vapour", "About 50% too high, because Henry's law only holds below 25 °C"], "correct": 2, "explain": "The gas at the surface is saturated with water vapour; P_sat(40 °C) = 7.38 kPa (steam tables), so the dry-air partial pressure is 93.6 kPa and using 101 kPa overstates the dissolved fraction by 101/93.6 − 1 ≈ 8%.", "distractors": {"0": "The correction is on the gas side (partial pressure of dry air), and it lowers the answer, not raises it.", "1": "Henry's constant relates the dry gas partial pressure to the dissolved fraction; the vapour correction is the user's job.", "3": "Henry's law holds at 40 °C with the appropriate constant; the error here is only the vapour correction."}, "topic": "Phase equilibrium"}, {"id": "equil-s3-q6", "text": "Ammonia is far more soluble in water than oxygen is. Highly soluble gases such as NH3 depart from the dilute-solution assumption, so measured equilibrium data are used instead.", "distractors": {"0": "H is inversely related to solubility: a poorly soluble gas such as O2 has H = 45,000 bar at 300 K.", "3": "Raoult's law is for volatile ideal solutions; a sparingly soluble gas in a liquid is a Henry's-law situation, and ammonia obeys neither well.", "2": "The phase rule counts degrees of freedom; it never gives the value of a composition."}, "topic": "Phase equilibrium"}, {"id": "equil-s3-q7", "text": "For a two-component liquid in equilibrium with its vapour (two phases), the Gibbs phase rule gives IV = 2. A test asks: if the temperature and the liquid composition are fixed, what else is determined?", "options": ["Both the total pressure and the vapour composition", "Only the total pressure; the vapour composition remains free", "Only the vapour composition; the pressure remains free", "Nothing further, because two variables have been used up and two more remain"], "correct": 0, "explain": "With IV = 2, fixing T and x_liquid uses both degrees of freedom, so P and the vapour mole fractions follow, as Raoult's law shows (P = Σ x_i P_sat,i, y_i = x_i P_sat,i/P).", "distractors": {"1": "Once P and T and x are known, Raoult's law fixes each y_i as x_i P_sat,i/P; nothing is left free.", "2": "P is also fixed: it is the sum of the partial pressures set by T and the liquid composition.", "3": "IV = 2 means exactly two intensive variables can be chosen; after that, every other intensive property is fixed."}, "topic": "Phase equilibrium"}], "THERMO/compflow/s1": [{"id": "compflow-s1-q1", "text": "Air at 300 K is at rest in a large tank. (σ = 5.670 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²·K⁴.)", "options": ["12.0 W", "2340 W", "25.0 W", "1989 W"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Q̇ = εσA(T_s⁴ − T_surr⁴) = 0.85 × 5.670×10⁻⁸ × 2.5 × (393.15⁴ − 293.15⁴) = 1989 W.", "distractors": {"2": "Used Celsius in T⁴; the Stefan-Boltzmann law needs absolute temperatures.", "0": "Wrote (T_s − T_surr)⁴; the law uses the difference of fourth powers, T_s⁴ − T_surr⁴.", "1": "Treated the pipe as a blackbody; multiply by its emissivity 0.85."}, "topic": "Radiation"}, {"id": "pa-q62", "text": "Air flows parallel to a smooth flat plate with a Reynolds number at the trailing edge of Re_L = 2.4 × 10⁵ and Pr = 0.72. Rigid: P₂ = 100 × 419.9/300 = 140.0 kPa.", "distractors": {"2": "Used c_p; in a rigid tank the work raises U, so ΔT = W/(m c_v).", "3": "Treated the process as having no energy input because Q = 0; the paddle work still raises U.", "0": "Used Celsius temperatures in P₂/P₁ = T₂/T₁; the ratio needs kelvin."}, "topic": "Exam strategy"}, {"id": "pa-q65", "text": "For a closed system, under which conditions may the heat transfer be computed as Q = m c_p (T₂ − T₁)?", "options": ["A quasi-equilibrium constant-pressure process of an ideal gas with constant c_p, in which boundary work is the only work", "A constant-pressure process in which a paddle wheel also does work", "A constant-volume process of an ideal gas", "Any process of an ideal gas, because Δh = c_p ΔT always holds"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Q − W_b = ΔU with W_b = PΔV at constant P gives Q = ΔH. With an ideal gas and constant c_p, ΔH = m c_pΔT. The result needs constant pressure, quasi-equilibrium and no other work mode.", "distractors": {"3": "Δh = c_pΔT always holds for an ideal gas, but Q equals ΔH only at constant pressure with only boundary work.", "2": "At constant volume Q = ΔU = m c_v ΔT; using c_p over-predicts Q by about 40% for air.", "1": "With other work present, the balance is Q − W_other = ΔH, so Q ≠ m c_p ΔT."}, "topic": "The full-course review"}], "THERMO/oa_sim/sim": [{"id": "oa-q1", "text": "A US-made air receiver has an internal volume of 2.5 ft³. Working in SI (1 ft³ = 0.0283168 m³, 1 psi = 6.8948 kPa, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K), what mass of air does it hold?", "options": ["0.779 kg", "0.694 kg", "0.433 kg", "10.85 kg"], "correct": 0, "explain": "V = 2.5 × 0.0283168 = 0.07079 m³; P = (120 + 14.7) psia × 6.8948 = 928.7 kPa absolute; T = (70 − 32)/1.8 + 273.15 = 294.26 K. m = PV/(RT) = 928.7 × 0.07079/(0.287 × 294.26) = 0.779 kg.", "distractors": {"2": "Uses 529.67, the temperature in degrees Rankine, as if it were kelvin; Rankine must be divided by 1.8 before use with R in kJ/kg·K.", "1": "Uses the gauge reading (827 kPa) instead of the absolute 928.7 kPa; the ideal-gas law needs absolute pressure.", "3": "Converts 70 °F to 21.1 °C and puts the Celsius value into PV = mRT; only an absolute temperature (294.26 K) is allowed."}, "topic": "Units, dimensions and the numbers you will use every day"}, {"id": "oa-q2", "text": "For one kilogram of ideal gas in an internally reversible process, the first law gives δq = c_v dT + (RT/v) dv, and the exactness test shows this differential is inexact. Which statement about repairing it is correct?", "options": ["Dividing by T gives c_v dT/T + R dv/v, which passes the exactness test; the new exact differential is ds, so 1/T is an integrating factor", "Multiplying by T gives an exact differential equal to du, the internal energy change", "No factor can repair it: heat is a path function, so any multiple of δq is also inexact", "Dividing by P gives an exact differential equal to dv, because Pv = RT removes the temperature dependence"], "correct": 0, "explain": "With M = c_v/T and N = R/v: ∂M/∂v = 0 and ∂N/∂T = 0, so the test passes. δq_rev/T = ds is exact, which is how entropy enters the course: 1/T turns the path function δq into the change of a property.", "distractors": {"2": "Path-dependence of δq does not stop a multiplier from producing an exact differential; 1/T does exactly that and defines entropy.", "1": "T·δq = c_v T dT + RT²/v dv fails the test: ∂(c_v T)/∂v = 0 but ∂(RT²/v)/∂T = 2RT/v ≠ 0.", "3": "δq/P = (c_v v/RT) dT + dv; the cross-derivatives c_v/(RT) and 0 differ, so it is still inexact and is certainly not dv."}, "topic": "The calculus you need"}, {"id": "oa-q3", "text": "A 0.40 m³ nitrogen bottle is connected to a U-tube manometer filled with oil of specific gravity 0.88. The oil stands 80 cm higher on the open side, the barometer reads 98.0 kPa, and the gas is at 30 °C. With R = 0.2968 kJ/kg·K for nitrogen and g = 9.81 m/s², what mass of nitrogen is in the bottle?", "options": ["0.466 kg", "0.910 kg", "4.71 kg", "0.0307 kg"], "correct": 0, "explain": "ΔP = ρgh = 880 × 9.81 × 0.80 = 6906 Pa = 6.906 kPa; P = 98.0 + 6.906 = 104.906 kPa absolute. m = PV/(RT) = 104.906 × 0.40/(0.2968 × 303.15) = 0.466 kg.", "distractors": {"3": "Uses only the manometer reading (6.9 kPa gauge) as the gas pressure; the ideal-gas law needs gauge plus atmospheric.", "1": "Uses the density of mercury (13,600 kg/m³) for the manometer fluid; the fluid is oil with ρ = 0.88 × 1000 = 880 kg/m³.", "2": "Puts 30 (°C) into PV = mRT instead of 303.15 K, inflating the mass tenfold."}, "topic": "Pressure, temperature and the zeroth law"}, {"id": "oa-q4", "text": "A diver at 25 m depth in a freshwater lake (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²) exhales a bubble. The water there is at 8 °C; at the surface the air pressure is 101.3 kPa and the water is at 20 °C. Treating the bubble air as an ideal gas that reaches the local water temperature, by what factor has its volume grown when it reaches the surface?", "options": ["3.42", "8.55", "3.57", "2.52"], "correct": 2, "explain": "P at depth = 101.3 + 1000 × 9.81 × 25/1000 = 346.55 kPa. A student objects that the process cannot be treated as quasi-equilibrium because the gas never has time to settle. Which reply is the sound engineering judgement?", "options": ["Quasi-equilibrium holds only if the piston speed is below the mean molecular speed divided by the number of molecules", "Pressure disturbances cross the gas at the speed of sound, about 350 m/s, hundreds of times faster than the piston; quasi-equilibrium is a good model", "The student is right: any process with a moving boundary is non-quasi-equilibrium, so ∫P dV cannot be used", "Quasi-equilibrium requires the process to be isothermal, so it holds only if the cylinder is cooled"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Quasi-equilibrium means the system passes through a sequence of near-equilibrium states. Pressure differences inside a gas even out at the speed of sound (≈ √(1.4 × 287 × 300) ≈ 347 m/s for air), so a piston moving at 0.5 m/s is roughly 700 times slower: the idealisation used for engine and compressor analyses is justified.", "distractors": {"2": "Quasi-equilibrium is judged by comparing the process speed with the rate of internal equilibration, not by whether the boundary moves.", "0": "This invented criterion has no basis; the comparison is between piston speed and the speed at which pressure waves cross the gas.", "3": "A quasi-equilibrium process can follow any path (isothermal, polytropic, adiabatic); it only requires near-uniform states at every instant."}, "topic": "State, process, cycle and the state postulate"}, {"id": "oa-q6", "text": "A cylinder holds 0.8 kg of air at 100 kPa and 300 K under a piston resting on stops. Using constant specific heats (c_v = 0.718, c_p = 1.005, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K), how much heat was added in total?", "options": ["758.2 kJ", "964.8 kJ", "861.5 kJ", "689.3 kJ"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Constant volume to lift-off: T₂ = 300 × 250/100 = 750 K. Constant pressure to 2V₁: T₃ = 2 × 750 = 1500 K. W_b = mR(T₃ − T₂) = 0.8 × 0.287 × 750 = 172.2 kJ; ΔU = m c_v (T₃ − T₁) = 0.8 × 0.718 × 1200 = 689.28 kJ; Q = ΔU + W_b = 861.5 kJ.", "distractors": {"1": "Treats the whole process as constant-pressure (Q = m c_p ΔT); the first leg is at constant volume and does no work.", "0": "Evaluates the boundary work at the initial 100 kPa; the piston moves at the lift-off pressure of 250 kPa.", "3": "Counts only ΔU and forgets the boundary work done while the piston rises at 250 kPa."}, "topic": "The first law for closed systems and the energy balance"}, {"id": "oa-q7", "text": "Air (k = 1.4) expands in a piston-cylinder along a polytropic path with n = 1.3, and its temperature falls. What is true of the heat transfer during this expansion?", "options": ["Heat flows out of the air, because the temperature decreases", "No conclusion is possible without knowing the pressures, because the polytropic work formula needs P₂V₂ and P₁V₁", "Heat flows into the air: the boundary work exceeds the fall in internal energy, so q = w − |Δu| > 0 even though the temperature drops", "The process is adiabatic, because any expansion in which the temperature falls must be adiabatic"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Per kg: w = R(T₁ − T₂)/(n − 1) = R ΔT_drop/0.3 and Δu = −c_v ΔT_drop = −R ΔT_drop/0.4. So q = Δu + w = R ΔT_drop (1/0.3 − 1/0.4) = +0.833 R ΔT_drop > 0: heat enters while the gas cools, because the gas does more work than it loses in internal energy.", "distractors": {"3": "Only n = k is adiabatic for an ideal gas; with n = 1.3 < 1.4 the gas cools more slowly than it would adiabatically, so heat must enter.", "0": "A falling temperature does not fix the sign of Q; the energy balance q = Δu + w decides it, and here w is larger than the drop in u.", "1": "The sign follows from n alone: w = R(T₁ − T₂)/(n − 1) and |Δu| = c_v(T₁ − T₂) = R(T₁ − T₂)/(k − 1), and w > |Δu| whenever n < k."}, "topic": "Work"}, {"id": "oa-q8", "text": "A rigid tank holds 2.0 kg of air at 300 K. How much heat is needed, and what would the room-temperature constant-c_v shortcut have given?", "options": ["2191.6 kJ (the constant c_p shortcut gives 2010 kJ)", "2010 kJ (from c_p = 1.005 kJ/kg·K)", "1436 kJ (the tables agree to within 1%)", "1617.5 kJ (the constant c_v = 0.718 shortcut gives 1436 kJ, 11% low)"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Rigid tank, no work: Q = m(u₂ − u₁) = 2.0 × (1022.82 − 214.07) = 1617.5 kJ. Classify the electrical energy for two choices of system: (a) the water in the kettle only; (b) the whole room, including air, kettle and water.", "options": ["Heat in both cases, because the end effect is that everything gets warmer", "Work in both cases, because the source is electrical", "(a) Heat, since it reaches the water from the hotter element across a temperature difference; (b) work, since it enters the room as electric current and Q = 0", "(a) work and (b) heat, because the room air transfers heat to the walls"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Heat is energy crossing a boundary because of a temperature difference; work is any other energy interaction. With the water as the system, the energy arrives from the hotter element: heat. With the whole insulated room as the system, the only crossing is the electric current: electrical work in, Q = 0, and ΔU of the room equals W_e,in.", "distractors": {"0": "Whether energy is heat or work depends on what crosses the chosen boundary, not on the final effect; electricity crossing the room boundary is work.", "1": "Once the element is outside the system boundary (case a), the energy reaches the water by conduction and convection across a temperature difference: heat.", "3": "This reverses the classification; the room is insulated, so no heat crosses its boundary at all, and the water receives heat from the element."}, "topic": "Forms of energy and energy transfer by heat"}, {"id": "oa-q10", "text": "A rigid 0.5 m³ tank holds steam at 1 MPa and 300 °C (v = 0.25799 m³/kg, u = 2793.6, h = 3051.6 kJ/kg). It cools to 100 °C, where v_f = 0.001043, v_g = 1.6718 m³/kg, u_f = 419.06, u_g = 2506.0, h_f = 419.17 and h_g = 2675.6 kJ/kg. Neglecting pressure drops and taking T₀ = 298.15 K, what is the rate of exergy destruction?", "options": ["294.4 kW", "84.8 kW", "126.6 kW", "7.11 kW"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Q̇ = 1.5 × 4.18 × 50 = 313.5 kW; air exit T = 500 − 313.5/(3.0 × 1.005) = 396.02 K.
