Ẋ_dest = 298.15 × 0.2845 = 84.8 kW.", "distractors": {"3": "Multiplies the entropy generation by T₀ = 25 (°C); the Gouy-Stodola relation needs the absolute temperature, 298.15 K.", "2": "Computes the exergy of the heat as if all of it left the air at 500 K, Q(1 − T₀/500); the air cools as it gives up heat, and the water receives it at 293-343 K.", "0": "Counts only the water stream’s entropy increase; the air loses entropy as it cools, and the destruction is T₀ times the net."}, "topic": "Exergy balance and exergy destruction"}, {"id": "oa-q31", "text": "A well-insulated tank of ice-water at 0 °C sits in a 25 °C, 100 kPa environment. What can be said about the exergy of its contents?", "options": ["It is negative, because the contents are colder than the dead state", "It is zero, because the contents have less energy than the environment, not more", "It is positive only if the tank pressure exceeds 100 kPa", "It is positive: a heat engine could run with the environment as its hot reservoir and the tank as its cold reservoir until the tank warms to 25 °C"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The dead state is 25 °C and 100 kPa. The tank differs from it, so the combined system (tank + environment) can deliver work, e.g. by an engine taking heat from the 298 K air and rejecting it to the 273 K tank. Exergy is zero only at the dead state and positive everywhere else, which is why a cold store is a work reservoir.", "distractors": {"0": "Exergy is never negative; any departure from the dead state, hotter or colder, offers work potential.", "1": "Exergy measures the possibility of useful work, which exists whenever a temperature difference with the environment exists.", "2": "The temperature difference alone provides work potential; pressure is a separate contribution."}, "topic": "Exergy, dead state and reversible work"}, {"id": "oa-q32", "text": "A rigid, completely evacuated chamber of 1.5 m³ sits in a 25 °C, 100 kPa atmosphere. What is the maximum useful work obtainable by opening it to the atmosphere through an ideal device, for example by letting the atmosphere push a frictionless piston into it?", "options": ["0 kJ", "−150 kJ", "150 kJ", "Unbounded, because an ideal pump would need infinite work to reach zero pressure"], "correct": 2, "explain": "The chamber differs from the dead state only in pressure. As the atmosphere pushes a piston in, it does P₀V of work on the piston, and nothing else changes, so all of it can be delivered as useful work: X = P₀V = 100 kPa × 1.5 m³ = 150 kJ. This is the surroundings-work term P₀(V − V₀) of the exergy balance acting in reverse.", "distractors": {"0": "Argues that an empty chamber holds no energy; exergy is a property of system plus environment, and the atmosphere can do P₀V of work filling the space.", "1": "Exergy cannot be negative; being below P₀ is a departure from the dead state and is a work potential, not a debt.", "3": "Confuses the work needed to evacuate with the work obtainable from the evacuated chamber; the atmosphere pushing in can deliver at most P₀V."}, "topic": "Exergy of a fixed mass and of a flow stream; second-law efficiency"}, {"id": "oa-q33", "text": "A regenerative gas turbine has pressure ratio 8, compressor inlet 300 K and turbine inlet 1300 K. The compressor and turbine isentropic efficiencies are 0.82 and 0.86 and the regenerator effectiveness is 0.75. With cold-air-standard properties (c_p = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, k = 1.4), what is the thermal efficiency?", "options": ["44.8%", "29.0%", "58.2%", "37.0%"], "correct": 3, "explain": "T₂s = 300 × 8^0.2857 = 543.4 K, T₂ = 300 + 243.4/0.82 = 596.9 K. T₄s = 1300/1.8114 = 717.7 K, T₄ = 1300 − 0.86 × 582.3 = 799.2 K. Regenerator: T₅ = 596.9 + 0.75 × (799.2 − 596.9) = 748.6 K. w_net = 1.005[(1300 − 799.2) − (596.9 − 300)] = 205.0 kJ/kg; q_in = 1.005(1300 − 748.6) = 554.1 kJ/kg; η = 37.0%.", "distractors": {"2": "Uses the ideal-regenerator formula 1 − (T₁/T₃)r_p^((k−1)/k), which assumes isentropic machines and effectiveness 1.", "0": "Uses the ideal simple-Brayton formula 1 − 1/r_p^((k−1)/k), ignoring both component losses and regeneration.", "1": "Ignores the regenerator and charges the combustor with c_p(T₃ − T₂); the regenerator preheats the air to 748.6 K first."}, "topic": "The Brayton cycle"}, {"id": "oa-q34", "text": "An ideal Diesel cycle has compression ratio 18 and starts compression at 300 K; 1100 kJ/kg of heat is added. Under cold-air-standard assumptions (c_p = 1.005, c_v = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, k = 1.4), what is its thermal efficiency?", "options": ["60.5%", "68.5%", "62.5%", "47.5%"], "correct": 2, "explain": "T₂ = 300 × 18^0.4 = 953.3 K. T₃ = 953.3 + 1100/1.005 = 2047.8 K, so r_c = 2.148. η = 1 − (1/18^0.4)(r_c^1.4 − 1)/[1.4(r_c − 1)] = 62.5%, below the Otto value at the same r (68.5%), as expected.", "distractors": {"3": "Leaves k out of the denominator of the cutoff term (r_c^k − 1)/[k(r_c − 1)].", "0": "Adds the heat with c_v, as in an Otto cycle; Diesel heat addition is at constant pressure, so T₃ − T₂ = q_in/c_p, giving a smaller cutoff ratio.", "1": "Uses the Otto formula 1 − 1/r^(k−1); the cutoff-ratio bracket must multiply r^(1−k) for a Diesel cycle."}, "topic": "The Otto and Diesel cycles"}, {"id": "oa-q35", "text": "An ideal Otto cycle is operated with a fixed compressor-inlet temperature T₁ and a fixed peak temperature T₃ (a materials limit), and the compression ratio is raised step by step. What happens?", "options": ["Efficiency reaches a maximum at an intermediate r and then falls", "Efficiency and net work per kilogram both rise continuously with r", "Both efficiency and net work fall, because the peak temperature limits the heat input", "Efficiency keeps rising with r, but the net work per kilogram first rises and then falls, reaching zero when T₂ reaches T₃"], "correct": 3, "explain": "η = 1 − r^(1−k) depends on r alone and increases. But q_in = c_v(T₃ − T₂) with T₂ = T₁r^(k−1) shrinks as r rises, and w_net = η q_in tends to zero as T₂ → T₃. The net work peaks at an intermediate r (at T₂ = √(T₁T₃)), which is why designers watch both quantities.", "distractors": {"1": "At fixed T₃, less and less heat can be added as T₂ climbs, so the net work must eventually fall even though the efficiency rises.", "0": "For the cold-air Otto cycle η = 1 − r^(1−k) rises monotonically with r; it is the net work, not the efficiency, that peaks.", "2": "The efficiency depends only on r and increases with it; only the work per kilogram is squeezed by the T₃ cap."}, "topic": "The Otto and Diesel cycles"}, {"id": "oa-q36", "text": "A Brayton cycle is given an ever-larger number of compression stages with intercooling and expansion stages with reheating, plus an ideal regenerator. What does it approach?", "options": ["The simple Brayton cycle with its efficiency still fixed at 1 − 1/r_p^((k−1)/k)", "The Ericsson cycle: isothermal compression and expansion with constant-pressure regeneration, so its efficiency approaches the Carnot value 1 − T_min/T_max", "The Stirling cycle, because both have isothermal compression and expansion", "The Otto cycle, because heat addition becomes effectively instantaneous"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Infinitely many intercooled stages make compression isothermal at T_min; infinitely many reheats make expansion isothermal at T_max; the regenerator transfers heat between the constant-pressure legs. That is the Ericsson cycle, whose efficiency with perfect regeneration equals Carnot’s.", "distractors": {"2": "The Stirling cycle regenerates at constant volume; the many-stage Brayton regenerates at constant pressure, which is the Ericsson cycle.", "0": "Intercooling and reheating make compression and expansion approach isothermal, and with regeneration the efficiency depends on temperatures, not on r_p.", "3": "Heat addition in the limit is isothermal at constant temperature in the expansion stages, not at constant volume."}, "topic": "Jet propulsion and the Stirling and Ericsson cycles"}, {"id": "oa-q37", "text": "A six-cylinder, four-stroke engine has a total displacement of 3.0 L and must deliver 90 kW of net power at 2400 rpm. What mean effective pressure must its cycle achieve?", "options": ["1500 kPa", "9000 kPa", "750 kPa", "25.0 kPa"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Ẇ = MEP × V_d × N/n_R with n_R = 2 for a four-stroke engine. MEP = 2 × 90 kW/(0.0030 m³ × 40 rev/s) = 1500 kPa ≈ 1.50 MPa, typical of a turbocharged engine.", "distractors": {"1": "Uses the displacement of one cylinder (0.5 L) with the power of all six.", "2": "Assumes one power stroke per revolution; a four-stroke engine completes one cycle every two revolutions, so W = MEP × V_d × N/2.", "3": "Leaves the speed in rev/min; it must be converted to rev/s (2400/60 = 40 rev/s)."}, "topic": "Air-standard assumptions, Carnot as a benchmark and reciprocating engines"}, {"id": "oa-q38", "text": "An ideal regenerative Rankine cycle has one open feedwater heater at 0.6 MPa. Enthalpies (kJ/kg): condensate h₁ = 251.42, after pump I h₂ = 252.01, heater exit (sat. liquid) h₃ = 670.38, after pump II h₄ = 680.72, turbine inlet (10 MPa, 550 °C) h₅ = 3502.0, extraction h₆ = 2755.8, turbine exit (20 kPa) h₇ = 2226.2. What is the thermal efficiency?", "options": ["44.8%", "36.2%", "50.1%", "41.7%"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Heater: y = (h₃ − h₂)/(h₆ − h₂) = 0.1671. w_T = (h₅ − h₆) + (1 − y)(h₆ − h₇) = 1187.3 kJ/kg; w_P = (1 − y)(h₂ − h₁) + (h₄ − h₃) = 10.83 kJ/kg; q_in = h₅ − h₄ = 2821.3 kJ/kg. η = (1187.3 − 10.83)/2821.3 = 41.7%.", "distractors": {"1": "Charges the boiler with h₅ − h₂; the boiler receives feedwater from pump II at h₄, after the heater has done its work.", "0": "Lets the full flow expand to 20 kPa and pass pump I; the extracted fraction y leaves the turbine at h₆ and never reaches the condenser.", "2": "Scales the boiler heat by (1 − y); all the steam passes through the boiler, and only the LP turbine and pump I carry the reduced flow."}, "topic": "Regeneration with open and closed feedwater heaters"}, {"id": "oa-q39", "text": "A 15 MPa, 600 °C reheat cycle currently reheats at 4 MPa. A designer drops the reheat pressure to 0.5 MPa, still reheating to 600 °C. The turbine exhaust becomes dry, yet the cycle efficiency falls. Why?", "options": ["The high-pressure turbine exhaust becomes wet, which destroys the efficiency gain", "Lower reheat pressure raises the condenser pressure, shrinking the expansion", "The pump work rises sharply because the feedwater must now be pumped against the reheat pressure", "Most of the reheat heat is now added at low temperature, so the average temperature of heat addition falls, and much of it leaves in a superheated exhaust"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Reheat helps efficiency only if the reheat heat enters at an average temperature at least as high as the rest of the boiler. At 0.5 MPa the steam starts reheating near 150 °C, so the extra heat is low-grade, and the exhaust leaves superheated, raising q_out. Optimum reheat pressures are typically about a quarter of the boiler pressure.", "distractors": {"2": "Pumps work between the condenser and boiler pressures, which have not changed; reheat pressure does not enter the pump work.", "1": "The condenser pressure is set by the cooling water, not by the reheat pressure.", "0": "The HP exhaust is only slightly wet (x ≈ 0.97), and in the ideal cycle moisture costs nothing; the drop comes from adding the reheat heat at low temperature."}, "topic": "Raising efficiency"}, {"id": "oa-q40", "text": "A gas turbine burns fuel at 330 MW and delivers 120 MW. Its exhaust, 420 kg/s at 790 K (c_p = 1.005 kJ/kg·K), is cooled to a 410 K stack in an HRSG that raises steam from feedwater at 199.88 kJ/kg to 8 MPa, 500 °C (3399.5 kJ/kg). The steam runs an ideal Rankine cycle with net work 1261.1 kJ/kg. What is the combined-cycle efficiency?", "options": ["85.0%", "75.8%", "55.5%", "61.1%"], "correct": 2, "explain": "HRSG: Q̇ = 420 × 1.005 × (790 − 410) = 160.4 MW, so ṁ_steam = 160398/(3399.5 − 199.88) = 50.13 kg/s. Ẇ_steam = 50.13 × 1261.1 = 63.2 MW. η = (120 + 63.2)/330 = 55.5%.", "distractors": {"3": "Cools the exhaust to 300 K in the HRSG; the gas leaves at the 410 K stack, so only 380 K of cooling is recovered.", "1": "Adds the two cycle efficiencies; the steam cycle runs on the gas turbine’s rejected heat, not on a second supply of fuel, so efficiencies do not add.", "0": "Counts the heat given to the steam as output; only the steam cycle’s net work (63.2 MW) is useful output."}, "topic": "Deviations from ideal, cogeneration and combined gas-vapour cycles"}, {"id": "oa-q41", "text": "An engineer proposes letting the condenser of an ideal Rankine plant subcool the condensate 15 K below saturation before the pump, while keeping the same condenser pressure. What is the effect on the ideal-cycle efficiency?", "options": ["It rises, because denser subcooled liquid needs less pump work", "It rises, because the condenser pressure effectively falls to the saturation pressure of the colder liquid", "It falls slightly: the boiler must now supply extra sensible heat at the lowest temperatures of the cycle, and the condenser rejects the same extra amount", "It is unchanged, because the extra heat added in the boiler is exactly returned in the condenser"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Subcooling lowers h₁ and h₂ by about c ΔT = 4.18 × 15 ≈ 63 kJ/kg. Both q_in and q_out rise by that amount, so w_net is unchanged while q_in grows, and η = w_net/q_in drops. Plants tolerate a little subcooling only to keep the pump from cavitating.", "distractors": {"0": "The change in v, and so in pump work, is a fraction of a percent of a few kJ/kg; the extra low-temperature heat input dominates.", "1": "The condenser pressure is set by the condensing steam at its saturation temperature; cooling the liquid afterwards does not lower it.", "3": "The extra heat added and rejected are equal, but adding equal Q to both q_in and q_out lowers w_net/q_in; it also lowers the mean heat-addition temperature."}, "topic": "The Carnot vapour cycle and the ideal Rankine cycle"}, {"id": "oa-q42", "text": "A cogeneration plant sends 10 kg/s of steam at 7 MPa, 500 °C (h = 3411.4 kJ/kg) into an ideal turbine. 3 kg/s is extracted at 500 kPa (h = 2739.3) for a process heater that returns saturated liquid (h = 640.09); the rest expands to 10 kPa (h = 2153.6) and leaves the condenser as saturated liquid (h = 191.81). The two liquids mix before the boiler; pump work is negligible. What is the utilisation factor?", "options": ["53.2%", "35.1%", "59.8%", "55.5%"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Ẇ_T = 10(3411.4 − 2739.3) + 7(2739.3 − 2153.6) = 10821 kW. Q̇_p = 3(2739.3 − 640.09) = 6298 kW. Feedwater h = (3 × 640.09 + 7 × 191.81)/10 = 326.29 kJ/kg; Q̇_in = 10(3411.4 − 326.29) = 30851 kW. ε_u = (Ẇ + Q̇_p)/Q̇_in = 55.5%.", "distractors": {"1": "This is the thermal efficiency, W/Q_in; the utilisation factor also counts the process heat as useful output.", "0": "Charges the boiler as if all feedwater arrived at the condenser enthalpy (191.81 kJ/kg); the process return mixes in at 640.09 kJ/kg, raising the feedwater to 326.29 kJ/kg.", "2": "Takes the process heater outlet at the condenser liquid enthalpy; the heater returns saturated liquid at 500 kPa, h = 640.09 kJ/kg."}, "topic": "Deviations from ideal, cogeneration and combined gas-vapour cycles"}, {"id": "oa-q43", "text": "An ideal R-134a heat pump runs between 0.24 MPa and 1.2 MPa: h = 247.30 kJ/kg entering the compressor (saturated vapour), 280.84 kJ/kg leaving it, and 117.80 kJ/kg leaving the condenser (saturated liquid). It heats a house at 20 °C from outdoor air at −2 °C. What is its second-law efficiency?", "options": ["29.0%", "78.6%", "36.5%", "39.4%"], "correct": 2, "explain": "COP_HP = (h₂ − h₃)/(h₂ − h₁) = 163.04/33.54 = 4.861. Reversible limit between the reservoirs: 293.15/22 = 13.32. η_II = 4.861/13.32 = 36.5%.", "distractors": {"0": "Uses COP_R = (h₁ − h₄)/(h₂ − h₁) for a machine whose job is heating; the useful effect is q_H = h₂ − h₃.", "3": "Divides by the refrigerator Carnot COP, T_L/(T_H − T_L); a heat pump is compared with T_H/(T_H − T_L).", "1": "Takes the reversible COP between the refrigerant saturation temperatures (46.3 °C and −5.4 °C); the benchmark is a reversible machine between the house and the outdoor air."}, "topic": "The reversed Carnot cycle and the ideal vapour-compression cycle"}, {"id": "oa-q44", "text": "A 5-ton R-134a refrigerator takes vapour into the compressor at 0.12 MPa and −15 °C (h = 242.88 kJ/kg); isentropic compression to 0.9 MPa would give h = 286.39 kJ/kg, and the compressor efficiency is 0.80. The liquid leaves the condenser at 0.9 MPa and 30 °C. Tables: h_f at 30 °C = 93.58, h_f at 0.9 MPa = 101.64 kJ/kg. What power does the compressor draw? (1 ton = 3.517 kW)", "options": ["6.41 kW", "4.10 kW", "1.82 kW", "6.77 kW"], "correct": 0, "explain": "h₄ = h₃ ≈ h_f(30 °C) = 93.58 kJ/kg; q_L = 242.88 − 93.58 = 149.30 kJ/kg. ṁ = 17.585/149.30 = 0.1178 kg/s. w_in = (286.39 − 242.88)/0.80 = 54.39 kJ/kg. Ẇ = 0.1178 × 54.39 = 6.41 kW.", "distractors": {"2": "Treats 5 tons as 5 kW; one ton of refrigeration is 3.517 kW, so the load is 17.585 kW.", "1": "Multiplies the isentropic work by η_C; a compressor needs more work than the ideal one, so divide by 0.80.", "3": "Uses h_f at 0.9 MPa for the condenser exit; the liquid is subcooled to 30 °C, so h ≈ h_f at 30 °C, which gives more cooling per kg."}, "topic": "Actual cycles, refrigerant selection and heat pump systems"}, {"id": "oa-q45", "text": "A gas refrigeration cycle takes air into the compressor at 255 K and compresses it through a pressure ratio of 4 (η_C = 0.80). The air is cooled to 300 K, expanded in a turbine (η_T = 0.85) that helps drive the compressor, and then absorbs heat from the cold space until it returns to 255 K. With c_p = 1.005 kJ/kg·K and k = 1.4, what is the COP?", "options": ["0.537", "2.058", "0.743", "0.248"], "correct": 0, "explain": "T₂s = 255 × 4^0.2857 = 378.9 K, T₂ = 255 + 123.9/0.80 = 409.9 K. T₄s = 300/1.4860 = 201.9 K, T₄ = 300 − 0.85 × 98.1 = 216.6 K. COP = (T₁ − T₄)/[(T₂ − T₁) − (T₃ − T₄)] = 38.4/(154.9 − 83.4) = 0.537.", "distractors": {"3": "Charges the whole compressor work to the cycle and forgets the turbine work, which offsets part of it.", "2": "Takes the refrigeration effect from the isentropic turbine exit T₄s; the real turbine exit is warmer (216.6 K), so each kilogram absorbs less heat.", "1": "Uses the ideal-cycle formula 1/(r_p^((k−1)/k) − 1); component losses cut the COP of a gas cycle drastically."}, "topic": "Cascade, multistage, absorption and gas refrigeration cycles"}, {"id": "oa-q46", "text": "Frost builds up on the evaporator coil of a freezer. With the thermostat still holding the cabinet at −18 °C, why does the energy use per unit of cooling rise?", "options": ["The COP is unaffected; only the cooling capacity falls, so the energy use per unit of cooling is the same", "Frost adds thermal resistance, so the refrigerant must evaporate at a lower temperature and pressure, and the compressor works across a larger pressure ratio", "The frost melts inside the evaporator and the extra latent heat has to be removed a second time", "The frost raises the condenser pressure, because ice is a good conductor"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Heat must cross air film + frost + coil wall to the refrigerant. More resistance needs a larger temperature difference, so the evaporating temperature (and pressure) drops. COP falls, as the reversed-Carnot bound T_L/(T_H − T_L) already predicts, and compressor work per kilogram rises. Defrost cycles exist for this reason.", "distractors": {"2": "The frost stays frozen on the coil at −18 °C; its effect is to insulate the coil, not to recirculate latent heat.", "3": "Frost is a poor conductor (it is porous ice); it affects the evaporator side, and the condenser pressure is set by the room.", "0": "A lower evaporating temperature lowers COP; it is the same Carnot argument, COP rises with T_L and falls as T_L drops."}, "topic": "Actual cycles, refrigerant selection and heat pump systems"}, {"id": "oa-q47", "text": "In a mountain village the air pressure is 70 kPa. Using the Clausius-Clapeyron equation with the normal boiling point (101.42 kPa at 100 °C), h_fg = 2256.4 kJ/kg held constant, and R = 0.4615 kJ/kg·K for water vapour, at what temperature does water boil there? (The saturation table gives 89.93 °C.)", "options": ["99.2 °C", "89.7 °C", "110.9 °C", "−26.0 °C"], "correct": 1, "explain": "ln(P₂/P₁) = (h_fg/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂) gives 1/T₂ = 1/373.15 − (0.4615/2256.4) ln(70/101.42) = 2.755722 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹, so T₂ = 362.88 K = 89.73 °C, within 0.20 K of the table value because h_fg varies little over 10 K.", "distractors": {"2": "Flips the sign of the logarithm term, so a lower pressure gives a higher boiling point; ln(P₂/P₁) < 0 must lower T.", "0": "Puts 100 (°C) in 1/T₁ and reads the result as Celsius; the Clapeyron equation needs kelvin.", "3": "Uses R_u = 8.314 with a per-kg h_fg; the units only balance with R = R_u/M = 0.4615 kJ/kg·K."}, "topic": "The Clapeyron equation and general relations for du, dh, ds, cv and cp"}, {"id": "oa-q48", "text": "You need the change of entropy of a gas with specific volume at constant temperature, but you can only measure P, v and T. Which relation gives it, and what does it predict for a van der Waals gas, P = RT/(v − b) − a/v²?", "options": ["(∂s/∂v)_T = (∂P/∂T)_v = R/(v − b), so Δs at constant T is R ln[(v₂ − b)/(v₁ − b)], independent of the attraction constant a", "It cannot be found from P-v-T data; a calorimeter is always needed for entropy", "(∂s/∂v)_T = −(∂v/∂T)_P, so Δs at constant T depends on the thermal expansion coefficient", "(∂s/∂v)_T = (∂P/∂T)_v = R/(v − b) − a/(Tv²), so the attraction constant lowers the entropy change"], "correct": 0, "explain": "From da = −s dT − P dv, the exactness test gives (∂s/∂v)_T = (∂P/∂T)_v. For van der Waals, (∂P/∂T)_v = R/(v − b). Integrating at constant T: Δs = R ln[(v₂ − b)/(v₁ − b)]. The a term drops out because it does not depend on T.", "distractors": {"2": "That Maxwell relation is (∂s/∂P)_T = −(∂v/∂T)_P, with P as the variable held apart; for changes in v the relation from the Helmholtz function applies.", "3": "Differentiating P = RT/(v − b) − a/v² at constant v, the a/v² term has no T in it and drops out.", "1": "The Maxwell relations exist precisely to turn unmeasurable entropy derivatives into measurable P-v-T derivatives."}, "topic": "Partial derivatives, the Gibbs functions and the Maxwell relations"}, {"id": "oa-q49", "text": "Winter air at 5 °C and 40% relative humidity (101.325 kPa) is heated to 22 °C and then humidified with steam to 45% relative humidity at 22 °C. P_sat is 0.8726 kPa at 5 °C and 2.6453 kPa at 22 °C. How much water must be added per kilogram of dry air?", "options": ["5.24 g", "0.83 g", "0.270 g", "7.39 g"], "correct": 0, "explain": "ω₁ = 0.622 × 0.40 × 0.8726/(101.325 − 0.3490) = 0.00215 kg/kg (unchanged by heating). ω₂ = 0.622 × 0.45 × 2.6453/(101.325 − 1.1904) = 0.00739 kg/kg. Water added = ω₂ − ω₁ = 0.00524 kg/kg = 5.24 g per kg of dry air.", "distractors": {"2": "Evaluates the 45% target with P_sat at 5 °C; the target is set at 22 °C, where P_sat is three times larger.", "1": "Assumes the relative humidity stays at 40% during heating; heating at constant ω lowers φ, and ω₁ must be found at 5 °C.", "3": "This is the final humidity ratio; the outdoor air already carries 2.15 g/kg, which the humidifier does not have to supply."}, "topic": "Air-conditioning processes and cooling towers"}, {"id": "oa-q50", "text": "A compressor takes in atmospheric air at 100 kPa, 25 °C and 60% relative humidity and delivers it to a receiver at 400 kPa, where it cools back to 25 °C (P_sat = 3.1698 kPa). What fraction of the water vapour that entered condenses in the receiver?", "options": ["75.4%", "40.0%", "58.8%", "0%"], "correct": 2, "explain": "ω₁ = 0.622 × (0.6 × 3.1698)/(100 − 1.9019) = 0.01206 kg/kg.
